articles.title: Disproof of Erdős Problem 1 on distinct subset sums
articles.statement:
There is no real number $C > 0$
such that for every natural number $N \ne 0$ and every finite set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$
whose distinct subsets have distinct sums, $C \cdot 2^{|A|} < N$.

Resolved false: Disproved: machine-checked disproof recorded in the FormalConjectures source
record. Source: Lean 4 disproof of Erdos Problem 1 (proof by GPT-6 Astra in the FrontierMath
Erdos benchmark; repository by T. Adamczewski), tadamcz/erdos1 at commit

articles.title: Erdős Problem 650: matching integers to distinct multiples
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, let
$f(m)$ be the largest natural number $r$ such that for every natural number $N$, every set
$A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ with exactly $m$ elements and every real $x \ge 1$, there are
distinct $a_1, \dots, a_r \in A$ and distinct natural numbers $b_1, \dots, b_r$ in the open
interval $(x, x + 2N)$ with $a_i \mid b_i$ for every $i$. Then $f(m) = \min(m,
\lceil 2\sqrt{m}\,\rceil)$ for every natural number $m$; it is not the case that
$f(m) \le \sqrt{m}$ for every natural number $m$; $\sqrt{m} \le f(m)$ for every natural number
$m$; and $f(m^2) \le 2m$ for every natural number $m$.

Solved by Erdős–Surányi [ErSu59], Erdős–Selfridge [Er78], [Er86c] and van Doorn–Li–Tang [VLT26].

## Sources

- [VLT26] W. van Doorn, Y. Li and Q. Tang, Optimal bounds for an Erdős problem on matching integers to distinct multiples, arXiv:2603.28636 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28636; W. van Doorn, Lean formalization of Erdős Problem 650 (Aristotle-assisted), https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/c100ed4a4429e987a9555ee428a1aa524a46e16d/ErdosProblem650.lean.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 650
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be Erdős's matching function for multiples in
intervals. The statement is the conjunction of four claims: for every natural number $m$,
$f(m) = \min(m, \lceil 2\sqrt{m}\,\rceil)$; it is not the case that $f(m) \le \sqrt{m}$ for every
natural number $m$; $\sqrt{m} \le f(m)$ for every natural number $m$; and $f(m^2) \le 2m$ for
every natural number $m$.

articles.title: Erdős–Pomerance bounds for the diagonal interval length
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$,
let $f(n, m)$ be the least natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains
distinct multiples of $1, \dots, n$. For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large
natural numbers $n$,

$$
\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{e}} - \varepsilon\right) n \sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}} < f(n, n) <
(2 + \varepsilon)\, n \sqrt{\log n}.
$$

## Sources

- the constants are read from the paper text (arXiv:2601.16972, same paper, Lemma 3), since the record's are garbled; they agree with the record's `√2e > 1.21` remark (`2/√e ≈ 1.213`).
- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Lemma 3, quoting Erdős and Pomerance.

articles.title: Characterization of the least interval length
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, let
$f(n, m)$ be the least natural number $K$ such that the interval $(m, m + K]$ contains distinct
multiples of $1, \dots, n$. Then for every natural number $L$, $f(n, m) \le L$ if and only if
the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct multiples of $1, \dots, n$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`).

articles.title: An inequality between diagonal and shifted interval lengths
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and
$m$, let $f(n, m)$ be the least natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains
distinct multiples of $1, \dots, n$. Then for all positive integers $k$ and $n$,
$kn + f(kn, kn) \le k^2 n + f(n, k^2 n)$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Lemma 2.

articles.title: The least interval length for $n = 1$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, let $f(n, m)$ be
the least natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct multiples of
$1, \dots, n$. Then $f(1, m) = 1$ for every natural number $m$: the interval $(m, m + 1]$
contains the multiple $m + 1$ of $1$, and the empty interval $(m, m]$ contains nothing.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`).

articles.title: Least interval length containing distinct multiples
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$,
$f(n, m)$ is the least natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct
multiples of $1, \dots, n$.

Such an $L$ always exists, so the least one is well defined.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`, after Erdős and Pomerance).

articles.title: Shifting the interval can greatly increase the least length
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and
$m$, let $f(n, m)$ be the least natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains
distinct multiples of $1, \dots, n$. For all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$ there is a
positive integer $m$ with

$$
f(n, m) - f(n, n) > \frac{0.36\, n \log n}{\log \log n}.
$$

Since $f(n, m)$ is periodic in $m$ with period $\operatorname{lcm}(1, \dots, n)$, this says that
$\max_{m \ge 1} f(n, m) - f(n, n) > 0.36\, n \log n / \log \log n$ for all large $n$, the form
stated in the source.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Some interval contains distinct multiples
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $m$ there is a
natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct multiples of
$1, \dots, n$.

For example, $L = n(m + 1)$ works, with $a_i = i(m + 1)$ for $1 \le i \le n$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`).

articles.title: Erdős's matching function for multiples in intervals
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, $f(m)$ is
the largest natural number $r$ such that for every natural number $N$, every set
$A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ with exactly $m$ elements and every real $x \ge 1$, there are
distinct $a_1, \dots, a_r \in A$ and distinct natural numbers $b_1, \dots, b_r$ in the open
interval $(x, x + 2N)$ with $a_i \mid b_i$ for every $i$.

articles.title: The least interval length is admissible
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, let $f(n, m)$
be the least natural number $L$ such that the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct multiples
of $1, \dots, n$. Then the interval $(m, m + f(n, m)]$ contains distinct multiples of
$1, \dots, n$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`).

articles.title: Distinct multiples of $1, \dots, n$ in an interval
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $m$ and $L$,
the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct multiples of $1, \dots, n$ when there are pairwise
distinct natural numbers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ with $m < a_i \le m + L$ and $i \mid a_i$ for every
$1 \le i \le n$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`, after Erdős and Pomerance).

articles.title: Lengthening the interval preserves distinct multiples
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $m$, $L$
and $L'$ with $L \le L'$, if the interval $(m, m + L]$ contains distinct multiples of
$1, \dots, n$, then so does the interval $(m, m + L']$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn, *On the Length of an Interval That Contains Distinct Multiples of the First n Positive Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A7, Section 1 (definition of `f(n, m)`).

articles.title: Balanced partitions of $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$ exist
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the set of
maximum overlaps of $A$ and $B$, taken over all pairs of disjoint finite sets of integers $A$ and
$B$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ and $|A| = |B|$, is nonempty.

For example, $A = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $B = \{n + 1, \dots, 2n\}$ is such a pair.

articles.title: Notation $C_{1b}$
articles.statement: We write $C_{1b}$ for the continuous Erdős minimum-overlap constant.

articles.title: Admissible pairs for the continuous minimum-overlap problem
articles.statement:
A pair of functions
$f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is admissible when $f$ and $g$ are almost everywhere measurable
with respect to Lebesgue measure, take values in $[0, 1]$ at every point, vanish at every point
outside the support interval $[-1, 1]$, satisfy $f(t) + g(t) = 1$ for every $t \in [-1, 1]$, and
satisfy $\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t)\,dt = 1$.

Since measurability is only required almost everywhere, Lebesgue-null modifications of Borel
functions are included. Integrability and the bounds on the overlap follow from these conditions.

articles.title: The continuous constant $C_{1b}$ is the largest asymptotic overlap constant
articles.statement:
Call a real
number $c$ a universal asymptotic lower bound when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
positive integer $N_0$ such that for every $N \ge N_0$ and all disjoint finite sets
$A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2N\}$ and $|A| = |B|$, some integer $x$
satisfies $(c - \varepsilon) N \le \#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = x\}$. Then the continuous
Erdős minimum-overlap constant $C_{1b}$ is a universal asymptotic lower bound, and every
universal asymptotic lower bound $c$ satisfies $c \le C_{1b}$.

## Sources

- Haugland 2016 and the uniform partition clause of Optimization Problems 1b.

articles.title: The proposition that $C_{1b}$ is the largest asymptotic overlap constant
articles.statement:
Call a real
number $c$ a universal asymptotic lower bound when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
positive integer $N_0$ such that for every $N \ge N_0$ and all disjoint finite sets
$A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2N\}$ and $|A| = |B|$, some integer $x$
satisfies $(c - \varepsilon) N \le \#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = x\}$. This is the
proposition that the continuous Erdős minimum-overlap constant $C_{1b}$ is a universal asymptotic
lower bound and that every universal asymptotic lower bound $c$ satisfies $c \le C_{1b}$.

## Sources

- Haugland 2016; Optimization Problems, Constant 1b.

articles.title: The normalized minimum overlap tends to $C_{1b}$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$ let $M(N)$ be
the Erdős minimum overlap function: the least, over all pairs of disjoint finite sets
$A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2N\}$ and $|A| = |B|$, of the largest
number of pairs $(a, b) \in A \times B$ with a given difference $a - b$. Then $M(N)/N$ tends to
the continuous Erdős minimum-overlap constant $C_{1b}$ as $N \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Haugland 2016 and Optimization Problems 1b.

articles.title: The proposition that $M(N)/N$ tends to $C_{1b}$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$ let $M(N)$ be
the Erdős minimum overlap function: the least, over all pairs of disjoint finite sets
$A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2N\}$ and $|A| = |B|$, of the largest
number of pairs $(a, b) \in A \times B$ with a given difference $a - b$. This is the proposition
that $M(N)/N$ tends to the continuous Erdős minimum-overlap constant $C_{1b}$ as $N \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Haugland 2016; Optimization Problems, Constant 1b.

articles.title: The continuous minimum-overlap constant is at most $1/2$
articles.statement:
The continuous Erdős
minimum-overlap constant $C_{1b}$ satisfies $C_{1b} \le 1/2$.

The bound is witnessed by the admissible pair $f = g$ with value $1/2$ on $[-1, 1]$ and $0$
elsewhere.

articles.title: The continuous Erdős minimum-overlap constant
articles.statement:
For an admissible pair $(f, g)$ let
$S(f, g)$ be its pair score, the supremum over $x \in [-2, 2]$ of
$\int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,g(x + t)\,dt$. The continuous minimum-overlap constant $C_{1b}$ is the
supremum of the set of real numbers $c$ such that $c \le S(f, g)$ for every admissible pair
$(f, g)$.

## Sources

- Optimization Problems, Constant 1b.

articles.title: Continuous overlap integrand
articles.statement:
For functions $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and real
numbers $x$ and $t$, the overlap integrand is $f(t)\,g(x + t)$.

articles.title: Continuous overlap values
articles.statement:
For functions $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the set of
overlap values of $f$ and $g$ is the image of the translation interval $[-2, 2]$ under the overlap
$x \mapsto \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,g(x + t)\,dt$.

articles.title: Continuous overlap
articles.statement:
For functions $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a translation
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, the overlap of $f$ and $g$ at $x$ is $\int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,g(x + t)\,dt$, the
integral of the overlap integrand over the support interval $[-1, 1]$.

The integral is the Lebesgue (Bochner) integral, which is $0$ when the integrand is not
integrable.

articles.title: Continuous pair score
articles.statement:
For functions $f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the pair score of
$f$ and $g$ is the supremum of the overlap values $\int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,g(x + t)\,dt$ over the
translations $x \in [-2, 2]$.

As with every supremum of real numbers here, it is $0$ when the set is not bounded above; for
admissible pairs the overlap values lie in $[0, 1]$.

articles.title: Continuous support interval
articles.statement:
The support interval of the continuous minimum-overlap
problem is the closed interval $[-1, 1]$ of real numbers.

Functions in the continuous model are extended by zero outside this interval.

articles.title: Translation interval of the continuous overlap model
articles.statement:
The translation interval of the
continuous minimum-overlap model is the closed interval $[-2, 2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Universal lower bound in the continuous overlap model
articles.statement:
Call a pair of functions
$f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ admissible when $f$ and $g$ are almost everywhere measurable,
take values in $[0, 1]$, vanish outside $[-1, 1]$, satisfy $f + g = 1$ on $[-1, 1]$, and
$\int_{\mathbb{R}} f = 1$, and let the pair score $S(f, g)$ be the supremum over $x \in [-2, 2]$
of $\int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\, g(x + t)\, dt$. A real number $c$ is a universal lower bound when
$c \le S(f, g)$ for every admissible pair $(f, g)$.

articles.title: Universal asymptotic lower bound for discrete overlaps
articles.statement:
A real number $c$ is a
universal asymptotic lower bound when for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a positive integer
$N_0$ such that for every $N \ge N_0$ and all disjoint finite sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$
with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2N\}$ and $|A| = |B|$, some integer $x$ satisfies
$(c - \varepsilon) N \le \#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = x\}$.

The positive size threshold $N_0$ is chosen before the size $N$ and the partition.

articles.title: Erdős's lower bound $C_{1b} \ge 1/4$
articles.statement:

$C_{1b}$ satisfies $1/4 \le C_{1b}$.

## Sources

articles.title: The minimum overlap is attained
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ there are disjoint finite
sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ and $|A| = |B|$ such that
the minimum overlap $M(n)$ equals the maximum overlap of $A$ and $B$, the supremum over
$k \in \mathbb{Z}$ of $\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = k\}$.

articles.title: The minimum overlap bounds every balanced partition
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let
$A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ be disjoint finite sets with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ and
$|A| = |B|$. Then the minimum overlap $M(n)$ is at most the maximum overlap of $A$ and $B$,
the supremum over $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ of $\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = k\}$.

articles.title: Erdős minimum overlap function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $M(n)$ is the least value of
the maximum overlap of $A$ and $B$, the supremum over $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ of
$\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = k\}$, taken over all pairs of disjoint finite sets
$A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ with $A \cup B = \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ and $|A| = |B|$.

articles.title: The maximum overlap is attained
articles.statement:
For finite sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ there is an
integer $k$ such that the maximum overlap of $A$ and $B$, the supremum over $j \in \mathbb{Z}$
of $\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = j\}$, equals
$\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = k\}$.

articles.title: Maximum overlap
articles.statement:
For finite sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, the maximum overlap of $A$
and $B$ is the natural number obtained as the supremum over all integers $k$ of
$\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = k\}$.

articles.title: Normalized minimum overlap
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, the normalized minimum overlap is
the real number $M(N) / N$, where $M(N)$ is the Erdős minimum overlap function; for $N = 0$
the quotient is $0$ by the convention $x / 0 = 0$.

articles.title: Overlaps are bounded by the maximum overlap
articles.statement:
For finite sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$
and every integer $k$, the overlap $\#\{(a, b) \in A \times B : a - b = k\}$ is at most the
maximum overlap of $A$ and $B$.

articles.title: Overlap count of two finite sets of integers
articles.statement:
For finite sets $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$
and an integer $k$, the overlap of $A$ and $B$ at $k$ is the number of pairs
$(a, b) \in A \times B$ with $a - b = k$.

articles.title: Odd numbers $1 < n < 2^{50}$ are squarefree plus a power of two
articles.statement:
Every odd natural
number $n$ with $1 < n < 2^{50}$ can be written as $n = s + 2^k$, where $s$ is a squarefree
positive integer and $1 \le k \le 13$.

This is a finite verification of a conjecture of Erdős, which is open for all odd $n$.

## Sources

- Christian Hercher, *On the Sum of a Squarefree Integer and a Power of Two*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.3.1, Theorem 5 (`jis-2025-25.3.1-thm-5`).

articles.title: Number of Hurwitz quaternions of a given norm
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz quaternion is a quaternion
$q = x_0 + x_1 i + x_2 j + x_3 k$ whose rational coordinates $x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3$ are either all
integers or all halves of odd integers, and its norm is
$\mathrm{Nm}(q) = x_0^2 + x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2$. For every positive integer $N$, the number of
Hurwitz quaternions of norm $N$ is $24 \sum_{d \mid N,\ d \text{ odd}} d$, that is, $24$ times
the sum of the odd divisors of $N$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Counting Hurwitz quaternions of bounded norm
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz quaternion is a quaternion whose
four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves of odd integers; its norm is the
sum of the squares of its coordinates. For a natural number $N$ let $S(N)$ be the set of nonzero
Hurwitz quaternions of norm at most $N$.

(a) There is a real constant $C$ such that $\bigl| |S(N)| - \pi^2 N^2 \bigr| \le C N \log N$ for
every natural number $N \ge 2$.

(b) For every positive integer $M$ there is a real constant $C$ such that, for every natural
number $N \ge 2$, the number $c_M(N)$ of Hurwitz quaternions whose norm is a positive integer
$n \le N$ coprime to $M$ satisfies

$$\Bigl| c_M(N) - \pi^2 N^2 \cdot \frac{\varphi(2M)}{M}
\prod_{p \mid M} \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{p^2}\Bigr) \Bigr| \le C N \log N,$$

where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function and the product runs over the primes $p$ dividing $M$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Density of Hurwitz quaternions with norm in Rankin's greedy set
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz quaternion is a
quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves of odd integers;
its norm is the sum of the squares of its coordinates. For a natural number $N$ let $S(N)$ be the
set of nonzero Hurwitz quaternions of norm at most $N$. Let $G$ be the set of positive integers
$n$ such that, for every prime $p$, the base-$3$ digits of the exponent $\nu_p(n)$ of $p$ in $n$
include no $2$ (this is Rankin's greedy set of positive integers avoiding 3-term geometric
progressions), and let $H_G$ be the set of Hurwitz quaternions whose norm lies in $G$. With
$f(x) = \prod_{i \ge 0} \bigl(1 + x^{-3^i}\bigr)$, the ratio $|H_G \cap S(N)| / |S(N)|$ tends,
as $N \to \infty$, to

$$\frac{6}{\pi^2} \, f(4) \prod_{p > 2} \Bigl( f(p) - \frac{f(p^2)}{p} \Bigr),$$

the product running over the odd primes $p$.

The paper writes this constant as $(f(2^2)/\zeta(2)) \prod_{p > 2} (f(p) - f(p^2)/p)$, using
$1/\zeta(2) = 6/\pi^2$, and gives its value as approximately $0.782643$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Theorem 7 (restated as the unnumbered theorem of the introduction).

articles.title: Density of Hurwitz quaternions whose norm has prescribed prime exponents
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz
quaternion is a quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves
of odd integers; its norm is the sum of the squares of its coordinates. For a natural number $N$
let $S(N)$ be the set of nonzero Hurwitz quaternions of norm at most $N$. Let $A$ be a set of
natural numbers, let $G$ be the set of positive integers $n$ such that for every prime $p$ the
exponent $\nu_p(n)$ of $p$ in $n$ lies in $A$, and let $H_G$ be the set of Hurwitz quaternions
whose norm lies in $G$. Then the ratio $|H_G \cap S(N)| / |S(N)|$ tends, as $N \to \infty$, to

$$\frac{6}{\pi^2} \Bigl( \sum_{k \in A} 2^{-2k} \Bigr)
\prod_{p > 2} \Bigl( \sum_{k \in A} p^{-k} - \frac{1}{p} \sum_{k \in A} p^{-2k} \Bigr),$$

the product running over the odd primes $p$. Here $6/\pi^2 = 1/\zeta(2)$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Many disjoint geometric progressions among Hurwitz quaternions
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz quaternion is a
quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves of odd integers;
its norm is the sum of the squares of its coordinates. For a natural number $N$ let $S(N)$ be the
set of nonzero Hurwitz quaternions of norm at most $N$. Fix a Hurwitz quaternion $R$ of norm $2$,
and for a natural number $N$ let $E(N)$ be the set of triples $(bR^{3n}, bR^{3n+1}, bR^{3n+2})$,
where $n$ is a natural number and $b$ is a Hurwitz quaternion whose norm is an odd integer at
most $N / 2^{3n+2}$. Then for every $N$, every triple in $E(N)$ has the form $(a, aR, aR^2)$ with
all three entries in $S(N)$, and two distinct triples in $E(N)$ have no entry in common.
Moreover there is a real constant $C$ such that

$$\Bigl| |E(N)| - \frac{\pi^2 N^2}{21} \Bigr| \le C N (\log N)^2$$

for every natural number $N \ge 2$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Lemma 12.

articles.title: Hurwitz quaternions of square norm that are not a unit times a square
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz
quaternion is a quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves
of odd integers; its norm is the sum of the squares of its coordinates, and a Hurwitz unit is a
Hurwitz quaternion of norm $1$. Let $r$ be a positive integer that is not a sum of three squares
of integers, or that is divisible by an odd integer greater than $24$. Then some Hurwitz
quaternion $Q$ of norm $r^2$ cannot be written as $Q = UR^2$ with $U$ a Hurwitz unit and $R$ a
Hurwitz quaternion of norm $r$. If $r$ is not a sum of three squares of integers, then $Q = r$,
viewed as a quaternion with zero imaginary part, is such a quaternion.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Proposition 20.

articles.title: The quaternion greedy set and the norm preimage of Rankin's set differ infinitely
articles.statement:
A
Hurwitz quaternion is a quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all
halves of odd integers; the norm $\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ of a quaternion $q$ is the sum of the squares of
its coordinates. Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a set of quaternions such that a quaternion $q$ lies in
$\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $q$ is a nonzero Hurwitz quaternion and there are no
$a \in \mathcal{G}$ and Hurwitz quaternion $r \ne 0$ with norm $\mathrm{Nm}(r) \ne 1$,
$ar \in \mathcal{G}$ and $q = ar^2$ (this recursion on the norm characterizes the quaternion
greedy set). Let $G^*_3$ be Rankin's greedy set, the set of positive integers $n$ such that for
every prime $p$ the base-$3$ digits of the exponent of $p$ in $n$ include no digit $2$, and let
$S(G^*_3)$ be the set of Hurwitz quaternions whose norm lies in $G^*_3$. Then both
$\mathcal{G} \setminus S(G^*_3)$ and $S(G^*_3) \setminus \mathcal{G}$ are infinite.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Proposition 19.

articles.title: Quaternions of prime-square norm separating the greedy set from Rankin's set
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz
quaternion is a quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves
of odd integers; its norm $\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ is the sum of the squares of its coordinates, and a
Hurwitz unit is a Hurwitz quaternion of norm $1$. Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a set of quaternions such
that a quaternion $q$ lies in $\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $q$ is a nonzero Hurwitz quaternion
and there are no $a \in \mathcal{G}$ and Hurwitz quaternion $r \ne 0$ with $\mathrm{Nm}(r) \ne 1$,
$ar \in \mathcal{G}$ and $q = ar^2$ (this recursion on the norm characterizes the quaternion
greedy set). Let $G^*_3$ be Rankin's greedy set, the set of positive integers $n$ such that for
every prime $\ell$ the base-$3$ digits of the exponent of $\ell$ in $n$ include no digit $2$, and
let $S(G^*_3)$ be the set of Hurwitz quaternions whose norm lies in $G^*_3$. Let $p$ be a prime
and $Q$ a Hurwitz quaternion of norm $p^2$ that cannot be written as $Q = UR^2$ with $U$ a
Hurwitz unit and $R$ a Hurwitz quaternion of norm $p$. Then
$Q \in \mathcal{G} \setminus S(G^*_3)$ and $Q^2 \in S(G^*_3) \setminus \mathcal{G}$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Proposition 21.

articles.title: The quaternion greedy set is not determined by norms
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz quaternion is a quaternion
whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves of odd integers; the norm
$\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ of a quaternion $q$ is the sum of the squares of its coordinates. Let
$\mathcal{G}$ be a set of quaternions such that a quaternion $q$ lies in $\mathcal{G}$ if and only
if $q$ is a nonzero Hurwitz quaternion and there are no $a \in \mathcal{G}$ and Hurwitz quaternion
$r \ne 0$ with norm $\mathrm{Nm}(r) \ne 1$, $ar \in \mathcal{G}$ and $q = ar^2$ (this recursion on
the norm characterizes the quaternion greedy set). Then for every set $G$ of positive integers,
$\mathcal{G}$ is not the set of Hurwitz quaternions whose norm lies in $G$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Proposition 18.

articles.title: Squarefree norms and the lower density of the quaternion greedy set
articles.statement:
A Hurwitz quaternion is
a quaternion whose four rational coordinates are either all integers or all halves of odd integers;
the norm $\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ of a quaternion $q$ is the sum of the squares of its coordinates. For a
natural number $N$ let $S(N)$ be the set of nonzero Hurwitz quaternions of norm at most $N$. Let
$\mathcal{G}$ be a set of quaternions such that a quaternion $q$ lies in $\mathcal{G}$ if and only
if $q$ is a nonzero Hurwitz quaternion and there are no $a \in \mathcal{G}$ and Hurwitz quaternion
$r \ne 0$ with norm $\mathrm{Nm}(r) \ne 1$, $ar \in \mathcal{G}$ and $q = ar^2$ (this recursion on
the norm characterizes the quaternion greedy set). Then $\mathcal{G}$ contains every Hurwitz
quaternion whose norm is a squarefree natural number, and

$$\liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{|\mathcal{G} \cap S(N)|}{|S(N)|} \ge \frac{60}{7 \pi^2 \zeta(3)},$$

where $\zeta(3) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n^{-3}$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Proposition 17.

articles.title: Bounds on the supremum of upper densities of geometric-progression-free Hurwitz sets
articles.statement:
Let
$Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ be the set of Hurwitz quaternions, the rational quaternions whose four
coordinates are all integers or all lie in $\mathbb{Z} + \tfrac12$, and let $\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ be
the sum of the squares of the coordinates of $q$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ let $S(N)$ be the set of
nonzero $q \in Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ with $\mathrm{Nm}(q) \le N$, and define the upper density of a
set $A$ of quaternions as $\limsup_{N \to \infty} |A \cap S(N)| / |S(N)|$. Call
$A \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ free of 3-term geometric progressions if there are no
$a, r \in Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ with $a \ne 0$, $r \ne 0$ and $\mathrm{Nm}(r) \ne 1$ such that $a$,
$ar$ and $ar^2$ all lie in $A$. Let $\bar m_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ be the supremum of the upper
densities of such sets. Then $17665627/18662400 \le \bar m_{\mathrm{Hur}} \le 20/21$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Theorem 14 (restated as the unnumbered theorem of the introduction).

articles.title: Upper density of Hurwitz quaternions with norms in a lacunary union of intervals
articles.statement:
Let
$Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ be the set of Hurwitz quaternions, the rational quaternions whose four
coordinates are all integers or all lie in $\mathbb{Z} + \tfrac12$, and let $\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ be
the sum of the squares of the coordinates of $q$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ let $S(N)$ be the set of
nonzero $q \in Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ with $\mathrm{Nm}(q) \le N$, and define the upper density of a
set $A$ of quaternions as $\limsup_{N \to \infty} |A \cap S(N)| / |S(N)|$. For a natural number
$M$ let $T_M$ be the set of positive integers in $(M/48, M/45] \cup (M/40, M/36] \cup
(M/32, M/27] \cup (M/24, M/12] \cup (M/9, M/8] \cup (M/4, M]$, and let
$\mathcal{S} = \bigcup_{i \ge 1} T_{N_i}$ with $N_i = 48^{2^i}$. Then the set of
$q \in Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ with $\mathrm{Nm}(q) \in \mathcal{S}$ has upper density
$17665627/18662400$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Lemma 10 (the set `𝒮` from Section 4.1).

articles.title: Upper bound for geometric-progression-free Hurwitz sets
articles.statement:
Let $Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ be the
set of Hurwitz quaternions, the rational quaternions whose four coordinates are all integers or
all lie in $\mathbb{Z} + \tfrac12$, and let $\mathrm{Nm}(q)$ be the sum of the squares of the
coordinates of $q$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ let $S(N)$ be the set of nonzero
$q \in Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ with $\mathrm{Nm}(q) \le N$. Let $A \subseteq Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ be free
of 3-term geometric progressions: there are no $a, r \in Q_{\mathrm{Hur}}$ with $a \ne 0$,
$r \ne 0$ and $\mathrm{Nm}(r) \ne 1$ such that $a$, $ar$ and $ar^2$ all lie in $A$. Then the
upper density $\limsup_{N \to \infty} |A \cap S(N)| / |S(N)|$ of $A$ is at most $20/21$.

## Sources

- Asada, Fang, Fourakis, Manski, McNew, Miller, Moreland, Yamin, and Zhang, *Avoiding 3-Term Geometric Progressions in Hurwitz Quaternions*, J. Integer Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.7, Lemma 13.

articles.title: Natural density of the even numbers
articles.statement:
The set of even natural numbers has natural
density $1/2$.

articles.title: Finite sets have natural density zero
articles.statement:
Every finite set of natural numbers has natural
density $0$.

articles.title: Density of a set
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a preorder in which every set
$\{x \in \beta \mid x \le b\}$ is finite, let $S, A \subseteq \beta$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$,
and write $\beta_{\lt b} = \{x \in \beta \mid x < b\}$. The set $S$ has density $\alpha$ relative to
$A$ if the partial density
$\lvert S \cap A \cap \beta_{\lt b} \rvert / \lvert A \cap \beta_{\lt b} \rvert$, taken to be $0$ when
the denominator is $0$, tends to $\alpha$ as $b \to \infty$ in $\beta$.

By default $A = \beta$; for $\beta = \mathbb{N}$ this is the natural density of $S$.

articles.title: Two-sided natural density
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of integers has two-sided natural density
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ if $\lvert S \cap [-N, N] \rvert / (2N + 1)$ tends to $\alpha$ as the
natural number $N$ tends to infinity, where $[-N, N]$ is the set of integers $m$ with
$-N \le m \le N$.

articles.title: Logarithmic density
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of natural numbers has logarithmic density
$d \in \mathbb{R}$ if
$\frac{1}{\log n} \sum_{k \in A,\, k \le n} \frac{1}{k}$
tends to $d$ as $n \to \infty$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm, the term $1/k$ for $k = 0$
is taken to be $0$, and the whole expression is taken to be $0$ when $\log n = 0$.

Logarithmic density is a weaker notion than natural density: if a set has natural density $d$,
then it also has logarithmic density $d$, but the converse is false.

articles.title: Positive density
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a preorder in which every set
$\{x \in \beta \mid x \le b\}$ is finite, and let $S, A \subseteq \beta$. The set $S$ has positive
density relative to $A$ if there is a real number $\alpha > 0$ such that $S$ has density $\alpha$
relative to $A$. By default $A = \beta$.

articles.title: Sets of nonzero natural density are infinite
articles.statement:
If a set $S$ of natural numbers has
natural density $\alpha$ with $\alpha \neq 0$, then $S$ is infinite.

articles.title: Two-sided partial density
articles.statement:
For a set $S$ of integers and a natural number $N$, the
two-sided partial natural density of $S$ at $N$ is $\lvert S \cap [-N, N] \rvert / (2N + 1)$,
where $[-N, N]$ is the set of integers $m$ with $-N \le m \le N$.

articles.title: Lower density
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a preorder in which every set $\{x \in \beta \mid x \le b\}$
is finite, and let $S, A \subseteq \beta$. The lower density of $S$ relative to $A$ is the limit
inferior, as $b \to \infty$ in $\beta$, of the partial densities of $S$ relative to $A$ at $b$.
By default $A = \beta$.

articles.title: Partial density
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a preorder in which every set $\{x \in \beta \mid x \le b\}$
is finite, let $S, A \subseteq \beta$ and $b \in \beta$, and write
$A_{\lt b} = \{x \in A \mid x < b\}$. The partial density of $S$ relative to $A$ at $b$ is the
proportion $\lvert S \cap A_{\lt b} \rvert / \lvert A_{\lt b} \rvert$ of elements of $A_{\lt b}$ that lie
in $S$, taken to be $0$ when $A_{\lt b}$ is empty. By default $A = \beta$.

## Sources

- inspired by https://github.com/b-mehta/unit-fractions

articles.title: The whole order has density one
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a partial order with a least element
and at least two elements, in which every closed interval $[a, b]$ is finite. Then the set of
all elements of $\beta$ has density $1$ (relative to all of $\beta$).

articles.title: Upper density
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a preorder in which every set $\{x \in \beta \mid x \le b\}$
is finite, and let $S, A \subseteq \beta$. The upper density of $S$ relative to $A$ is the limit
superior, as $b \to \infty$ in $\beta$, of the partial densities of $S$ relative to $A$ at $b$.
By default $A = \beta$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 1196 on primitive sets
articles.statement:
There is a function $o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
with $o(x) \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$ such that for every natural number $x > 0$ and every
primitive set $A$ of natural numbers contained in $[x, \infty)$, the series
$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a \log a}$ is summable and $\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a \log a} < 1 + o(x)$.
Here a set of natural numbers is primitive if no element divides a different element, and the
term for $a = 1$, where $\log a = 0$, is taken to be $0$.

Resolved true: Resolved affirmatively (GPT-5.4 Pro prompted by Price; account [ABLLPSTT26]), per
erdosproblems.com/1196. Source: B. Alexeev, K. Barreto, Y. Li, J. D. Lichtman, L. Price, J. I.
Shah, Q. Tang, T. Tao, Primitive sets and von Mangoldt chains: Erdős Problem #1196 and beyond,
arXiv:2605.00301 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00301. Moved from
`OpenConjectures/NumberTheory/ErdosProblem1196`.

articles.title: Asymptotic primitive set bound
articles.statement:
The statement that there is a function
$o : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $o(x) \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$ such that for every natural
number $x > 0$ and every primitive set $A$ of natural numbers contained in $[x, \infty)$, the
series $\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a \log a}$ is summable and
$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a \log a} < 1 + o(x)$. Here a set of natural numbers is primitive if
no element divides a different element, and the term for $a = 1$, where $\log a = 0$, is taken
to be $0$.

articles.title: Primitive set in a commutative monoid
articles.statement:
A subset $A$ of a commutative monoid $M$ is
primitive if for all $x, y \in A$ with $x \mid y$, the elements $x$ and $y$ are associated,
that is, $x u = y$ for some unit $u$ of $M$. In $\mathbb{N}$, where $1$ is the only unit, this
says that no element of $A$ divides a different element of $A$.

articles.title: Erdős cofactor threshold
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the cofactor threshold $h(n)$ is the
largest natural number $m$ such that for every set $A$ of exactly $n$ positive integers, the set
$\{a/\gcd(a,b) : a, b \in A\}$ has at least $m$ elements.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 539: square-root lower bound for the cofactor threshold
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$n$, let $h(n)$ be the largest natural number $m$ such that for every set $A$ of exactly $n$
positive integers, the set $\{a/\gcd(a,b) : a, b \in A\}$ has at least $m$ elements. Then
$\sqrt{n} = O(h(n))$ as $n \to \infty$: there are a real constant $C$ and an $n_0$ such that
$\sqrt{n} \le C\,h(n)$ for all natural numbers $n \ge n_0$.

This lower bound was proved by Erdős and Szemerédi. The open problem of determining the exact
order of growth of $h(n)$ is not part of this statement.

## Sources

- J. Schmitt, T. Gehrunger, J. Dekoninck, G. Bérczi, U. Kreitner, L. Price, D. Holmes, ProofCouncil: An LLM Agent for Solving Open Mathematical Problems, arXiv:2607.09474 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09474.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 539
articles.statement:
Let $h(n)$ denote the cofactor threshold of $n$. The
statement is that $\sqrt{n} = O(h(n))$ as $n \to \infty$, that is, there are a real constant $C$
and an $n_0$ such that $\sqrt{n} \le C\,h(n)$ for all natural numbers $n \ge n_0$.

articles.title: Cofactor lower bound
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, $m$ is a cofactor lower bound for
$n$ when, for every set $A$ of exactly $n$ positive integers, the set
$\{a/\gcd(a,b) : a, b \in A\}$ has at least $m$ elements.

Members of $A$ are required to be positive since the quotient $a/\gcd(a,b)$ is undefined at
$a = b = 0$.

articles.title: Dense sets with controlled gcd defect
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be Euler's number. There is an absolute
constant $C > 0$ with the following property. Let $C_0 > 0$ be real, and let $F_{C_0}$ be the
growth function of the dense-set construction. Then there is a set $A$ of natural numbers such
that, writing $S_A(x) = \sum_{n \in A,\ 1 \le n \le x} 1/n$ for its harmonic sum up to $x$ and
$\mathcal{E}_A(x)$ for its gcd defect up to $x$, the following two statements hold. First, there
is a constant $K > 0$ with $F_{C_0}(x)/K \le S_A(x) \le K\, F_{C_0}(x)$ for all sufficiently large
real $x$. Second, there is a function $\varepsilon : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$\varepsilon(x) \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$ such that
$\mathcal{E}_A(x) \le C\,(\exp(e^2 C_0^2) - 1 + \varepsilon(x))$ for all sufficiently large
real $x$.

The factor $e^2$ follows the journal version of the source; the arXiv preprint prints
$\exp(C_0^2)$, but its proof, through the factor $e^\ell$ of (35), gives $e^2 C_0^2$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Theorem 2(i).

articles.title: Dense sets with unusually large least common multiples
articles.statement:
Let $\operatorname{Log}_2$ and
$\operatorname{Log}_3$ be the second and third iterated truncated logarithms. For a set $A$ of
natural numbers and real $x$, write $S_A(x) = \sum_{n \in A,\ 1 \le n \le x} 1/n$, and write
$L_A(x)$ for the sum of $1/\operatorname{lcm}(n, m)$ over all ordered pairs $(n, m)$ with
$n, m \in A$, $1 \le n \le x$ and $1 \le m \le x$. Then for every real $C_0 > 0$ there is a set
$A$ of natural numbers with the following two properties. First, there is a function
$\varepsilon : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\varepsilon(x) \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$ such that
for all sufficiently large real $x$,
$S_A(x) = \exp((C_0/2 + \varepsilon(x))(\operatorname{Log}_2 x)^{1/2} \operatorname{Log}_3 x)$.
Second, there is a constant $K > 0$ such that $L_A(x) \le K\, S_A(x)^2$ for all sufficiently
large real $x$.

The source presents this as a negative answer to Erdős problem #442. Its accompanying claim that
the exponent is optimal is made precise by Theorem 2(ii) and is stated separately.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Baby version of the dense-set construction
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be Euler's number, let
$\operatorname{Log}_2$ and $\operatorname{Log}_3$ be the second and third iterated truncated
logarithms, and for a set $B$ of natural numbers and real $x$ write
$S_B(x) = \sum_{n \in B,\ 1 \le n \le x} 1/n$ and $\mathcal{E}_B(x)$ for the gcd defect of $B$ up
to $x$. There is an absolute constant $C > 0$ such that for every real $C_0 > 0$ there are sets
$A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots$ of natural numbers with the following property: for every $\varepsilon > 0$
there are a real $\delta > 0$ and a natural number $k_0$ such that for every natural number
$k \ge k_0$ and every real $x$ with $|C_0 (\operatorname{Log}_2 x)^{1/2} - k| \le \delta k$, there
is a real $\eta$ with $|\eta| \le \varepsilon$ and
$S_{A_k}(x) = \exp((C_0/2 + \eta)(\operatorname{Log}_2 x)^{1/2} \operatorname{Log}_3 x)$, and
moreover $\mathcal{E}_{A_k}(x) \le C(\exp(e^2 C_0^2) - 1 + \varepsilon)$.

In the source this is Proposition 1, a simplified version of the construction for Theorem 2(i)
(its lead-in sentence refers to Theorem 2(ii)): the sets $A_k$ satisfy (31) and the bound (21)
in the range (32), with all $o(1)$ terms taken as $k \to \infty$. Above, these $o(1)$ terms are
written with $\varepsilon$, $\delta$ and $k_0$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Proposition 1, (31) and (32), with (21).

articles.title: Logarithmic gcd moment
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a real number $x$, the
logarithmic gcd moment of $A$ up to $x$ is the sum of $\gcd(n, m)/(nm)$ over all ordered pairs
$(n, m)$ with $n, m \in A$, $1 \le n \le x$ and $1 \le m \le x$.

When $A \cap [1, x]$ is nonempty, dividing by $\big(\sum_{n \in A,\ 1 \le n \le x} 1/n\big)^2$
gives the expected value of $\gcd(n, m)$ for $n$ and $m$ drawn independently from $A \cap [1, x]$,
each with probability proportional to $1/n$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Equation (9).

articles.title: The gcd defect of the empty set
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the gcd defect of the empty
set up to $x$ equals $-1$.

The harmonic sum of the empty set is $0$, and division by $0$ gives $0$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Equation (9).

articles.title: Gcd defect
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a real number $x$, let
$S_A(x) = \sum_{n \in A,\ 1 \le n \le x} 1/n$ be the harmonic sum of $A$ up to $x$, and let
$G_A(x)$ be the sum of $\gcd(n, m)/(nm)$ over all ordered pairs $(n, m)$ with $n, m \in A$,
$1 \le n \le x$ and $1 \le m \le x$. The gcd defect of $A$ up to $x$ is
$\mathcal{E}_A(x) = G_A(x)/S_A(x)^2 - 1$, where division by $0$ gives $0$; in particular
$\mathcal{E}_A(x) = -1$ when $A$ has no element in $[1, x]$.

When $A$ has an element in $[1, x]$, $\mathcal{E}_A(x) + 1$ is the expected value of
$\gcd(n, m)$ for $n$ and $m$ drawn independently from $A \cap [1, x]$, each with probability
proportional to $1/n$, so $\mathcal{E}_A(x)$ is the quantity $\mathbb{E} \gcd(n, m) - 1$ of the
source.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Equation (9).

articles.title: Growth function of the dense-set construction
articles.statement:
Let $\operatorname{Log}_2$ be the second
iterated truncated logarithm. For real numbers $C_0$ and $x$, let $k$ be the natural number
$\max(\lceil C_0 \sqrt{\operatorname{Log}_2 x}\,\rceil - 1, 0)$, and set
$h = \operatorname{Log}_2 x - k^2/C_0^2 + 1$, $x' = \exp(\exp((k + 1)^2/C_0^2))$,
$h' = \operatorname{Log}_2 x' - k^2/C_0^2 + 1$ and $\psi = 1 + h^2/h'$. The growth function at
$(C_0, x)$ is $F_{C_0}(x) = \psi\, k^{2k} / (C_0^{2k}\, k!)$. Here division by $0$ gives $0$ and
$0^0 = 1$.

In the source, $h'$ is the value at $x_{k+1} = x'$ of the expression defining $h$, with $k$ kept
fixed, and $F_{C_0}(x)$ is written $\psi(x)\, k^{2k} C_0^{-2k}/k!$; the function is used only for
$C_0 > 0$ and sufficiently large $x$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Equations (13)--(15).

articles.title: Double reciprocal lcm sum of the empty set
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the double sum of
reciprocal least common multiples of the empty set up to $x$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Equation (12).

articles.title: Double sum of reciprocal least common multiples
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a
real number $x$, the double sum of reciprocal least common multiples of $A$ up to $x$ is the
real number $\sum 1/\operatorname{lcm}(n, m)$, summed over all ordered pairs $(n, m)$ with
$n, m \in A$, $1 \le n \le x$ and $1 \le m \le x$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Equation (12).

articles.title: The empty set has no elements up to any bound
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the finite set
of elements $n$ of the empty set with $1 \le n \le x$ is empty.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Elements of a set up to a bound
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a real number $x$,
this is the finite set of positive integers $n \in A$ with $n \le x$; it is empty when $x < 1$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: The truncated logarithm is at least one
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the truncated
logarithm $\operatorname{Log} x = \max(\log x, 1)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Log} x \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Products of a fixed number of distinct primes
articles.statement:
For a set $\mathcal{P}$ of natural numbers
and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathcal{P}^{[k]}$ is the set of squarefree natural numbers $n$ whose prime
divisors all lie in $\mathcal{P}$ and which have exactly $k$ distinct prime divisors; that is, the
products of exactly $k$ distinct primes from $\mathcal{P}$. In particular,
$\mathcal{P}^{[0]} = \{1\}$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Lemma 1 notation.

articles.title: At most zero primes means exactly zero primes
articles.statement:
For every set $\mathcal{P}$ of natural
numbers, $\mathcal{P}^{[\le 0]} = \mathcal{P}^{[0]}$, where $\mathcal{P}^{[\le k]}$ and
$\mathcal{P}^{[k]}$ are the products of at most, respectively exactly, $k$ distinct primes from
$\mathcal{P}$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Lemma 1 notation.

articles.title: Products of at most a fixed number of distinct primes
articles.statement:
For a set $\mathcal{P}$ of natural
numbers and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathcal{P}^{[\le k]}$ is the set of natural numbers that lie in
$\mathcal{P}^{[j]}$ for some $j \le k$, where $\mathcal{P}^{[j]}$ is the set of products of exactly
$j$ distinct primes from $\mathcal{P}$; that is,
$\mathcal{P}^{[\le k]} = \bigcup_{j \le k} \mathcal{P}^{[j]}$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Lemma 1 notation.

articles.title: Harmonic sums over products of distinct primes
articles.statement:
There are constants $c > 0$ and $C > 0$
such that the following holds. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a set of primes, let $k$ be a natural number,
let $x \ge 1$ be real, and put $S = \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P},\, p \le x} 1/p$,
$T_k = \sum_{n \in \mathcal{P}^{[k]},\, n \le x} 1/n$ and
$T_{\le k} = \sum_{n \in \mathcal{P}^{[\le k]},\, n \le x} 1/n$, where $\mathcal{P}^{[k]}$ and
$\mathcal{P}^{[\le k]}$ are the sets of products of exactly $k$, respectively at most $k$,
distinct primes from $\mathcal{P}$. If $k \le cS$, then
$S^k/(C\,k!) \le T_k \le C\,S^k/k!$ and $S^k/(C\,k!) \le T_{\le k} \le C\,S^k/k!$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Lemma 1.

articles.title: The harmonic sum over the empty set vanishes
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$,
$\sum_{n \in \emptyset,\, n \le x} 1/n = 0$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Harmonic sum of a set up to a bound
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a real number
$x$, this is the finite sum $\sum_{n \in A,\, 1 \le n \le x} 1/n$ of the reciprocals of the
positive integers in $A$ that are at most $x$; it is $0$ when $x < 1$.

The sum starts at $n = 1$, matching the paper's convention that natural numbers are positive.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Second iterated truncated logarithm
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$, the second iterated truncated
logarithm is $\operatorname{Log}_2 x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log} x)$, where
$\operatorname{Log}$ is the truncated logarithm.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Third iterated truncated logarithm
articles.statement:
For real $x$, let
$\operatorname{Log} x = \max(\log x, 1)$ be the truncated logarithm, where $\log$ is the natural
logarithm extended by $\log x = \log |x|$ for $x < 0$ and $\log 0 = 0$, and let
$\operatorname{Log}_2 x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log} x)$. The third iterated truncated
logarithm is the function on all of $\mathbb{R}$ given by
$\operatorname{Log}_3 x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log}_2 x)$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Truncated logarithm
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$, the truncated logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log} x = \max(\log x, 1)$. Here $\log$ is extended to all reals by $\log 0 = 0$
and $\log x = \log |x|$ for $x < 0$, so the definition is total; the paper uses it only for
$x > 0$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Notation.

articles.title: Harmonic sums of sets with small gcd defect
articles.statement:
For a set $A$ of natural numbers and a real
number $x$, let $S_A(x)$ be the sum of $1/n$ over $n \in A$ with $1 \le n \le x$, and let the
defect of $A$ at $x$ be the sum of $\gcd(n, m)/(nm)$ over $n, m \in A$ with $1 \le n, m \le x$,
divided by $S_A(x)^2$, minus $1$ (the defect is $-1$ when $S_A(x) = 0$). Let
$\operatorname{Log} x = \max(\log x, 1)$ be the truncated logarithm, let
$\operatorname{Log}_2 x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log} x)$ and let
$\operatorname{Log}_3 x = \operatorname{Log}(\operatorname{Log}_2 x)$. For every real
$C_0 > 0$ there are a function $e : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $e(x) \to 0$ as
$x \to \infty$ and a real $x_0$ such that for every real $x \ge x_0$ and every set $A$ of natural
numbers whose defect at $x$ is at most $C_0^2$,

$$S_A(x) \le \exp\bigl((C_0 + e(x)) (\operatorname{Log}_2 x)^{1/2} \operatorname{Log}_3 x\bigr).$$

The function $e$ and the threshold $x_0$ are chosen before $x$ and $A$, so the $o(1)$ error is
uniform in $A$.

## Sources

- Terence Tao, *Dense Sets of Natural Numbers with Unusually Large Least Common Multiples*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A100, Theorem 2(ii).

articles.title: Natural numbers with at most $r$ distinct prime factors
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $r$,
$n$ has at most $r$ distinct prime factors when $n = 0$ or at most $r$ distinct primes divide $n$;
the number $0$ is counted as having no prime factors.

## Sources

- EP-851 [Erdős Problems].

articles.title: Sums of a power of two and a prime
articles.statement:
A natural number $m$ is of this form when
$m = 2^k + p$ for some natural number $k$ and some prime $p$.

## Sources

- Romanoff's theorem in EP-851 [Erdős Problems].

articles.title: Sums of a power of two and a number with few prime factors
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$, a
natural number $m$ is of this form when $m = 2^k + n$ for some natural numbers $k$ and $n$ such
that $n = 0$ or at most $r$ distinct primes divide $n$.

## Sources

- EP-851 [Erdős Problems].

articles.title: Erdős Problem 851 is true
articles.statement:
The set of natural numbers of the form $2^k + p$, with $k$ a natural
number and $p$ prime, has positive lower density. Moreover, for every real number
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $r$ such that the set of natural numbers of the form
$2^k + n$, with $k$ and $n$ natural numbers and with $n = 0$ or at most $r$ distinct primes dividing
$n$, has lower density at least $1 - \varepsilon$.

Romanoff proved the positive-density clause in 1934; Price and GPT-5.2 Pro proved the near-one
density statement affirmatively in 2026.

## Sources

- Lean proof of Erdős Problem 851, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos851.lean#L37; Yuchen Ding and Wenguang Zhai, A generalization of the Romanoff theorem, arXiv:2401.15892v3 (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15892v3.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 851
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts two things. First, the set of natural numbers
of the form $2^k + p$, with $k$ a natural number and $p$ prime, has positive lower density
(Romanoff's theorem). Second, for every real number $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number
$r$ such that the set of natural numbers of the form $2^k + n$, with $k$ and $n$ natural numbers
and with $n = 0$ or at most $r$ distinct primes dividing $n$, has lower density at least
$1 - \varepsilon$.

## Sources

- EP-851 [Erdős Problems].

articles.title: Erdős Problem 793 has a positive answer
articles.statement:
Let $F(n)$ be the largest size of a set
$A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ such that $a \nmid bc$ whenever $a, b, c \in A$ with $a \ne b$ and
$a \ne c$ ($b = c$ is allowed), and let $\pi(n)$ be the number of primes at most $n$. Then there
is a real constant $C > 0$ such that $(F(n) - \pi(n)) / (n^{2/3} / (\log n)^2) \to C$ as
$n \to \infty$.

Chojecki (2026, Theorem 1.1) proves this with $C = 27/2$.

## Sources

- P. Chojecki, The Second Term for Strongly 2-Primitive Sets, arXiv preprint (2026), arXiv:2607.15306, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15306.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 793
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let $F(n)$ be the largest size
of a set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ with $a \nmid bc$ for all $a, b, c \in A$ such that
$a \ne b$ and $a \ne c$, and let $\pi(n)$ be the number of primes at most $n$. This is the
proposition that there is a real constant $C > 0$ such that
$(F(n) - \pi(n)) / (n^{2/3} / (\log n)^2) \to C$ as $n \to \infty$.
Equivalently, $F(n) = \pi(n) + (C + o(1))\, n^{2/3} / (\log n)^2$.

articles.title: Maximum size of a good subset
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $F(n)$ is the largest size of a
good subset of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, defined as the supremum of the sizes of the good sets
$A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$.

articles.title: Sets in which no element divides the product of two others
articles.statement:
A finite set $A$ of natural
numbers is good when every element of $A$ is positive and no $a \in A$ divides $bc$ for any
$b, c \in A$ with $a \ne b$ and $a \ne c$; here $b = c$ is allowed.

articles.title: Polynomial values plus reciprocals
articles.statement:
For a polynomial $p$ with rational coefficients,
$A_p$ is the set of rational numbers $p(n) + 1/n$, where $n$ ranges over the positive
integers.

articles.title: Strong completeness of polynomial values plus reciprocals (Erdős Problem 351)
articles.statement:
For every
polynomial $p$ with rational coefficients and positive leading coefficient, let $A_p$ be the set
of rational numbers $p(n) + 1/n$, where $n$ ranges over the positive integers. Then $A_p$ is
strongly complete: for every finite set $B$ of rational numbers there is an integer $N_0$ such
that every integer $m \ge N_0$ is the sum of the elements of some finite subset of
$A_p \setminus B$.

Resolved true: The maintained Erdős Problems page marks Problem 351 proved in the affirmative
and records that the positive solution follows from the positive solution of Problem 283.

## Sources

- plby/lean-proofs, https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/Util/PolynomialEgyptianSums.lean#L10266.

articles.title: The strong completeness statement of Erdős Problem 351
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that for
every polynomial $p$ with rational coefficients and positive leading coefficient, the set $A_p$
of rational numbers $p(n) + 1/n$, where $n$ ranges over the positive integers, is strongly
complete.

articles.title: Strongly complete sets of rationals
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of rational numbers is strongly complete
when, for every finite set $B$ of rational numbers, there is an integer $N_0$ such that every
integer $m \ge N_0$ is the sum of the elements of some finite subset of $A \setminus B$.

articles.title: Interval sums with unbounded representation counts (Erdős Problem 358)
articles.statement:
There is a
strictly increasing sequence $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ of positive integers such that the
number $f(n)$ of pairs $(u, v)$ of natural numbers with $u \le v$ and
$a_u + a_{u+1} + \cdots + a_v = n$ tends to infinity as $n \to \infty$.

Resolved true: Resolved by Tao's February 2026 construction of a set A of positive integers with
f(n) >> log n for all large n, hence f(n) -> infinity (Erdos Problems record 358, [Ta26]).

## Sources

- Terence Tao, construction of a set A of positive integers with f(n) >> log n for Erdos Problem 358, February 2026, https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf.

articles.title: The interval-sum conjecture of Erdős Problem 358
articles.statement:
This is the proposition that there is a
strictly increasing sequence $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ of positive integers whose interval-sum
representation count $f(n)$, the number of pairs $(u, v)$ of natural numbers with $u \le v$ and
$a_u + a_{u+1} + \cdots + a_v = n$, tends to infinity as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Interval-sum representation count
articles.statement:
For a sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of natural
numbers and a natural number $n$, $f_a(n)$ is the number of pairs $(u, v)$ of natural numbers
with $u \le v$ and $a_u + a_{u+1} + \cdots + a_v = n$, and $f_a(n) = 0$ if there are infinitely
many such pairs.

The sequence is indexed from $0$ rather than from $1$ as in the source; this does not change the
count. When the sequence is strictly increasing with positive terms there are only finitely many
such pairs, so $f_a(n)$ is then the true number of representations.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 845 is false
articles.statement:
There is a real number $C > 0$ such that the set of all sums
$\sum_{(k, l) \in B} 2^k 3^l$, where $B$ is a nonempty finite set of pairs of natural numbers such
that $\max_{(k, l) \in B} 2^k 3^l \le C \min_{(k, l) \in B} 2^k 3^l$, does not have natural
density $0$.

Van Doorn and Everts obtain a counterexample with $C = 6$.

## Sources

- Wouter van Doorn and Anneroos R. F. Everts, Smooth sums with small spacings, arXiv:2511.04585v1 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04585v1.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 845
articles.statement:
The proposition asserts that for every real number $C > 0$, the set of
all sums $\sum_{(k, l) \in B} 2^k 3^l$, where $B$ is a nonempty finite set of pairs of natural
numbers such that $\max_{(k, l) \in B} 2^k 3^l \le C \min_{(k, l) \in B} 2^k 3^l$, has natural
density $0$.

articles.title: Lower bound for the number of sums of consecutive prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots$
be the primes and let $k > 1$ be a natural number. For a natural number $x$ let $s_k(x)$ be the
number of pairs $(\ell, m)$ of integers with $0 \le \ell < x$ and $1 \le m \le x$ such that
$p_{\ell+1}^k + \cdots + p_{\ell+m}^k \le x$, and let $M(x, k)$ be the largest $m \le x$ with
$p_1^k + \cdots + p_m^k \le x$. Then $M(x, k)^2 / 2 \le s_k(x)$ for every $x$, and for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, for all sufficiently large $x$,
$(1 - \varepsilon) (k + 1)^2 x^{2/(k+1)} / \bigl(2 (\log x)^{2k/(k+1)}\bigr) \le M(x, k)^2 / 2$.

## Sources

- Cathal O'Sullivan, Jonathan P. Sorenson, and Aryn Stahl, *Algorithms and Bounds on the Sums of Powers of Consecutive Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A4, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Upper bound for the number of sums of consecutive prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots$
be the primes and let $k > 1$ be a natural number. For a natural number $x$ let $s_k(x)$ be the
number of pairs $(\ell, m)$ of integers with $0 \le \ell < x$ and $1 \le m \le x$ such that
$p_{\ell+1}^k + \cdots + p_{\ell+m}^k \le x$. Then for every real $\varepsilon > 0$, for all
sufficiently large $x$,
$s_k(x) \le (1 + \varepsilon)\, c_k\, x^{2/(k+1)} / (\log x)^{2k/(k+1)}$, where
$c_k = \frac{k^2}{k-1} (k + 1)^{1 - 1/k}$.

## Sources

- Cathal O'Sullivan, Jonathan P. Sorenson, and Aryn Stahl, *Algorithms and Bounds on the Sums of Powers of Consecutive Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A4, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Counting sums of a fixed number of consecutive prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots$
be the primes. For natural numbers $k > 1$, $m > 0$ and $x$, the number of integers $n \le x$ of
the form $n = p_{\ell+1}^k + p_{\ell+2}^k + \cdots + p_{\ell+m}^k$ for some $\ell \ge 0$ is at
most $\pi(\lfloor (x/m)^{1/k} \rfloor)$, the number of primes up to $(x/m)^{1/k}$.

## Sources

- Cathal O'Sullivan, Jonathan P. Sorenson, and Aryn Stahl, *Algorithms and Bounds on the Sums of Powers of Consecutive Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A4, Lemma 1 (quoted from [6]).

articles.title: Upper bound for the number of gleeful representations
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, \dots$ be
the primes in increasing order, and for natural numbers $k$ and $x$ let $s_k(x)$ be the number
of pairs $(n, m)$ of natural numbers with $m \ge 1$ and $p_{n+1}^k + \cdots + p_{n+m}^k \le x$.
Let $k > 1$, $M_0 \ge 6$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $p_1^k + \cdots + p_{M_0}^k \le x$. Put
$y = M_0$, let $\log$ be the natural logarithm, and set

$$A = \frac{\log(y/2)}{\log y},$$



$$B = \frac{\log(y+1)}{\log y} + \frac{\log\log((y+1)^2)}{\log y} \cdot \frac{k}{k+1},$$



$$C = \Big(\frac{y}{y-1}\Big)^{1/(k+1)} B^{k/(k+1)}, \qquad E = 1 + \frac{1}{(k+1)A - 1},$$



$$F = \Big(\frac{y+1}{y}\Big)^{(k-1)/k} 4^{(k-1)/(k(k+1))} C^{(k-1)/k} E,$$

$U = 1.25506\,F$ and $c_k = \frac{k^2}{k-1} (k+1)^{(k-1)/k}$. Then

$$s_k(x) \le c_k \cdot \frac{x^{2/(k+1)}}{(\log x)^{2k/(k+1)}} \cdot U.$$

The paper prints the exponent of $\log x$ as $k/(k+1)$; its proof ends with $2k/(k+1)$, which
is stated here and implies the printed bound because $\log x \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sara Moore and Jonathan P. Sorenson, *Explicit Bounds and Parallel Algorithms for Counting Multiply Gleeful Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A84, Theorem 1 and its proof, with `c_k, A, B, C, E, F, U` from Section 2.

articles.title: Lower bound for the number of gleeful representations
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, \dots$ be
the primes in increasing order, and for natural numbers $k$ and $x$ let $s_k(x)$ be the number
of pairs $(n, m)$ of natural numbers with $m \ge 1$ and $p_{n+1}^k + \cdots + p_{n+m}^k \le x$.
Let $k > 1$, $M_0 \ge 6$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $p_1^k + \cdots + p_{M_0}^k \le x$. Put
$y = M_0$, let $\log$ be the natural logarithm, and set

$$D = \frac{y}{y+3} \Big(\frac{\log(y/2)}{\log y + 2 \log\log(y+2)}\Big)^{k/(k+1)}$$

and $L = \frac{y-1}{y} D^2$. Then

$$\frac{(k+1)^2}{2} \cdot \frac{x^{2/(k+1)}}{(\log x)^{2k/(k+1)}} \cdot L \le s_k(x).$$

The paper prints the exponent of $\log x$ as $k/(k+1)$; its proof gives $2k/(k+1)$, which is
stated here. The printed form contradicts the upper bound for $s_k(x)$ for large $x$.

## Sources

- Sara Moore and Jonathan P. Sorenson, *Explicit Bounds and Parallel Algorithms for Counting Multiply Gleeful Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A84, Theorem 2 and its proof, with `D`, `L` from Section 2.

articles.title: Lower bound for the maximal gleeful chain length
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, \dots$ be the
primes in increasing order. Let $k > 1$, $M_0 \ge 6$, $M \ge M_0$ and $x$ be natural numbers with
$p_1^k + \cdots + p_M^k \le x < p_1^k + \cdots + p_{M+1}^k$. Put $y = M_0$ and

$$D = \frac{y}{y+3} \Big(\frac{\log(y/2)}{\log y + 2 \log\log(y+2)}\Big)^{k/(k+1)},$$

where $\log$ is the natural logarithm. Then

$$\frac{(k+1)\, x^{1/(k+1)}}{(\log x)^{k/(k+1)}} \cdot D \le M.$$

## Sources

- Sara Moore and Jonathan P. Sorenson, *Explicit Bounds and Parallel Algorithms for Counting Multiply Gleeful Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A84, Lemma 2, with `D` from Section 2.

articles.title: Bounds for the logarithm of the maximal gleeful chain length
articles.statement:
Let
$p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, \dots$ be the primes in increasing order. Let $k > 1$, $M_0 \ge 6$, $M \ge M_0$
and $x$ be natural numbers with $p_1^k + \cdots + p_M^k \le x < p_1^k + \cdots + p_{M+1}^k$.
Put $y = M_0$, let $\log$ be the natural logarithm, and set

$$A = \frac{\log(y/2)}{\log y},$$



$$B = \frac{\log(y+1)}{\log y} + \frac{\log\log((y+1)^2)}{\log y} \cdot \frac{k}{k+1}.$$

Then

$$\frac{\log x}{k+1} \cdot \frac{1}{B} \le \log M < \frac{\log x}{k+1} \cdot \frac{1}{A}.$$

## Sources

- Sara Moore and Jonathan P. Sorenson, *Explicit Bounds and Parallel Algorithms for Counting Multiply Gleeful Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A84, Lemma 3, with `A`, `B` from Section 2.

articles.title: Upper bound for the maximal gleeful chain length
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, \dots$ be the
primes in increasing order. Let $k > 1$, $M_0 \ge 6$, $M \ge M_0$ and $x$ be natural numbers with
$p_1^k + \cdots + p_M^k \le x < p_1^k + \cdots + p_{M+1}^k$. Put $y = M_0$,

$$B = \frac{\log(y+1)}{\log y} + \frac{\log\log((y+1)^2)}{\log y} \cdot \frac{k}{k+1}$$

and $C = (y/(y-1))^{1/(k+1)} B^{k/(k+1)}$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm. Then

$$M < 4^{1/(k+1)} \cdot \frac{(k+1)\, x^{1/(k+1)}}{(\log x)^{k/(k+1)}} \cdot C.$$

## Sources

- Sara Moore and Jonathan P. Sorenson, *Explicit Bounds and Parallel Algorithms for Counting Multiply Gleeful Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A84, Lemma 1, with `B`, `C` from Section 2.

articles.title: Length of the longest sum of consecutive prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots$ be the
primes, let $k > 1$ be a natural number, and for a natural number $x$ let $M(x, k)$ be the
largest $m \le x$ with $p_1^k + p_2^k + \cdots + p_m^k \le x$. Then
$M(x, k) \sim (k + 1)\, x^{1/(k+1)} / (\log x)^{k/(k+1)}$ (asymptotic equivalence) as $x \to \infty$
through the natural numbers.

## Sources

- Cathal O'Sullivan, Jonathan P. Sorenson, and Aryn Stahl, *Algorithms and Bounds on the Sums of Powers of Consecutive Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A4, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Large integers as a practical number plus two polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $s > 3$ be a natural
number and, for a natural number $x$, let $P_s(x) = (s-2)\binom{x}{2} + x$ be the $x$-th
$s$-gonal number, so that $P_s(0) = 0$. There is a natural number $N$ such that every natural
number $n > N$ can be written as $n = q + P_s(x) + P_s(y)$ with $q$ a practical number and
$x, y$ natural numbers.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Theorem 2 (`jis-2024-24.5.1-thm-2`).

articles.title: Sums of two polygonal numbers modulo an odd prime
articles.statement:
For a natural number $s > 3$ and a
natural number $x$, let $P_s(x) = (s-2)\binom{x}{2} + x$ be the $x$-th $s$-gonal number. For
every odd prime $p$ and every natural number $n > 0$ there are natural numbers $x, y > 0$ with
$P_s(x) + P_s(y) \equiv n \pmod{p}$.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 6 (arXiv Lemma 4.1; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-6`).

articles.title: Parity of sums of two polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $s > 3$ and a natural
number $x$, let $P_s(x) = (s-2)\binom{x}{2} + x$ be the $x$-th $s$-gonal number. For every
natural number $n > 0$ there are natural numbers $x, y > 0$ such that
$P_s(x_1) + P_s(y_1) \equiv n \pmod{2}$ for all natural numbers $x_1, y_1 > 0$ with
$x_1 \equiv x \pmod{4}$ and $y_1 \equiv y \pmod{4}$.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 7 (arXiv Lemma 4.2; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-7`).

articles.title: Every positive integer is a practical number plus a triangular number
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n > 0$ there are a practical number $q$ and a natural number $k$ with
$n = q + k(k+1)/2$; the case $k = 0$, where the triangular number is $0$, is allowed.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Theorem 1 (`jis-2024-24.5.1-thm-1`).

articles.title: Sums of two polygonal numbers modulo prime powers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $s > 3$ and a
natural number $x$, let $P_s(x) = (s-2)\binom{x}{2} + x$ be the $x$-th $s$-gonal number. There
is a prime $p$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ and $p \nmid s - 2$ such that for all natural numbers
$k > 0$ and $n > 0$ there are natural numbers $x, y > 0$ with
$P_s(x) + P_s(y) \equiv n \pmod{p^k}$.

The paper's statement asks only for an odd prime; the condition $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ is the
choice made in its proof via Lemma 8 (arXiv Lemma 4.3).

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 9 (arXiv Lemma 4.4; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-9`).

articles.title: Sums of two squares modulo prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.
For all natural numbers $n > 0$ and $k > 0$ there are natural numbers $x, y > 0$ with
$x^2 + y^2 \equiv n \pmod{p^k}$ and $p \nmid y$.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 8 (arXiv Lemma 4.3; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-8`).

articles.title: Square roots modulo powers of two
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m > 0$ and $n > 0$ there is
a natural number $x$ with $1 \le x \le 2^m - 1$ and $x^2 \equiv 8n + 1 \pmod{2^{m+2}}$.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 3 (arXiv Lemma 3.1; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-3`).

articles.title: Quadratic upper bound for polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $s > 3$ and a natural
number $x$, let $P_s(x) = (s-2)\binom{x}{2} + x$ be the $x$-th $s$-gonal number. For every natural
number $c$ there is a natural number $A$ such that $2 P_s(2cx) \le A x^2$ for every natural
number $x \ge 1$.

The paper states this only for one specific prime $c$, the prime chosen in Lemma 9 (arXiv
Lemma 4.4), and for real $x$; here $c$ is an arbitrary natural number and $x$ is a natural number.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 10 (arXiv Lemma 4.5; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-10`).

articles.title: Practical numbers divisible by neither 3 nor 4
articles.statement:
If $q$ is a practical number that is
divisible by neither $3$ nor $4$, then $q = 1$ or $q = 2$.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 11 (arXiv Lemma 4.6; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-11`).

articles.title: Products of a practical number with small factors
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a practical number and let
$\sigma(m)$ denote the sum of the positive divisors of $m$. Then for every natural number $n$
with $1 \le n \le \sigma(m) + 1$, the product $mn$ is a practical number.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 4 (arXiv Lemma 3.2; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-4`), quoting Margenstern.

articles.title: Exceptions to sums of a practical number and polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
(a) Let $s \ge 3$ with
$s \equiv 0$ or $s \equiv 4 \pmod{12}$. Then there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ that
cannot be written as $n = q + p_s(m)$ with $q$ a practical number and $m \ge 0$ an integer, where
$p_s(m)$ is the $m$-th $s$-gonal number. (b) For every natural number $M$ there is a natural
number $S$ such that for every $t \ge S$ there are at least $M$ positive integers $n$ that cannot
be written as $n = q + p_t(x) + p_t(y)$ with $q$ a practical number and integers $x, y \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Proposition 12 (arXiv Proposition 4.7; `jis-2024-24.5.1-prop-12`).

articles.title: Odd squares and triangular numbers
articles.statement:
For every odd natural number $x$, the number
$(x^2 - 1)/8$ is a triangular number: there is a natural number $k$ with
$(x^2 - 1)/8 = p_3(k)$, where $p_3(k) = k(k+1)/2$ is the $k$-th $3$-gonal number.

## Sources

- Sai Teja Somu and Duc Van Khanh Tran, *On Sums of Practical Numbers and Polygonal Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.1, Lemma 5 (arXiv Lemma 3.3; `jis-2024-24.5.1-lem-5`).

articles.title: Formula for the adelic norm
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field. For every idele $a$ of $K$ (with
$R = \mathcal{O}_K$), the adelic norm of $a$ equals
$\bigl(\prod_w \|a_w\|_w^{m_w}\bigr) \cdot \prod_v \|a_v\|_v$, where $w$ runs over the infinite
places of $K$, $\|\cdot\|_w$ is the absolute value on the completion $K_w$ extending $w$, $m_w$ is
$1$ for a real place and $2$ for a complex place, $v$ runs over the height-one primes of
$\mathcal{O}_K$, $\|\cdot\|_v$ is the normalized absolute value on the completion $K_v$, and the
product over $v$ is the product of its finitely many factors different from $1$.

articles.title: Product formula for principal ideles
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field. For every
$x \in K^\times$, the principal idele of $x$ (its image under the diagonal embedding of $K^\times$
into the topological idele group, with $R = \mathcal{O}_K$) has adelic norm $1$.

articles.title: Adelic norm
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. For each
infinite place $w$ of $K$ let $K_w$ be the completion of $K$ at $w$, with the absolute value
