articles.title: Rearick's characterization of multiplicative functions
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real-valued arithmetic
function with $f(1) > 0$, and let $L(f)$ be its Rearick logarithm. Then $f$ is multiplicative
(that is, $f(1) = 1$ and $f(mn) = f(m) f(n)$ whenever $m$ and $n$ are coprime) if and only if
$L(f)(m) = 0$ for every natural number $m$ that is not a prime power, including $m = 0$ and
$m = 1$.

## Sources

- Rearick logarithm support characterization of multiplicative arithmetic functions, after Huilan Li and Trueman MacHenry, arXiv:1009.1892v1, <https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.1892>, lines 444-450 (Rearick logarithm definition) and 706-708 (Rearick Theorem 4). Real-valued domain closure with `f 1 > 0` after Pong, arXiv:1504.03263v2, <https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.03263>, lines 174-195; positivity also supplies the nonzero premise for the Dirichlet inverse.

articles.title: Rearick logarithm
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a real-valued arithmetic function with $f(1) > 0$, and let
$f^{-1}$ be its Dirichlet inverse. The Rearick logarithm of $f$ is the arithmetic function $L(f)$
with $L(f)(0) = 0$, $L(f)(1) = \log f(1)$, and
$L(f)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d) \, f^{-1}(n/d) \log d$ for $n > 1$.

articles.title: Value of the square-splitting convolution at a positive integer
articles.statement:
For complex arithmetic
functions $f$ and $g$ and every natural number $n \ne 0$, the square-splitting convolution of $f$
and $g$ takes the value $(f \star g)(n) = \sum_{d \in A(n)} f(d)\, g(n/d)$ at $n$, where $A(n)$ is
the square-splitting divisor set of $n$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2.

articles.title: Square-splitting convolution as a bivariate Dirichlet convolution
articles.statement:
Let $\star$ be the
square-splitting convolution. For all complex arithmetic functions $f$ and $g$, every squarefree
natural number $u$ and every natural number $v \ge 1$,

$$(f \star g)(u v^2) = \sum_{u_1 \mid u} \sum_{v_1 \mid v} f(u_1 v_1^2)\, g((u/u_1)(v/v_1)^2).$$

Moreover, for every function $F : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ there is exactly
one complex arithmetic function $f$ with $f(u v^2) = F(u, v)$ for every squarefree $u$ and every
$v \ge 1$.

Thus $f \mapsto \big((u, v) \mapsto f(u v^2)\big)$ is a bijection from complex arithmetic functions
onto functions on $\{(u, v) : u \text{ squarefree},\ v \ge 1\}$, and it turns $\star$ into the
bivariate Dirichlet convolution
$(\Phi \odot \Psi)(u, v) = \sum_{u_1 \mid u} \sum_{v_1 \mid v} \Phi(u_1, v_1)\, \Psi(u/u_1, v/v_1)$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Ring axioms for the square-splitting convolution
articles.statement:
For all complex arithmetic functions
$f$, $g$ and $h$, the square-splitting convolution $\star$ satisfies $f \star g = g \star f$,
$(f \star g) \star h = f \star (g \star h)$, $f \star (g + h) = f \star g + f \star h$ and
$\varepsilon \star f = f$, where $\varepsilon$ is the arithmetic function with $\varepsilon(1) = 1$
and $\varepsilon(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 1$.

With pointwise addition, these identities make the complex arithmetic functions a commutative ring
under $\star$ with identity $\varepsilon$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Inverse of a multiplicative function under the square-splitting convolution
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a
multiplicative complex arithmetic function (an arithmetic function $h$ is multiplicative when
$h(1) = 1$ and $h(mn) = h(m)\, h(n)$ for coprime $m$ and $n$), let $\star$ be the square-splitting
convolution, and let $\varepsilon$ be the arithmetic function with $\varepsilon(1) = 1$ and
$\varepsilon(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 1$. Then there is a complex arithmetic function $g$ with
$f \star g = \varepsilon$ such that every complex arithmetic function $g'$ with
$f \star g' = \varepsilon$ equals $g$. Moreover, $g$ is multiplicative; for every prime $p$ and
every $k \ge 1$, $\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} f(p^{2j})\, g(p^{k-2j}) = 0$ if $k$ is even and
$\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} (f(p^{2j}) g(p^{k-2j}) + f(p^{2j+1}) g(p^{k-2j-1})) = 0$ if $k$ is
odd; $g(1) = 1/f(1)$; and for every prime $p$, $g(p) = -f(p)/f(1)^2$,
$g(p^2) = -f(p^2)/f(1)^2$ and $g(p^3) = \big(2 f(p) f(p^2) - f(p^3) f(1)\big)/f(1)^3$.

Multiplicativity includes $f(1) = 1$, so the source's hypothesis $f(1) \ne 0$ holds automatically.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 5.

articles.title: The square-splitting convolution preserves multiplicativity
articles.statement:
If $f$ and $g$ are
multiplicative complex arithmetic functions, then their square-splitting convolution $f \star g$
is multiplicative. Here an arithmetic function $h$ is multiplicative when $h(1) = 1$ and
$h(mn) = h(m)\, h(n)$ for all coprime $m$ and $n$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Square-splitting convolution
articles.statement:
For complex arithmetic functions $f$ and $g$, the
square-splitting $A$-convolution of Narkiewicz type is the arithmetic function $f \star g$ given by
$(f \star g)(n) = \sum_{d \in A(n)} f(d)\, g(n/d)$ for $n \ge 1$ and $(f \star g)(0) = 0$. Here
$A(n) = \{u_1 v_1^2 : u_1 \mid u(n),\ v_1 \mid v(n)\}$ is the square-splitting divisor set of $n$,
where $u(n)$ is the squarefree part of $n$ and $n = u(n) v(n)^2$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2 and Theorem 4 (`F = 1 ⋆ f` means `F(n) = ∑_{d ∈ A(n)} f(d)`).

articles.title: Dirichlet series of the square-splitting divisor function
articles.statement:
Let $\tau^\star(n) = |A(n)|$ be
the number of elements of the square-splitting divisor set $A(n)$, and let
$H(s) = \prod_p (1 - 3p^{-2s} + 2p^{-3s})$, where $p$ runs over the primes. For every complex
number $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the series $\sum_{k \ge 0} \tau^\star(p^k) p^{-ks}$
converges to $(1 + 2p^{-s})/(1 - p^{-2s})^2$ for each prime $p$, and the Dirichlet series
$\sum_{n \ge 1} \tau^\star(n) n^{-s}$ equals both $\prod_p (1 + 2p^{-s})/(1 - p^{-2s})^2$ and
$\zeta(s)^2 \zeta(2s)^2 H(s)$. Moreover, for every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$ the series
$\sum_p |-3p^{-2s} + 2p^{-3s}|$ converges (so the product defining $H(s)$ converges absolutely),
$H$ is holomorphic on the half-plane $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$, and $H(1) \ne 0$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Average order of the square-splitting divisor function
articles.statement:
Let $\tau^\star(n) = |A(n)|$ be
the number of elements of the square-splitting divisor set $A(n)$, let $\gamma$ be the
Euler–Mascheroni constant, and let $A_\tau = \prod_p (1 - 1/(p+1)^2)$ and
$B_\tau = 6 \sum_p \log p / ((p-1)(p+1)(p+2))$, where $p$ runs over the primes. Then, as the real
number $x$ tends to infinity,
$\sum_{1 \le n \le x} \tau^\star(n) - A_\tau x \log x - A_\tau (2\gamma - 1 - B_\tau - c) x$ is
$O(x^{1/2} (\log x)^3)$, where $c = 2\zeta'(2)/\zeta(2)$.

These constants are the ones forced by the Dirichlet series of $\tau^\star$: with
$H(s) = \prod_p (1 - 3p^{-2s} + 2p^{-3s})$, one has $A_\tau = \zeta(2)^2 H(1)$ and
$-B_\tau - 2\zeta'(2)/\zeta(2) = 4\zeta'(2)/\zeta(2) + H'(1)/H(1)$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 10.

articles.title: The square-splitting divisor set of $1$
articles.statement:
Let
$A(n) = \{u_1 v_1^2 : u_1 \mid u(n),\ v_1 \mid v(n)\}$ be the square-splitting divisor set of
$n \ge 1$, where $u(n)$ is the squarefree part of $n$ and $v(n)$ is the positive integer with
$n = u(n) v(n)^2$. Then $A(1) = \{1\}$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Basic properties of the square-splitting divisor sets
articles.statement:
Let
$A(n) = \{u_1 v_1^2 : u_1 \mid u(n),\ v_1 \mid v(n)\}$ be the square-splitting divisor set of
$n$, where $u(n)$ is the squarefree part of $n$ and $n = u(n) v(n)^2$ for $n \ge 1$. Then
(i) for every $n \ge 1$, both $1$ and $n$ belong to $A(n)$, and every element of $A(n)$ divides
$n$; (ii) for all coprime natural numbers $m$ and $n$, $A(mn) = \{ab : a \in A(m),\ b \in A(n)\}$;
and (iii) for every $n \ge 1$, $|A(n)| = d(u(n))\, d(v(n))$ and $|A(n)| = 2^{\omega(u(n))} d(v(n))$,
where $d(k)$ is the number of divisors of $k$ and $\omega(k)$ is the number of distinct prime
factors of $k$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Square-splitting divisors
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n \ge 1$ with prime factorization
$n = \prod_p p^{e_p}$, let $u(n) = \prod_p p^{e_p \bmod 2}$ and
$v(n) = \prod_p p^{\lfloor e_p/2 \rfloor}$, and let $u(0) = v(0) = 1$. The set of
square-splitting divisors of $n$ is $A(n) = \{u_1 v_1^2 : u_1 \mid u(n),\ v_1 \mid v(n)\}$, where
$u_1$ and $v_1$ range over the positive divisors of $u(n)$ and $v(n)$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Möbius function of the square-splitting convolution
articles.statement:
Let $\star$ be the square-splitting
convolution, $\mathbf{1}$ the constant function $1$ on the positive integers, $\varepsilon$ the
identity element ($\varepsilon(1) = 1$ and $\varepsilon(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 1$), and let $\mu_\star$
be any complex-valued arithmetic function with $\mathbf{1} \star \mu_\star = \varepsilon$. Then
$\mu_\star(n) = \mu(u(n))\,\mu(v(n))$ for every $n \ge 1$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function,
$u(n)$ is the product of the primes dividing $n$ to an odd power and $v(n)$ is the positive
integer with $n = u(n)\,v(n)^2$. For every prime $p$, $\mu_\star(p) = \mu_\star(p^2) = -1$,
$\mu_\star(p^3) = 1$ and $\mu_\star(p^k) = 0$ for every $k \ge 4$. For every complex $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,

$$\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\mu_\star(n)}{n^s} = \prod_p \left(1 - p^{-s} - p^{-2s} + p^{-3s}\right)
= \frac{1}{\zeta(s)\,\zeta(2s)}.$$

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Möbius inversion for the square-splitting convolution
articles.statement:
Let $\star$ be the
square-splitting convolution, $\mathbf{1}$ the constant function $1$ on the positive integers,
$\varepsilon$ the identity element ($\varepsilon(1) = 1$ and $\varepsilon(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 1$),
and let $\mu_\star$ be any complex-valued arithmetic function with
$\mathbf{1} \star \mu_\star = \varepsilon$. Then for all complex-valued arithmetic functions $f$
and $F$, $F = \mathbf{1} \star f$ if and only if $f = \mu_\star \star F$; that is,
$F(n) = \sum_{d \in A(n)} f(d)$ for every $n \ge 1$ if and only if
$f(n) = \sum_{d \in A(n)} \mu_\star(d)\,F(n/d)$ for every $n \ge 1$, where $A(n)$ is the set of
square-splitting divisors of $n$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Support and density of the square-splitting Möbius function
articles.statement:
Let $\star$ be the
square-splitting convolution, $\mathbf{1}$ the constant function $1$ on the positive integers,
$\varepsilon$ the identity element ($\varepsilon(1) = 1$ and $\varepsilon(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 1$),
and let $\mu_\star$ be any complex-valued arithmetic function with
$\mathbf{1} \star \mu_\star = \varepsilon$. Then for every $n \ge 1$, $\mu_\star(n) \ne 0$ if and
only if every prime exponent of $n$ is at most $3$. The proportion of the integers
$1 \le n \le N$ with $\mu_\star(n) \ne 0$ tends to $\prod_p (1 - p^{-4})$ as $N \to \infty$, and
$\prod_p (1 - p^{-4}) = 1/\zeta(4)$. Finally,
$\sum_{1 \le n \le x} |\mu_\star(n)|^2 \sim x/\zeta(4)$ as $x \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 11.

articles.title: A square-splitting divisor function and its Euler product
articles.statement:
Let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$, let $\sigma_\beta(m) = \sum_{d \mid m} d^\beta$ for $\beta \in \mathbb{C}$
(complex powers), and let $f(n) = \sigma_\alpha(u(n))\,\sigma_{2\alpha}(v(n))$, where $u(n)$ is
the product of the primes dividing $n$ to an odd power and $v(n)$ is the positive integer with
$n = u(n)\,v(n)^2$. Then $f(1) = 1$ and $f(mn) = f(m)\,f(n)$ for all coprime $m$ and $n$. For
every prime $p$ and every $b \ge 0$, $f(p^{2b}) = \sum_{j=0}^{b} p^{2j\alpha}$ and
$f(p^{2b+1}) = (1 + p^\alpha) \sum_{j=0}^{b} p^{2j\alpha}$. For every complex $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > \max(1, 1 + \operatorname{Re} \alpha)$, for every prime $p$

$$\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{f(p^k)}{p^{ks}}
= \frac{1 + p^{-s} + p^{-(s-\alpha)}}{(1 - p^{-2s})(1 - p^{-(2s-2\alpha)})},$$

the series $\sum_{n \ge 1} f(n)\,n^{-s}$ converges absolutely, and

$$\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{f(n)}{n^s}
= \zeta(2s)\,\zeta(2s - 2\alpha) \prod_p \left(1 + p^{-s} + p^{-(s-\alpha)}\right).$$

The paper identifies $f$ with its divisor function $\sigma_{\star,\alpha}$; that identification is
not part of this statement.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 6.

articles.title: The square-splitting totient function
articles.statement:
Let $A(n)$ be the set of square-splitting divisors
of $n$, and let $\varphi_\star$ be any integer-valued arithmetic function with
$\sum_{d \in A(n)} \varphi_\star(d) = n$ for every $n \ge 1$. Then $\varphi_\star$ is
multiplicative and $\varphi_\star(1) = 1$. For every prime $p$, $\varphi_\star(p) = p - 1$, and
for every $b \ge 1$, $\varphi_\star(p^{2b}) = (p^2 - 1)\,p^{2b-2}$ and
$\varphi_\star(p^{2b+1}) = (p - 1)(p^2 - 1)\,p^{2b-2}$. Moreover, for every $n \ge 1$,

$$\varphi_\star(n) = \varphi(u(n))\,v(n)^2 \prod_{p \mid v(n)} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^2}\right),$$

where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function, $u(n)$ is the product of the primes dividing $n$ to
an odd power and $v(n)$ is the positive integer with $n = u(n)\,v(n)^2$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Average order of the square-splitting totient function
articles.statement:
Let $A(n)$ be the set of
square-splitting divisors of $n$, and let $\varphi_\star$ be any integer-valued arithmetic function
with $\sum_{d \in A(n)} \varphi_\star(d) = n$ for every $n \ge 1$. Then the product
$M = \prod_p \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^2} + \frac{(p-1)^2}{p^5}\right)$ converges absolutely, that is,
$\sum_p \left|\frac{(p-1)^2}{p^5} - \frac{1}{p^2}\right| < \infty$, and for every
$0 < \varepsilon < 1/2$,

$$\sum_{1 \le n \le x} \varphi_\star(n) = \frac{M}{2}\,x^2 + O(x^{1+\varepsilon})
\quad (x \to \infty).$$

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Square-splitting decomposition
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ne 0$ with prime
factorization $n = \prod_p p^{e_p}$, we have $n = u(n)\,v(n)^2$, where
$u(n) = \prod_p p^{e_p \bmod 2}$ and $v(n) = \prod_p p^{\lfloor e_p/2 \rfloor}$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2.

articles.title: Squarefree part of one
articles.statement:
We have $u(1) = 1$, where $u(n)$ is the product of the primes
dividing $n$ to an odd power.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2.

articles.title: Squarefree part
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n \ge 1$ with prime factorization
$n = \prod_p p^{e_p}$, its squarefree part is $u(n) = \prod_p p^{e_p \bmod 2}$, the product of the
primes dividing $n$ to an odd power. By convention $u(0) = 1$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2 (`n = u(n) v(n)²`, Theorems 2 and 3).

articles.title: The square-root part of $1$ is $1$
articles.statement:
We have $v(1) = 1$, where for $n \ge 1$ the
square-root part $v(n)$ is the product of $p^{\lfloor e/2 \rfloor}$ over the prime powers $p^e$
exactly dividing $n$.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2.

articles.title: The square-root part of a natural number
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$ with prime factorization
$n = \prod_p p^{e_p}$, the square-root part of $n$ is $v(n) = \prod_p p^{\lfloor e_p/2 \rfloor}$;
by convention $v(0) = 1$. For $n \ge 1$, $v(n)^2$ is the largest square dividing $n$, and
$n = u(n)\, v(n)^2$ where $u(n) = n / v(n)^2$ is squarefree.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Section 2.

articles.title: Partial-sum asymptotics for a Riemann zeta quotient times a Dirichlet series
articles.statement:
Let
$f, g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and let $\sigma_0 < 1/2$ be a real number. Suppose that the
Dirichlet series $G(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} g(n) n^{-s}$ converges absolutely for
$\operatorname{Re} s > \sigma_0$, that $G(1) \ne 0$, and that for every complex $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ the Dirichlet series $F(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} f(n) n^{-s}$ converges
absolutely and $F(s) = \zeta(s)^2 G(s) / \zeta(2s)$, where $\zeta$ is the Riemann zeta
function. Then, as the real number $x$ tends to infinity,

$$
\sum_{1 \le n \le x} f(n) = \frac{G(1)}{\zeta(2)}\, x \log x +
\frac{G(1)}{\zeta(2)} \left(2\gamma - 1 + \frac{G'(1)}{G(1)} -
\frac{2\zeta'(2)}{\zeta(2)}\right) x + O\big(x^{1/2} (\log x)^3\big),
$$

where $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant and $G'$, $\zeta'$ are complex derivatives.

The hypothesis $G(1) \ne 0$ is added so that the quotient $G'(1)/G(1)$ is meaningful.

## Sources

- Champak Talukdar and Helen K. Saikia, *A Square-Splitting A-Convolution of Narkiewicz Type*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A56, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Explicit bounds for the summatory function of $\mu(n)/n$
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be the Möbius function.
For every real $x \ge 33$,

$$\Bigl| \sum_{1 \le n \le x} \frac{\mu(n)}{n} \Bigr| < \frac{0.19}{\log x},$$

and for every real $x > 1$,

$$\Bigl| \sum_{1 \le n \le x} \frac{\mu(n)}{n} \Bigr| < \frac{546}{(\log x)^2}.$$

These bounds improve the estimates $0.2185/\log x$ and $726/(\log x)^2$ of the source's
equation (e4).

## Sources

- Olivier Bordellès, "Some Explicit Estimates for the Möbius Function," Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.11.1, Theorem, items (a) and (b), lines 118–127, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Bordelles2/bordelles21.tex

articles.title: Asymptotic count of $k$-tuples with at least $r$ coprime pairs
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and
$r \ge 1$. For a set $E$ of pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $A_E$ be the coprimality
density of the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set $E$, and put

$$C'_{k,r} = \sum_{j=r}^{k(k-1)/2} (-1)^{j-r} \binom{j-1}{r-1} \sum_{|E| = j} A_E,$$

where the inner sum runs over all sets $E$ of exactly $j$ such pairs. Then there is a real
constant $C$ such that for every integer $N \ge 2$, the number of tuples
$(n_1, \dots, n_k) \in \{1, \dots, N\}^k$ with $\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for at least $r$ pairs
$a < b$ differs from $C'_{k,r} N^k$ by at most $C N^{k-1} (\log N)^{k-1}$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-11`).

articles.title: Inclusion–exclusion for at least $r$ coprime pairs
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $r \ge 1$, and let
$n = (n_1, \dots, n_k)$ be a tuple of natural numbers (zero allowed). Let $\beta'_r(n)$ be $1$ if
$\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for at least $r$ pairs $a < b$, and $0$ otherwise. For a set $E$ of pairs
$(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $\delta_E(n)$ be $1$ if $\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for every
$(a, b) \in E$, and $0$ otherwise. Then

$$\beta'_r(n) = \sum_{j=r}^{k(k-1)/2} (-1)^{j-r} \binom{j-1}{r-1} \sum_{|E| = j} \delta_E(n),$$

where the inner sum runs over all sets $E$ of exactly $j$ such pairs.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Lemma 6 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-lem-6`).

articles.title: The coprimality density of the empty graph is $1$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the
coprimality density of the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with no edges equals $1$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 1, display (A_G_version).

articles.title: Hu's independent-set formula for the coprimality density
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number, let
$E$ be a set of pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $G$ be the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$
with edge set $E$, and let $A_G$ be its coprimality density. For $0 \le m \le k$, let $i_m(G)$ be
the number of independent sets of $G$ of size $m$, that is, of sets $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$
with $|S| = m$ such that no edge of $E$ has both endpoints in $S$. Then

$$A_G = \prod_p \sum_{m=0}^{k} \frac{i_m(G)}{p^m} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^{k-m},$$

the product running over all primes $p$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Prime-power Euler product for the coprimality density
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let $E$ be a set of
pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $G$ be the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set
$E$, and let $A_G$ be its coprimality density. For natural numbers $n_1, \dots, n_k$ let
$\delta_G(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ be $1$ if $\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for every $(a, b) \in E$, and $0$
otherwise. Then

$$A_G = \prod_p \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^k \sum_{\nu \in \mathbb{N}^k}
\frac{\delta_G(p^{\nu_1}, \dots, p^{\nu_k})}{p^{\nu_1 + \dots + \nu_k}},$$

the product running over all primes $p$ and the sum over all $k$-tuples $\nu$ of natural numbers
(zero allowed).

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-9`).

articles.title: Möbius-convolution series for the coprimality density
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let $E$ be a set of
pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $G$ be the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set
$E$, and let $A_G$ be its coprimality density. Let $\delta_G(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ be $1$ if
$\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for every $(a, b) \in E$, and $0$ otherwise, and for a tuple
$n = (n_1, \dots, n_k)$ of positive integers let

$$(\mu * \delta_G)(n) = \sum_{d_1 \mid n_1, \dots, d_k \mid n_k}
\mu(d_1) \cdots \mu(d_k) \, \delta_G(n_1/d_1, \dots, n_k/d_k),$$

the sum running over positive divisors $d_i$ of $n_i$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function. Then

$$A_G = \sum_{n_1, \dots, n_k \ge 1} \frac{(\mu * \delta_G)(n)}{n_1 \cdots n_k}.$$

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-9`).

articles.title: Vertex-cover Euler product for the coprimality density
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let $E$ be a set of
pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $G$ be the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set
$E$, and let $A_G$ be its coprimality density. Let $J \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$ be a vertex cover
of $G$, that is, every edge of $E$ has an endpoint in $J$. For $L \subseteq J$ let $N(L)$ be the
set of vertices adjacent to some vertex of $L$. Then

$$A_G = \prod_p \sum_{L} \left(\frac{1}{p}\right)^{|L|}
\left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^{|J \setminus L| + |N(L) \setminus J|},$$

where the product runs over all primes $p$ and the sum over all independent sets $L \subseteq J$
of $G$, that is, subsets of $J$ such that no edge of $E$ has both endpoints in $L$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-9`).

articles.title: Coprimality density of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number and let $E$ be a set of ordered
pairs $(a, b)$ of vertices in $\{1, \dots, k\}$, the edge set of a graph $G$. For $F \subseteq E$
let $v(F)$ be the number of distinct vertices that occur in some pair of $F$. The coprimality
density of $G$ is the real number

$$A_G = \prod_p \sum_{F \subseteq E} \frac{(-1)^{|F|}}{p^{v(F)}},$$

the product running over all primes $p$.

When every edge $(a, b)$ has $a < b$, this is the Arias de Reyna–Heyman form of the asymptotic
density of the $k$-tuples $(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ of positive integers with $\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for
every edge $(a, b)$ of $G$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 1, display (A_G_version).

articles.title: Dirichlet series of the coprimality indicator
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let $E$ be a set of pairs
$(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $G$ be the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set $E$, and
let $J$ be a vertex cover of $G$, that is, every edge of $E$ has an endpoint in $J$. Let
$\delta_G(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ be $1$ if $\gcd(n_a, n_b) = 1$ for every $(a, b) \in E$, and $0$
otherwise. For $L \subseteq J$ let $N(L)$ be the set of vertices adjacent to some vertex of $L$.
Then for all complex numbers $s_1, \dots, s_k$ with $\operatorname{Re} s_i > 1$ for every $i$,

$$\sum_{n_1, \dots, n_k \ge 1} \frac{\delta_G(n_1, \dots, n_k)}{n_1^{s_1} \cdots n_k^{s_k}} =
\zeta(s_1) \cdots \zeta(s_k) \prod_p \sum_{L} \prod_{\ell \in L} p^{-s_\ell}
\prod_{i \in (J \setminus L) \cup (N(L) \setminus J)} \left(1 - p^{-s_i}\right),$$

where $\zeta$ is the Riemann zeta function, the product runs over all primes $p$, and the sum over
all independent sets $L \subseteq J$ of $G$, that is, subsets of $J$ such that no edge of $E$ has
both endpoints in $L$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 7 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-7`).

articles.title: Absolute convergence of the vertex-cover Euler product
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, let $E$ be a set of
pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a < b \le k$, let $G$ be the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set
$E$, and let $J$ be a vertex cover of $G$, that is, every edge of $E$ has an endpoint in $J$. For
$L \subseteq J$ let $N(L)$ be the set of vertices adjacent to some vertex of $L$. For complex
numbers $s = (s_1, \dots, s_k)$ and a prime $p$ put

$$D'_{G,p}(s) = \sum_{L} \prod_{\ell \in L} p^{-s_\ell}
\prod_{i \in (J \setminus L) \cup (N(L) \setminus J)} \left(1 - p^{-s_i}\right),$$

the sum running over all independent sets $L \subseteq J$ of $G$, that is, subsets of $J$ such that
no edge of $E$ has both endpoints in $L$. Suppose that $\operatorname{Re} \sum_{i \in T} s_i > 1$
for every set $T$ of at least two vertices each of which lies on some edge of $E$. Then
$\sum_p |D'_{G,p}(s) - 1| < \infty$, the sum running over all primes $p$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 7 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-7`).

articles.title: Asymptotic count of tuples coprime along the edges of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and let $E$
be a set of pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < j < k$, the edge set of a graph $G$ on the vertices
$0, \dots, k-1$. Let $d_G$ be the maximum degree of $G$, that is, the largest number of pairs in
$E$ that contain a single vertex; let $\delta_G$ be the coprimality indicator and $A_G$ the
coprimality density of $G$. Then there is a real constant $C$ such that for every integer
$N \ge 2$,

$$\Bigl|\sum_{n \in \{1, \dots, N\}^k} \delta_G(n) - A_G N^k\Bigr| \le C N^{k-1} (\log N)^{d_G}.$$

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Coprimality indicator of the empty graph
articles.statement:
Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $G$ be the graph
on $k$ vertices with no edges, and let $\delta_G$ be its coprimality indicator. Then
$\delta_G(n) = 1$ for every $n = (n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}) \in \mathbb{N}^k$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, remark after display (def_delta_G).

articles.title: Multiplicativity of the coprimality indicator
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, k-1$ given by an arbitrary set $E$ of ordered pairs of vertices, with coprimality
indicator $\delta_G$. If $m, n \in \mathbb{N}^k$ satisfy
$\gcd(m_0 m_1 \cdots m_{k-1}, n_0 n_1 \cdots n_{k-1}) = 1$, then
$\delta_G(m_0 n_0, \dots, m_{k-1} n_{k-1}) = \delta_G(m)\, \delta_G(n)$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Lemma 4 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-lem-4`).

articles.title: Coprimality indicator of a single edge: examples
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be the graph on the two
vertices $0, 1$ with the single edge $(0, 1)$, with coprimality indicator $\delta_G$. Then
$\delta_G(2, 3) = 1$ and $\delta_G(2, 4) = 0$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, display (def_delta_G).

articles.title: Coprimality indicator of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a set of ordered pairs $(i, j)$ of indices in
$\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, the edge set of a graph $G$ on these $k$ vertices. For
$n = (n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}) \in \mathbb{N}^k$, the coprimality indicator $\delta_G(n)$ is the
natural number $1$ if $\gcd(n_i, n_j) = 1$ for every $(i, j) \in E$, and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, display (def_delta_G).

articles.title: Number of coprime pairs: examples
articles.statement:
The triple $(2, 3, 4)$ has exactly two coprime pairs
of components, and the triple $(6, 10, 15)$ has none, that is, its components are pairwise
non-coprime.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, displays (def_beta) and (def_beta_exact).

articles.title: Number of coprime pairs
articles.statement:
For $n = (n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}) \in \mathbb{N}^k$, the number of
coprime pairs of $n$ is the number of index pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < j < k$ and
$\gcd(n_i, n_j) = 1$.

In the paper's notation, $\beta_r(n) = 1$ exactly when this count is $r$, $\beta'_r(n) = 1$
exactly when it is at least $r$, and $\beta = \beta_0$.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, displays (def_beta), (def_beta_exact), (def_beta_least).

articles.title: Euler product for the mean value of a multiplicative function of several variables
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N}^k \to \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $f(a_0 b_0, \dots, a_{k-1} b_{k-1}) = f(a) f(b)$
for all $a, b \in \mathbb{N}^k$ with $\gcd(a_0 \cdots a_{k-1}, b_0 \cdots b_{k-1}) = 1$. Let $\mu$
be the Möbius function, and for $n \in \mathbb{N}^k$ with every $n_i \ge 1$ put
$(\mu * f)(n) = \sum_{d} \mu(d_0) \cdots \mu(d_{k-1}) f(n_0/d_0, \dots, n_{k-1}/d_{k-1})$, the
sum over all $d \in \mathbb{N}^k$ with each $d_i$ a positive divisor of $n_i$. For a prime $p$
and $\nu \in \mathbb{N}^k$ write $p^\nu = (p^{\nu_0}, \dots, p^{\nu_{k-1}})$ and
$|\nu| = \nu_0 + \dots + \nu_{k-1}$. Assume that the family $|(\mu * f)(p^\nu)| / p^{|\nu|}$,
indexed by the pairs of a prime $p$ and a nonzero $\nu \in \mathbb{N}^k$, is summable. Then there
is a complex number $M$ such that the averages

$$\frac{1}{x_0 \cdots x_{k-1}} \sum_{1 \le n_i \le x_i} f(n)$$

(the sum over all $n \in \mathbb{N}^k$ with $1 \le n_i \le x_i$ for every $i$) tend to $M$ as
$x \in \mathbb{N}^k$ tends to infinity in every coordinate jointly, and

$$M = \prod_p \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{p}\Bigr)^k \sum_{\nu} \frac{f(p^\nu)}{p^{|\nu|}},$$

the product running over all primes $p$ and the sum over all $\nu \in \mathbb{N}^k$.

The averages are taken over integer $x_i$; this is equivalent to real $x_i$, since only
$\lfloor x_i \rfloor$ enters the sum and $\lfloor x_i \rfloor / x_i \to 1$. The multiplicativity
hypothesis is the source's multivariable one, weaker than coordinatewise multiplicativity.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 3 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-3`).

articles.title: Asymptotic count of tuples with exactly $r$ coprime pairs
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $r \ge 0$.
For a set $E$ of pairs $(a, b)$ with $0 \le a < b < k$, let $A_E$ be the coprimality density of
the graph with edge set $E$, and put

$$C_{k,r} = \sum_{j=r}^{k(k-1)/2} (-1)^{j-r} \binom{j}{r} \sum_{|E| = j} A_E,$$

where the inner sum runs over the $j$-element sets $E$ of such pairs. Then there is a real
constant $C$ such that for every integer $N \ge 2$ the number $T_r(N)$ of tuples
$n \in \{1, \dots, N\}^k$ with exactly $r$ coprime pairs satisfies

$$|T_r(N) - C_{k,r} N^k| \le C N^{k-1} (\log N)^{k-1}.$$

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-thm-11`).

articles.title: Inclusion–exclusion for tuples with exactly $r$ coprime pairs
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, $r \ge 0$
and $n \in \mathbb{N}^k$, and let $\beta_r(n)$ be $1$ if $n$ has exactly $r$ coprime pairs and $0$
otherwise. For a set $E$ of pairs $(a, b)$ with $0 \le a < b < k$, let $\delta_E$ be the
coprimality indicator of the graph with edge set $E$. Then, as integers,

$$\beta_r(n) = \sum_{j=r}^{k(k-1)/2} (-1)^{j-r} \binom{j}{r} \sum_{|E| = j} \delta_E(n),$$

where the inner sum runs over the $j$-element sets $E$ of such pairs.

For $r = 0$ this is the paper's identity for $\beta = \beta_0$, the indicator of pairwise
non-coprime tuples.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Lemma 5 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-lem-5`).

articles.title: The Möbius series for pairwise non-coprime tuples equals the inclusion–exclusion sum
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$. For a $k$-tuple $n = (n_1, \dots, n_k)$ of positive integers let $\beta(n) = 1$
if the number of coprime pairs of $n$ is $0$, that is, if $\gcd(n_i, n_j) \ne 1$ for all
$1 \le i < j \le k$, and $\beta(n) = 0$ otherwise. Let
$(\mu * \beta)(n) = \sum_{d_1 \mid n_1, \dots, d_k \mid n_k} \mu(d_1) \cdots \mu(d_k)\,
\beta(n_1/d_1, \dots, n_k/d_k)$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function. Then

$$
\sum_{n} \frac{(\mu * \beta)(n)}{n_1 \cdots n_k}
  = \sum_{j=0}^{k(k-1)/2} (-1)^j \sum_{|E| = j} A_E,
$$

where the left sum runs over all $k$-tuples $n$ of positive integers, the inner sum on the right
runs over all sets $E$ of $j$ pairs $(i, i')$ with $1 \le i < i' \le k$, and $A_E$ is the
coprimality density of the graph on $\{1, \dots, k\}$ with edge set $E$.

In the source the common value is the density $C_k$ of pairwise non-coprime $k$-tuples. The
asymptotic count of such tuples is the case $r = 0$ of the count of $k$-tuples with exactly $r$
coprime pairs.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Corollary 12 (`jis-2024-24.8.5-cor-12`).

articles.title: A multiplicative function with prescribed prime-power values
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
commutative monoid with zero, let $g : \mathbb{N} \to R$, and let $f$ be a multiplicative
arithmetic function with values in $R$. If $f(p^m) = g(m)$ for every prime $p$ and every
$m \ge 1$, then $f$ is the multiplicative function with prime-power values $g$, that is, the
arithmetic function $n \mapsto \prod_{q \mid n} g(v_q(n))$ for $n \ge 1$, where $q$ runs over the
primes dividing $n$ and $v_q(n)$ is the exponent of $q$ in $n$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3 (a multiplicative function is determined by its values at the prime powers).

articles.title: Gcd with a coprime factor preserves unitary divisors
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be coprime natural
numbers. If $d$ is a unitary divisor of $mn$, then $\gcd(d, m)$ is a unitary divisor of $m$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Complete multiplicativity of $c^{\Omega}$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a monoid with zero and $c \in R$.
Let $c^{\Omega}$ be the arithmetic function $n \mapsto c^{\Omega(n)}$ for $n \ge 1$, where
$\Omega(n)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity. Then $c^{\Omega}$ is
completely multiplicative: for all natural numbers $m$ and $n$, its value at $mn$ is the product
of its values at $m$ and at $n$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Multiplicativity of the function with prescribed prime-power values
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
commutative monoid with zero and $g : \mathbb{N} \to R$. The arithmetic function
$n \mapsto \prod_{q \mid n} g(v_q(n))$ for $n \ge 1$, where $q$ runs over the primes dividing $n$
and $v_q(n)$ is the exponent of $q$ in $n$, is multiplicative.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Multiplicativity of $c^{\Omega}$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a monoid with zero and $c \in R$. The
arithmetic function $n \mapsto c^{\Omega(n)}$ for $n \ge 1$, where $\Omega(n)$ is the number of
prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity, is multiplicative.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: The unitary convolution of multiplicative functions is multiplicative
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
commutative semiring. If $f$ and $g$ are multiplicative arithmetic functions with values in $R$,
then their unitary convolution $f \sqcup g$, given by $(f \sqcup g)(n) = \sum_{d} f(d)\, g(n/d)$
with $d$ running over the unitary divisors of $n$, is multiplicative.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3 (`(𝓜, ⊔)` is a group).

articles.title: Products of unitary divisors of coprime numbers
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be coprime natural
numbers. If $a$ is a unitary divisor of $m$ and $b$ is a unitary divisor of $n$, then $ab$ is a
unitary divisor of $mn$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Value of the function with prescribed prime-power values
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative monoid
with zero, let $g : \mathbb{N} \to R$, and let $n \ne 0$ be a natural number. The multiplicative
function with value $g(m)$ at every prime power $p^m$ with $m \ge 1$ takes the value
$\prod_{q \mid n} g(v_q(n))$ at $n$, where $q$ runs over the primes dividing $n$ and $v_q(n)$ is
the exponent of $q$ in the factorization of $n$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: The function with prescribed prime-power values is $1$ at $1$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
monoid with zero and $g : \mathbb{N} \to R$. The multiplicative function with prime-power values
$g$, given by $n \mapsto \prod_{q \mid n} g(v_q(n))$ for $n \ge 1$ (with $q$ running over the
primes dividing $n$ and $v_q(n)$ the exponent of $q$ in $n$), takes the value $1$ at $n = 1$,
whatever $g(0)$ is.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: The function with prescribed prime-power values at a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
commutative monoid with zero and $g : \mathbb{N} \to R$. For every prime $p$ and every $m \ge 1$,
the multiplicative function with prime-power values $g$, given by
$n \mapsto \prod_{q \mid n} g(v_q(n))$ for $n \ge 1$ (with $q$ running over the primes dividing
$n$ and $v_q(n)$ the exponent of $q$ in $n$), takes the value $g(m)$ at $p^m$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Multiplicative function with prescribed values at prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
monoid with zero and let $g : \mathbb{N} \to R$. This is the arithmetic function $f$ with values
in $R$ given by $f(0) = 0$ and $f(n) = \prod_{p \mid n} g(v_p(n))$ for $n \ge 1$, where the product
runs over the primes $p$ dividing $n$ and $v_p(n)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $n$. It is
multiplicative, it takes the value $g(m)$ at every prime power $p^m$ with $m \ge 1$, and its value
at $1$ is the empty product $1$, so $g(0)$ never enters.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3 (a multiplicative function is determined by its values at the prime powers).

articles.title: Value of $c^{\Omega}$ at a positive integer
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a monoid with zero, let $c \in R$,
and let $c^{\Omega}$ be the arithmetic function with values in $R$ that is $0$ at $0$ and
$c^{\Omega(n)}$ at each $n \ge 1$, where $\Omega(n)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$ counted
with multiplicity. For every natural number $n \ne 0$, its value at $n$ is $c^{\Omega(n)}$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Value of $c^{\Omega}$ at $1$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a monoid with zero, let $c \in R$, and let
$c^{\Omega}$ be the arithmetic function with values in $R$ that is $0$ at $0$ and $c^{\Omega(n)}$ at
each $n \ge 1$, where $\Omega(n)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity.
Its value at $1$ is $1$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Value of $c^{\Omega}$ at prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a monoid with zero, let $c \in R$, and
let $c^{\Omega}$ be the arithmetic function with values in $R$ that is $0$ at $0$ and
$c^{\Omega(n)}$ at each $n \ge 1$, where $\Omega(n)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$ counted
with multiplicity. For every prime $p$ and every natural number $m$, its value at $p^m$ is $c^m$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: The arithmetic function $c^{\Omega}$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a monoid with zero and let $c \in R$. This
is the arithmetic function $c^{\Omega}$ with values in $R$ given by $c^{\Omega}(0) = 0$ and
$c^{\Omega}(n) = c^{\Omega(n)}$ for $n \ge 1$, where $\Omega(n)$ is the number of prime factors of
$n$ counted with multiplicity. It is completely multiplicative.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 2.

articles.title: Unitary convolution as a sum over unitary divisors
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a semiring and let $f$ and
$g$ be arithmetic functions with values in $R$. For every natural number $n$, their unitary
convolution $f \sqcup g$ satisfies $(f \sqcup g)(n) = \sum_{d \parallel n} f(d)\, g(n/d)$, where the
sum runs over the unitary divisors $d$ of $n$: for $n \ge 1$ these are the divisors $d$ of $n$
with $\gcd(d, n/d) = 1$, and for $n = 0$ there are none, so the sum is $0$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Unitary convolution at $1$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a semiring and let $f$ and $g$ be arithmetic
functions with values in $R$. Their unitary convolution $f \sqcup g$, defined by
$(f \sqcup g)(n) = \sum_{d \parallel n} f(d)\, g(n/d)$ over the unitary divisors $d$ of $n$,
satisfies $(f \sqcup g)(1) = f(1)\, g(1)$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Unitary convolution at prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a semiring and let $f$ and $g$ be
arithmetic functions with values in $R$. For every prime $p$ and every natural number $m \ge 1$,
their unitary convolution $f \sqcup g$ satisfies
$(f \sqcup g)(p^m) = f(1)\, g(p^m) + f(p^m)\, g(1)$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Unitary convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a semiring. The unitary convolution of two arithmetic
functions $f$ and $g$ with values in $R$ is the arithmetic function $f \sqcup g$ given by
$(f \sqcup g)(n) = \sum_{d \parallel n} f(d)\, g(n/d)$, where the sum runs over the unitary divisors
$d$ of $n$: for $n \ge 1$ these are the divisors $d$ of $n$ with $\gcd(d, n/d) = 1$, and $0$ has
no unitary divisors. In particular $(f \sqcup g)(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Unitary divisors of a prime power
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$ and every natural number $m$, the
unitary divisors of $p^m$, that is, the divisors $d$ of $p^m$ with $\gcd(d, p^m/d) = 1$, are
exactly $1$ and $p^m$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, *Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.7, Section 1.3.

articles.title: Vaughan's identity in a commutative ring
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\mu$ and
$\Lambda$ be arithmetic functions with values in $R$ (so $\mu(0) = \Lambda(0) = 0$), and let
$L : \mathbb{N} \to R$ be any function. Suppose that for every natural number $m$,
$\sum_{d \mid m} \mu(d)$ is $1$ if $m = 1$ and $0$ otherwise, and
$\Lambda(m) = \sum_{d \mid m} \mu(d) \, L(m/d)$, where both sums run over the $d$ with
$0 \le d \le m$ and $d \mid m$. Then for all natural numbers $U$, $V$ and $n$ with $V < n$,

$$\Lambda(n) = \sum_{b \mid n,\ b \le U} \mu(b) \, L(n/b) -
\sum_{b \mid n,\ b \le U} \ \sum_{c \le V,\ bc \mid n} \mu(b) \, \Lambda(c) +
\sum_{b \mid n,\ b > U} \ \sum_{c > V,\ bc \mid n} \mu(b) \, \Lambda(c),$$

where $b$ and $c$ range over $0, 1, \dots, n$.

When $R = \mathbb{R}$, $\mu$ is the Möbius function, $L = \log$ and $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt
function, the hypotheses hold and this is the classical Vaughan identity.

articles.title: Vaughan's identity
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\mu$ and $\Lambda$ be arithmetic
functions with values in $R$ (so $\mu(0) = \Lambda(0) = 0$), and let $L : \mathbb{N} \to R$ be
any function. Suppose that for every natural number $m$, $\sum_{d \mid m} \mu(d)$ is $1$ if
$m = 1$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\Lambda(m) = \sum_{d \mid m} \mu(d) \, L(m/d)$, where both sums
run over the $d$ with $0 \le d \le m$ and $d \mid m$. Then for all natural numbers $U \ge 1$,
$V \ge 1$ and $n > V$,

$$\Lambda(n) = \sum_{b \mid n,\ b \le U} \mu(b) \, L(n/b) -
\sum_{b \mid n,\ b \le U} \ \sum_{c \le V,\ bc \mid n} \mu(b) \, \Lambda(c) +
\sum_{b \mid n,\ b > U} \ \sum_{c > V,\ bc \mid n} \mu(b) \, \Lambda(c),$$

where $b$ and $c$ range over $0, 1, \dots, n$.

When $R = \mathbb{R}$, $\mu$ is the Möbius function, $L = \log$ and $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt
function, the hypotheses hold and this is the classical Vaughan identity.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaughan%27s_identity It follows from `vaughan_identity_general`; the hypotheses `hU` and `hV` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: The $B_\kappa$-free indicator twisted by the principal character, convolved with $\mu$
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers with $\kappa(p) \ge 1$
for every prime $p$, let $\xi$ be a natural number, let $q_{B_\kappa}$ be the indicator of
$B_\kappa$-free integers and let $\mu$ be the Möbius function. Put $w(d) = q_{B_\kappa}(d)$ if
$\gcd(d, \xi) = 1$ and $w(d) = 0$ otherwise, so that $w = q_{B_\kappa} \chi_\xi$ with $\chi_\xi$
the principal character modulo $\xi$, and let $(w * \mu)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} w(d) \mu(n/d)$, the
sum running over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$ (it is empty for $n = 0$). For $r \ge 1$ with
prime factorization $r = \prod_p p^{e_p}$ write $r^\kappa = \prod_p p^{\kappa(p) e_p}$, and set
$0^\kappa = 1$. Then for every natural number $n$ with $(w * \mu)(n) \ne 0$ there are natural
numbers $\ell$ and $r$ with $\ell \mid \xi$, $\gcd(r, \xi) = 1$ and $n = \ell r^\kappa$. Moreover,
for all natural numbers $\ell$ and $r$ with $\ell \mid \xi$, $\gcd(r, \xi) = 1$ and $r \ge 1$,
$(w * \mu)(\ell r^\kappa) = \mu(\ell) \mu(r)$.

The hypothesis $r \ge 1$ in the evaluation is needed: for $r = 0$ the formula is false. No
positivity of $\xi$ is assumed.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Lemma 6, Equation (23).

articles.title: Asymptotic for the divisor function summed over $B_\kappa$-free integers
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be
a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers and let $K \ge 2$ be the minimum of
$\kappa(p)$ over the primes $p$: $\kappa(p) \ge K$ for every prime $p$, with equality for some
prime. Let $q_{B_\kappa}$ be the indicator of $B_\kappa$-free integers, $\tau(n)$ the number of
positive divisors of $n$, $\gamma$ the Euler–Mascheroni constant and
$\Delta(x) = \sum_{1 \le n \le x} \tau(n) - x \log x - (2\gamma - 1) x$ the Dirichlet divisor
error term, and put

$$C_\kappa = \prod_p \Bigl(1 - \frac{\kappa(p) + 1}{p^{\kappa(p)}} +
\frac{\kappa(p)}{p^{\kappa(p)+1}}\Bigr),$$

the product running over all primes $p$. Then there is a real constant $\beta_\kappa$ such that
$E(x) = \sum_{1 \le n \le x} q_{B_\kappa}(n) \tau(n) - C_\kappa x \log x - \beta_\kappa x$
satisfies the following as $x \to \infty$. If $K \le 3$, then $E(x) = O(x^{1/K + \varepsilon})$
for every $\varepsilon > 0$. If $K \ge 4$, then for every real $\eta \ge 1/4$ with
$\Delta(x) = O(x^\eta)$, $E(x) = O(x^{\eta + \varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Asymptotic for the divisor function summed over $B_\kappa$-free integers in a progression
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers and let $K$ be the
minimum of $\kappa(p)$ over the primes $p$: $\kappa(p) \ge K$ for every prime $p$, with equality
for some prime. Assume $K \ge 2$ and $K \ne 3$. Let $a$ and $\xi$ be natural numbers with
$a < \xi$ and $\gcd(a, \xi) = 1$. Let $q_{B_\kappa}$ be the indicator of $B_\kappa$-free
integers, $\tau(n)$ the number of positive divisors of $n$ and $\varphi$ Euler's totient
function, and put

$$C_{\kappa,\xi} = \prod_{p \nmid \xi} \Bigl(1 - \frac{\kappa(p) + 1}{p^{\kappa(p)}} +
\frac{\kappa(p)}{p^{\kappa(p)+1}}\Bigr),$$

the product running over the primes $p$ that do not divide $\xi$. Let $\eta = 1/2$ if $K = 2$
and $\eta = 1/3$ if $K \ge 4$. Then there is a real constant $\tilde c$ such that for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, as $x \to \infty$,

$$\sum_{\substack{1 \le n \le x \\ n \equiv a \pmod{\xi}}} q_{B_\kappa}(n) \tau(n) =
\frac{\varphi(\xi)}{\xi^2} C_{\kappa,\xi} \, x \log x + \tilde c x + O(x^{\eta + \varepsilon}).$$

The case $K = 3$ is not covered by the paper's statement and is excluded.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Corollary 3, Equation (15).

articles.title: Values of the $B_\kappa$-free indicator
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a function from the natural
numbers to the natural numbers. For every natural number $n$, the indicator $q_{B_\kappa}$ of
$B_\kappa$-free integers satisfies $q_{B_\kappa}(n) = 1$ if $n \ne 0$ and no $p^{\kappa(p)}$ with
$p$ prime divides $n$, and $q_{B_\kappa}(n) = 0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Equations (11), (12).

articles.title: The $B_\kappa$-free indicator convolved with the Möbius function
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a
function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers with $\kappa(p) \ge 1$ for every prime
$p$, let $q_{B_\kappa}$ be the indicator of $B_\kappa$-free integers, let $\mu$ be the Möbius
function and let $*$ denote Dirichlet convolution. Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number with prime
factorization $n = \prod_p p^{e_p}$. If $\kappa(p)$ divides $e_p$ for every prime $p$, then
$(q_{B_\kappa} * \mu)(n) = \mu(n^{1/\kappa})$, where $n^{1/\kappa} = \prod_p p^{e_p/\kappa(p)}$;
otherwise $(q_{B_\kappa} * \mu)(n) = 0$.

The source indexes the exponents by the position of the prime ($\kappa_i$ for the $i$-th prime
$p_i$) and requires $b_i = p_i^{\kappa_i} > 1$, which is the hypothesis $\kappa(p) \ge 1$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Lemma 5, Equation (22).

articles.title: The integer $1$ is $B_\kappa$-free
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a function from the natural numbers
to the natural numbers with $\kappa(p) \ge 1$ for every prime $p$. Then the indicator
$q_{B_\kappa}$ of $B_\kappa$-free integers satisfies $q_{B_\kappa}(1) = 1$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Equation (12).

articles.title: The prime power $p^{\kappa(p)}$ is not $B_\kappa$-free
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a function from
the natural numbers to the natural numbers and let $p$ be a prime. Then the indicator
$q_{B_\kappa}$ of $B_\kappa$-free integers satisfies $q_{B_\kappa}(p^{\kappa(p)}) = 0$.

No positivity of $\kappa(p)$ is assumed; for $\kappa(p) = 0$ the statement is
$q_{B_\kappa}(1) = 0$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Equation (12).

articles.title: Indicator of $B_\kappa$-free integers
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a function from the natural numbers
to the natural numbers (only its values $\kappa(p)$ at primes $p$ matter) and let $B_\kappa$ be
the set of prime powers $p^{\kappa(p)}$. A natural number $n$ is $B_\kappa$-free if $n \ge 1$ and
no $p^{\kappa(p)}$ with $p$ prime divides $n$. The indicator $q_{B_\kappa}$ is the integer-valued
arithmetic function with $q_{B_\kappa}(n) = 1$ if $n$ is $B_\kappa$-free and
$q_{B_\kappa}(n) = 0$ otherwise.

The paper indexes the exponents by the position of the prime ($b_i = p_i^{\kappa_i}$); here
$\kappa$ is indexed by the prime itself. For constant $\kappa = k$ this is the indicator $q_k$ of
$k$-free integers.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Equations (2), (11), (12).

articles.title: Gcd expansion of a convolution of completely multiplicative functions at a product
articles.statement:
Let
$u$ and $v$ be complex-valued completely multiplicative arithmetic functions, meaning
$u(mn) = u(m) u(n)$ and $v(mn) = v(m) v(n)$ for all natural numbers $m$ and $n$. Let $u * v$ be
their Dirichlet convolution and $\mu$ the Möbius function. Then for all natural numbers $r$ and
$s$,

$$(u * v)(rs) = \sum_{m \mid \gcd(r, s)} \mu(m) u(m) v(m) (u * v)(r/m) (u * v)(s/m),$$

the sum running over the positive divisors $m$ of $\gcd(r, s)$ (it is empty when $r = s = 0$).

The paper takes $r, s$ positive; the identity also holds (both sides vanish) when $r$ or $s$
is $0$, so no positivity hypothesis is imposed.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Lemma 2, Equation (17).

articles.title: Asymptotic for the divisor function summed over $k$-free integers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a
natural number, let $q_k$ be the indicator of $k$-free integers (the indicator of
$B_\kappa$-free integers for the constant function $\kappa = k$), let $\tau(n)$ be the number of
positive divisors of $n$, let $\gamma$ be the Euler–Mascheroni constant, let
$\Delta(x) = \sum_{1 \le n \le x} \tau(n) - x \log x - (2\gamma - 1) x$ be the Dirichlet divisor
error term, and put

$$c_k = \prod_p \Bigl(1 - \frac{k + 1}{p^k} + \frac{k}{p^{k+1}}\Bigr),$$

the product running over all primes $p$. Then there is a real constant $\beta_k$ such that
$E(x) = \sum_{1 \le n \le x} q_k(n) \tau(n) - c_k x \log x - \beta_k x$ satisfies the following
as $x \to \infty$. If $k \le 3$, then $E(x) = O(x^{1/k + \varepsilon})$ for every
$\varepsilon > 0$. If $k \ge 4$, then for every real $\eta \ge 1/4$ with $\Delta(x) = O(x^\eta)$,
$E(x) = O(x^{\eta + \varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Sums of a Dirichlet convolution over multiples of $r$
articles.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be completely
multiplicative arithmetic functions with complex values, let $u * v$ be their Dirichlet
convolution, let $\mu$ be the Möbius function, and for real $y$ put
$D(y) = \sum_{1 \le j \le y} (u * v)(j)$. Then for every natural number $r$ and every real $x$,

$$
\sum_{1 \le j \le x/r} (u * v)(rj) =
\sum_{d \mid r} u(d)\, v(r/d) \sum_{m \mid d} \mu(m)\, v(m)\, D\left(\frac{x}{mr}\right),
$$

where $d$ and $m$ run over positive divisors and $x/0 = 0$, so both sides vanish for $r = 0$.

Both sides also vanish for $x < 1$; the source assumes $r \ge 1$ and $x \ge 1$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Lemma 3, Equation (20).

articles.title: Möbius expansion of weighted sums of a Dirichlet convolution
articles.statement:
Let $w$, $u$ and $v$ be
arithmetic functions with complex values, let $*$ denote Dirichlet convolution, let $\mu$ be the
Möbius function and put $g = w * \mu$. Then for every real $x$,

$$
\sum_{1 \le j \le x} w(j)\, (u * v)(j) =
\sum_{1 \le r \le x} g(r) \sum_{1 \le j \le x/r} (u * v)(rj),
$$

where $j$ and $r$ run over positive integers.

Both sides vanish for $x < 1$; the source assumes $x \ge 1$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Product formula for homogeneous sums of powers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let
$a, b \in R$ and let $\tau, \xi$ be natural numbers. Then

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{\tau+\xi} a^j b^{\tau+\xi-j} =
\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\tau} a^j b^{\tau-j}\right) \left(\sum_{i=0}^{\xi} a^i b^{\xi-i}\right) -
ab \left(\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1} a^j b^{\tau-1-j}\right)
\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\xi-1} a^i b^{\xi-1-i}\right),
$$

where a sum with upper limit $-1$ is zero.

In the source, $a$ and $b$ are the values $u(n)$ and $v(n)$ of complex arithmetic functions.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Lemma 1, Equation (16).

articles.title: Weighted summation of Dirichlet convolutions
articles.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be completely
multiplicative arithmetic functions with complex values, let $w$ be any arithmetic function with
complex values, let $*$ denote Dirichlet convolution, let $\mu$ be the Möbius function, put
$g = w * \mu$, and for real $y$ put $D(y) = \sum_{1 \le j \le y} (u * v)(j)$. Then for every
real $x$,

$$
\sum_{1 \le j \le x} w(j)\, (u * v)(j) =
\sum_{1 \le r \le x} g(r) \sum_{d \mid r} u(d)\, v(r/d) \sum_{m \mid d} \mu(m)\, v(m)\,
D\left(\frac{x}{mr}\right),
$$

where $r$, $d$ and $m$ run over positive integers.

Both sides vanish for $x < 1$; the source assumes $x \ge 1$.

## Sources

- André Pierro de Camargo, *Weighted Summation of Dirichlet Convolutions and Applications to Some Divisor Problems over k-Free and B-Free Integers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A75, Theorem 1, Equation (8).

articles.title: Euler product for mean values of coordinatewise multiplicative functions
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural
number, write $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$, and let $f \colon \mathbb{N}^k \to \mathbb{C}$
satisfy $f(a_1 b_1, \dots, a_k b_k) = f(a) f(b)$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{N}^k$ with
$\gcd(a_i, b_i) = 1$ for every $i$. For a prime $p$ and $\nu = (\nu_1, \dots, \nu_k) \in
\mathbb{N}^k$ write $p^\nu = (p^{\nu_1}, \dots, p^{\nu_k})$, $|\nu| = \nu_1 + \dots + \nu_k$ and

$$
(\mu * f)(p^\nu) = \sum_{d_1 \mid p^{\nu_1}, \dots, d_k \mid p^{\nu_k}}
\mu(d_1) \cdots \mu(d_k) \, f(p^{\nu_1} / d_1, \dots, p^{\nu_k} / d_k),
$$

where $\mu$ is the Möbius function and each $d_i$ runs over the positive divisors of $p^{\nu_i}$.
Suppose that the family $|(\mu * f)(p^\nu)| / p^{|\nu|}$, indexed by the pairs $(p, \nu)$ of a
prime $p$ and a nonzero $\nu \in \mathbb{N}^k$, is summable. Then there is a complex number $M$
such that

$$
\frac{1}{N^k} \sum_{n \in \{1, \dots, N\}^k} f(n) \to M \quad (N \to \infty)
$$

and

$$
M = \prod_p \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{p}\Bigr)^k \sum_{\nu \in \mathbb{N}^k} \frac{f(p^\nu)}{p^{|\nu|}},
$$

where the product runs over all primes and the product and the inner sums are unconditional (an
unconditional sum that does not converge is read as $0$, a product as $1$).

This is the Wintner–Ushiroya theorem (Ushiroya, Theorem 4; Tóth, Proposition 19) under a
stronger multiplicativity hypothesis: the source asks for $f(a_1 b_1, \dots, a_k b_k) = f(a) f(b)$
only when $\gcd(a_1 \cdots a_k, b_1 \cdots b_k) = 1$. The hypothesis used here forces $f$ to be a
product of one-variable multiplicative functions of the coordinates, and the proof reduces to the
one-variable Wintner theorem in each coordinate. The averages over the cubes $\{1, \dots, N\}^k$
are the diagonal of the source's multi-parameter limit, so they converge to the same value.

## Sources

- László Tóth, "On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components," Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem (unlabeled; multiplicative-function form), equation, lines 314–326, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL27/Toth/toth27.tex

articles.title: Wintner's mean-value theorem in several variables
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and let $f$ be a
complex-valued function on $k$-tuples of natural numbers. For a $k$-tuple
$n = (n_1, \dots, n_k)$ of positive integers put

$$
(\mu * f)(n) = \sum_{d_1 \mid n_1, \dots, d_k \mid n_k}
\mu(d_1) \cdots \mu(d_k) \, f(n_1/d_1, \dots, n_k/d_k),
$$

where $\mu$ is the Möbius function and the $d_i$ run over positive divisors. If the series

$$\sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^k} \frac{|(\mu * f)(m)|}{m_1 \cdots m_k}$$

converges, then

$$
\frac{1}{x_1 \cdots x_k} \sum_{n_1 = 1}^{x_1} \cdots \sum_{n_k = 1}^{x_k} f(n_1, \dots, n_k)
\to \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^k} \frac{(\mu * f)(m)}{m_1 \cdots m_k}
$$

as the integers $x_1, \dots, x_k$ all tend to infinity.

## Sources

- László Tóth, "On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components," Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, Theorem `Th_Wintner_gen`, lines 300–311, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL27/Toth/toth27.tex>. Proved by H. Ushiroya (2012) as a generalization of Wintner's classical one-variable theorem.

articles.title: Wintner's mean-value theorem
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a complex-valued arithmetic function, let $\mu$
be the Möbius function, and let $\mu * f$ be their Dirichlet convolution,
$(\mu * f)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d) f(n/d)$. If the series $\sum_{n \ge 1} |(\mu * f)(n)|/n$
converges, then

$$\frac{1}{x} \sum_{n=1}^{x} f(n) \to \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{(\mu * f)(n)}{n}$$

as the integer $x$ tends to infinity.

No multiplicativity, Euler product, quantitative error term, or alternating mean is assumed or
concluded.

## Sources

- László Tóth, *On the Asymptotic Density of k-tuples of Positive Integers with Pairwise Non-Coprime Components*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.5, mean-value definition and Theorem `Th_Wintner_gen`, lines 292–310 (the `k = 1` case identified at lines 297–298 as Wintner's classical theorem; the source theorem itself is Ushiroya's multivariable generalization), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL27/Toth/toth27.tex>.

articles.title: Biunitary triperfect numbers exactly divisible by $2^4$ and by $3^3$ or $3^4$
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be
a biunitary triperfect number, that is, a positive integer with $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where
$\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor sum. If the exact power of $2$ dividing $N$ is $2^4$ and the
exact power of $3$ dividing $N$ is $3^3$ or $3^4$, then $N = 2160$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 14 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-14`).

articles.title: Prime factors of the biunitary divisor sum of $41^g$
articles.statement:
For every integer $g \ge 1$, the
biunitary divisor sum $\sigma^{**}(41^g)$ has a prime factor $q$ with $q \notin \{2, 3, 5, 13\}$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 8 (V) (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-8`).

articles.title: Prime factors at least $5$ of biunitary divisor sums of prime powers
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$
and every integer $g \ge 2$ with $(p, g) \ne (2, 4)$, the biunitary divisor sum $\sigma^{**}(p^g)$
has a prime factor $q \ge 5$.

The excluded case is a genuine exception: $\sigma^{**}(2^4) = 1 + 2 + 8 + 16 = 27 = 3^3$. It is
not in the printed statement; the paper's proof applies Lemma 2.4 to $p^u + 1$ with
$g = 2u - 1 - \varepsilon$, and $(p, u) = (2, 3)$ is that lemma's exception.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 8 (I) (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-8`).

articles.title: Prime factors at least $7$ of biunitary divisor sums of odd prime powers
articles.statement:
For every odd
prime $p$ and every integer $g \ge 4$, the biunitary divisor sum $\sigma^{**}(p^g)$ has a prime
factor $q \ge 7$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 8 (II) (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-8`).

articles.title: Primitive prime factors of $a^n + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $a \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$ be integers with
$(a, n) \ne (2, 3)$, and if $n = 1$ suppose that $a + 1$ is not a power of $2$. Then $a^n + 1$
has a primitive prime factor $p$, that is, a prime $p$ that divides $a^n + 1$ but divides no
$a^m + 1$ with $1 \le m < n$, such that $p \equiv 1 \pmod{2n}$.

The second exception is not in the printed statement: for $a = 3$, $n = 1$ the only prime factor
of $3 + 1 = 4$ is $2 \not\equiv 1 \pmod 2$; the paper's proof applies Lemma 2.3 to
$a^{2n} - 1$, whose exceptions include exactly this case.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 5 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-5`).

articles.title: Two prime factors of the biunitary divisor sum of $13^g$
articles.statement:
For every integer $g \ge 2$, the
biunitary divisor sum $\sigma^{**}(13^g)$ has two distinct prime factors $q_1$ and $q_2$, neither
of which lies in $\{2, 3, 41, 547\}$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 8 (IV) (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-8`).

articles.title: No biunitary triperfect number divisible by $27$ is exactly divisible by $2^5$
articles.statement:
Let $N$
be a biunitary triperfect number, that is, a positive integer with $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where
$\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor sum. If $3^3$ divides $N$, then the exact power of $2$
dividing $N$ is not $2^5$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 10 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-10`).

articles.title: No biunitary triperfect number divisible by $27$ is exactly divisible by $2^6$
articles.statement:
Let $N$
be a biunitary triperfect number, that is, a positive integer with $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where
$\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor sum. If $3^3$ divides $N$, then the exact power of $2$
dividing $N$ is not $2^6$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 11 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-11`).

articles.title: Biunitary triperfect numbers divisible by $27$ are divisible by $16$
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a
biunitary triperfect number, that is, a positive integer with $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where
$\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor sum. If $3^3$ divides $N$, then $2^4$ divides $N$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 9 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-9`).

articles.title: Biunitary triperfect numbers exactly divisible by $2^4$ and divisible by $3^5$ are prime to $5$
articles.statement:
**Biunitary triperfect numbers exactly divisible by $2^4$ and divisible by $3^5$ are prime
to $5$.** Let $N$ be a biunitary triperfect number, that is, a positive integer with
$\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where $\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor sum. If the exact power of $2$
dividing $N$ is $2^4$ and $3^5$ divides $N$, then $5$ does not divide $N$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 15 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-15`).

articles.title: No biunitary triperfect number has $3$-exponent $4$ and $2$-exponent at least $7$
articles.statement:
Let
$N$ be a positive integer with $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where $\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor
sum, and let $e$ and $f$ be the exponents of $2$ and $3$ in the prime factorization of $N$. If
$f \ge 3$, then $e \ge 7$ and $f = 4$ do not both hold.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 13 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-13`).

articles.title: No biunitary triperfect number has $3$-exponent $3$ and $2$-exponent at least $7$
articles.statement:
Let
$N$ be a positive integer with $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$, where $\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor
sum, and let $e$ and $f$ be the exponents of $2$ and $3$ in the prime factorization of $N$. If
$f \ge 3$, then $e \ge 7$ and $f = 3$ do not both hold.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 12 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-12`).

articles.title: Parity of the biunitary divisor sum
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$, the biunitary divisor
sum $\sigma^{**}(n)$ is odd if and only if $n = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$ (so $n = 1$ is
included).

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 2 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-2`).

articles.title: Primitive prime divisors of $a^n - 1$ are $1$ modulo $n$
articles.statement:
Let $a \ge 2$ and $n \ge 2$ be
natural numbers, and let $p$ be a primitive prime divisor of the integer sequence $m \mapsto
a^m - 1$ at index $n$, that is, a prime that divides $a^n - 1$ and divides no $a^m - 1$ with
$1 \le m < n$. Then $p \equiv 1 \pmod n$.

This is the congruence half of Bang's theorem. Its existence half (such a $p$ exists unless
$(a, n) = (2, 6)$, or $n = 2$ and $a + 1$ is a power of $2$) is the case $b = 1$ of the
Bang–Zsigmondy theorem.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 4 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-4`), quoting Bang.

articles.title: The only biunitary triperfect number divisible by $27$ is $2160$
articles.statement:
For every positive
integer $N$ divisible by $27$, $\sigma^{**}(N) = 3N$ if and only if $N = 2160$, where
$\sigma^{**}$ is the biunitary divisor sum.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Comparison bounds for the biunitary divisor sum of a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and
let $m \ge 1$ and $e \ge 2m - 1$ be natural numbers, and write $\sigma^{**}$ for the biunitary
divisor sum. Then, in $\mathbb{Q}$,
$\sigma^{**}(p^e)/p^e \ge \sigma^{**}(p^{2m})/p^{2m}$, and if moreover $e \ne 2m$, then
$\sigma^{**}(p^e)/p^e \ge \sum_{i=0}^{m} 1/p^i$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 3 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-3`).

articles.title: Lower bounds for the biunitary divisor sum of a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and
$e \ge 1$, and write $\sigma^{**}$ for the biunitary divisor sum. Then, in $\mathbb{Q}$,
$\sigma^{**}(p^e)/p^e \ge 1 + 1/p^2$; if moreover $e \ne 2$, then
$\sigma^{**}(p^e)/p^e \ge 1 + 1/p$; and if $e \ge 3$, then
$\sigma^{**}(p^e)/p^e \ge (1 + 1/p)(1 + 1/p^3)$.

## Sources

- Tomohiro Yamada, *Determining all Biunitary Triperfect Numbers of a Certain Form*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.5, Lemma 3 (`jis-2025-25.4.5-lem-3`).

articles.title: Prime factors of the biunitary divisor sum of a power of $3$
Prime factors of the biunitary divisor sum of a power of $2$
articles.statement:
Let $e$, $s$ and $\delta$
be natural numbers with $\delta \in \{0, 1\}$ and $e = 2s - 1 - \delta$, suppose $e \ge 6$ and
$e \notin \{8, 12\}$, and write $\sigma^{**}$ for the biunitary divisor sum. Then at least one of
the following holds:
(a) $\delta = 0$ and $\sigma^{**}(2^e)$ has two distinct prime factors $q_1, q_2$ with
$5 < q_i \le 2^s - 1$ for $i = 1, 2$;
(b) $5 \mid \sigma^{**}(2^e)$;
(c) $\sigma^{**}(2^e)$ has two distinct prime factors $q_1, q_2$ such that each $q_i$ equals
$2^{s-1} - 1$ or $2^s + 1$ or satisfies $5 < q_i$ and $q_i^2 \le 2^s - 3$, and if some $q_i$
