for an integer $k$. For a list $t = (t_1, \dots, t_s)$ of real numbers, let $L(t; r)$ and $U(t; r)$
be the lower and upper Lehmer bounds: the infimum and the supremum in $\mathbb{R}$ of
$\kappa_r(t_1, \dots, t_s, u_{s+1}, \dots, u_r)$ over all real numbers $u_{s+1}, \dots, u_r \ge 2$
such that $t_1, \dots, t_s, u_{s+1}, \dots, u_r$ is nondecreasing, where
$\kappa_r(y_1, \dots, y_r) = (y_1 \cdots y_r - 1) / ((y_1 - 1) \cdots (y_r - 1))$. Then for every
$s$ with $0 \le s \le r$ we have $L(x_1, \dots, x_s; r) \le k \le U(x_1, \dots, x_s; r)$, and
$L(x_1, \dots, x_s; r) = k$ if and only if $s = r$. Moreover $1 < k \le 2^r - 1$.

## Sources

- Grant Molnar and Guntas Singh, *Spoof Lehmer Factorizations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A33, Lemma 3.

articles.title: The exponent-one factorization on the bases 3 and 3
articles.statement:
The factorization with all exponents
one on the multiset of bases consisting of two copies of $3$ is the multiset consisting of two
copies of the pair $(3, 1)$, that is, $3 \cdot 3 = 3^1 \cdot 3^1$.

## Sources

- Grant Molnar and Guntas Singh, *Spoof Lehmer Factorizations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A33, Remark 3.

articles.title: Factorization with all exponents one
articles.statement:
For a finite multiset $x$ of natural numbers
$x_1, \dots, x_r$, this is the formal product $x_1 \cdots x_r = x_1^1 \cdots x_r^1$, that is,
the multiset of pairs $(x_1, 1), \dots, (x_r, 1)$, each consisting of a base $x_i$ and the
exponent $1$.

## Sources

- Grant Molnar and Guntas Singh, *Spoof Lehmer Factorizations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A33, Remark 3.

articles.title: Spoof totient of a unitary factorization
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x_1, \dots, x_r$, the spoof
totient of the spoof factorization $x_1 \cdots x_r$ with every exponent $1$ is
$\prod_{i=1}^{r} (x_i - 1)$, computed in the integers. This is Hasanalizade's spoof unitary
totient $\tilde{\varphi}^*(x_1 \cdots x_r)$.

## Sources

- Elchin Hasanalizade, *Some Remarks on a Paper of Molnar and Singh*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A100, Section 1 (definition of `φ̃*`).

articles.title: Spoof totient
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite multiset of pairs $(x_i, a_i)$ of natural numbers,
$i = 1, \dots, r$, viewed as the formal product $x_1^{a_1} \cdots x_r^{a_r}$. The spoof totient
of $F$ is the integer $\tilde\varphi(F) = \prod_{i=1}^{r} (x_i^{a_i} - x_i^{a_i - 1})$, where
the exponent $a_i - 1$ is truncated at $0$, so a pair with $a_i = 0$ contributes the factor $0$.

## Sources

- Grant Molnar and Guntas Singh, *Spoof Lehmer Factorizations*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A33, Definition 3.

articles.title: Lehmer's lemma for unitary spoof factorizations
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite multiset of integers,
write $E = \prod_{f \in F} f$ and $P = \prod_{f \in F} (f - 1)$, and let $k$, $\alpha$, $x$ and $y$
be integers with $\alpha = \pm 1$. If $k P = E + \alpha$ and $k P (x - 1)(y - 1) = E x y - 1$,
then $(\alpha x - E - \alpha)(\alpha y - E - \alpha) - (E^2 + \alpha E - \alpha) = 0$.

The second equation says that $F \cdot x \cdot y$ satisfies the unitary $k$-Lehmer equation
(Equation (3)). The paper takes $F$ with positive entries and $k \ge 2$; the identity holds for
every finite multiset of integers and every integer $k$.

## Sources

- Elchin Hasanalizade, *Some Remarks on a Paper of Molnar and Singh*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A100, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Thābit ibn Qurra's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number and put $p = 3 \cdot 2^n - 1$,
$q = 3 \cdot 2^{n-1} - 1$ and $r = 9 \cdot 2^{2n-1} - 1$. If $p$, $q$ and $r$ are all prime, then
$2^n p q < 2^n r$, the sum of the proper divisors of $2^n p q$ equals $2^n r$, and the sum of the
proper divisors of $2^n r$ equals $2^n p q$; that is, $2^n p q$ and $2^n r$ are distinct amicable
numbers.

Proof: Following Thabit ibn Qurra's construction as recorded in Dickson, *History of the Theory
of Numbers*, Vol. I, Ch. I, p. 39, and the cited Wikipedia account, compute full divisor sums by
multiplicativity and recover the proper-divisor sums by subtracting each number.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicable_numbers#Th%C4%81bit_ibn_Qurra_theorem

articles.title: Unitary divisor counts of unitary s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a unitary s-Zumkeller
number and let $q$ be the least unitary divisor of $n$ greater than $1$. If $q = 2$, then $n$ has
more than $2^6$ unitary divisors; if $q = 3$ or $q = 4$, then $n$ has more than $2^2$ unitary
divisors.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 12.

articles.title: Number of unitary divisors
articles.statement:
A positive integer $n$ with $m$ distinct prime factors has
exactly $2^m$ unitary divisors.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Lemma 2 (quoting Bege).

articles.title: Square of the product of the divisors
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$, let $T(n)$ be the
product of the positive divisors of $n$ and $\tau(n)$ their number. Then $T(n)^2 = n^{\tau(n)}$.

The paper writes this as $T(n) = n^{\tau(n)/2}$.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Lemma 1.

articles.title: Product of the divisors
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $T(n)$ is the product of all positive
divisors of $n$. For $n = 0$ the set of divisors is taken to be empty, so $T(0) = 1$.

articles.title: Odd s-Zumkeller numbers divisible by $3$ have at least eight prime factors
articles.statement:
Every odd
s-Zumkeller number divisible by $3$ has at least $8$ distinct prime factors.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 6(ii).

articles.title: Harmonic mean of squared divisors of even s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an even
s-Zumkeller number and let $\tau(n)$ be the number of positive divisors of $n$. Then
$\tau(n) / \sum_{d \mid n} d^{-2} \le 2\tau(n)/3$, where the sum runs over the positive divisors
$d$ of $n$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 9.

articles.title: Harmonic mean of squared divisors of s-Zumkeller numbers $2^\alpha(2^{\alpha+1}-1)$
articles.statement:
Let
$\alpha \ge 1$ be an integer, let $n = 2^\alpha (2^{\alpha+1} - 1)$ and let $\tau(n)$ be the
number of positive divisors of $n$. If $n$ is s-Zumkeller, then
$\tau(n) / \sum_{d \mid n} d^{-2} < 2^{2\alpha+3}/3$, where the sum runs over the positive
divisors $d$ of $n$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 10.

articles.title: $k$-m-perfect numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $n$ is $k$-m-perfect if
$T(n) = n^k$, where $T(n)$ is the product of the divisors of $n$.

articles.title: Odd s-Zumkeller numbers are perfect squares
articles.statement:
Every odd s-Zumkeller number is a perfect
square.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 7.

articles.title: $4$ is super-m-Zumkeller but not $k$-m-perfect for $k \ge 2$
articles.statement:
The number $4$ is
super-m-Zumkeller, and for no natural number $k \ge 2$ is $4$ a $k$-m-perfect number. This is the
paper's counterexample to the converse of Theorem 6.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Theorem 6.

articles.title: Criterion for super-m-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer, let $\tau(n)$ be the
number of positive divisors of $n$ and $T(n)$ their product. Then $n$ is super-m-Zumkeller if and
only if $8$ divides $\alpha \cdot \tau(n) \cdot \tau(T(n))$ for every prime $p$ dividing $n$,
where $\alpha$ is the exponent of $p$ in $n$.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Theorem 2.

articles.title: $k$-m-perfect numbers with $k$ a positive multiple of $4$ are super-m-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
Let
$k \ge 2$ be a natural number with $k \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. Then every natural number that is
$k$-m-perfect is super-m-Zumkeller.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Theorem 6.

articles.title: Super-m-Zumkeller prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $\alpha \ge 1$ an integer. Then
$p^\alpha$ is super-m-Zumkeller if and only if
$\alpha \equiv 0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13$ or $15 \pmod{16}$.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Theorem 3.

articles.title: Products of at least three distinct primes are super-m-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
For every finite set
$S$ of at least three primes, the product $\prod_{p \in S} p$ is super-m-Zumkeller.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Corollary 1.

articles.title: Powers of $2$ times at least three distinct odd primes are super-m-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be
a natural number and $S$ a finite set of at least three odd primes. Then $2^k \prod_{p \in S} p$
is super-m-Zumkeller.

The primes are required to be odd because the paper's proof uses that this number has
$(k+1)2^r$ divisors, where $r$ is the number of primes in $S$.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Odd powers of $2$ times two distinct odd primes are super-m-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be an odd
natural number and let $p$ and $q$ be distinct odd primes. Then $2^k p q$ is super-m-Zumkeller.

The primes are required to be odd because the paper's proof uses that this number has
$(k+1) \cdot 2^2$ divisors.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Super-m-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let $T(n)$ be the product of the
positive divisors of $n$ (for $n = 0$ the divisor set is taken to be empty, so $T(0) = 1$).
Then $n$ is *super-m-Zumkeller* if there is a set $A$ of positive divisors of $T(n)$ such that
the product of the elements of $A$ equals the product of the positive divisors of $T(n)$ that
are not in $A$; that is, the divisors of $T(n)$ split into two complementary sets, one of which
may be empty, with equal products.

articles.title: Properties of even s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an even s-Zumkeller number and let
$\sigma_2(n)$ be the sum of the squares of the positive divisors of $n$. Then $\sigma_2(n)$ is
even, some odd prime $p$ divides $n$ with an odd exponent in the prime factorization of $n$, and
$3n^2 \le 2\sigma_2(n)$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Criterion for even s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an even positive integer and let
$\sigma_2(n)$ be the sum of the squares of the positive divisors of $n$. Then $n$ is s-Zumkeller
if and only if there is a (possibly empty) set $S$ of proper divisors of $n$, not containing
$n/2$, such that $4 \sum_{d \in S} d^2 = 2\sigma_2(n) - 3n^2$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 2.

articles.title: $60$ is s-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
The number $60$ is s-Zumkeller: the squares of its proper divisors
$1, 2, 5, 30$ sum to $1^2 + 2^2 + 5^2 + 30^2 = 930$, which is half of the sum of the squares of
all proper divisors of $60$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Example 1.

articles.title: s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is s-Zumkeller if its proper divisors can be
split into two disjoint nonempty sets whose elements have equal sums of squares. Each of the two
sums is then $(\sigma_2(n) - n^2)/2$, where $\sigma_2(n)$ is the sum of the squares of the
positive divisors of $n$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Definition 1.

articles.title: Lower bounds for unitary s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a unitary s-Zumkeller
number, let $q$ be the least unitary divisor of $n$ greater than $1$, and for each prime $p$
dividing $n$ let $k_p$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Then, with both sums over all unitary
divisors $d$ of $n$ (including $n$ itself), $n^2 (2/q^2 + 1) \le \sum_d d^2$ and
$2/q^2 + 1 \le \sum_d 1/d^2$. Moreover $2/q^2 + 1 \le \prod_{p \mid n} (1 + p^{2k_p})/p^{2k_p}$,
the product running over the primes $p$ dividing $n$.

The number $q$ is the smallest of the prime powers $p^{k_p}$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 11.

articles.title: The number 60 is unitary s-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
The number $60$ is a unitary s-Zumkeller number: its
proper unitary divisors are $1, 3, 4, 5, 12, 15, 20$, and $20^2 + 3^2 + 1^2 = 410$ is half the sum
of their squares.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Example 2.

articles.title: Unitary s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is a unitary s-Zumkeller number when
its proper unitary divisors (the unitary divisors of $n$ other than $n$) split into two nonempty
disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ with equal sums of squares, $\sum_{d \in A} d^2 = \sum_{d \in B} d^2$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Definition 2.

articles.title: Lower bound for odd s-Zumkeller numbers divisible by 3
articles.statement:
Every odd s-Zumkeller number $n$
divisible by $3$ satisfies
$n \ge 12442607161209225 = (3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdot 17 \cdot 19 \cdot 23)^2$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 8.

articles.title: The number 6 is not s-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
The number $6$ is not an s-Zumkeller number: the squares of
its proper divisors sum to $1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 = 14$, and they admit no split into two parts with
equal sums.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Section 1.

articles.title: No odd unitary s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
There is no odd unitary s-Zumkeller number.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 13.

articles.title: The number 6 is not unitary s-Zumkeller
articles.statement:
The number $6$ is not a unitary s-Zumkeller
number.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Section 1.

articles.title: Product formulas for the sum of divisors
articles.statement:
Let $n \ne 0$ be a natural number, let
$\sigma(n)$ be the sum of the divisors of $n$, and for each prime $p$ dividing $n$ let $k_p$ be
the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Then, with products over the primes $p$ dividing $n$,

$$\sigma(n) = \prod_{p \mid n} \frac{p^{k_p + 1} - 1}{p - 1}$$

and

$$\frac{\sigma(n)}{n} = \prod_{p \mid n} \frac{p^{k_p + 1} - 1}{p^{k_p} (p - 1)}.$$

If moreover $n > 1$, then $\sigma(n)/n < \prod_{p \mid n} p/(p - 1)$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Lemma 1(i) (quoting Peng and Bhaskara Rao).

articles.title: Product formulas for the sum of squared divisors
articles.statement:
Let $n \ne 0$ be a natural number,
let $\sigma_2(n)$ be the sum of the squares of the divisors of $n$, and for each prime $p$
dividing $n$ let $k_p$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Then, with products over the primes $p$
dividing $n$,

$$\sigma_2(n) = \prod_{p \mid n} \frac{p^{2(k_p + 1)} - 1}{p^2 - 1}$$

and

$$\frac{\sigma_2(n)}{n^2} = \prod_{p \mid n} \frac{p^{2(k_p + 1)} - 1}{p^{2k_p} (p^2 - 1)}.$$

If moreover $n > 1$, then $\sigma_2(n)/n^2 < \prod_{p \mid n} p^2/(p^2 - 1)$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Lemma 1(ii) (quoting Peng and Bhaskara Rao).

articles.title: Even s-Zumkeller numbers are divisible by 6
articles.statement:
Every even s-Zumkeller number is divisible
by $6$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Sum of squares of unitary divisors
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$, the sum of the
squares of the unitary divisors of $n$ equals $\prod_{p} \left(1 + p^{2k_p}\right)$, where $p$
ranges over the distinct prime factors of $n$ and $k_p$ is the exponent of $p$ in $n$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Lemma 3(i) (quoting Subbarao and Warren).

articles.title: Even s-Zumkeller numbers are divisible by 3
articles.statement:
If $n$ is an even s-Zumkeller number, then
$3$ divides $n$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Super-m-Zumkeller numbers $n \ge 2$ have at least three divisors
articles.statement:
If a natural number
$n \ge 2$ is super-m-Zumkeller, then the number $\tau(n)$ of positive divisors of $n$ satisfies
$\tau(n) \ge 3$.

## Sources

- Harish Patodia, "Super m-Zumkeller Numbers", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Even s-Zumkeller numbers have at least three prime factors
articles.statement:
If $n$ is an even
s-Zumkeller number, then $n$ has at least $3$ distinct prime factors.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 6(i).

articles.title: Even s-Zumkeller numbers have at least twelve divisors
articles.statement:
If $n$ is an even s-Zumkeller
number, then $n$ has at least $12$ positive divisors.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 3.

articles.title: A prime-factor product bound for s-Zumkeller numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an s-Zumkeller number
and let $p_1$ be its least prime factor. Then

$$\frac{2}{p_1^2} + 1 < \prod_{p} \frac{p^2}{p^2 - 1},$$

where the product ranges over the distinct prime factors $p$ of $n$.

## Sources

- Jayanta Kalita and Helen K. Saikia, *A Study on Generalized Zumkeller Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A95, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Average number of prime factors of h-free integers
articles.statement:
Let $h \ge 2$ be an integer. Call a
positive integer $n$ $h$-free if every prime occurs in the factorization of $n$ with exponent less
than $h$, and write $\Omega(n)$ for the number of prime factors of $n$ counted with multiplicity
and $\zeta$ for the Riemann zeta function. Then, as the real number $x$ tends to infinity,

$$
\sum_{\substack{1 \le n \le x \\ n \ h\text{-free}}} \Omega(n)
= \frac{x \log\log x}{\zeta(h)} + O(x).
$$

## Sources

- Rafael Jakimczuk and Matilde Lalín, "The Number of Prime Factors on Average in Certain Integer Sequences," Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.2.3, Theorem, lines 110–117, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Lalin/lalin2.tex

articles.title: Benelux pairs of the first kind below $1.4 \cdot 10^{12}$
articles.statement:
Let $m < n$ be
non-negative integers with $n < 1.4 \cdot 10^{12}$. Then $m$ and $n$ have the same prime
factors and $m + 1$ and $n + 1$ have the same prime factors (that is, $(m, n)$ is a Benelux
pair of the first kind) if and only if $(m, n) = (75, 1215)$ or
$(m, n) = (2^k - 2, 2^{2k} - 2^{k+1})$ for some integer $k$ with $2 \le k \le 20$.

Here $0$ is taken to have no prime factors; for $m = 0$ both sides are false.

## Sources

- Christian Hercher, *On One of Erdős' Problems—An Efficient Search for Benelux Pairs*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.5, Theorem 1 a) (`jis-2025-25.8.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Benelux pairs of the second kind below $1.4 \cdot 10^{12}$
articles.statement:
Let $m < n$ be
non-negative integers with $n < 1.4 \cdot 10^{12}$. Then $m$ and $n + 1$ have the same prime
factors and $m + 1$ and $n$ have the same prime factors (that is, $(m, n)$ is a Benelux pair
of the second kind) if and only if $(m, n) = (35, 4374)$ or
$(m, n) = (2^k + 1, 2^{2k} + 2^{k+1})$ for some integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le 20$.

Here $0$ is taken to have no prime factors; for $m = 0$ both sides are false.

## Sources

- Christian Hercher, *On One of Erdős' Problems—An Efficient Search for Benelux Pairs*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.5, Theorem 1 b) (`jis-2025-25.8.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Solution of Erdős Problem 369, location variant
articles.statement:
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ and every
natural number $k \ge 2$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for every natural number
$n \ge N$ there is a natural number $a$ with $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor \le a + 1$ and $a + k \le n$
for which every prime factor $p$ of each of the $k$ consecutive integers $a + 1, \dots, a + k$
satisfies $p \le n^\varepsilon$.

## Sources

- Balog-Wooley 1998; Bober-Fretwell-Martin-Wooley 2020.
- Lean proof of EP-369 location variant (plby/lean-proofs), https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1d7b3f00780b85ed0462e79a1cd5650ee9055655/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos369.lean.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 369, location variant
articles.statement:
This is the statement that for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$ and every natural number $k \ge 2$ there is a natural number $N$ such that for
every natural number $n \ge N$ there is a natural number $a$ with $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor \le a + 1$
and $a + k \le n$ for which every prime factor $p$ of each of the $k$ consecutive integers
$a + 1, \dots, a + k$ satisfies $p \le n^\varepsilon$.

Erdős Problem 369 as written allows the run anywhere in $\{1, \dots, n\}$, which is trivially
true (take $1, \dots, k$ once $n^\varepsilon \ge k$); here the run must start at or after
$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 690 is false
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $k \ge 1$ such that the $k$-th
prime-factor density $d_k$ is not unimodal on the primes, that is, there is no prime $p_0$ such
that $d_k(p) \le d_k(q)$ for all primes $p$ and $q$ with $p \le q \le p_0$ and
$d_k(q) \le d_k(p)$ for all primes $p$ and $q$ with $p_0 \le p \le q$. Here $d_k(p)$ is the
natural density of the set of natural numbers whose $k$-th smallest prime factor is $p$ (an
unspecified real number if this density does not exist).

Cambie (Theorem 5) proves that $d_k$ is unimodal for $k = 1, 2, 3$ and not unimodal for
$4 \le k \le 20$; for example $d_4(13) = 31/5005 > d_4(17) = 206/36465 < d_4(19) = 1308/230945$.

## Sources

- S. Cambie, Resolution of Erdős' problems about unimodularity, arXiv preprint (2025), arXiv:2501.10333, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10333.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 690
articles.statement:
The proposition that for every natural number $k \ge 1$ the $k$-th
prime-factor density $d_k$ is unimodal on the primes: there is a prime $p_0$ such that
$d_k(p) \le d_k(q)$ for all primes $p$ and $q$ with $p \le q \le p_0$, and $d_k(q) \le d_k(p)$ for
all primes $p$ and $q$ with $p_0 \le p \le q$. Here $d_k(p)$ is the natural density of the set of
natural numbers whose $k$-th smallest prime factor is $p$ (an unspecified real number if this
density does not exist).

articles.title: The $k$-th smallest prime factor
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $n$ and $p$, $p$ is the $k$-th
smallest prime factor of $n$ when $n \ne 0$, $p$ is a prime dividing $n$, and exactly $k - 1$
primes dividing $n$ are smaller than $p$.

For $k = 0$ the count $k - 1$ is read as $0$ (truncated subtraction), so $k = 0$ and $k = 1$
agree.

articles.title: Unimodality on the primes
articles.statement:
A function $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ is unimodal on
the primes if there is a prime $p_0$ such that $f(p) \le f(q)$ for all primes $p$ and $q$ with
$p \le q \le p_0$, and $f(q) \le f(p)$ for all primes $p$ and $q$ with $p_0 \le p \le q$.

articles.title: The $k$-th prime-factor density
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $p$, let $S_{k,p}$ be the set
of natural numbers whose $k$-th smallest prime factor is $p$. The $k$-th prime-factor density
$d_k(p)$ is the natural density of $S_{k,p}$, that is, the limit of
$\lvert S_{k,p} \cap \{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\} \rvert / N$ as $N \to \infty$, when this limit
exists; otherwise $d_k(p)$ is an unspecified real number.

articles.title: Asymptotic count of cyclic and composite cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
For real $x$, let $A(x)$ be the
number of cyclic numbers $m$ with $1 \le m \le x$, and let $cc(x)$ be the number of composite
cyclic numbers $m \le x$, that is, cyclic numbers $m > 1$ that are not prime. Then, as
$x \to \infty$, $A(x) \sim cc(x)$ and $cc(x) \sim x e^{-\gamma} / \log \log \log x$, where
$\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Lemma 1.

articles.title: The cyclic counting functions vary regularly with index one
articles.statement:
For real $x$, let $A(x)$ be
the number of cyclic numbers $m$ with $1 \le m \le x$, let $\pi(x)$ be the number of primes
$p \le x$, and let $cc(x)$ be the number of composite cyclic numbers $m \le x$, that is, cyclic
numbers $m > 1$ that are not prime. Then for every real $\lambda > 0$, each of
$A(\lambda x) / A(x)$, $\pi(\lambda x) / \pi(x)$ and $cc(\lambda x) / cc(x)$ tends to $\lambda$
as $x \to \infty$.

Every prime is cyclic, so $\pi(x)$ is also the number of prime cyclic numbers $\le x$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Gaps between cyclic numbers under the Riemann hypothesis
articles.statement:
Assume the Riemann hypothesis.
Let $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots$ be the cyclic numbers in increasing order and $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots$ the
primes in increasing order. Then the gaps $d_n = c_{n+1} - c_n$ between consecutive cyclic
numbers satisfy $d_n = o(\sqrt{p_n} \log p_n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Mean and variance of the cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots$ be the cyclic numbers
in increasing order, so $c_1 = 1$. For $n \ge 1$ let $m(c,n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i$ be
the mean of $c_1, \dots, c_n$, and for $n \ge 2$ let
$v(c,n) = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (c_i - m(c,n))^2$ be their variance. Then, as
$n \to \infty$, $m(c,n) \sim c_n / 2$ and $v(c,n) \sim c_n^2 / 12$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Generalized Taylor's law for cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots$ be the cyclic
numbers in increasing order, so $c_1 = 1$. For $n \ge 1$ and a natural number $k$ let
$\mu'(c,n,k) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^k$ be the $k$-th moment of $c_1, \dots, c_n$, and
let $m(c,n) = \mu'(c,n,1)$ be their mean. Then for every natural number $k$, as $n \to \infty$,

$$
\mu'(c,n,k) \sim \frac{2^k}{1+k} \, m(c,n)^k.
$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Relation between the moments of the cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots$ be the
cyclic numbers in increasing order, so $c_1 = 1$, and for $n \ge 1$ and a natural number $k$ let
$\mu'(c,n,k) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^k$ be the $k$-th moment of $c_1, \dots, c_n$. Then
for all natural numbers $j \ge 1$ and $k$, as $n \to \infty$,

$$
\mu'(c,n,k) \sim \frac{(j+1)^{k/j}}{k+1} \, \mu'(c,n,j)^{k/j}.
$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Taylor's law for cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots$ be the cyclic numbers in
increasing order, so $c_1 = 1$. For $n \ge 1$ let $m(c,n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i$ be
the mean of $c_1, \dots, c_n$, and for $n \ge 2$ let
$v(c,n) = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (c_i - m(c,n))^2$ be their variance. Then for every real
$b$, as $n \to \infty$, $v(c,n) / m(c,n)^b$ tends to $\infty$ if $b < 2$, to $1/3$ if $b = 2$,
and to $0$ if $b > 2$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Joel E. Cohen, *Cyclic Numbers and Gaps*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A23, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
A positive integer $n$ is cyclic when $\gcd(n, \varphi(n)) = 1$, where
$\varphi$ is Euler's totient function.

articles.title: Cohen's Oppermann conjecture for cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > 1$ there are
cyclic numbers $c$ and $c'$ with $n^2 - n < c < n^2 < c' < n^2 + n$. Moreover, let $C_L(n)$ and
$C_R(n)$ be the numbers of cyclic numbers in $[n^2 - n, n^2]$ and in $[n^2, n^2 + n]$, and let
$A_L$, $A_R$ and $A$ be the left-hand, right-hand and simplified approximations for cyclic numbers
near squares. Then, as $n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers, $C_L(n) \sim A_L(n)$,
$A_L(n) \sim A(n)$, $C_R(n) \sim A_R(n)$ and $A_R(n) \sim A(n)$.

## Sources

- J. E. Cohen, *Conjectures about Primes and Cyclic Numbers*, J. Integer Seq. 28 (2025), Article 25.4.1.

articles.title: Simplified approximation for cyclic numbers near squares
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be the
Euler–Mascheroni constant and, for real $x$, let $L(x) = \log \log \log x$. The simplified
approximation is the function of the real variable $x$ given by

$$
\frac{x}{e^{\gamma} L(x)} \left(1 - \frac{\gamma}{L(x)}\right).
$$

Here $\log y$ means $\log |y|$, with $\log 0 = 0$, and a quotient by $0$ is $0$, so the expression
is defined for every real $x$. J. E. Cohen conjectures that, at $x = n$, it is asymptotic to
the number of cyclic numbers in $[n^2 - n, n^2]$ and to the number in $[n^2, n^2 + n]$.

articles.title: Cyclic numbers in the left Oppermann interval
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the
number of cyclic numbers $k$ with $n^2 - n \le k \le n^2$.

articles.title: Cyclic numbers in the right Oppermann interval
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the
number of cyclic numbers $k$ with $n^2 \le k \le n^2 + n$.

articles.title: Left-hand approximation for cyclic numbers near squares
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be the
Euler–Mascheroni constant and, for real $x$, let $L(x) = \log \log \log (x^2)$. The left-hand
approximation is the function of the real variable $x$ given by

$$
\frac{x}{e^{\gamma} L(x)} \left(1 - \frac{\gamma}{L(x)}\right).
$$

Here $\log y$ means $\log |y|$, with $\log 0 = 0$, and a quotient by $0$ is $0$, so the expression
is defined for every real $x$. J. E. Cohen conjectures that, at $x = n$, it is asymptotic to
the number of cyclic numbers in $[n^2 - n, n^2]$.

articles.title: Right-hand approximation for cyclic numbers near squares
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be the
Euler–Mascheroni constant and, for real $x$, let $L(x) = \log \log \log (x(x+1))$. The right-hand
approximation is the function of the real variable $x$ given by

$$
\frac{x}{e^{\gamma} L(x)} \left(1 - \frac{\gamma}{L(x)}\right).
$$

Here $\log y$ means $\log |y|$, with $\log 0 = 0$, and a quotient by $0$ is $0$, so the expression
is defined for every real $x$. J. E. Cohen conjectures that, at $x = n$, it is asymptotic to
the number of cyclic numbers in $[n^2, n^2 + n]$.

articles.title: Power sums of cyclic numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer. Let $c_n$ be the $n$-th cyclic
number ($c_1 = 1$), let $C(x)$ be the number of cyclic numbers $m \le x$, and let $\gamma$ be the
Euler–Mascheroni constant. Then, as $n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^k \sim \frac{n c_n^k}{k+1}
\sim \frac{n^{k+1} e^{k\gamma} (\log \log \log n)^k}{k+1},
$$

and, as $x \to \infty$ through the real numbers,

$$
\sum_{m \le x,\ m \text{ cyclic}} m^k \sim \frac{C(x)\, c_{C(x)}^k}{k+1}
\sim \frac{C(x)\, x^k}{k+1}
\sim \frac{x^{k+1}}{(k+1) e^{\gamma} \log \log \log x}
\left(1 - \frac{\gamma}{\log \log \log x}\right).
$$

## Sources

- Joel E. Cohen, *Conjectures about Primes and Cyclic Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.4.7, Theorem 1 (`jis-2025-25.4.7-thm-1`).

articles.title: Prime divisors of highly composite numbers form an initial segment
articles.statement:
If $H$ is a highly
composite number and $p \le q$ are primes with $q \mid H$, then $p \mid H$. In other words, the
set of primes dividing $H$ is an initial segment of the primes.

articles.title: Exponents of highly composite numbers are non-increasing
articles.statement:
If $H$ is a highly composite
number and $p \le q$ are primes, then the exponent of $q$ in the prime factorization of $H$ is at
most the exponent of $p$.

articles.title: Highly composite numbers
articles.statement:
A positive natural number is highly composite if it has strictly
more divisors than every smaller positive natural number.

articles.title: Counting integers whose prime factors are all $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a real
number such that $\sqrt{\ln x} \prod_{q \le x} (1 - 1/q) \to C$ as the natural number $x$ tends
to infinity, where $q$ runs over the primes with $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Let $g(x)$ be the number
of integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le x$ all of whose prime factors are $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ (so
$n = 1$ is counted). Then

$$g(x) \sim \sqrt{e^\gamma / \pi} \cdot \frac{C}{2} \cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{\ln x}}$$

as the natural number $x$ tends to infinity, where $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

In the source $C = C(4, 1)$ is the constant of Languasco and Zaccagnini; for $C = 1.29230\ldots$
the constant in front of $x / \sqrt{\ln x}$ is $0.48651\ldots$.

## Sources

- Jones and Zvonkin, *A Number-Theoretic Problem Concerning Pseudo-Real Riemann Surfaces*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A75, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Raikov's Tauberian theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ be nonnegative real numbers whose
Dirichlet series $F(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} a_n n^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$,
and let $\alpha < 1$ be real. Suppose that $H$ is a function holomorphic on an open set containing
the half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\, s \ge 1$ and nonzero on that half-plane, and that
$F(s) = H(s) / (s - 1)^{1 - \alpha}$ for $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$, with the principal branch of the
power. Then

$$\sum_{n=1}^{x} a_n \sim \frac{H(1)}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \frac{x}{(\ln x)^\alpha}$$

as the natural number $x$ tends to infinity.

The paper allows any real $\alpha$; for $\alpha = 1$ the statement fails: $a_1 = 1$, $a_n = 0$
otherwise and $H = 1$ give $F = 1 = H / (s - 1)^0$, but $\Gamma$ has a pole at $0$ and
$\sum_{n \le x} a_n = 1$. The analytic continuation of $F$ across $\mathrm{Re}\, s = 1$,
$s \neq 1$, assumed in the paper, follows from the representation through $H$.

## Sources

- Jones and Zvonkin, *A Number-Theoretic Problem Concerning Pseudo-Real Riemann Surfaces*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A75, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Consecutive polynomial family
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A family
$L_0, \dots, L_{k-1}$ of polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is consecutive when
$L_{i+1} - L_i = 1$ for every $i$ with $i + 1 < k$.

articles.title: Bound for $1/\zeta$ from the Riemann hypothesis
articles.statement:
Assume the Riemann hypothesis, and let
$1/2 < \sigma \le 1$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ be real. Then there are real constants $C$ and $t_0$,
depending on $\sigma$ and $\varepsilon$, such that $|1/\zeta(\sigma + it)| \le C |t|^{\varepsilon}$
for every real $t$ with $|t| \ge t_0$.

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Vinogradov–Korobov bound for $1/\zeta$
articles.statement:
Write $s = \sigma + it$ and
$g(T) = (\log T)^{2/3} (\log \log T)^{1/3}$. There are real constants $C > 0$, $K$ and
$T_0 \ge 3$ such that for every real $T$ and every complex $s$ with $T_0 < t \le T$ and
$\sigma \ge 1 - C / g(T)$, we have $\zeta(s) \ne 0$ and $|1/\zeta(s)| \le K g(T)$.

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Coarse zeta factorization of the squareful $2^{\omega(n)}$ Dirichlet series
articles.statement:
Let
$\omega(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of $n$, call $n$ squareful when $n \ne 0$ and
$p^2 \mid n$ for every prime $p \mid n$ (that is, $n$ is $2$-full), and let
$F(s) = \sum_{n \text{ squareful}} 2^{\omega(n)} n^{-s}$. There is a sequence
$h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ whose Dirichlet series $H(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} h(n) n^{-s}$
converges absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/5$, such that for every complex $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$,

$$F(s) = \frac{\zeta(2s)^2 \zeta(3s)^2}{\zeta(4s)} H(s).$$

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Fine zeta factorization of the squareful $2^{\omega(n)}$ Dirichlet series
articles.statement:
Let
$\omega(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of $n$, call $n$ squareful when $n \ne 0$ and
$p^2 \mid n$ for every prime $p \mid n$ (that is, $n$ is $2$-full), and let
$F(s) = \sum_{n \text{ squareful}} 2^{\omega(n)} n^{-s}$. There is a sequence
$h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ whose Dirichlet series $H(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} h(n) n^{-s}$
converges absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/15$, such that for every complex $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$,

$$F(s) = \frac{\zeta(2s)^2 \zeta(3s)^2 \zeta(7s)^2 \zeta(8s)^4 \zeta(12s)^5 \zeta(13s)^{14}
\zeta(14s)^5}{\zeta(4s) \zeta(5s)^2 \zeta(6s)^3 \zeta(10s)^5 \zeta(11s)^6} H(s).$$

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Asymptotic for the sum of $2^{\omega(n)}$ over squareful $n$
articles.statement:
Let $\omega(n)$ be the
number of distinct prime factors of $n$, and let $f(n) = 2^{\omega(n)}$ if $n$ is squareful
($n \ne 0$ and $p^2 \mid n$ for every prime $p \mid n$; so $f(1) = 1$) and $f(n) = 0$ otherwise.
There are real constants $C_1$, $C_2$, $C_3$, $C_4$, $c > 0$, $K$ and $x_0$ such that for every
real $x \ge x_0$,

$$\Bigl|\sum_{1 \le n \le x} f(n) - \bigl(C_1 x^{1/2} \log x + C_2 x^{1/2} +
C_3 x^{1/3} \log x + C_4 x^{1/3}\bigr)\Bigr| \le
K x^{1/4} \exp\Bigl(c \Bigl(\frac{\log x}{\log \log x}\Bigr)^{1/3}\Bigr).$$

The paper writes the coefficient as $c_\varepsilon$, "for some $c > 0$", after "let
$\varepsilon > 0$": a constant chosen after $\varepsilon$, not a product with an arbitrarily small
factor. Its proof (equations (28)–(30)) produces, with $T$ the height parameter of its contour,
the exponent $(4 + \varepsilon) c (\log T / \log \log T)^{1/3}$ with $\varepsilon$ small and
$c > 0$ the fixed constant of its contour shift to $\operatorname{Re} s = 1/4 - c/g(T)$, where
$g(T) = (\log T)^{2/3} (\log \log T)^{1/3}$, chosen in terms of the Vinogradov–Korobov
zero-free region and the bound for $1/\zeta$ there (its Lemmas 5 and 6), so the coefficient
stays bounded away from $0$ and the statement is one existential $c > 0$.

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Uniform fourth-moment bound for the Riemann zeta function
articles.statement:
There are real constants $C$
and $T_0$ such that for every real $\sigma$ with $1/2 \le \sigma \le 1$ and every real
$T \ge T_0$,

$$\int_1^T |\zeta(\sigma + it)|^4 \, dt \le C T (\log T)^4.$$

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Lindelöf bound from the Riemann hypothesis
articles.statement:
Assume the Riemann hypothesis, and let
$\varepsilon > 0$ be real. Then there are real constants $C$ and $t_0$ such that
$|\zeta(\sigma + it)| \le C |t|^{\varepsilon}$ for all real $\sigma$ and $t$ with
$1/2 \le \sigma \le 1$ and $|t| \ge t_0$.

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Vinogradov–Korobov zero-free region
articles.statement:
There are real constants $C > 0$ and $t_0 \ge 3$
such that $\zeta(\sigma + it) \ne 0$ for all real $\sigma$ and $t$ with $|t| \ge t_0$ and
$\sigma \ge 1 - C / \bigl((\log |t|)^{2/3} (\log \log |t|)^{1/3}\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Kampamolla Venkatasubbareddy and Ayyadurai Sankaranarayanan, *On the Distribution of the Restricted Sequence of Integers 2^{ω(n)}*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A110, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Odd-to-even ratio of $k$-full numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$. For a natural number $N$ let
$K_o(N)$ and $K_e(N)$ be the numbers of odd and of even $k$-full numbers $n \le N$. Then
$K_o(N)/K_e(N) \to 2 - 2^{1 - 1/k}$ as $N \to \infty$.

The counts up to a real $x$ depend only on $\lfloor x \rfloor$, so this is the same as the limit
as $x \to \infty$ through the reals.

## Sources

- Sunanta Srisopha and Teerapat Srichan, *The Odd/Even Dichotomy for the Set of Numbers That Are Both k-Full and l-Free*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A106, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Odd-to-even ratio of $k$-full, $l$-free numbers
articles.statement:
Let $2 \le k < l$. Call a natural number
$n$ a $[k, l]$-integer if it is $k$-full and $l$-free, that is, $n \ge 1$ and every prime $p$
dividing $n$ satisfies $p^k \mid n$ and $p^l \nmid n$. For a natural number $N$ let $O_{k,l}(N)$
and $E_{k,l}(N)$ be the numbers of odd and of even $[k, l]$-integers $n \le N$. Then
$O_{k,l}(N)/E_{k,l}(N) \to (2 - 2^{1 - 1/k})/(1 - 2^{1 - l/k})$ as $N \to \infty$.

The counts up to a real $x$ depend only on $\lfloor x \rfloor$, so this is the same as the limit
as $x \to \infty$ through the reals.

## Sources

- Sunanta Srisopha and Teerapat Srichan, *The Odd/Even Dichotomy for the Set of Numbers That Are Both k-Full and l-Free*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A106, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Odd-to-even ratio of $l$-free numbers
articles.statement:
Let $l \ge 2$. For a natural number $N$ let $O(N)$
and $E(N)$ be the numbers of odd and of even $l$-free positive integers $n \le N$. Then
$O(N)/E(N) \to 2^l/(2^l - 2)$ as $N \to \infty$.

This is the case $k = 1$ of the odd-to-even ratio for $k$-full, $l$-free numbers, since every
positive integer is $1$-full.

## Sources

- Sunanta Srisopha and Teerapat Srichan, *The Odd/Even Dichotomy for the Set of Numbers That Are Both k-Full and l-Free*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A106, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Characterization of power-free numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $n$ is $k$-free
if and only if $k \ge 2$, $n > 0$, and $p^k$ does not divide $n$ for any prime $p$.

articles.title: A natural number is 2-free if and only if it is squarefree
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$n$ is $2$-free if and only if $n$ is squarefree, that is, $d^2$ divides $n$ only for $d = 1$.

articles.title: Power-free natural numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A natural number $n$ is
$k$-free when $k \ge 2$, $n > 0$, and $p^k$ does not divide $n$ for any prime $p$.

articles.title: Power-freeness is monotone in the exponent
articles.statement:
If a natural number $n$ is $k$-free and
$k \le l$, then $n$ is $l$-free.

articles.title: A k-free number has no prime k-th power divisor
articles.statement:
If a natural number $n$ is $k$-free and
$p$ is a prime, then $p^k$ does not divide $n$.

articles.title: Divisors of k-free numbers are k-free
articles.statement:
If a natural number $n$ is $k$-free and $m$ divides
$n$, then $m$ is $k$-free.

articles.title: Power-free numbers are positive
articles.statement: If a natural number $n$ is $k$-free, then $n > 0$.

articles.title: The exponent of a power-free number is at least two
articles.statement:
If a natural number $n$ is $k$-free,
then $k \ge 2$.

articles.title: Factorization criterion for $k$-full numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $n$ be natural numbers with
$n \ne 0$, and write $v_p(n)$ for the exponent of a prime $p$ in the prime factorization of
$n$. Then $n$ is $k$-full if and only if $k \le v_p(n)$ for every prime $p$ dividing $n$.

articles.title: The $1$-full numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is $1$-full if and only if $n \ne 0$, since
$p^1 = p$ divides $n$ for every prime $p$ dividing $n$.

The source considers only $k$-full numbers with $k \ge 2$.

articles.title: The $0$-full numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is $0$-full if and only if $n \ne 0$, since
$p^0 = 1$ divides $n$ for every prime $p$.

The source considers only $k$-full numbers with $k \ge 2$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of $k$-fullness in $k$
articles.statement:
Let $j \le k$ be natural numbers. Every $k$-full
natural number is $j$-full.

articles.title: For $k \ge 2$, $k$-full numbers are $2$-full
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a natural number. Every
$k$-full natural number is $2$-full.

articles.title: One is $k$-full
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the number $1$ is $k$-full: it is nonzero
and has no prime divisors.

articles.title: The $2$-full numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is $2$-full if and only if $n \ne 0$ and $p^2$
divides $n$ for every prime $p$ dividing $n$. These are the squarefull (also called powerful)
numbers.

articles.title: $k$-full numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A natural number $n$ is $k$-full if
$n \ne 0$ and $p^k$ divides $n$ for every prime $p$ dividing $n$.

The definition makes sense for every $k$; the source considers only $k \ge 2$.

articles.title: Zero is not $k$-full
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the number $0$ is not $k$-full.

The source works with positive integers.

articles.title: The powerful part of $n$ divides $n$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the powerful part
of $n$ divides $n$.

articles.title: Prime exponents of the powerful part
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $p$, write $v_p(n)$ for
the exponent of $p$ in the prime factorization of $n$ (it is $0$ when $p$ is not a prime factor
of $n$). Then the exponent of $p$ in the powerful part of $n$ equals $v_p(n)$ if $v_p(n) \ge 2$,
and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Powerful part of a natural number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n \ge 1$ and a prime $p$, let
$v_p(n)$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$. The powerful (or $2$-full) part of $n$ is the product of
the prime powers $p^{v_p(n)}$ over the primes $p$ dividing $n$ with $v_p(n) \ge 2$ (and $1$ if
there are none). The powerful part of $0$ is defined to be $1$.

articles.title: Arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of powerful numbers
articles.statement:
For every integer $k \ge 3$
there are positive integers $a$ and $d$ such that each of the $k$ numbers $a + id$ with
$0 \le i < k$ is powerful: every prime that divides $a + id$ has its square dividing $a + id$.

## Sources

- Tsz Ho Chan, "Arithmetic Progressions Among Powerful Numbers", Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023), Article 23.1.1, Theorem `thm-longAP`, source lines 97–99, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL26/Chan/chan33.tex>. The paper notes the result is not new (see remark 2 in [H] there) and includes a proof for completeness. Powerful (squarefull) means every prime divisor appears with exponent at least two; nonconstant is `0 < d`. It follows from `arbitrarily_long_arithmetic_progressions_of_powerful_numbers_general`, which states powerfulness as `Nat.IsKFull 2`; the hypothesis `hk` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Arithmetic progressions of 2-full numbers of every length
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k$ there are positive integers $a$ and $d$ such that $a + id$ is $2$-full (powerful) for every
natural number $i < k$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 937 holds (Bajpai–Bennett–Chan)
articles.statement:
There are infinitely many pairs of natural
numbers $(a, d)$ with $d > 0$ such that the four numbers $a$, $a + d$, $a + 2d$, $a + 3d$ are
powerful (each is nonzero and divisible by $p^2$ for every prime $p$ dividing it) and pairwise
coprime. That is, there are infinitely many four-term arithmetic progressions of pairwise coprime
powerful numbers.

## Sources

- Prajeet Bajpai, Michael A. Bennett, and Tsz Ho Chan, Arithmetic progressions in squarefull numbers, International Journal of Number Theory 20 (2024), 19–45, https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet-getitem?mr=4688726. Resolved true: Resolved true by Bajpai–Bennett–Chan; a proof is available in an external Lean development.

articles.title: Statement of Erdős Problem 937
articles.statement:
There are infinitely many pairs of natural numbers
$(a, d)$ with $d > 0$ such that the four numbers $a$, $a + d$, $a + 2d$, $a + 3d$ are powerful
(each is nonzero and divisible by $p^2$ for every prime $p$ dividing it) and pairwise coprime;
that is, infinitely many four-term arithmetic progressions of pairwise coprime powerful numbers.

articles.title: Four-term progressions of pairwise coprime powerful numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and
$d$, the numbers $a$, $a + d$, $a + 2d$, $a + 3d$ form a four-term arithmetic progression of
pairwise coprime powerful numbers when $d > 0$, each of the four numbers is powerful (that is,
$2$-full: nonzero and divisible by $p^2$ for every prime $p$ dividing it), and any two of the
four numbers are coprime.

articles.title: Only $1$ is rough and smooth at the same bound
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural
numbers. If $n$ is $k$-rough and $n$ is positive with every prime factor less than
$k + 1$, then $n = 1$.

articles.title: A prime is rough exactly above the bound
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $k$ with $p$
prime, $p$ is $k$-rough if and only if $k < p$.

articles.title: Roughness through the list of prime factors
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $n$ is
$k$-rough if and only if $n \neq 0$ and every prime in the list of prime factors of $n$
(with multiplicity) is greater than $k$.

articles.title: Characterization of rough numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $n$ is $k$-rough
if and only if $n \neq 0$ and every prime $p$ dividing $n$ satisfies $k < p$.

articles.title: A product is rough exactly when both factors are
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$, $n$ and
$k$, the product $mn$ is $k$-rough if and only if both $m$ and $n$ are $k$-rough.

articles.title: The number $1$ is rough
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the number $1$ is $k$-rough.

This holds vacuously, since $1$ has no prime divisors.

articles.title: Rough numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers. Then $n$ is $k$-rough if $n \neq 0$
and every prime $p$ dividing $n$ satisfies $k < p$; that is, $n$ is positive and has no prime
factor at most $k$.

In particular $0$ is not rough, and $1$ is $k$-rough for every $k$ by vacuity.

## Sources

- Pandey, arXiv 2307.14890v1, footnote definition (`hybrid.tex` line 91).

articles.title: Prime divisors of a rough number exceed the bound
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $k$ and $p$ be natural
numbers. If $n$ is $k$-rough and $p$ is a prime dividing $n$, then $k < p$.

articles.title: Rough numbers other than $1$ lie in Mathlib's rough numbers up to a bound
articles.statement:
Let $n$,
$N$ and $k$ be natural numbers. If $n$ is $k$-rough, $n \le N$ and $n \ne 1$, then $n$ belongs
to the set of natural numbers $m$ with $1 \le m \le N$ that are not $(k+1)$-smooth, where $m$ is
$(k+1)$-smooth when $m > 0$ and every prime factor of $m$ is less than $k + 1$; for $m \ge 1$,
not being $(k+1)$-smooth means having a prime factor $p \ge k + 1$.

This set is Mathlib's set of rough numbers up to $N$ at bound $k + 1$. It asks only for some
prime factor $p \ge k + 1$, while $k$-roughness asks that every prime factor exceed $k$.

articles.title: Products of rough numbers are rough
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$, $n$ and $k$, if $m$ and
$n$ are both $k$-rough, then $mn$ is $k$-rough.

articles.title: Rough numbers are nonzero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, every $k$-rough natural number $n$
satisfies $n \ne 0$.

articles.title: Divisors of rough numbers are rough
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. If a natural number $m$
is $k$-rough and $d$ is a nonzero divisor of $m$, then $d$ is $k$-rough.

articles.title: Roughness is antitone in the bound
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $l$ be natural numbers with $l \le k$.
Every $k$-rough natural number is $l$-rough.

articles.title: Rough numbers are positive
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, every $k$-rough natural number
$n$ satisfies $n > 0$.

articles.title: Natural numbers with the same prime divisors
articles.statement:
Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ have the same
prime support when every prime $p$ divides $a$ if and only if it divides $b$.

articles.title: Entry 30 coefficients are multiplicative
articles.statement:
For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$
and all coprime $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Entry 30 coefficients $c_a$ satisfy
$c_a(mn) = c_a(m)\,c_a(n)$.

articles.title: Closed form of the Entry 30 coefficients
articles.statement:
For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$
and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ne 0$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n)$ equals the product of
$a(p)$ over the prime factors $p$ of $n$ when $n$ is squarefree, and $c_a(n) = 0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Entry 30 coefficients vanish at nonzero non-squarefree natural numbers
articles.statement:
For every
function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $n \ne 0$ that is not
squarefree, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n)$ is $0$.

articles.title: Entry 30 coefficients at squarefree integers
articles.statement:
For every function
$a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every squarefree $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ne 0$, the Entry 30
coefficient $c_a(n)$ is the product of $a(p)$ over the prime factors $p$ of $n$.

articles.title: The Entry 30 coefficient at one
articles.statement:
For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, the
Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(1)$ is $1$.

articles.title: Entry 30 coefficients vanish at higher prime powers
articles.statement:
For every function
$a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, every prime $p$ and every $e \ge 2$, the Entry 30 coefficient
satisfies $c_a(p^e) = 0$.

articles.title: Entry 30 coefficients at primes
articles.statement:
For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and
every prime $p$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(p)$ equals $a(p)$.

articles.title: The Entry 30 coefficient at zero
articles.statement:
For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, the
Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(0)$ is $0$.

articles.title: Coefficients for Entry 30
articles.statement:
For a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n) \in \mathbb{C}$ is $0$ when $n = 0$. When
$n \ne 0$ it is the product, over the prime factors $p$ of $n$, of the local factor of $a$ at $p$
with exponent the multiplicity of $p$ in $n$. The local factor at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $1$
for $e = 0$, $a(p)$ for $e = 1$, and $0$ for $e \ge 2$.

articles.title: Entry 30 local factors vanish at exponents at least two
articles.statement:
For every function
$a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, every $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $e \ge 2$, the Entry 30 local
factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $0$.

articles.title: Local factor at exponent one
articles.statement:
For every $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural
number $p$, the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $1$ is $a(p)$.

articles.title: Local factor at exponent zero
articles.statement:
For every $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural
number $p$, the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $0$ is $1$.

articles.title: Local factor
articles.statement:
Given $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and natural numbers $p$ and $e$,
the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $1$ if $e = 0$, $a(p)$ if $e = 1$, and $0$
if $e \ge 2$.

articles.title: Non-squarefree term, explicit form
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$, the
$j$-th term of the Dirichlet series over non-squarefree integers equals $0$ if $j + 1$ is
squarefree and $(j + 1)^{-s}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Terms of the Dirichlet series over non-squarefree integers
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a
natural number $j$, put $n = j + 1$; the $j$-th term is $0$ if $n$ is squarefree and $n^{-s}$
otherwise. As $j$ ranges over the natural numbers, these are the terms of $\sum n^{-s}$ over
non-squarefree $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Odd-count squarefree term, explicit form
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$,
the $j$-th term of the Dirichlet series over squarefree integers with an odd number of prime
factors equals $(j + 1)^{-s}$ if $j + 1$ is squarefree and has an odd number of distinct prime
factors, and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Terms over squarefree integers with an odd number of prime factors
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$
and a natural number $j$, put $n = j + 1$; the $j$-th term is $n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree and
has an odd number of distinct prime factors, and $0$ otherwise. As $j$ ranges over the natural
numbers, these are the terms of $\sum n^{-s}$ over squarefree $n \ge 1$ with an odd number of
prime factors.

articles.title: Explicit form of the signed coefficient
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number
$n \ne 0$, the signed coefficient of $n$ equals $-n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree with an odd number
of distinct prime factors, $n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree with an even number of distinct prime
factors, and $0$ if $n$ is not squarefree.

articles.title: Signed multiplicative coefficient
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $n$, let
$a(p) = -p^{-s}$ for natural numbers $p$. The signed coefficient of $n$ is $0$ if $n = 0$ and,
for $n \ne 0$, the product over the prime factors $p$ of $n$ of the local factor of $a$ at $p$
with exponent the multiplicity of $p$ in $n$, where the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent
$e$ is $1$ for $e = 0$, $a(p)$ for $e = 1$, and $0$ for $e \ge 2$.

articles.title: Squarefree term, explicit form
articles.statement:
For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$, the $j$-th
term of the Dirichlet series over squarefree integers equals $(j + 1)^{-s}$ if $j + 1$ is
squarefree and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Terms of the Dirichlet series over squarefree integers
articles.statement:
For a complex number $s$ and a
natural number $j$, let $n = j + 1$; the $j$-th squarefree term is $n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree
and $0$ otherwise, so the series of these terms over $j \ge 0$ is $\sum n^{-s}$ over the
squarefree $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 844 is true
articles.statement:
For every natural number $N$, the largest size of a set
$A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ such that $ab$ is not squarefree for all $a, b \in A$ (including
$a = b$) is the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le N$ that are even or not squarefree.

## Sources

- B. Alexeev, D. Mixon, and W. Sawin, The independence and clique cover numbers of the squarefree graph, arXiv:2507.01928 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01928; Erdős Problems, Problem 844 (including Desmond Weisenberg's proof), https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/844.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 844
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, let $E_N$ be the set of integers $n$ with
$1 \le n \le N$ that are even or not squarefree. The statement that for every natural number $N$,
the largest size of a set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ such that $ab$ is not squarefree for all
$a, b \in A$ (including $a = b$) is the size of $E_N$.

articles.title: Even or odd non-squarefree numbers up to a bound
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, the set of
integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le N$ that are even or not squarefree, that is, the even numbers in
$\{1, \dots, N\}$ together with the odd non-squarefree numbers in $\{1, \dots, N\}$.

articles.title: Euler product for the Entry 30 coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and let
$c > 1$ be real with $|a(p)| \le p^{-c}$ for every prime $p$. Write $f_a(n)$ for the Entry 30
coefficient of $a$ at $n$ (it is $0$ at $n = 0$; for $n \ge 1$ it is the product of $a(p)$ over
the primes $p \mid n$ if $n$ is squarefree, and $0$ otherwise). Then the product of $1 + a(p)$
over all primes $p$ converges unconditionally to $1 + \sum_{n \ge 2} f_a(n)$.

articles.title: Ramanujan's squarefree Dirichlet series (Entry 30)
articles.statement:
(i) Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$
and let $c > 1$ be real with $|a(p)| \le p^{-c}$ for every prime $p$, and write $f_a(n)$ for the
Entry 30 coefficient of $a$ at $n$. Then the family $(f_a(n))_{n \ge 2}$ is summable; for every
$n \ge 1$, $f_a(n)$ is the product of $a(p)$ over the primes $p \mid n$ if $n$ is squarefree and
$0$ otherwise; and the product of $1 + a(p)$ over all primes $p$ converges unconditionally to
$1 + \sum_{n \ge 2} f_a(n)$. (ii) Let $s$ be a complex number with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.
Then for every $n \ge 1$ the Entry 30 coefficient at $n$ of $p \mapsto -p^{-s}$ is $-n^{-s}$ if
$n$ is squarefree with an odd number of distinct prime factors, $n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree
with an even number of distinct prime factors, and $0$ if $n$ is not squarefree; $\zeta(s) \ne 0$
and $\zeta(2s) \ne 0$; the series of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ is summable with sum
$\zeta(s)/\zeta(2s)$; the series of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ with an odd number of
distinct prime factors is summable with sum $(\zeta(s)^2 - \zeta(2s))/(2\zeta(s)\zeta(2s))$; and
the series of $n^{-s}$ over the non-squarefree $n \ge 1$ is summable with sum
$\zeta(s)(\zeta(2s) - 1)/\zeta(2s)$.

## Sources

- Bruce C. Berndt, Ramanujan's Notebooks, Part I, Chapter 5, Entry 30, pp. 131–132.

articles.title: Summability of the Entry 30 coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and let
$c > 1$ be real with $|a(p)| \le p^{-c}$ for every prime $p$. Then the Entry 30 coefficients
$f_a(n)$ of $a$ (equal to $0$ at $n = 0$; for $n \ge 1$, the product of $a(p)$ over the primes
$p \mid n$ if $n$ is squarefree, and $0$ otherwise) form a summable family over $n \ge 2$.

articles.title: Summability of the non-squarefree terms
articles.statement:
For every complex number $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the series of $n^{-s}$ over the non-squarefree $n \ge 1$ is summable.

articles.title: Summability of the odd squarefree terms
articles.statement:
For every complex number $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the series of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ with an odd number
of distinct prime factors is summable.

articles.title: Summability of the squarefree terms
articles.statement:
For every complex number $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the series of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ is summable.

articles.title: Sum of $n^{-s}$ over non-squarefree $n$
articles.statement:
For every complex number $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the sum of $n^{-s}$ over the non-squarefree $n \ge 1$ equals
$\zeta(s)(\zeta(2s) - 1)/\zeta(2s)$.

articles.title: Sum of $n^{-s}$ over squarefree $n$ with an odd number of prime factors
articles.statement:
For every complex
number $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the sum of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ with
an odd number of distinct prime factors equals $(\zeta(s)^2 - \zeta(2s))/(2\zeta(s)\zeta(2s))$.

articles.title: Sum of $n^{-s}$ over squarefree $n$
articles.statement:
For every complex number $s$ with
$\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the sum of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ equals
$\zeta(s)/\zeta(2s)$.

articles.title: Primes completing a four-term prime-power divisibility
articles.statement:
Assume $(\ast)$: for all natural
numbers $a$, $f$, $g$ with $1 \le a \le f$, $\gcd(a, f) = 1$ and $4 \mid f$, and $g$ an odd prime
dividing $f$ with Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{g}{a}\right) = -1$, there is a prime
$\ell \equiv a \pmod f$ such that $g$ is a primitive root modulo $\ell$. Let $p$, $q$, $r$ be
distinct odd primes, at least one of which is congruent to $3$ or $5$ modulo $8$. Then there are
infinitely many primes $s$, distinct from $p$, $q$ and $r$, for each of which there are
infinitely many quadruples $(e_1, e_2, e_3, e_4)$ of positive integers with
$pqrs \mid p^{e_1} + q^{e_2} + r^{e_3} + s^{e_4}$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Fang–Chen theorem on shortest weakly prime-additive multiples
articles.statement:
For every positive integer
$m$, there are infinitely many weakly prime-additive numbers $n$ with $m \mid n$ and length
$\kappa_n = 3$ if and only if $8 \nmid m$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Theorem 5 (Fang and Chen, Corollary 1.1).

articles.title: Weakly prime-additive multiples of length four
articles.statement:
Assume $(\ast)$: for all natural numbers
$a$, $f$, $g$ with $1 \le a \le f$, $\gcd(a, f) = 1$ and $4 \mid f$, and $g$ an odd prime dividing
$f$ with Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{g}{a}\right) = -1$, there is a prime $\ell \equiv a \pmod f$
such that $g$ is a primitive root modulo $\ell$. Then for every positive integer $m$ there are
infinitely many weakly prime-additive numbers $n$ with $m \mid n$ and length $\kappa_n = 4$.

The paper states $(\ast)$ with the Kronecker symbol; since $a$ is coprime to $f$ and $4 \mid f$,
$a$ is odd, so it is the Jacobi symbol.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Weakly prime-additive multiples of length at most four
articles.statement:
Assume $(\ast)$: for all natural
numbers $a$, $f$, $g$ with $1 \le a \le f$, $\gcd(a, f) = 1$ and $4 \mid f$, and $g$ an odd prime
dividing $f$ with Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{g}{a}\right) = -1$, there is a prime
$\ell \equiv a \pmod f$ such that $g$ is a primitive root modulo $\ell$. Then for every positive
integer $m$ there are infinitely many weakly prime-additive numbers $n$ with $m \mid n$ and
length $\kappa_n \le 4$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Thirty is a sum of powers of three of its prime divisors
articles.statement:
The number $30$ is a sum of
positive powers of three distinct prime divisors of $30$, namely $30 = 2 + 3 + 5^2$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Section 1, Definition.

articles.title: Sums of powers of distinct prime divisors
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $t$, $n$ is a sum
of positive powers of $t$ distinct prime divisors of $n$ when there are a set $s$ of $t$ distinct
primes, each dividing $n$, and positive integers $e_p$ for $p \in s$ such that
$n = \sum_{p \in s} p^{e_p}$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Section 1, Definition (after Erdős and Hegyvári).

articles.title: Thirty is weakly prime-additive
articles.statement:
The number $30$ is weakly prime-additive.

Indeed, $30$ has the distinct prime divisors $2$, $3$, $5$ and $30 = 2 + 3 + 5^2$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Section 1, Definition.

articles.title: Weakly prime-additive numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is weakly prime-additive if it has at
least two distinct prime divisors and is a sum $n = \sum_{p \in s} p^{e_p}$ of positive powers
$p^{e_p}$, $e_p \ge 1$, over some set $s$ of distinct prime divisors of $n$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Section 1, Definition.

articles.title: The length is at most the size of any representation
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $t$,
if $n$ is a sum of positive powers of $t$ distinct prime divisors of $n$, then the length
$\kappa_n$ of $n$ is at most $t$.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Section 1, Definition (minimality of `κ_n`).

articles.title: Weakly prime-additive length
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the length $\kappa_n$ is the least
$t$ such that $n$ is a sum of positive powers of $t$ distinct prime divisors of $n$, and
$\kappa_n = 0$ when $n$ has no such representation.

## Sources

- Wing Hong Leung, *On the Weakly Prime-Additive Numbers with Length 4*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A9, Section 1, Definition.

articles.title: Unimodular solutions of a polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $R$ and $S$ be commutative semirings with $S$ an
$R$-algebra, and let $f$ be a multivariate polynomial over $R$ in variables indexed by a type
$\sigma$. Then $f$ has a solution in $S$ if there is a vector $x \in S^\sigma$ whose components
generate the unit ideal of $S$ and such that $f(x) = 0$, where $f$ is evaluated at $x$ through
the algebra map $R \to S$.

articles.title: Hypersurfaces of bounded height
articles.statement:
For a real number $A$, $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$ is the set of
degree-$d$ hypersurfaces $V \in \mathbb{V}_{d,n}$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$ whose height is at most $A$,
where the height of $V$ is the height of the chosen nonzero homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$
that represents $V$.

articles.title: Height of a rational polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a multivariate polynomial with rational
coefficients. Multiply the coefficients of $f$ by the least common multiple of their denominators
and divide the resulting integers by their greatest common divisor; this gives the primitive
integer coefficient vector $(a_m)_m$ of $f$, indexed by the monomials $m$ in the support of $f$.
The height of $f$ is the Euclidean norm $\sqrt{\sum_m a_m^2}$ of this vector. The zero polynomial
has height $0$.

articles.title: Local density of everywhere locally soluble hypersurfaces
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and
$n$ and a real number $A$, let $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$ be the set of degree-$d$ hypersurfaces in
$\mathbb{P}^n$ of height at most $A$, and let $\mathbb{V}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{d,n}$ be the set of
everywhere locally soluble ones. The local density $\rho^{\mathrm{loc}}_{d,n}$ is the limit, as
$A \to \infty$, of the number of elements of
$\mathbb{V}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{d,n} \cap \mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$ divided by the number of elements of
$\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$, a quotient taken to be $0$ when $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$ is empty; when this
limit does not exist, $\rho^{\mathrm{loc}}_{d,n}$ is an unspecified real number.

By a theorem of Poonen–Voloch [17, Th. 3.6], this limit exists (and is positive) when
$d \ge 2$, $n \ge 2$ and $(d, n) \ne (2, 2)$, and equals a product of local densities over all
places of $\mathbb{Q}$.

articles.title: Everywhere locally soluble hypersurfaces
articles.statement:
$\mathbb{V}^{\mathrm{loc}}_{d,n}$ is the set of
degree-$d$ hypersurfaces $V \in \mathbb{V}_{d,n}$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$ that are everywhere locally
soluble, that is, with $V(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}) \ne \emptyset$: the chosen homogeneous polynomial
representing $V$ has a solution in the adele ring $\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}$, namely a zero given by
$n + 1$ adeles that generate the unit ideal of $\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}$.

articles.title: Density of soluble Fano hypersurfaces
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $d \ge 2$,
$n \ge d$ and $(d, n) \ne (3, 3)$. Then the proportion $\rho_{d,n}(A)$ of degree-$d$
hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^n$ of height at most $A$ that have a rational point tends to the
local density $\rho^{\mathrm{loc}}_{d,n}$ as the real number $A$ tends to $\infty$.

## Sources

- T. Browning, P. L. Boudec, and W. Sawin, `The Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces`, Annals of Math, 197 (3) 2023. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_hasse_principle_random_fano` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Parameter space of hypersurfaces
articles.statement:
$\mathbb{V}_{d,n}$ is the projectivization of the
$\mathbb{Q}$-vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n + 1$ variables with
rational coefficients; its points are the degree-$d$ hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^n$ defined over
$\mathbb{Q}$. Since this space has dimension $N_{d,n} = \binom{n+d}{d}$, the number of degree-$d$
monomials in $n + 1$ variables, $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}$ is a copy of
$\mathbb{P}^{N_{d,n} - 1}(\mathbb{Q})$.

articles.title: Proportion of soluble hypersurfaces of bounded height
articles.statement:
For a real number $A$,
$\rho_{d,n}(A)$ is the proportion of hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$, the degree-$d$
hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^n$ of height at most $A$, that have a rational point: it is the
number of $V \in \mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$ with $V(\mathbb{Q}) \ne \emptyset$ divided by the number of
elements of $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$, taken to be $0$ when $\mathbb{V}_{d,n}(A)$ is empty. Here
$V(\mathbb{Q}) \ne \emptyset$ means that the chosen homogeneous polynomial representing $V$ has a
nonzero rational zero.

articles.title: Adele ring of the rationals
articles.statement:
$\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q}$, also written $\mathbb{A}$, is the
adele ring of $\mathbb{Q}$.

articles.title: Height lower bound on $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ when $|a|$ is small
articles.statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$
with $ab \ne 0$ and $4a^3 + 27b^2 \ne 0$, let $\lVert p \rVert = \sqrt{2 + a^2 + b^2}$, and suppose
$1 + |a| < \lVert p \rVert^{1/2}/1.782$. For $u, v \in \mathbb{Q}$ let
$H(u, v) = \max(|U|, |V|, |W|)$, where $U, V, W$ are coprime integers with
$(U : V : W) = (u : v : 1)$. Then every rational solution $(u, v)$ of $v^2 = u^3 + au + b$ with
$uv \ne 0$ satisfies $H(u, v) > \lVert p \rVert^{1/6}/1.634$.

## Sources

- Dimitrios Poulakis, *Lower Bounds for the Height of Rational Points of Elliptic Curves*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A66, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Height lower bounds on $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ when $b = \pm a$, $b = 0$ or $a = 0$
articles.statement:
Let
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $4a^3 + 27b^2 \ne 0$, and for $u, v \in \mathbb{Q}$ let
$H(u, v) = \max(|U|, |V|, |W|)$, where $U, V, W$ are coprime integers with
$(U : V : W) = (u : v : 1)$. Consider the rational solutions $(u, v)$ of $v^2 = u^3 + au + b$.
(a) If $b = a$, every solution has $H(u, v) \ge (|a|/4)^{1/3}$.
(b) If $b = -a$, every solution with $H(u, v) < (|a|/4)^{1/3}$ is $(1, 1)$ or $(1, -1)$.
(c) If $b = 0$, every solution with $H(u, v) < (|a|/4)^{1/3}$ is $(0, 0)$.
(d) If $a = 0$, every solution has $H(u, v) \ge (|b|/3)^{1/3}$.

In (b) the points $(1, \pm 1)$ and the point at infinity need not form a subgroup of order
three: for $a = 5$, doubling $(1, 1)$ gives $(14, -53)$.

## Sources

- Dimitrios Poulakis, *Lower Bounds for the Height of Rational Points of Elliptic Curves*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A66, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Height lower bounds on $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ when $a = \pm 1$ or $b = \pm 1$
articles.statement:
Let
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $4a^3 + 27b^2 \ne 0$, and for $u, v \in \mathbb{Q}$ let
$H(u, v) = \max(|U|, |V|, |W|)$, where $U, V, W$ are coprime integers with
$(U : V : W) = (u : v : 1)$. Consider the rational solutions $(u, v)$ of $v^2 = u^3 + au + b$.
(a) If $a = \pm 1$ and $b \notin \{0, 1, -1\}$, every solution has $H(u, v) \ge (|b|/5)^{1/3}$.
(b) If $a \notin \{0, 1, -1\}$ and $b = -1$, every solution has $H(u, v) \ge (|a|/5)^{1/3}$.
(c) If $a \notin \{0, 1, -1\}$ and $b = 1$, every solution with $H(u, v) < (|a|/5)^{1/3}$ is
$(0, 1)$ or $(0, -1)$.

## Sources

- Dimitrios Poulakis, *Lower Bounds for the Height of Rational Points of Elliptic Curves*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A66, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Height of a point on $y^2 = x^3 + ax - b$ versus the height of its $x$-coordinate
articles.statement:
Let
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a \ne 0$, $b > 0$ and $4a^3 + 27b^2 \ne 0$. For $u \in \mathbb{Q}$
let $H(u) = \max(|u_0|, u_1)$, where $u = u_0/u_1$ in lowest terms with $u_1 > 0$, and for
$u, v \in \mathbb{Q}$ let $H(u, v) = \max(|U|, |V|, |W|)$, where $U, V, W$ are coprime integers
with $(U : V : W) = (u : v : 1)$. Then every rational solution $(u, v)$ of
$v^2 = u^3 + au - b$ satisfies $H(u, v) < \sqrt{1 + |a|}\, H(u)^{3/2}$.

## Sources

- Dimitrios Poulakis, *Lower Bounds for the Height of Rational Points of Elliptic Curves*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A66, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Apollonian group
articles.statement:
The Apollonian group is the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$
generated by the four matrices $S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$, where $S_i$ agrees with the $4 \times 4$
identity matrix except in row $i$, which has entry $-1$ in column $i$ and entry $2$ in each of
the other three columns.

## Sources

- S. Haag, C. Kertzer, J. Rickards, and K. E. Stange, `The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false`, Annals of Math, 200 (2) 2024, start of Section 3.

articles.title: Curvature set
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a primitive Apollonian circle packing, viewed as an orbit of
integral primitive Descartes quadruples. The curvature set of $A$ is the set of all integers
that occur as an entry of some quadruple in $A$.

articles.title: Descartes matrix
articles.statement:
The Descartes matrix is the $4 \times 4$ integer matrix $M$ with
$M_{ii} = 1$ for every $i$ and $M_{ij} = -1$ for $i \ne j$. It is the matrix of the Descartes
form: for $v = (a, b, c, d) \in \mathbb{Z}^4$ one has
$v^{\mathsf T} M v = 2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2) - (a + b + c + d)^2$.

articles.title: Descartes orthogonal group action
articles.statement:
Let $Q$ be the set of vectors
$(a, b, c, d) \in \mathbb{Z}^4$ with $(a + b + c + d)^2 = 2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2)$ and
$\gcd(a, b, c, d) = 1$. For every matrix $X$ in the Descartes orthogonal group and every $v \in Q$,
the vector $Xv$ lies in $Q$, so the Descartes orthogonal group acts on $Q$ by $v \mapsto Xv$.

articles.title: Descartes orthogonal group
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be the Descartes matrix. The Descartes orthogonal
group is the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ consisting of the matrices $X$ with
