$X^{\mathsf T} M X = M$, that is, the invertible integer matrices that preserve the Descartes
form $2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2) - (a + b + c + d)^2$.

articles.title: General linear group action on primitive vectors
articles.statement:
Call $v \in \mathbb{Z}^4$ primitive
when the greatest common divisor of its four entries is $1$. For every
$X \in \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ and every primitive $v$, the vector $Xv$ is primitive, so
$\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ acts on the primitive vectors of $\mathbb{Z}^4$ by $v \mapsto Xv$.

articles.title: Integral primitive Descartes quadruple
articles.statement:
An integral primitive Descartes quadruple is a
vector $(a, b, c, d) \in \mathbb{Z}^4$ such that $a + b + c + d > 0$, the Descartes equation
$(a + b + c + d)^2 = 2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2)$ holds, and $\gcd(a, b, c, d) = 1$.

## Sources

- S. Haag, C. Kertzer, J. Rickards, and K. E. Stange, `The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false`, Annals of Math, 200 (2) 2024, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Missing curvature set
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a primitive Apollonian circle packing. The missing
curvature set of $A$ is the set of positive integers $n$ that do not lie in the curvature set
of $A$ but are congruent modulo $24$ to some element of the curvature set of $A$.

## Sources

- S. Haag, C. Kertzer, J. Rickards, and K. E. Stange, `The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false`, Annals of Math, 200 (2) 2024, start of Section 1.2.

articles.title: Number of missing curvatures
articles.statement:
For a primitive Apollonian circle packing $A$ and a real
number $N$, the number of missing curvatures of $A$ up to $N$ is the number of elements $n$ of
the missing curvature set of $A$ with $n \le N$, regarded as a real number.

articles.title: Primitive Apollonian circle packing
articles.statement:
A primitive Apollonian circle packing is an orbit of
the transformation group acting on the set of integral primitive Descartes quadruples.

articles.title: The Apollonian generator $S_2$
articles.statement:
$S_2$ is the element of $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ given
by the $4 \times 4$ integer matrix whose second row is $(2, -1, 2, 2)$ and whose other rows are
those of the identity matrix; it is its own inverse. Acting on column vectors, it sends
$(a, b, c, d)$ to $(a, 2a - b + 2c + 2d, c, d)$.

It is one of the four generators of the Apollonian group defined at the start of Section 3 of
Haag, Kertzer, Rickards and Stange.

articles.title: The Apollonian generator $S_3$
articles.statement:
$S_3$ is the element of $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ given
by the $4 \times 4$ integer matrix whose third row is $(2, 2, -1, 2)$ and whose other rows are
those of the identity matrix; it is its own inverse. Acting on column vectors, it sends
$(a, b, c, d)$ to $(a, b, 2a + 2b - c + 2d, d)$.

It is one of the four generators of the Apollonian group defined at the start of Section 3 of
Haag, Kertzer, Rickards and Stange.

articles.title: The Apollonian generator $S_4$
articles.statement:
$S_4$ is the element of $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ given
by the $4 \times 4$ integer matrix whose fourth row is $(2, 2, 2, -1)$ and whose other rows are
those of the identity matrix; it is its own inverse. Acting on column vectors, it sends
$(a, b, c, d)$ to $(a, b, c, 2a + 2b + 2c - d)$.

It is one of the four generators of the Apollonian group defined at the start of Section 3 of
Haag, Kertzer, Rickards and Stange.

articles.title: The Apollonian generator $S_1$
articles.statement:
$S_1$ is the element of $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ given
by the $4 \times 4$ integer matrix whose first row is $(-1, 2, 2, 2)$ and whose other rows are
those of the identity matrix; it is its own inverse. Acting on column vectors, it sends
$(a, b, c, d)$ to $(-a + 2b + 2c + 2d, b, c, d)$.

It is one of the four generators of the Apollonian group defined at the start of Section 3 of
Haag, Kertzer, Rickards and Stange.

articles.title: Infinitely many packings with many missing curvatures
articles.statement:
For a primitive Apollonian circle
packing $\mathcal{A}$ and a real number $N$, let $M_{\mathcal{A}}(N)$ be the number of missing
curvatures of $\mathcal{A}$ up to $N$. There are infinitely many primitive Apollonian circle
packings $\mathcal{A}$ such that $\sqrt{N} = O(M_{\mathcal{A}}(N))$ as $N$ tends to infinity.
In other words, for these packings the number of missing curvatures up to $N$ is
$\Omega(\sqrt{N})$.

## Sources

- S. Haag, C. Kertzer, J. Rickards, and K. E. Stange, `The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false`, Annals of Math, 200 (2) 2024. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_local_global_apollonian_circle_packings` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: A packing with no square curvatures
articles.statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the primitive Apollonian circle
packing generated by the integral primitive Descartes quadruple $(-3, 5, 8, 8)$. For every
integer $n$, $n^2$ does not belong to the curvature set of $\mathcal{A}$.

## Sources

- S. Haag, C. Kertzer, J. Rickards, and K. E. Stange, `The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false`, Annals of Math, 200 (2) 2024. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_local_global_apollonian_circle_packings` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Action of the transformation group on integral primitive Descartes quadruples
articles.statement:
Each
element $g$ of the transformation group sends an integral primitive Descartes quadruple $v$ to
$g v$, by matrix–vector multiplication: this is the restriction of the action of the
transformation group on $\mathbb{Z}^4$ to the set of integral primitive Descartes quadruples,
which is closed under the action.

articles.title: The transformation group preserves integral primitive Descartes quadruples
articles.statement:
For every $g$ in the transformation group, $g$ maps the set of integral primitive Descartes
quadruples into itself: if $v \in \mathbb{Z}^4$ is an integral primitive Descartes quadruple,
then so is $g v$.

articles.title: The transformation group
articles.statement:
The transformation group is the subgroup of
$\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})$ generated by the Apollonian group together with all $4 \times 4$
permutation matrices.

articles.title: The Mazur class of abelian groups
articles.statement:
An abelian group $T$ is in the Mazur class when it is
isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ for some $n \in \{1, 2, \ldots, 10, 12\}$, or to
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2m\mathbb{Z}$ for some $m \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$.

articles.title: Mazur's torsion theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$. The torsion
subgroup of the group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points of $E$ is finite and has at most $16$
elements.

Only this bound is stated, not Mazur's full list of the fifteen possible torsion subgroups.

## Sources

- B. Mazur, *Modular curves and the Eisenstein ideal*, Publ. Math. IHÉS 47 (1977), 33–186, doi:10.1007/BF02684339, <https://www.numdam.org/item/?id=PMIHES_1977__47__33_0>.

articles.title: Mazur's torsion theorem
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$, given by a
Weierstrass equation. The torsion subgroup of the group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points of $E$
is in the Mazur class: it is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ for some
$n \in \{1, 2, \ldots, 10, 12\}$, or to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2m\mathbb{Z}$ for
some $m \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$.

## Sources

- B. Mazur, *Modular curves and the Eisenstein ideal*, Publ. IHÉS 47 (1977). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §139. Problem `mazur_torsion` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Multivariable Hensel lemma over the p-adic integers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let
$f \in \mathbb{Z}_p[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}_p^n$, and suppose that for some index
$i$ the $p$-adic absolute values satisfy $|f(a)|_p < |(\partial f / \partial x_i)(a)|_p^2$, that
is, $\operatorname{ord}_p f(a) > 2 \operatorname{ord}_p (\partial f / \partial x_i)(a)$. Then
there is a point $x \in \mathbb{Z}_p^n$ with $f(x) = 0$.

## Sources

- Renz Jimwel Mina and Jerico Bacani, *Rank of the Elliptic Curve y^2=x^3-2pqx*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A51, Lemma 1, quoted there as Hensel's lemma.

articles.title: Odd-rank curves y² = x³ − 2pqx: rank one, three or five case
articles.statement:
Let $p \ne q$ be primes
with $p \equiv q \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ and Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = 1$, and let
$E$ be the elliptic curve $y^2 = x^3 - 2pqx$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the rank of the group
$E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points is odd, then it equals $1$, $3$ or $5$.

The odd-rank hypothesis stands for the parity conjecture for $E$.

## Sources

- Renz Jimwel Mina and Jerico Bacani, *Rank of the Elliptic Curve y^2=x^3-2pqx*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A51, Theorem 1 (iii).

articles.title: Odd-rank curves y² = x³ − 2pqx: rank one or three cases
articles.statement:
Let $p \ne q$ be primes and let
$E$ be the elliptic curve $y^2 = x^3 - 2pqx$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, and write
$\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)$ for the Legendre symbol. Suppose that $p \equiv q \equiv 1 \pmod 8$
and $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = -1$, or that $p \equiv q \equiv 7 \pmod 8$, or that
$p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, $q \equiv 3, 5$ or $7 \pmod 8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) = 1$. If the
rank of the group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points is odd, then it equals $1$ or $3$.

The odd-rank hypothesis stands for the parity conjecture for $E$.

## Sources

- Renz Jimwel Mina and Jerico Bacani, *Rank of the Elliptic Curve y^2=x^3-2pqx*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A51, Theorem 1 (ii).

articles.title: Odd-rank curves y² = x³ − 2pqx: rank one cases
articles.statement:
Let $p \ne q$ be primes and let $E$ be
the elliptic curve $y^2 = x^3 - 2pqx$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Suppose that
$(p \bmod 8, q \bmod 8)$ is one of $(3, 3)$, $(3, 5)$, $(3, 7)$, $(5, 5)$, $(5, 7)$, or that
$p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, $q \equiv 3, 5$ or $7 \pmod 8$ and the Legendre symbol
$\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)$ equals $-1$. If the rank of the group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational
points is odd, then it equals $1$.

The odd-rank hypothesis stands for the parity conjecture for $E$. The case with $p$ and $q$
interchanged is the same curve.

## Sources

- Renz Jimwel Mina and Jerico Bacani, *Rank of the Elliptic Curve y^2=x^3-2pqx*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A51, Theorem 1 (i).

articles.title: Odd-rank curves y² = x³ − 2pqx: a rank three family
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a positive integer such
that $p = 272r^2 + 120r + 9$ and $q = 2p + 9 = 544r^2 + 240r + 27$ are both prime, and let $E$
be the elliptic curve $y^2 = x^3 - 2pqx$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the rank of the group
$E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points is odd, then it equals $3$.

The odd-rank hypothesis stands for the parity conjecture for $E$.

## Sources

- Renz Jimwel Mina and Jerico Bacani, *Rank of the Elliptic Curve y^2=x^3-2pqx*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A51, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: even squarefree, three or more primes
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an even squarefree natural number with at least three prime factors, let $P$ be its
largest prime factor and $d = n / P$, and let $g(n)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic
progression in the absolute least reduced residue system modulo $n$. Then
$\lfloor P - 2P/d \rfloor \le g(n) \le P - 1$, and if $d \ge 2P$ then $g(n) = P - 1$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues modulo 5
articles.statement:
The length $g(5)$ of the
longest arithmetic progression in the absolute least reduced residue system modulo $5$ is $2$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Example 1(i).

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: odd squarefree composite moduli
articles.statement:
Let
$n > 1$ be an odd squarefree natural number that is not prime, let $P$ be its largest prime
factor and $d = n / P$, and let $g(n)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic progression in the
absolute least reduced residue system modulo $n$. Then
$g(n) = \lfloor P - (P + 1)/(2d) \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: neither squarefree nor prime power
articles.statement:
Let
$n > 1$ be a natural number that is neither squarefree nor a prime power, let
$\operatorname{rad}(n)$ be the product of the distinct primes dividing $n$ and $P$ the largest
prime factor of $n$, and let $g(n)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic progression in the
absolute least reduced residue system modulo $n$. Then
$g(n) = \max(n / \operatorname{rad}(n), P - 1)$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: primes congruent to 3 mod 4
articles.statement:
For a
prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, the length $g(p)$ of the longest arithmetic progression in the
absolute least reduced residue system modulo $p$ is $(p + 1)/2$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: primes congruent to 1 mod 4
articles.statement:
For a
prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, the length $g(p)$ of the longest arithmetic progression in the
absolute least reduced residue system modulo $p$ is $(p - 1)/2$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and
$r \ge 1$, with $r \ge 2$ when $p$ is odd. Then the length $g(p^r)$ of the longest arithmetic
progression in the absolute least reduced residue system modulo $p^r$ is $p^{r-1}$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progressions of absolute least residues: twice an odd prime
articles.statement:
For an odd prime
$p$, the length $g(2p)$ of the longest arithmetic progression in the absolute least reduced
residue system modulo $2p$ is $p - 1$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Longest progression in the absolute least reduced residues
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$,
let $R(n)$ be the set of integers $a$ with $1 - \lceil n/2 \rceil \le a \le n - \lceil n/2 \rceil$
and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, the system of absolute least reduced residues modulo $n$. Then $g(n)$ is
the largest $s \ge 0$ for which there are an integer $b$ and a positive integer $d$ with
$b + i d \in R(n)$ for every $0 \le i < s$: the length of the longest arithmetic progression
with positive common difference contained in $R(n)$. Equivalently,
$g(n) = f_{-\lceil n/2 \rceil}(n)$, where $f_m(n)$ is the same length for the set
$R_m(n)$ of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Section 1.

articles.title: Length bound for progressions in a reduced residue window
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an integer and $n$
a natural number, and let $R_m(n)$ be the set of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and
$\gcd(a, n) = 1$. If $b$ is an integer, $d$ a positive integer and $s$ a natural number such
that $b + i d \in R_m(n)$ for every $0 \le i < s$, then $s \le n$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6 (`R_m(n) ⊆ [m + 1, m + n]`).

articles.title: Average longest progression length for non-squarefree moduli
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be a natural
number that is not squarefree, $\operatorname{rad}(n)$ the product of its distinct prime factors
and $\operatorname{gpf}(n)$ its largest prime factor, and suppose that
$\operatorname{gpf}(n) - 1 \le n / \operatorname{rad}(n)$. For an integer $m$ let $f_m(n)$ be the
length of the longest arithmetic progression with positive common difference contained in the
set $R_m(n)$ of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then
$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} f_m(n) = \frac{n}{\operatorname{rad}(n)}$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Maximum longest progression length over all reduced residue windows
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be a
natural number, $\operatorname{rad}(n)$ the product of its distinct prime factors and
$\operatorname{gpf}(n)$ its largest prime factor. For an integer $m$ let $f_m(n)$ be the length of
the longest arithmetic progression with positive common difference contained in the set $R_m(n)$
of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then the largest value of
$f_m(n)$ over all integers $m$ is $\max(n / \operatorname{rad}(n), \operatorname{gpf}(n) - 1)$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Minimum longest progression length modulo a prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. For an integer $m$ let $f_m(p)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic
progression with positive common difference contained in the set $R_m(p)$ of integers $a$ with
$m + 1 \le a \le m + p$ and $\gcd(a, p) = 1$. Then the least value of $f_m(p)$ over all integers
$m$ is $(p + 1) / 2$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Minimum longest progression length modulo a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. For an integer $m$ let $f_m(p)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic
progression with positive common difference contained in the set $R_m(p)$ of integers $a$ with
$m + 1 \le a \le m + p$ and $\gcd(a, p) = 1$. Then the least value of $f_m(p)$ over all integers
$m$ is $(p - 1) / 2$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Minimum longest progression length modulo a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $r > 1$ a
natural number. For an integer $m$ let $f_m(p^r)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic
progression with positive common difference contained in the set $R_m(p^r)$ of integers $a$ with
$m + 1 \le a \le m + p^r$ and $\gcd(a, p^r) = 1$. Then the least value of $f_m(p^r)$ over all
integers $m$ is $p^{r-1}$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 3.

articles.title: The longest progression length is at most the modulus
articles.statement:
For every integer $m$ and natural
number $n$, $f_m(n) \le n$, where $f_m(n)$ is the length of the longest arithmetic progression
with positive common difference contained in the set $R_m(n)$ of integers $a$ with
$m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6 (`R_m(n)` has at most `n` elements).

articles.title: Minimum longest progression length when $n$ is neither squarefree nor a prime power
articles.statement:
Let
$n > 1$ be a natural number that is neither squarefree nor a prime power, $\operatorname{rad}(n)$
the product of its distinct prime factors and $\operatorname{gpf}(n)$ its largest prime factor.
For an integer $m$ let $f_m(n)$ be the length of the longest arithmetic progression with positive
common difference contained in the set $R_m(n)$ of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and
$\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then $f_m(n) \ge n / \operatorname{rad}(n)$ for every integer $m$, and
$f_m(n) \le \max(n / \operatorname{rad}(n), \operatorname{gpf}(n) - 1)$ for some integer $m$.
If moreover $\operatorname{gpf}(n) - 1 \le n / \operatorname{rad}(n)$, then the least value of
$f_m(n)$ over all integers $m$ is $n / \operatorname{rad}(n)$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Squarefree bound for progressions with a fixed difference
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an integer, $n > 1$
a squarefree natural number with largest prime factor $\operatorname{gpf}(n)$, and $d > 0$ a
natural number. Then $f_m(d, n) \le \operatorname{gpf}(n) - 1$, where $f_m(d, n)$ is the length of
the longest arithmetic progression with common difference $d$ contained in the set $R_m(n)$ of
integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Lemma 1(ii).

articles.title: Prime bound for progressions with a fixed difference
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an integer, $n > 1$ and
$d > 0$ natural numbers, and $p$ a prime that divides $n$ but not $d$. Then $f_m(d, n) \le p - 1$,
where $f_m(d, n)$ is the length of the longest arithmetic progression with common difference $d$
contained in the set $R_m(n)$ of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

## Sources

- Chaninat Phothila, Natthakan Thoket and Narakorn Rompurk Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Lemma 1(i).

articles.title: Longest progression with a given common difference
articles.statement:
For an integer $m$ and natural numbers
$n$ and $d$, let $R_m(n)$ be the set of integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and
$\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then $f_m(d, n)$ is the supremum of the natural numbers $s$ for which some
integer $b$ has $b + i d \in R_m(n)$ for every natural number $i < s$. For $d > 0$ every such $s$
is at most $n$, so $f_m(d, n)$ is the length of the longest arithmetic progression with common
difference $d$ contained in $R_m(n)$; the paper uses it only for $d > 0$, and for $d = 0$ the
definition gives $0$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Section 2.

articles.title: Length of the longest arithmetic progression in a reduced residue system
articles.statement:
For an
integer $m$ and a natural number $n$, let $R_m(n)$ be the reduced residue system of the
integers $a$ with $m + 1 \le a \le m + n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then $f_m(n)$ is the largest
natural number $s$ for which there are an integer $b$ and a positive integer $d$ such that
$b, b + d, \dots, b + (s - 1)d$ all lie in $R_m(n)$. So it is the length of the longest
arithmetic progression with positive common difference contained in $R_m(n)$, where a single
term counts as a progression of length $1$, and $f_m(n) = 0$ when $R_m(n)$ is empty.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Section 1.

articles.title: The reduced residue system $R_{-3}(5)$
articles.statement:
The reduced residue system $R_{-3}(5)$ of the
integers $a$ with $-2 \le a \le 2$ and $\gcd(a, 5) = 1$ is $\{-2, -1, 1, 2\}$: an integer $a$
lies in $R_{-3}(5)$ if and only if $a$ is one of $-2$, $-1$, $1$, $2$.

Since $\lceil 5/2 \rceil = 3$, this is the system $R(5) = R_{-\lceil 5/2 \rceil}(5)$ of absolute
least reduced residues modulo $5$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Example 1(i).

articles.title: The reduced residue system $R_m(n)$
articles.statement:
For an integer $m$ and a natural number $n$, the
reduced residue system $R_m(n)$ modulo $n$ is the finite set
$R_m(n) = \{a \in \mathbb{Z} : m + 1 \le a \le m + n,\ \gcd(a, n) = 1\}$.

## Sources

- Phothila, Thoket and Kanasri, *Length of the Longest Arithmetic Progressions in a Certain Reduced Residue System*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A6, Section 1.

articles.title: Reflection congruence for binomial coefficients modulo a prime
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and
natural numbers $j$ and $k$ with $j \le k \le p - 2$,

$$\binom{p-j}{k+1} + (-1)^k \binom{k+j}{k+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}.$$

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Lemma 11.

articles.title: Expansion of $\binom{sp-1}{k}$ modulo $p^3$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $s$ an integer
and $k$ a natural number with $1 \le k \le p - 1$, and let $H_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} i^{-1}$ and
$H_{k,2} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (i^2)^{-1}$ be the harmonic numbers of orders one and two in
$\mathbb{Z}/p^3\mathbb{Z}$. Then in $\mathbb{Z}/p^3\mathbb{Z}$

$$
\frac{1}{k!} \prod_{i=1}^{k} (sp - i) =
(-1)^k \Bigl(1 - sp\,H_k + \frac{s^2 p^2}{2} \bigl(H_k^2 - H_{k,2}\bigr)\Bigr),
$$

where $1/k!$ and $1/2$ are inverses in $\mathbb{Z}/p^3\mathbb{Z}$; the left side is the
binomial coefficient $\binom{sp-1}{k}$.

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Lemma 5.

articles.title: Delannoy triangle entry $T(np-1, p-1; 1)$ modulo $p^3$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime and
$n \ge 1$ a natural number, let $q_p(2) = (2^{p-1} - 1)/p$ be the Fermat quotient of $2$, and
let $T(a, b; 1)$ denote the entry of the ordinary Riordan Pascal-like triangle with $r = 1$
(the Delannoy triangle). Then

$$T(np - 1, p - 1; 1) \equiv 1 + (n - 1)\,p\,q_p(2)\,\bigl(2 - p\,q_p(2)\bigr) \pmod{p^3}.$$

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Theorem 4.

articles.title: Delannoy triangle entries $T(2p, p; 1)$ and $T(2p-1, p-1; 1)$ modulo $p^3$
articles.statement:
Let
$p \ge 5$ be a prime, let $q_p(2) = (2^{p-1} - 1)/p$ be the Fermat quotient of $2$, and let
$T(n, k; 1)$ denote the entry of the ordinary Riordan Pascal-like triangle with $r = 1$ (the
Delannoy triangle). Then

$$T(2p, p; 1) \equiv 3 + 2p\,q_p(2) - p^2 q_p(2)^2 \pmod{p^3}$$

and

$$T(2p-1, p-1; 1) \equiv 1 + 2p\,q_p(2) - p^2 q_p(2)^2 \pmod{p^3}.$$

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Harmonic numbers of order two modulo $m$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $k$, the
harmonic number $H_{k,2}$ of order two modulo $m$ is the residue $\sum_{i=1}^{k} (i^2)^{-1}$
in $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, where $(i^2)^{-1}$ is the inverse of $i^2$ modulo $m$ when $i$ is
coprime to $m$; for other $i$ it is the conventional value that Mathlib assigns to the
inverse of a non-unit.

articles.title: Harmonic numbers modulo $m$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $k$, the harmonic number
$H_k$ modulo $m$ is the residue $\sum_{i=1}^{k} i^{-1}$ in $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, where
$i^{-1}$ is the inverse of $i$ modulo $m$ when $i$ is coprime to $m$; for other $i$ it is the
conventional value that Mathlib assigns to the inverse of a non-unit.

articles.title: A binomial sum through central Delannoy numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$,

$$4 \sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{k}{j} \binom{k+j}{k+1} = D_{k+1} - 3 D_k,$$

where $D_n = A_{1,1}(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} \binom{n+i}{i}$ is the binomial-power
number with $r = s = 1$, that is, the $n$-th central Delannoy number.

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Lemma 13.

articles.title: Sum of the Delannoy triangle entries in rows $0$ to $p - 1$ modulo $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an
odd prime and let $T(n, k; 1)$ denote the entry of the ordinary Riordan Pascal-like triangle
with $r = 1$ (the Delannoy triangle). Then

$$\sum_{n=0}^{p-1} \sum_{k=0}^{n} T(n, k; 1) \equiv \left(\frac{2}{p}\right) \pmod{p},$$

where $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)$ is the Legendre symbol.

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Theorem 9.

articles.title: Sum of $H_k 2^k / k$ over $1 \le k \le p - 1$ modulo $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime, let
$q_p(2) = (2^{p-1} - 1)/p$ be the Fermat quotient of $2$, and let $H_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} 1/i$
be the harmonic number modulo $p$, where $1/i$ is the inverse of $i$ modulo $p$. Then

$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{H_k\, 2^k}{k} \equiv -q_p(2)^2 \pmod{p}.$$

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Lemma 7.

articles.title: Sums of $2^k/k$ and $2^k/k^2$ over $1 \le k \le p - 1$
articles.statement:
Let $p > 3$ be a prime and let
$q_p(2) = (2^{p-1} - 1)/p$ be the Fermat quotient of $2$. Then

$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{2^k}{k} \equiv -2\,q_p(2) \pmod{p^2}$$

and

$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{2^k}{k^2} \equiv -q_p(2)^2 \pmod{p},$$

where $1/k$ is the inverse of $k$ modulo $p^2$ and $1/k^2$ the inverse of $k^2$ modulo $p$.

## Sources

- Chahinaze Djadi and Hacène Belbachir, "Congruence Properties for the Delannoy Triangle Coefficients", Lemma 6.

articles.title: Euler–Fermat congruence modulo prime powers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $a$, every prime $p$
and every natural number $r \ge 1$, we have $a^{p^r} \equiv a^{p^{r-1}} \pmod{p^r}$.

articles.title: Euler–Fermat congruence modulo prime powers, for positive bases
articles.statement:
For every positive natural
number $a$, every prime $p$ and every natural number $r \ge 1$, we have
$a^{p^r} \equiv a^{p^{r-1}} \pmod{p^r}$.

## Sources

- G. Everest, A. J. van der Poorten, Y. Puri, and T. Ward, "Integer Sequences and Periodic Points," Journal of Integer Sequences 5 (2002), Article 02.2.3, Corollary; public TeX: <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL5/Ward/ward2.tex>. It follows from `euler_fermat_prime_power_congruence_general`; the hypothesis `ha` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Formula for the Fermat quotient
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, the
Fermat quotient satisfies $q_p(a) = (a^{p-1} - 1)/p$, where $/$ is integer division rounding
down.

articles.title: Fermat quotient
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, the Fermat quotient
is the integer $q_p(a) = (a^{p-1} - 1)/p$, where $/$ is integer division rounding down. The
division is exact, since $p$ divides $a^{p-1} - 1$ by Fermat's little theorem.

articles.title: Fermat quotient times the prime
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, the
Fermat quotient $q_p(a)$ satisfies $p \, q_p(a) = a^{p-1} - 1$.

articles.title: Lifting the exponent for odd primes
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $a \ne b$ be integers
such that $p$ divides $a - b$ but does not divide $ab$, and let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number.
Then

$$v_p(a^n - b^n) = v_p(n) + v_p(a - b),$$

where $v_p$ denotes the $p$-adic valuation.

articles.title: Lifting a congruence to one along powers of the modulus
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $n$ and $a$ be natural
numbers. If $a \equiv 1 \pmod p$, then $a^{p^n} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^{n+1}}$.

The modulus $p$ need not be prime.

articles.title: Prime-power lifting of a congruence to one
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $n$ and $a$ be
positive integers. If $a \equiv 1 \pmod p$, then $a^{p^n} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^{n+1}}$.

## Sources

- Hacène Belbachir and Celia Salhi, "The Generalized Bi-Periodic Fibonacci Sequence Modulo m," Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.9.4, Theorem, lines 340–341, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Salhi/salhi4.tex>. It follows from `pow_pow_modEq_one_of_modEq_one`; the hypotheses `hp`, `hn` and `ha` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Both first inverses extremal, odd–even case
articles.statement:
Let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be Euclidean
switching data with $r_0$ odd and $r_1$ even. Then $2|s_1| = r_0 - 1$ and $2|s_2| = r_1$ hold
simultaneously if and only if $r_1 = 2$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 7.

articles.title: Both first inverses extremal, odd–odd case
articles.statement:
Let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be Euclidean
switching data with $r_0$ and $r_1$ both odd. Then $2|s_1| = r_0 - 1$ and $2|s_2| = r_1 - 1$
hold simultaneously if and only if $r_0 = r_1 + 2$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 6.

articles.title: First inverses not both extremal, even–odd case
articles.statement:
Let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be
Euclidean switching data with $r_0$ even and $r_1$ odd. Then $2|s_1| < r_0$ or
$2|s_2| < r_1 - 1$; that is, $|s_1| < r_0/2$ or $|s_2| < (r_1 - 1)/2$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 8.

articles.title: Bézout coefficients are modular inverses
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be coprime positive integers,
and let $x$ and $y$ be integers with $xm + yn = 1$. Then $xm \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ and
$yn \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$; that is, $x$ is an inverse of $m$ modulo $n$ and $y$ is an inverse of
$n$ modulo $m$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 1.

articles.title: The Euclidean Bézout coefficients are smallest in absolute value
articles.statement:
Let $m > n > 1$ be
integers, write $g = \gcd(m, n)$, and let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be Euclidean switching data
with $r_0 = m/g$ and $r_1 = n/g$. Then for all integers $x$ and $y$ with $xm + yn = g$, we have
$|s_2| \le |x|$ and $|s_1| \le |y|$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 5.

articles.title: The Euclidean Bézout coefficients are least absolute inverses
articles.statement:
Let $m > n > 1$ be
integers, write $g = \gcd(m, n)$, and let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be Euclidean switching data
with $r_0 = m/g$ and $r_1 = n/g$. Then $s_2 m + s_1 n = g$, $s_2$ is the least absolute inverse
of $m/g$ modulo $n/g$, and $s_1$ is the least absolute inverse of $n/g$ modulo $m/g$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 4.

articles.title: Rankin's minimality of the Euclidean Bézout pair
articles.statement:
Let $m > n > 1$ be integers, write
$g = \gcd(m, n)$, and let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be Euclidean switching data with
$r_0 = m/g$ and $r_1 = n/g$. Then for all integers $x$ and $y$ with $xm + yn = g$, we have
$s_2^2 + s_1^2 \le x^2 + y^2$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Modular inverse switching
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $\gcd(m, n) = 1$,
and let $t$ be an integer with $\gcd(|t|, n) = 1$. Then $m = kn + t$ for some integer $k$ if
and only if there are integers $x$ and $y$ with $xt \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, $yn \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$
and $xm + yn = 1$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 2.

articles.title: Euclidean switching data
articles.statement:
A natural number $N$, a sequence $r_0, r_1, \dots$ of natural
numbers and a sequence $s_0, s_1, \dots$ of integers form Euclidean switching data when
$N \ge 1$; $r_0 > r_1 > \cdots > r_{N+1} = 1$, with $r_0, \dots, r_{N+1}$ all positive; for each
$i = 1, \dots, N$ there is a positive integer $q_i$ with $r_{i-1} = q_i r_i + r_{i+1}$;
$s_{N+1} = 1$; and $s_{i+1} r_{i-1} + s_i r_i = 1$ for each $i = 1, \dots, N$.

These are the remainders $r_i$ of the Euclidean algorithm on $(r_0, r_1)$ and the inverses $s_i$
of $r_i$ modulo $r_{i-1}$ in §3 of Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of
Modular Inverse Switching Formulas" (Equations (4), (5) and (6)).

articles.title: Every switching inverse is a least absolute inverse
articles.statement:
Let $(r_i)$, $(s_i)$ and $N$ be
Euclidean switching data. Then for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le N + 1$, $s_i$ is the least
absolute inverse of $r_i$ modulo $r_{i-1}$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Corollary 1.

articles.title: Least absolute inverses propagate down the Euclidean sequence
articles.statement:
Let $r_0, r_1, \ldots$ be
natural numbers, $s_0, s_1, \ldots$ integers and $N \ge 1$ such that $(r, s, N)$ is Euclidean
switching data: $r_0 > r_1 > \cdots > r_{N+1} = 1$ are the successive remainders of the Euclidean
algorithm, $s_{N+1} = 1$, and $s_{i+1} r_{i-1} + s_i r_i = 1$ for $1 \le i \le N$. If
$1 \le j \le N$ and $s_{j+1}$ is the least absolute inverse of $r_{j+1}$ modulo $r_j$, then $s_j$
is the least absolute inverse of $r_j$ modulo $r_{j-1}$.

## Sources

- Spiros Konstantogiannis, "The Euclidean Algorithm as a Sequence of Modular Inverse Switching Formulas", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Least absolute inverse
articles.statement:
For integers $x$ and $a$ and a natural number $n$, $x$ is the
least absolute inverse of $a$ modulo $n$ when $xa \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ and $-n < 2x \le n$, that is,
when $x$ is an inverse of $a$ modulo $n$ in the half-open interval $-n/2 < x \le n/2$.

For even $n$ the endpoint $n/2$ is included and $-n/2$ is excluded; this is also the choice the
Euclidean recurrence produces.

articles.title: Power sums vanish modulo a prime
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $e \ge 0$ be an integer such
that $p - 1$ does not divide $e$ whenever $e \ge 1$. Then $p$ divides $\sum_{t=1}^{p} t^e$.

For $e = 0$ the sum is $p$. The source states the lemma for odd primes; for $p = 2$ the
hypothesis forces $e = 0$.

## Sources

- Christian Ballot, "On a Congruence of Kimball and Webb Involving Lucas Sequences," Journal of Integer Sequences 17 (2014), Article 14.1.3, Lemma, lines 223–225, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Ballot/ballot7.tex

articles.title: Gauss's theorem on primitive roots modulo prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime
and let $g$ be a natural number that is a primitive root modulo $p$, where a primitive
root modulo $n$ is a residue class modulo $n$ of multiplicative order $\varphi(n)$. Then
there is a natural number $k$ such that $g + kp$ is a primitive root modulo $p^\ell$ for
every $\ell \ge 2$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Theorem 1.

articles.title: The lift of order $p - 1$ of a primitive root
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let
$g$ be a natural number that is a primitive root modulo $p$, that is, a residue class
modulo $p$ of multiplicative order $\varphi(p) = p - 1$. Let $P_g$ be the set of units
$x$ modulo $p^2$ with $x \equiv g \pmod p$. Then exactly one $x \in P_g$ has
multiplicative order $p - 1$ modulo $p^2$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Corollary 1.

articles.title: Unique order-preserving element of a fiber modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime,
let $x_0$ be a unit modulo $p^2$, and let $P_{x_0}$ be the set of units $x$ modulo $p^2$
with $x \equiv x_0 \pmod p$. There is exactly one $x \in P_{x_0}$ whose multiplicative
order modulo $p^2$ equals the multiplicative order of its reduction modulo $p$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Exactly one lift of a primitive root fails modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime
and let $g$ be a natural number that is a primitive root modulo $p$, where a primitive
root modulo $n$ is a residue class modulo $n$ of multiplicative order $\varphi(n)$. Then
there is exactly one $m \in \{0, 1, \dots, p - 1\}$ such that $g + mp$ is not a primitive
root modulo $p^2$, and $g + kp$ is a primitive root modulo $p^2$ for every other
$k \in \{0, 1, \dots, p - 1\}$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Corollary 1.

articles.title: Unique order-preserving lift modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $a$ be
a natural number coprime to $p$. Writing $\operatorname{ord}_n(b)$ for the multiplicative
order of $b$ modulo $n$, there is exactly one $m \in \{0, 1, \dots, p - 1\}$ such that
$\operatorname{ord}_{p^2}(a + mp) = \operatorname{ord}_p(a)$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Fibers of reduction modulo $p$ on units modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and a unit
$a$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$, the fiber $P_a$ is the set of units $x$ of
$\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$ with $x \equiv a \pmod p$, that is, the units whose image under the
reduction map $(\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z})^\times \to (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ equals the
image of $a$.

articles.title: Endomorphisms of the units modulo $p^2$ respect the fibers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd
prime, let $f$ be a group endomorphism of $(\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z})^\times$, and let
$a$ be a unit modulo $p^2$. Writing $P_b$ for the set of units $x$ modulo $p^2$ with
$x \equiv b \pmod p$, the image of $P_a$ under $f$ is contained in $P_{f(a)}$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Multiplicative order modulo $n$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $a$,
$\operatorname{ord}_n(a)$ is the multiplicative order of the residue class of $a$ in the
unit group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ when $a$ is coprime to $n$, and $0$
otherwise.

articles.title: The order of $a + kp$ modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $a$ and $k$ be
natural numbers with $a$ coprime to $p$. Writing $\operatorname{ord}_n(b)$ for the
multiplicative order of $b$ modulo $n$, the order $\operatorname{ord}_{p^2}(a + kp)$ is
either $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ or $p \cdot \operatorname{ord}_p(a)$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Lemma 1.

articles.title: Power maps on the fibers modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $a$ be a unit
modulo $p^2$, and let $n$ be a natural number coprime to $p$ and to the multiplicative
order of $a$. Writing $P_b$ for the set of units $x$ modulo $p^2$ with
$x \equiv b \pmod p$, the map $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $P_a$, maps $P_a$ onto
$P_{a^n}$, and preserves the multiplicative order of every element of $P_a$.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Lemma 4.

articles.title: Primitive roots modulo $p^\ell$ of the form $g^p + kp$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let
$g$ be a natural number that is a primitive root modulo $p$. If $k$ is a natural number not
divisible by $p$, then $g^p + kp$ is a primitive root modulo $p^\ell$ for every natural number
$\ell > 1$.

Here a natural number $a$ is a primitive root modulo $n$ when its residue class in
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is a primitive $\varphi(n)$-th root of unity, where $\varphi$ is Euler's
totient function.

## Sources

- V. P. Ramesh and S. Sivakumar, "A Note on Gauss's Theorem on the Primitive Roots Modulo `p^ℓ`", Theorem 3.

articles.title: Reduction of units modulo $p^2$ to units modulo $p$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, this is
the group homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z})^\times \to (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$
induced on units by the reduction ring homomorphism
$\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, which sends the class of $x$ modulo $p^2$ to
the class of $x$ modulo $p$.

articles.title: Carmichael's function on coprime products
articles.statement:
For coprime natural numbers $m, n > 1$,
the Carmichael function $\lambda$ satisfies
$\lambda(mn) = \operatorname{lcm}(\lambda(m), \lambda(n))$.

## Sources

- Benjamin Huang and Shuguang Li, "Notes on the Number of Primitive λ-roots mod n and Its Multiplicative Properties", Lemma 1.

articles.title: The count $\Delta_q(n)$ for primitive λ-roots
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda$ be the Carmichael function
and, for natural numbers $p$ and $m$, let $v_p(m)$ be the exponent of $p$ in the prime
factorization of $m$ (taken to be $0$ when $p$ is not prime or $m = 0$). For natural numbers
$q$ and $n$, the natural number $\Delta_q(n)$ is defined as follows. If $q = 2$, $v_2(n) = 3$
and $v_2(\lambda(n)) = 1$, then $\Delta_q(n)$ is one more than the number of distinct prime
factors of $n$. Otherwise, if $q$ divides $\lambda(n)$, then $\Delta_q(n)$ is the number of
prime factors $p$ of $n$ (there are none when $n = 0$) such that $q^{v_q(\lambda(n))}$ divides
$\lambda(p^{v_p(n)})$. In all remaining cases $\Delta_q(n) = 0$.

The argument $q$ is intended to be prime; the definition is the displayed formula for every
natural $q$.

articles.title: Huang–Li inequality for the local factors $h_q$
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda$ be the Carmichael function,
and let $\Delta_q$ and $h_q$ be the count and the local factor for primitive λ-roots. Let
$m, n > 1$ be coprime natural numbers and let $q$ be a prime dividing $\lambda(mn)$. Then
$h_q(m)\,h_q(n) \le h_q(mn)$. Moreover, $h_q(m)\,h_q(n) < h_q(mn)$ if and only if at least one
of the following holds: $0 < \Delta_q(m) < \Delta_q(mn)$; $0 < \Delta_q(n) < \Delta_q(mn)$; or
$\Delta_q(m) > 0$, $\Delta_q(n) > 0$, and $\Delta_q(mn)$ equals $\Delta_q(m)$ or $\Delta_q(n)$.

## Sources

- Benjamin Huang and Shuguang Li, "Notes on the Number of Primitive λ-roots mod n and Its Multiplicative Properties", Lemma 2.

articles.title: The local factor $h_q(n)$ for primitive λ-roots
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta_q(n)$ be the count for
primitive λ-roots. For natural numbers $q$ and $n$, the rational number $h_q(n)$ equals $1$ if
$\Delta_q(n) = 0$, and $1 - 1/q^{\Delta_q(n)}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Supermultiplicativity of the number of primitive λ-roots
articles.statement:
Let $R(n)$ be the number of
primitive λ-roots modulo $n$. For coprime natural numbers $m, n > 1$, we have
$R(m)\,R(n) \le R(mn)$, and $R(mn) = R(m)\,R(n)$ if and only if $m = 2$ and $n$ is odd, or
$n = 2$ and $m$ is odd.

## Sources

- Benjamin Huang and Shuguang Li, "Notes on the Number of Primitive λ-roots mod n and Its Multiplicative Properties", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Number of primitive λ-roots
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $R(n)$ is the number of units $a$
of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ whose multiplicative order equals $\lambda(n)$, where $\lambda$ is
the Carmichael function.

articles.title: Many values of a smooth diagonal form modulo a prime
articles.statement:
For a natural number $B$ and real
$\eta > 0$, let $A(B, B^\eta)$ be the set of integers $1 \le x \le B$ all of whose prime factors
are at most $B^\eta$. There is a real-valued function $g$ on the natural numbers with
$g(k) = O(\log \log k / \log k)$ as $k \to \infty$ such that for every $k \ge 2$ there is
$\eta_0 > 0$ with the following property. Let $0 < \eta \le \eta_0$ and let $n \ge 1$ satisfy
$2n \ge 5$ if $k = 2$, $2n \ge 8$ if $k = 3$, and $2n \ge k (\log k + \log \log k + 2 + g(k))$
if $k \ge 4$. Then there is $C > 0$ such that for every prime $p$, every natural number $B \ge 1$
with $n B^k \le p$ and all integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ not divisible by $p$, the set of residues
modulo $p$ of $a_1 x_1^k + \dots + a_n x_n^k$ with $x \in A(B, B^\eta)^n$ has at least $C B^k$
elements.

## Sources

- Todd Cochrane, Misty Ostergaard, Craig Spencer, and Kathryn Wilson, *A Note on Small Solutions to Diagonal Congruences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A14, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Diagonal congruences in $k$ variables are solvable
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $k \ge 1$. For
all integers $a_1, \dots, a_k$ not divisible by $p$ and every integer $c$, there are integers
$x_1, \dots, x_k$ with $a_1 x_1^k + \dots + a_k x_k^k \equiv c \pmod p$.

Equivalently, $\Gamma(k, p) \le k$, where $\Gamma(k, p)$ is the least $n$ such that every such
congruence in $n$ variables is solvable; extra variables can be set to $0$.

## Sources

- Todd Cochrane, Misty Ostergaard, Craig Spencer, and Kathryn Wilson, *A Note on Small Solutions to Diagonal Congruences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A14, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Small solutions of diagonal congruences
articles.statement:
There is a real-valued function $g$ on the natural
numbers with $g(k) = O(\log \log k / \log k)$ as $k \to \infty$ such that for every $k \ge 2$
there is a constant $C > 0$ with the following property. Let $n$ satisfy $n \ge 9$ if $k = 2$,
$n \ge 12$ if $k = 3$, and $n \ge \frac{3}{2} k (\log k + \log \log k + 2 + g(k))$ if $k \ge 4$.
Then for every prime $p$, every integer $c$ and all integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ not divisible by
$p$, the congruence $a_1 x_1^k + \dots + a_n x_n^k \equiv c \pmod p$ has a solution in natural
numbers $x_1, \dots, x_n$ with $1 \le x_i \le C p^{1/k}$ for every $i$.

## Sources

- Todd Cochrane, Misty Ostergaard, Craig Spencer, and Kathryn Wilson, *A Note on Small Solutions to Diagonal Congruences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A14, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Sum-product sets cover the integers modulo a prime
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let
$A_1, A_2, A_3, D$ be subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $|A_1| |A_2| |A_3| |D| > p^3$.
Then every residue class modulo $p$ can be written as $a_1 d + a_2 + a_3$ with $a_1 \in A_1$,
$d \in D$, $a_2 \in A_2$ and $a_3 \in A_3$; that is, $A_1 D + A_2 + A_3 = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Todd Cochrane, Misty Ostergaard, Craig Spencer, and Kathryn Wilson, *A Note on Small Solutions to Diagonal Congruences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A14, Lemma 3, quoting Lemma 8.3 of their reference [5] (a consequence of Sárközy's Corollary A).

articles.title: Smooth solutions of diagonal equations (Chow–Lindqvist–Prendiville)
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$N$ and real $\eta > 0$, let $A(N, N^\eta)$ be the set of integers $1 \le x \le N$ all of whose
prime factors are at most $N^\eta$. There is a real-valued function $g$ on the natural numbers
with $g(k) = O(\log \log k / \log k)$ as $k \to \infty$ such that for every $k \ge 2$ there is
$\eta_0 > 0$ with the following property. Let $c_1, \dots, c_s$ be nonzero integers such that
$\sum_{i \in I} c_i = 0$ for some nonempty $I \subseteq \{1, \dots, s\}$, and suppose $s \ge 5$
if $k = 2$, $s \ge 8$ if $k = 3$, and $s \ge k (\log k + \log \log k + 2 + g(k))$ if $k \ge 4$.
Then for every $0 < \eta \le \eta_0$ there are a natural number $N_0$ and constants
$C_1, C_2 > 0$ such that for all $N \ge N_0$ the number of $x \in A(N, N^\eta)^s$ with
$c_1 x_1^k + \dots + c_s x_s^k = 0$ is at least $C_1 N^{s-k}$ and at most $C_2 N^{s-k}$.

## Sources

- Todd Cochrane, Misty Ostergaard, Craig Spencer, and Kathryn Wilson, *A Note on Small Solutions to Diagonal Congruences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A14, Theorem 2, quoting Chow, Lindqvist and Prendiville, *Rado's criterion over squares and higher powers*, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 23 (2021), Theorem B.1.

articles.title: Thue's lemma, general form
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $n$ be integers with $n > 1$ and
$\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then there exist nonzero integers $x$ and $y$ with $|x| < \sqrt{n}$,
$|y| < \sqrt{n}$ and $x \equiv a y \pmod{n}$. Unlike the source form of Thue's lemma, no lower
bound on $a$ is assumed.

articles.title: Thue's lemma
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $n$ be integers with $a > 1$, $n > 1$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Then
there exist nonzero integers $x$ and $y$ with $|x| < \sqrt{n}$, $|y| < \sqrt{n}$ and
$x \equiv a y \pmod{n}$.

The hypothesis $a > 1$ follows the source and is not needed for the conclusion.

## Sources

- Bencheng Li, Steven J. Miller, Tudor Popescu, Daniel Sarnecki, and Nawapan Wattanawanichkul, "Modeling Random Walks to Infinity on Primes in Z[√2]", Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.6.1, Lemma [Thue's lemma], lines 217–218, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Miller/miller11.tex>. Original: V. Shoup, "A Computational Introduction to Number Theory and Algebra", Cambridge University Press, 2005, p. 43.

articles.title: The Wilson quotient sum Z(n) modulo n
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Morozov's
Wilson quotient sum $Z(n)$ is an integer; moreover $Z(n) \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ if $n$ is neither
$1$ nor prime, and $Z(n) \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$ if $n = 1$ or $n$ is prime.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Theorem 3.

articles.title: A primality criterion from the Wilson quotient sum Z(2n − 1)
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, Morozov's Wilson quotient sum $Z(2n - 1)$ is an integer, and it is divisible by $n$
if and only if $n = 1$ or $n$ is prime.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Theorem 4.

articles.title: The Wilson quotient sum is an integer
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$, Morozov's
Wilson quotient sum $Z(n)$ is an integer.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Theorem 1.

articles.title: The sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum Z⁺(2n) modulo 2n
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural
number. Morozov's sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum $Z^+(2n)$ is an integer; it satisfies
$Z^+(2n) \equiv 0 \pmod{2n}$ if $n = 2$ or $n$ is neither $1$ nor prime, and
$Z^+(2n) \equiv n + 1 \pmod{2n}$ if $n$ is an odd prime.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Theorem 5, equations (8) and (9).

articles.title: When the sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum is a natural number
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, Morozov's sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum $Z^+(n)$ is a natural number if and only
if $n$ is even, $n = 1$, or $n$ is prime.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Factorial form of the Wilson quotient identity
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, the Wilson
quotient $W(p)$ of $p$ satisfies $(p-1)! = p \, W(p) - 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- M. Avitabile and S. Mattarei, arXiv:2308.16034, `AH.tex` lines 315–321, display $(p-1)! = -1 + p \, w_p$, where $w_p$ is the Wilson quotient.

articles.title: Exactness of the Wilson quotient
articles.statement:
For every prime $p$, the Wilson quotient $W(p)$ of $p$
satisfies $p \, W(p) = (p-1)! + 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.

By Wilson's theorem $p$ divides $(p-1)! + 1$, so the division defining $W(p)$ is exact.

## Sources

- M. Avitabile and S. Mattarei, arXiv:2308.16034, `AH.tex` lines 315–321, which uses $(p-1)! = -1 + p \, w_p$, where $w_p$ is the Wilson quotient.

articles.title: A generalized Wilson criterion for primality
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $k < n$ be natural
numbers. Then $(-1)^k \, k! \, (n - k - 1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$ if and only if $n = 1$ or $n$
is prime.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Corollary 1.

articles.title: A Bernoulli–harmonic congruence for the sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an
odd prime, let $B_m$ denote the Bernoulli numbers, and let $H_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} 1/j$ denote the
harmonic numbers, with $H_0 = 0$. Then $p$ divides the numerator, in lowest terms, of the
rational number

$$Z^+(p) - \Bigl(B_{2(p-1)} - B_{p-1} - \sum_{k=0}^{p-1} (-1)^k H_k\Bigr),$$

where $Z^+(p)$ is Morozov's sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum.

This is the congruence obtained by summing the paper's Equation (7). The printed simplification
of the alternating harmonic sum to $H_{p-1}/2$ is false already at $p = 3$.

## Sources

- Ivan V. Morozov, "On Quotients of a More General Theorem of Wilson", Theorem 6 and Equation (7).

articles.title: Wilson's theorem modulo $p^2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and, for $1 \le k \le p - 1$, let
$q_p(k)$ be the Fermat quotient of $k$, the integer with $k^{p-1} = 1 + p\, q_p(k)$. Then

$$
(p - 1)! \equiv -1 + p \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} q_p(k) \pmod{p^2}.
$$

## Sources

- Claire Levaillant, "Wilson's Theorem Modulo `p^2` Derived from Faulhaber Polynomials", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Morozov's Wilson quotients
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $M_k(n)$ is the rational
number

$$M_k(n) = \frac{1 + (-1)^k \, k! \, (n - k - 1)!}{n},$$

where $n - k - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers and division by $0$ gives $0$.

articles.title: Morozov's sign-adjusted Wilson quotients
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $M_k^+(n)$ is
the rational number

$$M_k^+(n) = \frac{(-1)^k + k! \, (n - k - 1)!}{n},$$

where $n - k - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers and division by $0$ gives $0$.

articles.title: Morozov's Wilson quotient sum
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $Z(n)$ is the rational number
$Z(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} M_k(n)$, where $M_k(n)$ are Morozov's Wilson quotients.

articles.title: Morozov's sign-adjusted Wilson quotient sum
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $Z^+(n)$ is the
rational number $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} M_k^+(n)$, where $M_k^+(n) = ((-1)^k + k!\,(n-k-1)!)/n$ is
Morozov's sign-adjusted quotient.

articles.title: Wilson quotient
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, the Wilson quotient is the integer
$W(p) = \lfloor ((p-1)! + 1) / p \rfloor$ for $p \ge 1$, and $W(0) = 0$.

For a prime $p$, Wilson's theorem $p \mid (p-1)! + 1$ makes the division exact. The definition is
total on $\mathbb{N}$; the source defines $W_p$ only for odd primes $p$.

## Sources

- Y. Matsuno, *A resolution of Kellner's conjectures on Wilson quotients*, arXiv:2607.10106v1, lines 44–51.

articles.title: Alternating binomial sum identities
articles.statement:
For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write
$\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$ for the generalized binomial coefficient. Let $m$, $n$
and $k$ be natural numbers. Then for every natural number $j \le m$,

$$\sum_{s=j}^{m} (-1)^{s-j} \binom{n}{s} \binom{s}{j} = (-1)^{m-j} \binom{n}{j} \binom{n-j-1}{m-j}
= \binom{n}{j} \binom{m-n}{m-j},$$

and

$$\sum_{j=0}^{m} (-1)^{m-j} \binom{n}{j} \binom{n-j-1}{m-j} \binom{n-j}{k} =
\binom{n}{k} \binom{m-k}{m},$$



$$\sum_{j=0}^{\min(m, k)} (-1)^{m-j} \binom{n}{j} \binom{n-j-1}{m-j} \binom{n-j}{k-j} =
\binom{n}{k} \binom{k+m-n}{m}.$$

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Carlitz's block harmonic congruence
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime and let $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then in $\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$

$$\sum_{r=1}^{p-1} (kp + r)^{-1} = 0.$$

Each $kp + r$ with $1 \le r \le p - 1$ is prime to $p$, so these inverses are genuine inverses
modulo $p^2$.

Cited original: L. Carlitz, "A note on Wolstenholme's theorem", American
Mathematical Monthly 61 (1954), 174–176.

## Sources

- Jerry Metzger and Thomas Richards, "A Prisoner Problem Variation", <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Metzger/metz1.tex>, lines 657–662.

articles.title: $\binom{np}{mp}$ as a quotient of products
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $m$ and $n$ be
natural numbers with $1 \le m \le n$. Then

$$\binom{np}{mp} = \frac{\binom{n}{m} \prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \binom{(n-m+j+1)p-1}{p-1}}
{\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \binom{(j+1)p-1}{p-1}} = \frac{\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \binom{(n-m+j+1)p}{p}}
{\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \binom{(j+1)p}{p}}.$$

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Congruences for $\binom{tp}{p}$ modulo $p^5$, $p^6$ and $p^7$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 11$ be a prime
and $t$ a natural number. Write $H_{p-1}^{(r)} = \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} 1/j^r$ for the harmonic number of
order $r$ and $H_{p-1}(1, 1) = \sum_{1 \le i < j \le p-1} 1/(ij)$. For rational numbers $x$, $y$
and a natural number $s$, write $x \equiv y \pmod{p^s}$ when $x = y$ or $v_p(x - y) \ge s$, where
$v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$. Then

$$\binom{tp}{p} \equiv t + (-t^5 + 2t^4 - t^2) \, p \, H_{p-1}^{(1)} +
t^3 (t-1)^2 p^2 H_{p-1}(1, 1) \pmod{p^7},$$



$$\binom{tp}{p} \equiv t + (-t^5 + 2t^4 - t^2) \, p \, H_{p-1}^{(1)} -
\frac{t^3 (t-1)^2}{2} \, p^2 H_{p-1}^{(2)} \pmod{p^6},$$

and

$$\binom{tp}{p} \equiv t + t^2 (t-1) \, p \, H_{p-1}^{(1)} \pmod{p^5}.$$

The double sum $H_{p-1}(1, 1)$ is taken over $i < j$; under this reading the first two
congruences agree modulo $p^6$.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 10.

articles.title: Equivalent forms of Wolstenholme's congruence
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime and let $n$ and
$k$ be natural numbers. Then the congruences $\binom{2p}{p} \equiv 2$, $\binom{np}{p} \equiv n$ and
$\binom{np}{kp} \equiv \binom{n}{k}$ modulo $p^3$ are equivalent.

By Wolstenholme's theorem all three hold for every such $p$.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Coefficients of $(x + 1)^{jp} (x^p + 1)^{n-j}$
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $j$ and $k$ be natural numbers and
$p$ a positive integer, and let $d = \max(n - j, 0)$. Then the coefficient of $x^{kp}$ in the
polynomial $(x + 1)^{jp} (x^p + 1)^{d}$ is

$$\sum_{s=0}^{\min(j, k)} \binom{jp}{sp} \binom{d}{k - s}.$$

The source takes $p$ prime; here $p$ is any positive integer.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Divisibility of the polynomial parts by $k(n-k)/2$
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number and $n$ an
integer. For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$,
and for a rational number $x$ write $(x)_r = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)$ for the falling factorial. Then
there is a polynomial $Q \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ such that for every natural number $k$

$$\binom{m-k}{m} + \binom{k+m-n}{m} + (-1)^{m+1} \binom{n-1}{m} - 1 = \frac{k(n-k)}{2} \, Q(k),$$

and for all natural numbers $i$ and $j$ with $1 \le i < j$ there is a polynomial
$Q \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ such that for every natural number $k$

$$\frac{(n-k)_{j-i} \, (k)_i + (n-k)_i \, (k)_{j-i}}{j!} \binom{m-n}{\max(m-j, 0)} =
\frac{k(n-k)}{2} \, Q(k).$$

For $j \le m$ the left-hand sides are the polynomial parts of the coefficients
$C'_{00}(m, n, k)$ and $C'_{ji}(m, n, k)$ of Theorem 4 (the halving at $j = 2i$ does not affect
divisibility); agreement at every natural number $k$ amounts to divisibility by $k(n-k)/2$
in $\mathbb{Q}[k]$.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Coefficient bound for the divided derivatives $D^n/n!$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $B$ a
normed vector space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ whose norm is ultrametric. Let $(a_k)_{k \ge 0}$ be a
sequence in $B$ and $C$ a real number with $\|a_k\| \le C$ for every $k$. Then for all natural
numbers $n$ and $k$,

$$\Big\| \binom{k+n}{n} a_{k+n} \Big\| \le C.$$

The vectors $\binom{k+n}{n} a_{k+n}$ are the coefficients of $D^n f / n!$ for
$f = \sum_k a_k t^k$, so this is the coefficientwise form of the bound $\|D^n / n!\| \le 1$ on
the Tate algebra $B\{t\}$ with the sup norm.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Higher $p$-adic mean value theorem
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $|\cdot|$ be the $p$-adic
absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and let $B$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ whose
norm is ultrametric. Let $N$ and $m$ be natural numbers with $1 \le m \le p$, let
$f(t) = \sum_{j\lt N} a_j t^j$ be a polynomial with coefficients $a_j \in B$, and let
$t, h \in \mathbb{Q}_p$ with $|t| \le 1$. Suppose that $|h| \le p^{-1/(p-m)}$ if $m < p$, that
$|h| \le p^{-1/p}$ if $m = p$, and that $C \ge 0$ is a real number with
$\|j(j-1)\cdots(j-m+1) \, a_j\| \le C$ for every $j < N$. Then

$$\Big\| f(t+h) - \sum_{q\lt m} \sum_{q \le j < N} \binom{j}{q} t^{j-q} h^q a_j \Big\| \le
\Big| \frac{h^m}{m} \Big| \, C.$$

The inner sum $\sum_{q \le j < N} \binom{j}{q} t^{j-q} a_j$ is $f^{(q)}(t)/q!$, and the least
admissible $C$ is the sup of the norms of the coefficients of $f^{(m)}$.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Congruence form of the higher $p$-adic mean value theorem
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let
$|\cdot|$ be the $p$-adic absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and let $B$ be a normed vector space
over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ whose norm is ultrametric. Let $N$ and $m$ be natural numbers with
$1 \le m \le p$, let $f(t) = \sum_{j\lt N} a_j t^j$ with $a_j \in B$, let $t, h \in \mathbb{Q}_p$
with $|t| \le 1$, and let $w$ be a real number with
$\|j(j-1)\cdots(j-m+1) \, a_j\| \le p^{-w}$ for every $j < N$. Write

$$R = \Big\| f(t+h) - \sum_{q\lt m} \sum_{q \le j < N} \binom{j}{q} t^{j-q} h^q a_j \Big\|$$

and let $v_p(h)$ be the $p$-adic valuation of $h$, taken to be $0$ when $h = 0$. Then
$R \le p^{-(m v_p(h) + w)}$ if $m < p$ and $v_p(h) \ge 1/(p-m)$;
$R \le p^{-(p v_p(h) + w - 1)}$ if $m = p$ and $v_p(h) \ge 1/p$; and $R = 0$ if $h = 0$.

Reading a congruence modulo $p^v$ in $B$ as norm at most $p^{-v}$, the first two bounds say
$f(t+h) \equiv \sum_{q\lt m} f^{(q)}(t) h^q / q!$ modulo $p^{m v_p(h) + w}$ and
$p^{p v_p(h) + w - 1}$ respectively.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ with the coefficients $\bar C_{ji}$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime,
let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $m + 1 < p$, and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer
$x$ and a natural number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and set
$\binom{x}{r} = 0$ for negative $r$. Let

$$\bar C_{00} = \left( \binom{m-k}{m} + \binom{k+m-n}{m} + (-1)^{m+1} \binom{n-1}{m} - 1 \right)
\binom{n}{k},$$

let $\bar C_{ji} = \binom{n}{j} \binom{m-n}{m-j} \binom{n-j}{k-i}$, and let

$$X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \bar C_{00} -
\sum_{1 \le i < j \le m} \bar C_{ji} \binom{jp}{ip}.$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{m+1} \ne 0$ and
$v_p(X) \ge m + 1 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{m+1}\big)$, where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation on
$\mathbb{Q}$. With $v_p(0) = \infty$ this says $X \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{m+1+v_p(\binom{n}{m+1})}}$.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Lemma 4.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ with symmetrized coefficients
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime,
let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $m + 1 < p$, and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer
$x$ and a natural number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, for a rational
number $x$ write $(x)_r = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)$ for the falling factorial, and let $v_p$ be the
$p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$. Put

$$
C'_{00} = \left(\binom{m-k}{m} + \binom{k+m-n}{m} + (-1)^{m+1} \binom{n-1}{m} - 1\right)
\binom{n}{k}
$$

and, for $2 \le j \le m$ and $1 \le i \le \lfloor j/2 \rfloor$,

$$
C'_{ji} = \varepsilon_{ji} \, \frac{(n-k)_{j-i} \, (k)_i + (n-k)_i \, (k)_{j-i}}{j!}
\binom{m-n}{m-j} \binom{n}{k},
$$

where $\varepsilon_{ji} = 1/2$ if $j = 2i$ and $\varepsilon_{ji} = 1$ otherwise. Let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - C'_{00} -
\sum_{j=2}^{m} \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor j/2 \rfloor} C'_{ji} \binom{jp}{ip}.
$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{m+1} \ne 0$ and
$v_p(X) \ge m + 1 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{m+1}\big)$. That is, $\binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k}$ is
congruent to $C'_{00} + \sum_{j, i} C'_{ji} \binom{jp}{ip}$ modulo
$p^{m+1+v_p(\binom{n}{m+1})}$, and equal to it when $\binom{n}{m+1} = 0$.

The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 4.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ modulo $p^5$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 11$ be a prime, let $k$ be a
natural number and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write
$\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be the $p$-adic valuation on
$\mathbb{Q}$. Put $C_{00} = -(k^2 - kn + 2n^2 - 15n + 35)/6$, $C_{21} = (n-4)(n-3)/2$,
$C_{31} = (n-2)(4-n)/3$, $C_{41} = (2k^2 - 2kn + n^2 - 3n + 4)/12$ and
$C_{42} = (n-k-1)(k-1)/12$, and let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \frac{k(n-k)}{2} \binom{n}{k} \Big(C_{00} +
C_{21} \binom{2p}{p} + C_{31} \binom{3p}{p} + C_{41} \binom{4p}{p} + C_{42} \binom{4p}{2p}\Big).
$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{5} \ne 0$ and $v_p(X) \ge 5 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{5}\big)$; that
is, $X \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{5+v_p(\binom{n}{5})}}$, and $X = 0$ when $\binom{n}{5} = 0$.

The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Proposition 4.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ modulo $p^4$ via $\binom{2p}{p}$ alone
articles.statement:
Let
$p \ge 7$ be a prime, let $k$ be a natural number and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer $x$
and a natural number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be the
$p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$, with the convention $v_p(0) = 0$. Let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \frac{nk(n-k)}{4} \binom{n}{k} \left(\binom{2p}{p} - 2\right).
$$

Then either $X = 0$ or $v_p(X) \ge 4 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{4}\big)$. In particular, when
$\binom{n}{4} = 0$, that is $n \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, the conclusion is only that $X = 0$ or
$v_p(X) \ge 4$.

Equality cannot be demanded when $\binom{n}{4} = 0$: for $p = 7$, $n = 3$ and $k = 1$ one has
$X = 100842 = 6 \cdot 7^5$. The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered
here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 6.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ modulo $p^4$ via $\binom{2p}{p}$ and $\binom{3p}{p}$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 7$ be a prime, let $k$ be a natural number and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer
$x$ and a natural number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be
the $p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$. Let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \frac{k(n-k)}{2} \binom{n}{k} \left((n - 4) +
(3 - n) \binom{2p}{p} + \frac{n - 2}{3} \binom{3p}{p}\right).
$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{4} \ne 0$ and $v_p(X) \ge 4 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{4}\big)$; that
is, $X \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{4+v_p(\binom{n}{4})}}$, and $X = 0$ when $\binom{n}{4} = 0$.

The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Proposition 3.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ modulo $p^7$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 11$ be a prime, let $k$ be a
natural number and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write
$\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be the $p$-adic valuation on
$\mathbb{Q}$. Put

$$
C_{00} = -\frac{1}{360} \big(2k^4 - 4k^3 n + 11k^2 n^2 - 9k n^3 + 6n^4 - 105k^2 n + 105k n^2 -
105n^3 + 350k^2 - 350kn + 700n^2 - 2205n + 3248\big),
$$

$C_{21} = (6-n)(5-n)(4-n)(3-n)/24$, $C_{31} = (n-2)(6-n)(5-n)(4-n)/18$,
$C_{41} = (6-n)(5-n)(2k^2 - 2kn + n^2 - 3n + 4)/24$,
$C_{42} = (n-k-1)(k-1)(6-n)(5-n)/24$,
$C_{51} = (4-n)(n-6)(3k^2 - 3kn + n^2 - 2n + 3)/60$,
$C_{52} = (k+1-n)(k-1)(n-4)(n-6)/60$,

$$
C_{61} = \frac{1}{360} \big(2k^4 - 4k^3 n + 6k^2 n^2 - 4k n^3 + n^4 - 30k^2 n + 30k n^2 -
10n^3 + 70k^2 - 70kn + 35n^2 - 50n + 48\big),
$$

$C_{62} = (n-k-1)(k-1)(2k^2 - 2kn + n^2 - 5n + 12)/360$ and
$C_{63} = (n-k-1)(n-k-2)(k-1)(k-2)/360$, and let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \frac{k(n-k)}{2} \binom{n}{k} \Big(C_{00} +
\sum_{j=2}^{6} \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor j/2 \rfloor} C_{ji} \binom{jp}{ip}\Big).
$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{7} \ne 0$ and $v_p(X) \ge 7 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{7}\big)$; that
is, $X \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{7+v_p(\binom{n}{7})}}$, and $X = 0$ when $\binom{n}{7} = 0$.

Two coefficients differ from the printed paper and follow its Definition 1 and Theorem 4:
$C_{00}$ has the prefactor $-1/360$ (printed $-1/720$), and $C_{63}$ has the factor
$(n-k-1)(n-k-2)$ (printed $(k-n-1)(k-n-2)$). With the printed values the congruence fails
already modulo $p$, for instance at $p = 11$, $n = 7$, $k = 1$. The paper allows
$n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Proposition 6.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ modulo $p^6$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 11$ be a prime, let $k$ be a
natural number and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write
$\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be the $p$-adic valuation on
$\mathbb{Q}$. Put $C_{00} = (n-6)(n^2 - nk - 6n + k^2 + 15)/12$,
$C_{21} = (5-n)(4-n)(3-n)/6$, $C_{31} = (n-2)(n-5)(n-4)/6$,
$C_{41} = (2k^2 - 2kn + n^2 - 3n + 4)(5-n)/12$, $C_{42} = (k+1-n)(k-1)(n-5)/12$,
$C_{51} = (n-4)(3k^2 - 3kn + n^2 - 2n + 3)/60$ and $C_{52} = (n-k-1)(k-1)(n-4)/60$, and let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \frac{k(n-k)}{2} \binom{n}{k} \Big(C_{00} +
\sum_{j=2}^{5} \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor j/2 \rfloor} C_{ji} \binom{jp}{ip}\Big).
$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{6} \ne 0$ and $v_p(X) \ge 6 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{6}\big)$; that
is, $X \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{6+v_p(\binom{n}{6})}}$, and $X = 0$ when $\binom{n}{6} = 0$.

The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Proposition 5.

articles.title: The congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$ modulo $p^3$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime, let $k$ be a
natural number and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write
$\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be the $p$-adic valuation on
$\mathbb{Q}$. Let

$$
X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - \frac{k(n-k)}{2} \binom{n}{k} \left(\binom{2p}{p} - 2\right).
$$

Then either $X = 0$, or $\binom{n}{3} \ne 0$ and $v_p(X) \ge 3 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{3}\big)$; that
is, $X \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{3+v_p(\binom{n}{3})}}$, and $X = 0$ when $\binom{n}{3} = 0$.

The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Proposition 2.

articles.title: The general congruence for $\binom{np}{kp}$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $m$ and $k$ be
natural numbers with $m + 1 < p$, and let $n$ be an integer. For an integer $x$ and a natural
number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, and let $v_p$ be the $p$-adic
valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$. For natural numbers $j$ and $l$ put

$$
c_j = \sum_{s=0}^{\min(j, k)} \binom{jp}{sp} \binom{n-j}{k-s}, \qquad
d_l = \binom{n}{l} \sum_{j=0}^{l} (-1)^{l-j} \binom{l}{j} c_j,
$$

and let $X = \binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} - (d_1 + \cdots + d_m)$. Then either $X = 0$, or
$\binom{n}{m+1} \ne 0$ and $v_p(X) \ge m + 1 + v_p\big(\binom{n}{m+1}\big)$. That is,
$\binom{np}{kp} - \binom{n}{k} \equiv d_1 + \cdots + d_m$ modulo $p^{m+1+v_p(\binom{n}{m+1})}$,
with equality when $\binom{n}{m+1} = 0$.

The paper allows $n \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $n$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Congruences modulo $p^7$ for $\binom{\alpha p - 1}{p - 1} \binom{(\alpha + 1)p - 1}{p - 1}$ and $\binom{2p - 1}{p - 1}^{-1}$
articles.statement:
**Congruences modulo $p^7$ for $\binom{\alpha p - 1}{p - 1} \binom{(\alpha + 1)p - 1}{p - 1}$
and $\binom{2p - 1}{p - 1}^{-1}$.** Let $p \ge 11$ be a prime and let $\alpha$ be an integer. For
an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write $\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$, let
$H_{p-1}^{(r)} = \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} 1/j^r$ be the harmonic number of order $r$, and let $v_p$ be the
$p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$. Put

$$
X = \binom{\alpha p - 1}{p - 1} \binom{(\alpha + 1)p - 1}{p - 1} - 1 +
(\alpha p)^2 H_{p-1}^{(2)} - \frac{(\alpha p)^4}{2} \Big(\big(H_{p-1}^{(2)}\big)^2 -
H_{p-1}^{(4)}\Big)
$$

and

$$
Y = \binom{2p - 1}{p - 1}^{-1} - 1 - p^2 H_{p-1}^{(2)} -
\frac{p^4}{2} \Big(\big(H_{p-1}^{(2)}\big)^2 + H_{p-1}^{(4)}\Big).
$$

Then either $X = 0$ or $v_p(X) \ge 7$, and either $Y = 0$ or $v_p(Y) \ge 7$.

The paper allows $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}_p$; only integers $\alpha$ are covered here.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Theorem 13.
