articles.title: Binomial coefficients with upper index $-np$
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers
with $p \ge 1$ and $k \ge 1$. For an integer $x$ and a natural number $r$ write
$\binom{x}{r} = x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)/r!$. Then

$$
\binom{-np}{kp} = (-1)^{kp} \, \frac{n}{k} \binom{(n+k)p - 1}{kp - 1} =
(-1)^{kp} \, \frac{n}{n+k} \binom{(n+k)p}{kp}.
$$

The paper takes $p$ prime.

## Sources

- Walid Kehila, *An Extension of Wolstenholme's Theorem by Binomial Coefficients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A32, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Wolstenholme's congruence for odd powers
articles.statement:
Let $\nu \ge 1$ be odd and let $p$ be a prime with
$p \ge \nu + 4$. Then in $\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{p-1} (t^{\nu})^{-1} = 0,
$$

where each $t^{\nu}$ is invertible modulo $p^2$ because $1 \le t < p$.

For $\nu = 1$ this is Wolstenholme's congruence of 1862; the general statement is Theorem 131 of
Hardy and Wright and was first studied by Leudesdorf.

## Sources

- Christian Ballot, "On a Congruence of Kimball and Webb Involving Lucas Sequences," Journal of Integer Sequences 17 (2014), Article 14.1.3, Theorem, lines 94–99, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Ballot/ballot7.tex

articles.title: Wolstenholme's theorem
articles.statement:
If $p \ge 5$ is prime, then $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k^{-1} = 0$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$, where $k^{-1}$ is the inverse of $k$ modulo $p^2$.

articles.title: Non-intersecting integers admit no covering system of divisor form
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and let $D$ be the finite set of divisors of $n$ greater than $1$, taken empty when $n = 0$.
Call $n$ non-intersecting if there are integers $a_d$, one for each natural number $d$, such that
for all distinct natural numbers $d, d' > 1$ dividing $n$ (every $d$ divides $0$), if the classes
$a_d \pmod d$ and $a_{d'} \pmod{d'}$ have an integer in common, then $d$ and $d'$ are coprime. If
$n$ is non-intersecting, then there are no integers $b_d$ for $d \in D$ such that every integer
lies in the class $b_d \pmod d$ for some $d \in D$.

The families $(a_d)$ and $(b_d)$ are independent; in particular, no family of classes
$a_d \pmod d$ for $d \in D$ with the coprime-overlap property covers the integers.

## Sources

- Sarosh Adenwalla, "A Question of Erdős and Graham on Covering Systems", Theorem 3.2.

articles.title: Covering systems have reciprocal-moduli sum at least one
articles.statement:
Let $d_1, \dots, d_t$ be
positive integers and $a_1, \dots, a_t$ integers such that every integer $z$ satisfies
$z \equiv a_i \pmod{d_i}$ for some $i$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^t 1/d_i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sarosh Adenwalla, "A Question of Erdős and Graham on Covering Systems", Lemma 2.2.

articles.title: Covering system
articles.statement:
A covering system of a commutative semiring $R$ is a finite family of cosets
$r_i + I_i = \{r_i + a : a \in I_i\}$, where each $I_i$ is an ideal of $R$ different from both
$\{0\}$ and $R$, whose union is all of $R$. In the case $R = \mathbb{Z}$, this corresponds to a
choice of finitely many congruences $x \equiv r_i \pmod{n_i}$ with moduli $n_i \ge 2$ such that
every integer satisfies at least one of them.

articles.title: Reflection isomorphism of exact covering system digraphs
articles.statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$d_1, \dots, d_r$, $a_1, \dots, a_r$ and $k$ be integers, and put $a_i' = -a_i + (d_i - 1)k$.
Then the map $x \mapsto -(x + k)$ is a digraph isomorphism from
$G(d_1 n + a_1, \dots, d_r n + a_r)$ onto $G(d_1 n + a_1', \dots, d_r n + a_r')$.

The paper's exact-covering hypothesis on the rules is not needed.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Translation isomorphism of exact covering system digraphs
articles.statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$d_1, \dots, d_r$, $a_1, \dots, a_r$ and $k$ be integers, and put $a_i' = a_i - (d_i - 1)k$.
Then the map $x \mapsto x + k$ is a digraph isomorphism from
$G(d_1 n + a_1, \dots, d_r n + a_r)$ onto $G(d_1 n + a_1', \dots, d_r n + a_r')$.

The paper's exact-covering hypothesis on the rules is not needed.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Out-neighbours in a two-rule digraph
articles.statement:
For all integers $d_1, d_2, a_1, a_2, x, y$, the
digraph $G(d_1 n + a_1, d_2 n + a_2)$ has an edge $x \to y$ iff $y = d_1 x + a_1$ or
$y = d_2 x + a_2$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 1 (definition of `G_S`).

articles.title: Edge relation of an exact covering system digraph
articles.statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$d_1, \dots, d_r$ and $a_1, \dots, a_r$ be integers. The digraph
$G(d_1 n + a_1, \dots, d_r n + a_r)$ has vertex set $\mathbb{Z}$ and an edge $x \to y$ iff
$y = d_i x + a_i$ for some $i \in \{1, \dots, r\}$.

When the pairs $(a_i, d_i)$ form an exact covering system this is the paper's digraph $G_S$;
the definition itself places no condition on the $d_i$ and $a_i$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 1 (definition of `G_S`).

articles.title: Digit representations and connected digraphs
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$ be a natural number, let
$D$ be an integer with $|D| = d$, and let $a_1, \dots, a_d$ be integers such that for every
integer $n$ there is exactly one $i$ with $D \mid n - a_i$. Let
$G = G(Dn + a_1, \dots, Dn + a_d)$. Then every integer $z$ can be written as
$z = \sum_{j=0}^{k} b_j D^j$ with $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and digits
$b_0, \dots, b_k \in \{a_1, \dots, a_d\}$ if and only if the underlying undirected graph of $G$
is connected and $0$ lies on a directed cycle of $G$.

The paper also states that the representation is unique; that clause is omitted here.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 14.

articles.title: Cyclic vertices in every residue class
articles.statement:
Let $a_1, a_2$ be integers with $a_1 - a_2$
odd. Then every residue class modulo $|a_1 - a_2|$ contains a vertex that lies on a directed
cycle of $G(-2n + a_1, -2n + a_2)$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Descendants modulo the difference of offsets
articles.statement:
Let $a_1, a_2, x, y$ be integers and
$k \in \mathbb{N}$. If $y$ is a $k$-descendant of $x$ in $G(-2n + a_1, -2n + a_2)$, that is,
the end of a directed walk of exactly $k$ edges from $x$, then

$$y \equiv (-2)^k x + a_1 \cdot \frac{1 - (-2)^k}{3} \pmod{|a_1 - a_2|}.$$

The quotient is an integer because $3$ divides $1 - (-2)^k$.

The exact-covering condition on $a_1, a_2$ is not needed.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Cycles of $G(-2n, -2n + a)$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an odd natural number and $G = G(-2n, -2n + a)$.
A cycle of $G$ is a list $(c_1, \dots, c_t)$, $t \ge 1$, of distinct integers with edges
$c_1 \to c_2, \dots, c_{t-1} \to c_t$ and $c_t \to c_1$; a vertex is cyclic if it lies on a
cycle. For an integer $x$ let $\hat{x}$ be the representative of $x$ modulo $a$ in the interval
$(-a/3, 2a/3]$, and let $\operatorname{ord}_q(-2)$ be the multiplicative order of $-2$ modulo
$q$. Then:
(i) for every integer $m$, $G$ has a loop at $m$ iff $m = 0$ or $3m = a$;
(ii) an integer $m$ is cyclic iff $-a \le 3m \le 2a$;
(iii) if $3 \nmid a$, then $G$ has exactly $a$ cyclic vertices and each residue class modulo
$a$ contains exactly one of them; if $3 \mid a$, then $G$ has exactly $a + 1$ cyclic vertices,
each residue class modulo $a$ other than the class of $2a/3$ contains exactly one of them, and
the two-vertex list $(-a/3, 2a/3)$ is a cycle of $G$;
(iv) the list $(\widehat{(-2)^k})_{0 \le k < \operatorname{ord}_a(-2)}$ is a cycle of $G$, and
for every integer $b$ with $-a < 3b < 2a$, $b \ne 0$ and $3b \ne a$, so is the list
$(\widehat{b(-2)^k})_{0 \le k < \operatorname{ord}_{a/\gcd(a, b)}(-2)}$;
(v) if $a = t a'$ with $t, a' \in \mathbb{N}$, then a list $C$ of integers is a cycle of
$G(-2n, -2n + a')$ iff the list $tC$ obtained by multiplying every entry by $t$ is a cycle of
$G$.

The paper also assumes $a'$ odd in (v); this follows from $a$ odd.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 10.

articles.title: Connectivity of $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$
articles.statement:
For an even integer $a$, the underlying undirected
graph of $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ is connected iff $a = 1 + 3^m$ or $a = 1 - 3^m$ for some
integer $m \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 15.

articles.title: Shortest walks to $\pm(a - 1)$ in $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ be an integer and
$a = 1 + 3^m$ or $a = 1 - 3^m$. Then in $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ the least $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such
that $a - 1$ is a $k$-descendant of $0$ (the end of a directed walk of exactly $k$ edges from
$0$) is $3^m$, and the least $k$ such that $-(a - 1)$ is a $k$-descendant of $0$ is also $3^m$.

The paper states this for every $a \notin \{0, 2\}$, which is false: for $a = 6$ the shortest
walk from $0$ to $5$ has $4$ edges. Its proof uses that the cycle through $0$ has $|a - 1|$
edges, which holds when the digraph has a single component.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Single-component degree-2 ECSDs up to isomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $d_1, d_2 \in \{2, -2\}$ and let
$a_1, a_2$ be integers with $a_1 - a_2$ odd. If the exact covering system digraph
$G(d_1 n + a_1, d_2 n + a_2)$, with an edge $m \to d_i m + a_i$ for every integer $m$ and
$i = 1, 2$, has a single component, that is, any two integers are joined by a path in its
underlying undirected graph, then it is isomorphic as a digraph to $G(2n, -2n + 1)$ or to
$G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ for some integer $a$ with $a = 0$, $a = 2$ or $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Degree-2 ECSDs with one component and $0$ on a cycle
articles.statement:
Let $d_1, d_2 \in \{2, -2\}$ and let
$a_1, a_2$ be integers with $a_1 - a_2$ odd, excluding the case $d_1 = d_2 = -2$ with
$|a_1 - a_2| = 1$. Consider the exact covering system digraph $G(d_1 n + a_1, d_2 n + a_2)$, with
an edge $m \to d_i m + a_i$ for every integer $m$ and $i = 1, 2$. It has a single component (any
two integers are joined by a path in its underlying undirected graph) and a directed walk of
positive length from $0$ back to $0$ if and only if one of the following holds: $d_1 = 2$,
$d_2 = -2$, $a_1 = 0$ and $a_2 = \pm 1$; or $d_1 = -2$, $d_2 = 2$, $a_2 = 0$ and $a_1 = \pm 1$;
or $d_1 = d_2 = -2$, $|a_1 - a_2| = 3^m$ for some integer $m \ge 0$, neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is
divisible by $3$, and $\max(|a_1|, |a_2|) \le 2|a_1 - a_2| - 1$.

The excluded case behaves differently: $G(-2n + 1, -2n + 2)$ has a single component and the
cycle $(0, 1)$, although $\max(1, 2) = 2 > 2 \cdot 1 - 1$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 17.

articles.title: Cycles of the digraph $G(2n, -2n + a)$
articles.statement:
For an integer $b$ write $G_b$ for the digraph
$G(2n, -2n + b)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, with an edge $m \to 2m$ and an edge $m \to -2m + b$ for every
integer $m$. Let $a$ be an odd natural number. Then (i) $G_a$ has a loop at $m$ if and only if
$m = 0$ or $3m = a$; (ii) $G_a$ has a directed walk of positive length from $m$ back to $m$ if
and only if $0 \le m < a/2$; (iii) for all natural numbers $t$ and $a'$ with $a = t a'$, a list
$(c_1, \dots, c_s)$ of integers is a cycle of $G_{a'}$ if and only if $(t c_1, \dots, t c_s)$ is
a cycle of $G_a$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Descendants in the digraph $G(2n, -2n + a)$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $m$ be integers and let
$k \ge 1$. In the digraph $G(2n, -2n + a)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, with an edge $x \to 2x$ and an edge
$x \to -2x + a$ for every integer $x$, the $k$-descendants of $m$ (the ends of directed walks of
exactly $k$ edges from $m$) are exactly the integers $2^k m$, the integers $2^k m - ba$ and
$-(2^k m - ba)$ for natural numbers $b$ with $1 \le b < 2^{k-1}$, and $-(2^k m - 2^{k-1} a)$.

This holds for every integer $a$, not only for odd $a$, for which $G(2n, -2n + a)$ is an exact
covering system digraph.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Cycles of the digraph $G(2n, 2n - a)$
articles.statement:
For an integer $b$ write $G_b$ for the digraph
$G(2n, 2n - b)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, with an edge $m \to 2m$ and an edge $m \to 2m - b$ for every
integer $m$. Let $a$ be an odd natural number, write $x \bmod a$ for the residue of $x$ in
$\{0, \dots, a - 1\}$, and write $\operatorname{ord}(2, q)$ for the multiplicative order of $2$
modulo $q$. Then (i) $G_a$ has a loop at $m$ if and only if $m = 0$ or $m = a$; (ii) $G_a$ has a
directed walk of positive length from $m$ back to $m$ if and only if $0 \le m \le a$; (iii) the
list $(2^k \bmod a)_{0 \le k < \operatorname{ord}(2, a)}$ is a cycle of $G_a$; for every integer
$b$ with $1 \le b < a$ the list $(b 2^k \bmod a)_{0 \le k < \operatorname{ord}(2, a/\gcd(a, b))}$
is a cycle of $G_a$; and every cycle of $G_a$ with more than one vertex is a rotation of one of
these lists for some integer $b$ with $1 \le b < a$; (iv) for all natural numbers $t$ and $a'$
with $a = t a'$, a list $(c_1, \dots, c_s)$ of integers is a cycle of $G_{a'}$ if and only if
$(t c_1, \dots, t c_s)$ is a cycle of $G_a$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Normal form of the ECSDs $G(2n + a_1, 2n + a_2)$
articles.statement:
For all integers $a_1, a_2$ with
$a_1 - a_2$ odd, the exact covering system digraph $G(2n + a_1, 2n + a_2)$, with an edge
$m \to 2m + a_1$ and an edge $m \to 2m + a_2$ for every integer $m$, is isomorphic as a digraph
to $G(2n, 2n - a)$ for some odd natural number $a$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Normal forms of the ECSDs $G(-2n + a_1, -2n + a_2)$
articles.statement:
For all integers $a_1, a_2$ with
$a_1 - a_2$ odd, the exact covering system digraph $G(-2n + a_1, -2n + a_2)$, with an edge
$m \to -2m + a_1$ and an edge $m \to -2m + a_2$ for every integer $m$, is isomorphic as a
digraph to one of the following: $G(-2n, -2n + a)$ for an odd natural number $a$ (Type 3.1);
$G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ for an even natural number $a$ with $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ (Type 3.2); or
$G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ for an even integer $a$ with $a \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (Type 3.3).

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Bounds on the cyclic vertices of $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ when $a \equiv 2 \pmod 3$
articles.statement:
Let $a$
be an even integer with $a \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, and let $m$ be an integer such that the digraph
$G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, with an edge $x \to -2x + 1$ and an edge $x \to -2x + a$
for every integer $x$, has a directed walk of positive length from $m$ back to $m$. If $a \ge 2$,
then $-(a - 1)/3 < m < 2a/3$; if $a \le -2$, then $-2(|a| + 1)/3 < m < (|a| + 3)/3$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 12.

articles.title: Cyclic vertices of $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ and their residues when $a \equiv 2 \pmod 3$
articles.statement:
Let
$a$ be an even integer with $a \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, and call an integer $m$ cyclic if the digraph
$G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, with an edge $x \to -2x + 1$ and an edge $x \to -2x + a$
for every integer $x$, has a directed walk of positive length from $m$ back to $m$. Then: if
$a \ge 2$, every integer $m$ with $-(a - 1)/3 < m < 2a/3$ is cyclic; if $a \le -2$, every integer
$m$ with $-2(|a| + 1)/3 < m < (|a| + 3)/3$ is cyclic; every residue class modulo $|a - 1|$
contains a cyclic integer; and there are a least cyclic integer $\ell$ and a greatest cyclic
integer $h$ such that $\ell \equiv h \pmod{|a - 1|}$, the list $(\ell, h)$ is a cycle, and any
two distinct cyclic integers that are congruent modulo $|a - 1|$ are $\ell$ and $h$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 13.

articles.title: Cyclic vertices of $G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ when $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an even
natural number with $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ and let $m$ be an integer. The digraph
$G(-2n + 1, -2n + a)$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, with an edge $x \to -2x + 1$ and an edge $x \to -2x + a$
for every integer $x$, has a directed walk of positive length from $m$ back to $m$ if and only
if $-(a - 1)/3 < m < 2a/3$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 11.

articles.title: Normal form of Type 2 exact covering system digraphs
articles.statement:
Let $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ with
$a_1 - a_2$ odd, and write $G(2n + a_1, -2n + a_2)$ for the exact covering system digraph on
$\mathbb{Z}$ with an edge $m \to n$ exactly when $n = 2m + a_1$ or $n = -2m + a_2$. Then there is
an odd natural number $a$ such that $G(2n + a_1, -2n + a_2)$ is isomorphic as a digraph to
$G(2n, -2n + a)$, the digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$ with an edge $m \to n$ exactly when $n = 2m$ or
$n = -2m + a$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Two-vertex cycles of a digraph on the integers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$. The list $(x, y)$ is a cycle of $R$ if and only if $x \ne y$ and $R$ has both
edges $x \to y$ and $y \to x$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 2 (2-cycles).

articles.title: One-vertex cycles of a digraph on the integers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$x \in \mathbb{Z}$. The one-element list $(x)$ is a cycle of $R$ if and only if $R$ has a loop
$x \to x$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 2 (cycles of length 1).

articles.title: Cycles of a digraph on the integers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$, given by its edge
relation. A list $c = (c_1, \dots, c_t)$ of integers is a cycle of $R$ when it is nonempty, its
entries are pairwise distinct, and $R$ has the edges $c_1 \to c_2, \dots, c_{t-1} \to c_t$ and
$c_t \to c_1$ (for $t = 1$ this means a loop $c_1 \to c_1$).

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 2 (cycles `C = (c₁, …, c_t)`).

articles.title: The $1$-descendants are the out-neighbours
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $n$ is a $1$-descendant of $m$ in $R$ if and only if $R$ has an edge
$m \to n$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 1 (definition of successor).

articles.title: The only $0$-descendant of a vertex is itself
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $n$ is a $0$-descendant of $m$ in $R$ if and only if $n = m$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 1 (definition of `k`-descendant).

articles.title: $k$-descendants in a digraph on the integers
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a digraph on $\mathbb{Z}$, let
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $n$ is a $k$-descendant of $m$ in $R$ when
there is a directed walk of exactly $k$ edges from $m$ to $n$, that is, integers
$m = x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k = n$ such that $R$ has an edge $x_{i-1} \to x_i$ for every
$1 \le i \le k$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Section 1 (definition of `k`-descendant).

articles.title: Negabinary representations with digits $1$ and $a$
articles.statement:
Let $a \in \mathbb{Z}$. Every integer
$z$ can be written as $z = \sum_{j=0}^{k} b_j (-2)^j$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and digits
$b_0, \dots, b_k \in \{1, a\}$ if and only if $a = 1 + 3^m$ or $a = 1 - 3^m$ for some integer
$m \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Negabinary representations with two digits
articles.statement:
Let $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ with
$|a_1 - a_2| \ne 1$. Every integer $z$ can be written as $z = \sum_{j=0}^{k} b_j (-2)^j$ for some
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and digits $b_0, \dots, b_k \in \{a_1, a_2\}$ if and only if
$|a_1 - a_2| = 3^m$ for some integer $m \ge 0$, neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is divisible by $3$, and
$\max\{|a_1|, |a_2|\} \le 2|a_1 - a_2| - 1$.

The hypothesis $|a_1 - a_2| \ne 1$ restricts the printed statement, which fails when
$|a_1 - a_2| = 1$: the digits $\{1, 2\}$ represent every integer, yet $\max\{1, 2\} = 2 > 1$.
The paper's alternative $\{a_1, a_2\} = \{0, \pm 1\}$ lies in the excluded case and is dropped.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Nine divides $n$ when $n > 3$ and $3n$ divides $2^n + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $n > 3$ be a natural
number. If $3n$ divides $2^n + 1$, then $9$ divides $n$.

For odd $n$ the hypothesis says that $n$ divides the integer $(2^n + 1)/3$, which is the form
in the paper; for even $n$ it never holds, since $3$ does not divide $2^n + 1$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Lemma 4, quoting [3].

articles.title: Divisibility of $1 - (-2)^{3k}$ from $1 - (-2)^k$
articles.statement:
For every integer $n$ and every
natural number $k$, if $3n$ divides $1 - (-2)^k$, then $9n$ divides $1 - (-2)^{3k}$.

Since $3$ always divides $1 - (-2)^k$, this is equivalent to: if $n$ divides
$(1 - (-2)^k)/3$, then $3n$ divides $(1 - (-2)^{3k})/3$. The paper states it for positive $n$
and $k$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Divisibility of $2^{3n} + 1$ from $2^n + 1$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, if $3n$
divides $2^n + 1$, then $9n$ divides $2^{3n} + 1$.

Equivalently, if $3$ divides $2^n + 1$ and $n$ divides $(2^n + 1)/3$, then $3n$ divides
$(2^{3n} + 1)/3$. For $n = 0$ the hypothesis fails, so positivity is not assumed.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Bounding the power of $3$ dividing $2^{3k} + 1$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $k$, if
$3^{m+1}$ does not divide $2^k + 1$, then $3^{m+2}$ does not divide $2^{3k} + 1$.

For odd $k$, where $3$ divides $2^k + 1$, this says: if $3^m$ does not divide $(2^k + 1)/3$,
then $3^{m+1}$ does not divide $(2^{3k} + 1)/3$. For even $k$ the conclusion holds since $3$
does not divide $2^{3k} + 1$.

## Sources

- Dana Neidmann, *Exact Covering System Digraphs of Degree 2 and Non-Standard Binary Representations of Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A107, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Fraenkel's Bernoulli recurrence for exact covers
articles.statement:
Let $q \ge 2$, $m \ge 1$ and $M$ be
natural numbers, and for $i = 1, \dots, q$ let $n_i$ be a positive integer and $a_i$ an integer
with $0 \le a_i < n_i$. Suppose the residue classes $a_i \bmod n_i$, counted with repetition,
form an exact $M$-cover of $\mathbb{Z}$: every integer $k$ satisfies $k \equiv a_i \pmod{n_i}$
for exactly $M$ indices $i$. Then

$$
B_m \Big(M - \sum_{i=1}^{q} n_i^{m-1}\Big) =
\sum_{i=1}^{q} n_i^{m-1} \sum_{s=0}^{m-1} \binom{m}{s} B_s \Big(\frac{a_i}{n_i}\Big)^{m-s},
$$

where $B_s$ is the $s$-th Bernoulli number, with the convention $B_1 = -\frac{1}{2}$.

Only this direction of the source's equation (23) is stated; the converse, Beebee's variant with
a parameter $x$, and Porubsky's weighted variant are not.

## Sources

- Yevgenya Movshovich, "Raabe's Identity and Covering Systems," Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.2.8, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Movshovich/movsho5.tex>. Equation (23); lines 228–241.

articles.title: Fraenkel's Bernoulli recurrence for exact covers by any number of classes
articles.statement:
Let $q$, $M$
and $m \ge 1$ be natural numbers, and for $i = 1, \dots, q$ let $n_i$ be a positive integer and
$a_i$ an integer with $0 \le a_i < n_i$. Suppose the residue classes $a_i \bmod n_i$, counted
with repetition, form an exact $M$-cover of $\mathbb{Z}$: every integer $k$ satisfies
$k \equiv a_i \pmod{n_i}$ for exactly $M$ indices $i$. Then

$$
B_m \Big(M - \sum_{i=1}^{q} n_i^{m-1}\Big) =
\sum_{i=1}^{q} n_i^{m-1} \sum_{s=0}^{m-1} \binom{m}{s} B_s \Big(\frac{a_i}{n_i}\Big)^{m-s},
$$

where $B_s$ is the $s$-th Bernoulli number, with the convention $B_1 = -\frac{1}{2}$.

The source assumes $q \ge 2$; the identity holds without that assumption.

articles.title: Multiplicity of an indexed system of residue classes
articles.statement:
Given $k \in \mathbb{N}$, moduli
$m_0, \dots, m_{k-1} \in \mathbb{N}$ and residues $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in \mathbb{Z}$, the
multiplicity of an integer $z$ is the number of indices $i < k$ with $z \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$.

Indices are counted separately, so a residue class listed several times is counted that many
times; a modulus $m_i = 0$ makes the condition $z = r_i$.

articles.title: Exact covers by residue classes
articles.statement:
Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$m_0, \dots, m_{k-1} \in \mathbb{N}$ be moduli and $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in \mathbb{Z}$ residues,
and let $M \in \mathbb{N}$ and $T \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$. The system of residue classes
$r_i \bmod m_i$ is an exact $M$-cover of $T$ when $k \ge 2$, every $m_i$ is positive, every
$z \in T$ satisfies $z \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$ for exactly $M$ indices $i < k$, and every integer
$z \notin T$ satisfies $z \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$ for no index $i < k$.

Indices are counted separately, so a residue class listed several times counts that many times.

articles.title: Hough's minimum modulus theorem
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $N$ such that no finite set of
residue classes covering $\mathbb{Z}$ has pairwise distinct moduli that are all at least $N$.
Hence the conjecture of Open Garden problem OPG-493 is false.

## Sources

- Bob Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), 361-382; arXiv:1307.0874, https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.0874.

articles.title: Covering systems with arbitrarily large distinct moduli (OPG-493)
articles.statement:
The statement that
for every natural number $N$ there are finitely many residue classes $a_1 \bmod m_1, \dots,
a_k \bmod m_k$ that cover $\mathbb{Z}$ (every integer lies in at least one of them) whose moduli
are pairwise distinct and all at least $N$.

articles.title: Replacing the largest prime factor of the modulus set
articles.statement:
Let $m, L \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$p \ge m$ be a prime with $p \nmid L$, let $q > p$ be the largest prime dividing $L$, and write
$\nu_q(L)$ for the exponent of $q$ in $L$. Suppose there are residues $r_d \in \mathbb{Z}$, one
for each divisor $d \ge m$ of $L$, such that every integer $x$ satisfies $x \equiv r_d \pmod d$
for some such $d$. Then the same holds with $L$ replaced by $p^{\nu_q(L)} L / q^{\nu_q(L)}$:
there are residues $s_d \in \mathbb{Z}$, one for each divisor $d \ge m$ of
$p^{\nu_q(L)} L / q^{\nu_q(L)}$, such that every integer $x$ satisfies $x \equiv s_d \pmod d$
for some such $d$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Lemma 6.

articles.title: A distinct covering system with minimum modulus 7 and moduli of lcm 15120
articles.statement:
There is a
distinct covering system, that is, a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with
$r \in \mathbb{Z}$, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and no two with the same modulus, such that every
integer satisfies at least one of them, whose moduli are all at least $7$, include $7$, and have
least common multiple $15120$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Theorem 5.

articles.title: A distinct covering system with moduli from 6 to 168
articles.statement:
There is a distinct covering
system, that is, a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with $r \in \mathbb{Z}$,
$m \in \mathbb{N}$ and no two with the same modulus, such that every integer satisfies at least
one of them, whose moduli all lie between $6$ and $168$ and include both $6$ and $168$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Theorem 2; the paper's witness is due to Ognian Trifonov.

articles.title: Merging the p classes whose modulus is divisible by a prime power
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a
covering system with positive moduli: a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with
$r \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $m \ge 1$ such that every integer satisfies at least one of them. Let $p$
be a prime and $a \ge 1$, and suppose exactly $p$ congruences of $C$ have modulus divisible by
$p^a$, with moduli $p^a m_1, \dots, p^a m_p$. Then for some $r \in \mathbb{Z}$, replacing these
$p$ congruences by the single congruence $x \equiv r \pmod{p^{a-1} \operatorname{lcm}(m_1,
\dots, m_p)}$ still gives a covering system.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Lemma 2, quoting Dalton–Trifonov, Corollary 9.

articles.title: Krukenberg's conjecture for minimum modulus five
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a distinct covering
system: a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with $r \in \mathbb{Z}$ and
$m \in \mathbb{N}$, no two with the same modulus, such that every integer satisfies at least one
of them. If every modulus of $C$ is at least $5$ and some modulus equals $5$, then some modulus
of $C$ is at least $108$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Discarding the classes whose modulus is divisible by a large prime power
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a
distinct covering system: a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with
$r \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$ (where $x \equiv r \pmod 0$ means $x = r$), no two
with the same modulus, such that every integer satisfies at least one of them. Let
$B \in \mathbb{N}$ be at least every modulus of $C$, let $p$ be a prime and $a \ge 1$. If
$B < p^a (p + 1)$, then the congruences of $C$ whose modulus is not divisible by $p^a$ still
cover every integer.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Lemma 1, quoting Krukenberg, Corollary 2.3, and Dalton–Trifonov, Corollary 8.

articles.title: Swapping two residues modulo a prime in a covering system
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a covering system
with positive moduli: a finite set of congruences $x \equiv a \pmod m$ with $a \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $m \ge 1$ such that every integer satisfies at least one of them. Let $L$ be the least
common multiple of its moduli, $p$ a prime dividing $L$, and $a_1 < a_2 \le p - 1$ natural
numbers. For a prime $\ell$ write $\nu_\ell(L)$ for the exponent of $\ell$ in $L$, and let
$C_p(\alpha)$ be the set of congruences $x \equiv a \pmod m$ in $C$ with $p \mid m$ and
$a \equiv \alpha \pmod p$. Let $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $t \equiv a_2 - a_1 \pmod{p^{\nu_p(L)}}$
and $t \equiv 0 \pmod{q^{\nu_q(L)}}$ for every prime $q \ne p$ dividing $L$. Then the
congruences of $C$ outside $C_p(a_1) \cup C_p(a_2)$, together with $x \equiv a + t \pmod m$ for
each $x \equiv a \pmod m$ in $C_p(a_1)$ and $x \equiv a - t \pmod m$ for each
$x \equiv a \pmod m$ in $C_p(a_2)$, form a covering system.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Lemma 4, from the author's thesis, Lemma 2.13.

articles.title: Translating a covering system
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a covering system: a finite set of
congruences $x \equiv a_i \pmod{m_i}$ with $a_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $m_i \in \mathbb{N}$ (where
$x \equiv a_i \pmod 0$ means $x = a_i$) such that every integer satisfies at least one of them.
Then for every $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ the congruences $x \equiv a_i + t \pmod{m_i}$ also form a
covering system.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Least common multiple of a covering system with minimum modulus five
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a
distinct covering system: a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with
$r \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$, no two with the same modulus, such that every integer
satisfies at least one of them. If every modulus of $C$ is at least $5$ and some modulus equals
$5$, then the least common multiple of the moduli of $C$ is at least $1440$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Least common multiple of a covering system with minimum modulus six
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a
distinct covering system: a finite set of congruences $x \equiv r \pmod m$ with
$r \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$, no two with the same modulus, such that every integer
satisfies at least one of them. If every modulus of $C$ is at least $6$ and some modulus equals
$6$, then the least common multiple of the moduli of $C$ is at least $5040$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Mirsky–Newman bound for distinct covering systems
articles.statement:
Let $a_1 \bmod m_1, \dots,
a_k \bmod m_k$ be residue classes that cover $\mathbb{Z}$, that is, every integer lies in at
least one of them. If the moduli $m_1, \dots, m_k$ are pairwise distinct and all at least $2$,
then $\sum_{i=1}^{k} 1/m_i > 1$.

## Sources

- Jonah Klein, *On a Conjecture of Krukenberg and a Problem of Dalton and Trifonov*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A38, Lemma 5, quoting Mirsky and Newman.

articles.title: Strict covering system
articles.statement:
A covering system of a commutative semiring $R$, given by cosets
$r_i + I_i$, is strict if the ideals $I_i$ are pairwise distinct. In the case $R = \mathbb{Z}$, this
means that the congruences defining it have pairwise distinct moduli.

This corresponds to the notion of covering system that Erdős and Graham use.

## Sources

- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

articles.title: Totalized cubic residue symbol
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field that is the third cyclotomic
extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, and let $\zeta \in K$ be a
primitive cube root of unity. For $a, n \in \mathcal{O}_K$, the value is $0$ if $n = 0$;
otherwise it is the product, over the prime ideals $P$ in the factorization of the principal
ideal $(n)$ counted with multiplicity, of the totalized prime-ideal cubic symbol of $a$ at $P$
(which is $1$ unless $P$ is a nonzero prime ideal whose absolute norm is coprime to $3$).

articles.title: Cubic residue symbol modulo an element
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field that is the third
cyclotomic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, let $\zeta \in K$ be
a primitive cube root of unity and let $\omega$ be $\zeta$ regarded as an element of
$\mathcal{O}_K$. For $a \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and a cubic residue denominator $n$ (that is,
$n \neq 0$ and the absolute norm of the principal ideal $(n)$ is coprime to $3$), the cubic
residue symbol $(a/n)_3$ is the product, over the prime ideals $P$ in the factorization of $(n)$
counted with multiplicity, of the value that is $0$ if $a \in P$ and otherwise the unique
$c \in \{1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ with $c \equiv a^{(N(P) - 1)/3} \pmod{P}$, where $N(P)$ is the
absolute norm of $P$. Each such $P$ is a nonzero prime ideal whose absolute norm is coprime
to $3$.

articles.title: Cubic residue denominators
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field that is the third cyclotomic
extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. An element $n \in \mathcal{O}_K$
is a cubic residue denominator when $n \neq 0$ and the absolute norm of the principal ideal
$(n)$ is coprime to $3$.

articles.title: Totalized prime-ideal cubic symbol
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field that is the third
cyclotomic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, let $\zeta \in K$ be
a primitive cube root of unity and let $\omega$ be $\zeta$ regarded as an element of
$\mathcal{O}_K$. For an ideal $P$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $a \in \mathcal{O}_K$: if $P$ is a
nonzero prime ideal whose absolute norm $N(P)$ is coprime to $3$, the value is $0$ when
$a \in P$, and otherwise the unique $c \in \{1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ with
$c \equiv a^{(N(P) - 1)/3} \pmod{P}$; for every other ideal $P$ the value is $1$.

articles.title: Cubic residue symbol at a prime ideal
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field that is the third
cyclotomic extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, let $\zeta \in K$ be
a primitive cube root of unity and let $\omega$ be $\zeta$ regarded as an element of
$\mathcal{O}_K$. For a nonzero prime ideal $P$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ whose absolute norm $N(P)$ is
coprime to $3$ and for $a \in \mathcal{O}_K$, the cubic residue symbol $(a/P)_3$ is $0$ if
$a \in P$, and otherwise the unique $c \in \{1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ with
$c \equiv a^{(N(P) - 1)/3} \pmod{P}$.

articles.title: Eisenstein's lemma for Jacobi symbols (odd coprime form)
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be odd natural
numbers that are coprime. Then the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ equals $(-1)^{S}$,
where $S = \sum_{i=1}^{(b-1)/2} \lfloor ia/b \rfloor$.

articles.title: Eisenstein's lemma for Jacobi symbols
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive odd natural numbers that
are coprime. Then the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ equals $(-1)^{S}$, where
$S = \sum_{i=1}^{(b-1)/2} \lfloor ia/b \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Damanvir Singh Binner, "Generalization of a Result of Sylvester Related to the Frobenius Coin Problem", Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.8.4, Theorem `Eisenstein`, lines 272-278, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Binner/binner13.tex>. It follows from `eisenstein_lemma_jacobi_symbol_general`; the hypotheses `ha_pos` and `hb_pos` are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol at odd numbers for integers congruent to 3 mod 4
articles.statement:
Let $\chi_4$ be the
nontrivial Dirichlet character modulo $4$, so $\chi_4(n) = 1$ for $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and
$\chi_4(n) = -1$ for $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Let $D$ be an integer with $D \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and
let $p$ be an odd natural number. Then $\chi_4(p) \cdot \left(\frac{p}{|D|}\right) =
\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$, where $\left(\frac{p}{|D|}\right)$ is the Jacobi symbol and
$\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$ is the Kronecker symbol.

For $D > 0$ the factor $\chi_4(p)$ is the sign from quadratic reciprocity; for $D < 0$ it is
the value $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right) = \chi_4(p)$.

articles.title: Fundamental discriminant
articles.statement:
An integer $D$ is a fundamental discriminant if either $D$ is
squarefree and $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, or $D = 4m$ for some squarefree integer $m$ with
$m \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ or $m \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

With this definition $D = 1$ is a fundamental discriminant and $D = 0$ is not.

articles.title: Jacobi symbol of $4m$ at an odd denominator
articles.statement:
For every integer $m$ and every odd natural
number $p$, the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{4m}{p}\right)$ equals $\left(\frac{m}{p}\right)$.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol at odd primes for negative integers congruent to 1 mod 4
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a
negative integer with $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and let $p$ be an odd prime. Then the Jacobi symbol
$\left(\frac{p}{|D|}\right)$ equals the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol at odd primes for integers congruent to 1 mod 4
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an integer
with $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and let $p$ be an odd prime. Then the Jacobi symbol
$\left(\frac{p}{|D|}\right)$ equals the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$.

This covers $D$ of either sign. The congruence condition cannot be dropped: for $D = 3$ and
$p = 7$ the Jacobi symbol is $1$ while the Kronecker symbol is $-1$.

articles.title: Quadratic reciprocity for the Kronecker symbol, positive $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a
positive integer with $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and let $p$ be an odd prime. Then the Jacobi symbol
$\left(\frac{p}{|D|}\right)$ equals the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$.

The congruence condition cannot be dropped: for $D = 3$ and $p = 7$ the Jacobi symbol
$\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)$ is $1$, while the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)$ is
$-1$.

articles.title: Jacobi symbol of $2m$ at an odd denominator
articles.statement:
For every integer $m$ and every odd natural
number $p$, the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{2m}{p}\right)$ equals
$\chi_8(p) \left(\frac{m}{p}\right)$, where $\chi_8$ is the Dirichlet character modulo $8$ with
$\chi_8(n) = 1$ for $n \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 8$, $\chi_8(n) = -1$ for $n \equiv \pm 3 \pmod 8$, and
$\chi_8(n) = 0$ for even $n$.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol at a prime
articles.statement:
For an integer $D$ and a natural number $p$, the Kronecker
symbol of $D$ at $p$ is the Kronecker symbol of $D$ at two if $p = 2$, the Legendre symbol
$\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$ if $p$ is an odd prime, and $0$ if $p$ is not prime.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol at two
articles.statement:
For an integer $D$, the Kronecker symbol of $D$ at $2$ is $0$
if $D$ is even, $1$ if $D \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 8$, and $-1$ if $D \equiv \pm 3 \pmod 8$.

articles.title: Kronecker–Jacobi bridge for 4m with m ≡ 3 mod 4
articles.statement:
Even `m % 4 = 3` subcase for odd `p`: reduce `4 * m` to `m`, identify
`kroneckerSym` with `jacobiSym` at odd denominators, then apply the `D % 4 = 3`
bridge to `m` itself. Covers prime and composite odd denominators alike.

articles.title: Kronecker and Jacobi symbols agree at odd primes
articles.statement:
For every integer $D$ and every prime
$p \ne 2$, the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$ equals the Jacobi symbol
$\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol with a prime denominator
articles.statement:
For every integer $D$ and every prime $p$,
the Kronecker symbol $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$ equals the Kronecker symbol of $D$ at the
prime $p$.

articles.title: Kronecker symbol
articles.statement:
For an integer $D$ and a natural number $n$, the Kronecker symbol
$\left(\frac{D}{n}\right)$ is defined as follows. If $n = 0$, it is $1$ when $D = \pm 1$ and $0$
otherwise. If $n \ge 1$ and $n = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k$ is the factorization of $n$ into primes,
listed with multiplicity, it is the product of the Kronecker symbols of $D$ at the primes
$p_1, \ldots, p_k$ (the empty product $1$ when $n = 1$).

articles.title: Quadratic Dirichlet character of a fundamental discriminant
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a fundamental
discriminant. Then there is a unique integer-valued Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $|D|$ such
that $\chi(n \bmod |D|) = \left(\frac{D}{n}\right)$ for every natural number $n$, where
$\left(\frac{D}{n}\right)$ is the Kronecker symbol.

## Sources

- Joshua Males, Andreas Mono, Larry Rolen, and Ian Wagner, *Central L-values of newforms and local polynomials*, arXiv:2306.15519v5, subsection "L-functions and L-values", line 455. Exact source sentence: "One may also consider L-functions associated to a Dirichlet character chi_D = (D / dot), namely ...". This is the existence and uniqueness of the integer-valued Dirichlet character of level `Int.natAbs D` evaluating as the positive-denominator Kronecker symbol `kroneckerSym D` at every natural `n`, assuming `IsFundamentalDiscriminant D`. No primitivity or conductor claim belongs to this item.

articles.title: Numbers congruent to 6 mod 8 are not squares
articles.statement:
If a natural number $n$ satisfies
$n \equiv 6 \pmod 8$, then $n$ is not the square of a natural number.

articles.title: Numbers congruent to 3 mod 8 are not squares
articles.statement:
If a natural number $n$ satisfies
$n \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, then $n$ is not the square of a natural number.

articles.title: A number that is 6 mod 8 minus a smaller square is not a square
articles.statement:
Let $N$ and $k$ be
natural numbers with $N \equiv 6 \pmod 8$ and $k^2 < N$. Then $N - k^2$ is not the square of a
natural number.

articles.title: Squares of integers modulo 8
articles.statement:
For every integer $x$, the remainder of $x^2$ on division
by $8$, taken in $\{0, 1, \dots, 7\}$, is $0$, $1$ or $4$.

articles.title: Squares of natural numbers modulo 8
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, the remainder of $r^2$
on division by $8$ is $0$, $1$ or $4$.

articles.title: Odd squares modulo 16
articles.statement:
For every odd natural number $k$, either $k^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{16}$
and $k \equiv 1$ or $7 \pmod 8$, or $k^2 \equiv 9 \pmod{16}$ and $k \equiv 3$ or $5 \pmod 8$.

articles.title: Linear Legendre-symbol sums vanish
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $b$ and $c$ be
integers with $p \nmid b$. Then the Legendre symbols $\left(\frac{b\ell + c}{p}\right)$ for
$\ell = 0, 1, \dots, p - 1$ sum to $0$.

## Sources

- This is the first corollary of Theorem `thm1` in Ram Krishna Pandey and Anshumaan Parashar, *On Certain Sums with Quadratic Expressions Involving the Legendre Symbol*, Journal of Integer Sequences 21 (2018), Article 18.4.7, lines 190–193, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL21/Pandey/pandey14.tex>. The proof here reindexes Mathlib's `quadraticChar_sum_zero` through the affine permutation `x ↦ b * x + c` of `ZMod p`.

articles.title: Alternating series with a three-step continued fraction pattern
articles.statement:
Let $(u_i)_{i \ge 0}$
be positive integers with $u_0 = 1$, and let $x$ be an irrational real number with
$\sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i / u_i = x$. Write $x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ for its continued fraction
expansion and $p_n / q_n = [a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n]$ for its convergents, with $q_0 = 1$ and
$q_1 = a_1$. Suppose that for every $n \ge 0$ we have
$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i / u_i = p_{n+1} / q_{n+1}$, $u_{3n+2} \mid u_{3n+3}$,
$u_{3n+2} - u_{3n+1} = \bigl(\prod_{j=0}^{\lfloor 3n/2 \rfloor} u_{3n-2j+1} / u_{3n-2j}\bigr)^2$
and $u_{3n+4} - u_{3n+3} = (u_{3n+3} / u_{3n+2})^2 (u_{3n+2} - u_{3n+1})$. Then
(i) $u_n = q_n q_{n+1}$ for every $n \ge 0$, (ii) for every $n \ge 0$ there is a natural number
$m$ with $a_{3n+4} = m \, q_{3n+2}$, and (iii) $a_{3n+3} = 1$ for every $n \ge 0$ and
$a_{3n+2} = 1$ for every $n \ge 1$.

The product runs over the quotients $u_{k+1} / u_k$ for $k = 3n, 3n - 2, 3n - 4, \dots$, ending
at $k = 1$ when $n$ is odd and at $k = 0$ when $n$ is even. The condition $a_{3n+2} = 1$ is
stated only for $n \ge 1$, because it can fail at $n = 0$: the continued fraction
$[0; 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 1, 19, 1, 1, 699, \dots]$ with $u_n = q_n q_{n+1}$ satisfies every hypothesis
and has $a_2 = 2$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Theorem 10 (`jis-2025-25.1.4-thm-10`).

articles.title: Alternating series with a two-step continued fraction pattern
articles.statement:
Let $(u_i)_{i \ge 0}$ be
positive integers with $u_0 = 1$, and let $x$ be an irrational real number with
$\sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i / u_i = x$. Write $x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ for its continued fraction
expansion and $p_n / q_n = [a_0; a_1, \dots, a_n]$ for its convergents, with $q_0 = 1$ and
$q_1 = a_1$. Suppose that for every $n \ge 0$ we have
$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i / u_i = p_{n+1} / q_{n+1}$, $u_{2n+1} \mid u_{2n+2}$ and
$u_{2n+3} = \bigl(\prod_{j=0}^{n} u_{2j+2} / u_{2j+1}\bigr)^2 + u_{2n+2}$. Then
(i) $u_n = q_n q_{n+1}$ for every $n \ge 0$, (ii) for every $n \ge 0$ there is a natural number
$m$ with $a_{2n+3} = m \, q_{2n+1}$, and (iii) $a_{2n+2} = 1$ for every $n \ge 1$.

Part (iii) is stated only for $n \ge 1$, because it can fail at $n = 0$: the continued fraction
$[0; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 32, 1, 1280, \dots]$, continued by $a_{2n+4} = 1$ and
$a_{2n+3} = q_{2n+1}$, with $u_n = q_n q_{n+1}$ (here $q = 1, 1, 3, 4, 7, 32, 39, 1280, \dots$)
satisfies every hypothesis and has $a_2 = 2$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Theorem 4 (`jis-2025-25.1.4-thm-4`).

articles.title: Three-step pattern as an alternating series
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a natural number, let
$(\omega_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be positive integers, and let $(q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the convergent
denominators of the three-step pattern for $\beta$ and $(\omega_n)$. Then the series
$\sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i / (q_i q_{i+1})$ converges absolutely, and its sum $x$ has continued
fraction expansion $[a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ with $a_0 = 0$, $a_1 = \omega_0$, and
$a_{3n+2} = a_{3n+3} = 1$ and $a_{3n+4} = \omega_{n+1} q_{3n+2}^\beta$ for every $n \ge 0$; that is,
$x = [0; \omega_0, 1, 1, \omega_1 q_2^\beta, 1, 1, \omega_2 q_5^\beta, \dots]$.

The paper assumes $\beta \ge 1$; the statement here also allows $\beta = 0$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Proposition 8, under the hypotheses (e3) of Section 2.2.

articles.title: Small values of the three-step pattern denominators
articles.statement:
For $\beta = 1$ and $\omega_n = 1$
for all $n$, the convergent denominators $q_0, \dots, q_7$ of the three-step pattern are
$1, 1, 2, 3, 8, 11, 19, 220$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Section 2.2, display (e33).

articles.title: Convergent denominators of the three-step pattern
articles.statement:
For a natural number $\beta$ and a
sequence $(\omega_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of natural numbers, define natural numbers $q_n$ by $q_0 = 1$,
$q_1 = \omega_0$, and for every $n \ge 0$, $q_{3n+2} = q_{3n+1} + q_{3n}$,
$q_{3n+3} = q_{3n+2} + q_{3n+1}$ and $q_{3n+4} = \omega_{n+1} q_{3n+3} q_{3n+2}^\beta + q_{3n+2}$.

When the $\omega_n$ are positive, these are the convergent denominators of the continued fraction
$[0; \omega_0, 1, 1, \omega_1 q_2^\beta, 1, 1, \omega_2 q_5^\beta, \dots]$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Section 2.2, displays (e3) and (e33).

articles.title: Irrationality exponent of the three-step pattern
articles.statement:
Let $\beta \ge 1$ be a natural number,
let $(\omega_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be positive integers, let $(q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the convergent
denominators of the three-step pattern for $\beta$ and $(\omega_n)$, and let
$x = \sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i / (q_i q_{i+1})$. Let $L$ be the limit superior, in the extended real
numbers, of $\ln \omega_n / \ln q_{3n}$ as $n \to \infty$. Then $x$ is Liouville with exponent $p$
for every real $p < 2 + \beta + L$, that is, for each such $p$ there is a constant $C$ such that
$0 < |x - m/k| < C / k^p$ for infinitely many positive integers $k$, each with some integer $m$.
Moreover $2 + \beta \le 2 + \beta + L$, and $x$ is transcendental.

In other words, the irrationality exponent of $x$ satisfies $\mu(x) \ge 2 + \beta + L$, where $L$
may be $+\infty$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Two-step pattern as an alternating series
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a natural number, let
$(\omega_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be positive integers, and let $(q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the convergent
denominators of the two-step pattern for $\beta$ and $(\omega_n)$. Then the series
$\sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i / (q_i q_{i+1})$ converges absolutely, and its sum $x$ has continued
fraction expansion $[a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ with $a_0 = 0$, $a_1 = \omega_0$, and
$a_{2n+2} = 1$ and $a_{2n+3} = \omega_{n+1} q_{2n+1}^\beta$ for every $n \ge 0$; that is,
$x = [0; \omega_0, 1, \omega_1 q_1^\beta, 1, \omega_2 q_3^\beta, 1, \dots]$.

The paper assumes $\beta \ge 1$; the statement here also allows $\beta = 0$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Proposition 2, under the hypotheses (e2) of Section 2.1.

articles.title: Small values of the two-step pattern denominators
articles.statement:
For $\beta = 1$ and $\omega_n = 1$ for
all $n$, the convergent denominators $q_0, \dots, q_7$ of the two-step pattern are
$1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 18, 23, 432$ (the paper's first example).

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Section 2.1, first example.

articles.title: Convergent denominators of the two-step pattern
articles.statement:
For a natural number $\beta$ and a
sequence $(\omega_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of natural numbers, define natural numbers $q_n$ by $q_0 = 1$,
$q_1 = \omega_0$, and for every $n \ge 0$, $q_{2n+2} = q_{2n+1} + q_{2n}$ and
$q_{2n+3} = \omega_{n+1} q_{2n+1}^\beta q_{2n+2} + q_{2n+1}$.

When the $\omega_n$ are positive, these are the convergent denominators of the continued fraction
$[0; \omega_0, 1, \omega_1 q_1^\beta, 1, \omega_2 q_3^\beta, 1, \dots]$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Section 2.1, displays (e2) and (e22).

articles.title: Irrationality exponent of the two-step pattern
articles.statement:
Let $\beta \ge 1$ be a natural number,
let $(\omega_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be positive integers, let $(q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the convergent
denominators of the two-step pattern for $\beta$ and $(\omega_n)$, and let
$x = \sum_{i \ge 0} (-1)^i / (q_i q_{i+1})$. Let $L$ be the limit superior, in the extended real
numbers, of $\ln \omega_n / \ln q_{2n}$ as $n \to \infty$. Then $x$ is Liouville with exponent $p$
for every real $p < 2 + \beta + L$, that is, for each such $p$ there is a constant $C$ such that
$0 < |x - m/k| < C / k^p$ for infinitely many positive integers $k$, each with some integer $m$.
Moreover $2 + \beta \le 2 + \beta + L$, and $x$ is transcendental.

In other words, the irrationality exponent of $x$ satisfies $\mu(x) \ge 2 + \beta + L$, where $L$
may be $+\infty$.

## Sources

- Khalil Ayadi, Chiheb Ben Bechir, and Maher Saadaoui, *Continued Fractions with Predictable Patterns and Transcendental Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.4, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Bounded partial quotients for a cubic of Ayadi et al
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 2$ and let
$A \in \mathbb{F}_2[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $2\ell$ whose constant and linear coefficients
are both $1$, that is, $A = x^{2\ell} + \sum_{i=2}^{2\ell-1} e_i x^i + x + 1$ with
$e_i \in \mathbb{F}_2$. If $\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_2((x^{-1}))$ has positive degree in $x$ (the
largest exponent of $x$ occurring in $\alpha$ is positive) and satisfies
$x^\ell \alpha^3 + A \alpha^2 + 1 = 0$, then $\alpha$ has bounded partial quotients.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Baum–Sweet: cubics with bounded partial quotients
articles.statement:
Let $p \in \mathbb{F}_2[x]$ have degree
at least $1$. If $f \in \mathbb{F}_2((x^{-1}))$ satisfies $f^3 + p^{-1} f + 1 = 0$, then $f$ has
bounded partial quotients.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Theorem 1 (quoting Baum and Sweet, Corollary 3).

articles.title: Baum–Sweet: explicit continued fractions of roots
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 0$ and let
$P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_2[x]$ with $P + Q^{2^n} \ne 0$ and $P + Q^{2^n} \ne 1$. Then some
$f \in \mathbb{F}_2((x^{-1}))$ satisfies $f^{2^n+1} + Q f^{2^n} + P f + QP + 1 = 0$ and has partial
quotients $b_0 = Q$ and $b_k = P^{2^{(k-1)n}} + Q^{2^{kn}}$ for all $k \ge 1$, that is,
$f = [Q; P + Q^{2^n}, P^{2^n} + Q^{2^{2n}}, P^{2^{2n}} + Q^{2^{3n}}, \dots]$.

The paper also claims that this root is unique, which fails: for $n = 0$, $P = x$ and $Q = 0$ the
equation $f(f + x) = 1$ has the two roots $[0; x, x, \dots]$ and $[x; x, x, \dots]$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Theorem 3 (quoting Baum and Sweet).

articles.title: Baum–Sweet: unbounded partial quotients for higher degrees
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ and let
$g \in \mathbb{F}_2[x]$ have degree at least $1$. If $f \in \mathbb{F}_2((x^{-1}))$ satisfies
$f^{2^n+1} + g^{-1} f + 1 = 0$, then $f$ does not have bounded partial quotients.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Theorem 2 (quoting Baum and Sweet, Theorem 5).

articles.title: Baum–Sweet cubic: partial quotients of degree at most 2
articles.statement:
If
$\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_2((x^{-1}))$ satisfies $x\alpha^3 + \alpha + x = 0$, then every partial
quotient $b_n$ of $\alpha$, $n \ge 0$, has degree at most $2$ in $x$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Lasjaunias's bound on the next partial quotient
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field, let
$A, B, C, D \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ with $\Delta = AD - BC \ne 0$ and $C \ne 0$, and let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_q((x^{-1}))$ be irrational with $\alpha = (A\alpha^q + B)/(C\alpha^q + D)$.
Write $|y| = |x|^{\deg y}$ for the absolute value on $\mathbb{F}_q((x^{-1}))$, where $\deg y$ is
the largest exponent of $x$ occurring in $y \ne 0$, and write $P_n/Q_n$ for the convergents and
$b_n$ for the partial quotients of $\alpha$. Let $n \ge 0$, let $P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ be
coprime with $Q \ne 0$ and $P/Q = P_n/Q_n$, and suppose $|\alpha - P/Q| < |\alpha - A/C|$. Put
$R_1 = DP - BQ$, $S_1 = -CP + AQ$ and $\delta_1 = \gcd(R_1, S_1)$. If $R_1/\delta_1$ or
$S_1/\delta_1$ is not a $q$-th power in $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$, then
$|b_{n+1}| < |\Delta|\,|\delta_1|^{-2}$.

The hypothesis $C \ne 0$, which makes $A/C$ meaningful, is implicit in the paper.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 5 (quoting Lasjaunias, Lemma 1).

articles.title: Lasjaunias's criterion for unbounded partial quotients
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite
field, let $A, B, C, D \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ with $\Delta = AD - BC \ne 0$ and $C \ne 0$, and let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_q((x^{-1}))$ be irrational with $\alpha = (A\alpha^q + B)/(C\alpha^q + D)$.
Write $|y| = |x|^{\deg y}$ for the absolute value on $\mathbb{F}_q((x^{-1}))$, where $\deg y$ is
the largest exponent of $x$ occurring in $y \ne 0$, and write $P_n/Q_n$ for the convergents and
$b_n$ for the partial quotients of $\alpha$. Suppose that for some $n \ge 0$ there are coprime
$P, Q \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ with $Q \ne 0$ and $P/Q = P_n/Q_n$ such that
$|\alpha - P/Q|^q < |\alpha^q + D/C|$, $|\alpha - P/Q|^{q-1} < |\Delta|\,|C\alpha^q + D|^2$ and
$|b_{n+1}|^{q-1} > |\Delta|$. Then $\alpha$ does not have bounded partial quotients.

In the paper these conditions read $|\alpha - P/Q| < |\alpha^q + D/C|^{1/q}$,
$|\alpha - P/Q| < |\Delta|^{1/(q-1)} |C\alpha^q + D|^{2/(q-1)}$ and
$|b_{n+1}| > |\Delta|^{1/(q-1)}$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 8 (quoting Lasjaunias).

articles.title: Small roots of a hyperquadratic equation have unbounded partial quotients
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field, let $\ell \ge 1$ and let $D \in \mathbb{F}_q[x]$ with
$D(0) \ne 0$. Write $|y| = |x|^{\deg y}$ for the absolute value on $\mathbb{F}_q((x^{-1}))$, where
$\deg y$ is the largest exponent of $x$ occurring in $y \ne 0$. If
$\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_q((x^{-1}))$ is irrational, satisfies $x\alpha^{q+1} + D\alpha + x^\ell = 0$
and $|\alpha| < |x|^{-((q-1)\ell + 1)}$, then $\alpha$ does not have bounded partial quotients.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Complete quotients of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$. The
complete quotients of the continued fraction expansion of $\alpha$ are $\alpha_0 = \alpha$ and
$\alpha_{n+1} = (\alpha_n - [\alpha_n])^{-1}$ for $n \ge 0$, where $[\beta]$ is the polynomial part
of $\beta$ and $0^{-1} = 0$. So the complete quotients become $0$ after a finite expansion ends.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1, (1.3).

articles.title: Denominators of the convergents
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ and let
$b_0, b_1, \dots$ be its partial quotients. The denominators of the convergents of $\alpha$ are
given by $Q_{-1} = 0$, $Q_0 = 1$ and $Q_{n+1} = b_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 0$. They are
indexed from $0$ here: the $k$-th term of the sequence is $Q_{k-1}$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: Numerators of the convergents of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ have partial quotients $b_0, b_1, \dots$. The numerators of the
convergents of $\alpha$ are $P_{-1} = 1$, $P_0 = b_0$ and $P_{n+1} = b_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ for
$n \ge 0$. The sequence is indexed with a shift of one: its term at $n \ge 0$ is $P_{n-1}$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: The convergent $P_1 / Q_1$ of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ have partial quotients $b_0, b_1, \dots$. Let $P_n$ and $Q_n$ be the
numerators and denominators of its convergents, given by $P_{-1} = 1$, $Q_{-1} = 0$, $P_0 = b_0$,
$Q_0 = 1$, $P_{n+1} = b_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ and $Q_{n+1} = b_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$. Then
$P_1 = b_1 b_0 + 1$ and $Q_1 = b_1$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: Basic properties of the convergents of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ be irrational, with partial quotients $b_0, b_1, \dots$ and convergents
$P_n / Q_n$, where $P_{-1} = 1$, $Q_{-1} = 0$, $P_0 = b_0$, $Q_0 = 1$,
$P_{n+1} = b_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ and $Q_{n+1} = b_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$. For a Laurent series
$y = \sum_m c_m x^{-m}$ let $v(y)$ be its order, the least $m$ with $c_m \ne 0$, and let
$v(0) = 0$; thus $|y| = |x|^{-v(y)}$ for $y \ne 0$. For $\beta \in K((x^{-1}))$ write
$[b_k, \dots, b_n, \beta] = b_k + 1/(b_{k+1} + 1/(\cdots + 1/(b_n + 1/\beta)))$. Then:
(i) for every $n \ge 0$ and every $\beta \ne 0$ such that $[b_k, \dots, b_n, \beta] \ne 0$ for
all $1 \le k \le n$, $(\beta P_n + P_{n-1}) / (\beta Q_n + Q_{n-1}) = [b_0, \dots, b_n, \beta]$;
(ii) $P_n Q_{n-1} - P_{n-1} Q_n = (-1)^{n+1}$ for every $n \ge 0$;
(iii) $Q_{n-1} \ne 0$ and $v(Q_n) < v(Q_{n-1})$ for every $n \ge 1$;
(iv) $v(Q_n) = v(b_1) + \dots + v(b_n)$ for every $n \ge 1$;
(v) $v(\alpha - P_n / Q_n) = -v(b_{n+1}) - 2 v(Q_n)$ for every $n \ge 1$;
(vi) $v(Q_n \alpha - P_n) < v(Q_{n+1} \alpha - P_{n+1})$ for every $n \ge 1$.

Part (iii) fails at $n = 0$ because $Q_{-1} = 0$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Close rational approximations and convergents
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ be irrational, with partial quotients $b_0, b_1, \dots$ and convergents
$P_n / Q_n$, where $P_{-1} = 1$, $Q_{-1} = 0$, $P_0 = b_0$, $Q_0 = 1$,
$P_{n+1} = b_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ and $Q_{n+1} = b_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$. For a Laurent series
$y = \sum_m c_m x^{-m}$ let $v(y)$ be its order, the least $m$ with $c_m \ne 0$, and let
$v(0) = 0$. Let $P, Q \in K[x]$ be coprime with $Q \ne 0$.
(i) If $v(Q \alpha - P) = s + \deg Q$ for some integer $s \ge 1$, then there are $n \ge 0$ and
$c \in K \setminus \{0\}$ with $P = c P_n$, $Q = c Q_n$ and $v(b_{n+1}) = -s$.
(ii) If $v(Q \alpha - P) = \deg Q$, then there are $n \ge 0$ and $c, d \in K \setminus \{0\}$
with $P = c P_n + d P_{n-1}$ and $Q = c Q_n + d Q_{n-1}$.

With $|y| = |x|^{-v(y)}$, the hypothesis of (i) reads $|Q \alpha - P| = |x|^{-s} |Q|^{-1}$ and
its conclusion $|b_{n+1}| = |x|^s$; the hypothesis of (ii) reads $|Q \alpha - P| = |Q|^{-1}$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 3 (generalizing Baum and Sweet, Lemma 1).

articles.title: Laurent series with bounded partial quotients
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. A Laurent series
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ with partial quotients $b_0, b_1, \dots$ has bounded partial quotients
if there is an integer $B$ such that for every $n \ge 0$ and every integer $k > B$ the
coefficient of $x^k$ in $b_n$ is zero, that is, every nonzero $b_n$ is a polynomial in $x$ of
degree at most $B$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: The variable $x$ times $x^{-1}$ is one
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. In $K((x^{-1}))$, the
product of the variable $x$ and the series $x^{-1}$ (coefficient $1$ at $x^{-1}$ and $0$
elsewhere) is $1$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: The variable $x$ of $K((x^{-1}))$
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. Formal Laurent series in $x^{-1}$
over $K$ are realized as Laurent series $\sum_n c_n X^n$ in $X = x^{-1}$, and the variable $x$
is the series $X^{-1}$, with coefficient $1$ at $X^{-1}$ and $0$ elsewhere.

A series $\alpha = \sum_n c_n x^{-n} \ne 0$ has absolute value $|\alpha| = |x|^{-v(\alpha)}$,
where its order $v(\alpha)$ is the least $n$ with $c_n \ne 0$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: Irrational Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. A Laurent series $\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$
is irrational if $Q \alpha \ne P$ for all polynomials $P, Q \in K[x]$ with $Q \ne 0$, where
polynomials are embedded in $K((x^{-1}))$ by sending $x$ to the variable $x$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: Degree identities at convergents of a Möbius–Frobenius fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a finite
field with $q$ elements, let $A, B, C, D \in K[x]$ with $\Delta = AD - BC \ne 0$ and $C \ne 0$,
and let $\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ be irrational with $\alpha = (A \alpha^q + B) / (C \alpha^q + D)$.
Let $b_0, b_1, \dots$ be the partial quotients of $\alpha$ and $P_n / Q_n$ its convergents, where
$P_{-1} = 1$, $Q_{-1} = 0$, $P_0 = b_0$, $Q_0 = 1$, $P_{n+1} = b_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ and
$Q_{n+1} = b_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$. For a Laurent series $y = \sum_m c_m x^{-m}$ let $v(y)$ be its
order, the least $m$ with $c_m \ne 0$, and let $v(0) = 0$; thus $|y| = |x|^{-v(y)}$ for
$y \ne 0$. Let $n \ge 0$, let $P, Q \in K[x]$ be coprime with $Q \ne 0$ and $P Q_n = Q P_n$,
and put $R_1 = DP - BQ$, $S_1 = -CP + AQ$, $R_2 = AP^q + BQ^q$ and $S_2 = CP^q + DQ^q$, with
the degree of the zero polynomial taken to be $0$. Then:
(i) if $v(\alpha - A/C) < v(\alpha - P/Q)$, then
$v(S_1 \alpha^q - R_1) = \deg S_1 - \deg \Delta - v(b_{n+1})$;
(ii) if $v(\alpha^q + D/C) < q \, v(\alpha - P/Q)$, then
$v(S_2 \alpha - R_2) = \deg S_2 - \deg \Delta - q \, v(b_{n+1})$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 7, (3.7) and (3.8).

articles.title: Difference identities for a Möbius–Frobenius fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a finite field with
$q$ elements, let $A, B, C, D \in K[x]$ with $\Delta = AD - BC \ne 0$, and let
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ be irrational with $\alpha = (A \alpha^q + B) / (C \alpha^q + D)$. Let
$P, Q \in K[x]$ with $Q \ne 0$, put $R_1 = DP - BQ$, $S_1 = -CP + AQ$, $R_2 = AP^q + BQ^q$ and
$S_2 = CP^q + DQ^q$, and assume $S_1 \ne 0$ and $S_2 \ne 0$. Then
$\alpha^q - R_1 / S_1 = \Delta (Q \alpha - P) / ((A - C \alpha) S_1)$ and
$\alpha - R_2 / S_2 = \Delta (Q \alpha - P)^q / ((C \alpha^q + D) S_2)$.

For $C \ne 0$ the conditions $S_1 \ne 0$ and $S_2 \ne 0$ say $P/Q \ne A/C$ and
$(P/Q)^q \ne -D/C$. The source also assumes $\gcd(A, B, C, D) = 1$ and that $P/Q$ is a
convergent of $\alpha$ in lowest terms; the identities do not need these hypotheses.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Frobenius acts on continued fractions of Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a finite field with
$q$ elements and let $\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$, with partial quotients $b_0, b_1, \dots$ and
convergent numerators and denominators $P_n, Q_n$, where $P_{-1} = 1$ and $Q_{-1} = 0$. Then for
every $n \ge 0$ the $n$-th partial quotient of $\alpha^q$ is $b_n^q$, and for every $n \ge -1$
the convergent numerator and denominator of $\alpha^q$ of index $n$ are $P_n^q$ and $Q_n^q$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 2.

articles.title: First step of the continued fraction of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$. The partial quotient $b_0$ of $\alpha$ is its polynomial part
$[\alpha]$, and the complete quotient $\alpha_1$ is $(\alpha - [\alpha])^{-1}$, where
$0^{-1} = 0$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1, (1.3).

articles.title: Partial quotients of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, $\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ and
$n \ge 0$. The $n$-th partial quotient of $\alpha$ is $b_n = [\alpha_n]$, the polynomial part of
the $n$-th complete quotient $\alpha_n$ of $\alpha$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1, (1.3).

articles.title: Coefficients of the polynomial part of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and write
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ as $\alpha = \sum_n c_n x^{-n}$. For every integer $n$, the coefficient
of $x^{-n}$ in the polynomial part $[\alpha]$ is $c_n$ if $n \le 0$ and $0$ if $n > 0$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1, (1.3).

articles.title: Polynomial parts of the variable and its inverse
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. In
$K((x^{-1}))$ the polynomial part of $x$ is $x$, and the polynomial part of $x^{-1}$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1, (1.3).

articles.title: Polynomial part of a Laurent series
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and write a Laurent series
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ as $\alpha = \sum_n c_n x^{-n}$. Its polynomial part is
$[\alpha] = \sum_{n \le 0} c_n x^{-n}$, the sum of the terms in nonnegative powers of $x$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1, (1.3).

articles.title: Distance from an irrational Laurent series to its convergents
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let
$\alpha \in K((x^{-1}))$ be irrational with convergents $P_n/Q_n$ ($n \ge 0$), and for nonzero
$y \in K((x^{-1}))$ let $|y| = |x|^{\deg y}$, where $\deg y$ is the largest exponent of $x$
occurring in $y$ and $|x| > 1$ is fixed. (i) If $|\alpha| \ge 1$, then
$|\alpha - P_n/Q_n| < |\alpha|$ for all $n \ge 0$. (ii) If $|\alpha| < 1$, then
$|\alpha - P_0/Q_0| = |\alpha|$ and $|\alpha - P_n/Q_n| < |\alpha|$ for all $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Polynomials are not irrational
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. For every polynomial $P \in K[x]$,
the image of $P$ in $K((x^{-1}))$ is not irrational.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: The polynomial variable embeds as the Laurent variable
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. The
embedding $K[x] \to K((x^{-1}))$ sends the polynomial $x$ to the element $x$ of
$K((x^{-1}))$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: Polynomials as Laurent series in the inverse variable
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. The embedding
$K[x] \to K((x^{-1}))$ is the $K$-algebra homomorphism that sends $x$ to the element $x$ of
$K((x^{-1}))$, that is, it evaluates a polynomial at $x$.

## Sources

- Tuangrat Chaichana, Natthaphong Chitmung, and Vichian Laohakosol, *Certain Algebraic Formal Laurent Series with Bounded Partial Quotients*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A57, Section 1.

articles.title: Recurrence for the convergent denominators
articles.statement:
