$q$, and let $F_M = \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} |F(t)|$ (taken to be $0$ if $|F|$ is unbounded). For
all real numbers $x > 0$ and $y$,

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor y \rfloor} \frac{s_q(n)}{n} \, F\left(\frac{\log(x/n)}{\log q}\right) \le
F_M \sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor y \rfloor} \frac{s_q(n)}{n}.$$

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Reciprocal digit sums weighted by powers of the logarithm
articles.statement:
Let $q \ge 2$ and $j \ge 1$ be
integers, and let $s_q(n)$ denote the sum of the base-$q$ digits of $n$. As the real number $x$
tends to infinity,

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \frac{s_q(n)}{n} \log^j n =
\frac{(q - 1) \log^{j+2} x}{2 (j + 2) \log q} + O\left(\log^{j+1} x\right).$$

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Exact formulas for the reciprocal digit sums
articles.statement:
Let $q \ge 2$ be an integer and let $s_q(n)$
denote the sum of the base-$q$ digits of $n$. Let $F$ be the Trollope–Delange fluctuation and $J$
the remainder of the Trollope–Delange formula in base $q$, and for real $x$ put
$G(x) = \int_1^x F(\log u / \log q) \, du / u$, $H(x) = \int_1^x G(u) \, du / u$,
$K(x) = \int_1^x J(u) \, du / u^2$ and $L(x) = \int_1^x K(u) \, du / u$. Then for every real
number $x \ge 1$,

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \frac{s_q(n)}{n} = \frac{(q - 1) \log^2 x}{4 \log q} +
\frac{(q - 1) \log x}{2 \log q} + F\left(\frac{\log x}{\log q}\right) + G(x) + \frac{J(x)}{x} +
K(x)$$

and

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \frac{s_q(n) \log n}{n} = \frac{(q - 1) \log^3 x}{6 \log q} +
\frac{(q - 1) \log^2 x}{4 \log q} + \log x \cdot F\left(\frac{\log x}{\log q}\right) +
(\log x - 1) \, G(x) - H(x) + \frac{J(x) \log x}{x} + (\log x - 1) \, K(x) - L(x).$$

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1, equations (4) and (5).

articles.title: The double remainder integral vanishes at $1$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$, let $J$ be
the remainder of the Trollope–Delange formula in base $q$ and
$L(x) = \int_1^x \frac{1}{u} \int_1^u \frac{J(v)}{v^2} \, dv \, du$. Then $L(1) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Double integral of the Trollope–Delange remainder
articles.statement:
For a natural number $q$ and a real
number $x$, let $J$ be the remainder of the Trollope–Delange formula in base $q$. Then $L(x)$ is
the real number

$$L(x) = \int_1^x \frac{1}{u} \left( \int_1^u \frac{J(v)}{v^2} \, dv \right) du,$$

where the integrals are oriented, so that $\int_a^b = -\int_b^a$ when $b < a$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1 (definition of `L`).

articles.title: The remainder integral vanishes at $1$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$, let $J$ be the
remainder of the Trollope–Delange formula in base $q$ and $K(x) = \int_1^x J(u) \, du / u^2$.
Then $K(1) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Weighted integral of the Trollope–Delange remainder
articles.statement:
For a natural number $q$, let $J$
be the remainder of the Trollope–Delange formula in base $q$. For a real number $x$, define
$K(x) = \int_1^x J(u)/u^2 \, du$, an oriented interval integral (so
$K(x) = -\int_x^1 J(u)/u^2 \, du$ when $x < 1$) that is taken to be $0$ when $J(u)/u^2$ is not
integrable on the interval between $1$ and $x$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1 (definition of `K`).

articles.title: The Trollope–Delange remainder vanishes at zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$, the
remainder $J$ of the Trollope–Delange formula in base $q$ satisfies $J(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Trollope–Delange remainder
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number, write $s_q(n)$ for the sum of the
base-$q$ digits of a natural number $n$ (with $s_q(n) = n$ when $q \le 1$), and let $h$ be
Delange's series in base $q$. For a real number $x$, let $n_x$ be the floor of $x$ when
$x \ge 0$ and $n_x = 0$ when $x < 0$. The remainder of the Trollope–Delange formula is
$J(x) = (1 + n_x - x)\, s_q(n_x) - h(x)$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 1 (definition of `J`).

articles.title: Periodicity of the Trollope–Delange fluctuation
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$ and every
real number $x$, the Trollope–Delange fluctuation $F$ in base $q$ satisfies $F(x + 1) = F(x)$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Theorem 1 (`F` is `1`-periodic).

articles.title: Trollope–Delange fluctuation
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number and let $h$ be Delange's series
in base $q$. The Trollope–Delange fluctuation in base $q$ is the function of a real number $x$
given by $F(x) = \frac{q - 1}{2}(1 + \lfloor x \rfloor - x) +
q^{1 + \lfloor x \rfloor - x}\, h(q^{x - \lfloor x \rfloor - 1})$, where $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is
the floor of $x$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Theorem 1 (definition of `F`).

articles.title: Delange's function is eventually bounded
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q \ge 2$, Delange's
function $g$ in base $q$ satisfies $g(x) = O(1)$ as $x \to +\infty$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Delange's function vanishes at zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$, Delange's function $g$
in base $q$ satisfies $g(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Delange's function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $q$, Delange's function in base $q$ is the
function of a real number $x$ given by
$g(x) = \int_0^x \left(\lfloor q t \rfloor - q \lfloor t \rfloor - \frac{q - 1}{2}\right) dt$,
where $\lfloor \cdot \rfloor$ is the floor function.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Theorem 1 (definition of `g`).

articles.title: Delange's series vanishes at zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $q$, Delange's series $h$ in
base $q$ satisfies $h(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Delange's series
articles.statement:
For a natural number $q$, let $g$ be Delange's function in base $q$.
Delange's series in base $q$ is the function of a real number $x$ given by
$h(x) = \sum_{r \ge 0} g(q^r x)/q^r$, where the sum is taken to be $0$ when the series is not
summable.

## Sources

- Ka Lun Wong and Erdenebileg Erdenebat, *Asymptotics of Partial Sums of Dirichlet Convolutions of Digital Sum Functions in Arbitrary Bases*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A43, Theorem 1 (definition of `h`).

articles.title: Grundman's bound on consecutive Niven numbers
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ and $a \ge 1$ be integers.
Then for some $i$ with $0 \le i \le 2b$, the integer $a + i$ is not divisible by the sum of its
base-$b$ digits. Equivalently, the $2b + 1$ consecutive integers $a, a + 1, \dots, a + 2b$ are not
all $b$-Niven numbers, where a $b$-Niven number is a positive integer divisible by the sum of its
base-$b$ digits.

## Sources

- Michael Gohn, Joshua Harrington, Sophia Lebiere, Hani Samamah, Kyla Shappell, and Tony W. H. Wong, "Arithmetic Progressions of b-Prodigious Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.8.7, line 149, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Wong/wong42.tex>, citing as the original result Heidi Grundman, "Sequences of consecutive n-Niven numbers," Fibonacci Quarterly 32 (1994), 174–175.

articles.title: A common iterate of the negative-base digit-square map falls below twice the squared base
articles.statement:
Let $b \le -7$ be an integer, let $S_{2,b}$ be the map sending an integer to the sum of the
squares of its base-$b$ digits, and write $S_{2,b}^k$ for its $k$-fold iterate. For every finite
set $A$ of positive integers there is an integer $k \ge 1$ such that $S_{2,b}^k(a) < 2b^2$ for
every $a \in A$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Lemma 2.2.

articles.title: A congruence for the negative-base digit-square map
articles.statement:
Let $b \le -12$ be an even integer,
let $S_{2,b}$ be the map sending an integer to the sum of the squares of its base-$b$ digits, and
let $v$ be an integer with $0 < v < 2b^2$. Then there are integers $w$ and $c$ with
$0 \le w < v$ and $0 \le c \le |b| - 2$ such that

$$S_{2,b}\bigl((|b| - 1)b + v - w - 1\bigr) -
S_{2,b}\bigl((|b| - 1)b^2 + |b| - 1 - w\bigr) + 5 + 2c \equiv 0 \pmod{|b| + 1}.$$

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Lemma 3.1.

articles.title: Smallest run of six consecutive happy numbers
articles.statement:
A natural number is happy when repeatedly
replacing it by the sum of the squares of its decimal digits reaches $1$ after finitely many
steps. Let $N_0 = 7899999999999959999999996$. The six consecutive integers
$N_0, N_0 + 1, \dots, N_0 + 5$ are all happy, and every natural number $m$ such that
$m, m + 1, \dots, m + 5$ are all happy satisfies $m \ge N_0$.

## Sources

- Robert Styer, "Smallest Examples of Strings of Consecutive Happy Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), Article 10.6.3, Proposition, lines 135–136, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Styer/styer5.tex

articles.title: Even bases at most $-4$ make every finite set of positive integers good
articles.statement:
Let $b \le -4$
be an even integer. Then every finite set of positive integers is $(2, b)$-good.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Theorem 3.2.

articles.title: Goodness pulls back along compositions of the digit-square map and the successor map
articles.statement:
Let $b \le -2$ be an integer, let $S_{2,b}$ be the map sending an integer to the sum of the
squares of its base-$b$ digits, and let $I(t) = t + 1$. Let $T$ be a finite set of positive
integers and let $F$ be a composition $F = f_1 \circ \dots \circ f_m$ with $m \ge 0$ (the empty
composition being the identity), where each $f_i$ is $S_{2,b}$ or $I$. If the image $F(T)$ is
$(2, b)$-good, then $T$ is $(2, b)$-good.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Lemma 2.1.

articles.title: Good sets for the digit-square map
articles.statement:
For an integer $b$, let $S_{2,b}$ be the base-$b$
digit-square map, which for $b \le -2$ sends an integer to the sum of the squares of its base-$b$
digits; write $S_{2,b}^k$ for its $k$-fold iterate, and let $U_{2,b}$ be the set of positive
integers $u$ with $S_{2,b}^m(u) = u$ for some $m \ge 1$. A finite set $T$ of integers is
$(2, b)$-good if for each $u \in U_{2,b}$ there are integers $n \ge 1$ and $k \ge 1$ such that
$S_{2,b}^k(t + n) = u$ for every $t \in T$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Arbitrarily long runs of consecutive happy numbers in even bases at most $-4$
articles.statement:
Let
$b \le -4$ be an even integer. For every natural number $N$ there is an integer $n$ such that
$n + i$ is $b$-happy for every $0 \le i < N$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Theorem 1.2.

articles.title: Arbitrarily long runs of consecutive happy numbers in bases $-4$, $-6$, $-8$, $-10$
articles.statement:
Let
$b \in \{-4, -6, -8, -10\}$. For every natural number $N$ there is an integer $n$ such that
$n + i$ is $b$-happy for every $0 \le i < N$.

This is part (3) of the Grundman–Harris theorem.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Theorem 1.1.

articles.title: Happy numbers in base $-3$
articles.statement:
There is an integer $n$ such that $n + 2i$ is $(-3)$-happy for
every natural number $i$, and an integer $a$ is $(-3)$-happy if and only if $a \equiv 1 \pmod 2$.

This is part (2) of the Grundman–Harris theorem.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Theorem 1.1.

articles.title: Happy numbers in base $-2$
articles.statement:
There is an integer $n$ such that $n + 3i$ is $(-2)$-happy for
every natural number $i$, and an integer $a$ is $(-2)$-happy if and only if $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.

This is part (1) of the Grundman–Harris theorem.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Theorem 1.1.

articles.title: $1$ is happy in every negative base
articles.statement:
For every integer $b \le -2$, the integer $1$ is
$b$-happy.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Arithmetic progressions of happy numbers in odd negative bases
articles.statement:
Let $b \le -3$ be an odd
integer. For every natural number $N$ there is an integer $n$ such that $n + 2i$ is $b$-happy for
every natural number $i < N$. Thus there are arbitrarily long finite arithmetic progressions with
common difference $2$ of $b$-happy integers.

This is part (4) of the theorem of Grundman and Harris.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Theorem 1.1.

articles.title: Happy integers in a negative base
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be an integer and let $S_{2,b}$ be the
base-$b$ digit-square sum, which for $b \le -2$ sends an integer to the sum of the squares of its
base-$b$ digits. An integer $a$ is $b$-happy if $S_{2,b}^k(a) = 1$ for some $k \ge 1$, where
$S_{2,b}^k$ denotes the $k$-th iterate of $S_{2,b}$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Cycles of the negative-base digit-square map
articles.statement:
For an integer $b$, let $S_{2,b}$ be the
base-$b$ digit-square sum, which for $b \le -2$ sends an integer to the sum of the squares of its
base-$b$ digits. Then $U_{2,b}$ is the set of positive integers $u$ such that $S_{2,b}^m(u) = u$
for some $m \ge 1$, that is, the positive integers lying on a cycle of $S_{2,b}$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Truncated digit-square sum in a negative base
articles.statement:
For an integer $b$, define $T_b(f, a)$ for a
natural number $f$ and an integer $a$ by recursion on $f$: $T_b(0, a) = 0$, $T_b(f + 1, 0) = 0$,
and for $a \ne 0$, $T_b(f + 1, a) = r^2 + T_b(f, (a - r)/b)$, where $r = a \bmod b$ is the
remainder of $a$ on division by $b$, with $0 \le r < |b|$ (for $b = 0$ one takes $r = a$ and
$(a - r)/b = 0$). For $b \le -2$, $T_b(f, a)$ is thus the sum of the squares of the first $f$
base-$b$ digits of $a$, counted from the least significant one.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: The digit-square sum of a single digit
articles.statement:
Let $b$ and $d$ be integers with $0 < d < -b$, so
that $b \le -2$ and $d$ is a nonzero base-$b$ digit. Then the base-$b$ digit-square sum $S_{2,b}$
satisfies $S_{2,b}(d) = d^2$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Sample values of the negative-base digit-square sum
articles.statement:
Write $S_{2,b}$ for the base-$b$
digit-square sum, which sends an integer to the sum of the squares of its base-$b$ digits. Then
$S_{2,-10}(-1) = 82$, $S_{2,-10}(10) = 82$ and $S_{2,-4}(5) = 11$. Indeed $-1 = 1 \cdot (-10) + 9$
and $10 = 1 \cdot (-10)^2 + 9 \cdot (-10) + 0$ have base-$(-10)$ digits $1, 9$ and $1, 9, 0$, and
$5 = 1 \cdot (-4)^2 + 3 \cdot (-4) + 1$ has base-$(-4)$ digits $1, 3, 1$ (most significant first).

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: The digit-square sum of zero
articles.statement:
For every integer $b$, the base-$b$ digit-square sum $S_{2,b}$
satisfies $S_{2,b}(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Sum of squared digits in a negative base
articles.statement:
Let $b \le -2$ be an integer. Every integer $a$
has an expansion $a = \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i b^i$ with digits $0 \le a_i \le |b| - 1$, unique up to
leading zero digits, and $S_{2,b}(a) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i^2$ is the sum of the squares of these
digits. The digits are produced from the least significant one by taking $a_0 = a \bmod b$ and
passing to $(a - a_0)/b$, until $0$ is reached.

The definition is made for every integer $b$, by running this digit extraction for at most
$2|a| + 2$ steps; for $b \le -2$ this suffices, since the quantity $2a$ (for $a \ge 0$) or
$2|a| + 1$ (for $a < 0$) strictly decreases at each step.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: One lies on a cycle of the negative-base digit-square map
articles.statement:
For every integer $b \le -2$,
$1 \in U_{2,b}$, where $U_{2,b}$ is the set of positive integers lying on a cycle of the base-$b$
digit-square sum $S_{2,b}$.

## Sources

- Helen G. Grundman, *Closing an Open Problem on Negative Base Happy Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/grundman11162023, Section 2.

articles.title: Scaled translate of a set
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $l$, a real number $x$ and a set
$U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the affine scale set $b^l U - b^l x$ is the image of $U$ under the map
$y \mapsto b^l y - b^l x$, that is, $\{\, b^l y - b^l x : y \in U \,\}$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Complementary digit power sum
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$ and $j$, let $d' = b - 1 - d$,
computed by natural-number subtraction (so $d' = 0$ when $d \ge b - 1$). The complementary digit
power sum $\gamma'_j$ is the real number $\sum_{0 \le a < b,\ a \ne d'} a^j$, the sum of the
$j$-th powers of the base-$b$ digits other than $d'$, with the convention $0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Properties of the complementary moment recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be natural
numbers, and let $(v_{j,m})_{j, m \ge 0}$ be any family of real numbers satisfying the
complementary moment recurrence for $b$ and $d$. Then $v_{j,0} = b$ for every $j$. For every $j$
and every $m \ge 1$: $0 < v_{j,m} \le b$; if $(b, d, j) = (2, 1, 0)$ then $v_{j,m} = 2$, and
otherwise $v_{j,m+1} < v_{j,m}$; and $v_{j+1,m} < v_{j,m}$. Finally, for every $m \ge 1$,
$v_{j,m} \to b/(m+1)$ as $j \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Complementary moment recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $b$ and $d$ be natural numbers, let $d' = b - 1 - d$
(natural-number subtraction), and let $\gamma'_i$ be the complementary digit power sum for $b$ and
$d$. A family $(v_{j,m})_{j, m \ge 0}$ of real numbers satisfies the complementary moment
recurrence when, for every $m \ge 0$,

$$
(b^{m+1} - b + 1)\, v_{0,m} = b^{m+1} + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \binom{m}{i} \gamma'_i \, v_{0,m-i},
$$

and, for every $j \ge 1$ and every $m \ge 0$,

$$
(b^{m+1} - b + 1)\, v_{j,m} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \binom{m}{i} \gamma'_i \, v_{j,m-i} +
\sum_{i=0}^{m} \binom{m}{i} (d')^i \, v_{j-1,m-i},
$$

with the convention $0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Complementary moment
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$, $k$ and $m$ with $d < b$, let $\mu_k$
be the Irwin measure for base $b$, digit $d$ and digit count $k$. The complementary moment is

$$
v_{k;m} = \int_{[0,1)} (1 - x)^m \, d\mu_k(x).
$$

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition before Corollary 2.

articles.title: Zero has no digits
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $b$ and $d$, the digit $d$ occurs $0$ times in
the minimal base-$b$ representation of $0$, which is empty.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Digit count
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$ and $n$, the digit count of $d$ in $n$ is the
number of occurrences of the digit $d$ in the minimal base-$b$ representation of $n$ (its base-$b$
digits without leading zeros). The representation of $0$ is empty, so $0$ has digit count $0$.

For the degenerate bases, the representation of $n \ne 0$ is the single digit $n$ when $b = 0$
and a string of $n$ ones when $b = 1$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Digit power sum
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$ and $j$, the digit power sum $\gamma_j$ is
the real number $\sum_{0 \le a < b,\ a \ne d} a^j$, the sum of the $j$-th powers of the base-$b$
digits other than $d$, with the convention $0^0 = 1$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base depth of a real number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $b$, a real number $x$ and a natural
number $l$, the number $x$ has base-$b$ depth $l$ when $x = z / b^l$ for some integer $z$, and for
no $q < l$ is there an integer $z$ with $x = z / b^q$. Thus $l$ is the least exponent for which
$x$ can be written as an integer divided by $b^l$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Integer length
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $n$, the integer length of $n$ in base $b$ is
the number of digits in the minimal base-$b$ representation of $n$ (its base-$b$ digits without
leading zeros); in particular $0$ has length $0$.

For the degenerate bases, the representation of $n \ne 0$ is the single digit $n$ when $b = 0$
and a string of $n$ ones when $b = 1$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Prefix reciprocal sums as integrals against the Irwin measure
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$
be natural numbers, let $n > 0$ and $k$ be natural numbers, let $k(n)$ be the number of
occurrences of the digit $d$ in the base-$b$ representation of $n$, and let $\mu_k$ be the Irwin
measure of base $b$ and digit $d$ with index $k$. Then the family that assigns $1/m$ to each
positive integer $m$ whose base-$b$ representation begins with that of $n$ and contains exactly
$k(n) + k$ occurrences of $d$, and $0$ to every other natural number $m$, is summable with sum
$\int_{[0,1)} \frac{1}{n + x}\, d\mu_k(x)$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Digit decomposition of the Irwin measures, positive index
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be
natural numbers, and for each natural number $j$ let $\mu_j$ be the Irwin measure of base $b$ and
digit $d$ with index $j$. Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be measurable and bounded on
$[0, b)$, and let $k \ge 1$. Then

$$\int_{[0,1)} f(bx)\, d\mu_k(x) =
\frac{1}{b} \sum_{a \ne d} \int_{[0,1)} f(a + x)\, d\mu_k(x) +
\frac{1}{b} \int_{[0,1)} f(d + x)\, d\mu_{k-1}(x),$$

where $a$ ranges over the digits $0, 1, \dots, b - 1$ other than $d$.

Measurability of $f$ is a hypothesis added to the paper's boundedness assumption.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Digit decomposition of the Irwin measure, zero index
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be natural
numbers, and let $\mu_0$ be the Irwin measure of base $b$ and digit $d$ with index $0$. For every
measurable function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is bounded on $[0, b)$,

$$\int_{[0,1)} f(bx)\, d\mu_0(x) = f(0) +
\frac{1}{b} \sum_{a \ne d} \int_{[0,1)} f(a + x)\, d\mu_0(x),$$

where $a$ ranges over the digits $0, 1, \dots, b - 1$ other than $d$.

Measurability of $f$ is a hypothesis added to the paper's boundedness assumption.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Local structure of the Irwin measures on half-open intervals
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be
natural numbers, and for each natural number $k$ let $\mu_k$ be the Irwin measure of base $b$ and
digit $d$ with index $k$. Let $x \in [0, 1)$ have base-$b$ depth $l$, that is, $l$ is the least
natural number such that $b^l x$ is an integer; let $X$ be a string of $l$ base-$b$ digits, read
most significant digit first, whose value $n(X)$ satisfies $n(X)/b^l = x$; and let $j$ be the
number of occurrences of $d$ in $X$. Let $l' \ge l$ be a natural number, put $j' = j$ if $d > 0$
and $j' = j + l' - l$ if $d = 0$, and let $k \ge j'$ be a natural number. Then for every set
$U \subseteq [x, x + b^{-l'})$, as real numbers,
$\mu_k(U) = b^{-l'} \mu_{k-j'}(b^{l'} U - b^{l'} x)$, where $b^{l'} U - b^{l'} x$ is the image
of $U$ under $y \mapsto b^{l'} y - b^{l'} x$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Local structure of the Irwin measures on cylinders
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be natural
numbers, and for each natural number $k$ let $\mu_k$ be the Irwin measure of base $b$ and digit
$d$ with index $k$. Let $x \in [0, 1)$ have base-$b$ depth $l$, that is, $l$ is the least natural
number such that $b^l x$ is an integer; let $X$ be a string of $l$ base-$b$ digits, read most
significant digit first, whose value $n(X)$ satisfies $n(X)/b^l = x$; and let $j$ be the number
of occurrences of $d$ in $X$. Then for every $k < j$ the restriction of $\mu_k$ to
$[x, x + b^{-l})$ is the zero measure, and for every $k \ge j$ and every subset
$U \subseteq [x, x + b^{-l})$, as real numbers $\mu_k(U) = b^{-l} \mu_{k-j}(b^l U - b^l x)$,
where $b^l U - b^l x$ is the image of $U$ under $y \mapsto b^l y - b^l x$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Proposition 8.

articles.title: Masses of intervals under the Irwin measures
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be natural numbers,
and for each natural number $k$ let $\mu_k$ be the Irwin measure of base $b$ and digit $d$ with
index $k$; masses below are taken as real numbers. First, for all reals $0 \le t < u \le 1$ and
every natural number $l'$ such that $b^{l'} t$ and $b^{l'} u$ are integers,
$\mu_k([t, u)) = bu - bt$ for every $k \ge l'$. Second, for every nonempty interval
$I \subseteq [0, 1)$, $\mu_k(I)$ tends to $b(\sup I - \inf I)$ as $k \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Proposition 9.

articles.title: Local structure of the Irwin measures on open intervals
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be
natural numbers, and for each natural number $k$ let $\mu_k$ be the Irwin measure of base $b$ and
digit $d$ with index $k$. Let $x \in [0, 1)$ have base-$b$ depth $l$, that is, $l$ is the least
natural number such that $b^l x$ is an integer; let $X$ be a string of $l$ base-$b$ digits, read
most significant digit first, whose value $n(X)$ satisfies $n(X)/b^l = x$; and let $j$ be the
number of occurrences of $d$ in $X$. Let $l' \ge l$ be a natural number, put $j' = j$ if $d > 0$
and $j' = j + l' - l$ if $d = 0$, and let $U \subseteq (x, x + b^{-l'})$. Then for every natural
number $k$: if $k < j'$ then $\mu_k(U) = 0$, and if $k \ge j'$ then, as real numbers,
$\mu_k(U) = b^{-l'} \mu_{k-j'}(b^{l'} U - b^{l'} x)$, where $b^{l'} U - b^{l'} x$ is the image
of $U$ under $y \mapsto b^{l'} y - b^{l'} x$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Irwin measure
articles.statement:
Let $b$, $d$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $d < b$. For a finite string
$X$ of base-$b$ digits (of any length, including the empty string, with leading zeros allowed),
read most significant digit first, let $|X|$ be its length and $n(X)$ the integer it represents.
The Irwin measure $\mu_k$ of base $b$ and digit $d$ with index $k$ is the measure on $\mathbb{R}$
obtained by summing, over all strings $X$ containing exactly $k$ occurrences of the digit $d$,
the point mass of weight $b^{-|X|}$ at $n(X)/b^{|X|}$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition of `μ_k`.

articles.title: Alternating series for the Irwin sum
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be natural numbers, let
$(u_{j;m})_{j, m \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of real numbers satisfying the ordinary moment
recurrence for $b$ and $d$, and let $k$ and $l \ge 1$ be natural numbers. For a natural number
$n$ write $c(n)$ for the number of occurrences of the digit $d$ in the base-$b$ expansion of $n$,
and let $H^{(k)}_{b,d}$ be the Irwin sum, the sum of $1/n$ over the positive integers $n$ with
$c(n) = k$. Then the family of real numbers indexed by $m \ge 1$

$$
(-1)^m \sum_{\substack{b^{l-1} \le n < b^l \\ c(n) \le k}} \frac{u_{k - c(n);m}}{n^{m+1}}
$$

is summable, with sum

$$
H^{(k)}_{b,d} - \sum_{\substack{1 \le n < b^{l-1} \\ c(n) = k}} \frac{1}{n} -
b \sum_{\substack{b^{l-1} \le n < b^l \\ c(n) \le k}} \frac{1}{n}.
$$

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Complementary-moment series for the Irwin sums
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be natural
numbers, let $k$ and $l \ge 1$ be natural numbers, and let $(v_{j,m})_{j, m \ge 0}$ be a family
of real numbers satisfying the complementary moment recurrence for $b$ and $d$. For a natural
number $n$ let $k(n)$ be the number of occurrences of $d$ in the base-$b$ representation of $n$,
and let $H^{(k)}$ be the Irwin sum, the sum of $1/n$ over the positive integers $n$ with
$k(n) = k$. Then the family indexed by $m \ge 1$ of

$$\sum_{b^{l-1} \le n < b^l,\ k(n) \le k} \frac{v_{k - k(n), m}}{(n + 1)^{m + 1}}$$

is summable, with sum

$$H^{(k)} - \sum_{1 \le n < b^{l-1},\ k(n) = k} \frac{1}{n} -
b \sum_{b^{l-1} \le n < b^l,\ k(n) \le k} \frac{1}{n + 1}.$$

The hypothesis $b > 1$ is the paper's standing assumption, in place of an isolated $b > 0$ in the
statement of Theorem 2.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Monotonicity and limit of the Irwin sums
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ be a base and $d < b$ a digit, and
for $k \ge 0$ let $H^{(k)}$ be the Irwin sum, the sum of $1/n$ over the positive integers $n$ whose
base-$b$ expansion contains exactly $k$ occurrences of $d$. If $d \ne 0$, then $k \mapsto H^{(k)}$
is strictly decreasing on $k \ge 1$; if $d = 0$, it is strictly decreasing on all $k \ge 0$. In
both cases $H^{(k)} \to b \log b$ as $k \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Lower bounds for the Irwin sum without the digit
articles.statement:
Let $b > 2$ be a base and let $d$ be a
nonzero digit, $0 < d < b$. Let $H^{(0)}$ be the Irwin sum of $1/n$ over the positive integers $n$
whose base-$b$ expansion does not contain $d$. Then
$b \log b - b \log(1 + 1/d) < H^{(0)}$ and $b \log(b/2) < H^{(0)}$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Irwin sum
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$ and $k$, the Irwin sum $H^{(k)}_{b,d}$ is the sum
of $1/n$ over the positive integers $n$ whose base-$b$ expansion contains exactly $k$ occurrences
of the digit $d$. It is taken as an unconditional sum of real numbers, with the value $0$ if this
family is not summable; positivity and convergence are results, not part of the definition.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Leading digits
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $l$ and $m$, let $L$ be the number of digits of
$m$ in base $b$. The leading-digits integer of $m$ is the natural-number quotient of $m$ by
$b^{\max(L - l,\, 0)}$, rounded down (with quotient $0$ when the divisor is $0$). For $b \ge 2$
and $L \ge l$ this is the integer formed by the first $l$ base-$b$ digits of $m$; when $L < l$
it is $m$ itself, and statements using this notion separately require $L \ge l$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, notation before Proposition 4.

articles.title: Limit of the prefix-restricted Irwin sums
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$, let $d < b$ be a digit and let $n$
be a positive integer. For every $k \ge 0$, the family of reciprocals $1/m$ of the positive
integers $m$ whose base-$b$ expansion begins with the base-$b$ expansion of $n$ and contains
exactly $k$ occurrences of $d$ is summable, and its sum tends to $b \log(1 + 1/n)$ as
$k \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Prefix-restricted Irwin sum
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$, $k$ and $n$, this is the sum of
the prefix-restricted reciprocal terms over all natural numbers $m$: the sum of $1/m$ over the
positive integers $m$ with at least as many base-$b$ digits as $n$, whose leading-digits integer
keeping as many digits as $n$ has equals $n$, and with exactly $k$ occurrences of $d$ in base
$b$. For $b \ge 2$ the middle condition says that the base-$b$ expansion of $m$ begins with that
of $n$. It is taken as an unconditional sum of real numbers, with the value $0$ if this family is
not summable; the results that take a limit of this sum also assert summability.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Prefix sums as complementary-moment series
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$, let $d < b$ be a digit, let $n$
be a positive integer, let $k(n)$ be the number of occurrences of $d$ in the base-$b$ expansion
of $n$, and let $k \ge k(n)$. Write $v_{j;m} = \int_{[0,1)} (1 - x)^m \, d\mu_j(x)$ for the
complementary moments of the Irwin measure $\mu_j$. Then there is a real number $S$ such that
the reciprocals $1/N$ of the positive integers $N$ whose base-$b$ expansion begins with that of
$n$ and contains exactly $k$ occurrences of $d$ have sum $S$, and the series
$\sum_{m \ge 0} v_{k - k(n);m} / (n+1)^{m+1}$ also has sum $S$. Moreover every term
$v_{k - k(n);m} / (n+1)^{m+1}$ of this series is positive, and the series is summable.

Positivity plus summability renders the paper's phrase "positive series with geometric
convergence"; no explicit ratio is asserted.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Prefix sums as alternating ordinary-moment series
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$, let $d < b$ be a digit, let
$n$ be a positive integer, let $k(n)$ be the number of occurrences of $d$ in the base-$b$
expansion of $n$, and let $k \ge k(n)$. Write $u_{j;m} = \int_{[0,1)} x^m \, d\mu_j(x)$ for the
ordinary moments of the Irwin measure $\mu_j$. Then there is a real number $S$ such that the
reciprocals $1/N$ of the positive integers $N$ whose base-$b$ expansion begins with that of $n$
and contains exactly $k$ occurrences of $d$ have sum $S$, and the series
$\sum_{m \ge 0} (-1)^m u_{k - k(n);m} / n^{m+1}$ also has sum $S$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Prefix-restricted reciprocal terms
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$, $k$, $n$ and $m$, write
$L(x)$ for the number of base-$b$ digits of $x$. The term is $1/m$ when $m$ is positive,
$L(n) \le L(m)$, the leading-digits integer of $m$ keeping its first $L(n)$ digits equals $n$,
and $m$ has exactly $k$ occurrences of $d$ in base $b$; otherwise the term is $0$. For $b \ge 2$
the leading-digits condition says that the base-$b$ expansion of $m$ begins with that of $n$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, notation before Proposition 4.

articles.title: Normalized value of a digit string
articles.statement:
For a base $b$ and a string $X$ of base-$b$ digits,
written most significant digit first, with integer value $n(X)$ and length $|X|$, the normalized
value of $X$ is the real number $n(X) / b^{|X|}$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition of `μ_k`.

articles.title: Properties of solutions of the ordinary moment recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $b > 1$ and $d < b$ be
natural numbers, and let $(u_{j;m})_{j, m \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of real numbers that
satisfies the ordinary moment recurrence for $b$ and $d$. Then $u_{j;0} = b$ for every $j$, and for
all $j$ and all $m \ge 1$: $u_{j;m} \ge 0$, with $u_{j;m} = 0$ if and only if $j = 0$, $b = 2$ and
$d = 1$; $u_{j;m+1} \le u_{j;m}$, with strict inequality when $u_{j;m} \ne 0$;
$u_{j;m} < u_{j+1;m}$; and $u_{j;m} \to b/(m+1)$ as $j \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Ordinary moment recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $b$ and $d$ be natural numbers, and for $i \ge 1$ let
$\gamma_i$ be the sum of the $i$-th powers of the base-$b$ digits $a \in \{0, \dots, b-1\}$ with
$a \ne d$. A family of real numbers $(u_{j;m})_{j, m \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfies the ordinary
moment recurrence for $b$ and $d$ when $u_{0;0} = b$, when for every $m \ge 1$

$$
(b^{m+1} - b + 1)\, u_{0;m} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \binom{m}{i} \gamma_i\, u_{0;m-i},
$$

and when for every $j \ge 1$ and every $m \ge 0$

$$
(b^{m+1} - b + 1)\, u_{j;m} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \binom{m}{i} \gamma_i\, u_{j;m-i} +
\sum_{i=0}^{m} \binom{m}{i} d^i\, u_{j-1;m-i}.
$$

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Ordinary moments of the Irwin measures
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $d$, $k$, $m$ with
$d < b$, the ordinary moment $u_{k;m}$ is the integral of $x^m$ over $[0,1)$ with respect to the
Irwin measure $\mu_k$ of base $b$ and digit $d$:

$$
u_{k;m} = \int_{[0,1)} x^m \, d\mu_k(x).
$$

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition before Corollary 1.

articles.title: The atom of the empty string is the unit Dirac mass at the origin
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $b$, the atom $b^{-|X|}\,\delta_{n(X)/b^{|X|}}$ of a base-$b$ digit string $X$ is the
Dirac measure $\delta_0$ when $X$ is the empty string.

This concerns the summand of the empty string alone, not the total mass that an Irwin measure
places at $0$ once all strings with the same value are combined.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition of `μ_k` and Remark `rem:zero`.

articles.title: Atom of a digit string
articles.statement:
For a natural number $b$ and a base-$b$ digit string $X$ of
length $|X|$ and integer value $n(X)$, the atom of $X$ is the measure
$b^{-|X|}\,\delta_{n(X)/b^{|X|}}$ on $\mathbb{R}$: the Dirac measure at the point $n(X)/b^{|X|}$,
scaled by the weight $b^{-|X|}$.

The Irwin measures are sums of these atoms.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition of `μ_k`.

articles.title: The empty digit string has value zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $b$, the integer value
of the empty base-$b$ digit string is $0$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Value of a digit string
articles.statement:
For a natural number $b$ and a base-$b$ digit string
$X = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_\ell$ with digits $x_i \in \{0, \dots, b-1\}$, written with the most
significant digit first, the integer value of $X$ is

$$
n(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} x_i\, b^{\ell - i},
$$

so the last digit $x_\ell$ has weight $b^0 = 1$.

These exponents correct a typo in the corresponding displayed formula of the source.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, Notation and Terminology.

articles.title: Weight of a digit string
articles.statement:
For a natural number $b$ and a base-$b$ digit string $X$ of
length $|X|$, the weight of $X$ is $b^{-|X|}$, regarded as an element of $[0, \infty]$.

## Sources

- Jean-François Burnol, *Measures for the Summation of Irwin Series*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A11, definition of `μ_k`.

articles.title: Structure of four-digit Kaprekar dynamics in odd bases
articles.statement:
Let $B > 3$ be an odd integer.
For a pair of natural numbers $d = (d_1, d_2)$, let $K(d) = (a - e, b - c)$, where
$a \ge b \ge c \ge e$ are the four numbers $d_1 - 1, B - 1, B - 1, B - d_1$ if $d_2 = 0$, and
$d_1, d_2 - 1, B - d_2 - 1, B - d_1$ if $d_2 \ne 0$, sorted in decreasing order (subtraction is
truncated at $0$). Let $X_B$ be the set of pairs with $1 \le d_1 < B$ and $d_2 \le d_1$, and let
$T_B$ be the set of pairs in $X_B$ with $0 < d_2 < d_1$ and $d_1$, $d_2$ both odd. Let
$\mathcal{P}$ be the set of two-element sets $S$ of subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$ such that
every $C \in S$ has the form $\{x, -x\}$ with $x \ne 0$. For a set $S$ of subsets of
$\mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$ let $2S = \{2C : C \in S\}$, where $2C = \{2y : y \in C\}$, and for
$d \in T_B$ let $\Phi(d) = \{\{u, -u\}, \{v, -v\}\}$, where $u$ and $v$ are the residues of
$(d_1 + d_2)/2$ and $(d_1 - d_2)/2$ modulo $B$. Then $K$ maps $T_B$ into itself, the third
iterate $K^3$ maps $X_B$ into $T_B$, $S \mapsto 2S$ maps $\mathcal{P}$ into itself, $\Phi$ is a
bijection from $T_B$ onto $\mathcal{P}$, and $\Phi(K(d)) = 2\,\Phi(d)$ for every $d \in T_B$.

Here a pair $(d_1, d_2) \in X_B$ stands for the four-digit base-$B$ numbers whose digits, sorted
as $a \ge b \ge c \ge e$, satisfy $a - e = d_1$ and $b - c = d_2$; the four numbers listed above
are the base-$B$ digits of their Kaprekar image, so $K$ is the Kaprekar map on these pairs.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, "Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases", Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Theorem `thm:structural`, lines 220-230, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL29/Ono/ono3.tex>.

articles.title: Number of Kaprekar cycles of maximal length
articles.statement:
Let $B > 3$ be odd, let $K_B$ be the
four-digit Kaprekar map and $X_B$ its state space, and put $q = (B - 1)/2$. If some point of
$X_B$ has minimal period $q$ under $K_B$, then exactly $q \lfloor (q - 1)/2 \rfloor$ points of
$X_B$ have minimal period $q$ under $K_B$.

Equivalently, $K_B$ then has exactly $\lfloor (q - 1)/2 \rfloor$ terminal cycles of length $q$
on $X_B$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Corollary 5 (`jis-2026-26.4.7-cor-5`).

articles.title: Explicit count of Kaprekar cycles of each length
articles.statement:
Let $B > 3$ be odd and $L \ge 1$, let
$K_B$ be the four-digit Kaprekar map and $X_B$ its state space, let $\varphi$ be Euler's totient
function, and let $\lambda(n)$ denote the projective order of $2$ modulo $n$. For $a \ge 1$ put

$$\mu_B(a) = \sum_{n \mid B,\ n > 1,\ \lambda(n) = a}
\left\lfloor \frac{\varphi(n)}{2a} \right\rfloor$$

and

$$N_B(L) = \mu_B(L) \left\lfloor \frac{L - 1}{2} \right\rfloor + \mu_B(2L) +
\binom{\mu_B(L)}{2} L + \sum_{a, b \mid L,\ a < b,\ \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) = L}
\mu_B(a)\, \mu_B(b) \gcd(a, b),$$

where $n$ ranges over positive divisors of $B$ and $a, b$ in the last sum range over positive
divisors of $L$. Then exactly $L \cdot N_B(L)$ points of $X_B$ have minimal period $L$ under
$K_B$.

Here $N_B(L)$ is the number of terminal cycles of length $L$ of $K_B$ on $X_B$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Theorem 24, with `μ_B` from display (14) (`jis-2026-26.4.7-thm-24`).

articles.title: Kaprekar difference
articles.statement:
Let $l$ be a list of $k$ natural numbers and let
$a_0 \le a_1 \le \dots \le a_{k-1}$ be its entries in increasing order. The Kaprekar difference of
$l$ is $\alpha_M - \alpha_L$, where $\alpha_M = \sum_{i\lt k} a_i 10^i$ and
$\alpha_L = \sum_{i\lt k} a_{k-1-i} 10^i$. When the entries are decimal digits, $\alpha_M$ is the
number written with the digits of $l$ in descending order and $\alpha_L$ is the number written
with them in ascending order (leading zeros allowed).

## Sources

- Haruo Iwasaki, *A New Classification of the Kaprekar Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article iwasaki06162024-ASrev2, Definition 1.1.

articles.title: Sizes of the Kaprekar state spaces in bases 3 and 7
articles.statement:
The four-digit Kaprekar state spaces
satisfy $|X_3| = 5$ and $|X_7| = 27$.

Both values agree with the general count $|X_B| = (B - 1)(B + 2)/2$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, display (2) and the proof of Corollary 27.

articles.title: The four-digit Kaprekar state space
articles.statement:
For a base $B$, the state space $X_B$ is the finite
set of pairs of natural numbers $(d_1, d_2)$ with $1 \le d_1 < B$ and $0 \le d_2 \le d_1$.

A nonconstant four-digit base-$B$ string with sorted digits $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge a_3 \ge a_4$ has
difference coordinates $(d_1, d_2) = (a_1 - a_4, a_2 - a_3)$, a point of $X_B$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, display (2).

articles.title: Sample values of the four-digit Kaprekar map
articles.statement:
The four-digit Kaprekar map satisfies
$K_{11}(5, 1) = (9, 1)$, $K_{11}(6, 0) = (5, 5)$ and $K_{11}(5, 5) = (2, 0)$ in base $11$, and
$K_7(3, 1) = (5, 1)$, $K_7(5, 1) = (5, 3)$ and $K_7(5, 3) = (3, 1)$ in base $7$.

In particular $(3, 1) \mapsto (5, 1) \mapsto (5, 3) \mapsto (3, 1)$ is a terminal cycle of $K_7$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Examples 7, 12 and 18.

articles.title: The four-digit Kaprekar map in difference coordinates
articles.statement:
For a base $B$ and a pair of
natural numbers $(d_1, d_2)$, the map $K_B$ forms the list of four digits
$[d_1 - 1, B - 1, B - 1, B - d_1]$ if $d_2 = 0$ and $[d_1, d_2 - 1, B - d_2 - 1, B - d_1]$ if
$d_2 > 0$, sorts it decreasingly as $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge a_3 \ge a_4$, and sets
$K_B(d_1, d_2) = (a_1 - a_4, a_2 - a_3)$. Subtraction of natural numbers is truncated at $0$;
for $1 \le d_1 < B$ and $0 \le d_2 \le d_1$ no truncation occurs.

For such $(d_1, d_2)$ the list holds the digits of the Kaprekar difference (largest minus
smallest arrangement) of any four-digit base-$B$ string with difference coordinates
$(d_1, d_2)$, as in paper displays (5) and (6).

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Section 2.1.

articles.title: Classification of decimal Kaprekar numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ and $0 < \alpha < 10^n$. Then
the Kaprekar map on $n$-digit strings fixes $\alpha$ if and only if $\alpha$ is the Kaprekar
difference of some string $s$ of exactly $n$ decimal digits of one of the following five forms,
where juxtaposition is concatenation, $(w)^k$ is the block $w$ repeated $k$ times, and in each
form the exponents are chosen independently with $x, x_1, x_2 \ge 1$ and $y, y_1, y_2 \ge 0$:
$(495)^x$; $6174\,(36)^y$; $(123456789)^x (36)^y$;
$(123456789)^{x_1} (36)^{x_2} (495)^{2x_2} (27)^{3x_2}$;
$(124578)^{x_1} (09)^{x_2} (123456789)^{y_1} (36)^{y_2}$.

The witness string must have length $n$: $495$ is the Kaprekar difference of $(495)^1$, but the
Kaprekar map on $4$-digit strings sends $495$ to $9081$.

## Sources

- Haruo Iwasaki, *A New Classification of the Kaprekar Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article iwasaki06162024-ASrev2, Theorem 3.1.

articles.title: The four-digit Kaprekar map sends 495 to 9081
articles.statement:
With $n = 4$, the number $495$ is padded to
the digit string $0495$, and the Kaprekar map sends it to $9540 - 0459 = 9081$.

## Sources

- Haruo Iwasaki, *A New Classification of the Kaprekar Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article iwasaki06162024-ASrev2, Definition 1.1.

articles.title: 6174 is fixed by the four-digit Kaprekar map
articles.statement:
The Kaprekar map with $n = 4$ sends $6174$
to itself: $7641 - 1467 = 6174$.

## Sources

- Haruo Iwasaki, *A New Classification of the Kaprekar Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article iwasaki06162024-ASrev2, Section 1.

articles.title: 495 is fixed by the three-digit Kaprekar map
articles.statement:
The Kaprekar map with $n = 3$ sends $495$ to
itself: $954 - 459 = 495$.

## Sources

- Haruo Iwasaki, *A New Classification of the Kaprekar Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article iwasaki06162024-ASrev2, Section 1.

articles.title: Kaprekar map
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $\alpha$, take the decimal digits of $\alpha$
(without leading zeros, and no digits at all for $\alpha = 0$) and, if there are fewer than $n$
of them, pad them with leading zeros to a string of exactly $n$ digits. The Kaprekar map sends
$\alpha$ to the Kaprekar difference $\alpha_M - \alpha_L$ of this digit string: the number with
these digits in descending order minus the number with them in ascending order. For
$\alpha < 10^n$ this is the Kaprekar transformation on the set $D_n$ of $n$-digit strings; for
$\alpha \ge 10^n$ nothing is padded and all digits of $\alpha$ are used.

## Sources

- Haruo Iwasaki, *A New Classification of the Kaprekar Numbers*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article iwasaki06162024-ASrev2, Definition 1.1.

articles.title: Maximal Kaprekar cycle length in odd bases
articles.statement:
Let $B > 3$ be odd, let $K_B$ be the
four-digit Kaprekar map and $X_B$ its state space, and let $\lambda(B)$ be the projective order
of $2$ modulo $B$. Every point of $X_B$ that is periodic for $K_B$ has minimal period at most
$(B - 1)/2$. Moreover, some point of $X_B$ has minimal period exactly $(B - 1)/2$ under $K_B$
if and only if $B \ge 7$, $B$ is prime and $\lambda(B) = (B - 1)/2$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Corollary 3 (`jis-2026-26.4.7-cor-3`).

articles.title: Long Kaprekar cycles force a prime base
articles.statement:
Let $B > 3$ be odd, let $K_B$ be the four-digit
Kaprekar map and $X_B$ its state space. Every point of $X_B$ that is periodic for $K_B$ has
minimal period at most $(B - 1)/2$, and if some point of $X_B$ has minimal period exactly
$(B - 1)/2$ under $K_B$, then $B$ is prime.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Corollary 22 (`jis-2026-26.4.7-cor-22`).

articles.title: Odd bases with a unique Kaprekar cycle
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 3$ be odd, let $K_B$ be the
four-digit Kaprekar map and $X_B$ its state space. There is a point $c \in X_B$, periodic for
$K_B$, whose forward orbit $\{K_B^k(c) : k \ge 0\}$ contains every point of $X_B$ that is
periodic for $K_B$, if and only if $B \in \{3, 5, 7\}$.

That is, $K_B$ has a unique terminal cycle on $X_B$ exactly when $B$ is $3$, $5$ or $7$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Corollary 27 (ii) (`jis-2026-26.4.7-cor-27`).

articles.title: Cycle lengths of doubling on pairs of projective classes
articles.statement:
Let $B > 3$ be odd. For
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$ write $[x] = \{x, -x\}$ and $2C = \{2c : c \in C\}$ for a subset
$C$ of $\mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$, and let $D$ be the doubling map sending a set $T$ of subsets of
$\mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$ to $\{2C : C \in T\}$. If $S = \{[r], [s]\}$ for nonzero
$r, s \in \mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$ with $[r] \ne [s]$, then $S$ is a periodic point of $D$ and
its minimal period is at most $\lambda(B)$, the projective order of $2$ modulo $B$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Lemma 20 (`jis-2026-26.4.7-lem-20`).

articles.title: Characterization of the projective order of 2
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $m$ be natural numbers with
$m > 0$. Suppose that $2^m \equiv 1$ or $2^m \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$, and that for every $k$ with
$0 < k < m$ neither $2^k \equiv 1$ nor $2^k \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$. Then the projective order of $2$
modulo $n$ is $\lambda(n) = m$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Definition 19, display (13).

articles.title: Values of the projective order of 2
articles.statement:
Writing $\lambda(n)$ for the projective order of $2$
modulo $n$, we have $\lambda(7) = 3$, $\lambda(9) = 3$, $\lambda(11) = 5$ and $\lambda(17) = 4$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Examples 7-10 and 23.

articles.title: Projective order of 2 is at most half the totient
articles.statement:
For every odd natural number $B > 3$,
the projective order of $2$ modulo $B$ satisfies $\lambda(B) \le \lfloor \varphi(B)/2 \rfloor$,
where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Lemma 21 (quoting Kay and Downes-Ward, Theorem 2) (`jis-2026-26.4.7-lem-21`).

articles.title: Projective order of 2
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the projective order of $2$ modulo $n$ is
the least $m > 0$ with $2^m \equiv 1$ or $2^m \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$,

$$\lambda(n) = \min \{m > 0 : 2^m \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{n}\},$$

and $\lambda(n) = 0$ when no such $m$ exists, which happens exactly when $n$ is even (including
$n = 0$, where congruence modulo $0$ is equality of integers). For odd $n$ these are the terms of
OEIS A003558, which lists $\lambda(2k + 1)$ at index $k$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Definition 19, display (13).

articles.title: At least two Kaprekar cycles whose length is the projective order of 2
articles.statement:
Let $\lambda(B)$
denote the projective order of $2$ modulo $B$. For every odd base $B > 17$, at least $2\lambda(B)$
points of the state space $X_B$ have minimal period exactly $\lambda(B)$ under the four-digit
Kaprekar map $K_B$.

Each terminal cycle of $K_B$ of length $\lambda(B)$ consists of $\lambda(B)$ such points, so this
says that $K_B$ has at least two terminal cycles of length $\lambda(B)$.

## Sources

- Evan Chen, Ken Ono, Richard E. Schwartz, and Dinesh Thakur, *Four-Digit Kaprekar Dynamics in Odd Bases*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.4.7, Corollary 27 (i) (`jis-2026-26.4.7-cor-27`).

articles.title: Keith number with given digits
articles.statement:
A natural number $N$ is a Keith number with digit list
$d = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ when $k \ge 2$, $d_i < 10$ for every $i$, $d_0 \ne 0$,
$N = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} d_i \cdot 10^{k-1-i}$ (so $d$ is the decimal representation of $N$, with at
least two digits), and $N = a_m$ for some $m \ge k$, where $(a_m)_{m \ge 0}$ is the Keith sequence
of $d$ indexed from $0$ (so $N$ occurs after the initial digits).

## Sources

- Martin Klazar and Florian Luca, *Counting Keith Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Definition in the introduction.

articles.title: Keith number
articles.statement:
A natural number $N$ is a Keith number when it is a Keith number with some
digit list: that is, $N$ has a decimal representation $d_0 d_1 \cdots d_{k-1}$ with $k \ge 2$
digits and leading digit $d_0 \ne 0$, and $N = a_j$ for some $j \ge k$, where $(a_m)_{m \ge 0}$ is
the Keith sequence of $(d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$: $a_m = d_m$ for $m < k$, and each later term is the
sum of the preceding $k$ terms.

## Sources

- Martin Klazar and Florian Luca, *Counting Keith Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Definition in the introduction.

articles.title: Keith sequence prefix
articles.statement:
Given a list $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ of natural numbers and
$j \in \mathbb{N}$, the Keith sequence prefix of $d$ at step $j$ is the list of length $k + j$
obtained from $d$ by appending, $j$ times, the sum of the last $k$ entries of the current list.
This is the recurrence used for Keith numbers.

## Sources

- Martin Klazar and Florian Luca, *Counting Keith Numbers*, Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Definition in the introduction.

articles.title: Keith sequence
articles.statement:
Given a list $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ of natural numbers, the Keith
sequence of $d$ is the sequence $(a_m)_{m \ge 0}$ with $a_m = d_m$ for $m < k$ and
$a_m = \sum_{i=m-k}^{m-1} a_i$ for $m \ge k$: after the initial entries, each term is the sum of
the preceding $k$ terms.

articles.title: Midy's theorem, general form
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $n$ a natural number such that $p$
divides $10^{2n} - 1$ but does not divide $10^n - 1$. Let $Q = (10^{2n} - 1)/p$ and write
$Q = 10^n H + L$ with $0 \le L < 10^n$, so that $L$ is the number formed by the last $n$ decimal
digits of $Q$ and $H$ the number formed by the remaining digits. Then $H + L = 10^n - 1$.

Midy's theorem in its usual form, where the decimal period of $1/p$ is exactly $2n$, is the
special case in which $p$ does not divide $10^m - 1$ for any $0 < m < 2n$.

articles.title: Midy's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $p \ne 2, 5$ be a prime and $n \ge 1$ an integer such that $p$ divides
$10^{2n} - 1$ and does not divide $10^m - 1$ for any $0 < m < 2n$, that is, the decimal period of
$1/p$ is $2n$. Let $Q = (10^{2n} - 1)/p$, whose decimal expansion padded with leading zeros to
$2n$ digits is the repetend of $1/p$, and write $Q = 10^n H + L$ with $0 \le L < 10^n$, so that
$H$ and $L$ are the two $n$-digit halves of the repetend. Then $H + L = 10^n - 1$.

The proof uses neither $p \ne 2, 5$ nor the minimality of the period beyond $p \nmid 10^n - 1$;
see Midy's theorem, general form.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midy%27s_theorem.

articles.title: Chinese remainder solutions with nonzero-digit product one
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 3$ and $w \ge 1$
be integers, and for $v = 1, \dots, w$ let $m_v$ be a positive integer and $r_v$ an integer.
Suppose the system of congruences $x \equiv r_v \pmod{m_v}$, $v = 1, \dots, w$, has an integer
solution, and $r_v = 0$ whenever $\gcd(m_v, b) \ne 1$. Then the system has a positive integer
solution $c$ with $p_b(c) = 1$, where $p_b(c)$ is the product of the nonzero base-$b$ digits
of $c$.

## Sources

- Michael Gohn, Joshua Harrington, Sophia Lebiere, Hani Samamah, Kyla Shappell, and Tony W. H. Wong, "Arithmetic Progressions of b-Prodigious Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.8.7, Lemma `lem:crt`, lines 178-180, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Wong/wong42.tex>.

articles.title: Prodigious numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $n$, the number $n$ is $b$-prodigious when
$b \ge 2$, $n > 0$, and $n$ is divisible by the product of the nonzero digits of $n$ in base $b$.

articles.title: Product of the nonzero digits
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $n$, this is the product of the
nonzero digits of $n$ in base $b$; it equals $1$ when $n = 0$. In the degenerate bases, the digits
of $n > 0$ are the single digit $n$ when $b = 0$, and $n$ copies of $1$ when $b = 1$.

articles.title: Units modulo $L$ whose square is not $1$
articles.statement:
Let $L \ge 1$, let $e$ be the exponent of $2$
in $L$ and let $f$ be the number of distinct odd prime factors of $L$. Then the number of
integers $0 \le j < L$ with $\gcd(j, L) = 1$ and $j^2 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{L}$ is
$\varphi(L) - 2^{f + g(e)}$, where $g(e) = \max(0, \min(2, e - 1))$.

In the paper these $j$ index the Class A columns of a repetend table.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Moduli with exactly $\varphi(L)$ units of even order $L$
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $L \ge 2$
be even. If the number of elements of multiplicative order $L$ in
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ equals $\varphi(L)$, then either $n = 4$ and $L = 2$, or $n = tq$
for some $t \in \{1, 2\}$ and some odd prime power $q$ with $L \mid \varphi(q)$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Corollary 5.

articles.title: Elements of order two modulo $n$
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$, the number of elements of
multiplicative order $2$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is $2^k - 1$ for some natural
number $k$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Corollary 6.

articles.title: Raising the base by multiples of $n$ shifts repetend digits linearly
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $j$ be
natural numbers, $n \ge 1$ and $b \ge 2$. For a base $B$ write
$d_j(B) = \lfloor m B^{j+1} / n \rfloor \bmod B$ for the $j$-th base-$B$ digit of $m/n$. Then
there is a natural number $c < n$ such that $d_j(b + tn) = d_j(b) + tc$ for every natural number
$t$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Moduli with exactly two small bases of order six
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. If exactly
two integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$ and $\gcd(b, n) = 1$ have multiplicative order $6$ modulo $n$,
then either $n = 3^k t \ge 9$ for some natural number $k$ and some $t \in \{1, 2\}$, or
$n = p^k t$ for some prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, some $k \ge 1$ and some $t \in \{1, 2\}$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 33.

articles.title: Small bases of order greater than two come in pairs
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and
every $L > 2$, the number of integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$ and $\gcd(b, n) = 1$ whose
multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $L$ is even.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Long division of a proper fraction
articles.statement:
Let $m < n$ be natural numbers and $b \ge 1$. For
$j \ge 0$ let $c_j = m b^j \bmod n$ (the remainders of the long division of $m/n$ in base $b$) and
$r_j = \lfloor b c_j / n \rfloor$ (its digits). Then for every $k \ge 0$

$$\frac{m}{n} = \sum_{i\lt k} \frac{r_i}{b^{i+1}} + \frac{c_k}{n b^k},$$

and $r_j n = b c_j - c_{j+1}$ for every $j \ge 0$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Long-division remainders and small bases of prime order
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $L$ be primes and
let $b$ be a natural number of multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$. Suppose $m = 1$, or
$2 \le m \le n - 1$ and $m$ has multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$. Then removing $1$ from the
set of remainders $\{m b^j \bmod n : 0 \le j < L\}$ leaves exactly the set of integers $a$ with
$2 \le a \le n - 1$ whose multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $L$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Corollary 2.

articles.title: A constraint on $b^2 + un$ between $2$ and $n - 2$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers and
$u$ an integer, and put $b_2 = b^2 + un$. If $2 \le b_2 \le n - 2$, then $b \ne u + 1$.

The paper states this for a small base $b$; here $b$ is any natural number.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 31.

articles.title: Order-six elements modulo a power of a prime congruent to $1$ mod $6$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, let $k \ge 1$ and put $n = p^k$. If $b \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ has
multiplicative order $6$, then $b \ne 0$, $2b \ne 1$, $b \ne 1$, $b \ne -1$ and $b \ne 2$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 16.

articles.title: The $p$-adic valuation of $B^2 - B + 1$ for a base of order $6p^j$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, let $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers with $j \ge 1$ and $i \ge 2j$, and
let $B$ be a natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $p^i$ is $6p^j$. Then the $p$-adic
valuation of $B^2 - B + 1$ is exactly $i - j$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Half-period symmetry of the repetend of $1/n$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number whose unit
group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is cyclic, let $L > 0$ be even, and let $b < n$ be a
natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $L$. For natural numbers $m$ write
$b_m = b^m \bmod n$ and $r_m = \lfloor b^{m+1}/n \rfloor \bmod b$, the $m$-th base-$b$ digit of
$1/n$. Then for every natural number $j$ we have $b_{j+L/2} = n - b_j$ and
$r_j + r_{j+L/2} = r_{L/2}$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 29.

articles.title: Powers of $b^y \bmod p^i$ that differ by one
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$,
let $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers with $j \ge 1$ and $i \ge 2j$, put $n = p^i$ and $Q = p^j$, and
let $b$ be a natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $6Q$. Let $f \in \{1, -1\}$,
let $y$ be a natural number with $y \equiv s \pmod 6$ for some $s \in \{1, -1\}$, and put $e = 1$
if $sf = 1$ and $e = 5$ if $sf = -1$. Let $d$ be a natural number with $d \equiv 2f \pmod 6$, and
let $k < 6Q$ be a natural number with $k \equiv f \pmod 6$ and $k \equiv b^e d \pmod Q$. Then, with
$B = b^y \bmod n$, we have $B^k \bmod n = (B^d \bmod n) + 1$.

Here $b^5$ stands for $b^{-1}$ modulo $Q$, as $b^6 \equiv 1 \pmod Q$, so $b^e$ is $b^{sf}$ modulo
$Q$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 11.

articles.title: Powers of a base of order $6p^j$ modulo $p^j$ depend only on the exponent modulo $6$
articles.statement:
Let
$p$ be a prime, let $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers with $j \ge 1$ and $i \ge 2j$, and let $b$ be a
natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $p^i$ is $6p^j$. If $y$ and $s$ are natural
numbers with $y \equiv s \pmod 6$, then $b^y \equiv b^s \pmod{p^j}$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 10.

articles.title: A power of $B$ equal to $B - 1$ modulo $p^i$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$,
let $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers with $j \ge 1$ and $i \ge 2j$, put $n = p^i$ and $Q = p^j$, and
let $B < n$ be a natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $6Q$. Let $z < 6Q$ be a
natural number with $z \equiv 2 \pmod 6$ such that $zB \equiv 1 \pmod Q$ or
$z \equiv 1 - B \pmod Q$. Then $B^z \bmod n = B - 1$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 9.

articles.title: Powers of a base of order $6$ modulo $tp^k$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$,
let $k \ge 1$ and $t \in \{1, 2\}$ be natural numbers, and put $n = tp^k$. Let $b_1 < n$ be a
natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $6$, write $b_m = b_1^m \bmod n$, and put
$H = 0$ if $t = 1$, $H = p^k$ if $t = 2$ and $b_1 < p^k$, and $H = -p^k$ if $t = 2$ and
$b_1 \ge p^k$. Then $b_2 = b_1 - 1 + H$, $b_3 = n - 1$, $b_4 = n - b_1$ and
$b_5 = n - b_1 + 1 - H$, and there is an integer $u$ with $b_1^2 = un + b_1 - 1 + H$,
$b_2^2 = un - b_1 + (H + 2b_1 - 1)H$ and $b_1 b_2 = un - 1 + (b_1 + 1)H$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 35.

articles.title: Relations among the powers $B^{zp^j} \bmod p^i$ for a base of order $6p^j$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a
prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, let $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers, put $n = p^i$ and $Q = p^j$,
and let $B$ be a natural number whose multiplicative order modulo $n$ is $6Q$. Write
$B_z = B^z \bmod n$. Then $B_{2Q} = B_Q - 1$, $B_{4Q} = B_{5Q} - 1$, $B_Q + B_{5Q} = n + 1$ and
$B_{3Q} = n - 1$; moreover $Q^2 \equiv Q \pmod{6Q}$.

Since $B^{6Q} \equiv 1 \pmod n$, the residues $B_{5Q}$ and $B_{4Q}$ are those of $B^{-Q}$ and
$B^{-2Q}$. The paper assumes $j \ge 1$ and $i \ge 2j$; these are not needed here.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 13.

articles.title: Block sums of a repetend
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 2$, $N$, $x < N$, $d \ge 1$ and $k \ge 1$ be natural
numbers, and let $a_i = \lfloor xB^{i+1}/N \rfloor \bmod B$ be the $i$-th base-$B$ digit of $x/N$.
Suppose $a_{i+dk} = a_i$ for every natural number $i$. Let
$S = \sum_{j\lt d} \sum_{i\lt k} a_{jk+i} B^{k-1-i}$ be the sum of the first $d$ blocks of $k$ digits,
each read as a base-$B$ number, and let $R = \sum_{j\lt d} (xB^{jk} \bmod N)$. Then
$SN = R(B^k - 1)$, and if $B^k - 1$ is coprime to $N$, then $B^k - 1$ divides $S$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Columns $j$ and $j^{-1}$ of a repetend table match
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $L \ge 1$ be natural
numbers, and consider the repetend table of $1/n$ whose rows are the natural numbers $1 \le b < n$
coprime to $n$ of multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$, and whose column $j$ holds the digits
$\lfloor b^{j+1}/n \rfloor \bmod b$. If $j$ and $j'$ are natural numbers with $j$ coprime to $L$,
$j^2 \not\equiv 1 \pmod L$ and $jj' \equiv 1 \pmod L$, then columns $j$ and $j'$ are equal as
multisets.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Column $4$ of the order-$6$ repetend table of $t p^k$ differs from columns $0$ and $5$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, let $k \ge 1$ and $t \in \{1, 2\}$, and put
$n = t p^k$. Let the rows be the integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$, $\gcd(b, n) = 1$ and
multiplicative order $6$ modulo $n$, and let column $j$ be the multiset of the digits
$\lfloor b^{j+1}/n \rfloor \bmod b$ over these rows. Then column $4$ is different from column $0$
and from column $5$.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 39.

articles.title: Columns $0$ and $5$ of the order-$6$ repetend table of $t p^k$ differ
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, let $k \ge 1$ and $t \in \{1, 2\}$, and put $n = t p^k$. Let the rows be
the integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$, $\gcd(b, n) = 1$ and multiplicative order $6$ modulo $n$, and
let column $j$ be the multiset of the digits $\lfloor b^{j+1}/n \rfloor \bmod b$ over these rows.
Then columns $0$ and $5$ are different.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 37.

articles.title: Class C matched columns of repetend tables
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 6$,
let $j \ge 1$ and $i \ge 2j$, and put $n = p^i$, $Q = p^j$ and $L = 6Q$. Let $b$ be a natural
number of multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$, and let $d, e < L$ be natural numbers with
$d \equiv b^2 \pmod Q$, $e \equiv b^4 \pmod Q$ and $d \equiv e \equiv 4 \pmod 6$. Let the rows be
the integers $c$ with $1 \le c < n$, $\gcd(c, n) = 1$ and multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$, and
let column $s$ be the multiset of the digits $\lfloor c^{s+1}/n \rfloor \bmod c$ over these rows.
Then columns $d$ and $e$ are equal.

Theorem 6 of the source also says when the digit difference between these columns is $0$; that
clause is not stated here.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Class B matched columns of repetend tables
articles.statement:
Let $a \ge 1$ and $L = 12a + 6$, let $p$ be a
prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod L$, let $k \ge 1$ and $n = p^k$, and let $b$ be a natural number of
multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$; write $b_i = b^i \bmod n$. Let the rows be the integers $c$
with $1 \le c < n$, $\gcd(c, n) = 1$ and multiplicative order $L$ modulo $n$, and let column $j$
be the multiset of the digits $\lfloor c^{j+1}/n \rfloor \bmod c$ over these rows. Then
$\lfloor (b_i + b_{i + L/3} + b_{i + 2L/3})/n \rfloor = 1$ for every $0 \le i < L$ coprime to $L$
if and only if columns $2a + 1$ and $4a + 2$ are equal and columns $8a + 4$ and $10a + 5$ are
equal.

The proportion conjectured in the source is not stated here.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Repetend tables with one or three rows have no matched columns
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$
and $L$, let the rows be the integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$, $\gcd(b, n) = 1$ and multiplicative
order $L$ modulo $n$, and let column $j$ be the multiset of the digits
$\lfloor b^{j+1}/n \rfloor \bmod b$ over these rows. If there are exactly one or exactly three
rows, then for all distinct $i, j < L$ columns $i$ and $j$ are different.

## Sources

- R. J. Booth and D. J. Horton, *Matched Column Sets in Repetend Tables*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A26, Lemma 27.

articles.title: Repetend tables with at most three rows have no matched columns
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$
and $L$, let the rows be the integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$, $\gcd(b, n) = 1$ and multiplicative
order $L$ modulo $n$, and let column $j$ be the multiset of the digits
$\lfloor b^{j+1}/n \rfloor \bmod b$ over these rows. If there are at least one and at most three
