$\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathrm{FIB}}(m)$ is the number of finite sets $T$ of indices $i \ge 2$ with
$\sum_{i \in T} F_i = m$, where $F_i$ are the Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$); that is,
the number of ways to write $m$ as a sum of Fibonacci numbers with distinct indices at least $2$
(OEIS A000119). Indices above $m + 1$ never occur because $F_{m+2} > m$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1 (base Fibonacci representations).

articles.title: Generalized Beatty sequences composed with the Wythoff sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio and, for integers $a$, $b$, $c$ and natural numbers $n$, let
$V(a, b, c)(n) = a \lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + bn + c$. Let $A(n) = \lfloor n\varphi \rfloor$ and
$B(n) = \lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + n$ be the lower and upper Wythoff sequences. For all integers
$p$, $q$, $r$ and every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$V(p, q, r)(A(n)) = V(p + q, p, r - p)(n)$ and $V(p, q, r)(B(n)) = V(2p + q, p + q, r)(n)$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Lemma 3.

articles.title: First differences of a generalized Beatty sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio, for
integers $p, q, r$ let $V(p, q, r)$ be the sequence $n \mapsto p\lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + qn + r$
on the natural numbers, and let $x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ be the infinite Fibonacci word. For all
integers $p, q, r$ and every $n \ge 1$, the difference $V(p, q, r)(n+1) - V(p, q, r)(n)$ equals
$p + q$ if $x_{n-1} = 1$ and $2p + q$ if $x_{n-1} = 0$. Conversely, for all integers $a, b$ and
every sequence $v$ of integers indexed by the natural numbers such that, for every $n \ge 1$,
$v(n+1) - v(n)$ equals $b$ if $x_{n-1} = 1$ and $a$ if $x_{n-1} = 0$, there is an integer $r'$
with $v(n) = V(a - b, 2b - a, r')(n)$ for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Generalized Beatty sequence at one
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. For all integers
$p, q, r$, the generalized Beatty sequence $V(p, q, r)(n) = p\lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + qn + r$
takes the value $V(p, q, r)(1) = p + q + r$ at $n = 1$, since $\lfloor \varphi \rfloor = 1$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 5.

articles.title: Generalized Beatty sequence at zero
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. For all integers
$p, q, r$, the generalized Beatty sequence $V(p, q, r)(n) = p\lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + qn + r$
takes the value $V(p, q, r)(0) = r$ at $n = 0$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 6 (`V₀`).

articles.title: Generalized Beatty sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. For integers $p, q, r$, the
generalized Beatty sequence $V(p, q, r)$ is the integer sequence defined for every natural number
$n$, including $n = 0$, by $V(p, q, r)(n) = p\lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + qn + r$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 5.

articles.title: Peeling off the leading letter of a digit block
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of integers, read
as the positions of the digits $1$ of an expansion. For every integer $k$, every natural number
$b$ and every finite word $w$ over the natural numbers, the word $bw$ (the letter $b$ followed by
$w$) occurs as a digit block of $S$ at position $k$ if and only if both $k \in S$ holds exactly
when $b = 1$, and $w$ occurs as a digit block of $S$ at position $k - 1$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 6.

articles.title: The empty digit block occurs everywhere
articles.statement:
For every finite set $S$ of integers, read as the
positions of the digits $1$ of an expansion, and every integer $k$, the empty word occurs as a
digit block of $S$ at position $k$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 6.

articles.title: Digit block of an expansion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a finite set of integers, read as the positions of
the digits $1$ of an expansion with digits $d_i$, so $d_i = 1$ if $i \in S$ and $d_i = 0$
otherwise. For an integer $k$ and a finite word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{m-1}$ over the natural
numbers, $w$ occurs as a digit block of $S$ at position $k$ when the digits
$d_k d_{k-1} \cdots d_{k-m+1}$, read from the highest position down, are the letters of $w$: for
every $i < m$, $d_{k-i} = 1$ holds exactly when $w_i = 1$. A letter $1$ stands for the digit $1$
and any other letter for the digit $0$; the empty word occurs at every position.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Sections 6 and 7 (digit blocks `d_{m-1} ⋯ d_0` and `d_{-1} ⋯ d_{-m}`).

articles.title: Base phi expansion of one
articles.statement:
The set $\{0\}$, read as the positions of the digits $1$, is a
base phi expansion of $1$: the expansion with a single digit $1$ at position $0$ has no two
adjacent digits $1$, and its value $\varphi^0$ equals $1$, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Table 1.

articles.title: Base phi expansion of zero
articles.statement:
The empty set of positions, the expansion with no digit $1$, is
a base phi expansion of $0$: it has no two adjacent digits $1$, and its value, the empty sum, is
equal to $0$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 1.

articles.title: Base phi expansion
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. A finite set $S$ of integers, read as
the positions of the digits $1$ of a finite expansion with digits $0$ and $1$, is a base phi
expansion of the natural number $N$ when it is a Bergman expansion (no two digits $1$ are
adjacent: $i \in S$ implies $i + 1 \notin S$) and its value $\sum_{i \in S} \varphi^i$ equals $N$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 1 (definition of `β(N)`).

articles.title: The expansion 10.01 is a Bergman expansion
articles.statement:
The base phi expansion $10.01$, with digits $1$
at positions $1$ and $-2$ and digits $0$ elsewhere, has no two adjacent digits $1$, so it is a
Bergman expansion.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1.

articles.title: Bergman expansions
articles.statement:
Encode a finite base phi expansion with digits $0$ and $1$ by the
finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ of positions of its digits $1$. The expansion is a Bergman
expansion when no two digits $1$ are adjacent, that is, $i + 1 \notin S$ for every $i \in S$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1 (Bergman representation).

articles.title: A golden mean flip from 10.01 to 1.11
articles.statement:
Applying the golden mean flip $100 \to 011$ at the
leading digit of $10.01$ (the digit $1$ at position $1$, followed by digits $0$ at positions $0$
and $-1$) gives $1.11$, the expansion with digits $1$ at positions $0$, $-1$ and $-2$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 2.

articles.title: Golden mean flips
articles.statement:
Encode a finite base phi expansion with digits $0$ and $1$ by the
finite set of positions of its digits $1$. An expansion $T$ arises from an expansion $S$ by a
golden mean flip $100 \to 011$ when there is a position $i \in S$ with $i - 1 \notin S$ and
$i - 2 \notin S$ such that $T = (S \setminus \{i\}) \cup \{i - 1, i - 2\}$: the digit $1$ at
position $i$ is replaced by digits $1$ at positions $i - 1$ and $i - 2$, which were $0$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Sections 1 and 2 (the map `T_i`).

articles.title: Lucas tilings of a list with a first interval
articles.statement:
Write $\Lambda_k = [\ell_k, h_k]$ for the
Lucas interval with left end $\ell_k$ and right end $h_k$. For all natural numbers $a$, $b$, $k$,
$t$ and every list $P$ of pairs of natural numbers, the list consisting of $(k, t)$ followed by
$P$ is a Lucas tiling of $[a, b]$ if and only if $\ell_k + t = a$ and $P$ is a Lucas tiling of
$[h_k + t + 1, b]$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 4.

articles.title: Lucas tilings by the empty list
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the empty list is a
Lucas tiling of $[a, b]$ if and only if $a = b + 1$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 4.

articles.title: Lucas tilings
articles.statement:
Write $\Lambda_k = [\ell_k, h_k]$ for the Lucas interval with left end
$\ell_k$ and right end $h_k$. For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and a list $P$ of pairs $(k, t)$ of
natural numbers, $P$ is a Lucas tiling of $[a, b]$ when the translated Lucas intervals
$\Lambda_k + t$, $(k, t) \in P$, taken in the order of $P$, are adjacent and their union is
$[a, b]$. Precisely, it is defined by recursion on $P$: the empty list is a Lucas tiling of
$[a, b]$ exactly when $a = b + 1$, and the list consisting of $(k, t)$ followed by $P$ is a Lucas
tiling of $[a, b]$ exactly when $\ell_k + t = a$ and $P$ is a Lucas tiling of $[h_k + t + 1, b]$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 4 ("a union of adjacent translations" of Lucas intervals).

articles.title: Recursion for the number of Knott expansions
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio, let
$N \ge 2$ and $n$ be natural numbers, and let $p_0, \dots, p_n$ be integers with
$p_{k+1} \ge p_k + 2$ for all $k < n$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \varphi^{p_k} = N$. Thus $N$ has the
base phi expansion $10^{s_n} \cdots 10^{s_1} 1$ with digits $1$ at positions $p_0 < \dots < p_n$,
where $s_k = p_k - p_{k-1} - 1$ for $1 \le k \le n$. Let $r_0, r_1, \dots$ be integers with
$r_0 = 1$; if $n \ge 1$, let $r_1 = s_1/2 + 1$ when $s_1$ is even and $r_1 = (s_1 + 1)/2 + 1$
when $s_1$ is odd; and for $2 \le k \le n$, let $r_k = (s_k/2 + 1)\, r_{k-1}$ when $s_k$ is even
and $r_k = ((s_k + 1)/2 + 1)\, r_{k-1} - r_{k-2}$ when $s_k$ is odd. Then the number of Knott
expansions of $N$ is $r_n$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 2.3.

articles.title: Knott expansions of Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$,
$F_1 = 1$). For every $n \ge 1$, the number of Knott expansions of $F_n$ is $F_n$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 3.2.

articles.title: Knott expansions of Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$, each of the Lucas numbers $L_{2n}$
and $L_{2n+1}$ (with $L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$) has exactly $2n + 1$ Knott expansions.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 3.3.

articles.title: Number of Knott expansions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, $\mathrm{Tot}_\kappa(N)$ is the
number of Knott expansions of $N$ (OEIS A289749).

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1.

articles.title: Knott expansions
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and $N$ a natural number. Encode a
finite base phi expansion with digits $0$ and $1$ by the finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ of the
positions of its digits $1$. The Knott expansions of $N$ are the expansions of value $N$ that
satisfy Knott's truncation rule: the set of all such $S$ with $\sum_{i \in S} \varphi^i = N$ that
satisfy Knott's condition.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1.

articles.title: Dekking's Theorem 4: the coding of the canonical splittings of Lucas intervals
articles.statement:
Write
$\Lambda_m = [\ell_m, h_m]$ for the Lucas interval with left end $\ell_m$ and right end $h_m$. For
every $n \ge 3$, every pair $(k, t)$ in the canonical splitting of $\Lambda_n$ has
$k \in \{3, 4, 5\}$, and the canonical splitting of $\Lambda_n$ is a Lucas tiling of
$[\ell_n, h_n]$. Let $\kappa$ be the map on finite words of natural numbers that replaces each
letter $3$ by the word $5$, each letter $4$ by $434$ and every other letter by $545$, and let
$C(\Lambda_m)$ be the word formed by the first components $k$ of the pairs $(k, t)$ of the
canonical splitting of $\Lambda_m$, in order. Then for every $n \ge 0$,
$C(\Lambda_{2n+4}) = \kappa^n(4)$ and $C(\Lambda_{2n+5}) = \kappa^n(5)$, where $\kappa^n$ is the
$n$-fold iterate of $\kappa$ applied to the one-letter word.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Endpoints of the Lucas interval $\Lambda_5$
articles.statement:
The Lucas interval $\Lambda_5$ has left end
$12$ and right end $17$, that is, $\Lambda_5 = [12, 17]$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 3.

articles.title: Endpoints of the Lucas interval $\Lambda_4$
articles.statement:
The Lucas interval $\Lambda_4$ has left end
$7$ and right end $11$, that is, $\Lambda_4 = [7, 11]$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 3.

articles.title: Right end of a Lucas interval
articles.statement:
Let $L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$, $L_{j+2} = L_{j+1} + L_j$ be the
Lucas numbers, and let the Lucas intervals be $\Lambda_{2n} = [L_{2n}, L_{2n+1}]$ and
$\Lambda_{2n+1} = [L_{2n+1} + 1, L_{2n+2} - 1]$. The right end of $\Lambda_m$ is $L_{m+1}$ when
$m$ is even and $L_{m+1} - 1$ when $m$ is odd.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 3 (Lucas intervals).

articles.title: Left end of a Lucas interval
articles.statement:
Let $L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = 1$, $L_{j+2} = L_{j+1} + L_j$ be the
Lucas numbers, and let the Lucas intervals be $\Lambda_{2n} = [L_{2n}, L_{2n+1}]$ and
$\Lambda_{2n+1} = [L_{2n+1} + 1, L_{2n+2} - 1]$. The left end of $\Lambda_m$ is $L_m$ when $m$
is even and $L_m + 1$ when $m$ is odd.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 3 (Lucas intervals).

articles.title: Endpoints of the Lucas interval $\Lambda_3$
articles.statement:
The Lucas interval $\Lambda_3$ has left end
$5$ and right end $6$, that is, $\Lambda_3 = [5, 6]$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 3.

articles.title: The initial term of a generalized Beatty set
articles.statement:
For all integers $p$, $q$ and $r$, the
integer $r$ belongs to the set $V_0(p, q, r)$ of terms $p \lfloor n\varphi \rfloor + qn + r$,
$n \ge 0$, of the generalized Beatty sequence, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio; indeed $r$
is its term at $n = 0$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Section 6.

articles.title: Natural expansions are counted by Fibonacci representations
articles.statement:
Write $F_k$ for the $k$-th
Fibonacci number. Let $N > 3$ be a natural number, let $S$ be a Bergman expansion of $N$ and let
$R$ be the lowest position of a digit $1$ in $S$. Then the number $\mathrm{Tot}_\nu(N)$ of natural
base phi expansions of $N$ equals the number $\mathrm{Tot}_{\mathrm{FIB}}(F_{2-R} N)$ of
representations of $F_{2-R} N$ as a sum of Fibonacci numbers with distinct indices at least $2$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 4.4.

articles.title: Recursion for the number of natural expansions
articles.statement:
Let $N$ and $n$ be natural numbers and
let $p_0, \dots, p_n$ be integers with $p_k + 2 \le p_{k+1}$ for $k < n$ such that the base phi
expansion with digits $1$ at positions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ represents $N$. Put
$s_k = p_k - p_{k-1} - 1$ for $1 \le k \le n$. Let $r_0, r_1, \dots$ be integers with
$r_0 = 1$ such that, if $n \ge 1$, $2 r_1 = s_1 + 2$ when $s_1$ is even and $2 r_1 = s_1 + 1$
when $s_1$ is odd, and for $2 \le k \le n$, $2 r_k = (s_k + 2) r_{k-1}$ when $s_k$ is even and
$2 r_k = (s_k + 3) r_{k-1} - 2 r_{k-2}$ when $s_k$ is odd. Then the number
$\mathrm{Tot}_\nu(N)$ of natural base phi expansions of $N$ equals $r_n$.

Compared with the recursion for the number of Knott expansions, only the value of $r_1$ for odd
$s_1$ differs, and $N \ge 2$ is not assumed.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 4.1.

articles.title: Natural expansions of Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{Tot}_\nu(N)$ for the number of
natural base phi expansions of a natural number $N$ and $F_k$ for the $k$-th Fibonacci number.
Then for every $n \ge 0$, $\mathrm{Tot}_\nu(F_{2n+2}) = F_{2n+1}$ and
$\mathrm{Tot}_\nu(F_{2n+3}) = F_{2n+3}$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Number of natural expansions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, $\mathrm{Tot}_\nu(N)$ is the
number of natural base phi expansions of $N$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Natural base phi expansions
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and $N$ a natural number.
Encode a finite base phi expansion with digits $0$ and $1$ by the finite set
$S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ of the positions of its digits $1$. The natural expansions of $N$ are the
Knott expansions $S$ of $N$ for which there is a Bergman expansion $T$ with
$\sum_{i \in T} \varphi^i = N$ whose lowest digit $1$ is at the same position as the lowest
digit $1$ of $S$, that is, $\min T = \min S$, where $S$ and $T$ both empty also counts as
equal.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: The expansion 0.11 violates Knott's truncation rule
articles.statement:
The finite base phi expansion
$0.11$, with digits $1$ at positions $-1$ and $-2$ and no others, ends in the digits $011$, so it
does not satisfy Knott's truncation rule.

It represents $1$, since $\varphi^{-1} + \varphi^{-2} = 1$ for the golden ratio $\varphi$, but
is not a Knott expansion of $1$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1, Equation (1.1).

articles.title: A base phi expansion of 1 ends in the digit 1
articles.statement:
The number $1$ lies in the occurrence
set of the one-letter digit block $1$ placed at position $0$ (the paper's $R_1$): some base phi
expansion of $1$ has the digit $1$ at position $0$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Theorem 6.

articles.title: The expansion 10.01 is a natural expansion of 2
articles.statement:
The finite base phi expansion $10.01$,
with digits $1$ exactly at positions $1$ and $-2$, is a natural base phi expansion of $2$.

It is the Bergman expansion of $2$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 4.

articles.title: Golden mean flips connect all expansions to the Bergman expansion
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a natural
number, let $S$ be a Bergman expansion of $N$ and let $T$ be any finite base phi expansion of
$N$ with digits $0$ and $1$. Then $T$ is obtained from $S$ by finitely many (possibly zero)
golden mean flips $100 \to 011$.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-2/dekking11102023, Theorem 2.1.

articles.title: Knott's truncation rule
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. Encode a finite base $\varphi$
expansion with digits $0$ and $1$ by the finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ of the positions of
its digits $1$, and write $a_i$ for its digit at position $i$. The expansion satisfies Knott's
condition when it does not end in the digits $0, 1, 1$: if $S$ is nonempty with least element $R$,
then $a_{R+2} a_{R+1} a_R \ne 011$, that is, it is not the case that both $R + 1 \in S$ and
$R + 2 \notin S$. The empty expansion satisfies the condition.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1, Equation (1.1).

articles.title: Canonical splitting and coding of unions of two Lucas intervals
articles.statement:
Let $L_m$ denote the
$m$-th Lucas number and $\Lambda_m$ the Lucas interval, so $\Lambda_{2k} = [L_{2k}, L_{2k+1}]$
and $\Lambda_{2k+1} = [L_{2k+1} + 1, L_{2k+2} - 1]$. For $n \ge 2$, let $P_n$ be the canonical
splitting of $\Lambda_{2n-1}$ followed by the canonical splitting of $\Lambda_{2n}$, a list of
translations $\Lambda_k + t$. Then every index $k$ occurring in $P_n$ is $3$, $4$ or $5$, and
the intervals of $P_n$, taken in order, are adjacent with union $[L_{2n-1} + 1, L_{2n+1}]$.
Moreover, for every $n \ge 0$ the list of indices $k$ of $P_{n+2}$ (the coding $C(\Xi_{n+2})$,
where $\Xi_n = \Lambda_{2n-1} \cup \Lambda_{2n}$) equals $\delta(h^n(b))$, where $h$ is the
morphism $a \mapsto aab$, $b \mapsto ab$ on words over $\{a, b\}$ and $\delta$ is the morphism
$a \mapsto 54$, $b \mapsto 34$.

## Sources

- F. Michel Dekking, *The Structure of Base Phi Expansions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A24, Theorem 5.

articles.title: A Knott expansion of two
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. The base $\varphi$ expansion
$1.11$, whose digits $1$ sit at the positions $0$, $-1$ and $-2$, is a Knott expansion of $2$:
its value is $1 + \varphi^{-1} + \varphi^{-2} = 2$ and it satisfies Knott's truncation rule.

## Sources

- Michel Dekking and Ad van Loon, *Counting Base Phi Representations*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Section 1.

articles.title: Normalized hyperfactorial digit vectors
articles.statement:
A vector $(h_1, \dots, h_k)$ of natural numbers
is normalized when either $k = 0$ or its last entry $h_k$ is nonzero. In particular the empty
vector is normalized; it is the canonical representation of zero.

articles.title: Hyperfactorial partition
articles.statement:
A hyperfactorial partition of a natural number $n$ consists of
a length $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and natural numbers $h_1, \dots, h_k$ such that $h_i \le 2i$ for
every $1 \le i \le k$, the digit vector is normalized (either $k = 0$ or $h_k \neq 0$), and

$$n = \sum_{i=1}^{k} h_i \cdot i!.$$

articles.title: $k$-Mahler functions
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A formal power series
$F \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ is a $k$-Mahler function when $k \ge 2$ and there exist a natural number
$d$ and polynomials $a_0(z), \dots, a_d(z) \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $a_0 \ne 0$ and $a_d \ne 0$
such that the following identity holds in $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$:

$$\sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i(z)\, F\bigl(z^{k^i}\bigr) = 0.$$

## Sources

- https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Bell/bell2.tex.

articles.title: Mahler substitution
articles.statement:
For a formal power series $F \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ and natural numbers
$k$ and $i$, let $m = k^i$; the power series $F(z^{k^i})$ is defined coefficientwise. When
$m \ge 1$, its coefficient of $z^n$ is the coefficient of $z^{n/m}$ in $F$ if $m$ divides $n$, and
$0$ otherwise; this is the substitution $z \mapsto z^m$ in $F$. When $m = 0$ (that is, $k = 0$ and
$i \ge 1$), it is the constant series equal to the constant term of $F$.

## Sources

- https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Bell/bell2.tex.

articles.title: Nishioka's theorem: algebraic Mahler functions are rational
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number
and let $F \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ be a $k$-Mahler function. If $F$ is algebraic over
$\mathbb{C}[z]$, that is, $P(F) = 0$ for some nonzero polynomial $P$ with coefficients in
$\mathbb{C}[z]$, then $F$ is rational: there are polynomials $p, q \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $q \ne 0$
and $qF = p$ in $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$.

## Sources

- Jason P. Bell, Michael Coons, and Eric Rowland, "The Rational-Transcendental Dichotomy of Mahler Functions", Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.2.10, Nishioka corollary lines 238–241, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Bell/bell2.tex>. The corollary is attributed to Ku. Nishioka, "Mahler Functions and Transcendence", Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1294, Theorem 5.1.7.

articles.title: Moves of a Beatty octal game decrease the heap
articles.statement:
For all real numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$
and all natural numbers $n$, $m$: if a move of the Beatty octal game for $\alpha$ and $\beta$
takes a heap of $n$ tokens to a heap of $m$ tokens, then $m < n$.

Consequently every play of the game terminates.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Moves of the Beatty octal game
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be real numbers. In the Beatty
octal game for $\alpha$ and $\beta$, a move takes a heap of $n$ tokens to a heap of $m$ tokens
exactly when one of the following holds: $n \ge 1$, $n = \lfloor k\alpha \rfloor$ for some
integer $k \ge 1$, and $m = 0$ (the whole heap is removed); or $m = n - i$ for some natural
number $i$ with $1 \le i < n$ and $i = \lfloor k\beta \rfloor$ for some integer $k \ge 1$
(removing $i$ tokens leaves a nonempty heap).

When $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complementary, so that every $i \ge 1$ lies in exactly one of the
Beatty sequences $\{\lfloor k\alpha \rfloor : k \ge 1\}$ and
$\{\lfloor k\beta \rfloor : k \ge 1\}$, this is the octal game with code
$0{\cdot}d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots$, where $d_i = 1$ if $i$ lies in the first sequence and $d_i = 2$ if
$i$ lies in the second.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 1.1 (octal codes) and the codes of the gold, silver and bronze games in Sections 2, 3, 4.

articles.title: Recurrence for the companion bronze numbers of the first type
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n$, the companion bronze numbers $C_n$ of the first type satisfy $C_{n+2} = 3C_{n+1} + C_n$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4.

articles.title: Companion bronze numbers of the first type
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ denote the bronze numbers, the
Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$: $B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$ and $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$. For every
natural number $n$, the $n$-th companion bronze number of the first type is the integer
$C_n = B_{n+1} - 2B_n$.

Thus $C_0 = C_1 = 1$, $C_{n+2} = 3C_{n+1} + C_n$, and $C_n = B_n + B_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4 (companion bronze numbers of the first type).

articles.title: Recurrence for the companion bronze numbers of the second type
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n$, the companion bronze numbers $D_n$ of the second type satisfy $D_{n+2} = 3D_{n+1} + D_n$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4.

articles.title: Companion bronze numbers of the second type
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ denote the bronze numbers, the
Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$: $B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$ and $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$. For every
natural number $n$, the $n$-th companion bronze number of the second type is the integer
$D_n = B_{n+1} - B_n$.

Thus $D_0 = 1$, $D_1 = 2$, $D_{n+2} = 3D_{n+1} + D_n$, and $D_n = 2B_n + B_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4 (companion bronze numbers of the second type).

articles.title: Initial companion bronze numbers
articles.statement:
The companion bronze numbers $C_n$ of the first type
satisfy $(C_0, C_1, C_2, C_3, C_4) = (1, 1, 4, 13, 43)$, and the companion bronze numbers $D_n$
of the second type satisfy $(D_0, D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4) = (1, 2, 7, 23, 76)$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4.

articles.title: P-positions of the bronze game
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha = (3 + \sqrt{13})/2$ and
$\beta = (5 + \sqrt{13})/6$, let $B_n$ be the bronze numbers, and let $C_n$ and $D_n$ be the
companion bronze numbers of the first and second type. Let $P$ be the set of natural numbers
$x$ such that $x = 0$ or $x \in \{B_{2k+1}, C_{2k+2}, D_{2k+2}\}$ for some natural number $k$.
Then, in the Beatty octal game for $\alpha$ and $\beta$, no move takes a heap whose size lies
in $P$ to a heap whose size lies in $P$, and from every heap whose size is not in $P$ some move
leads to a heap whose size lies in $P$.

So $P$ is stable and absorbing for the moves of the game; since every move decreases the heap,
this determines $P$ as the set of P-positions, the heap sizes from which the previous player
wins: $0, B_1, C_2, D_2, B_3, C_4, D_4, \ldots$

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 11.

articles.title: Bronze Lucas parameters
articles.statement:
The bronze Lucas parameters are the Lucas sequence parameters
$(P, Q) = (3, -1)$. The Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$ is the sequence of bronze numbers $B_n$, with
$B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$ and $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4 (bronze numbers).

articles.title: Metallic identities for the bronze numbers
Numeration by bronze and companion bronze numbers
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ be the bronze numbers
($B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$, $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$, the Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$), and let
$C_n = B_{n+1} - 2B_n$ and $D_n = B_{n+1} - B_n$ be the companion bronze numbers of the first and
second type. Let $R$ be the integer sequence with $R_{3m+1} = B_{2m+1}$, $R_{3m+2} = C_{2m+2}$
and $R_{3m} = D_{2m}$ for all $m \ge 0$. Then for every positive integer $t$ there are a natural
number $n \ge 1$ and natural numbers $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that $R_n \le t < R_{n+1}$,
$t = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k R_k$, $a_k = 0$ for every $k > n$, and: (3) $a_1 \le 3$, and
$a_2 = a_3 = 0$ if $a_1 = 3$; (4) for every $k > 1$, $a_k \le 4$ if $k \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ and
$a_k \le 1$ otherwise; (5) for every $k$ with $a_k = 4$, $a_{k-1} = a_{k+1} = 0$, $a_{k-3} < 4$
and $a_{k+3} < 4$, where an index below $0$ is read as $0$.

The paper's conditions (6) and (7) are omitted: no representation of $50$ satisfies (6)
together with (2)–(5), and the greedy representation $410 = 3B_5 + D_4 + D_2$
($327 + 76 + 7$; digits $a_7 = 3$, $a_6 = 1$, $a_3 = 1$) violates (7).

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 9 (1)–(5).

articles.title: Mixed bronze numeration
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ be the bronze numbers ($B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$,
$B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$, the Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$), and let $C_n = B_{n+1} - 2B_n$ and
$D_n = B_{n+1} - B_n$ be the companion bronze numbers of the first and second type. Let $R$ be
the integer sequence with $R_{3m} = D_{2m}$, $R_{3m+1} = 3B_{2m+1}$ and
$R_{3m+2} = B_{2m+1} + C_{2m+2}$ for all $m \ge 0$. Then for every positive integer $t$ there are
a natural number $n$ and natural numbers $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that $R_n \le t < R_{n+1}$,
$t = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k R_k$, $a_k = 0$ for every $k > n$, and: (3) $a_0 \le 2$, and
$a_0 \le 1$ if $a_1 = 1$ or $a_2 = 1$; (4) for every $k > 0$, $a_k \le 4$ if $3 \mid k$ and
$a_k \le 1$ otherwise; (5) for every $k$ with $a_k = 4$, $a_{k-1} = a_{k+1} = 0$,
$a_{k-3} < 4$ and $a_{k+3} < 4$; (6) for every $m \ge 0$, if $a_{3m+1} = 1$ then
$a_{3m+2} = 0$, and if $a_{3m+2} = 1$ then $a_{3m+1} = 0$; (7) for every $m \ge 1$ with
$a_{3m} = 3$, if $a_{3m+1} = 1$ or $a_{3m+2} = 1$ then $a_{3m-1} = a_{3m-2} = 0$, and if
$a_{3m-1} = 1$ or $a_{3m-2} = 1$ then $a_{3m+1} = a_{3m+2} = 0$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Numeration by odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers
($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$). For every positive integer $t$ there are a
natural number $n$ and natural numbers $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that
$F_{2n+1} \le t < F_{2n+3}$, $t = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k F_{2k+1}$, $a_0 \le 1$, $a_k \le 2$ for
every $k \ge 1$, $a_1 = 2$ and $a_0 = 1$ do not both hold, and for no $k$ do $a_{k+1} = 2$ and
$a_k = 2$ both hold.

Here $a_k$ is the coefficient the paper calls $a_{2k+1}$; the last two conditions exclude the
digit patterns $2F_3 + F_1$ and $2F_{2k+3} + 2F_{2k+1}$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Numeration by Pell and half-companion Pell numbers
articles.statement:
Let $P_n$ be the Pell numbers
($P_0 = 0$, $P_1 = 1$, $P_{n+2} = 2P_{n+1} + P_n$) and $H_n$ the half-companion Pell numbers
($H_0 = H_1 = 1$, $H_{n+2} = 2H_{n+1} + H_n$), and let $R_k = P_k$ for odd $k$ and
$R_k = H_k$ for even $k$. Then for every positive integer $t$ there are a natural number $n \ge 1$
and natural numbers $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that $R_n \le t < R_{n+1}$,
$t = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k R_k$, $a_1 \le 2$, $a_2 = 0$ if $a_1 = 2$, $a_{2k+1} \le 3$ and
$a_{2k} \le 1$ for every $k \ge 0$, and for every $k \ge 1$ with $a_{2k+1} = 3$ we have
$a_{2k} = a_{2k+2} = 0$, $a_{2k-1} < 3$ and $a_{2k+3} < 3$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Numeration by doubled Pell and half-companion Pell numbers
articles.statement:
Let $P_n$ be the Pell numbers
($P_0 = 0$, $P_1 = 1$, $P_{n+2} = 2P_{n+1} + P_n$) and $H_n$ the half-companion Pell numbers
($H_0 = H_1 = 1$, $H_{n+2} = 2H_{n+1} + H_n$), and let $R_k = 2P_k$ for odd $k$ and
$R_k = H_k$ for even $k$. Then for every positive integer $t$ there are a natural number $n$ and
natural numbers $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that $R_n \le t < R_{n+1}$,
$t = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k R_k$, $a_0 \le 1$, $a_0 = 0$ if $a_1 = 1$, $a_{2k} \le 3$ and
$a_{2k+1} \le 1$ for every $k \ge 0$, $a_{2k+2} < 3$ whenever $a_{2k} = 3$ ($k \ge 0$), and
$a_{2k-1} = a_{2k+1} = 0$ and $a_{2k-2} < 3$ whenever $a_{2k} = 3$ with $k \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers times the golden ratio
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers
($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$) and $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2$ the golden
ratio. For every natural number $k$,
$F_{2k+1} \varphi = F_{2k+2} + \left((\sqrt 5 - 1)/2\right)^{2k+1}$ and
$F_{2k+1} (1 + \varphi) = F_{2k+3} + \left((\sqrt 5 - 1)/2\right)^{2k+1}$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Floor of greedy bronze sums times $(3 + \sqrt{13})/2$
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ be the bronze numbers
($B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$, $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$, the Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$), and let
$C_n = B_{n+1} - 2B_n$ and $D_n = B_{n+1} - B_n$ be the companion bronze numbers of the first and
second type. Let $R$ and $R'$ be the integer sequences with $R_{3m+1} = B_{2m+1}$,
$R_{3m+2} = C_{2m+2}$, $R_{3m} = D_{2m}$ and $R'_{3m+1} = D_{2m+1}$, $R'_{3m+2} = B_{2m+2}$,
$R'_{3m} = C_{2m+1}$ for all $m \ge 0$. Let $n$ be a natural number and $a_1, a_2, \dots$ natural
numbers such that $\sum_{k=1}^{m-1} a_k R_k < R_m$ for every $1 \le m \le n + 1$, and let
$t = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k R_k$. Then
$\lfloor t (3 + \sqrt{13})/2 \rfloor = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k R'_{k+1}$.

The hypothesis says that the $a_k$ are the digits of the greedy representation of Theorem 9;
$n$ need not be minimal.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 10 (1).

articles.title: Floor of greedy mixed bronze sums times $(5 + \sqrt{13})/6$
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ be the bronze
numbers ($B_0 = 0$, $B_1 = 1$, $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$, the Lucas sequence $U(3, -1)$), and let
$C_n = B_{n+1} - 2B_n$ and $D_n = B_{n+1} - B_n$ be the companion bronze numbers of the first and
second type. Let $R$ and $R'$ be the integer sequences with $R_{3m} = D_{2m}$,
$R_{3m+1} = 3B_{2m+1}$, $R_{3m+2} = B_{2m+1} + C_{2m+2}$ and $R'_{3m} = D_{2m}$,
$R'_{3m+1} = B_{2m+1}$, $R'_{3m+2} = C_{2m+2}$ for all $m \ge 0$. Let $n$ be a natural number
and $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ natural numbers such that $\sum_{k=0}^{m-1} a_k R_k < R_m$ for every
$m \le n + 1$, and let $t = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k R_k$. Then
$\lfloor t (5 + \sqrt{13})/6 \rfloor = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k R'_{k+1}$.

The hypothesis says that the $a_k$ are the digits of the greedy representation of Theorem 8;
$n$ need not be minimal.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 10 (2).

articles.title: Floor of greedy odd-Fibonacci sums times $\varphi$ and $1 + \varphi$
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the
Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$) and
$\varphi = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2$ the golden ratio. Let $n$ be a natural number and $a_0, a_1, \dots$
natural numbers such that $\sum_{k=0}^{m-1} a_k F_{2k+1} < F_{2m+1}$ for every $m \le n + 1$, and
let $t = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k F_{2k+1}$. Then
$\lfloor t \varphi \rfloor = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k F_{2k+2}$ and
$\lfloor t (1 + \varphi) \rfloor = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k F_{2k+3}$.

The hypothesis says that the $a_k$ are the digits of the greedy representation of Theorem 1
(here $a_k$ is the paper's $a_{2k+1}$); $n$ need not be minimal and $t = 0$ is allowed.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Floor of greedy Pell sums times $1 + \sqrt 2$
articles.statement:
Let $P_n$ be the Pell numbers ($P_0 = 0$,
$P_1 = 1$, $P_{n+2} = 2P_{n+1} + P_n$) and $H_n$ the half-companion Pell numbers
($H_0 = H_1 = 1$, $H_{n+2} = 2H_{n+1} + H_n$). Let $R_k = P_k$ and $R'_k = H_k$ for odd $k$, and
$R_k = H_k$ and $R'_k = P_k$ for even $k$. Let $n$ be a natural number and $a_1, a_2, \dots$
natural numbers such that $\sum_{k=1}^{m-1} a_k R_k < R_m$ for every $1 \le m \le n + 1$, and let
$t = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k R_k$. Then $\lfloor t (1 + \sqrt 2) \rfloor = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k R'_{k+1}$.

The hypothesis says that the $a_k$ are the digits of the greedy representation of Theorem 5;
$n$ need not be minimal.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 6 (1).

articles.title: Floor of greedy sums of $2P_k$ and $H_k$ times $(2 + \sqrt 2)/2$
articles.statement:
Let $P_k$ be the Pell
numbers and $H_k$ the Pell–Lucas numbers ($H_0 = H_1 = 1$, $H_{k+2} = 2H_{k+1} + H_k$). Put
$R_k = 2P_k$ and $R'_k = P_k$ for odd $k$, and $R_k = R'_k = H_k$ for even $k$. Let $n$ be a
natural number and $a_0, a_1, \dots$ natural numbers such that $\sum_{k\lt m} a_k R_k < R_m$ for
every $m \le n + 1$, and let $t = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k R_k$. Then
$\lfloor t(2 + \sqrt 2)/2 \rfloor = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k R'_{k+1}$.

The hypothesis says that the $a_k$ are the digits of the greedy representation of $t$ by the
$R_k$; $n$ need not be minimal.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 6 (2).

articles.title: P-positions of the gold game
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and $F_n$ the Fibonacci
numbers ($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). In the gold game a heap of $n$ tokens may be removed entirely when
$n = \lfloor k\varphi \rfloor$ for some integer $k \ge 1$, and $i$ tokens may be removed from a
heap of $n > i$ tokens, leaving $n - i$, when $i = \lfloor k(1 + \varphi) \rfloor$ for some
integer $k \ge 1$ (the Beatty octal moves for $\varphi$ and $1 + \varphi$). Let $S$ be the set of
natural numbers consisting of $0$ and the $F_{2k+1}$ for $k \ge 1$, that is $0, 2, 5, 13, 34, \dots$
Then $S$ is stable: no move leads from a heap size in $S$ to a heap size in $S$. And $S$ is
absorbing: from every heap size outside $S$ some move leads to a heap size in $S$.

Since every move shrinks the heap, a stable and absorbing set is the set of P-positions, so the
P-positions of the gold game are exactly the heap sizes in $S$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Recurrence of the bronze numbers
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ be the bronze numbers, the terms of the Lucas
sequence $U(3, -1)$. For every natural number $n$, $B_{n+2} = 3B_{n+1} + B_n$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4 (bronze numbers).

articles.title: The first bronze numbers
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ be the bronze numbers, the terms of the Lucas sequence
$U(3, -1)$. Then $B_0, B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5$ are $0, 1, 3, 10, 33, 109$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Section 4 (bronze numbers).

articles.title: Odd Pell and even Pell–Lucas numbers times $1 + \sqrt 2$
articles.statement:
Let $P_n$ be the Pell numbers and
$H_n$ the Pell–Lucas numbers ($H_0 = H_1 = 1$, $H_{n+2} = 2H_{n+1} + H_n$). For every natural
number $k$, $P_{2k+1}(1 + \sqrt 2) = P_{2k+2} + (\sqrt 2 - 1)^{2k+1}$ and
$H_{2k}(1 + \sqrt 2) = H_{2k+1} + \sqrt 2\,(\sqrt 2 - 1)^{2k}$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Proposition 2 (1), (2).

articles.title: P-positions of the silver game
articles.statement:
Let $P_n$ be the Pell numbers and $H_n$ the Pell–Lucas
numbers ($H_0 = H_1 = 1$, $H_{n+2} = 2H_{n+1} + H_n$). In the silver game a heap of $n$ tokens
may be removed entirely when $n = \lfloor k(1 + \sqrt 2) \rfloor$ for some integer $k \ge 1$, and
$i$ tokens may be removed from a heap of $n > i$ tokens, leaving $n - i$, when
$i = \lfloor k(2 + \sqrt 2)/2 \rfloor$ for some integer $k \ge 1$ (the Beatty octal moves for
$1 + \sqrt 2$ and $(2 + \sqrt 2)/2$). Let $S$ be the set of natural numbers consisting of $0$ and
the $P_{2k+1}$ and $H_{2k+2}$ for $k \ge 0$, that is $0, 1, 3, 5, 17, 29, 99, \dots$ Then $S$ is
stable: no move leads from a heap size in $S$ to a heap size in $S$. And $S$ is absorbing: from
every heap size outside $S$ some move leads to a heap size in $S$.

Since every move shrinks the heap, a stable and absorbing set is the set of P-positions, so the
P-positions of the silver game are exactly the heap sizes in $S$.

## Sources

- Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen, and Craig Tennenhouse, *Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article G3, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Block averages of Shakov's sequence
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be Shakov's $2$-regular sequence.
For every natural number $n$,

$$
\frac{1}{2^n} \sum_{2^n \le t < 2^{n+1}} s(t) =
\frac{(5 + \sqrt{17})^n - (5 - \sqrt{17})^n}{2^{2n-1} \sqrt{17}},
$$

where the exponent $2n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$ (both sides are then $0$).

## Sources

- Anton Shakov, "A 2-Regular Sequence That Counts The Divisors of `n^2 + 1`", Proposition 7.

articles.title: Fibonacci squares plus one are eventually composite
articles.statement:
Let $F_k$ denote the $k$-th
Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. For every natural number $k \ge 4$, the number
$F_k^2 + 1$ is composite.

In the source's numbering of the Fibonacci numbers, which is shifted by one, this reads
"$F_n^2 + 1$ is composite for $n > 4$".

## Sources

- Anton Shakov, "A 2-Regular Sequence That Counts The Divisors of `n^2 + 1`", Corollary 10.

articles.title: Shakov's sequence counts the divisors of $m^2 + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be Shakov's $2$-regular
sequence and let $\tau(N)$ denote the number of positive divisors of $N$. Then $s(n) \ge 0$ for
every $n \ge 1$, and for every natural number $m$ the set $\{n \ge 1 : s(n) = m\}$ is finite
and has exactly $\tau(m^2 + 1)$ elements.

This is the coefficientwise form of the identity
$\sum_{m \ge 0} \tau(m^2 + 1) x^m = \sum_{n \ge 1} x^{s(n)}$ of formal power series.

## Sources

- Anton Shakov, "A 2-Regular Sequence That Counts The Divisors of `n^2 + 1`", Theorem 4.

articles.title: Primality of $n^2 + 1$ from the fibers of Shakov's sequence
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be Shakov's
$2$-regular sequence. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the number $n^2 + 1$ is prime if and
only if the set of natural numbers $m$ with $s(m) = n$ is exactly $\{2^n, 2^{n+1} - 1\}$.

## Sources

- Anton Shakov, "A 2-Regular Sequence That Counts The Divisors of `n^2 + 1`", Proposition 8.

articles.title: Shakov's auxiliary sequence
articles.statement:
The integer sequence $a$ with $a(0) = 0$, $a(1) = 1$ and,
for every $n \ge 2$, $a(n) = 2a(n-1)$ if $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, $a(n) = a(n-1) + 1$ if
$n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $a(n) = 2a(n-1) + 1$ if $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and $a(n) = a(n-1) - 1$ if
$n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

The value $a(0)$ plays no role in the recursion; the source's sequence starts at $n = 1$.

articles.title: Shakov's sequence takes Fibonacci values along the auxiliary sequence
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be
Shakov's $2$-regular sequence, let $a$ be Shakov's auxiliary sequence, and let $F_k$ denote the
$k$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$s(\max(a(n), 0)) = F_{n-1}$.

The source shows that $a(n)$ is a positive integer and numbers the Fibonacci numbers so that
this reads $s(a(n)) = F_n$.

## Sources

- Anton Shakov, "A 2-Regular Sequence That Counts The Divisors of `n^2 + 1`", Proposition 9.

articles.title: Shakov's $2$-regular sequence
articles.statement:
The integer sequence $s$ with $s(0) = s(1) = 0$,
$s(2) = s(3) = 1$ and, for every $k \ge 1$, $s(4k) = 2s(2k) - s(k)$,
$s(4k+1) = 2s(2k) + s(2k+1)$, $s(4k+2) = 2s(2k+1) + s(2k)$ and $s(4k+3) = 2s(2k+1) - s(k)$.

The value $s(0)$ plays no role in the recursion; the source's sequence starts at $n = 1$.

articles.title: Extending a signed power-of-two sum to a longer range
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$, $s$, $t$ and $\alpha$
be natural numbers, let $\beta = \nu_2(m + 1)$ be the exponent of $2$ in $m + 1$, and suppose that
$s + \beta \le t + 1$ and $2^\alpha \equiv 1 \pmod{(m + 1)/2^\beta}$. If an integer $n$ can be
written as $\sum_{j=s}^{t} \lambda_j 2^j$ with every $\lambda_j \in \{-1, m\}$, then $n$ can also be
written as $\sum_{j=s}^{t+\alpha} \mu_j 2^j$ with every $\mu_j \in \{-1, m\}$.

The source's hypothesis $t \ge s + \beta - 1$ is written as $s + \beta \le t + 1$ to cover the
case $\beta = 0$.

## Sources

- Ross, *A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results*, JIS 27 (2024), Article 24.7.5, Corollary 8 (`jis-2024-24.7.5-cor-8`): fix `m ≥ 1` and let `β = ν₂(m + 1)`. If `n` is a signed power-of-two sum over `[s, t]` with `t ≥ s + β - 1`, then `n` is also expressible over `[s, t + α]` whenever `2^α ≡ 1 [(m + 1) / 2^β]`.

articles.title: Interval and congruence characterization of signed power-of-two sums
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and
$s \le t$ be natural numbers and put $L = t - s + 1$. An integer $n$ can be written as
$\sum_{j=s}^{t} \lambda_j 2^j$ with every $\lambda_j \in \{-1, m\}$ if and only if
$-2^s (2^L - 1) \le n \le 2^s m (2^L - 1)$ and $n \equiv -2^s (2^L - 1) \pmod{2^s (m + 1)}$.

## Sources

- Ross, *A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results*, JIS 27 (2024), Article 24.7.5, Lemma 7 (`jis-2024-24.7.5-lem-7`): for `0 ≤ s ≤ t` and `m ≥ 1`, the integers of the form `∑_{j=s}^{t} λⱼ * 2^j` with `λⱼ ∈ {-1, m}` are precisely the integers `n` in the interval `[-2^s * (2^{t-s+1} - 1), 2^s * m * (2^{t-s+1} - 1)]` satisfying `n ≡ -2^s * (2^{t-s+1} - 1) [ZMOD 2^s * (m + 1)]`.

articles.title: Example of a signed power-of-two sum
articles.statement:
The integer $1$ can be written as
$\sum_{j=0}^{1} \lambda_j 2^j$ with every $\lambda_j \in \{-1, 3\}$, namely
$1 = 3 \cdot 2^0 + (-1) \cdot 2^1$.

## Sources

- Ross, *A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results*, JIS 27 (2024), Article 24.7.5, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Signed power-of-two sums
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$, $s$ and $t$, an integer $n$ is a signed
power-of-two sum with coefficients in $\{-1, m\}$ over the range $s \le j \le t$ if
$n = \sum_{j=s}^{t} \lambda_j 2^j$ for some integers $\lambda_j$ with every
$\lambda_j \in \{-1, m\}$.

## Sources

- Ross, *A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results*, JIS 27 (2024), Article 24.7.5, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Integers that are one plus a signed sum of powers of two
articles.statement:
An integer $n$ can be written as
$n = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_j 2^j$ for some $k \ge 1$ and some
$\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k \in \{-1, 1\}$ if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Ross, *A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results*, JIS 27 (2024), Article 24.7.5, Lemma 12 (`jis-2024-24.7.5-lem-12`): an integer `n` can be written as `1 + ∑_{j=1}^{k} λⱼ * 2^j` for some `k ≥ 1` and coefficients `λⱼ ∈ {-1, 1}` if and only if `n ≡ 3 [ZMOD 4]`.

articles.title: Bradley's inequality between the $\alpha$- and $\varphi$-mixing coefficients
articles.statement:
Let
$(X_j)_{j \ge 1}$ be random variables on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathbb{P})$ with values in
a measurable space, and let $k \ge 1$. Suppose a real number $c$ bounds every term defining the
$\varphi$-mixing coefficient $\varphi(k)$: for every $p \ge 1$, every event
$A \in \sigma(X_j : 1 \le j \le p)$ with $\mathbb{P}(A) > 0$ and every event
$B \in \sigma(X_j : j \ge k + p)$, $|\mathbb{P}(B \mid A) - \mathbb{P}(B)| \le c$. Then $c/2$
bounds every term defining the $\alpha$-mixing coefficient $\alpha(k)$: for every $p \ge 1$,
every event $A \in \sigma(X_j : 1 \le j \le p)$ and every event $B \in \sigma(X_j : j \ge k + p)$,
$|\mathbb{P}(A \cap B) - \mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)| \le c/2$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 18 (Bradley) (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-18`).

articles.title: Zeckendorf digit sequence of zero
articles.statement:
The Zeckendorf digit sequence of $0$ is the zero
sequence: all of its digits are $0$, because the Zeckendorf representation of $0$ is empty.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 2.2 (characteristic lemma for the map `i`).

articles.title: Zeckendorf digit sequence of a natural number
articles.statement:
Let $F_k$ be the Fibonacci numbers
($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = F_2 = 1$). Every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ has a unique Zeckendorf representation
$n = F_{k_1} + \dots + F_{k_m}$ with $k_1 > \dots > k_m \ge 2$ and no two consecutive indices.
The Zeckendorf digit sequence of $n$ is the binary sequence $(x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ with
$x_k = 1$ if $k$ is one of the indices $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and $x_k = 0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 2.2 (the map `i`).

articles.title: Prefix value of order one
articles.statement:
For every binary sequence $x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, the
prefix value of order $1$ is $v_1(x) = x_2 F_2$, where $F_2 = 1$ is the second Fibonacci number.
It equals $x_2$: it is $1$ if $x_2 = 1$ and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 3.1 (characteristic lemma: towers of order `1`).

articles.title: Prefix value of a digit sequence
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a binary sequence
$x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, the prefix value of order $k$ is the natural number
$v_k(x) = \sum_{i=2}^{k+1} x_i F_i$, where $F_i$ is the $i$-th Fibonacci number
($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). It is the value of the block $x_{k+1} \cdots x_2$ of the $k$ rightmost digits
of $x$, the name of the cylinder of order $k$ that contains $x$.

In the paper the levels of the two Rokhlin towers of order $k$ are level sets of $v_k$: the
large tower has levels $\{v_k = j - 1\}$ for $1 \le j \le F_{k+1}$, and the small tower has
levels $\{v_k = F_{k+1} + j - 1\}$ for $1 \le j \le F_k$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 3.1 (cylinders of order `k` and the two towers).

articles.title: The truncated variation vanishes for zero steps
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer and,
for a binary sequence $x$, let $s_k(x) = x_2 + \dots + x_k$ and
$\Delta_k^{(r)}(x) = s_k(T^r(x)) - s_k(x)$. Then $\Delta_k^{(0)}(x) = 0$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every binary sequence $x$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 4 (characteristic lemma for `Δ_k^{(r)}`).

articles.title: Truncated variation of the Zeckendorf digit sum
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer
$x \mapsto x + 1$ on binary sequences, and write $x + r = T^r(x)$ for its $r$-th iterate. For
$r, k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a binary sequence $x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, let
$s_k(x) = x_2 + \dots + x_k$. The truncated variation is the integer
$\Delta_k^{(r)}(x) = s_k(x + r) - s_k(x)$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 4 (definition of `s_k` and `Δ_k^{(r)}`).

articles.title: Counting values of the variation against the invariant measure
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be the
set of Zeckendorf-adic integers, $T$ the Zeckendorf odometer, and $\mathbb{P}$ a $T$-invariant
probability measure on binary sequences with $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$. Let $s(n)$ be the
number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\iota(n)$ be the
Zeckendorf digit sequence of $n$, let $\Delta^{(r)}$ and $\Delta_k^{(r)}$ be the variation and the
truncated variation on binary sequences, and let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio. Then for all
integers $r \ge 1$, $N \ge 1$, $k \ge 2$ and $d, d' \in \mathbb{Z}$,

$$\frac{1}{N}\,\#\{n < N : s(n + r) - s(n) = d,\ \Delta_k^{(r)}(\iota(n)) = d'\}
\le r\varphi^3\,\mathbb{P}(\Delta^{(r)} = d,\ \Delta_k^{(r)} = d')$$

and

$$\frac{1}{N}\,\#\{n < N : s(n + r) - s(n) = d\} \le r\varphi^3\,\mathbb{P}(\Delta^{(r)} = d).$$

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 26 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-26`).

articles.title: The variation is the eventual value of the truncated variations
articles.statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $x$ be a binary sequence and let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$. If the truncated variation
$\Delta_k^{(r)}(x)$ equals $d$ for all sufficiently large $k$, then the variation
$\Delta^{(r)}(x)$ equals $d$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 4 (characteristic lemma for `Δ^{(r)}`).

articles.title: Ergodic averages of the variation for functions of polynomial growth
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be
the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers, $T$ the Zeckendorf odometer, and $\mathbb{P}$ a
$T$-invariant probability measure on binary sequences with $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$. Let
$s(n)$ be the number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$r \ge 1$, and let $\Delta^{(r)}$ and $\Delta_k^{(r)}$ be the variation and the truncated
variation on binary sequences. Let $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ and let $\alpha \ge 1$ and
$C > 0$ be reals with $|f(n)| \le C|n|^\alpha + |f(0)|$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then
$f \circ \Delta^{(r)}$ is $\mathbb{P}$-integrable,

$$\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f\bigl(s(n + r) - s(n)\bigr)
\to \int f \circ \Delta^{(r)}\,d\mathbb{P}$$

as $N \to \infty$, and
$\int f \circ \Delta_k^{(r)}\,d\mathbb{P} \to \int f \circ \Delta^{(r)}\,d\mathbb{P}$
as $k \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 23 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-23`).

articles.title: Ergodic theorem for the Zeckendorf digit-sum variation
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability
measure on the digit sequences $x : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ that gives the complement of the
Zeckendorf-adic integers $\mathbb{X}$ measure zero and is preserved by the odometer $T$. Let
$r \ge 1$ and let $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ be such that $f \circ \Delta^{(r)}$ is
$\mu$-integrable, where $\Delta^{(r)}$ is the variation on $\mathbb{X}$. Write $s(n)$ for the
number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n$. Then

$$\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f\bigl(s(n + r) - s(n)\bigr) \to \int f(\Delta^{(r)}(x))\, d\mu(x)$$

as $N \to \infty$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 28 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-28`).

articles.title: When the variation $\Delta^{(1)}$ exists
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a Zeckendorf-adic integer with digits
$x_k$, and let $\Delta_k^{(1)}(x)$ be its truncated variation of order $k$ for $r = 1$. The
integer sequence $(\Delta_k^{(1)}(x))_k$ is eventually constant (equivalently, the variation
$\Delta^{(1)}(x) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \Delta_k^{(1)}(x)$ exists) if and only if there is
$d \ge 0$ such that either $x_{2d+3} = x_{2d+2} = 0$ and $x_{2i+1} = 1$, $x_{2i} = 0$ for
$1 \le i \le d$ (the cylinder $C_{00(10)^d}$), or $x_{2d+4} = x_{2d+3} = 0$, $x_{2d+2} = 1$ and
$x_{2i+1} = 0$, $x_{2i} = 1$ for $1 \le i \le d$ (the cylinder $C_{001(01)^d}$).

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 27 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-27`), first part.

articles.title: The variation $\Delta^{(1)}$ on the cylinder $C_{001(01)^d}$
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 0$ and let $x$ be a
Zeckendorf-adic integer in the cylinder $C_{001(01)^d}$, that is, one whose digits satisfy
$x_{2d+4} = x_{2d+3} = 0$, $x_{2d+2} = 1$ and $x_{2i+1} = 0$, $x_{2i} = 1$ for $1 \le i \le d$.
Write $\Delta_k^{(1)}(x)$ for the truncated variation of order $k$ and $\Delta^{(1)}(x)$ for the
variation, both for $r = 1$. Then $\Delta^{(1)}(x) = -d$, and for every $k \ge 2$:
$\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = -k/2$ if $k$ is even and $k \le 2d + 2$; $\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = (1 - k)/2$ if
$k$ is odd and $k \le 2d + 1$; $\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = (3 - k)/2$ if $k = 2d + 3$; and
$\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = -d$ if $k \ge 2d + 4$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 27 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-27`), second cylinder.

articles.title: The variation $\Delta^{(1)}$ on the cylinder $C_{00(10)^d}$
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 0$ and let $x$ be a
Zeckendorf-adic integer in the cylinder $C_{00(10)^d}$, that is, one whose digits satisfy
$x_{2d+3} = x_{2d+2} = 0$ and $x_{2i+1} = 1$, $x_{2i} = 0$ for $1 \le i \le d$. Write
$\Delta_k^{(1)}(x)$ for the truncated variation of order $k$ and $\Delta^{(1)}(x)$ for the
variation, both for $r = 1$. Then $\Delta^{(1)}(x) = 1 - d$, and for every $k \ge 2$:
$\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = (2 - k)/2$ if $k$ is even and $k \le 2d$; $\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = (1 - k)/2$ if
$k$ is odd and $k \le 2d + 1$; and $\Delta_k^{(1)}(x) = 1 - d$ if $k \ge 2d + 2$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 27 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-27`), first cylinder.

articles.title: The variation for $r = 0$ vanishes
articles.statement:
For every digit sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$,
not only for Zeckendorf-adic integers, the variation satisfies $\Delta^{(0)}(x) = 0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 4 (characteristic lemma for `Δ^{(r)}`).

articles.title: The variation of the Zeckendorf digit sum
articles.statement:
For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and a digit sequence
$x : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$, let $\Delta_k^{(r)}(x)$ be the truncated variation of order $k$. If
the integer sequence $(\Delta_k^{(r)}(x))_k$ is eventually constant, the variation
$\Delta^{(r)}(x) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \Delta_k^{(r)}(x)$ is its eventual value; otherwise
$\Delta^{(r)}(x) = 0$.

The value $0$ is a junk value. The paper shows that the Zeckendorf-adic integers at which the
limit does not exist form a finite set.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 4 (definition of `Δ^{(r)}` on `𝕏`).

articles.title: The Zeckendorf-adic integers
articles.statement:
The Zeckendorf-adic integers $\mathbb{X}$ are the digit
sequences $x = (x_k)_{k \ge 0}$ with $x_k \in \{0, 1\}$ such that $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two
consecutive digits are both $1$, that is, $x_k x_{k+1} = 0$ for every $k$.

Digit $k \ge 2$ carries the weight $F_k$ (with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$). The unused digits $x_0$ and
$x_1$ keep the paper's indexing, in which
$\mathbb{X} = \{x \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}} : x_k x_{k+1} = 0 \text{ for all } k \ge 2\}$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 2.2 (arXiv:2309.14285v2).

articles.title: An $\alpha$-mixing bound for the block variations
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
the digit sequences $x : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ that gives the complement of the
Zeckendorf-adic integers measure zero and is preserved by the odometer $T$. Let $r \ge 1$, let
$\rho(r)$ be the number of blocks of $r$ and $r[i]$ its block prefixes, and for
$1 \le i \le \rho(r)$ let $X_i(x) = \Delta^{(r[i] - r[i-1])}(T^{r[i-1]}(x))$, where $\Delta^{(m)}$
is the variation and $T^{m}$ the $m$-fold iterate of $T$. Let $k, p \ge 1$, let $A$ be
measurable for the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the $X_i$ with $1 \le i \le \min(p, \rho(r))$,
and let $B$ be measurable for the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the $X_i$ with
$k + p \le i \le \rho(r)$ (the trivial $\sigma$-algebra when there is no such $i$). Then, with
$\varphi$ the golden ratio,

$$|\mu(A \cap B) - \mu(A)\mu(B)| \le 12 (1 - 1/\varphi^8)^{k/6} + 1/\varphi^{2k}.$$

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Theorem 6 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-thm-6`) and its restatement in Section 7 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-thm-unnumbered-2`).

articles.title: The empty block prefix is zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, the block prefix $r[0]$,
formed by the first $0$ blocks of the Zeckendorf representation of $r$, equals $0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 7.1 (convention `r[0] := 0`).

articles.title: Block prefixes of a natural number
articles.statement:
The blocks of $r \in \mathbb{N}$ are the maximal runs
of Zeckendorf indices of $r$ in which consecutive indices differ by exactly $2$, listed from the
unit digit. For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the block prefix $r[i]$ is the sum of the Fibonacci numbers
$F_j$ over the indices $j$ in the first $i$ blocks of $r$, or in all blocks when $i$ exceeds the
number $\rho(r)$ of blocks. Thus $r[0] = 0$ and $r[i] = r$ for $i \ge \rho(r)$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 7.1 (definition of `r[i]`).

articles.title: Zero has no blocks
articles.statement:
The list of blocks of $0$ is empty; that is, the number $\rho(0)$ of
blocks of $0$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Definition 2 (characteristic lemma: `ρ(0) = 0`).

articles.title: Blocks of a Zeckendorf representation
articles.statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ have Zeckendorf
representation $r = F_{i_1} + \dots + F_{i_s}$ with $i_1 > \dots > i_s \ge 2$ (Fibonacci numbers
with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$). The blocks of $r$ are the maximal runs of successive terms of the list
$i_1, \dots, i_s$ in which each index is exactly $2$ less than the one before it (the maximal
factors $(10)^m$ of the expansion, a final $1$ at the unit position counting as $10$). The blocks
are listed from the unit digit, so the first block contains $i_s$ and the last contains $i_1$, and
each block lists its indices in decreasing order. The number of blocks of $r$ is $\rho(r)$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Definition 2 (blocks) and Section 7.1.

articles.title: $\mathrm{CST}_1$ is empty for every positive shift
articles.statement:
For every $r \ge 1$, the set
$\mathrm{CST}_1$ for the shift $r$ is empty.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 5.1 ("We observe `CST_1 = ∅`").

articles.title: The sets $\mathrm{CST}_k$
articles.statement:
Fix $r, k \in \mathbb{N}$. For a digit sequence
$x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\{0, 1\}$ let $v_k(x) = \sum_{i=2}^{k+1} x_i F_i$, where $F_i$
is the $i$-th Fibonacci number ($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). The set $\mathrm{CST}_k$ (for the shift $r$)
consists of the digit sequences $x$ such that either $v_k(x) + r < F_{k+1}$, or both
$F_{k+1} \le v_k(x)$ and $v_k(x) + r < F_{k+2}$.

In terms of the Rokhlin towers of order $k$, this is the union of the levels of the large and the
small tower except the $r$ highest levels of each tower.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 5.1 (definition of `CST_k`).

articles.title: The Zeckendorf Markov chain has the invariant law
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be the set of
Zeckendorf-adic integers: the digit sequences $x \in \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$
and no two consecutive digits equal to $1$. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
$\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with $\mu(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$ that is preserved by the odometer $T$. Let
$(\Omega, \nu)$ be a probability space and let $(U_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be independent measurable real
random variables on $\Omega$, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$. Then the law under $\nu$ of
the digit sequence $\omega \mapsto (y_j(\omega))_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ of the Zeckendorf Markov chain
driven by $(U_n(\omega))_{n \ge 0}$ is $\mu$.

The paper indexes the uniform variables from $2$, writing $U_{n+2}$ for the $U_n$ here; the
measure $\mu$ is the paper's $\mathbb{P}$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 20 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-20`).

articles.title: After a one, the Zeckendorf Markov chain emits a zero
articles.statement:
For every real sequence
$(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and every $j \ge 1$, if the digit $y_j$ of the chain driven by $(u_n)$ is $1$,
then $y_{j+1} = 0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 3.3 (characteristic lemma: `ψ(1, t) = 0`).

articles.title: The first step of the Zeckendorf Markov chain
articles.statement:
For every real sequence $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$,
the digit $y_2$ of the chain driven by $(u_n)$ is $1$ exactly when $u_0 < 1/\varphi^2$, where
$\varphi$ is the golden ratio. In the paper's notation, where $u_n = U_{n+2}$, this says that
$y_2 = 1$ if and only if $U_2 < 1/\varphi^2$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 3.3 (characteristic lemma for `(y_j)`).

articles.title: The Zeckendorf Markov chain
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio, and let $\psi(0, t) = 1$
if $t < 1/\varphi^2$, $\psi(0, t) = 0$ otherwise, and $\psi(1, t) = 0$. For a real sequence
$(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$, written $u_n = U_{n+2}$, the chain $(y_j)_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ is the sequence in
$\{0, 1\}$ with $y_0 = y_1 = 0$ and $y_j = \psi(y_{j-1}, U_j)$ for $j \ge 2$; that is,
$y_{n+2} = 1$ exactly when $y_{n+1} = 0$ and $u_n < 1/\varphi^2$.

The paper starts the chain at $y_1 = 0$; the extra digit $y_0 = 0$ matches the indexing of
Zeckendorf-adic digit sequences.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 3.3 (the maps `ψ` and `(y_j)`).

articles.title: Exactly $2r$ new-information cylinders carry each small value
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$, and let
$F_n$ denote the $n$-th Fibonacci number ($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). There is an integer $D$ such that for
every integer $d \le D$ there are exactly $2r$ pairs $(k, v)$ of natural numbers with
$v < F_{k+2}$ such that the Zeckendorf digit sequence $i(v)$ of $v$ lies in the new-information
zone $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ (for the shift $r$) and the variation $\Delta^{(r)}$ satisfies
$\Delta^{(r)}(i(v)) = d$.

A pair $(k, v)$ stands for the cylinder of order $k$ whose name is the Zeckendorf expansion of
$v$, so the $2r$ cylinders may have equal orders.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 37 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-37`).

articles.title: Shifting a new-information cylinder by two orders
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be the set of
Zeckendorf-adic integers: the digit sequences $x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\{0, 1\}$ with
$x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive digits equal to $1$. Let $r \ge 1$, $k \ge 2$ and
$y \in \mathbb{X}$. Suppose that every $x \in \mathbb{X}$ with $x_{k+1} = x_k = 0$ and $x_i = y_i$
for $2 \le i \le k - 1$ lies in the new-information zone $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ (for the shift $r$).
Then every $x \in \mathbb{X}$ with $x_{k+3} = x_{k+2} = 0$, $x_{k+1} = 1$, $x_k = 0$ and
$x_i = y_i$ for $2 \le i \le k - 1$ lies in $\mathrm{NIZ}_{k+2}$.

In the paper's cylinder notation, where $C_w$ is the set of points of $\mathbb{X}$ whose digits
ending at $x_2$ read $w$, and with $n_i = y_i$: $C_{00 n_{k-1} \cdots n_2} \subseteq \mathrm{NIZ}_k$
implies $C_{0010 n_{k-1} \cdots n_2} \subseteq \mathrm{NIZ}_{k+2}$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 33 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-33`).

articles.title: The variation by $F_\ell$ on $\mathrm{NIZ}_{\ell+2}$ is $0$
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 3$, let
$F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2, \dots$ be the Fibonacci numbers, and let $\Delta^{(F_\ell)}$ be the
variation of the Zeckendorf sum of digits under adding $F_\ell$ on the Zeckendorf-adic integers
$\mathbb{X}$. Then $\Delta^{(F_\ell)}(x) = 0$ for every $x \in \mathbb{X}$ in the
new-information zone $\mathrm{NIZ}_{\ell+2}$ of order $\ell + 2$ for $r = F_\ell$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 42 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-42`).

articles.title: Values of the variation by $F_\ell$ on $\mathrm{NIZ}_{\ell+1}$
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 3$, let
$F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2, \dots$ be the Fibonacci numbers, and let $\Delta^{(F_\ell)}$ be the
variation of the Zeckendorf sum of digits under adding $F_\ell$ on the Zeckendorf-adic integers.
For $v \in \mathbb{N}$ write $i(v)$ for the Zeckendorf-adic integer whose digits are the
Zeckendorf digits of $v$. Among the $v < F_{\ell+3}$ with $i(v)$ in the new-information zone
$\mathrm{NIZ}_{\ell+1}$ of order $\ell + 1$ for $r = F_\ell$, exactly $F_{\ell-1}$ satisfy
$\Delta^{(F_\ell)}(i(v)) = 0$ and exactly $F_{\ell-2}$ satisfy $\Delta^{(F_\ell)}(i(v)) = 1$.

Each such $v$ stands for the level (cylinder of order $\ell + 1$) whose name is its digits.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 41 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-41`).

articles.title: The variation by $F_\ell$ on $\mathrm{NIZ}_\ell$ is $1$
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 3$, let
$F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2, \dots$ be the Fibonacci numbers, and let $\Delta^{(F_\ell)}$ be the
variation of the Zeckendorf sum of digits under adding $F_\ell$ on the Zeckendorf-adic integers
$\mathbb{X}$. Then $\Delta^{(F_\ell)}(x) = 1$ for every $x \in \mathbb{X}$ in the
new-information zone $\mathrm{NIZ}_\ell$ of order $\ell$ for $r = F_\ell$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 40 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-40`).

articles.title: Points of $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ have leading digits $00$
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$ and $k \ge 2$, and
let $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ be the new-information zone of order $k$ for $r$. Every Zeckendorf-adic
integer $x = (x_i)_{i \ge 2}$ in $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ has $x_{k+1} = x_k = 0$, that is, the name
$x_{k+1} \cdots x_2$ of its cylinder of order $k$ starts with $00$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 32 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-32`).

articles.title: The new-information zones as tower levels
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 2$ and let $r$ satisfy
$F_\ell \le r < F_{\ell+1}$, where $F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2, \dots$ are the Fibonacci numbers. For
a Zeckendorf-adic integer $x = (x_i)_{i \ge 2}$ let $v_k(x) = \sum_{i=2}^{k+1} x_i F_i$, and let
