$\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ be the new-information zone of order $k$ for $r$. Then for every
Zeckendorf-adic integer $x$: $x \notin \mathrm{NIZ}_k$ whenever $2 \le k \le \ell - 1$;
$x \in \mathrm{NIZ}_\ell$ if and only if $v_\ell(x) + r < F_{\ell+1}$;
$x \in \mathrm{NIZ}_{\ell+1}$ if and only if $F_{\ell+1} \le v_{\ell+1}(x) + r < F_{\ell+2}$; and
for every $k > \ell + 1$, $x \in \mathrm{NIZ}_k$ if and only if $F_k \le v_k(x) + r$ and
$v_k(x) < F_k$.

Since level $j$ of the large tower of order $k$ is $\{v_k = j - 1\}$, this says that
$\mathrm{NIZ}_\ell$ consists of the first $F_{\ell+1} - r$ levels of the large tower of order
$\ell$, $\mathrm{NIZ}_{\ell+1}$ of the levels $F_{\ell+1} - r + 1, \dots, F_{\ell+2} - r$ of the
large tower of order $\ell + 1$, and $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ for $k > \ell + 1$ of the levels
$F_k - r + 1, \dots, F_k$ of the large tower of order $k$ (as subsets of the Zeckendorf-adic
integers).

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 29 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-29`).

articles.title: New-information zones lie in $\mathrm{CST}_k$
articles.statement:
For all $r, k \in \mathbb{N}$, the
new-information zone $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ of order $k$ for the shift $r$ is contained in the set
$\mathrm{CST}_k$ for the shift $r$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 5.1 (characteristic lemma for `NIZ_k`).

articles.title: Values of the variation on $\mathrm{NIZ}_{k+2}$ are shifted by $-1$
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 2$,
let $r$ satisfy $F_\ell \le r < F_{\ell+1}$, where $F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2, \dots$ are the
Fibonacci numbers, and let $k \ge \ell + 4$. Write $\Delta^{(r)}$ for the variation of the
Zeckendorf sum of digits under adding $r$ on the Zeckendorf-adic integers, $\mathrm{NIZ}_m$ for
the new-information zone of order $m$ for $r$, and $i(v)$ for the Zeckendorf-adic integer whose
digits are the Zeckendorf digits of $v \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for every integer $d$, the number
of $v < F_{k+4}$ with $i(v) \in \mathrm{NIZ}_{k+2}$ and $\Delta^{(r)}(i(v)) = d - 1$ equals
the number of $v < F_{k+2}$ with $i(v) \in \mathrm{NIZ}_k$ and $\Delta^{(r)}(i(v)) = d$.

Each $v < F_{m+2}$ stands for the cylinder of order $m$ whose name is its digits, so the values
of $\Delta^{(r)}$ on the cylinders in $\mathrm{NIZ}_{k+2}$ are those on the cylinders in
$\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ shifted by $-1$, with multiplicity.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Corollary 36 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-36`).

articles.title: Lifting a cylinder of $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ to order $k + 2$ lowers the variation by $1$
articles.statement:
Let $\ell \ge 2$, let $r$ satisfy $F_\ell \le r < F_{\ell+1}$, where $F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2,
\dots$ are the Fibonacci numbers, and let $k \ge \ell$. Write $\Delta^{(r)}$ for the variation
of the Zeckendorf sum of digits under adding $r$ on the Zeckendorf-adic integers $\mathbb{X}$,
and $\mathrm{NIZ}_k$ for the new-information zone of order $k$ for $r$. Let $y \in \mathbb{X}$
and $d \in \mathbb{Z}$. Let $C$ be the set of $x \in \mathbb{X}$ with $x_{k+1} = x_k = 0$ and
$x_i = y_i$ for $2 \le i \le k - 1$, and let $C'$ be the set of $x \in \mathbb{X}$ with
$x_{k+3} = x_{k+2} = 0$, $x_{k+1} = 1$, $x_k = 0$ and $x_i = y_i$ for $2 \le i \le k - 1$. If
$C \subseteq \mathrm{NIZ}_k$ and $\Delta^{(r)}(x) = d$ for every $x \in C$, then
$\Delta^{(r)}(x) = d - 1$ for every $x \in C'$.

In the paper's notation, $C = C_{00 n_{k-1} \cdots n_2}$ and $C' = C_{0010 n_{k-1} \cdots n_2}$
with $n_i = y_i$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 35 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-35`).

articles.title: New-information zone
articles.statement:
Let $F_1 = F_2 = 1, F_3 = 2, \dots$ be the Fibonacci numbers, and
for a digit sequence $x = (x_i)_{i \ge 0}$ with $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and $j \in \mathbb{N}$ let
$v_j(x) = \sum_{i=2}^{j+1} x_i F_i$. For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ let $\mathrm{CST}_j$ be the
set of digit sequences $x$ with $v_j(x) + r < F_{j+1}$, or with $F_{j+1} \le v_j(x)$ and
$v_j(x) + r < F_{j+2}$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the new-information zone of order $k$
for $r$ is $\mathrm{NIZ}_k = \mathrm{CST}_k \setminus \mathrm{CST}_{k-1}$, where $k - 1$ is read
as $0$ when $k = 0$ (so $\mathrm{NIZ}_0 = \emptyset$).

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 5.1 (definition of `NIZ_k`).

articles.title: The odometer on a point ending in $00$
articles.statement:
If a Zeckendorf-adic integer
$x = (x_k)_{k \ge 2}$ has $x_2 = x_3 = 0$, then the odometer $T(x) = x + 1$ sets the unit digit
$x_2$ to $1$ and leaves every other digit of $x$ unchanged.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 2.2 (case `ℓ = 0` of the definition of `T`).

articles.title: Conditional probability that prescribed later digits vanish
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences
with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive ones), let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer, and let
$\varphi$ be the golden ratio. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with
$\mu(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$ that is preserved by $T$. Let $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$k_0, \dots, k_\ell$ be natural numbers with $2 \le k_0 < k_1 < \dots < k_\ell$. Let
$A \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be a set such that whether $x \in A$ depends only on the digits
$x_2, \dots, x_{k_0}$, with $x_{k_0} = 0$ for every $x \in A$ and $\mu(A) > 0$. Then the event
$E = \{x : x_{k_i} = 0 \text{ for } 1 \le i \le \ell\}$ has conditional probability
$1/\varphi^\ell \le \mu(E \mid A) \le (2/\varphi^2)^\ell$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 21 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-21`).

articles.title: Mass of a cylinder under the invariant measure
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences
with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive ones), let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer, and let
$\varphi$ be the golden ratio. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with
$\mu(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$ that is preserved by $T$. Let $\ell \ge 2$ and $y \in \mathbb{X}$, and let
$C = \{x : x_i = y_i \text{ for } 2 \le i \le \ell\}$ be the cylinder of the digits
$y_\ell \cdots y_2$. Then $\mu(C) = 1/\varphi^\ell$ if $y_\ell = 1$, and
$\mu(C) = 1/\varphi^{\ell - 1}$ if $y_\ell = 0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 15 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-15`), cylinder formula.

articles.title: Mixing of the Zeckendorf digits under the invariant measure
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences
with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive ones), let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer, and let
$\varphi$ be the golden ratio. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with
$\mu(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$ that is preserved by $T$, and let $k, p \ge 1$. Let $A$ be a set that is
measurable for the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the digits $x_2, \dots, x_{p+1}$, with
$\mu(A) > 0$, and let $B$ be a set that is measurable for the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the
digits $x_j$ with $j \ge k + p + 1$. Then $|\mu(B \mid A) - \mu(B)| \le 2/\varphi^{2k}$.

For the coordinate process $X_j = x_{j+1}$ ($j \ge 1$) this bounds every term in the supremum
that defines the $\phi$-mixing coefficient $\phi(k)$, so $\phi(k) \le 2/\varphi^{2k}$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 19 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-19`).

articles.title: Renewal property of the invariant measure
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences
with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive ones) and let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer. Let
$\mu$ be a probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with $\mu(\mathbb{X}^c) = 0$ that is
preserved by $T$. Let $k \ge 2$, $\ell_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $y, z \in \mathbb{X}$, and let
$C = \{x : x_i = z_i \text{ for } 2 \le i \le \ell_0\}$. Let
$E_0 = \{x : x_{k+1} = 0 \text{ and } x_i = y_i \text{ for } 2 \le i \le k\}$ and
$E_1 = \{x : x_{k+1} = 1 \text{ and } x_i = y_i \text{ for } 2 \le i \le k\}$. Then
$\mu(\{x : x_{i+k} = z_i \text{ for } 2 \le i \le \ell_0\} \mid E_0) = \mu(C)$, and if
$y_k = 0$, then also
$\mu(\{x : x_{i+k+1} = z_i \text{ for } 2 \le i \le \ell_0\} \mid E_1) = \mu(C)$.

With the shift $(\sigma x)_i = x_{i+1}$, the two conditioned events are $\sigma^k x \in C$ and
$\sigma^{k+1} x \in C$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 16 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-16`).

articles.title: Adding $r$ across a window of four zero digits
articles.statement:
Write $F_j$ for the Fibonacci numbers
($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ let $Z(r)$ be the set of indices in the Zeckendorf
representation $r = \sum_{j \in Z(r)} F_j$ (all indices $\ge 2$, no two consecutive), and let
$r_j = 1$ if $j \in Z(r)$ and $r_j = 0$ otherwise. Let $\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$
be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive
ones), and write $x + n = T^n(x)$ for the $n$-th iterate of the Zeckendorf odometer $T$. Let
$x \in \mathbb{X}$ and $\ell \ge 2$ with $x_{\ell+1} = x_{\ell+2} = x_{\ell+3} = x_{\ell+4} = 0$,
and let $r < F_{\ell+3}$ with $r_{\ell+2} = 1$. Then either $(x + r)_{\ell+k} = r_{\ell+k}$ for
$k = 1, 2, 3, 4$, or $(x + r)_{\ell+1} = 0$ and $(x + r)_{\ell+3} = 1$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 11 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-11`).

articles.title: Adding a small $r$ leaves the high digits unchanged
articles.statement:
Write $F_j$ for the Fibonacci
numbers ($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). Let $\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of
Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive ones), and write
$x + r = T^r(x)$ for the $r$-th iterate of the Zeckendorf odometer $T$. Let $x \in \mathbb{X}$,
$\ell \ge 2$ and $r < F_{\ell+1}$, and suppose that $x_{\ell+2} = x_{\ell+3} = 0$. Then
$(x + r)_k = x_k$ for every $k \ge \ell + 3$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Lemma 10 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-lem-10`).

articles.title: Adding $r$ without low digits leaves the low digits unchanged
articles.statement:
Write $F_j$ for the
Fibonacci numbers ($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ let $Z(r)$ be the set of indices in
the Zeckendorf representation $r = \sum_{j \in Z(r)} F_j$ (all indices $\ge 2$, no two
consecutive), and let $r_j = 1$ if $j \in Z(r)$ and $r_j = 0$ otherwise. Let
$\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences
with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive ones), and write $x + n = T^n(x)$ for the $n$-th
iterate of the Zeckendorf odometer $T$. Let $x \in \mathbb{X}$ and $\ell \ge 2$ with
$x_\ell = x_{\ell+1} = 0$, and let $r$ satisfy $r_j = 0$ for $2 \le j \le \ell + 1$. Then
$(x + r)_n = x_n$ for every $n$ with $2 \le n \le \ell - 2$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Corollary 9 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-9`).

articles.title: The odometer on sequences without two consecutive zeros
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the Zeckendorf
odometer and let $x = (x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a digit sequence with $x_k \in \{0, 1\}$ such
that for every $k \ge 2$ we have $x_k = 1$ or $x_{k+1} = 1$. Then $T(x)$ is the zero sequence.

Among the Zeckendorf-adic integers, the sequences satisfying this hypothesis are the two whose
digits from index $2$ on alternate, $(10)^\infty$ and $(01)^\infty$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 2.2 (last two cases of the definition of `T`).

articles.title: Stopping condition for a block of size one
articles.statement:
Write $F_j$ for the Fibonacci numbers
($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ let $Z(r)$ be the set of indices in the Zeckendorf
representation $r = \sum_{j \in Z(r)} F_j$ (all indices $\ge 2$, no two consecutive), and let
$r_j = 1$ if $j \in Z(r)$ and $r_j = 0$ otherwise. Let $\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$
be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive
ones), and write $x + n = T^n(x)$ for the $n$-th iterate of the Zeckendorf odometer $T$. Let
$x \in \mathbb{X}$ and $\ell \ge 2$ with $x_i = 0$ for $\ell \le i \le \ell + 5$, and let $r$
satisfy $r_{\ell+1} = r_{\ell+5} = 0$ and $r_{\ell+3} = 1$. Let
$\tilde r = \sum_{j \in Z(r),\, j \le \ell} F_j$ be the part of $r$ of index at most $\ell$. Then
$(x + \tilde r + F_{\ell+3})_k = (x + \tilde r)_k = x_k$ for every $k \ge \ell + 4$, and
$(x + r)_k = (x + \tilde r + F_{\ell+3})_k = (x + \tilde r)_k$ for every $k$ with
$2 \le k \le \ell + 2$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Corollary 12 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-12`).

articles.title: Stopping condition for a block of size $m + 2$
articles.statement:
Write $F_j$ for the Fibonacci numbers
($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). For $r \in \mathbb{N}$ let $Z(r)$ be the set of indices in the Zeckendorf
representation $r = \sum_{j \in Z(r)} F_j$ (all indices $\ge 2$, no two consecutive), and let
$r_j = 1$ if $j \in Z(r)$ and $r_j = 0$ otherwise. Let $\mathbb{X} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$
be the set of Zeckendorf-adic integers (sequences with $x_0 = x_1 = 0$ and no two consecutive
ones), and write $x + n = T^n(x)$ for the $n$-th iterate of the Zeckendorf odometer $T$. Let
$x \in \mathbb{X}$, $\ell \ge 2$ and $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $x_i = 0$ for
$i \in \{\ell, \ell+1, \ell+2, \ell+3, \ell+2m+4, \ell+2m+5, \ell+2m+6, \ell+2m+7\}$, and let
$r$ satisfy $r_{\ell+1} = r_{\ell+2m+7} = 0$ and $r_{\ell+2i+3} = 1$ for $i = 0, \dots, m+1$.
Let $\tilde r = \sum_{j \in Z(r),\, j \le \ell} F_j$ be the part of $r$ of index at most $\ell$,
and let $S = \sum_{i=0}^{m+1} F_{\ell+2i+3}$. Then
$(x + \tilde r + S)_k = (x + \tilde r)_k = x_k$ for every $k \ge \ell + 2m + 7$, and
$(x + r)_k = (x + \tilde r + S)_k$ for every $k$ with $2 \le k \le \ell + 2m + 2$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Corollary 14 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-14`).

articles.title: Unique ergodicity of the Zeckendorf odometer
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{X}$ be the set of
Zeckendorf-adic integers, a subset of the space $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of digit sequences with its
product $\sigma$-algebra, and let $T$ be the Zeckendorf odometer on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$. There
is exactly one probability measure $\mu$ on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ such that
$\mu(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \mathbb{X}) = 0$ and $T$ preserves $\mu$, that is, $T$ is
measurable and $\mu(T^{-1}(A)) = \mu(A)$ for every measurable set $A$.

In other words, $(\mathbb{X}, T)$ is uniquely ergodic.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 15 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-15`), first part.

articles.title: The Zeckendorf odometer
articles.statement:
The odometer is the map $T$ on digit sequences
$x = (x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $x_k \in \{0, 1\}$ defined as follows. If $x_k = x_{k+1} = 0$
for some $k \ge 2$, let $k$ be the least such index; then $T(x)_j = 0$ for $j < k$, $T(x)_k = 1$
and $T(x)_j = x_j$ for $j > k$. If there is no such $k$, then $T(x)$ is the zero sequence.

On a Zeckendorf-adic integer, where digit $k \ge 2$ carries the weight of the Fibonacci number
$F_k$, the map $T$ is addition of $1$, and $x + r$ denotes $T^r(x)$ for $r \in \mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Section 2.2 (definition of `T`).

articles.title: Zeckendorf variation densities exist, with finite moments and mean zero
articles.statement:
For
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $s(n)$ be the number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n$. For
every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a function $\mu : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for every
$d \in \mathbb{Z}$ the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : s(n + r) - s(n) = d\}$ has natural density
$\mu(d)$, the series $\sum_{d \in \mathbb{Z}} |d|^k \mu(d)$ converges absolutely for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\sum_{d \in \mathbb{Z}} d \, \mu(d) = 0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Corollary 24 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-24`), with the remark after it for `r = 0`.

articles.title: Fibonacci shifts have the same Zeckendorf variation densities as shift one
articles.statement:
For
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $s(n)$ be the number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n$, and
let $F_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th Fibonacci number ($F_1 = F_2 = 1$). Let $\ell \ge 2$ and let
$\mu : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ be such that for every $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ the set
$\{n \in \mathbb{N} : s(n + 1) - s(n) = d\}$ has natural density $\mu(d)$. Then for every
$d \in \mathbb{Z}$ the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : s(n + F_\ell) - s(n) = d\}$ also has natural
density $\mu(d)$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Theorem 3 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-thm-3`, for `ℓ ≥ 3`) and its restatement in Section 6 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-thm-unnumbered-1`, for `ℓ ≥ 2`).

articles.title: Distribution of the Zeckendorf digit-sum variation for shift one
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$
let $s(n)$ be the number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n$, and let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio. For every $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : s(n + 1) - s(n) = d\}$
has natural density $0$ if $d \ge 2$, $1/\varphi^2$ if $d = 1$, and $1/\varphi^{2 - 2d}$ if
$d \le 0$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Proposition 39 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-prop-39`).

articles.title: Geometric negative tail of the Zeckendorf variation densities
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let
$s(n)$ be the number of terms in the Zeckendorf representation of $n$, and let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio. Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mu : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ be such that for
every $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ the set $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : s(n + r) - s(n) = d\}$ has natural density
$\mu(d)$. Then there is $D \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $\mu(d - 1) = \mu(d)/\varphi^2$ for every
integer $d \le D$.

## Sources

- Yohan Hosten, *On the Variation of the Sum of Digits in the Zeckendorf Representation: An Algorithm to Compute the Distribution and Mixing Properties*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.2, Corollary 1 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-1`) and its restatement in Section 5 (`jis-2024-24.3.2-cor-unnumbered-1`).

articles.title: Perfect powers with all decimal digits equal but one (Kihel–Luca)
articles.statement:
Fix a natural number
$l \ge 3$. There are only finitely many perfect $l$-th powers $y = x^l$ ($x \in \mathbb{N}$) whose
decimal digits are all equal but one, that is, some digit $c$ occurs in the decimal
representation of $y$ and exactly one digit position of $y$ holds a digit other than $c$, apart
from the powers $10^{ln}$ ($n \in \mathbb{N}$) and, when $l = 3$, the cubes $8 \cdot 10^{3n}$
($n \in \mathbb{N}$).

## Sources

- Omar Kihel and Florian Luca, "Perfect Powers with All Equal Digits but One," Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), Article 05.5.7, Theorem 1, lines 134–140, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Kihel/kihel7.tex.

articles.title: Palindromes in residue classes: a logarithmic error bound
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ be a natural
number, let $q$ be an odd natural number with $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$, and let $r$ be a natural
number with $r < q$. For natural numbers $m$, $q'$ and $r'$, write $A_b(m, q', r')$ for the number
of base-$b$ palindromes $n$ with $1 \le n \le m$ and $n \equiv r' \pmod{q'}$; thus $A_b(m, 1, 0)$
is the number of all base-$b$ palindromes in $[1, m]$. Then for every natural number $m \ge 1$,

$$\left| A_b(m, q, r) - \frac{A_b(m, 1, 0)}{q} \right| \le \frac{\log m}{2 \log b} + 2,$$

where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Corollary 12.

articles.title: Counting digit tuples by their sum modulo a divisor of the base minus one
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$,
$k$ and $q$ be natural numbers, all at least $1$, with $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$, and let $r$ be an
integer. For natural numbers $x$ and $y$ write $N_b(k, q, r, x, y)$ for the number of tuples
$(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of natural numbers with $x \le x_1 < y$, $x_i < b$ for $2 \le i \le k$, and
$x_1 + \dots + x_k \equiv r \pmod q$. Write $[P]$ for $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise,
$\lfloor a/q \rfloor$ for the integer part of $a/q$, and $r \bmod q$ and $a \bmod q$ for the least
nonnegative residues modulo $q$. Then, as rational numbers,

$$N_b(k, q, r, 0, b) = \frac{b^k - 1}{q} + [r \equiv 0 \pmod q],$$



$$N_b(k, q, r, 1, b) = \frac{b^k - b^{k-1}}{q},$$



$$N_b(k, q, r, 0, a) = \frac{a (b^{k-1} - 1)}{q} + \lfloor a/q \rfloor + [r \bmod q < a \bmod q],$$



$$N_b(k, q, r, 1, a) = \frac{(a - 1)(b^{k-1} - 1)}{q} + \lfloor a/q \rfloor +
[r \bmod q < a \bmod q] - [r \equiv 0 \pmod q].$$

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Lemma 5.

articles.title: A small value of the digit-sum congruence count
articles.statement:
In the notation $N_b(k, q, r, x, y)$
of the digit-sum congruence count, $N_3(2, 2, 0, 0, 3) = 5$: exactly five pairs $(x_1, x_2)$ of
natural numbers with $x_1, x_2 < 3$ have even sum.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Definition 3.

articles.title: Digit-sum congruence count
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $k$, $q$, $x$, $y$ and an integer $r$,
$N_b(k, q, r, x, y)$ is the number of tuples $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of natural numbers with
$x \le x_1 < y$ and $x_i < b$ for $2 \le i \le k$ such that $x_1 + \dots + x_k \equiv r \pmod q$.
The count is meant for $k \ge 1$; for $k = 0$ it is defined to equal its value for $k = 1$, the
number of natural numbers $x_1$ with $x \le x_1 < y$ and $x_1 \equiv r \pmod q$.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Definition 3.

articles.title: Two floor-function identities
articles.statement:
For every real number $x$, the sum
$\lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor -x \rfloor$ equals $0$ if $x$ is an integer and $-1$ otherwise.
For all real numbers $x$ and $y$, $\lfloor x + y \rfloor = \lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor y \rfloor$ if
$(x - \lfloor x \rfloor) + (y - \lfloor y \rfloor) < 1$, and
$\lfloor x + y \rfloor = \lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor y \rfloor + 1$ otherwise.

These are parts (iii) and (v) of the cited lemma; its remaining parts are not restated here.

## Sources

- Kritkhajohn Onphaeng, Tammatada Khemaratchatakumthorn, Phakhinkon Napp Phunphayap and Prapanpong Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Lemma 6 (`jis-2024-24.4.8-lem-6`).

articles.title: Palindromes up to a power of the base in residue classes
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$, $k \ge 1$ and
$q \ge 1$ be natural numbers and let $r$ be a natural number with $r < q$. Write $A_b(m, q, r)$
for the number of base-$b$ palindromes $n$ with $1 \le n \le m$ and $n \equiv r \pmod q$, and
$[r = 0]$ for $1$ if $r = 0$ and $0$ otherwise. If $q \mid b$, then

$$A_b(b^k, q, r) = \left(\frac{b}{q} - [r = 0]\right)
\frac{b^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} + b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} - 2}{b - 1}.$$

If $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$, then $A_b(b^k, q, r)$ equals
$(b^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} + b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} - 2)/q$ if $q$ is odd,
$(b - 1) b^{\lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor}/q$ if $q$ is even and $r$ is odd, and
$((b + 1) b^{\lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor} + 2 b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} - 4)/q$ if $q$ and $r$ are both
even. All these identities hold as identities of rational numbers.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Corollary 11.

articles.title: Palindromes in residue classes modulo a divisor of the base
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$, $m \ge 1$ and
$q \ge 1$ be natural numbers with $q \mid b$. Write $m = (a_k a_{k-1} \cdots a_0)_b$ in base $b$,
with leading digit $a_k$. Write $A_b(m, q, r)$ for the number of base-$b$ palindromes $n$ with
$1 \le n \le m$ and $n \equiv r \pmod q$, $C_b(m)$ for the palindromic half copy of $m$, and
$[P]$ for $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. Put

$$\alpha = \frac{b^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} + b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} - 2}{b - 1}, \quad
S = \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} a_{k-i} b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - i}, \quad
\delta = [C_b(m) \le m].$$

Then, as rational numbers,

$$A_b(m, q, 0) = \left(\frac{b}{q} - 1\right) \alpha +
\left\lfloor \frac{a_k - 1}{q} \right\rfloor b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} +
[a_k \equiv 0 \pmod q] (S + \delta),$$

and for every natural number $r$ with $r \bmod q > 0$,

$$A_b(m, q, r) = \frac{b \alpha}{q} +
\left\lceil \frac{a_k - (r \bmod q)}{q} \right\rceil b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} +
[a_k \equiv r \pmod q] (S + \delta).$$

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Palindromes in residue classes modulo a divisor of the base minus one
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$,
$m \ge 1$ and $q \ge 1$ be natural numbers with $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$, and let $r$ be a natural
number with $r < q$. Write $m = (a_k a_{k-1} \cdots a_0)_b$ in base $b$. Write $A_b(m, q, r)$ for
the number of base-$b$ palindromes $n$ with $1 \le n \le m$ and $n \equiv r \pmod q$, $C_b(m)$
for the palindromic half copy of $m$, $[P]$ for $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise, and
$t \bmod d$ for the least nonnegative residue of an integer $t$ modulo a positive integer $d$.
For $j \ge 0$ define integers $s_j$ and $r_j$ as follows. If $q$ is even and $2j \ne k$, let
$s_j = a_{k-j} \bmod (q/2)$ and
$r_j = \bigl(\lfloor r/2 \rfloor - \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} a_{k-i}\bigr) \bmod (q/2)$. If $q$ is odd
and $2j \ne k$, let $s_j = a_{k-j} \bmod q$ and
$r_j = \bigl(\frac{q+1}{2} r - \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} a_{k-i}\bigr) \bmod q$. If $2j = k$, let
$s_j = a_{k-j} \bmod q$ and $r_j = \bigl(r - 2 \sum_{i=0}^{k/2-1} a_{k-i}\bigr) \bmod q$. Put
$\delta = [C_b(m) \le m] \, [r_{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} = s_{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor}]$ and

$$m_1^* = \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor}
\left( \frac{2 a_{k-j} b^{\lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor - j} - 2 s_j}{q} + [r_j < s_j] \right),$$



$$m_2^* = \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - 1}
\frac{a_{k-j} (b - 1) b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - j - 1}}{q},$$



$$m_3^* = \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - 1}
\left( \frac{a_{k-j} (b + 1) b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - j - 1} - 2 s_j}{q} + [r_j < s_j] \right).$$

Then, as rational numbers, if $q$ is odd,

$$A_b(m, q, r) = \frac{b^{\lfloor (k+1)/2 \rfloor} - 1}{q} +
\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{a_{k-j} b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - j}}{q}
\right\rfloor + [r_j < s_j] \right) - [r = 0] + \delta,$$

and if $q$ is even, $A_b(m, q, r)$ equals $(b - 1) b^{(k-1)/2}/q$ when $k$ and $r$ are odd,
$((b + 1) b^{(k-1)/2} - 2)/q + m_1^* - [r = 0] + \delta$ when $k$ is odd and $r$ is even,
$\lfloor a_{k/2}/q \rfloor + m_2^* + [r_{k/2} < s_{k/2}] + \delta$ when $k$ is even and $r$ is
odd, and $2(b^{k/2} - 1)/q + \lfloor a_{k/2}/q \rfloor + m_3^* - [r = 0] +
[r_{k/2} < s_{k/2}] + \delta$ when $k$ and $r$ are both even.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Two small palindrome counts
articles.statement:
Write $A_b(m, q, r)$ for the number of base-$b$ palindromes
$n$ with $1 \le n \le m$ and $n \equiv r \pmod q$. Then $A_{10}(100, 1, 0) = 18$, the palindromes
being $1, \dots, 9$ and $11, 22, \dots, 99$, and $A_2(9, 2, 1) = 5$, the odd base-$2$ palindromes
up to $9$ being $1$, $3 = (11)_2$, $5 = (101)_2$, $7 = (111)_2$ and $9 = (1001)_2$.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Section 1.

articles.title: Palindromes in an arithmetic progression
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $m$, $q$ and $r$,
$A_b(m, q, r)$ is the number of base-$b$ palindromes $n$ with $1 \le n \le m$ and
$n \equiv r \pmod q$, where a natural number is a base-$b$ palindrome when its string of base-$b$
digits reads the same in both directions.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Section 1.

articles.title: Counting palindromes up to $m$ and by parity
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ and $m \ge 1$, and write
$m = (a_k a_{k-1} \cdots a_0)_b$ in base $b$, with leading digit $a_k \ne 0$. For natural numbers
$q$ and $r$, let $A_b(m, q, r)$ be the number of $b$-adic palindromes $n$ with $1 \le n \le m$
and $n \equiv r \pmod q$, and let $C_b(m)$ be the palindromic half copy of $m$. Put $\delta = 1$
if $C_b(m) \le m$ and $\delta = 0$ otherwise. Then
$A_b(m, 1, 0) = b^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} +
\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} a_{k-i} b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - i} + \delta - 2$.
If moreover $b$ is even, let
$\alpha = (b^{\lceil k/2 \rceil} + b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} - 2)/(b - 1)$ and
$S = \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} a_{k-i} b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor - i}$, let $\varepsilon_0 = 1$
if $a_k$ is even and $\varepsilon_0 = 0$ otherwise, and let $\varepsilon_1 = 1 - \varepsilon_0$.
Then $A_b(m, 2, 0) = (b/2 - 1)\alpha + \lfloor (a_k - 1)/2 \rfloor b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} +
\varepsilon_0 (S + \delta)$ and
$A_b(m, 2, 1) = b\alpha/2 + \lceil (a_k - 1)/2 \rceil b^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} +
\varepsilon_1 (S + \delta)$.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Corollary 8.

articles.title: Palindromic half copies of $5570$ in bases $5$ and $8$
articles.statement:
Write $C_b(m)$ for the
palindromic half copy of $m$ in base $b$. For $m = 5570 = (134240)_5 = (12702)_8$,
$C_5(m) = (134431)_5 = 5616$ and $C_8(m) = (12721)_8 = 5585$.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Definition 1 (example).

articles.title: Palindromic half copy
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $m \ge 1$, write
$m = (a_k a_{k-1} \cdots a_0)_b$ for the base-$b$ digits of $m$. The palindromic half copy of $m$
is $C_b(m) = \sum_{j=0}^{k} a_{\max(j, k - j)} b^j$: the $b$-adic palindrome with the same number
of digits as $m$ whose upper digits $a_k, \dots, a_{\lceil k/2 \rceil}$ are those of $m$ and whose
lower digits mirror them. For $m = 0$, which has no digits, $C_b(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- K. Onphaeng, T. Khemaratchatakumthorn, P. N. Phunphayap and P. Pongsriiam, *Exact Formulas for the Number of Palindromes in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.4.8, Definition 1.

articles.title: Even-length palindromic prime powers have base one less than a power of the prime
articles.statement:
Let
$p$ be a prime and let $n$ and $b \ge 2$ be natural numbers. If the base-$b$ representation of
$p^n$ is a palindrome with an even number of digits, then $b = p^x - 1$ for some natural number
$x$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Even-length palindromic powers of 2 have base one less than a power of 2
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and
$b \ge 2$ be natural numbers. If the base-$b$ representation of $2^n$ is a palindrome with an
even number of digits, then $b = 2^x - 1$ for some natural number $x$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Bases of binomial forms of powers of 2
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b \ge 2$, $\alpha \ge 1$ and $k \ge 1$
be natural numbers. If the base-$b$ digits of $2^n$, from the most significant to the least
significant, are $\alpha\binom{k}{k}, \alpha\binom{k}{k-1}, \dots, \alpha\binom{k}{0}$, then
$b = 2^x - 1$ for some natural number $x \le n$, and $\alpha = 2^i$ for some natural number $i$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Digits of a multiple of a power of one more than the base
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha \ge 1$, $k$ and $b$
be natural numbers with $\alpha\binom{k}{\lceil k/2 \rceil} < b$. Then the base-$b$
representation of $\alpha(1 + b)^k$ has exactly the $k + 1$ digits
$\alpha\binom{k}{k}, \alpha\binom{k}{k-1}, \dots, \alpha\binom{k}{0}$, from the most significant
to the least significant.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Digits of a power of the base and of its successor
articles.statement:
Let $z \ge 2$ and $n$ be natural
numbers. Then the base-$z$ digits of $z^n$ are a $1$ followed by $n$ zeros, and, if $n \ge 1$,
the base-$z$ digits of $z^n + 1$ are a $1$, then $n - 1$ zeros, then a $1$.

Part (III) of the source theorem is omitted: as printed ($z^n - 1 = (1, 1, \dots, 1)_z$) it is
false for $z \ge 3$, for example $3^2 - 1 = 8 = (2, 2)_3$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 7, parts (I) and (II).

articles.title: Powers of 2 have binomial forms in small bases
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$ there
are natural numbers $y$ and $b$ with $y \le \lceil \sqrt{2n} \rceil + 1$ and $2 \le b \le 2^y - 1$
such that $2^n$ has a base-$b$ representation in binomial form.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 5.

articles.title: The binomial form of 2023 in base 16
articles.statement:
The number $2023$ has a base-$16$ representation in
binomial form: its base-$16$ digits are $7, 14, 7$, that is
$7\binom{2}{2}, 7\binom{2}{1}, 7\binom{2}{0}$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Section 1.

articles.title: Sufficient condition for a binomial form of a power of 2
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $x$, $k$ and $r$ be
natural numbers with $k \ge 1$, $n = xk + r$ and $2^r\binom{k}{\lceil k/2 \rceil} < 2^x - 1$.
Then $2^n$ has a base-$(2^x - 1)$ representation in binomial form.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Binomial form
articles.statement:
A natural number $N$ has a base-$b$ representation in binomial form if
there are natural numbers $\alpha \ge 1$ and $k \ge 1$ such that the base-$b$ digits of $N$, from
the most significant to the least significant, are
$\alpha\binom{k}{k}, \alpha\binom{k}{k-1}, \dots, \alpha\binom{k}{0}$.

The one-digit case $k = 0$ is excluded as degenerate.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Section 1 (definition of binomial form).

articles.title: Brown's theorem on minimal palindromic base one less than the number
articles.statement:
Let $N \ge 1$ be a
natural number and let $b(N)$ be the smallest base $b \ge 2$ in which $N$ is a palindrome. If
$b(N) = N - 1$, then $N \in \{3, 4, 6\}$, or $N > 6$ and $N$ is prime.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 1, credited to K. Brown.

articles.title: The minimum palindromic base of two
articles.statement:
The smallest base $b \ge 2$ in which the number $2$
is a palindrome is $b(2) = 3$: in base $2$ the number $2$ is written $(1, 0)_2$, which is not a
palindrome, while in base $3$ it is the one-digit palindrome $(2)_3$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Table 1.

articles.title: Minimum palindromic base
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, $b(N)$ is the smallest base $b \ge 2$
in which $N$ is a palindrome, that is, in which the base-$b$ digits of $N$ read the same forwards
and backwards. Such a base exists: $0$ has no digits and is a palindrome in every base, and for
$N \ge 1$ the number $N$ is written with the single digit $N$ in base $N + 1$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Section 1.

articles.title: The Nagell–Ljunggren equation in natural numbers (Bugeaud–Mihăilescu)
articles.statement:
Let $x, y, n, q$
be natural numbers with $x \ge 2$, $y \ge 2$, $n \ge 3$ and $q \ge 2$ such that
$(x^n - 1)/(x - 1) = y^q$. If $q = 2$, or $3 \mid n$, or $4 \mid n$, or $q = 3$ and
$n \not\equiv 5 \pmod 6$, then $(x, y, n, q)$ is one of $(3, 11, 5, 2)$, $(7, 20, 4, 2)$ and
$(18, 7, 3, 3)$; these are $11^2 = (1,1,1,1,1)_3$, $20^2 = (1,1,1,1)_7$ and $7^3 = (1,1,1)_{18}$.

The ranges $x, y \ge 2$, $n \ge 3$, $q \ge 2$ are the standard ones for this equation (not
displayed in the paper).

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 8, quoting Bugeaud and Mihăilescu.

articles.title: Three-digit representations of powers of two with outer digits one
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and $b \ge 2$ a base. There is a digit $c \ne 2$ such that the base-$b$ representation of
$2^n$ is $(1, c, 1)_b$, that is, $2^n = 1 + cb + b^2$ with $0 \le c < b$, if and only if
(i) $2^n - 1 = kb$ for some natural number $k$ with $b \le k \le 2b - 1$, and (ii) it is not the
case that $n$ is even and $b = 2^{n/2} - 1$.

The excluded digit $c = 2$ gives the binomial form $(1, 2, 1)_b = (b + 1)^2$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Palindromic powers of two in a base one less than a power of two
articles.statement:
Let $x \ge 2$ and
$n \ge 1$ be natural numbers, let $b = 2^x - 1$, and suppose that the base-$b$ representation
$2^n = (c_k, \dots, c_0)_b$ is a palindrome with $k + 1$ digits. Then (1) $n > k(x - 1)$; and
(2) if $n = kx + r$ for a natural number $r$, and either $k \le x - r$, or $3 \le k \le x - r + 1$
and $x \ge 3$, then $c_i = 2^r \binom{k}{i}$ for $i = 0, \dots, k$, that is, the representation
is the binomial form $2^r (\binom{k}{k}, \dots, \binom{k}{0})_b$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Even-length palindromes are divisible by the base plus one
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ and let $N$ be a
natural number whose base-$b$ digits form a palindrome with an even number of digits. Then
$b + 1$ divides $N$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Three-digit binomial forms of powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $\alpha \ge 1$ be natural numbers
and let $b \ge 2$ be a base. The base-$b$ representation of $2^n$ is
$(\alpha, 2\alpha, \alpha)_b$ if and only if there is a natural number $i$ with $3i + 2 < n$,
$n \equiv i \pmod 2$, $\alpha = 2^i$ and $b = 2^{(n - i)/2} - 1$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Three-digit palindromic powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $b \ge 2$ be a
base, and let $c = 2^n \bmod b$. The base-$b$ representation of $2^n$ is a palindrome with exactly
three digits if and only if $b^2 + 1 \le 2^n \le b^3 - 1$, $c \ne 0$, and
$\frac{1}{b} \lfloor 2^n / b \rfloor - \frac{b - 1}{b} \le c \le
\frac{1}{b} \lfloor 2^n / b \rfloor$.

## Sources

- D. L. Kreher and D. R. Stinson, *On Minimum-Base Palindromic Representations of Powers of 2*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A69, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Edges of the closed walks $2 \to 8 \to 2$ and $9 \to 9$
articles.statement:
The closed walk with vertex
list $[2, 8]$ has edge list $[(2, 8), (8, 2)]$, and the closed walk with vertex list $[9]$
(a loop at $9$) has edge list $[(9, 9)]$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Example 2.

articles.title: Edge list of a closed walk
articles.statement:
For a list $[v_0, \dots, v_{r-1}]$ of natural numbers,
read as the vertex list of a closed walk, the edge list is
$[(v_0, v_1), \dots, (v_{r-2}, v_{r-1}), (v_{r-1}, v_0)]$: each vertex is paired with the
next one, and the last vertex with the first. A single vertex $[v_0]$ gives the loop
$[(v_0, v_0)]$, and the empty list gives the empty edge list.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 5 (cycles of `M`).

articles.title: Multiset union of cycle edges
articles.statement:
For a multiset $I$ of lists of natural numbers, each
read as the vertex list of a closed walk, write $C_j$ for the edge list of $j \in I$. The
multiset union $C_I = \biguplus_{j \in I} C_j$ is the multiset of all these edges, counted
with multiplicity: each list $j$ contributes its edges as often as $j$ occurs in $I$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3 (multiset cycle union `C_I`).

articles.title: Every mother-graph edge induces a carry transition
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural
numbers. If $(d_1, d_2)$ is an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, then there are natural
numbers $c_1$ and $c_2$ with $c_1 \le n - 1$ and $c_2 \le n - 1$ such that
$b c_2 - c_1 = n d_2 - d_1$ as integers.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Every permutiple has a cycle-preserving digit permutation
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$ and
$d_0, \dots, d_k$ be natural numbers and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ such
that $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ is an $(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple. Then there is a permutation
$\hat\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ such that $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ is also an
$(n, b, \hat\sigma)$-permutiple and the digits along each cycle of $\hat\sigma$ are distinct:
for all $j \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ and all $i \ge 0$, if $d_{\hat\sigma^i(j)} = d_j$ then
$\hat\sigma^i(j) = j$.

Unlike the paper, no assumption $1 < n < b$ is made.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Theorem 5, with Definition 5 (cycle-preserving permutations).

articles.title: $L$-Eulerian criterion for permutiple strings
articles.statement:
Let $1 < n < b$ and let $I$ be a
multiset of cycles of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, with multiset union of cycle edges $C_I$
and multi-image union $\Delta_I$. Then $\Delta_I$ is $L$-Eulerian if and only if there is
an $(n, b)$-permutiple string $s$ whose multiset of entries is $C_I$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Eulerian circuits through zero yield permutiple strings
articles.statement:
Let $1 < n < b$ and let $I$
be a multiset of cycles of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, with multiset union of cycle edges
$C_I$ and multi-image union $\Delta_I$. If $\Delta_I$ has an Eulerian circuit beginning
and ending at the zero state, then there is an $(n, b)$-permutiple string $s$ whose
multiset of entries is $C_I$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Eulerian circuit through the zero state
articles.statement:
Read a multiset $D$ of pairs of natural
numbers as the multi-edges $(c_1, c_2)$ of a directed multigraph. Then $D$ has an Eulerian
circuit beginning and ending with the zero state when there is a nonempty list of pairs
whose multiset of entries is $D$ (so it uses every multi-edge exactly once), in which each
multi-edge ends where the next one begins, the first one starts at $0$ and the last one
ends at $0$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Theorem 7 (hypothesis).

articles.title: Carries of the $(2, 4)$-Hoey–Sloane machine on $(0,0)(2,3)(1,2)(3,1)$
articles.statement:
On the input
string $(d_0, \hat d_0)(d_1, \hat d_1)(d_2, \hat d_2)(d_3, \hat d_3) = (0,0)(2,3)(1,2)(3,1)$,
the carries $c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4$ of the $(2, 4)$-Hoey–Sloane machine are $0, 0, 1, 1, 0$.

This is the $(2, 4)$-permutiple string of $(3, 1, 2, 0)_4 = 216 = 2 \cdot 108 =
2 \cdot (1, 2, 3, 0)_4$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Example 1.

articles.title: Carries of the Hoey–Sloane machine
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers and let
$(d_0, \hat d_0)(d_1, \hat d_1) \cdots (d_k, \hat d_k)$ be an input string of pairs of natural
numbers. The carries $c_0, c_1, c_2, \dots$ of the $(n, b)$-Hoey–Sloane machine on this string
are the integers given by $c_0 = 0$,

$$c_{j+1} = \left\lfloor \frac{n \hat d_j - d_j + c_j}{b} \right\rfloor \quad (0 \le j \le k)$$

and $c_{j+1} = 0$ for $j > k$, where division by $b = 0$ gives $0$.

The machine has a transition from the state $c_j$ on the input $(d_j, \hat d_j)$ when this
division is exact.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Section 4, Equation (2) (the Hoey-Sloane machine).

articles.title: Language of the Hoey–Sloane machine
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $b$, the language
$L$ of the $(n, b)$-Hoey–Sloane machine is the set of strings $s$ of pairs of natural
numbers such that the machine, reading $s$ from left to right, can go from state $0$ to
state $0$. In particular the empty string belongs to $L$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3.

articles.title: Two multi-edges of the $(4, 10)$-Hoey–Sloane multigraph
articles.statement:
In the
$(4, 10)$-Hoey–Sloane multigraph the label $(2, 8)$ sits on the multi-edge from state $0$
to state $3$, and the label $(1, 7)$ sits on the loop at state $3$: the Hoey–Sloane
transition sends $(2, 8)$ to $(0, 3)$ and $(1, 7)$ to $(3, 3)$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 6 and Figure 4.

articles.title: Hoey–Sloane transition of a digit pair
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $b$ and a pair
$e = (d_1, d_2)$ of natural numbers, the multi-edge of the $(n, b)$-Hoey–Sloane multigraph
carrying the label $e$ is $(c_1, c_2)$, where $c_1 = \lambda(d_1 + (b - n) d_2)$ with
$\lambda$ the least non-negative residue modulo $b$ (computed in the integers), and
$c_2 = \lfloor (n d_2 - d_1 + c_1) / b \rfloor$, replaced by $0$ when negative. For $b = 0$
the conventions are $x \bmod 0 = x$ and $x / 0 = 0$, and $c_1$ is likewise replaced by $0$
when negative.

For an edge $e$ of the $(n, b)$-mother graph with $1 < n < b$, the source shows that
$(c_1, c_2)$ is the unique solution of $b c_2 - c_1 = n d_2 - d_1$ with
$0 \le c_1, c_2 \le n - 1$, that is, the transition of the Hoey–Sloane machine with input $e$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 6 and the proof of Theorem 6.

articles.title: Hoey–Sloane words with permuted digits are unions of cycles
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $b \ge 2$
be natural numbers, and let $s = (d_0, \hat d_0) \cdots (d_k, \hat d_k)$ be an input string in
the language $L$ of the $(n, b)$-Hoey–Sloane machine such that $\hat d_j = d_{\sigma(j)}$ for all
$j$, for some permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, k\}$. Let
$E = \{(d_j, \hat d_j) : 0 \le j \le k\}$ be the set of inputs of $s$. Then every $e \in E$ lies
on a directed cycle with edges in $E$: there are $m \ge 0$ and pairwise distinct natural numbers
$v_0, \dots, v_m$ such that $(v_i, v_{i+1}) \in E$ for all $0 \le i \le m$, with indices taken
modulo $m + 1$, and $e = (v_i, v_{i+1})$ for some $i$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Runs of the Hoey-Sloane machine
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$, $c$ and $c'$ be natural numbers and let
$s = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_m$ be a finite string of inputs, each a pair of natural numbers. The
$(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane machine can go from state $c$ to state $c'$ reading $s$ from left to right
when there are natural numbers $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_m$ with $c_0 = c$ and $c_m = c'$ such that,
for each $1 \le i \le m$, the input $e_i$ moves state $c_{i-1}$ to state $c_i$ in one transition
of the $(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane machine. For the empty string ($m = 0$) this says $c = c'$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3.

articles.title: Hoey-Sloane transitions are transitions of the machine
articles.statement:
Let $1 < n < b$, let
$e = (d_1, d_2)$ be an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, and let $(c_1, c_2)$ be the Hoey-Sloane
transition of $e$, that is, $c_1 = \lambda(d_1 + (b - n) d_2)$ and $c_2 = (n d_2 - d_1 + c_1) / b$,
where $\lambda$ is the least non-negative residue modulo $b$. Then the input $e$ moves state $c_1$
to state $c_2$ in one transition of the $(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane machine.

By the uniqueness of Hoey-Sloane transitions (Theorem 5), it is the only transition labelled
by $e$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 6, from Theorems 5 and 6.

articles.title: Uniqueness of Hoey-Sloane transitions
articles.statement:
Let $n \le b$. If an input $e$ moves state $c_1$
to state $c_2$ and also moves state $\hat c_1$ to state $\hat c_2$, each in one transition of the
$(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane machine, then $c_1 = \hat c_1$ and $c_2 = \hat c_2$.

The paper assumes $1 < n < b$; here it is weakened to $n \le b$. For $n > b$ the claim can fail:
for $n = 3$ and $b = 1$ the input $(0, 0)$ moves $0$ to $0$ and also $1$ to $1$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Transitions of the Hoey-Sloane machine
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$, $c_1$, $c_2$, $d_1$ and $d_2$ be
natural numbers. The input $e = (d_1, d_2)$ moves state $c_1$ to state $c_2$ in one transition of
the $(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane machine $\Gamma$ when $c_1 < n$, $c_2 < n$, $(d_1, d_2)$ is an edge of
the $(n, b)$-mother graph, and $b c_2 - c_1 = n d_2 - d_1$ in the integers (Equation (1)).

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3, Equation (1).

articles.title: The string $(0,0)(2,3)(1,2)(3,1)$ lies in the $(2, 4)$-Hoey–Sloane language
articles.statement:
The input
string $(d_0, \hat d_0) \cdots (d_3, \hat d_3) = (0,0)(2,3)(1,2)(3,1)$ belongs to the language
$L$ of the $(2, 4)$-Hoey–Sloane machine.

This is the $(2, 4)$-permutiple string of $(3, 1, 2, 0)_4 = 216 = 2 \cdot 108 =
2 \cdot (1, 2, 3, 0)_4$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Example 1.

articles.title: Hoey–Sloane words
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers. An input string
$(d_0, \hat d_0) \cdots (d_k, \hat d_k)$ of pairs of natural numbers belongs to the language $L$
of the $(n, b)$-Hoey–Sloane machine when, with $c_0, \dots, c_{k+1}$ the carries of the machine
on this string, every input $(d_j, \hat d_j)$ is an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, $b$
divides $n \hat d_j - d_j + c_j$ for every $0 \le j \le k$, and $c_{k+1} = 0$.

So the walk starts in the state $c_0 = 0$, every transition is an exact division, and the walk
ends in the state $0$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Section 4 (the language `L` and `L`-walks).

articles.title: $L$-Eulerian multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a finite multiset of multi-edges $(x, y)$ between
natural numbers, and call a number a vertex of $D$ when it is an endpoint of some multi-edge in
$D$. The multigraph $D$ is $L$-Eulerian when $0$ is a vertex of $D$, every vertex $u$ of $D$
reaches every vertex $v$ of $D$ along a (possibly empty) directed path of multi-edges in $D$, and
for every natural number $c$ the number of multi-edges in $D$ ending at $c$ equals the number of
multi-edges in $D$ starting at $c$, counted with multiplicity.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 4 (definition of `L`-Eulerian, before Corollary 2).

articles.title: Cycles of the mother graph
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers. A list
$[v_0, \dots, v_{r-1}]$ of natural numbers is a (directed) cycle of the $(n, b)$-mother graph when
it is nonempty, has no repeated entry, and each of its edges
$(v_0, v_1), \dots, (v_{r-2}, v_{r-1}), (v_{r-1}, v_0)$ is an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph.
In particular a one-element list $[v]$ is a cycle when $(v, v)$ is an edge of the mother graph.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 5 (cycles of `M`).

articles.title: Sample edges of the $(4, 10)$-mother graph
articles.statement:
In the $(4, 10)$-mother graph, $(2, 8)$ and
$(9, 9)$ are edges and $(2, 1)$ is not. With $\lambda$ the least non-negative residue modulo
ten, $\lambda(2 + 6 \cdot 8) = 0 \le 3$ and $\lambda(9 + 6 \cdot 9) = 3 \le 3$, while
$\lambda(2 + 6 \cdot 1) = 8 > 3$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 4 and Example 1.

articles.title: An edge and a non-edge of the $(2, 4)$-mother graph
articles.statement:
In the $(2, 4)$-mother graph, the
pair $(0, 2)$ is an edge, since $\lambda(0 + (4 - 2) \cdot 2) = \lambda(4) = 0 \le 1$, and the
pair $(0, 1)$ is not an edge, since $\lambda(0 + (4 - 2) \cdot 1) = \lambda(2) = 2 > 1$, where
$\lambda$ is the least non-negative residue modulo $4$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Definition 4 and Example 1.

articles.title: Edges of the mother graph
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers. For natural numbers $x$
and $y$, the pair $(x, y)$ is an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph $M$ when $x < b$, $y < b$ and

$$\lambda(x + (b - n) y) \le n - 1,$$

where $\lambda(z)$ is the least non-negative residue of the integer $z$ modulo $b$, and $b - n$
and $n - 1$ are computed in the integers.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Definition 4 (the mother graph).

articles.title: $87912$ is a $(4, 10)$-permutiple by digit reversal
articles.statement:
The numeral
$(d_4, d_3, d_2, d_1, d_0)_{10} = 87912$ is a $(4, 10, \sigma)$-permutiple, where $\sigma$ is the
reversal $j \mapsto 4 - j$ of $\{0, \dots, 4\}$; that is, $87912 = 4 \cdot 21978$, and $21978$ has
the digits of $87912$ in reverse order.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Introduction.

articles.title: The permutiple string of $87912 = 4 \cdot 21978$
articles.statement:
The string of inputs
$(2, 8)(1, 7)(9, 9)(7, 1)(8, 2)$ is a $(4, 10)$-permutiple string. It is produced by the
$(4, 10)$-permutiple $87912 = 4 \cdot 21978$, whose multiplication reverses the digits.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3 and Table 1.

articles.title: Inputs of a permutiple string lie on mother-graph cycles
articles.statement:
Let $1 < n < b$ and let $s$ be
an $(n, b)$-permutiple string. Then every input $(d, \hat d)$ of $s$ is an edge of the
$(n, b)$-mother graph, and $\hat d$ reaches $d$ along a (possibly empty) directed path in the
graph whose edges are the inputs of $s$, so $(d, \hat d)$ lies on a directed cycle of that graph.
In this sense the inputs of $s$ form a union of cycles of the mother graph.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Corollary 1, quoting Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*.

articles.title: Permutiple strings
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers, and for natural numbers
$a_0, \dots, a_k$ write $(a_k, \dots, a_0)_b = \sum_{j=0}^{k} a_j b^j$. A string $s$ of inputs
(pairs of natural numbers) is an $(n, b)$-permutiple string when it belongs to the language $L$ of
the $(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane machine and there are a natural number $k$, natural numbers
$d_0, \dots, d_k$ and a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ such that $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$
is an $(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple, that is, every $d_j$ is less than $b$ and
$(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b = n (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$, and
$s = (d_0, d_{\sigma(0)})(d_1, d_{\sigma(1)}) \cdots (d_k, d_{\sigma(k)})$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3.

articles.title: Permutiples with a given digit permutation
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$ and $d_0, \dots, d_k$ be
natural numbers and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$. The numeral
$(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ is an $(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple when $d_j < b$ for every $j$ and

$$\sum_{j=0}^k d_j b^j = n \sum_{j=0}^k d_{\sigma(j)} b^j,$$

that is, $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b = n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Definition 1 (from Holt, *Some general results and open questions on palintiple numbers*).

articles.title: A word in the $(4, 10)$-Hoey-Sloane language
articles.statement:
The input string
$(2, 8)(1, 7)(9, 9)(7, 1)(8, 2)$ belongs to the language of the $(4, 10)$-Hoey-Sloane machine:
reading it from left to right, the machine can go from state $0$ to state $0$.

Writing $87912 = (d_4, \dots, d_0)_{10}$ and letting $\sigma$ be the digit reversal
$\sigma(j) = 4 - j$, so that $87912 = 4 \cdot (d_{\sigma(4)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_{10}$ is
$4 \cdot 21978$, the inputs are the pairs $(d_j, d_{\sigma(j)})$ for $j = 0, \dots, 4$; an
accepting run passes through the states $0, 3, 3, 3, 0, 0$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Section 2.3 and Example 2.

articles.title: Multi-image union of a multiset of cycles
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b$ be natural numbers and let $I$
be a multiset of vertex lists. Let $C_I$ be the multiset cycle union of $I$: the multiset sum,
over the lists in $I$, of their edges, where a nonempty list $[v_0, \dots, v_{r-1}]$ has the
edges $(v_0, v_1), \dots, (v_{r-2}, v_{r-1}), (v_{r-1}, v_0)$ and the empty list has none. The
multi-image union $\Delta_I$ is the multiset obtained by replacing each edge $e = (d_1, d_2)$ of
$C_I$, with its multiplicity, by the multi-edge $(c_1, c_2)$ of the $(n, b)$-Hoey-Sloane
multigraph that carries the label $e$: $c_1 = \lambda(d_1 + (b - n) d_2)$, where $\lambda$ is
the least non-negative residue modulo $b$ computed in the integers (the identity when $b = 0$),
and $c_2 = \lfloor (n d_2 - d_1 + c_1) / b \rfloor$ (taken to be $0$ when $b = 0$), with a
negative value of $c_1$ or $c_2$ replaced by $0$.

The labels are dropped, since they do not affect in- and out-degrees, connectivity or Eulerian
circuits.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Definition 7.

articles.title: Holt's residue condition for rearranged permutiples
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $b \ge 2$ be
natural numbers, let $d_0, \dots, d_k$ be natural numbers, and write $(e_k, \dots, e_0)_b$
for the base-$b$ numeral $\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j b^j$. Let $\sigma$, $\pi$ and $\tau$ be
permutations of $\{0, \dots, k\}$. If $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ is an $(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple
and $(d_{\pi(k)}, \dots, d_{\pi(0)})_b$ is an $(n, b, \tau)$-permutiple, then for every
$0 \le j \le k$

$$\lambda\bigl(d_j + (b - n)\, d_{\pi(\tau(\pi^{-1}(j)))}\bigr) \le n - 1,$$

where $\lambda(x)$ is the least non-negative residue of the integer $x$ modulo $b$ (the
difference $b - n$ is taken in the integers and may be negative).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is needed: for $n = 0$ the only permutiples have all digits zero
and the bound would read $0 \le -1$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Carry bound for permutiples
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let $\sigma$
be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$, and let $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ be an
$(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple, where $(e_k, \dots, e_0)_b$ denotes the base-$b$ numeral
$\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j b^j$. Let $c_0, c_1, \dots$ be the carries of the multiplication
$n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$. Then for every $0 \le j \le k$ we have
$c_j \le n - 1$ if $n \ge 1$, and $c_j = 0$ if $n = 0$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Theorem 2, quoting Holt's earlier paper; restated as Theorem 2 of Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13.

articles.title: Carry relation for permutiples
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $b \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let
$\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$, and let $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ be an
$(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple, where $(e_k, \dots, e_0)_b$ denotes the base-$b$ numeral
$\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j b^j$. Let $c_0, c_1, \dots$ be the carries of the multiplication
$n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$. Then for every $0 \le j \le k$,

$$b\, c_{j+1} - c_j = n\, d_{\sigma(j)} - d_j,$$

with both sides computed in the integers.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Theorem 1, quoting Holt's earlier paper; restated as Theorem 1 of Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13.

articles.title: First two carries of a permutiple multiplication
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$ and $d_0, \dots, d_k$
be natural numbers, let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$, and write
$(e_k, \dots, e_0)_b$ for the base-$b$ numeral $\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j b^j$. The carries
$c_0, c_1, \dots$ of the single-digit multiplication
$n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$, defined by $c_0 = 0$ and
$c_{j+1} = \lfloor (n d_{\sigma(j)} + c_j) / b \rfloor$ for $0 \le j \le k$, satisfy
$c_0 = 0$ and $c_1 = \lfloor n d_{\sigma(0)} / b \rfloor$, where division by $b = 0$ is
taken to give $0$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Section 2.

articles.title: Carries of a permutiple multiplication
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$ and $d_0, \dots, d_k$ be
natural numbers and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$. The carries of the
single-digit multiplication $n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$, where
$(e_k, \dots, e_0)_b$ denotes the base-$b$ numeral $\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j b^j$, are the
natural numbers $c_0, c_1, c_2, \dots$ defined by $c_0 = 0$,
$c_{j+1} = \lfloor (n d_{\sigma(j)} + c_j) / b \rfloor$ for $0 \le j \le k$, and
$c_{j+1} = 0$ for $j > k$. Division by $b = 0$ is taken to give $0$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *A Method for Finding All Permutiples with a Fixed Set of Digits from a Single Known Example*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A88, Section 2.

articles.title: Edge condition for permutiples
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, $b$ and $k$ be natural numbers, let $\sigma$
be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ and let $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ be an
$(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple, that is, $d_i < b$ for all $i$ and
$(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b = n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$. Then for every
$0 \le j \le k$, $\lambda(d_j + (b - n) d_{\sigma(j)}) \le n - 1$, where $\lambda$ is the least
non-negative residue modulo $b$ and $b - n$ is computed in the integers, so it may be negative.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is needed: for $n = 0$ the only permutiples have all digits zero and the
bound would read $0 \le -1$.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Theorem 3, quoting Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*.

articles.title: Graph of the permutiple 87912
articles.statement:
Let $(d_0, d_1, d_2, d_3, d_4) = (2, 1, 9, 7, 8)$ be
the decimal digits of $87912$, from the units digit up, and let $\sigma$ be the reversal
$\sigma(j) = 4 - j$ of $\{0, \dots, 4\}$. The edge set
$\{(d_j, d_{\sigma(j)}) : 0 \le j \le 4\}$ of the graph of these digits with digit
permutation $\sigma$ is exactly $\{(2, 8), (1, 7), (9, 9), (7, 1), (8, 2)\}$: the edges
$8 \rightleftarrows 2$ and $7 \rightleftarrows 1$ and a loop at $9$.

Here $87912 = 4 \cdot 21978$, and $21978$ is $87912$ with its digits reversed.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Figure 1.

articles.title: Conjugate rearrangements have the same graph
articles.statement:
Let $d_0, \dots, d_k$ be natural numbers
and let $\pi_1, \pi_2, \tau_1, \tau_2$ be permutations of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ with
$\pi_1 \tau_1 \pi_1^{-1} = \pi_2 \tau_2 \pi_2^{-1}$. Then the graph of the digits
$d_{\pi_1(0)}, \dots, d_{\pi_1(k)}$ with digit permutation $\tau_1$ and the graph of the digits
$d_{\pi_2(0)}, \dots, d_{\pi_2(k)}$ with digit permutation $\tau_2$ have the same edge set:

$$\{(d_{\pi_1(j)}, d_{\pi_1(\tau_1(j))}) : 0 \le j \le k\} =
\{(d_{\pi_2(j)}, d_{\pi_2(\tau_2(j))}) : 0 \le j \le k\}.$$

The source assumes, for a base $b$ and a multiplier $n$ with $1 < n < b$, that
$(d_{\pi_1(k)}, \dots, d_{\pi_1(0)})_b$ is an $(n, b, \tau_1)$-permutiple and that
$(d_{\pi_2(k)}, \dots, d_{\pi_2(0)})_b$ is an $(n, b, \tau_2)$-permutiple, together with a base
permutiple $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$; these hypotheses are not needed.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Permutiple graphs are unions of simple cycles of the mother graph
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$
and $b \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$, and
let $(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ be an $(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple, where $(e_k, \dots, e_0)_b$
denotes the base-$b$ numeral $\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j b^j$. Let
$E = \{(d_j, d_{\sigma(j)}) : 0 \le j \le k\}$ be the edge set of its graph. Then every
pair in $E$ is an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, and every $e \in E$ lies on a directed
cycle with distinct vertices all of whose edges are in $E$: there are $m \ge 0$ and pairwise
distinct natural numbers $v_0, \dots, v_m$ such that, with indices taken modulo $m + 1$,
$(v_i, v_{i+1}) \in E$ for every $0 \le i \le m$ and $e = (v_i, v_{i+1})$ for some $i$.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Theorem 6, with Definition 6 (permutiple classes and their graphs).

articles.title: Edge set of the graph of a numeral
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a base, let $d_0, \dots, d_k$ be
natural numbers, the digits of the base-$b$ numeral
$(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b = \sum_{j=0}^{k} d_j b^j$, and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of
$\{0, \dots, k\}$. The graph $G$ of these digits with digit permutation $\sigma$ has edge set

$$E = \{(d_j, d_{\sigma(j)}) : 0 \le j \le k\},$$

a finite set of ordered pairs of natural numbers; it does not depend on $b$.

The vertices of $G$ are all base-$b$ digits, so $G$ is determined by its edge set.

## Sources

- B. V. Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A13, Definition 3 (the graph of a permutiple).

articles.title: Edges of a permutiple's graph lie on cycles of the mother graph
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, $b$ and $k$
be natural numbers, let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ and let
$(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b$ be an $(n, b, \sigma)$-permutiple, that is, $d_i < b$ for all $i$ and
$(d_k, \dots, d_0)_b = n \cdot (d_{\sigma(k)}, \dots, d_{\sigma(0)})_b$. Its graph has the edges
$(d_i, d_{\sigma(i)})$ for $0 \le i \le k$. Then for every $0 \le j \le k$, the pair
$(d_j, d_{\sigma(j)})$ is an edge of the $(n, b)$-mother graph, and $d_j$ is reachable from
$d_{\sigma(j)}$ along edges of the graph of the permutiple (in zero steps when they are equal),
so the edge $(d_j, d_{\sigma(j)})$ lies on a directed cycle of that graph.

## Sources

- Benjamin V. Holt, *A Multigraph Characterization of Permutiple Strings*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A111, Theorem 4, quoting Holt, *Finding Permutiples of a Known Base and Multiplier*.

articles.title: Digit reversal
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$ and $n$ with $b \ge 2$, write
$n = \sum_{i\lt k} d_i b^i$ with digits $0 \le d_i < b$ and leading digit $d_{k-1} \ne 0$ (so $k = 0$
when $n = 0$). The base-$b$ reversal of $n$ is the natural number $\sum_{i\lt k} d_{k-1-i} b^i$. For
the bases $b = 0$ and $b = 1$ the reversal of $n$ is $n$ itself.

Trailing zeros of $n$ become leading zeros and are lost: in base $10$ the reversal of $120$ is
$21$.

articles.title: Basic reverse divisors
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k \ge 2$, the numbers
$11(10^k - 1)$ and $22(10^k - 1)$ both have exactly $k + 2$ decimal digits, the decimal
reversal of $11(10^k - 1)$ equals $9 \cdot 11(10^k - 1)$, and the decimal reversal of
$22(10^k - 1)$ equals $4 \cdot 22(10^k - 1)$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Theorem 1 (quoted from the literature).

articles.title: In base $B$, divisors of $B^2 - 1$ divide reversals of their multiples
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 2$ be
a natural number and let $n$ be a natural number dividing $B^2 - 1$. Then $n$ divides the
base-$B$ reversal of every multiple of $n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 5.

articles.title: Reverse divisors with at most seven digits
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a reverse divisor with $L$
decimal digits, where $L \le 7$. Then $n = 11(10^{L-2} - 1)$ or $n = 22(10^{L-2} - 1)$, where
$L - 2$ is read as $0$ when $L < 2$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Theorem 1 (quoted from the literature).

articles.title: Sufficient conditions for a multiple with divisible reversal
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number such that $\gcd(n, 10) = 1$, or $n$ equals its decimal reversal, or $n$ is a reverse
divisor. Then there is a natural number $k_0 \ge 1$ such that $n$ divides the decimal reversal
of $k_0 n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 6.

articles.title: Reverse divisors have at least four digits
articles.statement:
Every reverse divisor has at least four
decimal digits.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Theorem 1 (quoted from the literature).

articles.title: The positive integers with property $P^*$ are the divisors of $99$
articles.statement:
**The positive integers with property $P^*$ are the divisors of $99$.** A natural number
$n \ge 1$ has property $P^*$ if and only if $n$ divides $99$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Theorem 3.

articles.title: Unfolding property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**Unfolding property $P^*$.** A natural number $n$ has property $P^*$ if and only if $n$
divides the decimal reversal of every multiple of $n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Section 2 (terminology).

articles.title: Divisors of $99$ have property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**Divisors of $99$ have property $P^*$.** Every divisor of $99$ has property $P^*$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 1.

articles.title: Property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**Property $P^*$.** A natural number $n$ has property $P^*$ if $n$ divides the decimal
reversal of every multiple of $n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Section 2 (terminology).

articles.title: Infinitely many multiples with divisible reversal
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number not
divisible by $10$, and suppose that $n$ divides the decimal reversal of $k_0 n$ for some natural
number $k_0 \ge 1$. Then there are infinitely many natural numbers $k \ge 1$ such that $n$
divides the decimal reversal of $k n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 6.

articles.title: Complete Young graphs
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $g$, $k$ and $m$, the Young graph $Y(g, k)$ of
the $k$-reverse multiples in base $g$ is complete on $m$ nodes: the nodes other than its
distinguished starting node form the complete directed graph on $m$ nodes, so $Y(g, k)$ has
$m + 1$ nodes in all; the node $[0, 0]$ is one of these $m$ nodes, and the starting node has an
edge to every node except $[0, 0]$.

## Sources

- L. H. Kendrick, "Young Graphs: 1089 et al.", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Kendrick/ken1.tex>.
