Definition at lines 458-460: in the source's `K_m` convention, the nodes other than the distinguished starting node form the complete directed graph on `m` nodes, so the Young graph has `m + 1` total nodes including that distinguished start; `[0, 0]` is one of the `m` non-start nodes, and the starting node connects to every node except `[0, 0]`.

articles.title: Characterization of reverse divisors
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is a reverse divisor if and
only if $n > 0$ and there is a natural number $k \ge 2$ such that the decimal reversal of $n$
equals $kn$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Section 1 (terminology).

articles.title: Reverse divisor
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is a reverse divisor if $n > 0$ and there is a
natural number $k \ge 2$ such that the decimal reversal of $n$ equals $kn$. Since $n > 0$, such a
$k$ is unique; it is called the quotient of $n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Section 1 (terminology).

articles.title: Characterization of retained nodes
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a set, let $P$ be a predicate on $V$ and
let $\prec$ be a binary relation on $V$. A node $v \in V$ is retained with respect to $P$ and
$\prec$ if and only if $P(v)$ holds or there is a node $w \in V$ with $P(w)$ and $v \prec w$.

articles.title: Retained node
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a set, let $P$ be a predicate on $V$ (the pivot nodes) and let
$\prec$ be a binary relation on $V$. A node $v \in V$ is retained with respect to $P$ and $\prec$
if $P(v)$ holds or there is a node $w \in V$ with $P(w)$ and $v \prec w$.

articles.title: A product congruent to $11$ modulo a power of ten
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, let
$a = (10^r - 1) \cdot 100 + 89$, the integer whose decimal digits are $r$ nines followed by $89$,
and let $b = 10^{r+2} - 1$, the integer whose decimal digits are $r + 2$ nines. Then the
remainder of $ab$ modulo $10^{r+2}$ is $11$; that is, the last $r + 2$ decimal digits of $ab$ are
$r$ zeros followed by $11$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Lemma 4.

articles.title: For $k \ge 2$, the number $11 \cdot (10^k - 1)$ lacks property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**For $k \ge 2$, the number $11 \cdot (10^k - 1)$ lacks property $P^*$.** For every natural
number $k \ge 2$, the number $11 \cdot (10^k - 1)$ does not have the property $P^*$.

In the source these numbers $1089, 10989, 109989, \dots$ are the basic reverse divisors with
quotient $9$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Lemma 2.

articles.title: No reverse divisor has property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**No reverse divisor has property $P^*$.** If $n$ is a reverse divisor, then $n$ does not have
the property $P^*$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 4.

articles.title: Positive integers sharing a factor with $10$ lack property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**Positive integers sharing a factor with $10$ lack property $P^*$.** If $n \ge 1$ is a
natural number with $\gcd(n, 10) \ne 1$, then $n$ does not have the property $P^*$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 2.

articles.title: Reverse divisors with quotient $4$ lack property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**Reverse divisors with quotient $4$ lack property $P^*$.** If $n > 0$ is a natural number
whose decimal reversal equals $4n$, then $n$ does not have the property $P^*$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Lemma 1.

articles.title: Palindromes with property $P^*$
articles.statement:
**Palindromes with property $P^*$.** Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number that is a decimal
palindrome, that is, whose decimal reversal equals $n$. If $n$ has the property $P^*$, then $n$
is one of $1$, $3$, $9$, $11$, $33$ and $99$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Proposition 3.

articles.title: Reverse divisors have quotient $4$ or $9$
articles.statement:
If $n$ is a reverse divisor, then the decimal
reversal of $n$ equals $4n$ or $9n$.

## Sources

- Mohamed Ayad and Rachid Bouchenna, "Which Integer Divides the Reverse of Any of Its Multiples?", Theorem 1 (quoted from the literature).

articles.title: Characterization of complete Young graphs
articles.statement:
Let $g$, $k$ and $m$ be natural numbers with
$2 \le k < g$ and $m \ge 2$. Then the Young graph $Y(g, k)$ is complete on $m$ nodes if and only
if

$$\left\lfloor \frac{\gcd(g - k,\, k^2 - 1)}{k + 1} \right\rfloor = m - 1.$$

## Sources

- Corollary at lines 574-576 of L. H. Kendrick, "Young Graphs: 1089 et al.", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Kendrick/ken1.tex>. In the source's `K_m` convention, the nodes other than the distinguished starting node form the complete directed graph on `m` nodes, so the Young graph has `m + 1` total nodes including that distinguished start; `[0, 0]` is one of the `m` non-start nodes. Natural-number division represents the source floor because all quantities are nonnegative and the denominator is positive. The hypothesis is `2 ≤ m`, not `1 ≤ m`. The corollary rests on a theorem whose proof starts "Since $s_1$ exists", so it needs `m - 1 ≥ 1`. For `m = 1` the class `K_1` contains no Young graph: every Young graph is connected and contains `[0, 0]`, so the starting node has an edge to some node other than `[0, 0]`, while a graph in `K_1` has none. With `1 ≤ m`, `(g, k) = (10, 9)` and `m = 1` give `gcd(1, 80) / 10 = 0 = m - 1`, but `Y(10, 9)` is the 1089 graph, not in `K_1`.

articles.title: Sloane's endpoint formula for reverse multiples
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $k$ be integers with
$2 \le k < g$, and let $N = (a_n a_{n-1} \cdots a_0)_g$ have base-$g$ digits
$a_0, \dots, a_n \in \{0, \dots, g - 1\}$, with units digit $a_0$ and leading digit $a_n \ne 0$.
Suppose $N$ is a $(g, k)$ reverse multiple, that is, $k N = (a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n)_g$, and that
$a_0 + a_n = g$. Then $(k + 1) a_n = g$; in particular $k + 1$ divides $g$ and
$a_n = g / (k + 1)$.

## Sources

- L. H. Kendrick, *Young Graphs: 1089 et al.*, Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.9.7, Corollary `cor:lastdig1089` (Sloane's Conjecture 3.5) and proof, lines 418–424, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Kendrick/ken1.tex>.

articles.title: Sutcliffe's theorem on two- and three-digit reverse multiples
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $k$ be
integers with $2 \le k < g$, and let $a$ and $b$ be base-$g$ digits, $0 \le a, b < g$, with
$a \ne 0$, such that $(a\,b)_g$ is a $(g, k)$ reverse multiple, that is,
$k (a g + b) = b g + a$. Then $a + b < g$, so $a + b$ is a base-$g$ digit, and
$(a\,(a + b)\,b)_g$ is again a $(g, k)$ reverse multiple, that is,
$k (a g^2 + (a + b) g + b) = b g^2 + (a + b) g + a$.

This is the forward implication of Sutcliffe's theorem; the converse is not included.

## Sources

- L. H. Kendrick, *Young Graphs: 1089 et al.*, Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.9.7, Remark `rem:truncate` (quoting Sutcliffe's Theorem 3), lines 203–205, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Kendrick/ken1.tex>.

articles.title: Label of an edge in the Young graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, let $P$ be a
predicate on its vertices, let $\prec$ be a binary relation on its vertices, and let $e$ be an
edge of $G$ whose source and target are both retained with respect to $P$ and $\prec$, viewed as
an edge of the Young graph of $G$ with respect to $P$ and $\prec$. The label of $e$ in the Young
graph is its label in $G$.

articles.title: Source of an edge in the Young graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, let $P$ be a
predicate on its vertices, let $\prec$ be a binary relation on its vertices, and let $e$ be an
edge of $G$ whose source and target are both retained with respect to $P$ and $\prec$, viewed as
an edge of the Young graph of $G$ with respect to $P$ and $\prec$. The source of $e$ in the Young
graph, viewed as a vertex of $G$, is the source of $e$ in $G$.

articles.title: Target of an edge in the Young graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph, let $P$ be a
predicate on its vertices, let $\prec$ be a binary relation on its vertices, and let $e$ be an
edge of $G$ whose source and target are both retained with respect to $P$ and $\prec$, viewed as
an edge of the Young graph of $G$ with respect to $P$ and $\prec$. The target of $e$ in the Young
graph, viewed as a vertex of $G$, is the target of $e$ in $G$.

articles.title: Young graph of a labeled directed graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a labeled directed graph with vertex
set $V$, edge set $E$ and label set $L$, let $P$ be a predicate on $V$ and let $\prec$ be a binary
relation on $V$. The Young graph of $G$ with respect to $P$ and $\prec$ is the labeled directed
graph with label set $L$ whose vertices are the vertices of $G$ that are retained with respect to
$P$ and $\prec$, whose edges are the edges of $G$ whose source and target are both retained, and
in which each edge has the same source, target and label as in $G$.

articles.title: Carry equations for reverse multiples, general form
articles.statement:
Let $g, k, n$ be natural numbers
with $2 \le k < g$, and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ be natural numbers with $a_i < g$ for every $i$.
Then $k \sum_{i\lt n} a_i g^i = \sum_{i\lt n} a_{n-1-i} g^i$ if and only if there is a unique sequence
of natural numbers $r_0, \dots, r_n$ with $r_0 = 0$, $r_n = 0$ and, for every $i < n$,
$r_{i+1} < k$ and $k a_i + r_i = a_{n-1-i} + r_{i+1} g$.

No hypothesis is placed on $n$ or on the end digits $a_0$ and $a_{n-1}$; in particular $n$ may be
$0$.

articles.title: Carry equations for reverse multiples
articles.statement:
Let $g, k, n$ be natural numbers with
$2 \le k < g$ and $n \ge 1$, and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ be natural numbers with $a_i < g$ for
every $i$, $a_{n-1} \ne 0$ and $a_0 \ne 0$. Then $k \sum_{i\lt n} a_i g^i = \sum_{i\lt n} a_{n-1-i} g^i$,
that is, $k$ times the number with base-$g$ digits $a_{n-1}, \dots, a_0$ (most significant first)
equals the number with these digits reversed, if and only if there is a unique sequence of natural
numbers $r_0, \dots, r_n$ with $r_0 = 0$, $r_n = 0$ and, for every $i < n$, $r_{i+1} < k$ and
$k a_i + r_i = a_{n-1-i} + r_{i+1} g$.

The carry $r_{i+1}$ here is the source's $r_i$.

## Sources

- L. H. Kendrick, *Young Graphs: 1089 et al.*, Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.9.7, subsection `subsec:eqtns`, lines 128–154 (the column equations for `kN = Reverse_g(N)`, Young's bound `r_i ≤ k - 1`, and equation `eq:rmdig`), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Kendrick/ken1.tex>. It follows from `young_reverse_multiple_carry_path_iff_general`; the hypotheses `hfirst` and `hlast` (and `hn`, which only serves to state them) are unused and keep the source's shape.

articles.title: Young's theorem on reverse multiples
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $2 \le k < g$.
A $(g, k)$ reverse multiple is a list of base-$g$ digits $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n$, most significant
first, with $n \ge 2$, $d_1 \ne 0$, $d_n \ne 0$ and $d_i < g$ for every $i$, such that $k$ times
the number $\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i g^{n-i}$ equals the number $\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{n+1-i} g^{n-i}$
whose digits are those of the first in reverse order. Consider the graph whose nodes are pairs
$(r, s)$ of natural numbers, with an edge labeled $(a, b)$ from $(r, s)$ to $(r', s')$ whenever
$k b + s = a + s' g$ and $k a + r' = b + r g$. A path is a sequence of nodes $v_0, \dots, v_m$
together with a sequence of labels $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m$ such that $m \ge 1$, $v_0 = (0, 0)$,
both coordinates of every node are less than $k$, both coordinates of every label are less
than $g$, both coordinates of $\ell_1$ are nonzero, and for each $j$ the label $\ell_j$ labels an
edge from $v_{j-1}$ to $v_j$. A node $(r, s)$ is an even pivot if $r = s$, and an odd pivot if
for some $c < g$ there is an edge labeled $(c, c)$ from $(r, s)$ to $(s, r)$.

Then there is a bijection from the $(g, k)$ reverse multiples with an even number of digits to
the paths whose last node is an even pivot, and a bijection from the $(g, k)$ reverse multiples
with an odd number of digits to the paths whose last node is an odd pivot. Under both
bijections, a reverse multiple $d_1, \dots, d_n$ is sent to a path with labels
$(d_1, d_n), (d_2, d_{n-1}), \dots, (d_h, d_{n+1-h})$, where $h = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$; in the
odd case, if $(r, s)$ is the last node of that path, there is an edge labeled
$(d_{h+1}, d_{h+1})$ from $(r, s)$ to $(s, r)$.

## Sources

- L. H. Kendrick, *Young Graphs: 1089 et al.*, Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.9.7, Theorem [Young's Theorem], lines 192-197, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Kendrick/ken1.tex>, after Theorems 1 and 2 of Young's first paper on reverse multiples.

articles.title: Squares with two blocks of repeated digits
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a perfect square whose decimal
representation, read from the most significant digit, consists of $r \ge 1$ copies of a digit
$a$ with $1 \le a \le 9$ followed by $s \ge 1$ copies of a digit $b$ with $0 \le b \le 9$. Then
$n$ is one of $16$, $25$, $36$, $49$, $64$, $81$, $144$, $225$, $441$, $1444$ and $7744$, or
there is a natural number $i$ such that $n = 10^{2i}$, $n = 4 \cdot 10^{2i}$ or
$n = 9 \cdot 10^{2i}$.

## Sources

- Omar Kihel and Florian Luca, "Perfect Powers With All Equal Digits But One," Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), Article 05.5.7, Theorem, lines 273–279, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Kihel/kihel7.tex

articles.title: Triangular repdigits
articles.statement:
The positive triangular numbers $n(n+1)/2$ with $n \ge 1$ whose
decimal representation consists of a single repeated digit are exactly $1$, $3$, $6$, $55$, $66$
and $666$.

## Sources

- Christian Hercher and Karl Fegert, "Triangular Numbers With a Single Repeated Digit", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Real numbers with a common continued fraction prefix are close
articles.statement:
Let $\xi$ and $\xi'$ be
real numbers with continued fraction expansions $[a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$ and
$[a_0'; a_1', a_2', \dots]$, computed by $\xi_0 = \xi$, $a_i = \lfloor \xi_i \rfloor$ and
$\xi_{i+1} = 1/(\xi_i - a_i)$, stopping when $\xi_i = a_i$ (so an expansion is finite exactly when
the number is rational). Let $k \ge 0$ be an integer, and suppose that $a_0 = a_0'$ and that for
each $1 \le i \le k$ either both expansions have a digit of index $i$ and $a_i = a_i'$, or neither
has one. Then $|\xi - \xi'| \le 2^{1-k}$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Lemma 5, quoted from Cusick and Flahive, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Convergents and the Lagrange approximability
articles.statement:
Let $\xi$ be an irrational real number,
with complete quotients $\xi_0 = \xi$ and $\xi_{k+1} = 1/\{\xi_k\}$, where $\{x\}$ is the
fractional part of $x$, and digits $a_k = \lfloor \xi_k \rfloor$, so that
$\xi = [a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$. For $k \ge 1$ let
$c_k = a_k + [0; a_{k-1}, \dots, a_1] + \{\xi_k\}$, where the middle term is $0$ when $k = 1$.
Then for every $k \ge 1$ the convergent $p/q = [a_0; a_1, \dots, a_{k-1}]$, written in lowest terms
with $q > 0$, satisfies $(-1)^k / (q^2 (p/q - \xi)) = c_k$. Moreover, the $1$-Lagrange
approximability $\lambda_1(\xi)$ equals $\limsup_{k \to \infty} c_k$, taken in the extended reals.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 4, parts (a) and (c), quoted from Cusick and Flahive, Appendix 1.

articles.title: Common minimum of the $n$-Lagrange and $n$-Markoff spectra
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$
there is a real number $\alpha$ that is the least element both of the $n$-Lagrange spectrum $L_n$
and of the $n$-Markoff spectrum $M_n$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 12.

articles.title: Hall's ray in the $n$-Lagrange spectrum
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$ be the classical Lagrange spectrum and
let $F$ (Freĭman's constant) be the infimum of the real numbers $c$ with
$[c, \infty) \subseteq L_1$. Then for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$[nF, \infty) \subseteq L_n \subseteq M_n$, where $L_n$ is the $n$-Lagrange spectrum and
$M_n$ is the $n$-Markoff spectrum.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 14.

articles.title: The $n$-Lagrange spectrum is closed
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the $n$-Lagrange spectrum
$L_n$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 19.

articles.title: The $n$-Markoff spectrum is closed
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the $n$-Markoff spectrum
$M_n$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 11.

articles.title: Markoff points in the $p$-Lagrange spectrum
articles.statement:
Let $x \le y \le z$ be positive integers with
$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 3xyz$ (a sorted Markoff triple), let $\lambda_z = \sqrt{9 - 4/z^2}$, let
$D = 9z^2 - 4$ if $z$ is odd and $D = (9z^2 - 4)/4$ if $z$ is even, and let $p$ be a prime.
Call $p$ a principal norm if $|u^2 + Duv + \frac{D^2 - D}{4} v^2| = p$ for some integers $u, v$,
that is, if some element $u + v \frac{D + \sqrt{D}}{2}$ of the quadratic order $\mathcal{O}_D$ has
norm $\pm p$. Then: (a) if $p$ is a principal norm, then $\lambda_z$ lies in the $p$-Lagrange
spectrum $L_p$; (b) if $\lambda_z \in L_p$ and, for every sorted Markoff triple
$(x', y', z') \ne (x, y, z)$ with $z' \le z$, the rational number $(9z^2 - 4)/(9z'^2 - 4)$ is not
a square in $\mathbb{Q}$, then $p$ is a principal norm.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 26; the printed `λ_p ∈ L_p` is read as `λ_z ∈ L_p`, as in the proof.

articles.title: Congruence conditions for Markoff points in the $p$-Lagrange spectrum
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
and let $L_p$ be the $p$-Lagrange spectrum. Then: (a) $\sqrt{5} \in L_p$ if and only if
$p \equiv 0, \pm 1 \pmod 5$; (b) $2\sqrt{2} \in L_p$ if and only if $p \equiv 2, \pm 1 \pmod 8$;
(c) $\sqrt{221}/5 \in L_p$ if and only if $p$ is a square modulo $13$ and modulo $17$;
(d) $\sqrt{1517}/13 \in L_p$ if and only if $p$ is a square modulo $37$ and modulo $41$;
(e) $\sqrt{7565}/29 \in L_p$ if and only if $p$ is a square modulo $5$, modulo $17$ and modulo
$89$. Here $p$ is a square modulo $m$ when $p \equiv a^2 \pmod m$ for some integer $a$; this
includes the case $p \equiv 0 \pmod m$.

Part (f) of the source, for $10\sqrt{26}/17$, is omitted: as printed it fails at $p = 17$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Corollary 27.

articles.title: Membership in the $n$-Lagrange spectrum
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and real number
$\alpha$, $\alpha$ lies in the $n$-Lagrange spectrum $L_n$ if and only if $\alpha = \lambda_n(\xi)$
for some irrational real number $\xi$, where $\lambda_n$ is the $n$-Lagrange approximability.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (3).

articles.title: Membership in the $n$-Markoff spectrum
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and real number
$\alpha$, $\alpha$ lies in the $n$-Markoff spectrum $M_n$ if and only if $\alpha = \mu_n(\xi, \xi')$
for some distinct irrational real numbers $\xi$ and $\xi'$, where $\mu_n$ is the $n$-Markoff
approximability.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (4).

articles.title: Isolated minimum of the $p$-Lagrange spectrum for primes below 2000
articles.statement:
For every prime
$p < 2000$, the $p$-Lagrange spectrum $L_p$ has a least element $\alpha$ with the following
properties: $\alpha$ is an isolated point of $L_p$, that is, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that
every $\beta \in L_p$ with $|\beta - \alpha| < \varepsilon$ equals $\alpha$; $\alpha$ is
irrational; and $\alpha = \sqrt{r}$ for some rational number $r$.

This is Conjecture 1 of the source for primes below 2000.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Theorem 2, with Conjecture 1.

articles.title: The $n$-approximabilities as maxima over divisors
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $\lambda_n$ and
$\mu_n$ be the $n$-Lagrange and $n$-Markoff approximabilities, and let $\xi \ne \xi'$ be irrational
real numbers. Then $\lambda_n(\xi) = \max_{g \mid n} \lambda_1(g\xi)$ and
$\mu_n(\xi, \xi') = \max_{g \mid n} \mu_1(g\xi, g\xi')$, where $g$ runs over the positive divisors
of $n$ and the maxima are taken in the extended reals.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 6.

articles.title: The $1$-Lagrange approximability is the classical one
articles.statement:
For every real number $\xi$, the
$1$-Lagrange approximability of $\xi$ is

$$\lambda_1(\xi) = \limsup_{s/t \to \xi} \frac{1}{t^2 \, |s/t - \xi|},$$

taken in the extended reals, where the limsup is over rational numbers $s/t \ne \xi$, written in
lowest terms with $t > 0$, tending to $\xi$. That is, the factor $\gcd(t, 1)$ in the definition
equals $1$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equations (1) and (3).

articles.title: $n$-Lagrange approximability
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a real number $\xi$, the
$n$-Lagrange approximability of $\xi$ is the element of the extended reals

$$\lambda_n(\xi) = \limsup_{s/t \to \xi} \frac{\gcd(t, n)}{t^2 \, |s/t - \xi|},$$

where the limsup is over rational numbers $s/t \ne \xi$, written in lowest terms with $t > 0$,
tending to $\xi$. For $n = 1$ this is the classical Lagrange approximability $\lambda(\xi)$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (3).

articles.title: The $n$-Lagrange spectrum is the closure of its quadratic-irrational values
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$,
let $\lambda_n$ be the $n$-Lagrange approximability, and let $P_n$ be the set of real numbers
$\alpha$ such that $\alpha = \lambda_n(\xi)$ for some quadratic irrational $\xi$, that is, an
irrational real number with $a\xi^2 + b\xi + c = 0$ for some integers $a \ne 0$, $b$, $c$. Then
the $n$-Lagrange spectrum $L_n$ is the closure of $P_n$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 20.

articles.title: The $n$-Lagrange spectrum lies in the $n$-Markoff spectrum, with attained suprema
articles.statement:
Let
$n \ge 1$, let $L_n$ and $M_n$ be the $n$-Lagrange and $n$-Markoff spectra, and let $\mu_n$ be the
$n$-Markoff approximability. Then $L_n \subseteq M_n$. Moreover, for every $\alpha \in L_n$ there
are distinct irrational real numbers $\xi$ and $\xi'$ with $\mu_n(\xi, \xi') = \alpha$ at which the
supremum defining $\mu_n(\xi, \xi')$ is attained: some pair of integers $(s, t) \ne (0, 0)$
satisfies

$$\frac{\gcd(t, n)\,|\xi - \xi'|}{|s - t\xi|\,|s - t\xi'|} = \alpha.$$

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 9.

articles.title: $n$-Lagrange spectrum
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the $n$-Lagrange spectrum $L_n$ is the set
of real numbers $\alpha$ such that $\lambda_n(\xi) = \alpha$ for some irrational real number
$\xi$, where $\lambda_n$ is the $n$-Lagrange approximability; only finite values of $\lambda_n$
count. For $n = 1$ this is the classical Lagrange spectrum $L$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (3).

articles.title: Symmetry of the $n$-Markoff approximability
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and all real
numbers $\xi$ and $\xi'$, the $n$-Markoff approximability satisfies
$\mu_n(\xi, \xi') = \mu_n(\xi', \xi)$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (4).

articles.title: $n$-Markoff approximability
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and real numbers $\xi$ and $\xi'$, the
$n$-Markoff approximability is the supremum in the extended reals

$$\mu_n(\xi, \xi') = \sup_{(s,t) \ne 0} \frac{\gcd(t, n)\,|\xi - \xi'|}{|s - t\xi|\,|s - t\xi'|}$$

over all pairs of integers $(s, t) \ne (0, 0)$. A term whose denominator is $0$, which happens only
when $\xi$ or $\xi'$ is rational, counts as $0$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (4).

articles.title: Attained suprema in the $n$-Markoff spectrum
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $M_n$ be the $n$-Markoff
spectrum, and let $\mu_n$ be the $n$-Markoff approximability. For every $\alpha \in M_n$ there are
distinct irrational real numbers $\xi$ and $\xi'$ with $\mu_n(\xi, \xi') = \alpha$ at which the
supremum defining $\mu_n(\xi, \xi')$ is attained: some pair of integers $(s, t) \ne (0, 0)$
satisfies

$$\frac{\gcd(t, n)\,|\xi - \xi'|}{|s - t\xi|\,|s - t\xi'|} = \alpha.$$

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 10.

articles.title: The $n$-Markoff spectrum
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and irrational numbers $\xi \ne \xi'$,
the $n$-Markoff approximability $\mu_n(\xi, \xi')$ is the extended real number
$\sup_{(s, t) \in \mathbb{Z}^2 \setminus \{0\}}
\gcd(t, n) \, |\xi - \xi'| / (|s - t\xi| \, |s - t\xi'|)$. The $n$-Markoff spectrum $M_n$ is the
set of real numbers $\alpha$ such that $\mu_n(\xi, \xi') = \alpha$ for some irrational numbers
$\xi \ne \xi'$. For $n = 1$ this is the classical Markoff spectrum $M$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Introduction, equation (4).

articles.title: Divisibility inclusions of the $n$-Lagrange and $n$-Markoff spectra
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$
be natural numbers with $m \ge 1$, $n \ge 1$ and $m \mid n$, and write $L_k$ and $M_k$ for the
$k$-Lagrange and $k$-Markoff spectra. Then $L_n \subseteq L_m$ and $M_n \subseteq M_m$; in
particular $L_n \subseteq L_1$ and $M_n \subseteq M_1$, where $L_1$ and $M_1$ are the
classical Lagrange and Markoff spectra.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Corollary 7, equations (8) and (9).

articles.title: The prime $67$ and continued fraction digits $1$ and $2$
articles.statement:
For an irrational real
number $\xi$, define its complete quotients by $\xi_0 = \xi$ and $\xi_{k+1} = 1/\{\xi_k\}$,
where $\{\cdot\}$ denotes the fractional part, and its continued fraction digits by
$a_k = \lfloor \xi_k \rfloor$. Let $p < 2000$ be a prime. Then there is no irrational $\xi$
such that the digits of both $\xi$ and $p\xi$ eventually all lie in $\{1, 2\}$ if and only
if $p = 67$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Scaled classical spectra lie in the $n$-spectra
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number and
write $L_k$ and $M_k$ for the $k$-Lagrange and $k$-Markoff spectra, so that $L_1$ and $M_1$
are the classical Lagrange and Markoff spectra. Then $n\alpha \in L_n$ for every
$\alpha \in L_1$ and $n\alpha \in M_n$ for every $\alpha \in M_1$; that is,
$n L_1 \subseteq L_n$ and $n M_1 \subseteq M_n$.

## Sources

- Brandon Dong, Soren Dupont, Evan M. O'Dorney and W. Theo Waitkus, *Raney Transducers and the Lowest Point of the n-Lagrange Spectrum*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A47, Proposition 13.

articles.title: Chosen basis of a rational subspace
articles.statement:
For a rational subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, this
is a fixed choice of a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of the lattice $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, indexed by
$\{0, \dots, \dim V - 1\}$ and viewed as an $\mathbb{R}$-basis of $V$.

articles.title: Diophantine exponent
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and let $k$ be a natural
number. For subspaces $v$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ write $\operatorname{dist}(v, x)$ for the distance
between the subspaces $v$ and $x$, and for a rational subspace $v$ write $H(v)$ for its height.
The diophantine exponent $\beta_k(x)$ of $x$ for approximation by $k$-dimensional rational
subspaces is the infimum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the set of real numbers $\beta > 0$ for
which there is a real number $c > 0$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(v, x) \ge c \, H(v)^{-\beta}$
for every $k$-dimensional rational subspace $v$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$. In particular
$\beta_k(x) = \infty$ when there is no such $\beta$.

articles.title: Distance from a line to a subspace
articles.statement:
For a line $x$ through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$
and a subspace $y$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ is the infimum,
over all lines $y'$ contained in $y$, of the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y')$ between the
lines $x$ and $y'$. When $y = 0$ there is no such line and the value is $0$.

articles.title: Distance between lines
articles.statement:
For lines $x$ and $y$ through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the
distance $\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ is $\sin \theta$, where $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle
between nonzero vectors spanning $x$ and $y$. This is the usual distance on the projective
space.

articles.title: Distance between subspaces
articles.statement:
For subspaces $x$ and $y$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, the distance
$\operatorname{dist}(x, y)$ is defined as follows. If $\dim y \le \dim x$, it is the supremum,
over all lines $y'$ contained in $y$, of the distance $\operatorname{dist}(y', x)$ from the line
$y'$ to the subspace $x$. If $\dim y > \dim x$, it is the supremum, over all lines $x'$ contained
in $x$, of the distance $\operatorname{dist}(x', y)$ from the line $x'$ to the subspace $y$. A
supremum over no lines is $0$.

articles.title: Height of a rational subspace
articles.statement:
For a rational subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ of dimension
$k$, let $v_1, \dots, v_k$ be the chosen basis of the lattice $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$. The height of
$V$ is $H(V) = \lVert v_1 \wedge \dots \wedge v_k \rVert$, where the exterior power
$\bigwedge^k \mathbb{R}^d$ carries the inner product whose value on decomposable elements
$u_1 \wedge \dots \wedge u_k$ and $w_1 \wedge \dots \wedge w_k$ is the Gram determinant
$\det(\langle u_i, w_j \rangle)_{i,j}$.

articles.title: Integer points of a subspace
articles.statement:
For a subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, this is the set
$V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of integer points of $V$, as a $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule of $V$.

articles.title: The integer lattice
articles.statement:
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule of $\mathbb{R}^d$
spanned by the standard basis vectors, that is, the lattice of points with integer coordinates.

articles.title: Rational subspace
articles.statement:
A subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is rational if $V \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$
is a full-rank lattice in $V$, that is, a discrete subgroup of $V$ that spans $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$.

The paper does not state which definition of rational subspace it uses; this one is common
and is the most convenient for defining heights of rational subspaces.

articles.title: Dirichlet's principle in Grassmann varieties
articles.statement:
Let $d$, $l$ and $k$ be natural numbers with
$d \ge 2$, $0 < l < d$ and $1 \le k \le l$, and for a subspace $x$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ write
$\beta_k(x)$ for the diophantine exponent of $x$ for approximation by $k$-dimensional rational
subspaces. Then every $l$-dimensional subspace $x$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfies
$\beta_k(x) \ge \frac{d}{k(d - l)}$. Moreover, some $l$-dimensional subspace $x$ of
$\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfies $\beta_k(x) = \frac{d}{k(d - l)}$.

## Sources

- N. de Saxcé, `Rational approximations to linear subspaces`, Annals of Math, 203 (3) 2026. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_linear_subspaces` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Real algebraic numbers of bounded degree
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the type of
real numbers $\alpha$ that are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ and whose minimal polynomial over
$\mathbb{Q}$ has degree at most $n$.

## Sources

- the lean-eval source ranged over `ℂ`; the classical exponent in Poëls' theorem uses real algebraic approximants, so this is restricted to `ℝ` (recorded as a Lean variant).

articles.title: Classical exponent of approximation by algebraic numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a
real number $\xi$, let $H(\alpha)$ denote the height of a real algebraic number $\alpha$. The
classical exponent $\omega^*_n(\xi)$ is the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the set of real numbers
$\omega > 0$ for which there are infinitely many real algebraic numbers $\alpha$ of degree at
most $n$ with $0 < |\xi - \alpha| \le H(\alpha)^{-\omega - 1}$.
It is $0$ when this set is empty.

articles.title: Height of a real algebraic number
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic number, let $p$ be its
monic minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$, and let $D$ be the least common multiple of the
denominators of the nonzero coefficients of $p$. The height $H(\alpha)$ is the largest absolute
value of a coefficient of the integer polynomial $D p$. For a real number that is not algebraic
over $\mathbb{Q}$, the height is $0$.

Equivalently, $H(\alpha)$ is the largest absolute value of a coefficient of the minimal polynomial
of $\alpha$ scaled to have coprime integer coefficients.

articles.title: Approximation exponents admitting infinitely many solutions
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number,
$\xi$ a real number, and $H(\alpha)$ the height of a real algebraic number $\alpha$. This is the
set of real numbers $\omega > 0$ for which there are infinitely many real algebraic numbers
$\alpha$ of degree at most $n$ with $0 < |\xi - \alpha| \le H(\alpha)^{-\omega - 1}$.

When $n \ge 1$ and $\xi$ is irrational, this set contains the interval $(0, 1)$ by Dirichlet's
theorem.

## Sources

- `ω` here is `ω⋆` in the paper.

articles.title: Poëls' lower bound for the classical exponent
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and let
$a = 1/(2 - \log 2)$. For every real number $\xi$ that is transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$, the
classical exponent of approximation to $\xi$ by real algebraic numbers of degree at most $n$
satisfies $\omega^*_n(\xi) \ge a n$.

## Sources

- A. Poëls, `On approximation to a real number by algebraic numbers of bounded degree`, Annals of Math, 201 (1) 2025. Statement taken from https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/AnnalsChallenge. Problem `annals_on_approximation_of_reals` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Baker–Davenport reduction for an arbitrary denominator, absolute-value form
articles.statement:
For a real
number $x$ write $\lVert x \rVert = |x - \operatorname{round}(x)|$ for the distance from $x$ to a
nearest integer. Let $M$ and $q$ be natural numbers with $q > 0$, and let $\kappa$, $\mu$, $A$, $B$
be real numbers with $A > 0$ and $B > 1$. Put
$\varepsilon = \lVert \mu q \rVert - M \lVert \kappa q \rVert$ and suppose that $\varepsilon > 0$.
Then there are no natural numbers $r$, $s$, $w$ with $r \le M$,
$w \ge \log(Aq/\varepsilon) / \log B$ and $|r\kappa - s + \mu| < A B^{-w}$.

articles.title: Baker–Davenport reduction lemma, absolute-value form
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$ write
$\lVert x \rVert = |x - \operatorname{round}(x)|$ for the distance from $x$ to a nearest integer.
Let $M$ be a positive integer and $\kappa$ an irrational real number, and let $q$ be the
denominator of the $j$-th convergent of the continued fraction of $\kappa$ for some natural number
$j$, with $q > 6M$. Let $A$, $B$, $\mu$ be real numbers with $A > 0$ and $B > 1$. Put
$\varepsilon = \lVert \mu q \rVert - M \lVert \kappa q \rVert$ and suppose that $\varepsilon > 0$.
Then there are no positive integers $r$, $s$, $w$ with $r \le M$,
$w \ge \log(Aq/\varepsilon) / \log B$ and $0 < |r\kappa - s + \mu| < A B^{-w}$.

Of the hypothesis $q > 6M$ only $q > 0$ is used. The hypotheses that $M > 0$, that $\kappa$ is
irrational and that $q$ is a convergent denominator, and the positivity of $r$, $s$, $w$ and of
$|r\kappa - s + \mu|$, are not needed: the statement follows from the version for an arbitrary
positive denominator.

## Sources

- Eric F. Bravo, Carlos A. Gomez, and Florian Luca, "Product of Consecutive Tribonacci Numbers With Only One Distinct Digit," Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.6.3, Lemma `bd`, lines 285–292. Source URL <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Gomez/gomez3.tex>.

articles.title: Baker–Davenport reduction for an arbitrary denominator, one-sided form
articles.statement:
For a real number
$x$ write $\lVert x \rVert = |x - \operatorname{round}(x)|$ for the distance from $x$ to a nearest
integer. Let $N$ and $q$ be natural numbers with $q > 0$, and let $\gamma$, $\mu$, $A$, $B$ be real
numbers with $A > 0$ and $B > 1$. Put $\xi = \lVert \mu q \rVert - N \lVert \gamma q \rVert$ and
suppose that $\xi > 0$. Then there are no natural numbers $u$, $v$, $w$ with $u \le N$,
$w \ge \log(Aq/\xi) / \log B$ and $0 < u\gamma - v + \mu < A B^{-w}$.

articles.title: Baker–Davenport reduction lemma, one-sided form
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$ write
$\lVert x \rVert = |x - \operatorname{round}(x)|$ for the distance from $x$ to a nearest integer.
Let $N$ be a positive integer and $\gamma$ an irrational real number, and let $q$ be the
denominator of the $j$-th convergent of the continued fraction of $\gamma$ for some natural number
$j$, with $q > 6N$. Let $A$, $B$, $\mu$ be real numbers with $A > 0$ and $B > 1$. Put
$\xi = \lVert \mu q \rVert - N \lVert \gamma q \rVert$ and suppose that $\xi > 0$. Then there are
no positive integers $u$, $v$, $w$ with $u \le N$, $w \ge \log(Aq/\xi) / \log B$ and
$0 < u\gamma - v + \mu < A B^{-w}$.

Of the hypothesis $q > 6N$ only $q > 0$ is used. The hypotheses that $N > 0$, that $\gamma$ is
irrational and that $q$ is a convergent denominator, and the positivity of $u$, $v$ and $w$, are
not needed: the statement follows from the version for an arbitrary positive denominator.

## Sources

- Bilizimbéyé Edjeou, Amadou Tall, and Mohamed Ben Fraj Ben Maaouia, "Powers of Two as Sums of Three Lucas Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.8.8, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Edjeou/edj4.tex>, Lemma, lines 200–211.

articles.title: Nearest-integer estimate in the Baker–Davenport reduction
articles.statement:
For a real number $x$ write
$\lVert x \rVert = |x - \operatorname{round}(x)|$ for the distance from $x$ to a nearest integer.
Let $q$, $M$, $u$ be natural numbers with $u \le M$, let $v$ be an integer, and let $\kappa$ and
$\mu$ be real numbers. If $\varepsilon = \lVert \mu q \rVert - M \lVert \kappa q \rVert$, then
$\varepsilon \le q \, |u\kappa - v + \mu|$.

## Sources

- Nearest-integer Baker–Davenport reduction core: a named reusable arithmetic prerequisite stage extracted from Lemma (lines 285--292) of Eric F. Bravo, Carlos A. Gómez, and Florian Luca, "Product of Consecutive Tribonacci Numbers With Only One Distinct Digit", Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.6.3. <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Gomez/gomez3.tex>. Scope: the printed lemma defines nearest-integer distance by `‖x‖ = |x - round x|` and `ε := ‖μq‖ - M‖κq‖`; this stage records the reverse-triangle inequality used by the reduction argument. It does not claim to formalize the full lemma. The source's irrationality, continued-fraction, `q > 6M`, and logarithmic hypotheses belong to the later wrapper and are deliberately omitted from this arithmetic stage, as are the source's `0 < q` and `0 < ε`, which the inequality does not need. The explicit `heq` equality hypothesis is necessary: a prior default-valued epsilon binder did not assert the definition and made the statement false.

articles.title: Baker–Wüstholz theorem on linear forms in logarithms
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $K$ be a number
field of degree $d = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$, let $\varphi : K \to \mathbb{C}$ be a ring homomorphism,
and let $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$ be nonzero elements of $K$. Let $b_1, \dots, b_n$ be integers
and let $B \ge 2$ be a natural number with $|b_i| \le B$ for every $i$. With $\log$ the principal
branch of the complex logarithm, suppose that $\Lambda = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i \log \varphi(\alpha_i)$
is nonzero. Then

$$\log |\Lambda| \ge -C(n, d) \max\left(\log B, \frac{1}{d}\right) \prod_{i=1}^n h'(\alpha_i),$$

where $C(n, d)$ is the Baker–Wüstholz constant and $h'$ is the modified height with respect to
$\varphi$.

## Sources

- A. Baker, G. Wüstholz, Logarithmic forms and group varieties, J. reine angew. Math. 442 (1993), 19-62. Problem `bakerWustholz_linearForms_logs` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: The Baker–Wüstholz constant
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $d$, the Baker–Wüstholz constant
is the real number
$C(n, d) = 18 \cdot (n + 1)! \cdot n^{n+1} \cdot (32 d)^{n+2} \cdot \log(2nd)$.

articles.title: Modified height
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a number field of degree $d = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ and let
$\varphi : K \to \mathbb{C}$ be a ring homomorphism. For $\alpha \in K$, the modified height of
$\alpha$ with respect to $\varphi$ is

$$h'(\alpha) = \max\left(h(\alpha), \frac{|\log \varphi(\alpha)|}{d}, \frac{1}{d}\right),$$

where $\log$ is the principal branch of the complex logarithm (with $\log 0 = 0$) and $h(\alpha)$
is the absolute logarithmic Weil height of $\alpha$: $\frac{1}{d}$ times the sum of
$\log \max(1, |\alpha|_v)$ over the places $v$ of $K$, with the absolute values normalized so that
the product formula holds and each complex place counted twice.

articles.title: Matveev's lower bound for linear forms in logarithms (real case)
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a number
field of degree $D = [L : \mathbb{Q}]$ with a field embedding $f : L \to \mathbb{R}$, let $s \ge 1$
be a natural number, and let $\eta_1, \dots, \eta_s \in L$ satisfy $\eta_i \ne 1$ and
$f(\eta_i) > 0$ for every $i$. Let $d_1, \dots, d_s$ be nonzero integers and let $B$ be a real
number with $B \ge 1$ and $|d_i| \le B$ for every $i$. Let $A_1, \dots, A_s$ be real numbers with
$A_j \ge \max(D\,h(\eta_j), |\log f(\eta_j)|, 0.16)$ for every $j$, where $h$ is the absolute
logarithmic Weil height. Put $\Gamma = f(\eta_1)^{d_1} \cdots f(\eta_s)^{d_s} - 1$. If
$\Gamma \ne 0$, then

$$\log|\Gamma| > -1.4 \cdot 30^{s+3} \, s^{4.5} \, D^2 (1 + \log D)(1 + \log B) \, A_1 \cdots A_s.$$

No integrality is assumed on the $\eta_i$, so the statement also covers non-integral algebraic
numbers, such as the element in the source's application whose minimal polynomial has leading
coefficient $23$. The source states the bound with $B = \max_i |d_i|$; since the right-hand side
increases with $B$, any real $B \ge 1$ bounding every $|d_i|$ may be used.

## Sources

- Salah Eddine Rihane, Chèfiath Awero Adegbindin, and Alain Togbé, "Fermat Padovan And Perrin Numbers", Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.6.2, Section 2.1 and its Matveev theorem. Source URL <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Togbe/togbe16.tex>, definitions-and-theorem source lines 148–178, theorem lines 172–178. The source cites Bugeaud–Mignotte–Siksek, Theorem 9.4, as a modified consequence of E. M. Matveev, "An explicit lower bound for a homogeneous rational linear form in the logarithms of algebraic numbers, II", Izv. Math. 64 (2000), 1217–1269.

articles.title: Schmidt's subspace theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a finite set with at least two elements, and
for $i \in \sigma$ let $L_i(x) = \sum_{j \in \sigma} a_{ij} x_j$ be linear forms whose
coefficients $a_{ij} \in \mathbb{C}$ are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ and whose coefficient
vectors $(a_{ij})_{j \in \sigma}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{C}$. Let
$\varepsilon > 0$ be real. Then there is a finite set $S$ of nonzero vectors in
$\mathbb{Z}^\sigma$ such that every $x \in \mathbb{Z}^\sigma$ with
$\left|\prod_{i \in \sigma} L_i(x)\right| < \|x\|^{-\varepsilon}$, where
$\|x\| = \max_{j \in \sigma} |x_j|$, satisfies $\sum_{i \in \sigma} c_i x_i = 0$ for some $c \in S$.

Every proper subspace of $\mathbb{Q}^\sigma$ lies in a hyperplane $\sum_i c_i x_i = 0$ with a
nonzero integer vector $c$, so this is the usual form: these $x$ lie in finitely many proper
subspaces.

## Sources

- W.M. Schmidt, Diophantine approximation, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 785, Springer Verlag 1980, Chap. V,VI,VII. Problem `schmidt_subspace` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Roth's theorem with divisibility conditions
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic number, let
$0 < \varepsilon \le 1$, and let $S$ be a finite index set carrying, for each $l \in S$, a natural
number $p_l$ and reals $\mu_l, \nu_l \ge 0$ with $\sigma = \sum_{l \in S} (\mu_l + \nu_l)$ less
than $2 + \varepsilon$. Then there are only finitely many rationals $q$, written in lowest terms
with numerator $n$ and denominator $d \ge 1$, such that
$|\alpha - q| < 1/d^{2 + \varepsilon - \sigma}$ and there are exponents $a_l, b_l \in \mathbb{N}$
for $l \in S$ with $\prod_{l \in S} p_l^{a_l}$ dividing $n$, $\prod_{l \in S} p_l^{b_l}$ dividing
$d$, and $d^{\mu_l} \le p_l^{a_l}$ and $d^{\nu_l} \le p_l^{b_l}$ for every $l \in S$.

Taking $S$ empty gives the usual archimedean approximation statement.

articles.title: Ridout's $p$-adic extension of Roth's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\xi$ be an irrational real algebraic
number, let $\varepsilon > 0$, and let $S$ be a finite set of primes. For a rational number $r$,
write $r = p/q$ in lowest terms with $p \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $q \ge 1$, and let
$H(r) = \max(|p|, q)$ be its height. For a prime $\ell$, let $|\cdot|_\ell$ be the $\ell$-adic
absolute value on $\mathbb{Q}$, normalized by $|\ell|_\ell = \ell^{-1}$. Then only finitely many
rationals $r = p/q$ satisfy

$$\Bigl(\prod_{\ell \in S} |p|_\ell |q|_\ell\Bigr) |\xi - r| < \frac{1}{H(r)^{2 + \varepsilon}}.$$

The source prints the right side as $1/q^{2 + \varepsilon}$. Over all rationals that bound fails:
with $2 \in S$ and $\xi = \sqrt{2}$, every $r = 2^k$ with $k \ge 1$ gives left side
$1 - \sqrt{2}/2^k < 1$, so the height $H(r)$ is used instead.

Proof: The proof follows Roth's auxiliary-polynomial and index route, with the
S-adic integrality step supplied by valuation divisibility and a finite pigeonhole.

## Sources

- Boris Adamczewski, "The Many Faces of the Kempner Number", Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.2.15, `thmRi` environment, lines 736–746, attributed there to Ridout, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Adamczewski/adam6.tex>.

articles.title: Thue–Siegel–Roth theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational real number that is algebraic over
$\mathbb{Q}$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real. Then only finitely many rational numbers $q$
satisfy $|\alpha - q| < 1 / b^{2 + \varepsilon}$, where $b$ is the denominator of $q$ in lowest
terms.

Proof: The proof constructs Siegel's auxiliary polynomial, bounds its index at rational
approximation points by a Taylor estimate, and contradicts the inductive Roth lemma.

## Sources

- K. F. Roth, Rational approximations to algebraic numbers, Mathematika 2 (1955) 1–20; predecessors Thue 1909 and Siegel 1921; textbook in Schmidt, Diophantine Approximation

articles.title: Calegari–Dimitrov–Tang linear independence theorems
articles.statement:
Let
$\chi : \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ be given by $\chi(0) = 0$, $\chi(1) = 1$ and
$\chi(2) = -1$ (the nontrivial Dirichlet character modulo $3$), let $\zeta$ be the Riemann zeta
function and let $L(s, \chi)$ be the Dirichlet $L$-function of $\chi$. Then the complex numbers
$1$, $\zeta(2)$ and $L(2, \chi)$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Moreover, let $m$
and $n$ be integers, neither of them equal to $-1$ or $0$, with $10^6 |m - n| < |n|$, and put
$\ell_m = \log(1 + 1/m)$ and $\ell_n = \log(1 + 1/n)$. Then $\ell_m \ell_n$ is irrational, and if
$m \ne n$, the real numbers $1$, $\ell_m$, $\ell_n$ and $\ell_m \ell_n$ are linearly independent
over $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15403. Problem `cdt_linearIndependent` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Gelfond–Schneider theorem for every value of a complex power
articles.statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{C}$
be algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $a \neq 1$ and $b \notin \mathbb{Q}$, and let $z \in \mathbb{C}$
satisfy $e^z = a$. Then $e^{bz}$ is transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$.

The hypothesis $e^z = a$ already implies $a \neq 0$. Taking $z = \log a + 2 \pi i n$, where
$\log a$ is the principal logarithm and $n$ is an integer, recovers every branch of $a^b$.

## Sources

- A. O. Gelfond, *Sur le septième problème de Hilbert* (1934), and T. Schneider, *Transzendenzuntersuchungen periodischer Funktionen I. Transzendenz von Potenzen*, J. Reine Angew. Math. 172 (1935), 65–69, DOI 10.1515/crll.1935.172.65. Explicit arbitrary- and principal-branch applications occur in arXiv:2311.11127v1, arXiv:2607.23662v1, and arXiv:2608.17545v1. The Lean formalization in arXiv:2603.24823v1 states only the principal `Complex.cpow` value; this declaration records the arbitrary-logarithm form.

articles.title: Gelfond–Schneider theorem for real powers
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be real numbers that
are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, with $\alpha > 0$, $\alpha \neq 1$ and $\beta$ irrational. Then
the real power $\alpha^\beta$ is transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- A. O. Gelfond, Sur le septième problème de Hilbert, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 2 (1934) 1–6 and T. Schneider 1935 independent; textbook in Baker, Transcendental Number Theory

articles.title: Hermite–Lindemann theorem
articles.statement:
If $\alpha$ is a nonzero complex number that is algebraic over
$\mathbb{Q}$, then $e^{\alpha}$ is transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- C. Hermite, Sur la fonction exponentielle, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 77 (1873) for e; F. von Lindemann, Über die Zahl π, Math. Ann. 20 (1882) 213–225 extension to π; textbook in Baker, Transcendental Number Theory

articles.title: Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be a finite index set, let $\alpha_i$
($i \in \iota$) be pairwise distinct complex numbers that are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$, and let
$\beta_i$ ($i \in \iota$) be complex numbers that are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ and not all
zero. Then $\sum_{i \in \iota} \beta_i e^{\alpha_i} \neq 0$.

## Sources

- F. von Lindemann 1882 and K. Weierstrass, Zu Lindemann's Abhandlung Über die Ludolph'sche Zahl, 1885; textbook in Baker, Transcendental Number Theory

articles.title: Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem (universe-polymorphic form)
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be a finite index
set, let $\alpha_i$ ($i \in \iota$) be pairwise distinct complex numbers that are algebraic over
$\mathbb{Q}$, and let $\beta_i$ ($i \in \iota$) be complex numbers that are algebraic over
$\mathbb{Q}$ and not all zero. Then $\sum_{i \in \iota} \beta_i e^{\alpha_i} \neq 0$.

articles.title: Doubly exponential floors are Type 2 irrationality sequences for all but countably many bases
articles.statement:
**Doubly exponential floors are Type 2 irrationality sequences for all but countably many
bases.** For all real numbers $\alpha > 1$ outside a countable set, the sequence
$(\lfloor \alpha^{2^{n+1}} \rfloor)_{n \ge 0}$ is a Type 2 irrationality sequence: for every
sequence $(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of positive integers with $b_n / \lfloor \alpha^{2^{n+1}} \rfloor \to 1$,
the series $\sum_n 1 / b_n$ does not converge to a rational number.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Theorem 2 and the definition of Type 2 irrationality sequences preceding it.

articles.title: Characterization of the denominators of the Millin series
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a
sequence of positive integers with $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \le 2/3$ for all $n$ and
$\sum_n 1 / a_n = (5 - \sqrt 5) / 2$. Then $a_n = F_{2^{n+1}}$ for all $n \ge 0$, where $F_k$
is the $k$-th Fibonacci number ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$); that is, $a$ is the sequence
$F_2, F_4, F_8, \ldots$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Recovering a doubly exponential sequence from its reciprocal sum
articles.statement:
Let $\beta \ge 0$ and
$r$ be real numbers, and let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers with
$|a_n^2 / a_{n+1} - \beta| \le 1/3$ for all $n$ and $\sum_n 1 / a_n = r$. Write
$x_n = r - \sum_{k\lt n} 1 / a_k$. Then for every $n$ with $a_n \ge 8 (\beta + 1/3)^2$ we have
$a_n = \lfloor x_n^{-1} + \beta + 1/2 \rfloor$, that is, $a_n$ is the integer nearest to
$x_n^{-1} + \beta$, with halves rounded up. Moreover, if $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \to \beta$, then
$|x_n^{-1} + \beta - a_n| \to 0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Characterization of the Sylvester sequence
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of
positive integers with $2/3 \le a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \le 4/3$ for all $n$ and $\sum_n 1 / a_n = 1$.
Then $a_n = s_n(1)$ for all $n \ge 0$, where $(s_n(1))_{n \ge 0}$ is the generalized Sylvester
sequence with parameter $1$, that is, the Sylvester sequence $2, 3, 7, 43, \ldots$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Eventual vanishing of the pseudo-greedy gaps of a rational number
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a positive
rational number and let $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the gap sequence of the pseudo-greedy
expansion of $r$. Suppose that $\liminf_n \varepsilon_n \prod_{k\lt n} (1 - \varepsilon_k) \ge 0$,
that is, for every $\delta > 0$ we have $\varepsilon_n \prod_{k\lt n} (1 - \varepsilon_k) \ge -\delta$
for all sufficiently large $n$; or that $\varepsilon_n \ge 0$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
Then $\varepsilon_n = 0$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Erdős–Straus and Badea criterion for the Sylvester recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a
sequence of positive integers with $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \to 1$ such that $\sum_n 1 / a_n$ converges
to a rational number. Suppose that
$\liminf_n (a_0 \cdots a_{n-1} / a_n)(1 - a_n^2 / a_{n+1}) \ge 0$, that is, for every
$\delta > 0$ this quantity is at least $-\delta$ for all sufficiently large $n$; or that
$a_{n+1} \ge a_n^2 - a_n + 1$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Then
$a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Tails that are pseudo-greedy expansions
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive
integers with $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \to 1$ such that $\sum_n 1 / a_n$ converges. Then there is a
natural number $N$ such that, with $r = \sum_{k \ge 0} 1 / a_{N+k}$, the tail
$(a_{N+n})_{n \ge 0}$ is the pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$, and the gap sequence of this
expansion tends to $0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Convergence of the pseudo-greedy expansion
articles.statement:
For every real number $r > 0$, the
pseudo-greedy expansion $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of $r$ satisfies $\sum_n 1 / a_n = r$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Koizumi's conjecture is equivalent to the Erdős–Graham question
articles.statement:
The following are
equivalent. (1) For every positive rational number $r$ whose pseudo-greedy gap sequence
$(\varepsilon_n)_{n \ge 0}$ tends to $0$, we have $\varepsilon_n = 0$ for all sufficiently large
$n$. (2) Every sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of positive integers with $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \to 1$ such
that $\sum_n 1 / a_n$ converges to a rational number satisfies $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$ for
all sufficiently large $n$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Theorem 3, with Conjecture 1 and Question 1.

articles.title: Second term of the pseudo-greedy expansion of $1$
articles.statement:
The pseudo-greedy expansion
$(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of $1$ satisfies $a_1 = 3$.

The remainder after the first term $a_0 = 2$ is $1 - 1/2 = 1/2$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Example 1 (the expansion of `1` is the Sylvester sequence).

articles.title: The pseudo-greedy expansion of 1 starts with 2
articles.statement:
The first term $a_0$ of the
pseudo-greedy expansion of $1$ equals $2$, the first Sylvester number.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Example 1 (the expansion of `1` is the Sylvester sequence).

articles.title: Structure of the pseudo-greedy expansion of a rational
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be positive
integers, let $r = p/q$, and let $(x_n)$, $(a_n)$ and $(\varepsilon_n)$ be the remainder
sequence, the pseudo-greedy expansion and the gap sequence of $r$. Put
$d_n = q a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1}$ (so $d_0 = q$). Then there are positive integers $c_n$ and
integers $e_n$ ($n \ge 0$) such that for every $n$ we have $x_n = c_n / d_n$,
$\varepsilon_n = e_n / c_n$, $e_n \equiv d_n \pmod{c_n}$, $-c_n/2 \le e_n < c_n/2$,
$a_n = (d_n - e_n)/c_n + 1$, $c_{n+1} = c_n - e_n$ and $d_{n+1} = d_n a_n$. Moreover, as
$n \to \infty$, $c_n = O(a_0 \cdots a_{n-1} / a_n)$ and $c_n = O(1.5^n)$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Recursion for the pseudo-greedy expansion
articles.statement:
Let $r > 0$ be a real number, and let
$(a_n)$ be its pseudo-greedy expansion and $(\varepsilon_n)$ its gap sequence. Then for every
$n \ge 0$,

$$a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n^2}{1 - \varepsilon_n} - a_n + (1 - \varepsilon_{n+1}).$$

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Pseudo-greedy expansion
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a real number with pseudo-greedy remainder sequence
$(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$. The pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$ is the integer sequence
$a_n = \lfloor x_n^{-1} + 1 + 1/2 \rfloor$ for $n \ge 0$; that is, $a_n$ is the integer nearest
to $x_n^{-1} + 1$, with halves rounded up.

Here $0^{-1}$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Section 2 (definition of the pseudo-greedy expansion).

articles.title: The first gap of the expansion of 1 vanishes
articles.statement:
The first term $\varepsilon_0$ of the gap
sequence of the pseudo-greedy expansion of $1$ is $0$: the first remainder is $x_0 = 1$ and the
first term of the expansion is $a_0 = 2$, so $\varepsilon_0 = x_0^{-1} + 1 - a_0 = 1 + 1 - 2 = 0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Example 1 (`ε_n = 0` for the expansion of `1`).

articles.title: A vanishing gap stays zero
articles.statement:
Let $r > 0$ be a real number and let $(\varepsilon_n)$ be
the gap sequence of its pseudo-greedy expansion. For every $n \ge 0$, if $\varepsilon_n = 0$,
then $\varepsilon_{n+1} = 0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Gap sequence of the pseudo-greedy expansion
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a real number, and let $(x_n)$
be the remainder sequence and $(a_n)$ the pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$. The gap sequence of
$r$ is the real sequence $\varepsilon_n = x_n^{-1} + 1 - a_n$ for $n \ge 0$.

Here $0^{-1}$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Section 2 (definition of the gap sequence).

articles.title: Remainder recursion
articles.statement:
For every real number $r$ and every $n \ge 0$, the remainder
sequence $(x_n)$ and the pseudo-greedy expansion $(a_n)$ of $r$ satisfy $x_{n+1} = x_n - 1/a_n$.

Here $1/0$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Section 2 (definition of the remainder sequence).

articles.title: Pseudo-greedy remainder sequence
articles.statement:
For a real number $r$, the remainder sequence
$(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of the pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$ is defined by $x_0 = r$ and
$x_{n+1} = x_n - 1/a_n$, where $a_n = \lfloor x_n^{-1} + 1 + 1/2 \rfloor$ is the integer
nearest to $x_n^{-1} + 1$, with halves rounded up.

Here $0^{-1}$ and $1/0$ are read as $0$.

## Sources

- Junnosuke Koizumi, *Irrationality of the Reciprocal Sum of Doubly Exponential Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A28, Section 2 (definitions of the pseudo-greedy expansion and its remainder sequence).

articles.title: Counting $\beta$-Beatty terms between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with $1 < \alpha < 2$, let $\beta$ be a real number with
$\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, and let $B$ be the set of the numbers $\lfloor k\beta\rfloor$ for
positive integers $k$. Then for every positive integer $n$, the number of elements of $B$ in the
open interval $(\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor, \lfloor n\beta\rfloor)$ equals
$\lfloor n(2 - \alpha)\rfloor$.

By Beatty's theorem, the Beatty sequences of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are then complementary.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Theorem 3.

articles.title: The $\beta$-Beatty counts between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$ form a Beatty sequence
articles.statement:
**The $\beta$-Beatty counts between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$ form a
Beatty sequence.** Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with $1 < \alpha < 2$, let $\beta$ be a
real number with $\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, and let $B$ be the set of the numbers
$\lfloor k\beta\rfloor$ for positive integers $k$. Then there is a real number $r$ with
$0 < r < 1$ such that for every positive integer $n$, the number of elements of $B$ in the open
interval $(\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor, \lfloor n\beta\rfloor)$ equals $\lfloor nr\rfloor$.

By Beatty's theorem, the Beatty sequences of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are then complementary.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Increments of the $\beta$-Beatty counts between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$
articles.statement:
**Increments of the $\beta$-Beatty counts between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and
$\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$.** Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with $1 < \alpha < 2$, let $\beta$
be a real number with $\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, let $B$ be the set of the numbers
$\lfloor k\beta\rfloor$ for positive integers $k$, and for an integer $m$ let $r(m)$ be the number
of elements of $B$ in the open interval $(\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor, \lfloor m\beta\rfloor)$. Then for
every positive integer $n$, the difference $r(n + 1) - r(n)$ is $0$ or $1$, and it equals $1$ if
and only if $\lfloor (n + 1)\alpha\rfloor - \lfloor n\alpha\rfloor = 1$.

By Beatty's theorem, the Beatty sequences of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are then complementary.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Counting $\alpha$-Beatty terms between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with $1 < \alpha < 2$, let $\beta$ be a real number with
$\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, and let $A$ be the set of the numbers $\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor$ for
positive integers $k$. Then for every positive integer $n$, the number of elements of $A$ in the
open interval $(\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor, \lfloor n\beta\rfloor)$ equals
$\lfloor n(\beta - 2)\rfloor$.

By Beatty's theorem, the Beatty sequences of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are then complementary.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Increments of the $\alpha$-Beatty counts between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$
articles.statement:
**Increments of the $\alpha$-Beatty counts between $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and
$\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$.** Let $\beta$ be an irrational number with $\beta > 2$, let $\alpha$ be a
real number with $\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, let $A$ be the set of the numbers
$\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor$ for positive integers $k$, and for an integer $m$ let $c(m)$ be the number
of elements of $A$ in the open interval $(\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor, \lfloor m\beta\rfloor)$. Then for
every positive integer $n$, the difference $c(n + 1) - c(n)$ is $\lfloor\beta\rfloor - 2$ or
$\lfloor\beta\rfloor - 1$, and it equals $\lfloor\beta\rfloor - 2$ if and only if
$\lfloor (n + 1)\beta\rfloor - \lfloor n\beta\rfloor = \lfloor\beta\rfloor$.

By Beatty's theorem, the Beatty sequences of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are then complementary.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Beatty's theorem and its converse
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. The
set of the numbers $\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor$ for positive integers $k$ and the set of the numbers
$\lfloor k\beta\rfloor$ for positive integers $k$ are disjoint and their union is the set of
positive integers if and only if $\alpha$ is irrational and $\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$.

The hypothesis $\beta > 0$ cannot be dropped: for irrational $0 < \alpha < 1$ the number $\beta$
with $\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$ is negative, and the two sets do not partition the positive
integers.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Theorem 1 (Beatty–Rayleigh).

articles.title: Multiplicities of $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ are $k$ plus the indicator of a Beatty set
articles.statement:
Let
$k$ be a positive integer and let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with
$1/(k + 1) < \alpha < 1/k$. Then there is a real number $\delta > 0$ such that, writing $D$ for
the set of the numbers $\lfloor m\delta\rfloor$ for positive integers $m$, every non-negative
integer $t$ equals $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for exactly $k + 1$ positive integers $n$ if $t \in D$,
and for exactly $k$ positive integers $n$ if $t \notin D$.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Multiplicities of the values of $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for $1/(k + 1) < \alpha < 1/k$
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a positive integer and let $\alpha$ be a real number with
$1/(k + 1) < \alpha < 1/k$. Then every non-negative integer $t$ equals $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$
for exactly $k$ or exactly $k + 1$ positive integers $n$, there are infinitely many $t$ for which
it is exactly $k$, and there are infinitely many $t$ for which it is exactly $k + 1$.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Lemma 1.

articles.title: The values of $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ of each multiplicity form Beatty sets
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
positive integer and let $\alpha$ be an irrational number with $1/(k + 1) < \alpha < 1/k$. Then
there are real numbers $\gamma > 0$ and $\delta > 0$ such that the positive integers $t$ that
equal $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for exactly $k + 1$ positive integers $n$ are exactly the numbers
$\lfloor m\gamma\rfloor$ for positive integers $m$, and the positive integers $t$ that equal
$\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for exactly $k$ positive integers $n$ are exactly the numbers
$\lfloor m\delta\rfloor$ for positive integers $m$.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Multiplicity $k + 1$ for $\alpha$ is multiplicity $k$ for $\alpha/(1 - \alpha)$
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be
a positive integer, let $\alpha$ be a real number with $1/(k + 1) < \alpha < 1/k$, and let
$\beta = \alpha/(1 - \alpha)$. Then a non-negative integer $t$ equals $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for
exactly $k + 1$ positive integers $n$ if and only if it equals $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$ for exactly
$k$ positive integers $n$.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Polanco's floor identity for $\lfloor (\beta - 2) n \rfloor$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an
irrational real number with $1 < \alpha < 2$, let $\beta$ be a real number with
$\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, and write $a_n = \lfloor n\alpha \rfloor$ and
$b_n = \lfloor n\beta \rfloor$. Then for every positive integer $n$,

$$
\lfloor \alpha^{-1} b_n \rfloor - \lfloor \alpha^{-1} (a_n + 1) \rfloor
= \lfloor (\beta - 2) n \rfloor.
$$

Since $\alpha > 1$, Beatty's theorem says that the conditions "$\alpha$ is irrational and
$\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$" mean exactly that $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ and $(b_n)_{n \ge 1}$ are
complementary Beatty sequences.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Theorem 5, identity (8).

articles.title: Polanco's floor identity for $\lfloor (2 - \alpha) n \rfloor$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an
irrational real number with $1 < \alpha < 2$, let $\beta$ be a real number with
$\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$, and write $a_m = \lfloor m\alpha \rfloor$ and
$b_m = \lfloor m\beta \rfloor$ for integers $m$ (so $b_0 = 0$). Then for every positive
integer $n$,

$$
\lfloor \beta^{-1} (b_{n-1} + 1) \rfloor - \lfloor \beta^{-1} a_n \rfloor
= \lfloor (2 - \alpha) n \rfloor.
$$

Since $\alpha > 1$, Beatty's theorem says that the conditions "$\alpha$ is irrational and
$\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$" mean exactly that $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ and $(b_n)_{n \ge 1}$ are
complementary Beatty sequences.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Theorem 5, identity (7).

articles.title: Multiplicities of Polanco's skipping sequence
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer, let
$\alpha$ be an irrational real number with $(2k - 1)/k < \alpha < (2k + 1)/(k + 1)$, and let
$\beta$ be a real number with $\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} = 1$. Let
$A = \{\lfloor j\alpha \rfloor : j \ge 1\}$ and, for each positive integer $n$, let $c_n$ be
the number of elements of $A$ strictly between $\lfloor n\alpha \rfloor$ and
$\lfloor n\beta \rfloor$. Let $f(x) = 2 - 1/x$, let $f^{k-1}$ be its $(k-1)$-fold iterate, and
let $\delta = -1 + 1/f^{k-1}(\alpha - 1)$, that is,
$\delta = -1 + 1/(2 - 1/(2 - \cdots - 1/(\alpha - 1)))$ with $k - 1$ twos. Then for every
non-negative integer $m$, the number of positive integers $n$ with $c_n = m$ is $k$ if
$m = \lfloor j\delta \rfloor$ for some integer $j \ge 1$, and $k - 1$ otherwise, where an
infinite set is counted as having $0$ elements.

For $k = 1$ this gives $\delta = 1/(\alpha - 1) - 1 = \beta - 2$, and the multiplicity is one
or zero.

## Sources

- Geremias Polanco, *Decomposition of Beatty and Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A104, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Beatty term as a natural-number floor
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$ and every real
number $\alpha$, the Beatty term $b_n(\alpha)$ equals the natural-number floor of $n/\alpha$:
the largest natural number $m$ with $m \le n/\alpha$ when $n/\alpha \ge 0$, and $0$ when
$n/\alpha < 0$. Division by zero is read as $0$, so $n/0 = 0$.

articles.title: Beatty sequences are almost Beatty
articles.statement:
For every real number $\alpha$ with
$0 < \alpha < 1$, the sequence of Beatty terms $n \mapsto b_n(\alpha) = \lfloor n/\alpha \rfloor$,
indexed by the positive integers $n$, is an almost Beatty sequence for $\alpha$.

The proof takes the bound $B = 0$ and derives strict monotonicity and positivity from
$0 < \alpha < 1$.

articles.title: Beatty term
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$ and a real number $\alpha$, the Beatty term
$b_n(\alpha)$ is the natural number $\max(\lfloor n/\alpha \rfloor, 0)$: the $n$-th term
$\lfloor n \cdot (1/\alpha) \rfloor$ of the Beatty sequence of slope $1/\alpha$, truncated at
$0$. Division by zero is read as $0$, so $b_n(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Almost Beatty partition
articles.statement:
Given real numbers $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$, three
sequences $s_1, s_2, s_3$ of natural numbers indexed by the positive integers form an almost
Beatty partition when, for each $i$, the sequence $s_i$ is an almost Beatty sequence for
$\alpha_i$, and the three sequences form a three-way partition of the positive integers: their
ranges are pairwise disjoint and their union is the set of positive integers.

articles.title: Almost Beatty sequence
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. A sequence $(s_n)_{n \ge 1}$ of
natural numbers indexed by the positive integers is an almost Beatty sequence for $\alpha$ when
$0 < \alpha < 1$, the sequence is strictly increasing, $s_n > 0$ for every $n \ge 1$, and
there is a natural number $B$ with $|s_n - b_n(\alpha)| \le B$ for every $n \ge 1$, where
$b_n(\alpha)$ is the Beatty term, equal to $\lfloor n/\alpha \rfloor$ once $\alpha > 0$.

articles.title: Three-way partition of the positive integers
articles.statement:
Three sequences $s_1, s_2, s_3$ of natural
numbers indexed by the positive integers partition the positive integers when their ranges are
pairwise disjoint, that is, $s_i(m) \ne s_j(n)$ for all $i \ne j$ and all positive integers $m$
and $n$, and the union of their ranges is exactly the set of positive integers: a natural
number $k$ is a value of some $s_i$ if and only if $k > 0$.

articles.title: Uspensky's theorem on Beatty partitions
articles.statement:
For a real number $\alpha$ with
$0 < \alpha < 1$, let $B_\alpha = \{\lfloor n/\alpha \rfloor : n \text{ an integer}, n \ge 1\}$
be its Beatty sequence. Let $k \ge 3$ and let $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k$ be real numbers with
$0 < \alpha_i < 1$ for every $i$. Then $B_{\alpha_1}, \dots, B_{\alpha_k}$ do not partition the
positive integers: it is not the case both that $B_{\alpha_i} \cap B_{\alpha_j} = \emptyset$
for all $i \ne j$ and that $B_{\alpha_1} \cup \dots \cup B_{\alpha_k} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$.

No irrationality hypothesis is imposed on the $\alpha_i$.

## Sources

- A. J. Hildebrand, Xiaomin Li, Junxian Li, and Yun Xie, *Almost Beatty Partitions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.4.6, Theorem B (Uspensky's theorem), lines 234–236, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Hildebrand/hilde2.tex>; first proved by Uspensky in 1927 (lines 238–244).

articles.title: Erdős Problem 992 has a negative answer
articles.statement:
For a sequence of integers $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$, a real
number $\alpha$ and a natural number $N$, let $D(N)$ be the supremum, over rationals $p, q$ with
$0 \le p \le q \le 1$, of $\lvert A(p, q) - (q - p) N \rvert$, where $A(p, q)$ is the number of
indices $n < N$ for which the fractional part $\{\alpha x_n\}$ lies in $[p, q]$. It is not true
that for every strictly increasing sequence of integers $x_0 < x_1 < \cdots$, for almost every
$\alpha \in [0, 1]$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real constant $C$ with
$D(N) \le C \sqrt{N} (\log N)^{\varepsilon}$ for all sufficiently large $N$.

Berkes and Philipp construct an increasing integer sequence $(n_k)$ with
$\limsup_N \lvert \sum_{k \le N} \cos(2\pi n_k \alpha) \rvert / \sqrt{N \log N} = \infty$ for almost
