The stability gauge of Definition 3 is $\lVert m \rVert_K = \ell \mu + d - u$ whenever
$m / \rho^\ell \in T_u$, with a displacement $d$ independent of $m$; so this is the identity
$\lVert \rho n \rVert_K = \lVert n \rVert_K + \mu$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 6.

articles.title: The layer index of a quasi-arithmetical compact set is well defined (Proposition 5)
articles.statement:
Let
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a quasi-arithmetical compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$. For
each natural number $j$ let $K^{(j)}$ be the $j$-th iterated derived set of $K$ and
$T_j = K^{(j)} \setminus K^{(j+1)}$ its $j$-th layer. If $n, p, q, v, w$ are natural numbers with
$n / \rho^p \in T_v$ and $n / \rho^q \in T_w$, then $p \mu - v = q \mu - w$ as integers.

The paper takes $n$ positive; $n = 0$ is allowed here, and then the claim is vacuous because $0$
lies in no layer.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Quasi-arithmetical compact sets
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $\mu$ and $\rho$ be
natural numbers. Then $K$ is a quasi-arithmetical compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$
when $\rho \ge 2$, $K$ is a self-similar compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, and there
is a function $\kappa : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that
$K \setminus \{0\} = \{n / \rho^k : n, k \in \mathbb{N},\ \rho \nmid n,\ k \ge \kappa(n)\}$.

The paper's $\kappa$ is defined only on $\mathbb{N} \setminus \rho\mathbb{N}$; here its values at
multiples of $\rho$ are irrelevant.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 2.

articles.title: Quasi-arithmetical compact sets are self-similar
articles.statement:
If $K$ is a quasi-arithmetical compact
set of module $\mu$ and natural-number ratio $\rho$, then $K$ is a self-similar compact set of
module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 2.

articles.title: Enumerating the derived sets of a self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a self-similar
compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, let $n \ge 1$, and write $K^{(n)}$ for the $n$-th
derived set of $K$. Let $\alpha \mapsto K[\alpha]$ and $\alpha \mapsto K^{(n)}[\alpha]$ be
strictly decreasing maps from the ordinals $\alpha \le \omega^\omega$ onto $K$ and onto
$K^{(n)}$, respectively. Then $K^{(n)}[\alpha] = K[\omega^n (1 + \alpha)]$ (ordinal
arithmetic) for every ordinal $\alpha \le \omega^\omega$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Order type of a self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a self-similar compact set of module
$\mu \ge 1$ and ratio $\rho$. Then there is a strictly decreasing map $\alpha \mapsto K[\alpha]$
from the ordinals $\alpha \le \omega^\omega$ onto $K$ (so $K$ has order type $\omega^\omega + 1$
under the reverse order) with $K[\omega^\omega] = 0$, $K[0] > 0$ and $K \subseteq [0, K[0]]$.

The hypothesis $\mu \ge 1$ is the paper's convention that $\mu$ is a natural number; for
$\mu = 0$ the set $\{0\}$ would satisfy the definition.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Decomposition of a self-similar compact set into layers
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a self-similar
compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, and for $u \ge 0$ let
$T_u = K^{(u)} \setminus K^{(u+1)}$, where $K^{(u)}$ is the $u$-th derived set of $K$. Then

$$K = \{0\} \cup \bigcup_{n \ge 0} \bigcup_{0 \le u < \mu} \rho^{-n} T_u,$$

where $\rho^{-n} T_u = \{\rho^{-n} x : x \in T_u\}$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 2, equation (2).

articles.title: Limits across the last layer of a self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a self-similar
compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, with layers $T_u = K^{(u)} \setminus K^{(u+1)}$
for $u \ge 0$, where $K^{(u)}$ is the $u$-th derived set of $K$. Suppose that for every $u$,
$\alpha \mapsto T_u[\alpha]$ is a strictly decreasing map from the ordinals $\alpha < \omega^\omega$
onto $T_u$. Then for every ordinal $\alpha < \omega^\omega$,
$T_{\mu-1}[\omega \alpha + n] \to T_0[\alpha] / \rho$ as $n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers
(ordinal arithmetic in the index).

These hypotheses force $\mu \ge 1$, so $\mu - 1$ is a genuine index.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Limits between consecutive layers of a self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
self-similar compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, with layers
$T_u = K^{(u)} \setminus K^{(u+1)}$ for $u \ge 0$, where $K^{(u)}$ is the $u$-th derived set of
$K$. Suppose that for every $u$, $\alpha \mapsto T_u[\alpha]$ is a strictly decreasing map from
the ordinals $\alpha < \omega^\omega$ onto $T_u$. Then for every $u \ge 0$ and every ordinal
$\alpha < \omega^\omega$, $T_u[\omega \alpha + n] \to T_{u+1}[\alpha]$ as $n \to \infty$ through
the natural numbers (ordinal arithmetic in the index).

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Enumerating the higher layers of a self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a self-similar
compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, let $u \ge 1$, and let
$T_u = K^{(u)} \setminus K^{(u+1)}$, where $K^{(u)}$ is the $u$-th derived set of $K$. Let
$\alpha \mapsto K[\alpha]$ be a strictly decreasing map from the ordinals $\alpha \le \omega^\omega$
onto $K$, and $\alpha \mapsto T_u[\alpha]$ a strictly decreasing map from the ordinals
$\alpha < \omega^\omega$ onto $T_u$. Then $T_u[\alpha] = K[\omega^u (\alpha + 1)]$ (ordinal
arithmetic) for every ordinal $\alpha < \omega^\omega$.

The paper writes $0 \le \alpha \le \omega^\omega$; the layer has order type $\omega^\omega$, so the
range here is $\alpha < \omega^\omega$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Enumerating the isolated points of a self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a self-similar
compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, and let $T_0 = K \setminus K'$ be the set of
isolated points of $K$, where $K'$ is the derived set of $K$. Let $\alpha \mapsto K[\alpha]$ be a
strictly decreasing map from the ordinals $\alpha \le \omega^\omega$ onto $K$, and
$\alpha \mapsto T_0[\alpha]$ a strictly decreasing map from the ordinals $\alpha < \omega^\omega$
onto $T_0$. Then for every ordinal $\alpha < \omega^\omega$, $T_0[\alpha] = K[\alpha]$ if
$\alpha < \omega$, and $T_0[\alpha] = K[\alpha + 1]$ if $\omega \le \alpha$.

The paper writes $0 \le \alpha \le \omega^\omega$; the layer has order type $\omega^\omega$ (its
indices in $K$ are $0$ and the successor ordinals below $\omega^\omega$), so $T_0[\omega^\omega]$
is undefined and the range here is $\alpha < \omega^\omega$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Self-similar compact set
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a natural number and $\rho$ a real number. A set
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a self-similar compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$ when
$\rho > 1$, $K$ is nonempty and compact, $K \subseteq [0, \infty)$, $K$ is well ordered by the
reverse order $x \preceq y \iff x \ge y$ (every nonempty subset of $K$ has a largest element),
and $\rho K^{(\mu)} = K$, where $K^{(\mu)}$ is the $\mu$-th derived set of $K$ (the operation
$A \mapsto A'$ taking a set to its set of accumulation points, applied $\mu$ times) and
$\rho K^{(\mu)} = \{\rho x : x \in K^{(\mu)}\}$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 1.

articles.title: Layers of the derived set
articles.statement:
For a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $u \ge 0$, write
$T_u(A) = A^{(u)} \setminus A^{(u+1)}$ for the $u$-th layer of $A$, where $A^{(u)}$ is the $u$-th
derived set of $A$. Then for every set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and every $u \ge 0$,
$T_{u+1}(K) = T_u(K')$, where $K'$ is the derived set of $K$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, proof of Proposition 7.

articles.title: The zeroth layer is the set of isolated points
articles.statement:
For every set
$K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the layer $T_0$ of $K$ equals $K \setminus K'$, where $K'$ is the derived
set of $K$ (its set of accumulation points); that is, $T_0$ is the set of isolated points of $K$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Layers of the iterated derived sets
articles.statement:
For a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and a natural
number $u$, let $K^{(u)}$ be the $u$-th derived set of $K$ (the derived set, i.e. the set of
accumulation points, iterated $u$ times, with $K^{(0)} = K$). The layer of $K$ of index $u$ is
$T_u = K^{(u)} \setminus K^{(u+1)}$, the set of points of $K^{(u)}$ that are isolated in
$K^{(u)}$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Self-similarity equation
articles.statement:
If $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a self-similar compact set of
module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, then $\rho K^{(\mu)} = K$, where $K^{(\mu)}$ is the $\mu$-th derived
set of $K$ (the set of accumulation points, iterated $\mu$ times) and $\rho K^{(\mu)}$ is its
image under multiplication by $\rho$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 1, equation (1).

articles.title: Un-normalized stability gauge
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $\mu$, $\rho$ and $n$ be
natural numbers, and let $T_u$ denote the layer of $K$ of index $u$. Let $\ell$ be the least
natural number such that $n / \rho^\ell$ lies in some layer $T_u$ (division by $0$ gives $0$), and
let $u$ be the least index with $n / \rho^\ell \in T_u$. The un-normalized stability gauge of $n$
is the integer $\ell \mu - u$. If $n / \rho^\ell$ lies in no layer for any $\ell$, its value is $0$.

When $K$ is a quasi-arithmetical compact set of module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$, Proposition 5 of the
source says that $\ell \mu - u$ is the same for every $\ell$ and $u$ with $n / \rho^\ell \in T_u$;
taking the least $\ell$ only fixes a choice.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 3.

articles.title: The stability gauge vanishes at one
articles.statement:
For every set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and all
natural numbers $\mu$ and $\rho$, the stability gauge $n \mapsto \lVert n \rVert_K$ of $K$ with
module $\mu$ and ratio $\rho$ takes the value $0$ at $n = 1$, that is, $\lVert 1 \rVert_K = 0$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 3.

articles.title: Stability gauge
articles.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $\mu$ and $\rho$ be natural numbers, and
for a natural number $n$ let $g(n)$ be the un-normalized stability gauge of $n$ for $K$, $\mu$
and $\rho$: the integer $\ell \mu - u$, where $\ell$ is least such that $n / \rho^\ell$ lies in
some layer $T_u$ of $K$ and $u$ is the least such index (and $g(n) = 0$ if there is no such
$\ell$). The stability gauge of $n$ is the integer $\lVert n \rVert_K = g(n) - g(1)$. When such
an $\ell$ exists, this is $\ell \mu + d - u$ with the displacement $d = -g(1)$, chosen so that
$\lVert 1 \rVert_K = 0$.

The source defines the gauge only for quasi-arithmetical compact sets of module $\mu$ and ratio
$\rho$; this definition applies to every set $K$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Definition 3.

articles.title: Stable complexity of a stable number
articles.statement:
If $n$ is a stable natural number, then its
stable complexity equals its integer complexity: $\lVert n \rVert_{\mathrm{st}} = \lVert n \rVert$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Section 1.

articles.title: Stable complexity
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let $\lVert m \rVert$ denote the integer
complexity of a positive integer $m$, with $\lVert 0 \rVert = 0$, and let $a$ be the least natural
number such that $3^a n$ is stable, with $a = 0$ if there is none. The stable complexity of $n$
is the integer $\lVert n \rVert_{\mathrm{st}} = \lVert 3^a n \rVert - 3a$.

Altman and Zelinsky show that such an $a$ exists for $n \ge 1$, and any larger $a$ gives the
same value. For $n = 0$ there is none, so $\lVert 0 \rVert_{\mathrm{st}} = \lVert 0 \rVert = 0$.

## Sources

- J. Arias de Reyna, *Arithmetical Self-Similar Compact Sets*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A21, Section 1.

articles.title: Odd values of Bala's binomial sum are $1$ modulo $4$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let
$a(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{2n+1}{n+k+1} (-2)^k$. If $a(n)$ is odd, then $a(n) \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

The paper's $a(n)$ is A026641 (the number of even-outdegree nodes in all ordered trees with $n$
edges); its proof works with this binomial sum (Bala's formula, display (13)), which is taken as
the definition here.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 7 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-7`).

articles.title: The Bala–Somos parity conjectures
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$ let $p(k)$ be the number of
partitions of $k$. For natural numbers $m$ and $N$ let
$b_m(N) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} k^{2m+1} p(k) p(N-k)$ and $a(N) = \sum_{j=0}^{N} c(j)\, p(N-j)$, where
$c(0) = 0$ and $c(j) = \sum_{d \mid j,\ d \text{ odd}} (-1)^{j/d - 1}$ for $j \ge 1$. Then for all
$m \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$: (a) if $n$ is odd, then $n$ divides $b_m(n)$; (b) $n$ divides $b_m(2n)$,
and $b_m(2n)/n$ is odd if and only if $n$ and $p(n)$ are both odd; (c) $a(n)$ is odd if and only
if $n$ and $p(n)$ are both odd; (d) twice the fractional part of the rational number $b_1(n)/n$
equals $1$ if and only if $n$ is even and $n/2$ and $p(n/2)$ are both odd.

Here $c(j)$ is the coefficient of $x^j$ in $\sum_{k \ge 1} x^{2k-1}/(1 + x^{2k-1})$, so $a(N)$ is
the coefficient of $x^N$ in $\bigl(\sum_{k \ge 1} x^{2k-1}/(1 + x^{2k-1})\bigr)
\prod_{k \ge 1} 1/(1 - x^k)$ (A305123). The paper calls the left side of (d) $c(n)$, a different
sequence from the coefficients $c(j)$ above.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 8 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-8`).

articles.title: Inserting a digit and the digit sum
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ have the $\ell$ decimal digits
$d_{\ell-1} \dots d_1 d_0$, so that $n = \sum_{j\lt \ell} d_j 10^j$. Let $S(n)$ be the set of the
numbers $\sum_{j\lt i} d_j 10^j + x \cdot 10^i + \sum_{i \le j < \ell} d_j 10^{j+1}$ with
$0 \le i \le \ell$ and $x \in \{0, \dots, 9\}$, excluding $i = \ell$ with $x = 0$: these are the
numbers obtained by inserting one decimal digit $x$ anywhere in the decimal expansion of $n$,
without creating a leading zero. Then the number of elements of $S(n)$ that are at most $10n$,
that is, the position of $10n$ when $S(n)$ is listed in increasing order, equals the digit sum
$d_0 + d_1 + \dots + d_{\ell-1}$ of $n$ (A007953).

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 6 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-6`).

articles.title: The ceiling of $\cot(\pi/(2m))$ rises in steps of $0$ or $1$
articles.statement:
For $m \ge 1$ let
$g(m) = \lceil \cot(\pi/(2m)) \rceil$. Then for every $m \ge 1$, $g(m) \le g(m+1)$ and
$g(m+1) - g(m) \in \{0, 1\}$; and for every integer $n \ge 1$, the number of $m \ge 1$ with
$g(m) = n$ is $1$ or $2$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Lemma 9 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-lem-9`).

articles.title: Values taken once by the ceiling of $\cot(\pi/(2m))$
articles.statement:
For $m \ge 1$ let
$g(m) = \lceil \cot(\pi/(2m)) \rceil$. Let $r \ge 1$ and $m \ge 2$ be integers. Then $m$ is the
only integer $m' \ge 1$ with $g(m') = r$ if and only if $g(m-1) = r - 1$, $g(m) = r$ and
$g(m+1) = r + 1$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Lemma 11 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-lem-11`).

articles.title: Zakharov's conjecture on intersection points of cevians
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be affinely
independent points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $T$ the triangle they span; a cevian is a segment
joining a vertex of $T$ to a point of the open side opposite it. Let $n \ge 0$ and let
$c_1, \dots, c_n$ be cevians such that the interior of $T$ minus $c_1 \cup \dots \cup c_n$ has
exactly $\lceil (n+1)(n+2)/3 \rceil$ connected components. Then the number of points of the
interior of $T$ that lie on $c_i$ and on $c_j$ for some $i \ne j$ is $\lfloor n^2/3 \rfloor$
(A000212).

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Corollary 15 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-cor-15`).

articles.title: Zakharov's conjecture on regions cut by cevians
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be affinely independent
points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $T$ the triangle they span; a cevian is a segment joining a vertex
of $T$ to a point of the open side opposite it. The regions cut out by cevians
$c_1, \dots, c_n$ are the connected components of the interior of $T$ minus
$c_1 \cup \dots \cup c_n$. Then for every $n \ge 0$, the maximum number of regions cut out by
$n$ cevians (not necessarily distinct) is $\lceil (n+1)(n+2)/3 \rceil$ (A007980).

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 14 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-14`).

articles.title: A diagonal coefficient equal to a signed Franel number
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 0$, the
coefficient of $x^n y^n z^n$ in the integer polynomial
$(1 + x + y - z)^n (1 + x - y + z)^n (1 - x + y + z)^n$ equals
$(-1)^n \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^3$ (A000172).

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 2 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-2`).

articles.title: Triangular numbers near squares along $\lfloor n\sqrt{2} \rfloor$
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$n$ let $a = \lfloor n\sqrt{2} \rfloor$ (A001951) and $T_a = a(a+1)/2$. Then some integer $k$
satisfies $|T_a - k^2| \le \lfloor a/2 \rfloor$; that is, the distance from $T_a$ to the nearest
perfect square is at most $\lfloor a/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 3 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-3`).

articles.title: Fried's alternating binomial identity
articles.statement:
For integers $a$ and $b$ let $\binom{a}{b}$ be the
binomial coefficient when $a, b \ge 0$ (so $0$ when $b > a$), and $0$ when $a < 0$ or $b < 0$.
For natural numbers $n$, $r$, $s$ with $r \le n$ and $s \le 2r$, with all arguments computed in
the integers,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} \binom{2n-2r}{n-k} \binom{n-k}{n-2r+s}
\binom{2r-k-s}{n-s} = (-1)^n \binom{n}{2r-n} \binom{2n-2r}{n-s}.$$

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Lemma 1 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-lem-1`).

articles.title: Jeffery's conjecture on singletons of $\lfloor \cot(\pi/(2m)) \rfloor$
articles.statement:
Let
$f(m) = \lfloor \cot(\pi / (2m)) \rfloor$ for nonzero integers $m$. Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ list
the integers $k \ge 1$ for which exactly one integer $m \ge 2$ satisfies $f(-m) = -k$, and let
$b_1 < b_2 < \cdots$ list the integers $k \ge 2$ with $f(-k-1) < f(-k) < f(-k+1)$. Then for every
integer $n \ge 1$, $2a_n = b_n + n - 1$ (A223577, A223578).

If either list has fewer than $n$ terms, its $n$-th term is taken to be $0$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 12 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-12`).

articles.title: Counting arithmetic progressions in $\{1, \dots, n\}$
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the
number of subsets $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ with $|S| \ge 2$ that are arithmetic progressions,
that is, $S = \{a, a + d, \dots, a + (|S| - 1)d\}$ for some natural numbers $a$ and $d \ge 1$,
equals $\sum_{m=0}^{n-1} D(m)$, where $D(m) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \lfloor m/k \rfloor$ (A078567,
A006218).

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 5 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-5`).

articles.title: Counting $m$ with $\lceil \cot(\pi/(2m)) \rceil \le r$
articles.statement:
Let
$g(m) = \lceil \cot(\pi / (2m)) \rceil$ for integers $m \ge 1$, and call an integer $j$ a
singleton if exactly one integer $m \ge 1$ satisfies $g(m) = j$. For an integer $r \ge 1$, let
$s(r)$ be the number of singletons in $\{1, \dots, r\}$. Then the number of integers $m \ge 2$
with $g(m) \le r$ equals $2r - s(r)$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Lemma 10 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-lem-10`).

articles.title: Counting solutions of a repeating-decimal ratio equation
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, the number of natural numbers $x$ with $10^n \le x < 10^{n+1}$ for which there is a
natural number $k$ with $x \le k < 2x$ and $k / x = 1 + (x - 10^n) / (10^n - 1)$, computed in the
rationals, (OEIS A285273) equals $2^{\omega(10^n - 1)}$, where $\omega(m)$ is the number of
distinct prime factors of $m$.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 13 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-13`).

articles.title: Blomberg's conjecture on intersection points of two equal fans
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$,
$P = (-1, 0)$ and $Q = (1, 0)$. From $P$ draw the $n$ closed rays at angles $\pi - 2\pi s/n$ for
$0 \le s < n$, and from $Q$ the $n$ closed rays at angles $2\pi t/n$ for $0 \le t < n$. Then the
number of points that are $P$, $Q$, or a point off the $x$-axis lying on a ray from $P$ and on a
ray from $Q$ is $(n^2 + 7)/4$ for odd $n$ and $(n^2 - 6n + 16)/4$ for even $n$ (A338042).

Off the $x$-axis these are exactly the points where two rays meet; on the axis, rays meet only at
$P$, $Q$ or along overlapping segments, which are not counted.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Corollary 17 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-cor-17`).

articles.title: Intersection points of two fans of rays
articles.statement:
Let $m, n \ge 1$, $P = (-1, 0)$ and
$Q = (1, 0)$. From $P$ draw the $m$ closed rays at angles $\pi - 2\pi s/m$ for $0 \le s < m$, and
from $Q$ the $n$ closed rays at angles $2\pi t/n$ for $0 \le t < n$. Let
$h = \lfloor (m - 1)/2 \rfloor$. Then the number of points that are $P$, $Q$, or a point off the
$x$-axis lying on a ray from $P$ and on a ray from $Q$ is
$2 \sum_{s=1}^{h} \lceil ns/m - 1/2 \rceil + 2$ for odd $n$ and
$2 \sum_{s=1}^{h} \lceil ns/m \rceil - 2h + 2$ for even $n$.

Off the $x$-axis these are exactly the points where two rays meet; on the axis, rays meet only at
$P$, $Q$ or along overlapping segments, which the paper does not count.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Theorem 16 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-thm-16`).

articles.title: Blomberg's conjecture on regions cut out by two equal fans
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$, $P = (-1, 0)$
and $Q = (1, 0)$. From $P$ draw the $n$ closed rays at angles $\pi - 2\pi s/n$ for $0 \le s < n$,
and from $Q$ the $n$ closed rays at angles $2\pi t/n$ for $0 \le t < n$, and let $U$ be the union
of these rays. Then there is a real $R_0$ such that for every real $R \ge R_0$, if $K_R$ is the
convex hull of the points of $U$ on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = R^2$, the interior of $K_R$ minus $U$
has $(n^2 + 8n - 5)/4$ connected components for odd $n$ and $(n^2 + 2n)/4$ for even $n$
(A338041).

The points lie on the circle, so $K_R$ is the polygon joining consecutive points, and the
connected components are the regions into which the rays cut it.

## Sources

- Sela Fried, *Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.8, Corollary 21 (`jis-2026-26.1.8-cor-21`).

articles.title: Rising factorial between consecutive $k$-th powers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $n$ be natural numbers,
write $n^{\overline{k}} = n (n + 1) \cdots (n + k - 1)$ for the rising factorial, and let
$r = \lfloor (k^2 - 4k + 6)/4 \rfloor$ if $k$ is even and $r = \lfloor (k^2 - 6k + 11)/4 \rfloor$
if $k$ is odd. If $n \ge r$, then
$(n + \lfloor k/2 \rfloor - 1)^k \le n^{\overline{k}} \le (n + \lfloor k/2 \rfloor)^k$.

Both numerators are positive: $k^2 - 4k + 6 = (k - 2)^2 + 2$ and $k^2 - 6k + 11 = (k - 3)^2 + 2$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Lemma 1, Equation (8).

articles.title: Complementary pair determined by $a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n}$
articles.statement:
Sequences
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ form a complementary pair determined by this equation when they
form a complementary pair (both strictly increasing with positive terms, and every positive
integer is a term of exactly one of them) and they satisfy $b_0 = 1$ and $a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n}$
for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Complementary pair determined by $a_n = b_{hn} + b_{khn}$
articles.statement:
Sequences
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ form a complementary pair determined by this equation with
natural-number parameters $h$ and $k$ when they form a complementary pair (both strictly
increasing with positive terms, and every positive integer is a term of exactly one of them),
$h \ge 2$, $k \ge 2$, $b_0 = 1$, and $a_n = b_{hn} + b_{khn}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Complementary pair determined by $a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n} + 1$
articles.statement:
Sequences
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ form a complementary pair determined by this equation when they
form a complementary pair (both strictly increasing with positive terms, and every positive
integer is a term of exactly one of them) and they satisfy $b_0 = 1$ and
$a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n} + 1$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Complementary pair of sequences
articles.statement:
Two sequences $a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, indexed
from $0$, form a complementary pair when all their terms are positive, both are strictly
increasing, no term of $a$ equals a term of $b$, and every positive integer is a term of $a$ or
a term of $b$. In particular, the ranges of $a$ and $b$ partition the positive integers.

articles.title: Non-centered polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 3$; the centered $k$-gonal numbers are
$k j (j + 1)/2 + 1$ for $j \ge 0$. For $n \ge 1$ let $a(n)$ be the $n$-th nonnegative integer that
is not a centered $k$-gonal number (so $a(1) = 0$), and let $s = \lfloor \sqrt{2n/k} \rfloor$.
Then $a(n) = n + s$ if $k s (s + 1) < 2(n + s - 1)$, and $a(n) = n + s - 1$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Integers not of the form $m + 1^k + \cdots + m^k$
articles.statement:
Let $k > 1$. For $n \ge 1$ let $a(n)$
be the $n$-th positive integer that is not of the form $m + \sum_{i=1}^m i^k$ with $m \ge 1$, and
let $h = \lfloor ((k + 1) n)^{1/(k+1)} \rfloor$. Then $a(n) = n + h - 1$ if
$n \le \sum_{i=1}^h i^k$, and $a(n) = n + h$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 11 (third equivalent form).

articles.title: Interleaving formula when $f(m) - \alpha(m) \ge m$
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $f(1) \ge 1$ and $f(m + 1) \ge f(m) + m$ for all $m \ge 1$,
and for $n \ge 1$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $n$-th positive integer that is not a value $f(m)$ with
$m \ge 1$. Let $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(m - 1) \le \alpha(m) \le f(m)$ for
all $m \ge 2$, and let $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $h(n) \ge 1$ and
$\alpha(h(n)) \le n < \alpha(h(n) + 1)$ for all $n \ge 1$.
Suppose moreover that $f(m) - \alpha(m) \ge m$ for all $m \ge 2$. Then for every $n \ge 1$,
$f_P(n) = n + h(n)$ if $f(h(n)) < n + h(n)$, and $f_P(n) = n + h(n) - 1$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Interleaving formula when $f(m) - \alpha(m) < m$
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $f(1) \ge 1$ and $f(m + 1) \ge f(m) + m$ for all $m \ge 1$,
and for $n \ge 1$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $n$-th positive integer that is not a value $f(m)$ with
$m \ge 1$. Let $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(m - 1) \le \alpha(m) \le f(m)$ for
all $m \ge 2$, and let $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $h(n) \ge 1$ and
$\alpha(h(n)) \le n < \alpha(h(n) + 1)$ for all $n \ge 1$.
Suppose moreover that $f(m) - \alpha(m) < m$ for all $m \ge 1$. Then for every $n \ge 1$,
$f_P(n) = n + h(n) + 1$ if $f(h(n) + 1) \le n + h(n)$, and $f_P(n) = n + h(n)$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Complementary sequences from an interleaving function
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $f(1) \ge 1$ and $f(m + 1) \ge f(m) + m$ for all $m \ge 1$,
and for $n \ge 1$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $n$-th positive integer that is not a value $f(m)$ with
$m \ge 1$. Let $\alpha : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(m - 1) \le \alpha(m) \le f(m)$ for
all $m \ge 2$, and let $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $h(n) \ge 1$ and
$\alpha(h(n)) \le n < \alpha(h(n) + 1)$ for all $n \ge 1$.
Then for every $n \ge 1$, $f_P(n) = n + h(n) + 1$ if $f(h(n) + 1) \le n + h(n)$; otherwise
$f_P(n) = n + h(n) - 1$ if $n + h(n) \le f(h(n))$, and $f_P(n) = n + h(n)$ if not.

For increasing $\alpha$ with $\alpha(1) = 1$, the paper's choice of $h(n)$ as the largest
$m \ge 1$ with $\alpha(m) \le n$ satisfies the hypothesis on $h$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Complementary sequences from one evaluation of the counting function
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $f(1) \ge 1$ and $f(m + 1) \ge f(m) + m$ for all
$m \ge 1$, let $C(x)$ be the number of $m$ with $1 \le m \le x$ and $f(m) \le x$, and for
$n \ge 1$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $n$-th positive integer that is not a value $f(m)$ with $m \ge 1$.
Then for every $n \ge 1$, $f_P(n) = n + C(n) + 1$ if $f(C(n) + 1) \le n + C(n)$, and
$f_P(n) = n + C(n)$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Complementary sequences in two Lambek–Moser steps
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
satisfy $f(1) \ge 1$ and $f(m + 1) \ge f(m) + m$ for all $m \ge 1$, let $C(x)$ be the number of
$m$ with $1 \le m \le x$ and $f(m) \le x$, and for $n \ge 1$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $n$-th positive
integer that is not a value $f(m)$ with $m \ge 1$. Then $f_P(n) = n + C(n + C(n))$ for every
$n \ge 1$.

Under the hypotheses, $f(m) \ge m$ for all $m \ge 1$, so $C(x)$ is the number of all $m \ge 1$
with $f(m) \le x$, the counting function of the values of $f$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Rounding formula for the non-$k$-gonal numbers, every $k \ge 3$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 3$; the
$k$-gonal numbers are $(k - 2) j (j - 1)/2 + j$ for $j \ge 1$. For every $n \ge 1$, the $n$-th
positive integer that is not a $k$-gonal number equals
$n + \lfloor \sqrt{(2n - 2 + \lfloor (k + 1)/4 \rfloor)/(k - 2)} + 1/2 \rfloor$.

This corresponds to the shift $r = \lfloor (k + 1)/4 \rfloor - 2$ in the source.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 5 (last sentence).

articles.title: Rounding formula for the non-$k$-gonal numbers, $3 \le k \le 10$
articles.statement:
Let $3 \le k \le 10$;
the $k$-gonal numbers are $(k - 2) j (j - 1)/2 + j$ for $j \ge 1$. For every $n \ge 1$, the $n$-th
positive integer that is not a $k$-gonal number equals
$n + \lfloor \sqrt{2n/(k - 2)} + 1/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 4 (last sentence).

articles.title: Shifted formula for the non-polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 3$, let $r$ be a real number
with $-1 \le r \le k - 4$, and for $j \ge 1$ let $T(k, j) = (k - 2) j (j - 1)/2 + j$ be the
$k$-gonal numbers. For every integer $n \ge 1$, put $s = \lfloor \sqrt{(2n + r)/(k - 2)} \rfloor$.
Then the $n$-th positive integer that is not of the form $T(k, j)$ with $j \ge 1$ equals
$n + s + 1$ if $(k - 2) s (s + 1) < 2n$, and $n + s$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 5, Equation (4).

articles.title: Formula for the non-polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 3$, and for $j \ge 1$ let
$T(k, j) = (k - 2) j (j - 1)/2 + j$ be the $k$-gonal numbers. For every integer $n \ge 1$, put
$s = \lfloor \sqrt{2n/(k - 2)} \rfloor$. Then the $n$-th positive integer that is not of the form
$T(k, j)$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $n + s + 1$ if $(k - 2) s (s + 1) < 2n$, and $n + s$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 4, Equation (3).

articles.title: Two-case formula for the non-pyramidal numbers when $k \le 8$
articles.statement:
Let $3 \le k \le 8$, and
for $j \ge 1$ let $P(k, j) = j (j + 1) ((k - 2) j - (k - 5))/6$ be the $k$-gonal pyramidal
numbers. For every integer $n \ge 1$, put $s = \lfloor \sqrt[3]{6n/(k - 2)} \rfloor$. Then the
$n$-th positive integer that is not of the form $P(k, j)$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $n + s - 1$ if
$6n \le s (s - 1) (s (k - 2) + k + 1)$, and $n + s$ otherwise.

This extends Equation (7) of Corollary 4 from $k \le 5$ to $k \le 8$; the paper reports it after
checking small values of $n$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, remark after Corollary 4.

articles.title: Two-case formula for the non-pyramidal numbers when $k \le 5$
articles.statement:
Let $3 \le k \le 5$, and
for $j \ge 1$ let $P(k, j) = j (j + 1) ((k - 2) j - (k - 5))/6$ be the $k$-gonal pyramidal
numbers. For every integer $n \ge 1$, put $s = \lfloor \sqrt[3]{6n/(k - 2)} \rfloor$. Then the
$n$-th positive integer that is not of the form $P(k, j)$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $n + s - 1$ if
$6n \le s (s - 1) (s (k - 2) + k + 1)$, and $n + s$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Corollary 4, Equation (7).

articles.title: Formula for the non-pyramidal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $3 \le k \le 8$, and for $j \ge 1$ let
$P(k, j) = j (j + 1) ((k - 2) j - (k - 5))/6$ be the $k$-gonal pyramidal numbers. For every
integer $n \ge 1$, put $s = \lfloor \sqrt[3]{6n/(k - 2)} \rfloor$. Then the $n$-th positive
integer that is not of the form $P(k, j)$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $n + s + 1$ if
$6n \ge s^3 (k - 2) + 3 s^2 (k - 1) + s (2k - 1) + 6$; otherwise it equals $n + s - 1$ if
$6n \le s (s - 1) (s (k - 2) + k + 1)$, and $n + s$ if not.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 9, Equation (6).

articles.title: Formula for the non-second-pentagonal numbers
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, put
$s = \lfloor \sqrt{2n/3} \rfloor$. Then the $n$-th positive integer that is not a second
pentagonal number $(3j^2 + j)/2$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $n + s + 1$ if $s (3s + 5) + 4 \le 2n$, and
$n + s$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Formula for the non-second-polygonal numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k > 5$, and for $j \ge 1$ let
$S(k, j) = ((k - 2) j^2 + (k - 4) j)/2$ be the second $k$-gonal numbers. For every integer
$n \ge 1$, put $s = \lfloor \sqrt{2n/(k - 2)} \rfloor$. Then the $n$-th positive integer that is
not of the form $S(k, j)$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $n + s$ if $(k - 2) s (s + 1) < 2n + 4s$, and
$n + s - 1$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 7, Equation (5).

articles.title: Formula for the non-simplex numbers when $k \le 15$
articles.statement:
Let $1 < k \le 15$. For every
integer $n \ge 1$, put $R = \lfloor (k!\, n)^{1/k} \rfloor$ and let
$t = n + R - \lfloor k/2 \rfloor$, an integer. Then the $n$-th positive integer that is not a
$k$-simplex number $\binom{j + k - 1}{k}$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $t + 2$ if
$\binom{R + \lceil k/2 \rceil + 1}{k} \le t + 1$; otherwise it equals $t$ if
$t < \binom{R + \lceil k/2 \rceil}{k}$, and $t + 1$ if not.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Corollary 5.

articles.title: Formula for the non-simplex numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ satisfy $1 < k \le 5$, $k = 7$ or $k = 9$.
For every integer $n \ge 1$, put $R = \lfloor (k!\, n)^{1/k} \rfloor$ and let
$t = n + R - \lfloor k/2 \rfloor$, an integer. Then the $n$-th positive integer that is not a
$k$-simplex number $\binom{j + k - 1}{k}$ with $j \ge 1$ equals $t + 2$ if
$\binom{R + \lceil k/2 \rceil + 1}{k} \le t + 1$; otherwise it equals $t$ if
$t < \binom{R + \lceil k/2 \rceil}{k}$, and $t + 1$ if not.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 12, Equation (9).

articles.title: Formula for the non-square numbers
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the $n$-th positive
integer that is not a perfect square is $n + \lfloor \sqrt{n} + 1/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Corollary 3.

articles.title: The first non-square
articles.statement:
The smallest positive integer that is not the square of a positive
integer is $2$; that is, the first non-value of $m \mapsto m^2$ is $2$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Section 1 (the non-squares).

articles.title: The second non-square
articles.statement:
The second smallest positive integer that is not the square of a
positive integer is $3$; that is, the second non-value of $m \mapsto m^2$ is $3$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Section 1 (the non-squares).

articles.title: Integers missed by the sums $1^k + \dots + j^k$
articles.statement:
Let $k > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ be integers,
and let $h = \lfloor ((k+1)n)^{1/(k+1)} \rfloor$. Then the $n$-th smallest positive integer that
is not of the form $\sum_{i=1}^{j} i^k$ with $j \ge 1$ is $n + h - 1$ if
$n \le \sum_{i=1}^{h} (i^k - 1)$, and $n + h$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Theorem 10 (third equivalent form).

articles.title: Formula for the $n$-th non-triangular number
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, the $n$-th
smallest positive integer that is not a triangular number $j(j+1)/2$ with $j \ge 1$ is
$n + \lfloor \sqrt{2n} + 1/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Corollary 3.

articles.title: The $n$-th non-value of a sequence
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $n \ge 1$, the
$n$-th non-value of $f$ is the $n$-th smallest positive integer that is not of the form $f(m)$
with $m \ge 1$, or $0$ if fewer than $n$ such integers exist. At $n = 0$ it takes the same value
as at $n = 1$.

In the paper's notation, where $f = f_{\neg P}$ lists the positive integers without a property
$P$, the $n$-th non-value of $f$ is $f_P(n)$, the $n$-th term of the complementary sequence.

## Sources

- Chai Wah Wu, *Algorithms for Complementary Sequences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A95, Section 1 (definition of `f_P`).

articles.title: The subsequence-sum equation $a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n}$
articles.statement:
Sequences
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy this equation when $b_0 = 1$ and
$a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: The subsequence-sum equation $a_n = b_{hn} + b_{khn}$
articles.statement:
Sequences
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and natural numbers $h$ and $k$ satisfy the parametrized
subsequence-sum equation when $h \ge 2$, $k \ge 2$, $b_0 = 1$, and $a_n = b_{hn} + b_{khn}$ for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: The subsequence-sum equation $a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n} + 1$
articles.statement:
Sequences
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy this equation when $b_0 = 1$ and
$a_n = b_{2n} + b_{4n} + 1$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Dold congruences for binomial-power sequences
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$ and $s \ge 0$ be integers
and let $A_{r,s}(m) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k}^r \binom{m+k}{k}^s$. Then for every integer
$n \ge 1$, $n$ divides $\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, A_{r,s}(n/d)$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius
function and $d$ runs over the positive divisors of $n$.

articles.title: Non-negativity of the Möbius transform of binomial-power sequences
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$ and
$s \ge 0$ be integers and let $A_{r,s}(m) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k}^r \binom{m+k}{k}^s$.
Then for every integer $n \ge 1$, $\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, A_{r,s}(n/d) \ge 0$, where $\mu$
is the Möbius function and $d$ runs over the positive divisors of $n$.

articles.title: Binomial-power sequences
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $r$, $s$ and $n$, the binomial-power number
$A_{r,s}(n)$ is the natural number

$$A_{r,s}(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^r \binom{n+k}{k}^s.$$

Special cases include the central Delannoy numbers ($r = s = 1$), the Apéry numbers
($r = s = 2$) and the Franel numbers of order $r$ ($s = 0$).

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, "Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences," Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Theorem, lines 143–144, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL27/Zhang/zhang9.tex with `A(n,r,s)` at lines 120–122 and realizability at lines 86–93.

articles.title: Binomial-power sequences are Dold realizable
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$ and $s \ge 0$ be integers and
let $A_{r,s}(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^r \binom{n+k}{k}^s$. Then the integer sequence
$(A_{r,s}(n))_{n \ge 0}$ is Dold realizable: for every integer $n \ge 1$, the sum
$\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, A_{r,s}(n/d)$ over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$, where $\mu$ is
the Möbius function, is non-negative and divisible by $n$.

## Sources

- Zhang 2024, J. Integer Seq. 27, Article 24.3.3, Theorem 1.13.

articles.title: Binomial coefficients at multiples of a prime divisor
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let
$n \ge 1$ be an integer divisible by $p$. Then for every integer $\lambda \ge 0$ with
$\lambda p \ne n$,

$$\binom{n}{\lambda p} \equiv \binom{n/p}{\lambda} \pmod{p^e},$$

where $e = \max(\nu_p(n), \nu_p(n - \lambda p))$ and $\nu_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation; the
integer $n - \lambda p$ may be negative, and $\nu_p(n - \lambda p)$ is the valuation of its
absolute value.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Lemma 27 (`jis-2024-24.3.3-lem-27`).

articles.title: Helou–Terjanian congruence for primes $p \ge 5$
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 5$ be a prime and let $m$ and
$n$ be integers with $0 < m < n$. Then $\binom{np}{mp} \equiv \binom{n}{m} \pmod{p^e}$, where
$e = 3 + \max(\nu_p(m), \nu_p(n - m)) + \nu_p\big(\binom{n}{m}\big)$ and $\nu_p$ is the $p$-adic
valuation.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Lemma 26 (1) (`jis-2024-24.3.3-lem-26`).

articles.title: Helou–Terjanian congruence for $p = 3$
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be integers with $0 < m < n$.
Then $\binom{3n}{3m} \equiv \binom{n}{m} \pmod{3^e}$, where
$e = 2 + \max(\nu_3(m), \nu_3(n - m)) + \nu_3\big(\binom{n}{m}\big)$ and $\nu_3$ is the $3$-adic
valuation.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Lemma 26 (2) (`jis-2024-24.3.3-lem-26`).

articles.title: Helou–Terjanian congruence for $p = 2$
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be integers with $0 < m < n$.
Then $\binom{2n}{2m} \equiv \binom{n}{m} \pmod{2^e}$, where
$e = 1 + \max(\nu_2(m), \nu_2(n - m)) + \nu_2\big(\binom{n}{m}\big)$ and $\nu_2$ is the $2$-adic
valuation.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Lemma 26 (3) (`jis-2024-24.3.3-lem-26`).

articles.title: Domb-type sums are Dold realizable
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r \ge 1$, $s$ and $t$, the
integer sequence $(D(n, r, s, t))_{n \ge 0}$ of Domb-type sums
$D(n, r, s, t) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^r \binom{2k}{k}^s \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}^t$ is Dold
realizable.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Theorem 15 (`jis-2024-24.3.3-thm-15`).

articles.title: Dold realizable sequences satisfy the Dold congruences
articles.statement:
If an integer sequence
$(a(n))_{n \ge 0}$ is Dold realizable, then for every integer $n \ge 1$, $n$ divides
$\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, a(n/d)$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function and $d$ runs over the
positive divisors of $n$.

articles.title: Even-binomial-type sums are Dold realizable
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 1$, $s$, $t$ and $u$ be natural
numbers with $t + u \ge 1$, and let

$$T(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{2k}^r \binom{n+k}{k}^s \binom{2k}{k}^t \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}^u.$$

Then the integer sequence $(T(n))_{n \ge 0}$ is Dold realizable.

The hypothesis $t + u \ge 1$ is added to the source: for $t = u = 0$ the Möbius transform at
$n = 2$ is $T(2) - T(1) = 3^s$, which is odd, so the sequence is not Dold realizable.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Theorem 18 (`jis-2024-24.3.3-thm-18`).

articles.title: The Möbius transform of a Dold realizable sequence is non-negative
articles.statement:
If an integer sequence
$(a(n))_{n \ge 0}$ is Dold realizable, then for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, a(n/d) \ge 0$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function and $d$ runs over
the positive divisors of $n$.

articles.title: Criterion for Dold realizability
articles.statement:
Let $(a(n))_{n \ge 0}$ be an integer sequence and let
$\mu$ be the Möbius function. If for every integer $n \ge 1$ the sum
$\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, a(n/d)$ over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$ is divisible by $n$, and
for every integer $n \ge 1$ this sum is non-negative, then $a$ is Dold realizable.

articles.title: Dold realizable sequences
articles.statement:
An integer sequence $(a(n))_{n \ge 0}$ is Dold realizable when,
for every integer $n \ge 1$, the Möbius transform $\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, a(n/d)$ is divisible
by $n$ and non-negative, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function and $d$ runs over the positive
divisors of $n$.

The divisibility condition alone is the classical Dold condition.

## Sources

- Wójcik, Lemma 3, for an equivalent form of the Dold condition.

articles.title: Fermat sequence
articles.statement:
Given a sequence $b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, the Fermat sequence
generated by $b$ is the sequence $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ given by
$a_n = \sum_{m \mid n} m \, b_m$ for $n \ge 1$, the sum running over the positive divisors $m$
of $n$, and $a_0 = 0$.

The source defines the sequence only for positive indices; the value $a_0 = 0$ comes from
summing over the empty set of divisors of $0$.

## Sources

- B.-S. Du, S.-S. Huang, and M.-C. Li, *Newton, Fermat, and Exactly Realizable Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), lines 181–190, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Huang/huang11.tex>.

articles.title: Binomial-power sequences are almost realizable
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r \ge 1$ and $s$,
the binomial-power sequence $n \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^r \binom{n+k}{k}^s$ is almost
realizable.

Every Dold realizable sequence is almost realizable (take the multiplier $m = 1$), and the
binomial-power sequences are Dold realizable.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Definition 3 and Theorem 13.

articles.title: The zero sequence is almost realizable
articles.statement:
The constant sequence $a(n) = 0$ is almost
realizable.

It is realized by the self-map of the empty set, with multiplier $m = 1$.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Definition 3.

articles.title: Almost realizable sequences
articles.statement:
A sequence $a$ of natural numbers $a(0), a(1), \dots$ is
almost realizable when there is an integer $m \ge 1$ such that the integer sequence
$(m\, a(n))_{n \ge 0}$ is Dold realizable: for every $n \ge 1$, the sum
$\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, m\, a(n/d)$ over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$, where $\mu$ is the
Möbius function, is non-negative and divisible by $n$.

This is Miska and Ward's notion that some positive integer multiple of $a$ is realizable. The
value $a(0)$ is not used.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Definition 3.

articles.title: Dold sequences
articles.statement:
A sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of integers is a Dold sequence when
for every integer $m \ge 1$ there is an $m \times m$ matrix $A$ with integer entries such that
$a_n = \operatorname{tr}(A^n)$ for every $n$ with $1 \le n \le m$. The term $a_0$ is not
constrained.

## Sources

- Wójcik, *Binomial Transform and Dold Sequences*, Lemma 3; this equivalent trace characterization is taken here as the definition.

articles.title: Möbius transforms of sequences growing by a factor of at least $1.221$ are nonnegative
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a sequence of real numbers and $C \ge 1.221$ a real number such that $b(n) \ge 0$ and
$b(n+1) \ge C\, b(n)$ for every $n \ge 1$. Then for every $n \ge 1$, with $\mu$ the Möbius
function,

$$\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(n/d)\, b(d) \ge 0,$$

that is, the Dirichlet convolution $\mu * b$ is nonnegative at $n$.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Lemma 28 (`jis-2024-24.3.3-lem-28`).

articles.title: The Catalan, Motzkin and large Schröder numbers are not almost realizable
articles.statement:
None of the
following three sequences of non-negative integers is almost realizable: the Catalan numbers
$C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$, the Motzkin numbers $M(n)$, and the large Schröder numbers
$S(n)$ (OEIS A006318), given by $S(0) = 1$ and $S(n+1) = S(n) + \sum_{i=0}^{n} S(i) S(n-i)$.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Theorem 21 (`jis-2024-24.3.3-thm-21`).

articles.title: Dold congruences via prime-power congruences
articles.statement:
Let $(V(n))_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of
integers and let $\mu$ denote the Möbius function. Then
$V(n p^m) \equiv V(n p^{m-1}) \pmod{p^m}$ holds for all integers $n, m \ge 1$ and all primes $p$
if and only if $n$ divides $\sum_{d \mid n} \mu(n/d) V(d)$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Geng-Rui Zhang, *Realizability of Some Combinatorial Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.3, Lemma 30 (`jis-2024-24.3.3-lem-30`).

articles.title: Arithmetic billiards in a tilted rectangle
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
and let $l$ be an even natural number with $l + 3 \le p$. Put $m = l + 1$ if $2l + 5 \le p$ and
$m = p - (l + 1)$ otherwise, and let $R \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be the convex hull of the four
points $(0, m)$, $(m, 0)$, $(p/2, p/2 - m)$ and $(p/2 - m, p/2)$. Let $L$ be the set of integer
points on the boundary of $R$ other than $(0, m)$ and $(m, 0)$. Call a sequence $P_0, P_1, \ldots$
of integer points a billiard path if $P_0 = (0, m)$ and, for every $i < p - 1$, the point
$P_{i+1}$ lies on the boundary of $R$, differs from $P_i$, and has the same second coordinate as
$P_i$ when $i$ is even and the same first coordinate as $P_i$ when $i$ is odd. Then a billiard
path exists, and every billiard path $P$ maps $\{1, \ldots, p - 2\}$ bijectively onto $L$,
satisfies $P_{p-1} = (m, 0)$, and satisfies $P_{p-1-i} = (y_i, x_i)$ for every $i \le p - 1$,
where $P_i = (x_i, y_i)$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Lemma 16 (`lem:billiards`).

articles.title: Counting prime first nonintegral indices of $g_{k,2}$ for $k \le 10^7$
articles.statement:
Exactly
$8649270$ natural numbers $k$ with $2 \le k \le 10^7$ have the following property: for the
$(k, 2)$-Göbel sequence $g_{k,2}$ there is a prime $q$ such that $g_{k,2}(q)$ is not an integer
and $g_{k,2}(n)$ is an integer for every $1 \le n < q$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)- Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 26.

articles.title: The diagonal is zigzag-below every odd residue walk
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $l$ be
an odd natural number with $l < p$, and let $\tilde g_l$ be the residue walk of $l$ for $p$. Then
the diagonal $n \mapsto n$ is zigzag-below $\tilde g_l$ up to $p$: there is $m \le p$ such that
$n < \tilde g_l(n)$ for all $1 \le n \le m$ and $\tilde g_l(n) = n$ for all $m < n \le p$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 9.

articles.title: Existence and uniqueness of the sequence $a_{p,l}$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with
$p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and let $l$ be an even natural number with $l \le p - 3$. Then exactly one
function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies the defining conditions of $a_{p,l}$:
$a(n) = \pm 1$ for $1 \le n \le p - 1$, $a(n) = 0$ for $n = 0$ and for $n \ge p$, $a(1) = 1$,
$a(n) = a(p - n)$ for $1 \le n \le (p - 1)/2$, $a(n) = -a(l + 1 - n)$ for $1 \le n \le l/2$, and
$a(n) = a(l + 1 + n)$ for $1 \le n \le p - l - 2$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 17.

articles.title: Existence and uniqueness of the sequence $b_{l,s}$
articles.statement:
Let $l$ be an even natural number and
$s$ a natural number with $s \le l$ such that $2s + 1$ and $l + 1$ are coprime. Then exactly one
function $b : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies the defining conditions of $b_{l,s}$:
$b(n) = \pm 1$ for every integer $n$, $b(n + l + 1) = b(n)$ for every $n$, $b(1) = 1$,
$b(n) = -b(l + 1 - n)$ for every $n$ not divisible by $l + 1$, and $b(s - n) = b(s + 1 + n)$ for
every $n$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 20.

articles.title: The sequence $a_{p,l}$ is not multiplicative at an even index
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 13$ be a prime
with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, let $l$ be an even natural number with $2 \le l \le p - 3$, and let
$a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy the defining conditions of $a_{p,l}$. Then there is a
positive integer $m$ with $2m \le p - 3$ such that $a(2m) \ne a(2)\,a(m)$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 25.

articles.title: Equality of the left and right boundaries via Legendre symbols
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with
$p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and, for each $l$, let $\tilde g_l$ be the residue walk of $l$ for $p$.
Suppose that $l_0$ is the largest even $l < p$ with $\tilde g_l(p) = 0$, put $l_L = l_0 + 2$, and
suppose that $l_R$ is the smallest even $l < p$ with $\tilde g_l(p) = p$. Then $l_L = l_R$ if and
only if there is an even natural number $l \le p - 3$ such that
$\left(\frac{n}{p}\right) = -\left(\frac{l + 1 - n}{p}\right)$ for all $1 \le n \le l/2$ and
$\left(\frac{n}{p}\right) = \left(\frac{l + 1 + n}{p}\right)$ for all $1 \le n \le p - l - 2$,
where $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ is the Legendre symbol.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 15.

articles.title: Complementary sequences $b_{l,s}$ and $b_{l,l-s}$
articles.statement:
Let $l \ge 2$ be an even natural
number and $s \le l$ a natural number such that $2s + 1$ and $l + 1$ are coprime. Let
$b_1, b_2 : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy the defining conditions of $b_{l,s}$ and of
$b_{l,l-s}$ respectively. Then for every integer $n$, $b_1(n) = b_2(n)$ if $l + 1$ does not divide
$n$, and $b_1(n) = -b_2(n)$ if $l + 1$ divides $n$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Lemma 22.

articles.title: Translation and reflection identities for $b_{l,s}$
articles.statement:
Let $l \ge 2$ be an even natural
number and $s \le l$ a natural number such that $2s + 1$ and $l + 1$ are coprime, let
$b : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy the defining conditions of $b_{l,s}$, and write
$t = l/2 - s$. Then the following hold. (a) For every integer $n$ such that neither $n$ nor
$n + 2s + 1$ is divisible by $l + 1$, $b(n) = -b(n + 2s + 1)$. (b) If $s < l/2$, then for every
integer $n$ such that neither $n$ nor $n + 2t$ is divisible by $l + 1$, $b(n) = -b(n + 2t)$.
(c) If $s < l/2$, then for every integer $n$ such that neither $t - n$ nor $t + n$ is divisible
by $l + 1$, $b(t - n) = b(t + n)$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Lemma 23.

articles.title: Failure of the residue sequence detects non-integrality
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $r \ge 1$ be
integers, let $p$ be a prime, write $\nu_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation, and let $n \ge 1$ be an
integer with $\nu_p(n!) \le r$. Then the residue sequence $g_{k,p,r}$ takes the failure value $F$
at $n$, that is $g_{k,p,r}(n) = F$, if and only if the value $g_{k,2}(n)$ of the $(k, 2)$-Göbel
sequence has negative $p$-adic valuation, that is $g_{k,2}(n) \notin \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$.

This is Lemma 10 of Matsuhira, Matsusaka, and Tsuchida.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *On the Length over Which k-Göbel Sequences Remain Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A23, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Periodicity of the Göbel residue sequence in the exponent
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, $r \ge 1$,
and $k$, $l$ integers with $r + 1 \le k \le l$ and $k \equiv l \pmod{\varphi(p^r)}$, where
$\varphi$ is Euler's totient function. Write $\nu_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation. Then every
integer $n \ge 1$ with $\nu_p(n!) \le r$ satisfies $g_{k,p,r}(n) = g_{l,p,r}(n)$, where both
sides are values of the residue sequence (so either both are the failure value $F$ or both are
the same residue class).

This is Proposition 12 of Matsuhira, Matsusaka, and Tsuchida.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *On the Length over Which k-Göbel Sequences Remain Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A23, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Initial value of the Göbel residue sequence
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$, $p$, $r$, the
residue sequence satisfies $g_{k,p,r}(1) = 2 \bmod p^r$, the residue class of $2$ modulo $p^r$
(represented by the remainder of $2$ on division by $p^r$).

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *On the Length over Which k-Göbel Sequences Remain Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A23, Section 2 (definition of `g_{k,p,r}`).

articles.title: Failure of the Göbel residue sequence persists
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$, $p$, $r$ and
every $n \ge 1$, if the residue sequence takes the failure value at $n$, that is
$g_{k,p,r}(n) = F$, then $g_{k,p,r}(n + 1) = F$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *On the Length over Which k-Göbel Sequences Remain Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A23, Section 2 (definition of `g_{k,p,r}`).

articles.title: Example value of the Göbel residue sequence
articles.statement:
For $k = 2$, $p = 3$ and $r = 1$, the
residue sequence satisfies $g_{2,3,1}(2) = 0 \bmod 3$; in particular it is not the failure value
$F$. Indeed $g_{2,3,1}(1) = 2$ and
$(1 \cdot 2 + 2^2) \cdot 2^{-1} = 6 \cdot 2^{-1} \equiv 0 \pmod 3$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *On the Length over Which k-Göbel Sequences Remain Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A23, Section 2 (definition of `g_{k,p,r}`).

articles.title: The residue walk stays on the diagonal
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $l \le p - 1$ be a
natural number, and let $\tilde g_l$ be the residue walk of $l$ for $p$. If $1 \le m \le p$ and
$\tilde g_l(m) = m$, then $\tilde g_l(n) = n$ for every $n$ with $m \le n \le p$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Consecutive even residue walks form a zigzag chain when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $p$
be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and for a natural number $l$ write $\tilde g_l$ for the
residue walk of $p$ starting at $l$. Then for every even natural number $l$ with
$l + 2 \le p - 1$, the walk $\tilde g_l$ is zigzag-below $\tilde g_{l+2}$ up to $p$: there is
an $m \le p$ such that $\tilde g_l(n) < \tilde g_{l+2}(n)$ for $1 \le n \le m$ and
$\tilde g_l(n) = \tilde g_{l+2}(n)$ for $m < n \le p$. Writing $A \preceq B$ when $A$ is
zigzag-below $B$ up to $p$, these links form the chain
$\tilde g_0 \preceq \tilde g_2 \preceq \cdots \preceq \tilde g_{p-1}$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)- Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 11.

articles.title: Even residue walks lie zigzag-below the antidiagonal when $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $p$
be a prime with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, let $l < p$ be an even natural number, and write
$\tilde g_l$ for the residue walk of $p$ starting at $l$. Then $\tilde g_l$ is zigzag-below the
function $n \mapsto p - n$ up to $p$: there is an $m \le p$ such that $\tilde g_l(n) < p - n$
for $1 \le n \le m$ and $\tilde g_l(n) = p - n$ for $m < n \le p$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 10.

articles.title: Initial value of the residue walk
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $p$ and $l$, the residue walk
$\tilde g_l$ of $p$ starting at $l$ satisfies $\tilde g_l(1) = l$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Section 2 definition of `tilde g_l`.

articles.title: Recurrence of the residue walk at interior values
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $l$ and $n$ be natural numbers
with $n \ge 1$, write $\tilde g_l$ for the residue walk of $p$ starting at $l$, and write
$\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ for the Jacobi symbol. If $0 < \tilde g_l(n) < p$, then

$$\tilde g_l(n+1) = \max\bigl(0, \tilde g_l(n) + (\tfrac{n}{p})(\tfrac{\tilde g_l(n)}{p})\bigr).$$

The maximum with $0$ records the conversion of the integer sum back to a natural number; the sum
is never negative because $\tilde g_l(n) \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Section 2 definition of `tilde g_l`.

articles.title: The residue walk stays at $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $l$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $n \ge 1$,
and write $\tilde g_l$ for the residue walk of $p$ starting at $l$. If $\tilde g_l(n) = p$, then
$\tilde g_l(n+1) = p$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Section 2 definition of `tilde g_l`.

articles.title: The residue walk stays at $0$
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $l$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $n \ge 1$,
and write $\tilde g_l$ for the residue walk of $p$ starting at $l$. If $\tilde g_l(n) = 0$, then
$\tilde g_l(n+1) = 0$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Section 2 definition of `tilde g_l`.

articles.title: The residue walk $\tilde g_l$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $l$, write
$\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ for the Jacobi symbol. The residue walk
$\tilde g_l \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of $p$ starting at $l$ is defined by
$\tilde g_l(0) = 0$, $\tilde g_l(1) = l$ and, for every $n \ge 1$,
$\tilde g_l(n+1) = \tilde g_l(n) + \left(\frac{n}{p}\right)\left(\frac{\tilde g_l(n)}{p}\right)$
if $0 < \tilde g_l(n) < p$, and $\tilde g_l(n+1) = \tilde g_l(n)$ otherwise.

The sum in the first case is never negative, since $\tilde g_l(n) \ge 1$ there. The paper only
uses the indices $1 \le n \le p$; the value at $0$ and the values beyond $p$ totalize the walk.
For an odd prime $p$ the Jacobi symbol is the Legendre symbol.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Section 2 definition of `tilde g_l`.

articles.title: Residue sequence of the $k$-Göbel sequence
articles.statement:
Fix natural numbers $k$, $p$, $r$ and write
$\nu_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation. The residue sequence $g_{k,p,r}(n)$, meant for $n \ge 1$ with
$\nu_p(n!) \le r$, takes values in $\mathbb{Z}/p^{r - \nu_p(n!)}\mathbb{Z} \cup \{F\}$, where $F$
is a failure value; a residue class is represented by its least nonnegative representative. It
is defined by $g_{k,p,r}(0) = F$, $g_{k,p,r}(1) = 2 \bmod p^r$ and, for $n \ge 2$, as follows.
If $g_{k,p,r}(n-1) = F$ then $g_{k,p,r}(n) = F$. Otherwise let $g_{k,p,r}(n-1) = a$ and let $N$
be the least nonnegative residue of $(n-1)a + a^k$ modulo $p^{r - \nu_p((n-1)!)}$, with $a^k$
computed by modular exponentiation. If $N \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p^{\nu_p(n)}}$ then
$g_{k,p,r}(n) = F$; otherwise $g_{k,p,r}(n) = (N/p^{\nu_p(n)}) \cdot c \bmod p^{r - \nu_p(n!)}$,
where $c$ is the inverse of the quotient $n/p^{\nu_p(n)}$ modulo $p^{r - \nu_p(n!)}$ (it exists
when $p$ is prime; when no inverse exists, $c$ is the junk value that Mathlib's inverse in
$\mathbb{Z}/p^{r - \nu_p(n!)}\mathbb{Z}$ returns, which need not be $0$).

For a prime $p$ with $\nu_p(n!) \le r$ we have $\nu_p(n) + (r - \nu_p(n!)) = r - \nu_p((n-1)!)$,
so the reduction keeps exactly the information both the divisibility test and the next residue
need, and the recursion agrees with the source's, which tests and divides $(n-1)a + a^k$ itself.
Values with $\nu_p(n!) > r$ and at $n = 0$ are junk and never used.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *On the Length over Which k-Göbel Sequences Remain Integers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A23, Section 2 (definition of `g_{k,p,r}`, after Matsuhira, Matsusaka, and Tsuchida, Definition 9).

articles.title: Asymptotic expansion of the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence
articles.statement:
Let $k, l \ge 2$ be natural numbers
and let $g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. There are a real number $C > 1$ and real numbers
$a_1, a_2, \dots$ such that for every natural number $R$, as $n \to \infty$,

$$g_{k,l}(n) - C^{k^n} n^{1/(k-1)} \Bigl(1 + \sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{a_r}{n^r}\Bigr) =
O\Bigl(\frac{C^{k^n} n^{1/(k-1)}}{n^{R+1}}\Bigr).$$

In other words, $g_{k,l}(n) \sim C^{k^n} n^{1/(k-1)} \bigl(1 + \sum_{r \ge 1} a_r / n^r\bigr)$ as
an asymptotic expansion, generalizing Zagier's asymptotic for Göbel's sequence.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Theorem 4 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-thm-4`).

articles.title: Series formula and bound for the Göbel error
articles.statement:
Let $k, l \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let
$g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence, and let $C$ be a real number such that the real numbers
$C_{k,l}(n) = g_{k,l}(n)^{1/k^n}$ tend to $C$ as $n \to \infty$. Then for every natural number
$n \ge 1$ the error

$$\varepsilon_{k,l}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{\log(m + n)}{k^m} -
k^n \bigl(\log C_{k,l}(n) - \log C\bigr)$$

satisfies

$$\varepsilon_{k,l}(n) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^m}
\log\Bigl(1 + \frac{m + n - 1}{g_{k,l}(m + n - 1)^{k-1}}\Bigr) \le \frac{2n}{C^{(k-1) k^n}}.$$

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 12 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-12`).

articles.title: The Göbel error term decays faster than every power of $n$
articles.statement:
Let $k, l \ge 2$ be natural
numbers, let $g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence, and let $C$ be a real number such that the
real numbers $C_{k,l}(n) = g_{k,l}(n)^{1/k^n}$ tend to $C$ as $n \to \infty$. Then for every real
number $R > 0$, as $n \to \infty$,

$$\exp\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{\log(m + n)}{k^m}\Bigr) -
\Bigl(\frac{C_{k,l}(n)}{C}\Bigr)^{k^n} = O(n^{-R}).$$

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-thm-11`).

articles.title: The first non-integral term of $g_{2600725,2}$ is at index $9011$
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$ denote
the $(k,l)$-Göbel sequence. The rational number $g_{2600725,2}(9011)$ is not an integer, while
$g_{2600725,2}(n)$ is an integer for every natural number $n$ with $1 \le n < 9011$. Writing
$N_k$ for the first index at which $g_{k,2}$ is not an integer, as in the paper, this says
$N_{2600725} = 9011$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 26.

articles.title: Index-scaled Göbel terms with $k = (p-1)/2$ are congruent to the residue walk
articles.statement:
Let $p$
be an odd prime and $l \le p - 1$ a natural number. Write $k = (p-1)/2$, let $g_{k,l}$ be the
$(k,l)$-Göbel sequence, and let $\tilde g_l$ be the residue walk of $p$ starting at $l$. Then
(a) for every $1 \le n \le p$, the rational number $n\,g_{k,l}(n) - \tilde g_l(n)$ is either $0$
or has $p$-adic valuation at least $1$, that is,
$n\,g_{k,l}(n) \equiv \tilde g_l(n) \pmod{p}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$; and (b) $g_{k,l}(p)$ lies in
the localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, that is, has nonnegative $p$-adic valuation, if and only if
$\tilde g_l(p) = 0$ or $\tilde g_l(p) = p$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Odd starting values give a $p$-integral $p$-th term when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be
a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, write $k = (p-1)/2$, and let $g_{k,l}$ denote the
$(k,l)$-Göbel sequence. Then for every odd natural number $l < p$, the term $g_{k,l}(p)$ lies in
the localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, that is, its $p$-adic valuation is nonnegative.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)- Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 1(b), odd case.

articles.title: Göbel sequences at index $p$ for primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$ denote the
$(k, l)$-Göbel sequence and let $p$ be a prime with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Then for every natural
number $l < p$, the $p$-adic valuation of $g_{(p-1)/2,\,l}(p)$ is nonnegative (the valuation of
$0$ is taken to be $0$); that is, $g_{(p-1)/2,\,l}(p)$ lies in the localization
$\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 1(a).

articles.title: Unique boundary pair for Göbel sequences when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$ denote
the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence and let $p \ge 13$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Then there
is exactly one pair $(l_L, l_R)$ of even natural numbers with $2 \le l_L < l_R \le p-1$ such
that, for every even natural number $l < p$, the $p$-adic valuation of $g_{(p-1)/2,\,l}(p)$ is
nonnegative (the valuation of $0$ is taken to be $0$) if and only if $l < l_L$ or $l_R \le l$.

Thus the even $l < p$ split into the three intervals $l < l_L$, $l_L \le l < l_R$ and
$l_R \le l$, and $g_{(p-1)/2,\,l}(p)$ lies in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ exactly on the outer two.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 1(b), unique decomposition.

articles.title: Integrality of the early terms of $(k, l)$-Göbel sequences
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$ denote the
$(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. For all natural numbers $k, l \ge 2$ and $1 \le n \le 6$, the value
$g_{k,l}(n)$ is an integer. Moreover, for all natural numbers $k, l \ge 2$, the value $g_{k,l}(7)$
is not an integer if and only if $k \equiv 2 \pmod 6$ and $l \equiv 3 \pmod 7$.

Equivalently, if $N_{k,l}$ is the first index at which $g_{k,l}$ is not an integer, then
$\min_{k,l \ge 2} N_{k,l} = 7$, and $N_{k,l} = 7$ if and only if $k \equiv 2 \pmod 6$ and
$l \equiv 3 \pmod 7$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Theorem 2 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-thm-2`).

articles.title: Propagation of a congruence along the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let
$k, l, r \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let $g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence, and let $a, b$ be
natural numbers with $1 \le a < p$ and $b < p$. For rational numbers $x, y$ write
$x \equiv y \pmod{p^r}$ when $x = y$ or $\nu_p(x - y) \ge r$, where $\nu_p$ is the $p$-adic
valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$. If $g_{k,l}(a) \equiv b p^{r-1} \pmod{p^r}$, then
$n \, g_{k,l}(n) \equiv a b p^{r-1} \pmod{p^r}$ for every natural number $n$ with $a \le n < p$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 20 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-20`).

articles.title: A congruence class of non-integral Göbel sequences
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$ denote the
$(k, l)$-Göbel sequence, let $p \ge 13$ be a prime with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and let
$k = \frac{p-1}{2} q$ for a positive odd natural number $q$. Then there is an even natural number
$l$ with $2 \le l \le p-3$ such that for every positive natural number $l'$ with
$l' \equiv l \pmod p$, the $p$-adic valuation of $g_{k,l'}(p)$ is negative, and some
$g_{k,l'}(n)$ with $1 \le n \le p$ is not an integer.

Every such $k$ is positive and even, as the paper requires.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Corollary 2.

articles.title: A non-integral term of $g_{k,2}$ by index $29363$ for $2 \le k \le 10^{14}$
articles.statement:
Let
$g_{k,l}$ denote the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. For every natural number $k$ with
$2 \le k \le 10^{14}$, there is a natural number $n$ with $1 \le n \le 29363$ such that the
rational number $g_{k,2}(n)$ is not an integer.

Writing $N_k$ for the first index at which $g_{k,2}$ is not an integer, as in the paper, this
says $N_k \le 29363$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 29.

articles.title: A non-integral term of $g_{k,2}$ by index $9011$ for $2 \le k \le 10^7$
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$
denote the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. For every natural number $k$ with $2 \le k \le 10^7$, there
is a natural number $n$ with $1 \le n \le 9011$ such that the rational number $g_{k,2}(n)$ is
not an integer.

Writing $N_k$ for the first index at which $g_{k,2}$ is not an integer, as in the paper, this
says $N_k \le 9011$ for $2 \le k \le 10^7$; together with $N_{2600725} = 9011$, this makes $9011$
the largest of these thresholds. The paper also reports that each of these $N_k$ was determined
explicitly by computation; that claim is not part of this statement.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Theorem 26.

articles.title: Initial value of the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $l$, the
$(k, l)$-Göbel sequence $g_{k,l}$ satisfies $g_{k,l}(1) = l$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Definition 1.
