articles.title: Key $p$-adic properties of the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $N \ge 1$
be a natural number, let $r = \nu_p(N!)$, where $\nu_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$
(with $\nu_p(0) = 0$), and write $g_{k,l}$ for the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. Write
$\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ for the set of rational numbers $x$ with $\nu_p(x) \ge 0$, and for an integer
$s$ write $x \in p^s \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ when $x = 0$ or $\nu_p(x) \ge s$. Then:
(1) for all natural numbers $k, l \ge 1$, if $p > N$ then $g_{k,l}(N) \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$;
(2) for all natural numbers $k, l \ge 1$ and $1 \le n \le N$, if
$g_{k,l}(n) \notin \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ then $g_{k,l}(n + 1) \notin \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$;
(3) if $p \le N$, then for all natural numbers $k_1, k_2 \ge r$ with
$k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{\varphi(p^r)}$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function, all $l \ge 1$
and all $1 \le n \le N$: $g_{k_1,l}(n) \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ if and only if
$g_{k_2,l}(n) \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, and in that case
$g_{k_1,l}(n) - g_{k_2,l}(n) \in p^{r - \nu_p(n!)} \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$;
(4) if $p \le N$, then for all natural numbers $k, l_1, l_2 \ge 1$ with
$l_1 \equiv l_2 \pmod{p^r}$ and all $1 \le n \le N$: $g_{k,l_1}(n) \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ if and
only if $g_{k,l_2}(n) \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, and in that case
$g_{k,l_1}(n) - g_{k,l_2}(n) \in p^{r - \nu_p(n!)} \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 5 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-5`).

articles.title: Residues of the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence modulo $p^r$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let
$k, l, r \ge 2$ be natural numbers, and let $g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. Let $I$ be
the set of natural numbers $n$ with $1 \le n < p$ such that $g_{k,l}(n) = 0$ or
$\nu_p(g_{k,l}(n)) \ge r - 1$, where $\nu_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$; that is,
$g_{k,l}(n) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{r-1}}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$. Let $G$ be the set of residues of the
numbers $g_{k,l}(n)$, $n \in I$, in $\mathbb{Z}/p^r\mathbb{Z}$, the residue of a rational number
being its numerator times the inverse of its denominator. Then $G = \{0\}$ or $G$ has exactly as
many elements as $I$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Theorem 18 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-thm-18`).

articles.title: Strict decrease of the normalized Göbel roots
articles.statement:
Let $k, l \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let
$g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence, and let $C_{k,l}(n) = g_{k,l}(n)^{1/k^n}$, a real
number. Then $C_{k,l}(n) > C_{k,l}(n + 1) > 1$ for every natural number $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 7 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-7`).

articles.title: The normalized Göbel roots converge to a limit greater than 1
articles.statement:
Let $k, l \ge 2$ be natural
numbers and let $g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. There is a real number $C > 1$ such
that the real numbers $g_{k,l}(n)^{1/k^n}$ tend to $C$ as $n \to \infty$.

The paper defines $C_{k,l}$ as this limit.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Proposition 10 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-prop-10`).

articles.title: Integrality of Göbel sequences up to index 7 via finite $p$-adic checks
articles.statement:
Let $g_{k,l}$ be
the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence. For a prime $p$, call a rational number $x$ $p$-integral if
$x \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, that is, if $x = 0$ or its $p$-adic valuation $\nu_p(x)$ is
nonnegative. The following two statements are equivalent.

(i) For all natural numbers $k, l \ge 2$, the value $g_{k,l}(n)$ is an integer for every
$1 \le n \le 6$, and $g_{k,l}(7)$ is not an integer if and only if $k \equiv 2 \pmod 6$ and
$l \equiv 3 \pmod 7$.

(ii) $g_{k,l}(7)$ is $2$-integral for all $2 \le k \le 11$ and $1 \le l \le 16$; it is
$3$-integral for all $2 \le k \le 7$ and $1 \le l \le 9$; it is $5$-integral for all
$1 \le k \le 4$ and $1 \le l \le 5$; and for all $1 \le k \le 6$ and $1 \le l \le 7$, it is not
$7$-integral if and only if $(k, l) = (2, 3)$.

Statement (i) is Theorem 2 of the source.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 6 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-6`).

articles.title: Recursion for the (k, l)-Göbel sequence
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$, $l$ and $n \ge 1$,
the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence $g_{k,l}$ satisfies, in $\mathbb{Q}$,

$$(n + 1)\, g_{k,l}(n + 1) = g_{k,l}(n) \bigl(n + g_{k,l}(n)^{k-1}\bigr),$$

where $k - 1$ is truncated subtraction, so the exponent is $0$ when $k = 0$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Definition 1.

articles.title: Göbel's original sequence
articles.statement:
The $(2, 2)$-Göbel sequence $g_{2,2}$ satisfies
$g_{2,2}(2) = 3$, $g_{2,2}(3) = 5$, $g_{2,2}(4) = 10$ and $g_{2,2}(5) = 28$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Section 1.

articles.title: The (k, l)-Göbel sequence
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $l$, the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence
is the sequence of rational numbers $g_{k,l}(n)$, $n \ge 0$, given by $g_{k,l}(0) = 0$,
$g_{k,l}(1) = l$ and, for $n \ge 1$,

$$g_{k,l}(n + 1) = \frac{g_{k,l}(n) \bigl(n + g_{k,l}(n)^{k-1}\bigr)}{n + 1},$$

where $k - 1$ is truncated subtraction, so the exponent is $0$ when $k = 0$.

The paper indexes from $n = 1$ and takes $k, l \ge 2$ (Lemma 5 also admits $k, l \ge 1$); the
value at $n = 0$ is a convention and plays no role.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Definition 1.

articles.title: The sign sequence $a_{p,l}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $l$, a function
$a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is an $a_{p,l}$-sequence when all of the following hold:
$a(n) \in \{1, -1\}$ for $1 \le n \le p-1$; $a(n) = 0$ for $n = 0$ and for every $n \ge p$;
$a(1) = 1$; $a(n) = a(p-n)$ for $1 \le n \le \lfloor (p-1)/2 \rfloor$; $a(n) = -a(l+1-n)$ for
$1 \le n \le \lfloor l/2 \rfloor$; and $a(n) = a(l+1+n)$ for $1 \le n \le p-l-2$.

The values outside $1 \le n \le p-1$ are fixed to $0$ so that uniqueness of the paper's finite
sequence becomes uniqueness of the function.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 17.

articles.title: The periodic sign sequence $b_{l,s}$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$ and $s$, a function
$b : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is a $b_{l,s}$-sequence when all of the following hold:
$b(n) \in \{1, -1\}$ for every integer $n$; $b(n + l + 1) = b(n)$ for every integer $n$;
$b(1) = 1$; $b(n) = -b(l+1-n)$ for every integer $n$ not divisible by $l+1$; and
$b(s-n) = b(s+1+n)$ for every integer $n$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Proposition 20.

articles.title: Left boundary of the even Göbel residue walks
articles.statement:
Fix a natural number $p$ and, for each
natural number $l$, let $\tilde g_l$ denote the Göbel residue walk for $p$ starting at $l$. A
natural number $l_L$ is the left boundary for $p$ when there is an even natural number $l_0 < p$
with $\tilde g_{l_0}(p) = 0$ and $l_L = l_0 + 2$ such that every even natural number $l < p$
with $\tilde g_l(p) = 0$ satisfies $l \le l_0$. In other words, the set of even $l < p$ with
$\tilde g_l(p) = 0$ is nonempty and $l_L$ is its maximum plus $2$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, proof of Theorem 1.

articles.title: Right boundary of the even Göbel residue walks
articles.statement:
Fix a natural number $p$ and, for each
natural number $l$, let $\tilde g_l$ denote the Göbel residue walk for $p$ starting at $l$. A
natural number $l_R$ is the right boundary for $p$ when $l_R$ is even, $l_R < p$,
$\tilde g_{l_R}(p) = p$, and every even natural number $l < p$ with $\tilde g_l(p) = p$
satisfies $l_R \le l$. In other words, $l_R$ is the least even $l < p$ with $\tilde g_l(p) = p$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, proof of Theorem 1.

articles.title: Zigzag order on integer sequences
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and functions
$a, b : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$, $a$ lies zigzag-below $b$ up to $p$, written $a \preceq b$,
when there is a natural number $m \le p$ such that $a(n) < b(n)$ for all $1 \le n \le m$ and
$a(n) = b(n)$ for all $m < n \le p$.

The paper's point sets are represented by their integer-valued coordinate functions; values
outside $1 \le n \le p$ play no role.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)- Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Section 2 definition of `⪯`.

articles.title: The odd multiples of $(p-1)/2$ admit no finite subcover
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ write
$A_p = \{\tfrac{p-1}{2}(2m+1) : m \in \mathbb{N}\}$ for the set of odd multiples of $(p-1)/2$. For
every finite set $S$ of primes $q$ with $q \ge 13$ and $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, there is a natural
number $k$ that lies in $A_p$ for some prime $p \ge 13$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ but lies in no
$A_q$ with $q \in S$.

## Sources

- Yuh Kobayashi and Shin-ichiro Seki, *A Note on Non-Integrality of the (k, l)- Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.8, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Residue of an integer
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$ and every integer $z$, the residue
modulo $m$ of $z$, viewed as a rational number, is the image of $z$ in $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Section 4.

articles.title: Residue of a rational number modulo an integer
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$ and a rational
number $x = a/b$ in lowest terms with $b > 0$, the residue of $x$ modulo $m$ is the element
$a \cdot b^{-1}$ of $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. When $b$ is prime to $m$, $b^{-1}$ is the inverse
of $b$ modulo $m$, so the residue is the class $c$ with $b c \equiv a \pmod m$; for other $x$
the inverse, and hence the residue, is a conventional value with no arithmetic meaning.

For a prime $p$ and a natural number $r$, it is used to read congruences modulo $p^r$ in the
ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of rational numbers whose denominator is prime to $p$.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Section 4 (residues of `g_{k,l}(n)` modulo `p^r` in `ℤ_(p)`).

articles.title: Somos-type sequences lie below Göbel sequences
articles.statement:
Let $k, l \ge 2$ be natural numbers, let
$g_{k,l}$ be the $(k, l)$-Göbel sequence, and let $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy
$t(n + 1) = t(n)^k / (n + 1)$ for all $n \ge 0$. If $t(0)^k \le l$, then $t(n) \le g_{k,l}(n)$
for every $n \ge 1$.

The paper also assumes $t(0) > 1$; the statement holds without it (for even $k$, $t(n) \ge 0$
for $n \ge 1$; for odd $k$, $x \mapsto x^k$ is monotone), so that hypothesis is dropped.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 9 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-9`).

articles.title: Root asymptotics of Somos-type sequences
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a natural number, let
$\sigma_k = \exp\bigl(\sum_{m \ge 1} \log m / k^m\bigr)$ be the $k$-Somos constant, and let
$t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $t(n + 1) = t(n)^k / (n + 1)$ for all $n \ge 0$. If
$t(0) > \sigma_k$, then the sequence $n \mapsto t(n)^{1/k^n}$ is nonincreasing and converges to
some real number $c > 1$.

The sequence is constant from $n = 0$ to $n = 1$, so the paper's "decreases monotonically" is
read in the non-strict sense.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Lemma 8 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-lem-8`).

articles.title: Sondow–Hadjicostas asymptotic expansion
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a natural number. For $j \ge 1$
put $S_j = \sum_{i \ge 1} i^j / k^i$ and $b_j = (-1)^{j-1} S_j / j$, and for $r \ge 0$ let

$$a_r = \sum_{m_1 + 2 m_2 + \dots + r m_r = r} \ \prod_{j=1}^{r} \frac{b_j^{m_j}}{m_j!},$$

where the sum runs over the tuples $(m_1, \dots, m_r)$ of natural numbers satisfying the
constraint. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $E(n) = \exp\bigl(\sum_{s \ge 1} \log(s + n) / k^s\bigr)$
and, for a natural number $R$, let $P_R(n) = 1 + \sum_{r=1}^{R} a_r / n^r$. Then for every
natural number $R$,

$$E(n) - n^{1/(k-1)} P_R(n) = O\bigl(n^{1/(k-1)} / n^{R+1}\bigr)$$

as $n \to \infty$ through the natural numbers.

In the paper $S_j$ appears as $A_j(k) / (k - 1)^{j+1}$, with $A_j$ the Eulerian polynomial.

## Sources

- Gima, Matsusaka, Miyazaki, and Yara, *On Integrality and Asymptotic Behavior of the (k, l)-Göbel Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.8.1, Theorem 15, quoting Sondow and Hadjicostas (2007), Theorem 9 and Lemma 1 (`jis-2024-24.8.1-thm-15`).

articles.title: Some generalized Euclid sequence contains every prime
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite set of primes
and let $k$ be the number of elements of $P$. Then there is an injective sequence
$a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of primes such that $a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$ are exactly the elements of $P$,
every prime occurs in the sequence, and for every $n \ge k$ there is a set
$I \subseteq \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $a_n$ divides

$$\prod_{i \in I} a_i + \prod_{i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\} \setminus I} a_i.$$

This is an existence claim over all choices of $I$ and of the prime divisor, unlike the open
Euclid–Mullin conjecture about one specific sequence. For distinct primes $p_1, \dots, p_r$ and
any $J \subseteq \{1, \dots, r\}$, the number
$\prod_{i \in J} p_i + \prod_{i \in \{1, \dots, r\} \setminus J} p_i$ is coprime to
$p_1 \cdots p_r$, so a prime divisor of it is always new.

Proof: Booker's residue-set route, with an elementary squarefree count in place of Rogers'
density bound and Jacobi-sum character-sum bounds in place of the Hasse and Weil bounds.

## Sources

- Andrew R. Booker, "A Variant of the Euclid-Mullin Sequence Containing Every Prime," Journal of Integer Sequences 19 (2016), Article 16.6.4, Theorem, lines 132–136, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Booker/book3.tex

articles.title: The largest number built from $m$ copies of $l$
articles.statement:
Let $l > 1$ and $m \ge 1$ be natural
numbers. Then $l^m$ can be built from exactly $m$ copies of $l$ using addition and
multiplication, and every natural number that can be built from $m$ copies of $l$ in this way
is at most $l^m$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Lemma 1.

articles.title: Numbers built from copies of $l$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$, $k$ and $n$, the number $n$
can be built from $k$ copies of $l$ when $n$ is the value of an expression that uses exactly $k$
copies of $l$, combined by addition and multiplication with arbitrary parentheses. Inductively,
$l$ is built from $1$ copy, and if $x$ is built from $a$ copies and $y$ from $b$ copies, then
$x + y$ and $x y$ are built from $a + b$ copies.

articles.title: Integer complexity of a sum
articles.statement:
For all positive integers $a$ and $b$, the integer
complexity of $a + b$ is at most the sum of the integer complexities of $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Integer complexity as a minimum over factorizations and sums
articles.statement:
Write
$\lVert m \rVert$ for the integer complexity of a positive integer $m$, the least number of ones
needed to write $m$ using $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses. For every integer $n \ge 2$,
$\lVert n \rVert$ is the least element of the set consisting of the numbers
$\lVert d \rVert + \lVert n/d \rVert$ for the divisors $d \ge 2$ of $n$ and the numbers
$\lVert j \rVert + \lVert n - j \rVert$ for the integers $j$ with $1 \le j \le n/2$.

## Sources

- Juan Arias de Reyna, "Complexity of Natural Numbers", Proposition 1.

articles.title: Adding a small multiple of $l$ to a multiple of $l^2$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_l$ for the
$l$-complexity of $n$. Let $l > 1$, let $b \ge 1$ be a multiple of $l^2$, let $a$ be a natural
number with $a \le l - 1$, and let $n = b + a l$. Then $\|n\|_l = \|b\|_l + a$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 2.

articles.title: Even $n$ with $2^m < n \le 2^{m+1}$ and 2-complexity $m + 1$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the
2-complexity of $n$. Let $m \ge 1$ and let $n$ be an even natural number with
$2^m < n \le 2^{m+1}$. Then $\|n\|_2 = m + 1$ if and only if $n = 2^m + 2^t$ for some natural
number $t$ with $1 \le t \le m$.

The case $t = m$ gives $n = 2^{m+1}$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 3 and Theorem 1.

articles.title: Even numbers in $(2^m, 2^{m+1})$ with 2-complexity $m + 2$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the
2-complexity of $n$. Let $m \ge 3$ and let $n$ be an even natural number with
$2^m < n \le 2^{m+1}$. Then $\|n\|_2 = m + 2$ if and only if $n$ has one of the following
forms, where all exponents are natural numbers:
(a) $n = 2^m + 2^{m_2} + 2^{m_3}$ with $m > m_2 > m_3 \ge 1$;
(b) $n = 2^m + 2^{m_2} + 2^{m_3} + 2^{m_4}$ with $m > m_2 > m_3 > m_4 \ge 2$ and
$m + m_4 = m_2 + m_3$;
(c) $n = 2^m + 2^{m-3} + 2^{m_2} + 2^{m_2-1}$ with $m \ge m_2 + 3 \ge 6$;
(d) $n = 2^m + 2^{m-5} + 2^{m-6} + 2^{m-7}$ with $m \ge 10$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 4 and Theorem 1.

articles.title: Four forms of even numbers with 2-complexity $m + 2$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the
2-complexity of $n$. Let $m \ge 3$ and let $n$ be an even natural number with
$2^m < n \le 2^{m+1}$. Suppose that $n$ has one of the following forms, where all exponents
are natural numbers:
(a) $n = 2^m + 2^{m_2} + 2^{m_3}$ with $m > m_2 > m_3 \ge 1$;
(b) $n = 2^m + 2^{m_2} + 2^{m_3} + 2^{m_4}$ with $m > m_2 > m_3 > m_4 \ge 2$ and
$m + m_4 = m_2 + m_3$;
(c) $n = 2^m + 2^{m-3} + 2^{m_2} + 2^{m_2-1}$ with $m \ge m_2 + 3 \ge 6$;
(d) $n = 2^m + 2^{m-5} + 2^{m-6} + 2^{m-7}$ with $m \ge 10$.
Then $\|n\|_2 = m + 2$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Corollary 3.

articles.title: The $l$-complexity vanishes exactly on numbers that cannot be built
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $l$ and $n$, the $l$-complexity of $n$ is $0$ if and only if there is no $k$ such that
$n$ can be built from $k$ copies of $l$ using addition and multiplication.

articles.title: The $l$-complexity is at most the size of any build
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$, $k$ and
$n$, if $n$ can be built from $k$ copies of $l$ using addition and multiplication, then the
$l$-complexity of $n$ is at most $k$.

articles.title: The $l$-complexity of $l^m + l^{m'}$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_l$ for the $l$-complexity of $n$.
For natural numbers $l > 1$ and $m \ge m' \ge 1$, $\|l^m + l^{m'}\|_l = m + 1$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Corollary 1.

articles.title: A buildable number is built from as many copies as its $l$-complexity
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $l$ and $n$, if $n$ can be built from some number of copies of $l$ using addition and
multiplication, then $n$ can be built in this way from $c$ copies of $l$, where $c$ is the
$l$-complexity of $n$.

articles.title: An upper bound for the 2-complexity of a sum of distinct powers of two
articles.statement:
Write
$\|n\|_2$ for the $2$-complexity of $n$. Let $S$ be a nonempty finite set of positive integers
with $k$ elements and largest element $m_1$. Then $\|\sum_{e \in S} 2^e\|_2 \le m_1 + k - 1$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Lemma 3.

articles.title: The 2-complexity of a power of two and of a sum of two powers of two
articles.statement:
Write
$\|n\|_2$ for the $2$-complexity of $n$. For all natural numbers $m_1$ and $m_2$ with
$m_1 > m_2 \ge 1$, one has $\|2^{m_1}\|_2 = m_1$ and $\|2^{m_1} + 2^{m_2}\|_2 = m_1 + 1$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Bounds for the 2-complexity of $2^m \cdot 6^r$ when $8 \le r \le 9$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for
the $2$-complexity of $n$. For all natural numbers $m$ and $r$ with $8 \le r \le 9$, one has
$m + 3r - 1 \le \|2^m \cdot 6^r\|_2 \le m + 3r$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 5 and Theorem 2.

articles.title: The 2-complexity of $2^m \cdot 6^r$ for $1 \le r \le 7$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the
$2$-complexity of $n$. For all natural numbers $m$ and $r$ with $1 \le r \le 7$, one has
$\|2^m \cdot 6^r\|_2 = m + 3r$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 5 and Theorem 2.

articles.title: The 2-complexity of $2^m \cdot 10^r$ for $1 \le r \le 4$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the
$2$-complexity of $n$. For all natural numbers $m$ and $r$ with $1 \le r \le 4$, one has
$\|2^m \cdot 10^r\|_2 = m + 4r$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 6 and Theorem 2.

articles.title: Bounds for the 2-complexity of $2^m \cdot 10^5$
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the $2$-complexity
of $n$. For every natural number $m$, one has $m + 19 \le \|2^m \cdot 10^5\|_2 \le m + 20$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 6 and Theorem 2.

articles.title: The $l$-complexity of a natural number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$ and $n$, the
$l$-complexity $\|n\|_l$ of $n$ is the least number $k$ such that $n$ can be built from $k$
copies of $l$ using addition and multiplication (with arbitrary parentheses), and
$\|n\|_l = 0$ if $n$ cannot be built from copies of $l$ at all.

articles.title: Expressions bound the integer complexity from above
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. If
an expression $e$ has value $n$, then the integer complexity of $n$ is at most the number of
ones of $e$.

## Sources

- C4.

articles.title: The function $g$ bounds integer complexity from below
articles.statement:
Write $\lVert n \rVert$ for the
integer complexity of a positive integer $n$, the least number of ones needed to write $n$ using
$1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses. For a positive integer $n$, let $a$ be the largest natural
number with $3^a \le n$, and let $g(n) = 3a$ if $n < \frac{4}{3} \cdot 3^a$, $g(n) = 3a + 1$ if
$\frac{4}{3} \cdot 3^a \le n < 2 \cdot 3^a$, and $g(n) = 3a + 2$ if $n \ge 2 \cdot 3^a$. Then
$g(n) \le \lVert n \rVert$ for every positive integer $n$.

## Sources

- Juan Arias de Reyna, "Complexity of Natural Numbers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Lower-bound function for integer complexity
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let $a$ be the
largest natural number with $3^a \le n$ when $n \ge 1$, and let $a = 0$ when $n = 0$. The function
$g$ on the natural numbers is given by $g(n) = 3a$ if $n < \frac{4}{3} \cdot 3^a$,
$g(n) = 3a + 1$ if $\frac{4}{3} \cdot 3^a \le n < 2 \cdot 3^a$, and $g(n) = 3a + 2$ if
$n \ge 2 \cdot 3^a$.

articles.title: Integers above $2^a 3^b$ have complexity above $2a + 3b$ when $a \le 2$ and $2a + 3b \ge 2$
articles.statement:
Write $\lVert m \rVert$ for the integer complexity of a positive integer $m$, the least number
of ones needed to write $m$ using $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses. Let $a \le 2$ and $b$ be
natural numbers with $2a + 3b \ge 2$. Then every natural number $m > 2^a 3^b$ satisfies
$\lVert m \rVert > 2a + 3b$.

## Sources

- Juan Arias de Reyna, "Complexity of Natural Numbers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Integer complexity of a product
articles.statement:
For all positive integers $a$ and $b$, the integer
complexity of $ab$ is at most the sum of the integer complexities of $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Integer complexity of $2^a 3^b$ for $a \le 2$
articles.statement:
Write $\lVert n \rVert$ for the integer
complexity of a positive integer $n$, the least number of ones needed to write $n$ using $1$, $+$,
$\times$ and parentheses. For all natural numbers $a \le 2$ and $b$, not both zero,
$\lVert 2^a 3^b \rVert = 2a + 3b$.

## Sources

- Juan Arias de Reyna, "Complexity of Natural Numbers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Integer complexity
articles.statement:
The integer complexity of a positive integer $n$ is the least
number of ones in an expression whose value is $n$, that is, the least number of ones needed
to write $n$ using $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses.

## Sources

- C4. Implemented via Nat.find on proved existential predicate.

articles.title: Number of leaves of an $m$-ary expression
articles.statement:
The number of leaf selections of an $m$-ary
Mahler–Popken expression, counting repetitions: a leaf counts $1$, and the count of a sum or of a
product of two expressions is the sum of their counts.

articles.title: Number of ones in an expression
articles.statement:
The number of ones of an expression is the number of
occurrences of the constant $1$ in it: the constant $1$ has one, and both $e_1 + e_2$ and
$e_1 \times e_2$ have as many as $e_1$ and $e_2$ together.

## Sources

- C3.

articles.title: Integer complexity extended to all natural numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the value
$\lVert n \rVert$ is the integer complexity of $n$ when $n$ is positive, that is, the least number
of ones needed to write $n$ using $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses, and $\lVert 0 \rVert = 0$.

articles.title: Value of an $m$-ary expression
articles.statement:
The natural number expressed by an $m$-ary Mahler–Popken
expression: the leaf with index $i \in \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ has value $i + 1$, and the value of a
sum or of a product of two expressions is the sum or the product of their values.

articles.title: Value of an expression
articles.statement:
The value of an expression is the natural number obtained by
evaluating it: the constant $1$ has value $1$, the value of $e_1 + e_2$ is the sum of the values
of $e_1$ and $e_2$, and the value of $e_1 \times e_2$ is the product of their values.

## Sources

- C2.

articles.title: Every positive integer is the value of an expression
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n > 0$ there is an expression whose value is $n$.

## Sources

- C2/C4 existence side.

articles.title: Every positive integer has an $m$-ary expression
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m \ge 1$ and
$n \ge 1$, there is an $m$-ary Mahler–Popken expression whose value is $n$ (for instance a sum of
ones).

articles.title: Expressions built from one, addition and multiplication
articles.statement:
An expression is either the
constant $1$, or a sum $e_1 + e_2$ of two expressions, or a product $e_1 \times e_2$ of two
expressions. Expressions are formal syntax trees, so the tree structure plays the role of
parentheses.

## Sources

- C2.

articles.title: A criterion for lower bounds on integer complexity
articles.statement:
Write $\lVert n \rVert$ for the
integer complexity of a positive integer $n$, the least number of ones needed to write $n$ using
$1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses. Let $P$ be a real-valued function on the natural numbers with
$P(1) = 1$ such that $P(n + m) \le P(n) + P(m)$ and $P(nm) \le P(n) + P(m)$ for all positive
integers $n$ and $m$. Then $P(n) \le \lVert n \rVert$ for every positive integer $n$.

## Sources

- Juan Arias de Reyna, "Complexity of Natural Numbers", Proposition 2.

articles.title: Logarithmic bounds for the $l$-complexity
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_l$ for the $l$-complexity of
$n$. Let $l > 1$ be a natural number and let $n$ be a positive multiple of $l$. Then
$\log_l n \le \|n\|_l \le l \log_l n - 1$, where $\log_l$ is the real logarithm to base $l$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Proposition 1.

articles.title: A lower bound for the 2-complexity outside sums of two powers of two
articles.statement:
Write
$\|n\|_2$ for the $2$-complexity of $n$. Let $n$ be a positive even integer that cannot be
written as $2^a + 2^b$ with natural numbers $a \le b$. Then $\log_2 n + 1 \le \|n\|_2$.

Since $n$ is even, the hypothesis says that $n$ is neither a power of $2$ nor a sum of two
distinct powers of $2$.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: Logarithmic lower bound for integer complexity
articles.statement:
Write $\lVert n \rVert$ for the integer
complexity of a positive integer $n$, the least number of ones needed to write $n$ using $1$, $+$,
$\times$ and parentheses. For every positive integer $n$, $\log_2(1 + n) \le \lVert n \rVert$.

## Sources

- Juan Arias de Reyna, "Complexity of Natural Numbers", Corollary 1.

articles.title: Lower bound for the 2-complexity of even sums of five or more distinct powers of two
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the 2-complexity of $n$. Let $n \ge 1$ be an even natural number and let $S$
be a finite set of natural numbers with at least five elements such that $n = \sum_{e \in S} 2^e$.
Then $\log_2 n + 2 \le \|n\|_2$, where $\log_2$ is the real base-2 logarithm.

This is a particular case of Corollary 4 of the source.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Corollary 4.

articles.title: Lower bound $\log_2 n + 2$ for the 2-complexity (Zhang's Corollary 4)
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$
for the 2-complexity of $n$: the least number of copies of $2$ from which $n$ can be built using
addition and multiplication, and $0$ if $n$ cannot be built. Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers
with $n$ even, $n \ge 1$ and $2^m < n \le 2^{m+1}$. Suppose that $n \ne 2^a + 2^b$ for all
natural numbers $a \le b$, and that $n$ has none of Zhang's four exceptional forms for $m$.
Then $\log_2 n + 2 \le \|n\|_2$, where $\log_2$ is the real base-2 logarithm.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Corollary 4.

articles.title: Logarithmic bounds for the 2-complexity (Zhang's Lemma 3(3))
articles.statement:
Write $\|n\|_2$ for the
2-complexity of $n$: the least number of copies of $2$ from which $n$ can be built using addition
and multiplication, and $0$ if $n$ cannot be built. For every even natural number $n \ge 1$,
$\log_2 n \le \|n\|_2 \le 2 \log_2 n - 1$, where $\log_2$ is the real base-2 logarithm.

## Sources

- Pengcheng Zhang, "The 2-Complexity of Even Positive Integers", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Logarithmic lower bound for the binary Mahler–Popken complexity
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n \ge 1$, the $2$-ary (binary) Mahler–Popken complexity $\|n\|_2$ satisfies $\log_2 n \le \|n\|_2$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell, "A Binary Version of the Mahler-Popken Complexity Function", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Subadditivity of the $m$-ary complexity under addition
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m \ge 1$,
$a \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1$, the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity $\|\cdot\|_m$ satisfies
$\|a + b\|_m \le \|a\|_m + \|b\|_m$.

This is the analogue of subadditivity under addition for the classical integer complexity.

articles.title: The $m$-ary complexity eventually satisfies its recursion
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$m \ge 1$ there is $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$, the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity
$\|n\|_m$ equals the right-hand side of the recursion (9), that is, the least of the values
$\|d\|_m + \|n/d\|_m$ over divisors $d$ of $n$ with $d \ne 1$ and $d \ne n$, and the values
$\|\eta\|_m + \|n - \eta\|_m$ over $0 < \eta < n$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell, "A Binary Version of the Mahler-Popken Complexity Function", Proposition 1.

articles.title: Expressions bound the $m$-ary complexity from above
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $n$ and
every $m$-ary Mahler–Popken expression $e$ whose value is $n$, the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken
complexity $\|n\|_m$ is at most the number of leaves of $e$.

articles.title: Subadditivity of the $m$-ary complexity under multiplication
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$m \ge 1$, $a \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1$, the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity $\|\cdot\|_m$ satisfies
$\|a b\|_m \le \|a\|_m + \|b\|_m$.

This is the analogue of subadditivity under multiplication for the classical integer
complexity.

articles.title: The $1$-ary complexity is the integer complexity
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the
$1$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity $\|n\|_1$ equals the classical integer complexity of $n$, the
least number of ones needed to write $n$ using $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses.

This is the case $m = 1$ of Definition 1 in Campbell's paper (its Example 2).

articles.title: The $m$-ary complexity is positive
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, the
$m$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity $\|n\|_m$ is positive.

articles.title: The Mahler–Popken complexity is attained
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$,
there is an $m$-ary Mahler–Popken expression whose value is $n$ and whose number of leaves
(counted with repetition) equals the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity $\lVert n \rVert_m$.

articles.title: Recursion for the binary Mahler–Popken complexity
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 3$,
the binary ($2$-ary) Mahler–Popken complexity $\lVert n \rVert_2$ equals the minimum of the sums
$\lVert d \rVert_2 + \lVert n/d \rVert_2$ over the divisors $d$ of $n$ with $d \ne 1$ and
$d \ne n$, and of the sums $\lVert \eta \rVert_2 + \lVert n - \eta \rVert_2$ over $0 < \eta < n$.
This is the recursion (9) for $m = 2$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell, "A Binary Version of the Mahler-Popken Complexity Function", Proposition 1.

articles.title: Upper bound for the binary Mahler–Popken complexity
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 2$,
the binary ($2$-ary) Mahler–Popken complexity $\lVert n \rVert_2$ is at most
$\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + \nu_2(n) - 1$, where $\nu_2(n)$ is the number of ones in the base-$2$
expansion of $n$.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell, "A Binary Version of the Mahler-Popken Complexity Function", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Mahler–Popken complexity
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken
complexity $\lVert n \rVert_m$ is the smallest number of leaves (counted with repetition) of an
$m$-ary Mahler–Popken expression whose value is $n$: the smallest number of possibly repeated
selections from $\{1, \dots, m\}$ needed to express $n$ with addition, multiplication and legal
bracketing. If no expression has value $n$ (which happens exactly when $m = 0$ or $n = 0$), the
value is $0$.

articles.title: Mahler–Popken expressions
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken expressions
are the formal expressions built from leaves using the binary operations $+$ and $\times$; the
tree structure plays the role of brackets. Each leaf carries a label $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$
(so there are $m$ kinds of leaf), and a leaf with label $i$ stands for the number
$i + 1 \in \{1, \dots, m\}$.

articles.title: Right-hand side of the Mahler–Popken recursion
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, write
$\lVert k \rVert_m$ for the $m$-ary Mahler–Popken complexity of $k$. The recursion value of $n$
is the smallest of the sums $\lVert d \rVert_m + \lVert n/d \rVert_m$ over the divisors $d$ of
$n$ with $d \ne 1$ and $d \ne n$, and of the sums $\lVert \eta \rVert_m + \lVert n - \eta \rVert_m$
over $0 < \eta < n$; it is $0$ when there are no such sums. This is the right-hand side of the
recursion (9) in Campbell's paper.

articles.title: Integer-complexity expressions as $1$-ary Mahler–Popken expressions
articles.statement:
The translation of
an expression built from one, addition and multiplication into a $1$-ary Mahler–Popken expression
replaces each occurrence of $1$ by the leaf standing for $1$ and keeps every addition and
multiplication, so the expression tree is unchanged.

articles.title: Every build uses at least one copy
articles.statement:
If $n$ can be obtained from $k$ copies of $l$ using
addition and multiplication, then $k \ge 1$.

articles.title: Achievable numbers of ones
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$ and a natural number $c$, the
predicate holds when some expression has value $n$ and exactly $c$ ones.

## Sources

- replaces Set S.

articles.title: $1$-ary Mahler–Popken expressions as integer-complexity expressions
articles.statement:
The translation of a
$1$-ary Mahler–Popken expression into an expression built from one, addition and multiplication
replaces each leaf (the only leaf stands for $1$) by $1$ and keeps every addition and
multiplication, so the expression tree is unchanged.

articles.title: Zhang's four exceptional forms
Multiple-counting Jacobsthal sequence
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $x$, $\rho$ and $n$, the
multiple-counting Jacobsthal sequence $J_{x,\rho}(n)$ is the number of multiples of $\rho$ strictly
between $x^n$ and $x^{n+1}$, that is, the number of natural numbers $k$ with $x^n < k < x^{n+1}$
and $\rho \mid k$.

The source studies $2 \le x$ and $2 \le \rho$; the count itself is useful without those
restrictions.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Cilasun/cila5.tex>.

articles.title: The recurrence of a Newton sequence
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring and let
$a, c \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$ be such that $a$ is a Newton sequence generated by $c$. Then for
every natural number $n$ we have $a_{n+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_{n-j} c_{j+1} + (n+1) c_{n+1}$.

articles.title: Newton sequences
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring and let $a, c \colon \mathbb{N} \to R$.
The sequence $a$ is a Newton sequence generated by $c$ if for every natural number $n$,
$a_{n+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_{n-j} c_{j+1} + (n+1) c_{n+1}$.

Equivalently, $a_m = \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} a_{m-k} c_k + m c_m$ for every $m \ge 1$. The sequences in
the sources begin at index one, so $a_0$ and $c_0$ play no role. The two sources write the
factors in opposite orders, which agree because $R$ is commutative.

## Sources

- JIS VOL18/Wojcik, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Wojcik/wojcik6.tex>, lines 276–280; JIS VOL8/Huang, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Huang/huang11.tex>, lines 176–179.

articles.title: Odd Lichtenberg numbers
articles.statement:
The odd Lichtenberg numbers form the sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$
of natural numbers defined by $a_0 = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = 4 a_n + 1$, so the sequence begins
$1, 5, 21, 85, \dots$; these are the positive terms of OEIS A002450.

Equivalently, it is the self-generating sequence with seed $1$ and generating function
$k \mapsto 4k + 1$.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Hinz/hinz5.tex>.

articles.title: Counting integers with a given least prime factor in an interval
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $t$ be
positive integers and let $p$ be a prime. Let $N$ be the number of integers $m$ with
$a + 1 \le m \le a + t$ that are divisible by $p$ and by no prime $q < p$. Then

$$\left| N - \frac{t}{p} \prod_{q < p,\ q \text{ prime}} \left(1 - \frac{1}{q}\right) \right|
\le 2^{\pi(p-1)}$$

where $\pi$ is the prime-counting function.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Lemma 6 (`lem:Dp`).

articles.title: The first iterated remainder set is the remainder set
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
iterated remainder set $S_1(n)$ equals the remainder set
$S(n) = \{n \bmod k : 1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\}$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Section 2 (`S(n) = S_1(n)`).

articles.title: Iterated remainder sets of 35
articles.statement:
The iterated remainder sets of $35$ satisfy
$S_6(35) = \{0\}$ and $S_7(35) = \emptyset$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Section 2 (definition of `S_j(n)`).

articles.title: Iterated remainder sets
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the iterated remainder sets
$S_j(n)$, $j \ge 0$, are defined by $S_0(n) = \{1, \dots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\}$ and, for
$j \ge 0$, $S_{j+1}(n) = \{n \bmod k : k \in S_j(n),\ k \ne 0\}$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Section 2 (definition of `S_j(n)`).

articles.title: Maximal Pierce length via iterated remainder sets
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ and $t$ be natural
numbers, let $P(n)$ be the maximal Pierce length of $n$ and let $S_j(n)$ be the iterated
remainder sets of $n$. Then the following are equivalent: $P(n) = t + 1$; $S_t(n) = \{0\}$;
$S_t(n)$ has exactly one element and $S_{t+j}(n) = \emptyset$ for every $j \ge 1$.

This corrects the index of the printed lemma, $P(n) = t \iff S_{t+1}(n) = \{0\}$, which fails
for every $n \ge 3$: for example $P(5) = 3$, $S_2(5) = \{0\}$ and $S_4(5) = \emptyset$. The
paper derives the lemma from its Lemma 18 ($r \in S_j(n)$ if and only if $a_{j+1} = r$ for some
$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1 \le a \le n$, where $a_0 = a$ and $a_{i+1} = n \bmod a_i$), which
gives the index $P(n) - 1$. Lemma 18, and hence this lemma, needs $n \ge 3$: $P(2) = 1$ but
$S_0(2) = \{1\}$.

## Sources

- the forward direction of the first equivalence (for `t ≥ 1`) is proved as `S_eq_singleton_zero_of_maxLength_eq` in `FormalizedPapers/NumberTheory/BaraskarGokhaleJainKiezun2026`.
- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Lemma 19.

articles.title: Upper bound $1.3\, n / \log n$ for the prime-counting function
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n \ge 2$, the number $\pi(n)$ of primes at most $n$ satisfies
$\pi(n) \le 1.3\, n / \log n$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Lemma 7 (`lem:primecounting_ub`).

articles.title: The remainder-set constant
articles.statement:
The remainder-set constant is
$c = \sum_{p} \frac{1}{p(p+1)} \prod_{q < p} \left(1 - \frac{1}{q}\right)$, where $p$ runs
over all primes and, for each $p$, $q$ runs over the primes less than $p$.

Numerically, $c \approx 0.2296$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, equation `eq:asymp`.

articles.title: Asymptotic formula for the number of remainders
articles.statement:
Let $s(n)$ be the number of distinct
remainders $n \bmod k$ with $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and let $c$ be the remainder-set
constant. Then, as $n \to \infty$ over the natural numbers,
$s(n) - cn = O\bigl(n / (\log n \cdot \log \log n)\bigr)$, and $s(n)/n \to c$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Theorem 1 (`thm:asymp`).

articles.title: Consecutive differences of the number of remainders
articles.statement:
Let $s(n)$ be the number of
distinct remainders $n \bmod k$ with $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Then
$s(n+1) \le s(n) + 1$ for every $n \ge 1$; there is a real constant $C$ with
$s(n) - C \log \log n \le s(n+1)$ for all sufficiently large $n$; and for every natural number
$M$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $s(n+1) + M \le s(n)$, that is,
$\liminf_{n \to \infty} (s(n+1) - s(n)) = -\infty$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Theorem 2 (`thm:diffs`).

articles.title: Unbounded drops in the number of remainders
articles.statement:
Let $s(n)$ be the number of distinct
remainders $n \bmod k$ with $1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. For every natural number $M$
there are infinitely many $n$ with $s(n+1) + M \le s(n)$; equivalently,
$\liminf_{n \to \infty} (s(n+1) - s(n)) = -\infty$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Proposition 17 (`prop:diffs_unbounded`).

articles.title: The remainder count of 11
articles.statement:
The number $s(11)$ of distinct remainders $11 \bmod k$ for
$1 \le k \le 5$ equals $4$.

These remainders form the set $S(11) = \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ (Table 1 of the paper).

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Table 1.

articles.title: The remainder count of 12
articles.statement:
The number $s(12)$ of distinct remainders $12 \bmod k$ for
$1 \le k \le 6$ equals $2$.

This is a drop from $s(11) = 4$, the number of distinct remainders $11 \bmod k$ for
$1 \le k \le 5$ (Table 1 of the paper).

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Table 1.

articles.title: Remainder count
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, $s(n)$ is the number of elements of the
remainder set $S(n)$, that is, the number of distinct values of $n \bmod k$ for
$1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ (OEIS A283190).

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Section 1 (definition of `s(n)`).

articles.title: Remainder set
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the remainder set is
$S(n) = \{\, n \bmod k : 1 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \,\}$, the set of remainders of $n$
modulo the integers from $1$ to $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Section 1 (definition of `S(n)`).

articles.title: Tail of the sum of inverse prime squares
articles.statement:
As the natural number $n$ tends to infinity,
the sum $\sum_{p > n,\ p \text{ prime}} 1/p^2$ of the inverse squares of the primes greater
than $n$ is $O(1/(n \log n))$.

## Sources

- Omkar Baraskar and Ingrid Vukusic, *Bounds for Sets of Remainders*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.1.4, Lemma 8 (`lem:psquared_sum_est`).

articles.title: Positivity of the generalized Sylvester sequence
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the
term $s_k(n)$ of the generalized Sylvester sequence is positive.

articles.title: Recurrence for the generalized Sylvester sequence
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the
generalized Sylvester sequence $(s_k(n))_{k \ge 0}$ satisfies
$s_{k+1}(n) = s_k(n)^2 - s_k(n) + 1$.

articles.title: Initial term of the generalized Sylvester sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
generalized Sylvester sequence $(s_k(n))_{k \ge 0}$ satisfies $s_0(n) = n + 1$.

articles.title: Generalized Sylvester sequence
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the generalized Sylvester sequence
$(s_k(n))_{k \ge 0}$ is the sequence of natural numbers defined by $s_0(n) = n + 1$ and
$s_{k+1}(n) = s_k(n)^2 - s_k(n) + 1$ for $k \ge 0$.

The source indexes the sequence from one: its $s_1(n)$ is $s_0(n)$ here.

articles.title: Coprime solutions of $x^2 + 7 = 4y^n$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $x$ and $y$, the
conditions $n \ge 3$, $x \ge 1$, $y \ge 1$, $\gcd(x, y) = 1$ and $x^2 + 7 = 4y^n$ hold if and only
if $(n, x, y)$ is $(3, 5, 2)$, $(5, 11, 2)$ or $(13, 181, 2)$ (Luca–Tengely–Togbé).

## Sources

- F. Luca, Sz. Tengely, and A. Togbé, "On the Diophantine equation x² + C = 4yⁿ", Theorem 1.1, as quoted in Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Theorem 1, equation with C = 7.

articles.title: Coprime solutions of $x^2 + 3 = 4y^n$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $x$ and $y$, the
conditions $n \ge 3$, $x \ge 1$, $y \ge 1$, $\gcd(x, y) = 1$ and $x^2 + 3 = 4y^n$ hold if and only
if $n \ge 3$ and either $x = y = 1$ or $(n, x, y) = (3, 37, 7)$ (Luca–Tengely–Togbé).

## Sources

- F. Luca, Sz. Tengely, and A. Togbé, "On the Diophantine equation x² + C = 4yⁿ", Theorem 1.1, as quoted in Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Theorem 1, equation with C = 3.

articles.title: Mersenne numbers in the Sylvester sequence
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. The natural numbers $x$ such that $x = S_n$
for some $n$ and $x = 2^r - 1$ for some $r \ge 1$ are exactly $3$ and $7$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Corollary 1(a).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers of even index modulo 10
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $i \ge 1$,
$S_{2i} \equiv 7 \pmod{10}$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 2, congruence (9), even indices.

articles.title: Prime divisors congruent to 3 modulo 4 of Sylvester numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the
Sylvester sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $n \ge 1$, $S_n$ has a
prime divisor $p$ with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Corollary 1(d).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers modulo 1764
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester sequence,
$S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $n \ge 3$, $S_n \equiv 43 \pmod{1764}$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 1, congruence (7).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers modulo 36
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester sequence,
$S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $n \ge 2$, $S_n \equiv 7 \pmod{36}$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 1, congruence (6).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers modulo 4
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester sequence,
$S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $n \ge 1$, $S_n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 1, congruence (5).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers next to perfect powers
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $n$ other than $1$ and $2$ there
are no natural numbers $a \ge 2$ and $m \ge 2$ with $S_n = a^m + 1$ or $S_n = a^m - 1$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 3(b).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers are not perfect powers
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $n$ there are no natural numbers
$a \ge 2$ and $m \ge 2$ with $S_n = a^m$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 3(a).

articles.title: No Sylvester number is perfect
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the $n$-th Sylvester number
$S_n$ is not a perfect number.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Corollary 1(c).

articles.title: Sylvester numbers
articles.statement:
The Sylvester numbers $S_0, S_1, S_2, \dots$ are the natural numbers
given by $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$ for $n \ge 0$, so the sequence begins
$2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, \dots$. It is the generalized Sylvester sequence with parameter $1$.

articles.title: Sylvester numbers of odd index modulo 10
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For every $i \ge 1$,
$S_{2i+1} \equiv 3 \pmod{10}$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 2, congruence (9), odd indices.

articles.title: Alternating divisibility for Sylvester numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$ with
$1 \le k \le n$, the integer $S_k^2 + 1$ divides the integer $S_n - (-1)^{n-k} S_k$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 2, divisibility (8).

articles.title: Divisibility of differences of Sylvester numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Sylvester
sequence, $S_0 = 2$ and $S_{n+1} = S_n^2 - S_n + 1$. For all natural numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$
with $k \ge 1$, $m \ge k$ and $n \ge k$, the integer $(S_k - 1)^2$ divides $S_n - S_m$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Proposition 1, divisibility (4).

articles.title: The only triangular Sylvester number is $3$
articles.statement:
Let $S_n$ denote the $n$-th Sylvester
number. A natural number $x$ equals $S_n$ for some $n$ and satisfies $2x = m(m + 1)$ for some
natural number $m \ge 1$ if and only if $x = 3$.

## Sources

- Abderrahim Makki Naciri, "A Note on Sylvester's Sequence", Corollary 1(b).

articles.title: Bounds for the arithmetic derivative
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number, let $p$ be the
least prime factor of $n$, and let $\Omega(n)$ be the number of prime factors of $n$ counted with
multiplicity. Then the arithmetic derivative $D(n)$ satisfies

$$\Omega(n) \, n^{(\Omega(n) - 1)/\Omega(n)} \le D(n) \le \frac{n \log_p n}{p},$$

and each of the two inequalities is an equality if and only if $n$ is a prime power.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Lemma 1 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-lem-1`).

articles.title: Prime tetrations where the arithmetic derivative and the Collatz map commute
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be
the arithmetic derivative and $C$ the accelerated Collatz map. For a prime $p$,
$D(C(p^p)) = C(D(p^p))$ if and only if $C(p^p) = q^q$ for some prime $q$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 4 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-4`).

articles.title: Bounds on the factors of compatible semiprimes
articles.statement:
Suppose the semiprimes $pq$ and $rs$ are
compatible, where $q < p$. Then $r \ge 241$, $s \ge 241$, $3q < r < 3p$ and $3q < s < 3p$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Lemma 11 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-lem-11`).

articles.title: Prime roots give semiprime solutions
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be the arithmetic derivative and $C$ the
accelerated Collatz map. Let $p$ and $q$ be primes and let $t \ge 0$ be an integer with
$t^2 = p^2 - 22pq + q^2 - 8$. If $r = (p + q + t)/4$ and $s = (p + q - t)/4$ are both primes,
then $C(pq) = rs$ and $D(C(pq)) = C(D(pq))$.

The numbers $r$ and $s$ are the roots $(p + q \pm \sqrt{p^2 - 22pq + q^2 - 8})/4$ of
$2x^2 - (p + q)x + 3pq + 1 = 0$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 7 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-7`).

articles.title: The accelerated Collatz map on even numbers
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be the accelerated Collatz map and
$T$ the Collatz map. For every even natural number $n$, $C(n) = T(n)$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The accelerated Collatz map on odd numbers
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be the accelerated Collatz map and
$T$ the Collatz map. For every odd natural number $n$, $C(n) = T(T(n))$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Section 2.

articles.title: The accelerated Collatz map
articles.statement:
The accelerated Collatz map $C : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
sends a natural number $n$ to $n/2$ if $n$ is even and to $(3n + 1)/2$ if $n$ is odd.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Section 2.

articles.title: Positive solutions of the Collatz arithmetic differential equation are composite
articles.statement:
Let
$D$ be the arithmetic derivative and $C$ the accelerated Collatz map. Every positive integer $n$
with $D(C(n)) = C(D(n))$ is composite, that is, $n > 1$ and $n$ is not prime.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 3 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-3`).

articles.title: An example of compatible semiprimes
articles.statement:
The semiprimes $71 \cdot 1609 = 114239$ and
$349 \cdot 491$ are compatible.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Table 1.

articles.title: Compatible semiprimes
articles.statement:
Natural numbers $p, q, r, s$ form a compatible semiprime pair,
and the semiprimes $pq$ and $rs$ are called compatible, when $p, q, r, s$ are primes with
$2(r + s) = p + q$ and $2rs = 3pq + 1$; equivalently, $r$ and $s$ are the roots of
$2x^2 - (p + q)x + 3pq + 1 = 0$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Section 3, definition after Proposition 7.

articles.title: Compatible semiprimes modulo 5
articles.statement:
Let $p, q, r, s$ be primes with $2(r + s) = p + q$ and
$2rs = 3pq + 1$, so that the semiprimes $pq$ and $rs$ are compatible. Then one of $p, q$ is
congruent to $1$ and the other to $4$ modulo $5$, and likewise one of $r, s$ is congruent to $1$
and the other to $4$ modulo $5$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 12 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-12`).

articles.title: Compatible semiprimes modulo 4
articles.statement:
Let $p, q, r, s$ be primes with $2(r + s) = p + q$ and
$2rs = 3pq + 1$, so that the semiprime $pq$ is compatible with the semiprime $rs$. Then
$pq \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and one of $p, q$ is congruent to $1$ and the other to $3$ modulo $4$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 10 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-10`).

articles.title: Compatible semiprimes modulo 10
articles.statement:
Let $p, q, r, s$ be primes with $2(r + s) = p + q$ and
$2rs = 3pq + 1$, so that the semiprimes $pq$ and $rs$ are compatible. Then one of $p, q$ is
congruent to $1$ and the other to $9$ modulo $10$, and likewise one of $r, s$ is congruent to $1$
and the other to $9$ modulo $10$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 13 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-13`).

articles.title: Compatible semiprimes modulo 3
articles.statement:
Let $p, q, r, s$ be primes with $2(r + s) = p + q$ and
$2rs = 3pq + 1$, so that the semiprimes $pq$ and $rs$ are compatible. Then
$pq \equiv rs \equiv 2 \pmod 3$; moreover one of $p, q$ is congruent to $1$ and the other to $2$
modulo $3$, and likewise one of $r, s$ is congruent to $1$ and the other to $2$ modulo $3$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 8 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-8`).

articles.title: No special semiprime solves the derivative–Collatz equation
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be the arithmetic
derivative and let $C$ be the accelerated Collatz map, $C(n) = n/2$ for even $n$ and
$C(n) = (3n + 1)/2$ for odd $n$. Let $n$ be a positive integer with $D(C(n)) = C(D(n))$ and let
$p$ be a prime. Then $n \ne p^2$; if $p + 2$ is prime then $n \ne p(p + 2)$; if $p + 4$ is prime
then $n \ne p(p + 4)$; and if $2p + 1$ is prime then $n \ne p(2p + 1)$. Thus no such $n$ is the
square of a prime, a product of twin primes, a product of cousin primes, or the product of a
Sophie Germain prime and its safe prime.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Corollary 6 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-cor-6`).

articles.title: Positive solutions of the Collatz arithmetic differential equation are odd
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be
the arithmetic derivative and $C$ the accelerated Collatz map. Every positive integer $n$ with
$D(C(n)) = C(D(n))$ is odd.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 2 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-2`).

articles.title: Compatible semiprimes have odd prime factors
articles.statement:
Let $p, q, r, s$ be primes with
$2(r + s) = p + q$ and $2rs = 3pq + 1$, so that the semiprimes $pq$ and $rs$ are compatible.
Then $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$ are all odd.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Lemma 9 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-lem-9`).

articles.title: Prime gap bound for semiprime solutions
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be the arithmetic derivative and let $C$
be the accelerated Collatz map, $C(n) = n/2$ for even $n$ and $C(n) = (3n + 1)/2$ for odd $n$.
If $p$ and $q$ are primes with $q < p$ and $D(C(pq)) = C(D(pq))$, then
$p - q \ge 2\sqrt{30p^2 + 2} - 10p$.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Proposition 5 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-prop-5`).

articles.title: Reciprocals of compatible semiprimes have a finite sum
articles.statement:
Call a natural number $n$ a
compatible semiprime if $n = pq$ for primes $p, q$ for which there are primes $r, s$ with
$2(r + s) = p + q$ and $2rs = 3pq + 1$. The sum of $1/n$ over all compatible semiprimes $n$
converges.

## Sources

- Zachary P. Bradshaw, *On a Family of Solutions to Arithmetic Differential Equations Involving the Collatz Map*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.1.8, Theorem 14 (`jis-2025-25.1.8-thm-14`).

articles.title: Iterates of the Collatz map
articles.statement:
Let $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the Collatz map, which
sends $n$ to $n / 2$ if $n$ is even and to $3n + 1$ if $n$ is odd. For natural numbers $k$ and
$n$, the $k$-th Collatz iterate of $n$ is $T^k(n)$, the result of applying $T$ to $n$ exactly $k$
times: $T^0(n) = n$ and $T^{k+1}(n) = T(T^k(n))$.

articles.title: The Collatz map
articles.statement:
The Collatz map $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ sends a natural number
$n$ to $n / 2$ if $n$ is even and to $3n + 1$ if $n$ is odd.

articles.title: Collatz stopping time
articles.statement:
Let $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the Collatz map, which sends
$n$ to $n / 2$ if $n$ is even and to $3n + 1$ if $n$ is odd, and let $T^k$ denote its $k$-fold
iterate, with $T^0(n) = n$. For a natural number $n$, the Collatz stopping time of $n$ is
undefined if $n = 0$ or if $T^k(n) \ne 1$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$; otherwise it is the least
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $T^k(n) = 1$.

In the Collatz literature this quantity is often called the total stopping time.

articles.title: No Collatz $m$-cycles with $m \le 91$ (Hercher)
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the shortcut Collatz map on
the natural numbers, $T(c) = c/2$ for even $c$ and $T(c) = (3c+1)/2$ for odd $c$, and let $m$ be
a natural number with $m \le 91$. There are no natural numbers $n$ and $p > 0$ such that
$T^i(n) > 2$ for all $i < p$, $T^p(n) = n$, $T^k(n) \ne n$ for all $k$ with $0 < k < p$, and
exactly $m$ indices $i < p$ satisfy both $T^i(n) < T^{(i+1) \bmod p}(n)$ and
$T^i(n) < T^{(i+p-1) \bmod p}(n)$.

In words: no cycle of $T$ all of whose entries exceed $2$ (which excludes the trivial cycle
$1, 2, 1, 2, \dots$), taken with its minimal period $p$, has exactly $m$ entries lying cyclically
strictly below both neighbours.

## Sources

- Christian Hercher, "There are no Collatz m-Cycles with m ≤ 91," Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023), Article 23.3.5, Main Theorem, lines 541–543, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL26/Hercher/hercher5.tex with the operator at lines 104–111 and the m-cycle definition at lines 149–151.

articles.title: A perturbation at $q^{n+1}$ moves to $q^n$ under $T_{A,B}$
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, U, V$ be power
series in $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $A$, $B$ and $V$ odd (constant term $1$), let $T_{A,B}$ be the
$q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n \ge 0$ be an integer. Then there is an odd power series
$W \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $T_{A,B}(U + q^{n+1} V) = T_{A,B}(U) + q^n W$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Lemma 7 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-lem-7`).

articles.title: The $q$-Collatz map is conjugate to the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be odd
power series in $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ (constant term $1$), let $T_{A,B}$ be the $q$-analog of the
$3x+1$ map on $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, and let $T$ be the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers
$\mathbb{Z}_2$. Then there is a bijection $h : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with
$h^{-1}(T_{A,B}(h(x))) = T(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Theorem 2 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-thm-2`).

articles.title: Fixed points and the $2$-cycle of the $q$-Collatz map
articles.statement:
Let $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ be
odd (constant term $1$) and let $T_{A,B}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map. For every
$x \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, $T_{A,B}(x) = x$ holds exactly when $x = 0$ or $x = B/(A+q)$. Moreover,
for every $x \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, $T_{A,B}(T_{A,B}(x)) = x$ and $T_{A,B}(x) \ne x$ hold together
exactly when $x = B/(A+q^2)$ or $x = qB/(A+q^2)$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Lemma 13 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-lem-13`).

articles.title: Iterates of $T_{A,B}$ move a perturbation at $q^{n+1}$ to $q^{n+1-k}$
articles.statement:
Let $A, B, U, V$
be power series in $\mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $A$, $B$ and $V$ odd (constant term $1$), let
$T_{A,B}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers with
$k \le n + 1$. Write $T_{A,B}^k$ for the $k$-th iterate of $T_{A,B}$. Then there is an odd power
series $W \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $T_{A,B}^k(U + q^{n+1} V) = T_{A,B}^k(U) + q^{n+1-k} W$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Corollary 8 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-cor-8`).

articles.title: A perturbation at $q^n$ flips the parity of the $n$-th iterate
articles.statement:
Let
$A, B, U, V \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ with $A$, $B$ and $V$ odd (constant term $1$), let $T_{A,B}$ be
the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n \ge 0$ be an integer. Then the $n$-th iterates
$T_{A,B}^n(U + q^n V)$ and $T_{A,B}^n(U)$ have different constant terms.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Corollary 9 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-cor-9`).

articles.title: The map $T_{1+q,1}$ is conjugate to the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
articles.statement:
Let $T_q = T_{1+q,1}$
be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$ map with $A = 1 + q$ and $B = 1$, so that $T_q(x) = x/q$ if $q$
divides $x$ and $T_q(x) = ((1+q)x + 1)/q$ otherwise, and let $T$ be the $3x+1$ map on the
$2$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_2$. Then there is a bijection $h : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$
with $h^{-1}(T_q(h(x))) = T(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Corollary 3 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-cor-3`).

articles.title: Polynomial orbits of $T_{1,1+q^2}$
articles.statement:
Let $T = T_{1,1+q^2}$ be the $q$-analog of the $3x+1$
map with $A = 1$ and $B = 1 + q^2$. For every polynomial $p$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, some iterate
$T^k(p)$ with $k \ge 0$ lies in $\{0, 1 + q, 1, q\}$, the set formed by the fixed points $0$ and
$1 + q$ of $T$ and its $2$-cycle $\{1, q\}$. Moreover, for every $x \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, $T(x)$
is a polynomial if and only if $x$ is a polynomial.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Theorem 5 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-thm-5`).

articles.title: Parity vectors detect congruence modulo $q^{n+1}$
articles.statement:
Let $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ be odd
(constant term $1$), let $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}$ be the parity vector map of the $q$-analog $T_{A,B}$
of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n \ge 0$ be an integer. For all $a, b \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, we have
$\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(a) \equiv \mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(b) \pmod{2^{n+1}}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ if and only if
$q^{n+1}$ divides $a - b$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Theorem 11 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-thm-11`).

articles.title: Parity vectors induce bijections modulo $q^n$
articles.statement:
Let $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ be odd
(constant term $1$), let $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}$ be the parity vector map of the $q$-analog $T_{A,B}$
of the $3x+1$ map, and let $n \ge 1$ be an integer. Then there is a bijection
$e : \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]/(q^n) \to \mathbb{Z}/2^n\mathbb{Z}$ such that, for every
$a \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, $e$ sends the class of $a$ to the residue of $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(a)$
modulo $2^n$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Corollary 12 (`jis-2025-25.6.8-cor-12`).

articles.title: The parity vector of $0$
articles.statement:
For all $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the parity vector of $0$
under the $q$-analog $T_{A,B}$ of the $3x+1$ map is $0$, that is, $\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Definition 10.

articles.title: The parity vector of the q-analog 3x+1 map
articles.statement:
For power series
$A, B, x \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the parity vector of $x$ is the $2$-adic integer
$\mathrm{PV}_{A,B}(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} x_k 2^k \in \mathbb{Z}_2$, where $x_k \in \{0, 1\}$ is the
constant coefficient of the $k$-th iterate $T_{A,B}^k(x)$ of the $q$-analog $3x+1$ map $T_{A,B}$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Definition 10.

articles.title: The q-analog 3x+1 map on multiples of $q$
articles.statement:
For all power series
$A, B, y \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the $q$-analog $3x+1$ map satisfies $T_{A,B}(qy) = y$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T_{A,B}`).

articles.title: Zero is a fixed point of the q-analog 3x+1 map
articles.statement:
For all power series
$A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the $q$-analog $3x+1$ map satisfies $T_{A,B}(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T_{A,B}`).

articles.title: The q-analog of the 3x+1 map
articles.statement:
For a power series $y = \sum_n y_n q^n \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$,
write $y/q$ for the power series $\sum_n y_{n+1} q^n$: the constant term of $y$ is discarded and the
rest is divided by $q$. For power series $A, B \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, the map
$T_{A,B} : \mathbb{F}_2[[q]] \to \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$ is defined by $T_{A,B}(x) = x/q$ if the
constant term of $x$ is $0$, and $T_{A,B}(x) = (Ax + B)/q$ otherwise.

When $A$ and $B$ have constant term $1$, the numerator $Ax + B$ has constant term $0$ whenever
$x$ has constant term $1$, so in that case the division by $q$ is exact.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T_{A,B}`).

articles.title: Dividing a multiple of $q$ by $q$
articles.statement:
For every power series $y \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$,
applying the shift $\sum_n x_n q^n \mapsto \sum_n x_{n+1} q^n$ to $qy$ gives back $y$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (division by `q`).

articles.title: Division by $q$ in $\mathbb{F}_2((q))$
articles.statement:
For a power series
$x = \sum_n x_n q^n \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$, its shift is the power series $\sum_n x_{n+1} q^n$,
obtained by discarding the constant term of $x$ and dividing by $q$. In particular, the shift of
$qy$ is $y$ for every $y \in \mathbb{F}_2[[q]]$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (the quotients `x/q` and `(Ax+B)/q` in the definition of `T_{A,B}`).

articles.title: $3x + 1$ is even for odd $2$-adic $x$
articles.statement:
For every $2$-adic integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ whose
residue modulo $2$ is nonzero, the residue of $3x + 1$ modulo $2$ is zero.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T`).

articles.title: The $2$-adic $3x+1$ map swaps $1$ and $2$
articles.statement:
The $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
$T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ satisfies $T(1) = 2$ and $T(2) = 1$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T`).

articles.title: The $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
articles.statement:
The map $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ is defined by
$T(x) = x/2$ if $x$ is even and $T(x) = (3x+1)/2$ if $x$ is odd, where even and odd refer to the
residue of $x$ modulo $2$.

In both cases the numerator is divisible by $2$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$, so the division is exact.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T` extended to `ℤ₂`).

articles.title: Divisibility by $2$ from the residue modulo $2$
articles.statement:
If the residue modulo $2$ of a $2$-adic
integer $y \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ is zero, then $2$ divides $y$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (parity in `ℤ₂`, so that `T` is a self-map).

articles.title: Even branch of the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
articles.statement:
Let $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ be
the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers. For every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ whose residue modulo $2$
is zero, $2\,T(x) = x$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T`).

articles.title: Odd branch of the $2$-adic $3x+1$ map
articles.statement:
Let $T : \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbb{Z}_2$ be
the $3x+1$ map on the $2$-adic integers. For every $x \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ whose residue modulo $2$
is nonzero, $2\,T(x) = 3x + 1$.

## Sources

- Kenneth G. Monks, *On q-Analogs of the 3x+1 Dynamical System*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.6.8, Section 1 (definition of `T`).

articles.title: One-based residue
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $m$, the one-based residue of $a$ modulo
$m$ is $a \bmod m$ if this is nonzero, and $m$ if $a \bmod m = 0$ (here $a \bmod 0 = a$). This is
the residue convention used in Pelesko's recurrence.

articles.title: Conway–Hofstadter-like sequence
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number. A sequence
$c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a Conway–Hofstadter-like sequence of order $k$ when
$c(1) = c(2) = 1$ and, for every $n \ge 3$,

$$c(n) = c(i_n) + c(n - i_n),$$

where $i_n$ is the one-based residue of $k \, c(n-1)$ modulo $n - 1$: it equals
$k \, c(n-1) \bmod (n-1)$ when this is nonzero, and $n - 1$ otherwise.

The value $c(0)$ is not constrained.

articles.title: Binomial coefficients $\binom{p^k - p^{k-1}}{j}$ modulo $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime,
let $k \ge 2$, and let $j$ be an integer with $0 \le j \le p^k - p^{k-1}$. If $j = c\,p^{k-1}$
for an integer $c$, then $\binom{p^k - p^{k-1}}{j} \equiv (-1)^c \pmod{p}$; otherwise
$\binom{p^k - p^{k-1}}{j} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

## Sources

- Mark L. Lewis and Shannon M. Tefft, "The Maximum Length for Ducci Sequences on `ℤ_m^n` when `n` is Even", Lemma 2.

articles.title: Binomial coefficients $\binom{p^k - 1}{j}$ modulo $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $k \ge 1$,
and let $j$ be an integer with $0 \le j \le p^k - 1$. Then
$\binom{p^k - 1}{j} \equiv (-1)^j \pmod{p}$.

## Sources

- Mark L. Lewis and Shannon M. Tefft, "The Maximum Length for Ducci Sequences on `ℤ_m^n` when `n` is Even", Lemma 1.
