articles.title: Reduction of Ducci coefficients modulo $p$
articles.statement:
For integers $N \ge 1$, $r \ge 0$ and $s \ge 1$
write $a^{(N)}_{r,s} = \sum_{0 \le j \le r,\ j \equiv s - 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)} \binom{r}{j}$ for
the Ducci coefficients of length $N$. Let $p$ be a prime, let $k \ge 0$ and $n_1 \ge 2$ be
integers, and let $n = p^k n_1$. Then for every integer $c \ge 1$ and every integer $b$ with
$0 \le b < n_1$,
$a^{(n)}_{c p^k,\, b p^k + 1} \equiv a^{(n_1)}_{c,\, b + 1} \pmod{p}$.

## Sources

- Mark L. Lewis and Shannon M. Tefft, "The Maximum Length for Ducci Sequences on `ℤ_m^n` when `n` is Even", Lemma 4.

articles.title: Vanishing of Ducci coefficients modulo $p$
articles.statement:
For integers $N \ge 1$, $r \ge 0$ and $s \ge 1$
write $a^{(N)}_{r,s} = \sum_{0 \le j \le r,\ j \equiv s - 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)} \binom{r}{j}$ for
the Ducci coefficients of length $N$. Let $p$ be a prime, let $k \ge 0$ and $n_1 \ge 2$ be
integers, and let $n = p^k n_1$. Let $c \ge 1$, and let $s$ be an integer with $1 \le s \le n$
that is not of the form $b\,p^k + 1$ with $0 \le b < n_1$. Then
$a^{(n)}_{c p^k, s} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

## Sources

- Mark L. Lewis and Shannon M. Tefft, "The Maximum Length for Ducci Sequences on `ℤ_m^n` when `n` is Even", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Ducci coefficients
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $r$ and $s$, the Ducci coefficient is
$a_{r,s} = \sum_{0 \le j \le r,\ j \equiv s - 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)} \binom{r}{j}$, where $s - 1$
is read as $0$ when $s = 0$ and congruence modulo $0$ is equality.

For $1 \le s \le n$, $a_{r,s}$ is the coefficient of $x_s$ in the first entry of $D^r(x)$, where
the Ducci map $D$ on $\mathbb{Z}_m^n$ sends $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ to
$(x_1 + x_2, x_2 + x_3, \dots, x_n + x_1)$.

articles.title: Ducci predecessor criterion for even length
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 0$ be an integer, let $n \ge 2$ be
even, and write $\mathbb{Z}_m = \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ (so $\mathbb{Z}_0 = \mathbb{Z}$). A tuple
$x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathbb{Z}_m^n$ has a Ducci predecessor, that is, a tuple
$y \in \mathbb{Z}_m^n$ with $y_i + y_{i+1} = x_i$ for all $i$ (indices taken cyclically, so
$y_{n+1} = y_1$), if and only if $x_1 - x_2 + x_3 - \cdots + x_{n-1} - x_n = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_m$.

## Sources

- Mark L. Lewis and Shannon M. Tefft, "The Maximum Length for Ducci Sequences on `ℤ_m^n` when `n` is Even", Theorem 2.

articles.title: The grown prefix is a long iterate of $\tau_k$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau_k$ be the substitution sending
the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, extended letterwise to words, and
let $\mathrm{grow}_k(n)$ be the word obtained from the one-letter word $k$ by applying $\tau_k$
until it has more than $n$ letters, at most $n$ times. For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$ there
is an $m$ with $\mathrm{grow}_k(n) = \tau_k^m(k)$, and $\mathrm{grow}_k(n)$ has more than $n$
letters.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (prefixes `τ_k^j(k)` of `x_k`).

articles.title: Every iterate $\tau_k^j(k)$ starts with $k$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau_k$ be the substitution sending the
letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, extended letterwise to words. For all
natural numbers $k$ and $j$, the word $\tau_k^j(k)$, obtained by applying $\tau_k$ to the
one-letter word $k$ a total of $j$ times, has the form $k\,r$ for some word $r$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (`τ_k(k) = k 1`).

articles.title: Bracketing by the iterates of $L_k$
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 1$, let $\tau_k$ be the substitution
sending the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, let $x_k$ be its fixed
point starting with $k$, and let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the image under $\tau_k$ of the first
$n$ letters of $x_k$; write $L_k^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of $L_k$. For all $j \ge 0$ and
$m \ge 1$ there is a unique $n \ge 1$ with $L_k^j(n - 1) < m \le L_k^j(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 5 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-5`).

articles.title: Letter counts of the Hofstadter word as cardinalities
articles.statement:
Let $x_k$ be the fixed point,
starting with $k$, of the substitution sending the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter
$i$ to $i + 1$, and write $x_k[j]$ for its letter at index $j$. For every predicate $P$ on letters
and every $n$, the number $C_k^{(P)}(n)$ of letters satisfying $P$ in the prefix
$x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1]$ equals the number of indices $j < n$ with $P(x_k[j])$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 4.

articles.title: Witnesses that the letter counts of $x_k$ and $x_{k+1}$ are not ordered
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be the substitution sending the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other
letter $a$ to $a + 1$, let $x_k = x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be its fixed point beginning with $k$,
let $C_k^{(=i)}(n)$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $x_k[j] = i$, let $L_k(n)$ be the
length of the word $\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$, and write $L_k^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate
of $L_k$. For all natural numbers $i$ and $k$ with $3 \le i < k$, put $n = i + L_k^{2k+2}(1)$
and $m = i + L_{k+1}^{k+i}(1)$. Then $C_k^{(=i)}(n) < C_{k+1}^{(=i)}(n)$ and
$C_{k+1}^{(=i)}(m) < C_k^{(=i)}(m)$, so for these letters $i$ the letter counts of $x_k$ and
$x_{k+1}$ are not ordered.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 27 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-27`).

articles.title: Prefixes of $x_{k+1}$ contain no more letters $1$ than those of $x_k$
articles.statement:
Let $x_k$ be the
fixed point, starting with $k$, of the substitution sending the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every
other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, and let $C_k^{(=1)}(n)$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with
$x_k[j] = 1$. For $k \ge 1$ and every $n \ge 0$, $C_{k+1}^{(=1)}(n) \le C_k^{(=1)}(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 26 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-26`).

articles.title: Letter counts in the Hofstadter word
articles.statement:
Let $x_k$ be the fixed point, starting with $k$, of
the substitution sending the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, and write
$x_k[j]$ for its letter at index $j$. For a predicate $P$ on letters, $C_k^{(P)}(n)$ is the number
of letters satisfying $P$ in the prefix $x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1]$, that is,
$C_k^{(P)}(n) = \#\{0 \le j < n : P(x_k[j])\}$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 4.

articles.title: Growing from an iterate of $\tau_k$ gives an iterate of $\tau_k$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau_k$ be the
substitution sending the letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, extended
letterwise to words, and let $\mathrm{grow}_{k,n}^f(w)$ be the word obtained from $w$ by applying
$\tau_k$ until it has more than $n$ letters, at most $f$ times. For all $k, n, f, j$ there is an
$m$ with $\mathrm{grow}_{k,n}^f(\tau_k^j(k)) = \tau_k^m(k)$ such that $\tau_k^m(k)$ has more than
$n$ letters or $j + f \le m$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (prefixes `τ_k^j(k)` of `x_k`).

articles.title: Bounded growth of a word under $\tau_k$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau_k$ be the substitution sending the
letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, extended letterwise to words. Given
$n$, a bound $f$ and a word $w$, the result is $w$ if $f = 0$ or $w$ has more than $n$ letters,
and otherwise it is the result for the bound $f - 1$ and the word $\tau_k(w)$. Thus $\tau_k$ is
applied to $w$ until the word has more than $n$ letters, at most $f$ times.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (prefixes `τ_k^j(k)` of `x_k`).

articles.title: The shortest long iterate $\tau_k^j(k)$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau_k$ be the substitution sending the
letter $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, extended letterwise to words. For
natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $\mathrm{grow}_k(n)$ is the word obtained from the one-letter word
$k$ by applying $\tau_k$ until it has more than $n$ letters, at most $n$ times. Since
$\tau_k^j(k)$ has at least $j + 1$ letters, this is the shortest iterate $\tau_k^j(k)$ with more
than $n$ letters.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (prefixes `τ_k^j(k)` of `x_k`).

articles.title: The image length $L_k$ as a letter count
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$. Let $F_k$ be the generalized
Hofstadter function and $F_k^{k-1}$ its $(k-1)$-fold iterate, let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the
fixed point, beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every
other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the word
$\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$, and let $C_k^{(=k)}(n)$ be the number of indices $0 \le i < n$
with $x_k[i] = k$. Then for every natural number $n$, $L_k(n) = n + C_k^{(=k)}(n)$ and
$L_k(n) = n + F_k^{k-1}(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 9 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-9`).

articles.title: Basic properties of the iterates of $L_k$
Order of iterates of $L_k$ against order of iterates of $F_k$
articles.statement:
Let $F_k$ be the
generalized Hofstadter function, let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed point, beginning with
$k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to
$i + 1$, let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the word $\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$, and write
$f^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of a function $f$. Let $k, k' \ge 1$ and $j, j' \ge 0$. Then
$L_k^j(n) \le L_{k'}^{j'}(n)$ for every $n$ if and only if $F_{k'}^{j'}(n) \le F_k^j(n)$ for
every $n$. Moreover, for every natural number $n$:
(a) $L_k^j(n) \le L_{k'}^{j'}(n)$ if and only if $F_{k'}^{j'}(m) \le F_k^j(m)$ for
$m = L_k^j(n)$;
(b) $L_k^j(n) < L_{k'}^{j'}(n)$ if and only if $F_{k'}^{j'}(m) < F_k^j(m)$ for
$m = L_{k'}^{j'}(n)$;
(c) if $L_k^j(m) \le L_{k'}^{j'}(m)$ for $m = F_k^j(n)$, then $F_{k'}^{j'}(n) \le F_k^j(n)$;
(d) if $F_k^j(n) < F_{k'}^{j'}(n)$, then $L_{k'}^{j'}(m) < L_k^j(m)$ for $m = F_k^j(n)$.

In (d) the paper prints $m = F_{k'}^{j'}(n)$; its proof derives (d) as the contrapositive of
(c), which gives $m = F_k^j(n)$. The printed form fails for $k = 1$, $j = 1$, $k' = 4$,
$j' = 2$ and $n = 8$: $F_1(8) = 4 < F_4^2(8) = 5$, but $L_4^2(5) = L_1(5) = 10$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 19 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-19`).

articles.title: Comparing $L_{k+1}^{j+1}(1)$ with $L_k^j(1)$
articles.statement:
Let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed
point, beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every
other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the word
$\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$, and write $L_k^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of $L_k$. Let
$k \ge 1$, and take differences in $\mathbb{Z}$. Then $L_{k+1}^{j+1}(1) - L_k^j(1) = 1$ for
every $j \le 2k$; $2\bigl(L_{k+1}^{j+1}(1) - L_k^j(1)\bigr) = -(j - 2k - 1)(j - 2k + 2)$ for
every $j$ with $2k \le j \le 3k$; $L_{k+1}^{2k+2}(1) = L_k^{2k+1}(1)$; and
$L_{k+1}^{j+1}(1) < L_k^j(1)$ for every $j \ge 2k + 2$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Lemma 24 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-lem-24`).

articles.title: Iterates of $L_{k+1}$ lie below iterates of $L_k$
articles.statement:
Let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the
fixed point, beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every
other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the word
$\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$, and write $L_k^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of $L_k$. For
every $k \ge 1$, every $j \ge 0$ and every natural number $n$, $L_{k+1}^j(n) \le L_k^j(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Corollary 21 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-cor-21`).

articles.title: Points where $L_k^j$ exceeds $L_{k+1}^{j+1}$
articles.statement:
Let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed
point, beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every
other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the word
$\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$, and write $L_k^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of $L_k$. Let
$k \ge 1$. Then $L_{k+1}^{j+1}(2k + 3 - j) < L_k^j(2k + 3 - j)$ for every $j$ with
$k + 2 \le j \le 2k + 2$, and $L_{k+1}^{j+1}(1) < L_k^j(1)$ for every $j \ge 2k + 2$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Lemma 25 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-lem-25`).

articles.title: Comparing $L_k$ with $L_{k+1}$
articles.statement:
Let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed point,
beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other
letter $i$ to $i + 1$, let $L_k(n)$ be the length of the word $\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[n-1])$,
write $L_k^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of $L_k$, and let $C_k^{(=k)}(n)$ be the number of
indices $i < n$ with $x_k[i] = k$. For all $k \ge 1$, $n \ge 1$ and $j$ with $0 \le j \le k$:
$L_{k+1}(n) \le L_k(n)$, $C_{k+1}^{(=k+1)}(n) \le C_k^{(=k)}(n)$, and
$L_k^j(n) < L_{k+1}^{j+1}(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Theorem 20 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-thm-20`).

articles.title: The image length $L_k$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $L_k(n) = |\tau_k(x_k[0:n))|$
is the length of the word obtained by applying the substitution $\tau_k$, letter by letter, to
the prefix $x_k[0:n)$ formed by the first $n$ letters of the fixed point $x_k$ of $\tau_k$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 2.

articles.title: The prefix $x_k(0:n)$ letter by letter
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $x_k$ be
the fixed point of the substitution $\tau_k$ with letters $x_k[0], x_k[1], \dots$, and let
$x_k[0:n)$ be the word formed by the first $n$ letters of the shortest word $\tau_k^j(k)$ with
more than $n$ letters. Then $x_k[0:n) = x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots x_k[n-1]$, the empty word when
$n = 0$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 2.

articles.title: The prefix $x_k(0:n)$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, let $\tau_k$ be the
substitution $k \mapsto k\,1$, $i \mapsto i + 1$ for $i \ne k$, applied letter by letter to
words, and let $\tau_k^j$ be its $j$-fold iterate. Then $x_k[0:n)$ is the word formed by the
first $n$ letters of the shortest of the words $\tau_k^j(k)$, $j \ge 0$, that has more than $n$
letters.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 2.

articles.title: The Hofstadter substitution preserves prefixes
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be
the morphism of finite words over $\mathbb{N}$ that replaces the letter $k$ by the word $k\,1$ and
every other letter $i$ by $i + 1$. For every $k$ and all finite words $u$, $v$ over $\mathbb{N}$,
if $u$ is a prefix of $v$, then $\tau_k(u)$ is a prefix of $\tau_k(v)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (`τ_k` is a morphism).

articles.title: Consecutive iterates of the Hofstadter substitution on $k$ are nested
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$k$, let $\tau_k$ be the morphism of finite words over $\mathbb{N}$ that replaces the letter $k$ by
the word $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ by $i + 1$, and write $\tau_k^j(k)$ for the word
obtained by applying $\tau_k$ $j$ times to the one-letter word $k$. For all natural numbers $k$
and $j$, $\tau_k^j(k)$ is a prefix of $\tau_k^{j+1}(k)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (the fixed point `x_k` is the limit of `τ_k^j(k)`).

articles.title: The iterates of the Hofstadter substitution on $k$ form a chain of prefixes
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be the morphism of finite words over $\mathbb{N}$ that replaces the letter
$k$ by the word $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ by $i + 1$, and write $\tau_k^j(k)$ for the word
obtained by applying $\tau_k$ $j$ times to the one-letter word $k$. For every natural number $k$
and all natural numbers $i \le j$, $\tau_k^i(k)$ is a prefix of $\tau_k^j(k)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (the fixed point `x_k` is the limit of `τ_k^j(k)`).

articles.title: Iterates of the Hofstadter substitution on the letter $k$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $\tau_k$ be
the morphism of finite words over $\mathbb{N}$ that replaces the letter $k$ by the word $k\,1$ and
every other letter $i$ by $i + 1$, and write $\tau_k^j(k)$ for the word obtained by applying
$\tau_k$ $j$ times to the one-letter word $k$. For every natural number $j$: if $j \le k$, then
$\tau_k^j(k) = k\,1\,2 \cdots j$, the letter $k$ followed by $1, 2, \dots, j$; and if $j \ge k$,
then $\tau_k^j(k)$ is the concatenation $\tau_k^{j-1}(k)\,\tau_k^{j-k}(k)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 3 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-3`).

articles.title: The Hofstadter substitution on finite words
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, $\tau_k$ maps a
finite word $w$ over $\mathbb{N}$ to the concatenation, in order, of the words $\tau_k(a)$ for the
letters $a$ of $w$, where $\tau_k(k) = k\,1$ and $\tau_k(i) = i + 1$ for every letter $i \ne k$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2.

articles.title: The Hofstadter substitution on letters
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, the substitution
$\tau_k$ sends the letter $k$ to the word $k\,1$ and every other letter $i \in \mathbb{N}$ to the
one-letter word $i + 1$.

The rule $i \mapsto i + 1$ is used only for $1 \le i < k$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2.

articles.title: The letter $x_k(n)$ can be read off $\tau_k^n(k)$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be
the Hofstadter substitution on finite words over $\mathbb{N}$ ($k \mapsto k\,1$, $i \mapsto i + 1$
for $i \ne k$), let $x_k = x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be its fixed point, and write $\tau_k^n(k)$
for the word obtained by applying $\tau_k$ $n$ times to the one-letter word $k$. For all natural
numbers $k$ and $n$, $x_k[n]$ is the letter at position $n$ of $\tau_k^n(k)$, counting positions
from $0$ (this word has at least $n + 1$ letters).

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2.

articles.title: Letters of $x_k$ from the iterates $\tau_k^j(k)$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be
the Hofstadter substitution on finite words over $\mathbb{N}$ ($k \mapsto k\,1$, $i \mapsto i + 1$
for $i \ne k$), let $x_k = x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be its fixed point, and write $\tau_k^j(k)$
for the word obtained by applying $\tau_k$ $j$ times to the one-letter word $k$. For all natural
numbers $k$, $n$ and $j$, if $\tau_k^j(k)$ has more than $n$ letters, then $x_k[n]$ is the letter
at position $n$ of $\tau_k^j(k)$, counting positions from $0$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (the fixed point `x_k` is the limit of `τ_k^j(k)`).

articles.title: The letters of $x_k$ from the increments of the iterates of $F_k$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $F_k$
be the generalized Hofstadter function with $j$-th iterate $F_k^j$ ($F_k^0$ the identity), and
let $x_k = x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed point of the substitution $\tau_k$
($k \mapsto k\,1$, $i \mapsto i + 1$ for $i \ne k$). For every natural number $n$: for each $j$
with $1 \le j < k$, $x_k[n] = j$ if and only if $F_k^{j-1}(n+1) = F_k^{j-1}(n) + 1$ and
$F_k^j(n+1) = F_k^j(n)$; and $x_k[n] = k$ if and only if $F_k^{k-1}(n+1) = F_k^{k-1}(n) + 1$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 11 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-11`).

articles.title: First values of $x_2$, $x_3$ and $L_2$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, let $x_k$ be the fixed
point of the Hofstadter substitution $\tau_k$ ($k \mapsto k\,1$, $i \mapsto i + 1$ for $i \ne k$),
and let $L_2(n)$ be the length of $\tau_2(x_2[0] \cdots x_2[n-1])$. The first eight letters of
the Fibonacci word $x_2$ are $2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2$; the first eight letters of $x_3$ are
$3, 1, 2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1$; and $L_2(0), \dots, L_2(5)$ are $0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Figure 2.

articles.title: Letters of the Hofstadter fixed-point word
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, let $\tau_k$
be the substitution on letters in $\mathbb{N}$ that sends $k$ to the word $k\,1$ and every other
letter $i$ to $i + 1$, applied to words letter by letter, and let $\tau_k^j(k)$ be the word
obtained by applying $\tau_k$ $j$ times to the one-letter word $k$. Then $x_k[n]$ is the letter at
position $n$, counting from $0$, of the shortest word $\tau_k^j(k)$ with $j \ge 0$ that has more
than $n$ letters.

Since each word $\tau_k^j(k)$ is a prefix of $\tau_k^{j+1}(k)$, $x_k[n]$ is the letter at position
$n$ of the fixed point $x_k$ of $\tau_k$ that begins with $k$, and every word $\tau_k^j(k)$ with
more than $n$ letters has $x_k[n]$ at position $n$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2.

articles.title: Generalized Hofstadter function as a letter count
articles.statement:
Let $k > 1$ and $n \ge 0$. Let $F_k$ be
the generalized Hofstadter function, defined by $F_k(0) = 0$ and $F_k(m) = m - F_k^k(m - 1)$ for
$m \ge 1$, where $F_k^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate of $F_k$. Let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the
fixed point, beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every
other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, and for a property $P$ of letters let $C_k^{(P)}(n)$ be the number
of indices $0 \le i < n$ with $P(x_k[i])$. Then $F_k(n) = n - C_k^{(=1)}(n)$ and
$F_k(n) = C_k^{(\ne 1)}(n)$. Moreover, $F_k(n+1) = F_k(n)$ if and only if $x_k[n] = 1$, and
$F_k(n+1) = F_k(n) + 1$ whenever $x_k[n] \ne 1$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 10 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-10`).

articles.title: Recursion for the generalized Hofstadter function
articles.statement:
For every $k \ge 0$ and every $n \ge 1$,
the generalized Hofstadter function $F_k$ satisfies $F_k(n) = n - F_k^k(n - 1)$, where $F_k^k$
is the $k$-fold iterate of $F_k$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Galois insertion between iterated Hofstadter functions
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $j \ge 0$. Let
$F_k$ be the generalized Hofstadter function, let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed point,
beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter
$i$ to $i + 1$, let $L_k(m)$ be the length of the word $\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[m-1])$, and
write $f^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of a function $f$. Then for all $n, m \ge 0$,
$F_k^j(n) \le m$ if and only if $n \le L_k^j(m)$, so $F_k^j$ and $L_k^j$ form a Galois
connection; and $F_k^j(L_k^j(m)) = m$ for every $m \ge 0$, so it is a Galois insertion.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Corollary 7 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-cor-7`).

articles.title: Basic properties of the iterated Hofstadter functions
articles.statement:
Let $j, k \ge 1$, let $F_k$ be the
generalized Hofstadter function, and write $F_k^i$ for its $i$-fold iterate. Then
$F_k^j(1) = F_k^j(2) = 1$; $F_k^j(n) \ge 1$ for every $n \ge 1$; $F_k^j(n) < n$ for every
$n \ge 2$; $F_k(n+1) - F_k(n) = 1 - \bigl(F_k^k(n) - F_k^k(n-1)\bigr)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ for every
$n \ge 1$; $F_k^j(n+1)$ equals $F_k^j(n)$ or $F_k^j(n) + 1$ for every $n \ge 0$; and $F_k^j$ is
monotone and surjective from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ but not injective.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 2 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-2`).

articles.title: Iterated Hofstadter functions as letter counts
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 0$. Let $F_k$ be
the generalized Hofstadter function and $F_k^j$ its $j$-fold iterate, let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$
be the fixed point, beginning with $k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and
every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$, and for a property $P$ of letters let $C_k^{(P)}(m)$ be the
number of indices $0 \le i < m$ with $P(x_k[i])$. Then $F_k^{k-1}(n) = C_k^{(=k)}(n)$;
$F_k^j(n) = C_k^{(>j)}(n)$ for every $0 \le j < k$; and $F_k^{k+i-1}(n) = C_k^{(=i)}(n+i)$ for
every $1 \le i < k$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 8 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-8`).

articles.title: Eventual order of iterates of consecutive Hofstadter functions
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $F_k$ be
the generalized Hofstadter function, write $F_k^i$ for its $i$-fold iterate, let $\alpha > 0$ be
a root of $X^k + X - 1$, and let $\alpha' > 0$ be a root of $X^{k+1} + X - 1$. Then for all
sufficiently large $n$, $F_k(n) < F_{k+1}(n)$, $F_{k+1}^{k+1}(n) < F_k^k(n)$ and
$F_{k+1}^{k+2}(n) < F_k^{k+1}(n)$. Moreover, for every $j \ge 0$: if $j/(j+1) \le \alpha$ or
$j^2 \le k$, then $F_{k+1}^{k+j+1}(n) < F_k^{k+j}(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$; and if
$\alpha' \le j/(j+1)$ or $k < j$, then $F_k^{k+j}(n) < F_{k+1}^{k+j+1}(n)$ for all sufficiently
large $n$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Corollary 17 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-cor-17`).

articles.title: Eventual order of iterated Hofstadter functions from their growth rates
articles.statement:
Let $k, k' \ge 1$
and $j, j' \ge 0$, let $F_k$ be the generalized Hofstadter function, write $F_k^i$ for its
$i$-fold iterate, let $\alpha > 0$ be a root of $X^k + X - 1$, and let $\alpha' > 0$ be a root of
$X^{k'} + X - 1$. If $\alpha^j < \alpha'^{j'}$, then $F_k^j(n) < F_{k'}^{j'}(n)$ for all
sufficiently large $n$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Corollary 16 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-cor-16`).

articles.title: Iterates of consecutive Hofstadter functions are ordered
articles.statement:
For every $k \ge 1$, $j \ge 0$
and $n \ge 0$, $F_k^j(n) \le F_{k+1}^j(n)$, where $F_k$ is the generalized Hofstadter function and
$F_k^j$ is its $j$-fold iterate.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Theorem 22 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-thm-22`).

articles.title: Fibres of the iterated Hofstadter functions
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $j \ge 0$. Let $F_k$ be the
generalized Hofstadter function, let $x_k[0]\,x_k[1] \cdots$ be the fixed point, beginning with
$k$, of the substitution $\tau_k$ that sends $k$ to $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to $i + 1$,
let $L_k(m)$ be the length of the word $\tau_k(x_k[0] \cdots x_k[m-1])$, and write $f^j$ for the
$j$-fold iterate of a function $f$. Then for every $n \ge 1$, the set of $m$ with $F_k^j(m) = n$
is the interval $L_k^j(n-1) < m \le L_k^j(n)$; and for every $m \ge 1$,
$L_k^j(F_k^j(m) - 1) < m \le L_k^j(F_k^j(m))$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Theorem 6 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-thm-6`).

articles.title: Shifted order of iterates of consecutive Hofstadter functions
articles.statement:
Let $F_k$ denote the
generalized Hofstadter functions and write $f^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of a function $f$. For
every $k \ge 1$, every $j$ with $0 \le j \le k$ and every natural number $n$,
$F_{k+1}^{j+1}(n) \le F_k^j(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Theorem 23 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-thm-23`).

articles.title: Pointwise order of the generalized Hofstadter functions
articles.statement:
For every $k \ge 1$ and every
natural number $n$, the generalized Hofstadter functions satisfy $F_k(n) \le F_{k+1}(n)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Theorem 1 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-thm-1`).

articles.title: First values of Hofstadter's G and H
articles.statement:
Let $F_k$ denote the generalized Hofstadter
functions. For $n = 0, 1, \dots, 10$ the values $F_2(n)$ are $0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6$
and the values $F_3(n)$ are $0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7$.

Here $F_2$ is Hofstadter's $G$ (OEIS A005206) and $F_3$ is Hofstadter's $H$ (OEIS A005374).

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Figure 1.

articles.title: The generalized Hofstadter functions vanish at zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the
generalized Hofstadter function $F_k$ satisfies $F_k(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.1.

articles.title: Generalized Hofstadter function
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, the function
$F_k : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is given by $F_k(0) = 0$ and $F_k(n) = n - F_k^k(n - 1)$ for
$n \ge 1$, where $F_k^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate of $F_k$ (the identity when $k = 0$).

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.1.

articles.title: The fuel-bounded Hofstadter recursion is bounded by its argument
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$k$, $p$ and $n$, the fuel-bounded value $A_k(p, n)$ of the generalized Hofstadter recursion
satisfies $A_k(p, n) \le n$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.1 (`0 ≤ F_k(n) ≤ n`).

articles.title: Fuel-bounded generalized Hofstadter recursion
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $p$ and $n$, the
value $A_k(p, n)$ is defined by recursion on the fuel $p$, which bounds the recursion depth:
$A_k(0, n) = 0$ and $A_k(p + 1, n) = n - g^k(n - 1)$, where $g^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate of the
function $g(m) = A_k(p, m)$ and both subtractions are truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.4 (Rocq definition `recf`).

articles.title: Limits of Hofstadter iterates and letter frequencies
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and $j \ge 0$, let
$\alpha > 0$ satisfy $\alpha^k + \alpha - 1 = 0$ and let $\beta > 0$ satisfy
$\beta^k - \beta^{k-1} - 1 = 0$. Write $f^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of a function $f$ and let
$F_k$ be the generalized Hofstadter function. Let $\tau_k$ be the substitution on letters with
$\tau_k(k) = k\,1$ and $\tau_k(i) = i + 1$ for $1 \le i < k$, let $x_k$ be the infinite word fixed
by $\tau_k$ that is the limit of the words $\tau_k^m(k)$, write $x_k[m]$ for its letter at index
$m$ (counting from $0$) and $x_k[0:n)$ for its prefix of length $n$, let
$L_k(n) = |\tau_k(x_k[0:n))|$, and for a letter $i$ let $C_k^{(=i)}(n)$ be the number of indices
$m < n$ with $x_k[m] = i$. Then, as $n \to \infty$: $F_k^j(n)/n \to \alpha^j$;
$L_k^j(n)/n \to \beta^j$; $C_k^{(=i)}(n)/n \to \alpha^{k+i-1}$ for every $i$ with $1 \le i < k$;
and $C_k^{(=k)}(n)/n \to \alpha^{k-1}$. Moreover $\alpha^{k-1} = \beta - 1$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Theorem 14 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-thm-14`).

articles.title: Monotonicity and asymptotics of the Hofstadter constants
articles.statement:
For each integer $k \ge 1$ let
$\alpha_k$ be a positive zero of $X^k + X - 1$ and $\beta_k$ a positive zero of
$X^k - X^{k-1} - 1$. Then for every $k \ge 1$ we have $\alpha_k < \alpha_{k+1}$,
$\beta_{k+1} < \beta_k$, $1 + 1/k \le \beta_k \le 1 + 1/\sqrt{k}$ and
$\sqrt{k} \le \beta_k^{k-1} \le k$. Moreover $\beta_k \to 1$ and $\alpha_k \to 1$ as
$k \to \infty$, and $\alpha_k = 1 - \ln k / k + o(\ln k / k)$ and
$\beta_k = 1 + \ln k / k + o(\ln k / k)$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 13 and Definition 12 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-13`).

articles.title: Values with exactly one preimage under a Hofstadter function
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let
$\alpha > 0$ satisfy $\alpha^k + \alpha - 1 = 0$ and let $\beta > 0$ satisfy
$\beta^k - \beta^{k-1} - 1 = 0$. Write $f^j$ for the $j$-fold iterate of a function $f$ and let
$F_k$ be the generalized Hofstadter function. Let $\tau_k$ be the substitution on letters with
$\tau_k(k) = k\,1$ and $\tau_k(i) = i + 1$ for $1 \le i < k$, let $x_k$ be the infinite word fixed
by $\tau_k$ that is the limit of the words $\tau_k^m(k)$, write $x_k[0:n)$ for its prefix of
length $n$ and let $L_k(n) = |\tau_k(x_k[0:n))|$. Let $U_k(n)$ be the number of $j$ with
$0 \le j < n$ for which exactly one natural number $m$ satisfies $F_k(m) = j$. Then for every
$n \ge 1$, $U_k(n) = 2n - 1 - L_k(n - 1)$ and $U_k(n) = n - F_k^{k-1}(n - 1)$. Moreover
$U_k(n)/n \to 1 - \alpha^{k-1}$ as $n \to \infty$, and $1 - \alpha^{k-1} = 2 - \beta$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Proposition 18 (`jis-2026-26.3.3-prop-18`).

articles.title: The generalized Hofstadter substitution does not shorten words
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be the substitution on letters in $\mathbb{N}$ sending $k$ to the
two-letter word $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to the one-letter word $i + 1$. For every
finite word $w$ over $\mathbb{N}$, the word $\tau_k(w)$, obtained by replacing each letter of
$w$ by its image under $\tau_k$, is at least as long as $w$: $|w| \le |\tau_k(w)|$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (definition of `τ_k`).

articles.title: Letter images under the generalized Hofstadter substitution are nonempty
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $k$, let $\tau_k$ be the substitution on letters in $\mathbb{N}$ sending $k$ to
the two-letter word $k\,1$ and every other letter $m$ to the one-letter word $m + 1$. For every
natural number $i$, the image $\tau_k(i)$ of the letter $i$ has length at least $1$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (definition of `τ_k`).

articles.title: Growth of the iterated generalized Hofstadter substitution
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$
and $j$, let $\tau_k$ be the substitution on letters in $\mathbb{N}$ sending $k$ to the
two-letter word $k\,1$ and every other letter $i$ to the one-letter word $i + 1$, extended
letter by letter to finite words. The word $\tau_k^j(k)$, obtained by applying $\tau_k$
$j$ times to the one-letter word $k$, has length at least $j + 1$.

## Sources

- Pierre Letouzey, Shuo Li, and Wolfgang Steiner, *Pointwise Order of Generalized Hofstadter Functions G, H, and Beyond*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.3, Section 1.2 (the fixed point `x_k` is the limit of `τ_k^j(k)`).

articles.title: Closed form for Golomb-like sequences
articles.statement:
Let $y$ and $z$ be integers of opposite parity with
$y \ge 2$ and $z \ge 2 - y$, and put $c = (y + z - 1)/2$. There is exactly one strictly
increasing function $f$ from the positive integers to the positive integers such that
$f(1) = (y + z + 1)/2$ and $f(f(n)) = yn + z$ for every positive integer $n$. Moreover, for
every such $f$, every natural number $k$ and every integer $j$ with $-c\,y^k \le j < c\,y^k$,
the rational number

$$m = \frac{(y+1)\,c}{y-1}\, y^k - \frac{z}{y-1} + j$$

is a positive integer and

$$f(m) = \frac{2c}{y-1}\, y^{k+1} - \frac{z}{y-1} + \frac{(y+1)\,j}{2} + \frac{(y-1)\,|j|}{2}.$$

Proof: The construction tiles the positive integers by the source's blocks and verifies the
two slope regimes, followed by strong-induction uniqueness, as in Cloitre–Sloane–Vandermast,
Theorem Th1 and equations (Eq48a), (Eq48).

## Sources

- Benoit Cloitre, N. J. A. Sloane, and Matthew J. Vandermast, "Numerical Analogues of Aronson's Sequence," Journal of Integer Sequences 6 (2003), Article 03.2.2, Theorem, equations, lines 584–603, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Cloitre/cloitre2.tex

articles.title: Hinman–Kuca–Schlesinger–Sheydvasser weak rigidity theorem for Ulam sequences
articles.statement:
There
exist sequences of integers $(a_k)$, $(b_k)$, $(c_k)$, $(d_k)$ indexed by $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with
the following property. For every real $C > 0$ there is a natural number $N > 0$ such that for
every natural number $n \ge N$ with $n > 1$, and every sequence of natural numbers
$u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ with $u_0 = 1$ and $u_1 = n$ that is strictly increasing and in which, for
every $t \ge 2$, $u_t$ is the least natural number $m > u_{t-1}$ for which there is exactly one
pair of indices $(i, j)$ with $i < j < t$ and $u_i + u_j = m$, the following holds: for every
natural number $x$ with $1 \le x \le Cn$, $x$ is a term of the sequence $u$ if and only if
$a_k n + b_k \le x \le c_k n + d_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Integer polynomial map
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, an integer polynomial map from
$n$ variables to $m$ components is an $m$-tuple $F = (F_0, \dots, F_{m-1})$ of polynomials with
integer coefficients in the $n$ variables $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$.

articles.title: Iterates of an integer polynomial map modulo a natural number
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be an integer
polynomial map from $n$ variables to $n$ components, let $p$ be a natural number, and let
$\bar F \colon (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n \to (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$ be the map obtained by
reducing the coefficients of $F$ modulo $p$ and evaluating. For a natural number $k$ and
$x \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$, the $k$-th iterate of $F$ modulo $p$ at $x$ is $\bar F^k(x)$,
the result of applying $\bar F$ to $x$ exactly $k$ times; in particular $\bar F^0(x) = x$.

articles.title: Iterates of an integer polynomial map
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be an integer polynomial map from $n$
variables to $n$ components, viewed as the map $\mathbb{Z}^n \to \mathbb{Z}^n$ given by
evaluation. For a natural number $k$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, the $k$-th iterate of $F$ at $x$ is
$F^k(x)$, the result of applying $F$ to $x$ exactly $k$ times; in particular $F^0(x) = x$.

articles.title: Reduction of an integer polynomial map modulo a natural number
articles.statement:
Let
$F = (F_0, \dots, F_{m-1})$ be an integer polynomial map from $n$ variables to $m$ components and
let $p$ be a natural number. For $x \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$, the value of the reduction of
$F$ modulo $p$ at $x$ is $(\bar F_0(x), \dots, \bar F_{m-1}(x)) \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^m$,
where $\bar F_i$ is the polynomial obtained from $F_i$ by reducing its coefficients modulo $p$.

The definition allows an arbitrary natural modulus; the source applies it when $p$ is prime.

articles.title: Evaluation of an integer polynomial map
articles.statement:
Let $F = (F_0, \dots, F_{m-1})$ be an integer
polynomial map from $n$ variables to $m$ components. The value of $F$ at a point
$x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ is the point $(F_0(x), \dots, F_{m-1}(x)) \in \mathbb{Z}^m$.

articles.title: The EKG sequence
articles.statement:
A sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ of natural numbers is an EKG
sequence when $a_0 = 1$, $a_1 = 2$, and for every $n \ge 0$ the term $a_{n+2}$ is positive,
differs from each of $a_0, \dots, a_{n+1}$, satisfies $\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_{n+2}) > 1$, and
satisfies $a_{n+2} \le m$ for every positive integer $m$ that differs from each of
$a_0, \dots, a_{n+1}$ and has $\gcd(a_{n+1}, m) > 1$. Thus every term from $a_2$ on is the
least positive integer not used before that shares a factor greater than $1$ with the
previous term.

The indexing starts at $0$, so the source's $a_1 = 1$ and $a_2 = 2$ are $a_0$ and $a_1$ here.
The sequence begins $1, 2, 4, 6, 3, 9, 12, 8, 10, 5, \dots$

## Sources

- JIS source `hofman1.tex`, lines 99–100, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Hofman/hofman1.tex>; first terms at lines 104–112.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits of four
articles.statement:
The base-$3/2$ digit list of $4$, written least significant
digit first, is $(2, 1, 2)$; written most significant digit first, this is the paper's
$(212)_{3/2}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits are at most two
articles.statement:
For every natural number $N$, every digit $d$ in the
base-$3/2$ digit list of $N$ satisfies $d < 3$, that is, $d \in \{0, 1, 2\}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits of thirteen
articles.statement:
The base-$3/2$ digit list of $13$, written least
significant digit first, is $(2, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2)$; written most significant digit first, this
is the paper's $(210112)_{3/2}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Value of the base-3/2 digits
articles.statement:
For every natural number $N$, if
$(d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{k-1})$ is the base-$3/2$ digit list of $N$, least significant digit first,
then in $\mathbb{Q}$

$$2N = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} d_i \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^i.$$

Equivalently, the paper's expansion $\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} d_i (3/2)^i$ has value $N$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits
articles.statement:
The base-$3/2$ digit list of a natural number $N$, least significant
digit first, is defined by recursion on $N$: the list of $0$ is empty, and for $N \ge 1$ it is
the digit $d = 2N \bmod 3$ followed by the base-$3/2$ digit list of $(2N - d)/3$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Extremal points of the Josephus function near $2k - 2$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ be a natural
number and let $J_k$ be the Josephus function; call $m$ low extremal if $1 \le J_k(m) \le k - 1$,
and high extremal if $m + 1$ is low extremal. If $J_k(2k - 2) \le k - 1$, then $2k - 3$ is high
extremal and $2k - 2$ is low extremal. If $J_k(2k - 2) > k - 1$, then $2k - 2$ is high extremal
and $2k - 1$ is low extremal. In particular, $2k - 2$ is always a low or a high extremal point.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Corollary 7.

articles.title: The Josephus function has infinitely many fixed points
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k \ge 2$, the set of natural numbers $n$ with $J_k(n) = n$ is infinite, where $J_k$ is the
Josephus function.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Theorem 13.

articles.title: High extremal point of the Josephus function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $m$, the point
$m$ is a high extremal point of the Josephus function $J_k$ if $m + 1$ is a low extremal point
of $J_k$, that is, if $1 \le J_k(m + 1) \le k - 1$.

articles.title: $13$ is a fixed point of $J_3$
articles.statement:
The number $13$ is a fixed point of the Josephus function
$J_3$ (elimination step $3$), that is, $J_3(13) = 13$.

It is the third fixed point of $J_3$, after $1$ and $2$; the statement records only that $13$ is
a fixed point.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Section 2, Table 1.

articles.title: Fixed points of the Josephus function $J_3$
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is a fixed point of the
Josephus function $J_3$ (elimination step $3$) when $n \ge 1$ and $J_3(n) = n$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Section 1, Definition (Extremal and Fixed points).

articles.title: $3$ is a high extremal point but not a fixed point of $J_3$
articles.statement:
The number $3$ is a high
extremal point of the Josephus function $J_3$ (elimination step $3$) and is not a fixed point of
$J_3$; indeed $J_3(3) = 2$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Section 1, Definition (Extremal and Fixed points).

articles.title: High extremal points of the Josephus function $J_3$
articles.statement:
A natural number $n$ is a high
extremal point of the Josephus function $J_3$ (elimination step $3$) when $n \ge 1$ and either
$J_3(n) = n$ or $J_3(n) = n - 1$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Section 1, Definition (Extremal and Fixed points).

articles.title: Low extremal point of the Josephus function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $m$, the point
$m$ is a low extremal point of the Josephus function $J_k$ if $1 \le J_k(m) \le k - 1$, where
$k - 1$ is truncated at $0$.

articles.title: Linear growth of the Josephus function after a high extremal point
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and
$n_e \ge 2k - 3$ be natural numbers such that $n_e$ is a high extremal point of the Josephus
function $J_k$, that is, $1 \le J_k(n_e + 1) \le k - 1$, and write $j = J_k(n_e + 1)$. Then
$J_k(n_e + 1 + m) = j + km$ for every natural number
$m \le \lfloor (n_e - (j - 1)) / (k - 1) \rfloor$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Theorem 9.

articles.title: Linear growth of the Josephus function before a wrap-around
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, $n \ge 1$
and $m$ be natural numbers, let $J_k$ be the Josephus function and write $p = J_k(n)$. If
$p + km \le n + m$, then $J_k(n + m) = p + km$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Lemma 6.

articles.title: The Josephus function at the first wrap-around
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$, $n \ge 1$ and $m$ be
natural numbers and let $J_k$ be the Josephus function. Suppose that $m$ is the least natural
number with $J_k(n) + km > n + m$, and that moreover $J_k(n) + km \le 2(n + m)$. Then
$J_k(n + m) = J_k(n) + km - (n + m)$.

The second hypothesis, which allows only one wrap-around, is not in the printed lemma; without it
the statement fails at $k = 4$, $n = 1$, $m = 1$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Lemma 6.

articles.title: Josephus fixed points detected by the next value
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $n_p$ be natural
numbers with $n_p \ge k - 1$, and let $J_k$ be the Josephus function. Then $J_k(n_p) = n_p$ if
and only if $J_k(n_p + 1) = k - 1$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Proposition 4.

articles.title: The Josephus function just after a fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $n_p \ge 1$ be natural
numbers with $J_k(n_p) = n_p$, where $J_k$ is the Josephus function. Then $J_k(n_p + 1)$ is
determined as follows: (i) if $k \le n_p + 1$, then $J_k(n_p + 1) = k - 1$; (ii) if
$k = \ell(n_p + 1) + 1$ for some natural number $\ell \ge 1$, then $J_k(n_p + 1) = n_p + 1$;
(iii) if $k = \ell(n_p + 1) + k_1$ for some natural numbers $\ell \ge 1$ and $k_1$ with
$2 \le k_1 \le n_p$, then $J_k(n_p + 1) = k_1 - 1$; (iv) if $k = (\ell + 1)(n_p + 1)$ for some
natural number $\ell \ge 1$, then $J_k(n_p + 1) = n_p$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Proposition 4.

articles.title: The Josephus function at one
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k \ge 2$, the Josephus function
$J_k$ for elimination step $k$ satisfies $J_k(1) = 1$.

articles.title: Range of the Josephus function
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$, the
Josephus function $J_k$ for elimination step $k$ satisfies $1 \le J_k(n) \le n$.

articles.title: Josephus recurrence by number of wrap-arounds
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$ be natural
numbers, let $J_k$ be the Josephus function and write $p = J_k(n)$. If $\ell$ is a natural
number with $\ell(n+1) + 1 \le p + k \le (\ell+1)(n+1)$, then $J_k(n+1) = p + k - \ell(n+1)$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Euler recurrence for the Josephus function
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k \ge 2$ and
$n \ge 1$, the Josephus function $J_k$ for elimination step $k$ satisfies
$J_k(n+1) = ((J_k(n) + k - 1) \bmod (n+1)) + 1$.

articles.title: The Josephus function between consecutive fixed points
articles.statement:
For every natural number $\ell$,
let $a$ and $b$ be the $(\ell+1)$-th and $(\ell+2)$-th smallest fixed points of the Josephus
function $J_3$, and let $m = \nu_2(3a + 2)$ be the $2$-adic valuation of $3a + 2$. For every
natural number $n$ with $a + 1 \le n \le b$, put
$\mathfrak{m} = \lceil \log_{3/2}((2n + 1)/(3a + 2)) \rceil$; then, in the real numbers,

$$J_3(n) = 3n + 1 - \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^{m - \mathfrak{m}} (2b + 1).$$

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Digit count of consecutive Josephus fixed points
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus function
with elimination step $3$, let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th positive fixed point of $J_3$ in
increasing order (counting from $\ell = 0$), and let $m_\ell$ be the number of integers $n$ with
$n_\ell < n < n_{\ell+1}$ and $J_3(n) + 1 = n$ (the pure high extremal points between them).
For every $\ell$, the base-$3/2$ digit list of $n_{\ell+1}$ has exactly $m_\ell + 1$ more digits
than the base-$3/2$ digit list of $n_\ell$.

This is part (iv) of the cited Theorem 1.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits of the next Josephus fixed point, gap one
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus
function with elimination step $3$, let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th positive fixed point of $J_3$
in increasing order (counting from $\ell = 0$), and let $m_\ell$ be the number of integers $n$
with $n_\ell < n < n_{\ell+1}$ and $J_3(n) + 1 = n$ (the pure high extremal points between
them). For every $\ell$, if $m_\ell = 1$, then the base-$3/2$ digit list of $n_{\ell+1}$, least
significant digit first, is the digits $2, 0$ followed by the digit list of $n_\ell$.

This is part (ii) of the cited Theorem 1.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits of the next Josephus fixed point, gap at least two
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the
Josephus function with elimination step $3$, let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th positive fixed point
of $J_3$ in increasing order (counting from $\ell = 0$), and let $m_\ell$ be the number of
integers $n$ with $n_\ell < n < n_{\ell+1}$ and $J_3(n) + 1 = n$ (the pure high extremal points
between them). For every $\ell$, if $m_\ell \ge 2$, then the base-$3/2$ digit list of
$n_{\ell+1}$, least significant digit first, is the digit $2$, then $m_\ell - 1$ digits equal to
$1$, then the digit $0$, followed by the digit list of $n_\ell$.

Written most significant digit first, this appends to the digits of $n_\ell$ a $0$, then
$m_\ell - 1$ ones, then a $2$. This is part (iii) of the cited Theorem 1.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Base-3/2 digits of the next Josephus fixed point, gap zero
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus
function with elimination step $3$, let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th positive fixed point of $J_3$
in increasing order (counting from $\ell = 0$), and let $m_\ell$ be the number of integers $n$
with $n_\ell < n < n_{\ell+1}$ and $J_3(n) + 1 = n$ (the pure high extremal points between
them). For every $\ell$, if $m_\ell = 0$, then the base-$3/2$ digit list of $n_{\ell+1}$, least
significant digit first, is the digit $1$ followed by the digit list of $n_\ell$.

This is part (i) of the cited Theorem 1.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Second positive fixed point of the Josephus function for step three
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the
Josephus function with elimination step $3$. The second smallest positive integer $n$ with
$J_3(n) = n$ is $2$; in the zero-indexed enumeration $n_0 < n_1 < \cdots$ of these fixed points,
$n_1 = 2$, the paper's $n_p^{(2)}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Recurrence for consecutive fixed points of $J_3$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $\ell$, let $a$
and $b$ be the $(\ell+1)$-th and $(\ell+2)$-th smallest fixed points of the Josephus function
$J_3$, and let $m = \nu_2(3a + 2)$ be the $2$-adic valuation of $3a + 2$. Then exactly $m$
natural numbers $n$ with $a < n < b$ satisfy $J_3(n) = n - 1$ (the pure high extremal points
between $a$ and $b$), and $2^{m+1} b + 2^m = 3^m (3a + 2)$, that is,
$b = (3^m (3a + 2) - 2^m) / 2^{m+1}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Theorem 2.

articles.title: The third positive fixed point of $J_3$ is $13$
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus function with
step $3$ and let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th natural number $n \ge 1$ with $J_3(n) = n$, in
increasing order and counting from $\ell = 0$. Then $n_2 = 13$; this is the paper's $n_p^{(3)}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: The first positive fixed point of $J_3$ is $1$
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus function with
step $3$ and let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th natural number $n \ge 1$ with $J_3(n) = n$, in
increasing order and counting from $\ell = 0$. Then $n_0 = 1$; this is the paper's $n_p^{(1)}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Enumeration of the positive fixed points of $J_3$
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus function
with step $3$. For $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, $n_\ell$ is the $\ell$-th element, in increasing order
and counting from $\ell = 0$, of the set of natural numbers $n \ge 1$ with $J_3(n) = n$. Thus
$n_\ell$ is the paper's $n_p^{(\ell+1)}$.

If this set has at most $\ell$ elements, then $n_\ell = 0$ by convention.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: The second gap between positive fixed points of $J_3$ is $3$
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus
function with step $3$, let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th natural number $n \ge 1$ with
$J_3(n) = n$ (in increasing order, counting from $\ell = 0$), and let $g_\ell$ be the number of
natural numbers $n$ with $n_\ell < n < n_{\ell+1}$ and $J_3(n) + 1 = n$. Then $g_1 = 3$; this is
the paper's $\bar m_2 = 3$.

Here $n_1 = 2$ and $n_2 = 13$, and the three pure high extremal points counted are $3$, $5$ and $8$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Gaps between consecutive positive fixed points of $J_3$
articles.statement:
Let $J_3$ be the Josephus
function with step $3$ and let $n_\ell$ be the $\ell$-th natural number $n \ge 1$ with
$J_3(n) = n$, in increasing order and counting from $\ell = 0$. For $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, the gap
$g_\ell$ is the number of natural numbers $n$ with $n_\ell < n < n_{\ell+1}$ and
$J_3(n) + 1 = n$, that is, the number of pure high extremal points strictly between $n_\ell$ and
$n_{\ell+1}$. Thus $g_\ell$ is the paper's $\bar m_{\ell+1}$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *Fixed Points of the Josephus Function via Fractional Base Expansions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A54, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Unified recurrences for consecutive high extremal points of $J_3$
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $i$, let $a$ and $b$ be the $(i+1)$-th and $(i+2)$-th smallest high extremal points of the
Josephus function $J_3$. In the integers, put $r = a \bmod 2$, $f = a - J_3(a)$ and
$s = \lfloor (3a + 2 - r)/2 \rfloor \bmod 2$. Then

$$2b = 3a + 1 + (1 - r)(2f - 1), \qquad 2J_3(b) = 3a + (2 - 3r)(2f - 1),$$



$$b - J_3(b) = f - (1 - r)(2f - 1), \qquad b \bmod 2 = s - (1 - r)(1 - f)(2s - 1).$$

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Successive high extremal points of $J_3$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $i$, let $a$ and $b$ be
the $(i+1)$-th and $(i+2)$-th smallest high extremal points of the Josephus function $J_3$, and
put $f = a - J_3(a)$, $f' = b - J_3(b)$ and $r = a \bmod 2$. If $(f, r) = (1, 0)$, then
$2b = 3a + 2$ and $f' = 0$; if $(f, r) = (1, 1)$, then $2b = 3a + 1$ and $f' = 1$; if
$(f, r) = (0, 0)$, then $2b = 3a$ and $f' = 1$; if $(f, r) = (0, 1)$, then $2b = 3a + 1$ and
$f' = 0$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Josephus survivor function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, the Josephus function
$J_k(n)$ is defined by recursion on $n$: $J_k(0) = 0$ and
$J_k(n+1) = ((J_k(n) + k - 1) \bmod (n+1)) + 1$, where subtraction of natural numbers is
truncated at $0$.

For $k \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$, $J_k(n)$ is the one-based position of the sole survivor when every
$k$-th person is eliminated from a circle of $n$ people; the value $J_k(0) = 0$ only anchors the
recursion.

articles.title: $4$ is not a high extremal point of $J_3$
articles.statement:
The number $4$ is not a high extremal point of
the Josephus function $J_3$ (elimination step $3$).

Indeed $J_3(4) = 1$.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, *On the Recurrence Formula for Fixed Points of the Josephus Function*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A115, Section 1, Definition (Extremal and Fixed points).

articles.title: Linear-step bound at a low extremal point
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let
$J_k$ be the Josephus function, write $j = J_k(n+1)$, and suppose $j \le k - 1$. Then for every
natural number $m$, $j + km \le n + 1 + m$ holds if and only if
$m \le \lfloor (n - (j - 1)) / (k - 1) \rfloor$. Moreover, if $k - 2 + j \le n$, then
$\lfloor (n - (j - 1)) / (k - 1) \rfloor \ge 1$.

Since $1 \le J_k(n+1) \le n + 1$, the hypothesis says $j \in [1, k - 1]$, that is, $n + 1$ is a
low extremal point in the paper's sense, and none of the subtractions above is truncated.

## Sources

- Yunier Bello-Cruz and Roy Quintero-Contreras, "Analytical Study and Efficient Evaluation of the Josephus Function", Lemma 8.

articles.title: Affine expansion of a sequence
articles.statement:
For $r \in \mathbb{N}$, maps
$a, b : \{0, \dots, r - 1\} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a finite sequence $A = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of
natural numbers, $T(A)$ is the sequence of length $rn$ obtained by listing the blocks
$(a_i x_1 + b_i, \dots, a_i x_n + b_i)$ one after another for $i = 0, 1, \dots, r - 1$.

The order of the entries does not affect whether an entry repeats.

articles.title: Klarner's theorem (Erdős Problem 481)
articles.statement:
For every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and all maps
$a, b : \{0, \dots, r - 1\} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $a_i \ge 1$ for every $i$ and
$\sum_{i < r} 1 / a_i > 1$, let $T$ send a finite sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of natural numbers
to the sequence of all $a_i x_j + b_i$, listed in blocks for $i = 0, 1, \dots, r - 1$. Then,
starting from $A_1 = (1)$ with $A_{k+1} = T(A_k)$, some $A_k$ has a repeated entry.

This was first shown by Klarner and generalized by Kolpakov and Talambutsa.

## Sources

- T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problems, Problem #481, https://www.erdosproblems.com/481 (status PROVED (LEAN)); resolution: D. A. Klarner, A sufficient condition for certain semigroups to be free, J. Algebra (1982), 140-148; A. Kolpakov and A. Talambutsa, On free semigroups of affine maps on the real line, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (2022), 2301-2307, erdosproblems.com/481: true, first shown by Klarner; generalized by Kolpakov and Talambutsa, https://www.erdosproblems.com/481.

articles.title: Erdős Problem 481: repetitions under affine expansion
articles.statement:
The statement that for every
$r \in \mathbb{N}$ and all maps $a, b : \{0, \dots, r - 1\} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $a_i \ge 1$ for
every $i$ and $\sum_{i < r} 1 / a_i > 1$, if $T$ is the affine expansion of $a$ and $b$, sending a
finite sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of natural numbers to the sequence of all $a_i x_j + b_i$,
listed in blocks for $i = 0, 1, \dots, r - 1$ (the order does not affect whether an entry repeats),
then, starting from $A_1 = (1)$ with $A_{k+1} = T(A_k)$, some $A_k$ has a repeated entry.

articles.title: Infinitely many primes avoid $\gamma \alpha^n - \beta$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be
nonzero integers such that $\beta \ne \gamma \alpha^k$ and $\beta \alpha^k \ne \gamma$ for every
natural number $k$, that is, $\beta / \gamma$ is not $\alpha^k$ for any integer $k$. Then there
are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p$ divides none of the integers $\gamma \alpha^n - \beta$
with $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Lemma 3.2.

articles.title: Nilpotent polynomial at a point
articles.statement:
Let $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and $r \in \mathbb{Z}$, and
write $u^{(n)}$ for the $n$-fold iterate of $u$ as a map $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Then $u$ is
nilpotent at $r$ if $u^{(n)}(r) = 0$ for some $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Section 2.

articles.title: $x + 1$ is locally nilpotent at $1$
articles.statement:
Let $u(x) = x + 1 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and write
$u^{(m)}$ for the $m$-fold iterate of $u$ as a map $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Then for every
prime $p$ there is $m \ge 1$ such that $p$ divides $u^{(m)}(1)$.

One can take $m = p - 1$, since $u^{(p-1)}(1) = p$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Section 2, example (e).

articles.title: Weakly locally nilpotent polynomial at a point
articles.statement:
Let $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and
$r \in \mathbb{Z}$, and let $A$ be a set of natural numbers. Write $u^{(m)}$ for the $m$-fold
iterate of $u$ as a map $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Then $u$ is weakly locally nilpotent at $r$
outside $A$ if for every prime $p \notin A$ there is $m \ge 1$ such that $p$ divides
$u^{(m)}(r)$. For $A = \emptyset$ this is called locally nilpotent at $r$.

Only the primes in $A$ matter, so $A$ is usually taken to be a set of primes.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Section 2.

articles.title: Iterates of $x + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $u(x) = x + 1 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and write $u^{(m)}$ for its
$m$-fold iterate as a map $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$. For every integer $r$ and every natural
number $m$, $u^{(m)}(r) = r + m$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Section 2, example (e).

articles.title: Linear polynomials weakly locally nilpotent but not nilpotent at $1$
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite
set of primes, and let $c$ range over the positive integers all of whose prime factors lie in $A$.
A polynomial $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree $1$ is weakly locally nilpotent at $1$ outside $A$ and
not nilpotent at $1$ if and only if $u$ is one of: $x + c$; $x - c$ with $c \ne 1$; $cx + 1$ or
$-cx + 1$ with $c \ne 1$; or $-2x - 1$, the last only when $2 \in A$.

Writing $c = q_1^{s_1} \cdots q_k^{s_k}$ with the $q_i$ the primes of $A$, the condition $c \ne 1$
is the paper's $\sum s_i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Corollary 5.2.

articles.title: Classification of locally nilpotent polynomials at $-1$
articles.statement:
A polynomial $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$
of positive degree is locally nilpotent at $-1$ if and only if it has one of the following forms,
for some $p \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$: $(x+1)p(x)$ with $p \ne 0$; $-2x - 4 + p(x)(x+1)(x+2)$;
$2x^2 + 7x + 3 + p(x)(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)$; or $u = x - 1$.

These are the images of the polynomials locally nilpotent at $1$ under $u(x) \mapsto -u(-x)$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Corollary 4.2.

articles.title: Classification of locally nilpotent polynomials at $1$
articles.statement:
A polynomial $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$
of positive degree is locally nilpotent at $1$ if and only if it has one of the following forms,
for some $p \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$: $(x-1)p(x)$ with $p \ne 0$; $-2x + 4 + p(x)(x-1)(x-2)$;
$-2x^2 + 7x - 3 + p(x)(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)$; or $u = x + 1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Theorem 4.1.

articles.title: Classification of locally nilpotent polynomials at $0$
articles.statement:
A polynomial $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$
of positive degree is locally nilpotent at $0$ if and only if it has one of the following forms:
$x + b$ with $b \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b \ne 0$; $ax + b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b \ne 0$, $a$
divisible by at least one prime, and every prime divisor of $a$ dividing $b$; $x\,p(x)$ with
$p \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, $p \ne 0$; or $(x - a)p(x)$ with $a \in \mathbb{Z}$, $a \ne 0$, and
$p \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $p(0) = -1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Theorem 4.4.

articles.title: Locally nilpotent but not nilpotent polynomials at $\pm 1$
articles.statement:
The only polynomial
$u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of positive degree that is locally nilpotent at $1$ but not nilpotent at $1$
is $x + 1$, and the only polynomial of positive degree that is locally nilpotent at $-1$ but not
nilpotent at $-1$ is $x - 1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Corollary 4.3.

articles.title: Polynomials locally nilpotent but not nilpotent at $0$
articles.statement:
A polynomial $u \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$
of degree at least $1$ is locally nilpotent at $0$ and not nilpotent at $0$ if and only if either
$u = x + b$ for some integer $b \ne 0$, or $u = ax + b$ for some integers $a$ and $b$ with
$b \ne 0$ such that $a$ has at least one prime divisor and every prime divisor of $a$ divides $b$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Corollary 4.5.

articles.title: $x + 1$ is not nilpotent at $1$
articles.statement:
The polynomial $x + 1 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is not nilpotent
at $1$.

Writing $u(x) = x + 1$, the iterates satisfy $u^{(n)}(1) = n + 1 \ne 0$ for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Sayak Sengupta, *Locally Nilpotent Polynomials over Z*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A13, Section 2, example (e).

articles.title: Even-index recurrence for the Stern sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the
Stern sequence $s$ satisfies $s(2n) = s(n)$.

## Sources

- Stern sequence, OEIS A002487; JIS Lansing, lines 92-103; JIS Dennison, lines 80-85.

articles.title: Odd-index recurrence for the Stern sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the
Stern sequence $s$ satisfies $s(2n + 1) = s(n) + s(n + 1)$.

## Sources

- Stern sequence, OEIS A002487; JIS Lansing, lines 92-103; JIS Dennison, lines 80-85.

articles.title: Stern sequence at one
articles.statement:
The Stern sequence $s$ satisfies $s(1) = 1$.

## Sources

- Stern sequence, OEIS A002487; JIS Lansing, lines 92-103.

articles.title: Stern's diatomic sequence
articles.statement:
The Stern sequence is the function
$s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ defined by $s(0) = 0$, $s(1) = 1$, and, for every $n \ge 1$,
$s(2n) = s(n)$ and $s(2n + 1) = s(n) + s(n + 1)$.

## Sources

- Stern sequence ("Stern diatomic sequence", OEIS A002487); JIS Lansing, lines 92-103; JIS Dennison, lines 80-85.

articles.title: Stern sequence at zero
articles.statement:
The Stern sequence $s$ satisfies $s(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Stern sequence, OEIS A002487; JIS Lansing, lines 92-103.

articles.title: The sequence from $1, 2, 3$ dies after four terms
articles.statement:
Run the recurrence
$B(n) = B(n - B(n-1)) + B(n - B(n-2)) + B(n - B(n-3))$ from the initial conditions
$B(1) = 1$, $B(2) = 2$, $B(3) = 3$ without padding, so that a term whose recurrence refers to a
nonpositive index, or to an index not yet computed, cannot be computed. Then the sequence has
exactly four terms: $B(4)$ can be computed and $B(5)$ cannot.

## Sources

- Nathan Fox, *The Behavior of a Three-Term Hofstadter-Like Recurrence with Linear Initial Conditions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.4, proof of Theorem 1 (`B_3(4) = 6`).

articles.title: Exact length of a three-term Hofstadter-like sequence
articles.statement:
Take integer initial conditions
$B(1), \dots, B(m)$, and either pad the sequence with $B(n) = 0$ for every $n \le 0$ or leave it
unpadded. Continue it by $B(n) = B(n - B(n-1)) + B(n - B(n-2)) + B(n - B(n-3))$ for $n > m$,
where a term cannot be computed if this formula refers to an undefined index: a nonpositive
index in the unpadded case, or an index not yet computed. For a natural number $T$, the
sequence has exactly $T$ terms when $T \ge m$, the terms $B(1), \dots, B(T)$ can all be
computed, and $B(T + 1)$ cannot.

## Sources

- Nathan Fox, *The Behavior of a Three-Term Hofstadter-Like Recurrence with Linear Initial Conditions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.4, Section 1 ("dies after `n - 1` terms"; "ends" in the padded case).

articles.title: Computing further terms of a three-term Hofstadter-like sequence
articles.statement:
Given terms
$B(1), \dots, B(m)$, padded with $0$ at nonpositive indices or not, and a natural number $k$,
this is the list $B(1), \dots, B(m + k)$ obtained by computing $B(m + 1), \dots, B(m + k)$ one
after another from $B(n) = B(n - B(n-1)) + B(n - B(n-2)) + B(n - B(n-3))$. It is undefined if
one of these terms cannot be computed because the formula refers to an undefined index (a
nonpositive index in the unpadded case, or an index not yet computed).

## Sources

- Nathan Fox, *The Behavior of a Three-Term Hofstadter-Like Recurrence with Linear Initial Conditions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.4, Section 1.

articles.title: Five-cycle lemma for the three-term Hofstadter-like recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $K \ge 3$ be a
natural number, $\mu \ge 1$ an integer, and $a_4, \dots, a_K$ arbitrary integers. Let $B$ be
the sequence given by $B(n) = B(n - B(n-1)) + B(n - B(n-2)) + B(n - B(n-3))$, padded with
$B(n) = 0$ for $n \le 0$, with initial conditions
$1, 2, 3, a_4, \dots, a_K, K + \mu, 3, K + 3, K + \mu + 1, 5$ at the indices $1, \dots, K + 5$.
Then for all natural numbers $k$ and $r < 5$ with
$K + 1 \le K + 5k + r \le K + \lfloor (5\mu - 15)/2 \rfloor$, the term $B(K + 5k + r)$ can be
computed, and it equals $5$, $K + 3k + \mu$, $3$, $K + 5k + 3$ or $K + 3k + \mu + 1$ according
as $r = 0, 1, 2, 3$ or $4$.

## Sources

- Nathan Fox, *The Behavior of a Three-Term Hofstadter-Like Recurrence with Linear Initial Conditions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.7.4, Lemma 5, citing the author's thesis, Proposition 9.10 (`jis-2024-24.7.4-lem-5`).

articles.title: Death of the unpadded sequence from $1, \dots, N$ for $N = 3$, $4$ or $N \ge 10$
articles.statement:
Let
$N$ be a natural number with $N = 3$, $N = 4$ or $N \ge 10$, and let $B_N$ be the sequence with
initial conditions $B_N(i) = i$ for $1 \le i \le N$, continued without padding by the recurrence
$B_N(n) = B_N(n - B_N(n-1)) + B_N(n - B_N(n-2)) + B_N(n - B_N(n-3))$. Then $B_N$ dies: there is
a natural number $T$ such that $B_N(1), \dots, B_N(T)$ can be computed and $B_N(T + 1)$ cannot,
because the recurrence refers to a nonpositive index or to an index not yet computed.

## Sources
