- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Definition 3.13.

articles.title: Growth and positivity of Lucas sequences with positive discriminant
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be
integers with $P \neq 0$, $Q \neq 0$ and $D = P^2 - 4Q > 0$, and let $U = U(P, Q)$ and
$V = V(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequences. Then $|U_n| < |U_{n+1}|$ for every $n \ge 2$ and
$|V_n| < |V_{n+1}|$ for every $n \ge 1$; if $P > 0$, then $U_n > 0$ for every $n \ge 1$ and
$V_n > 0$ for every $n \ge 0$; and $|U_3| \ge 3$ unless $|P| = 1$ and $Q = -1$.

When $Q \neq 0$ and $D > 0$, the condition $P \neq 0$ is equivalent to the pair $(P, Q)$ being
nondegenerate (Theorem 2.1 of the source).

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 2.9.

articles.title: Classification of degenerate Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers, let
$\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $\alpha + \beta = P$ and $\alpha\beta = Q$ (so they are the
roots of $x^2 - Px + Q$), and let $D = P^2 - 4Q$. Let $(u_n)$ be the Lucas sequence of the first
kind with parameters $P, Q$, and let $(v_n)$ be the integer sequence with $v_0 = 2$, $v_1 = P$ and
$v_{n+2} = P v_{n+1} - Q v_n$ for all $n$. Suppose that $Q = 0$ or that $\alpha/\beta$ is a root
of unity. Then either (i) $Q = 0$, $D = P^2$, and $u_n = P^{n-1}$ and $v_n = P^n$ for every
$n \ge 1$; or there is a nonzero integer $M$ such that one of the following holds:
(ii) $\alpha/\beta = 1$, $P = 2M$, $Q = M^2$ and $D = 0$;
(iii) $\alpha/\beta = -1$, $P = 0$, $Q = M$ and $D = -4M$;
(iv) $\alpha/\beta$ is a primitive cube root of unity, $P = M$, $Q = M^2$ and $D = -3M^2$;
(v) $\alpha/\beta$ is a primitive fourth root of unity, $P = 2M$, $Q = 2M^2$ and $D = -4M^2$;
(vi) $\alpha/\beta$ is a primitive sixth root of unity, $P = 3M$, $Q = 3M^2$ and $D = -3M^2$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 2.1.

articles.title: Index of the Lucas pseudoprime congruences
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers with $Q \neq 0$ and
$D = P^2 - 4Q$. For a natural number $N$, the index is $N - (D/N)$, where $(D/N)$ is the Jacobi
symbol, replaced by $0$ when this difference is negative. For $N > 1$ the difference is positive.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, congruences (3.1), (3.4).

articles.title: Rank of appearance and super Lucas pseudoprimes
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers with $Q \neq 0$
such that the pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $D = P^2 - 4Q$, and write $\rho(m)$ for the rank
of appearance of $m$ in the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$. Let $N > 1$ be an odd number that is not
prime, with $\gcd(N, QD) = 1$, and for each prime $p \mid N$ let $k_p$ be the exponent of $p$ in
$N$ and let $m_p \ge k_p$ satisfy $\rho(p^{m_p}) = \rho(p)$ and $\rho(p^{m_p + 1}) \neq \rho(p)$.
Let $h$ be the least common multiple of the $\rho(p)$ over the primes $p \mid N$. Then
$\rho(N) = h$, and $N$ is a super Lucas pseudoprime with parameters $(P, Q)$ if and only if
$p \equiv (D/p) \pmod h$ for every prime $p \mid N$, where $(D/p)$ is the Jacobi symbol.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 3.16.

articles.title: Rank of appearance is at most any positive index of divisibility
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers
with $Q \neq 0$, let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequence, and write $\rho(m)$ for the rank of
appearance of a natural number $m$ in $U$. If $r > 0$ and $m \mid U_r$, then $\rho(m) \le r$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Section 2 (definition of `ρ` as a least index).

articles.title: Rank of appearance of $1$
articles.statement:
For all integers $P, Q$ with $Q \neq 0$, the rank of
appearance of $1$ in the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$ is $1$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Section 2 (definition of `ρ`).

articles.title: Properties of the rank of appearance in a Lucas sequence
The rank of appearance in a Lucas sequence is attained
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be a Lucas
sequence and $m$ a natural number. If $m \mid U_r$ for some positive integer $r$, then the rank of
appearance $\rho(m)$ of $m$ in $U$ is positive and $m \mid U_{\rho(m)}$.

Together with the bound $\rho(m) \le r$ for every positive $r$ with $m \mid U_r$, this makes
$\rho(m)$ the least such index.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Section 2 (definition of `ρ` as a least index).

articles.title: Rank of appearance in a Lucas sequence
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequence with
integer parameters $P$ and $Q \ne 0$. The rank of appearance $\rho(m)$ of a natural number $m$ in
$U$ is the least positive integer $r$ with $m \mid U_r$; when no positive $r$ has $m \mid U_r$,
$\rho(m) = 0$.

When $m \ge 1$ and $\gcd(m, Q) = 1$, such an $r$ always exists (the source defines $\rho(m)$ only
in this case); it can also exist when $\gcd(m, Q) \ne 1$. For $m = 0$ it need not exist even when
$\gcd(0, Q) = |Q| = 1$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Section 2.

articles.title: Shift congruence for the Lucas recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequence with
integer parameters $P$ and $Q \ne 0$, and let $(W_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of integers with
$W_{n+2} = P W_{n+1} - Q W_n$ for every $n \ge 0$. If $t \ge 0$ and $m$ are integers with
$m \mid U_t$ and $\gcd(m, Q) = 1$, then $W_{n+t} \equiv U_{t+1} W_n \pmod{m}$ for every $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 2.5.

articles.title: Composite terms of Lucas sequences with positive discriminant
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the
Lucas sequence with integer parameters $P \ne 0$ and $Q \ne 0$ such that $\gcd(P, Q) = 1$ and
$D = P^2 - 4Q > 0$, and let $m \ge 5$ be an odd integer. If $m$ is not prime, then $U_m$ is
composite; and $U_{2m}/P$ is always composite. Here an integer $N$ is composite when $|N| > 1$
and $|N|$ is not prime.

Since $D > 0$, the conditions $P \ne 0$ and $Q \ne 0$ say that $U$ is nondegenerate. The quotient
$U_{2m}/P$ is an integer because $P \mid U_{2m}$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Corollary 4.2.

articles.title: Divisibility of Lucas sequences at divisible indices
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ and
$V = V(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequences with integer parameters $P$ and $Q \ne 0$, and let $m$ and
$n$ be natural numbers with $m \mid n$. Then $U_m \mid U_n$, and if moreover $n/m$ is odd, then
$V_m \mid V_n$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Proposition 2.3 (iii), (iv).

articles.title: Lucas sequences under negation of the first parameter
articles.statement:
For integers $P$ and $Q \ne 0$ and
every natural number $n$, the Lucas sequences $U$ and $V$ satisfy
$U_n(-P, Q) = (-1)^{n+1} U_n(P, Q)$ and $V_n(-P, Q) = (-1)^n V_n(P, Q)$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Proposition 2.3 (vii), (viii).

articles.title: Lucas sequences modulo 3
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequence with integer parameters
$P$ and $Q \ne 0$, let $D = P^2 - 4Q$, and suppose $3 \nmid \gcd(P, Q)$. Then $U$ is periodic
modulo $3$ from index $1$ on: there is $k > 0$ with $U_{n+k} \equiv U_n \pmod 3$ for every
$n \ge 1$. If $3 \mid Q$, then $3 \nmid U_n$ for every $n \ge 1$. If $3 \mid P$, then for every
$n \ge 0$, $3 \mid U_n$ if and only if $2 \mid n$. If $3 \nmid P$ and $Q \equiv -1 \pmod 3$,
then for every $n \ge 0$, $3 \mid U_n$ if and only if $4 \mid n$. If $3 \nmid P$ and
$Q \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, then for every $n \ge 0$, $3 \mid U_n$ if and only if $3 \mid n$; moreover
$3 \mid D$.

The periodicity need not start at $n = 0$: for $P = 1$ and $Q = 3$, $U$ is $0, 1, 1, 1, \dots$
modulo $3$. The source's values $\rho(3) = 2, 4, 3$ of the rank of apparition are the least
positive indices these equivalences give.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 2.8.

articles.title: Lucas sequences modulo 2
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequence with integer parameters
$P$ and $Q \ne 0$, let $D = P^2 - 4Q$, and suppose $2 \nmid \gcd(P, Q)$. Then $U$ is periodic
modulo $2$ from index $1$ on: there is $k > 0$ with $U_{n+k} \equiv U_n \pmod 2$ for every
$n \ge 1$. If $P$ is odd and $Q$ is even, then $U_n$ is odd for every $n \ge 1$. If $P$ is even
and $Q$ is odd, then for every $n \ge 0$, $2 \mid U_n$ if and only if $2 \mid n$; moreover
$2 \mid D$. If $P$ and $Q$ are both odd, then for every $n \ge 0$, $2 \mid U_n$ if and only if
$3 \mid n$.

The periodicity need not start at $n = 0$: for $P = 1$ and $Q = 2$, $U$ is $0, 1, 1, 1, \dots$
modulo $2$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 2.7.

articles.title: Pseudoprime candidates from a Lucas sequence
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be the Lucas sequence with
integer parameters $P \ne 0$ and $Q \ne 0$ such that $\gcd(P, Q) = 1$ and $D = P^2 - 4Q > 0$.
Let $m > 1$ be an odd integer with $\gcd(m, PQD) = 1$, and assume $3 \nmid m$ when $P$ and $Q$
are both odd. Put $N_1 = U_m$ and $N_2 = U_{2m}/P$. Then $N_1$ and $N_2$ are positive and odd,
and $\gcd(N_1 N_2, PQD) = 1$. If $m$ is not prime, then $N_1$ and $N_2$ are composite, that is,
$|N_i| > 1$ and $|N_i|$ is not prime for $i = 1, 2$. If $P$ is odd, or $P \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ and
$Q \equiv -1 \pmod 4$, or $P \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ and $Q \equiv -1 \pmod 8$, then the Jacobi
symbols satisfy $(D/m) = (D/|N_1|) = (D/|N_2|)$.

Since $D > 0$, the conditions $P \ne 0$ and $Q \ne 0$ say that $U$ is nondegenerate. The quotient
$U_{2m}/P$ is an integer because $P \mid U_{2m}$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 6.1.

articles.title: $|U_m|$ is a strong Lucas and Frobenius pseudoprime when $Q = \pm 1$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be
integers with $Q = 1$ or $Q = -1$ such that the Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $U_n$
be the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$, and let $D = P^2 - 4Q$. Let $m \ge 5$ be either an odd prime or
a Lucas pseudoprime of the second kind for $(P, Q)$, with $\gcd(m, PD) = 1$ and with $3 \nmid m$
if $P$ is odd. Then $D > 0$, $\gcd(U_m, PD) = 1$, and $3 \nmid U_m$ if $P$ is odd. Suppose
moreover that $|U_m|$ is not prime whenever $m$ is prime and $Q = -1$, and that $P$ is odd, or
$P$ is even and $Q = -1$. Then $|U_m|$ is both a strong Lucas pseudoprime and a Frobenius
pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 6.3.

articles.title: When $|U_{2m}/P|$ is a Frobenius pseudoprime, for $Q = \pm 1$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers
with $Q = 1$ or $Q = -1$ such that the Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $U_n$ be the
Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$, and let $D = P^2 - 4Q$. Let $m \ge 5$ be either an odd prime or a Lucas
pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$, with $\gcd(m, PD) = 1$ and with $3 \nmid m$ if $P$ is odd, and write
$\left(\frac{D}{m}\right)$ for the Jacobi symbol. Suppose that $P$ is odd, or $P$ is even and
$Q = -1$, and put $N_2 = |U_{2m}/P|$. Then $D > 0$ and $N_2$ is a Lucas pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$.
Moreover, $N_2$ is a Frobenius pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$ if and only if:
$m \equiv \left(\frac{D}{m}\right) \pmod 6$ and $\left(\frac{D}{m}\right) = 1$, when $P$ is odd
and $Q = -1$; $m \equiv \left(\frac{D}{m}\right) \pmod 6$, when $P$ is odd and $Q = 1$; and
$m \equiv \left(\frac{D}{m}\right) \pmod 4$ and $\left(\frac{D}{m}\right) = 1$, when $P$ is even
and $Q = -1$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 6.10.

articles.title: $|U_{2m}/P|$ is a Lucas pseudoprime when $Q = \pm 1$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with
$Q = 1$ or $Q = -1$ such that the Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $U_n$ be the Lucas
sequence $U(P, Q)$, and let $D = P^2 - 4Q$. Let $m \ge 5$ be either an odd prime or a Lucas
pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$, with $\gcd(m, PD) = 1$ and with $3 \nmid m$ if $P$ is odd, and put
$N_2 = U_{2m}/P$. Then $D > 0$, $\gcd(N_2, PD) = 1$, and $3 \nmid N_2$ if $P$ is odd; and if $P$
is odd, or $P$ is even and $Q = -1$, then $|N_2|$ is a Lucas pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 6.6.

articles.title: Doubling formula $U_{2n} = U_n V_n$ for Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with
$Q \ne 0$, and let $U$ and $V$ be the Lucas sequences $U(P, Q)$ and $V(P, Q)$. Then
$U_{2n} = U_n V_n$ for every natural number $n$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Proposition 2.3 (i).

articles.title: Compositeness criteria for $|U_p|$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be coprime integers such that the
Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $U_n$ be the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$, let
$D = P^2 - 4Q$, and write $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ for the Jacobi symbol. Call a prime $p$
admissible if $p \ge 5$ and $\gcd(p, PQD) = 1$. Then the following hold.

First, if $Q$ is the square of an integer and $D > 0$, then for every admissible prime $p$, $|U_p|$
is greater than $1$, is not prime, and has at least two distinct prime factors.

Second, let $p$ be an admissible prime such that $2p + 1$ is prime and
$\left(\frac{D}{2p+1}\right) = \left(\frac{Q}{2p+1}\right) = 1$. Then $2p + 1 \mid |U_p|$ if
$|U_p| > 2p + 1$; and if $D > 0$, then $|U_p| > 2p + 1$ unless $p = 5$, $|P| = 1$ and $Q = -2$.

Third, if $D < 0$, there is a constant $C$ such that $|U_p| > 2p + 1$ for every prime $p \ge C$.

Fourth, let $p$ be an admissible prime such that $2p - 1$ is prime,
$\left(\frac{D}{2p-1}\right) = -1$ and $\left(\frac{Q}{2p-1}\right) = 1$. Then $2p - 1 \mid |U_p|$
if $|U_p| > 2p - 1$; and if $D > 0$, then $|U_p| > 2p - 1$ unless $p = 7$, $|P| = 1$ and $Q = -1$.

The source states the bound for $D < 0$ in both parts (ii) and (iii) of Theorem 5.1, as printed
with $2p + 1$ in each; the third claim above is that bound.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 5.1 (i)–(iii).

articles.title: $U_n$ divides none of $U_1, \dots, U_{n-1}$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with $P \ne 0$,
$Q \ne 0$ and $D = P^2 - 4Q > 0$, and let $U_n$ be the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$. Then for every
$n \ge 3$ and every $k$ with $0 < k < n$, $U_n$ does not divide $U_k$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Corollary 2.10.

articles.title: Parity of $U_m$ and $U_{2m}/P$ and their coprimality to $D$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be coprime
integers with $P \ne 0$ and $Q \ne 0$, let $U_n$ be the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$, and let
$D = P^2 - 4Q$. Let $m$ be an odd natural number with $\gcd(m, PQD) = 1$, and with $3 \nmid m$ if
$P$ and $Q$ are both odd. Then $U_m$ and $U_{2m}/P$ are odd, and each of them is coprime to $D$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 4.10.

articles.title: $P$ divides $U_{2n}$, and $V_n$ for odd $n$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with $Q \ne 0$,
and let $U$ and $V$ be the Lucas sequences $U(P, Q)$ and $V(P, Q)$. Then $P \mid U_{2n}$ for every
natural number $n$, and $P \mid V_n$ for every odd natural number $n$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Proposition 2.3 (v), (vi).

articles.title: When $p^{i+1}$ divides $U_{2n}$, for a prime power $p^i$ exactly dividing $P$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and
$Q$ be coprime integers with $Q \ne 0$, and let $U_n$ be the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$. Let $p$ be
a prime and $i \ge 1$ such that $p^i \mid P$ and $p^{i+1} \nmid P$. Then for every positive
integer $n$, $p^{i+1} \mid U_{2n}$ if and only if $p \mid n$.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Lemma 2.6, first claim.

articles.title: Lucas-type pseudoprime properties are unchanged by $P \mapsto -P$
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be
integers such that the Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $D = P^2 - 4Q$, and let $N > 1$
be an odd natural number with $\gcd(N, QD) = 1$. Then $N$ is a Lucas pseudoprime for $(P, Q)$ if
and only if it is one for $(-P, Q)$, and the same holds for Lucas pseudoprimes of the second
kind, Dickson pseudoprimes, Dickson pseudoprimes of the second kind, and Frobenius pseudoprimes.

## Sources

- Lawrence Somer and Michal Křížek, *On Lucas and Frobenius Pseudoprimes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A107, Theorem 4.7.

articles.title: Fibonacci prime divisibility
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime with $p > 2$ and $p \ne 5$, and let
$\left(\frac{5}{p}\right)$ be the Legendre symbol of $5$ modulo $p$. Then $p$ divides the
Fibonacci number $F_{p-1}$ if $\left(\frac{5}{p}\right) = 1$, and $p$ divides the Fibonacci
number $F_{p+1}$ otherwise. Since $\left(\frac{5}{p}\right) = \pm 1$, this says that $p$ divides
$F_{p - \left(\frac{5}{p}\right)}$.

## Sources

- Phakhinkon Phunphayap and Prapanpong Pongsriiam, "Explicit Formulas for the p-adic Valuations of Fibonomial Coefficients," Journal of Integer Sequences 21 (2018), Article 18.3.1, Lemma, item (i), lines 166–169, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL21/Pongsriiam/pong12.tex

articles.title: Zsigmondy primes divide the homogenized cyclotomic value
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be distinct
coprime positive integers and let $n \ge 2$. If $p$ is a primitive prime divisor of the term
$a^n - b^n$ of the integer sequence $(a^m - b^m)_{m \ge 0}$ (a Zsigmondy prime for $(a, b, n)$),
then $p$ divides the homogenized cyclotomic value $\Phi_n(a, b)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 5.

articles.title: A Zsigmondy prime $q$ that is not large satisfies $n = q - 1$
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be coprime
positive integers and let $n \ge 2$. If $q$ is a primitive prime divisor of the term $a^n - b^n$
of the integer sequence $(a^m - b^m)_{m \ge 0}$ and $q$ is not a large Zsigmondy prime for
$(a, b, n)$, then $n = q - 1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Avcı's classification of large Zsigmondy primes
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be coprime positive
integers and let $n > 1$. There is a large Zsigmondy prime for $(a, b, n)$ if and only if none
of the following holds: $n = 2$ and $a + b = 2^s$ or $a + b = 3 \cdot 2^s$ for some natural
number $s$; $n = 4$ and $(a, b) \in \{(2, 1), (3, 1)\}$; $n = 6$ and
$(a, b) \in \{(2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2), (5, 1), (5, 4)\}$; $n = 10$ and
$(a, b) \in \{(2, 1), (3, 2)\}$; $n = 12$ and $(a, b) = (2, 1)$; $n = 18$ and $(a, b) = (2, 1)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Theorem 1 (the converse is the classification in the proof of Theorem 1).

articles.title: A size criterion for a large Zsigmondy prime
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be distinct coprime
positive integers and let $n \ge 3$. If $(n + 1) q < \Phi_n(a, b)$ for every prime factor $q$ of
$n$, where $\Phi_n(a, b)$ is the homogenized cyclotomic value, then there is a large Zsigmondy
prime for $(a, b, n)$.

Equivalently, the hypothesis asks that $n + 1$ times the greatest prime factor of $n$ be less
than $\Phi_n(a, b)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Large Zsigmondy primes for exponents $n > 1$ outside six values
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be coprime
positive integers and let $n > 1$ with $n \notin \{2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 18\}$. Then there is a
large Zsigmondy prime for $(a, b, n)$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 8.

articles.title: Bounds for homogenized cyclotomic values
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be positive integers and let
$n \ge 1$. Then the homogenized cyclotomic value $\Phi_n(a, b)$ satisfies
$(a - b)^{\varphi(n)} \le \Phi_n(a, b) \le (a + b)^{\varphi(n)}$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's
totient function.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 3 (ii) (quoted from reference [6]).

articles.title: Homogenized cyclotomic values at $pn$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, $n$ a positive integer and
$a, b$ integers, and write $\Phi_m(a, b)$ for the homogenized cyclotomic value. If $p \mid n$,
then $\Phi_{pn}(a, b) = \Phi_n(a^p, b^p)$. If $p \nmid n$, then
$\Phi_{pn}(a, b) \cdot \Phi_n(a, b) = \Phi_n(a^p, b^p)$.

The paper states the case $p \nmid n$ as a quotient; here it is cleared of its denominator.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 3 (iii) (quoted from reference [6]).

articles.title: Homogenized cyclotomic values at $p^\beta k$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $\beta \ge 1$ and
$k \ge 1$ be integers with $p \nmid k$, and let $a, b$ be integers; write $\Phi_m(a, b)$ for the
homogenized cyclotomic value. Then
$\Phi_{p^\beta k}(a, b) = \Phi_{pk}(a^{p^{\beta - 1}}, b^{p^{\beta - 1}})$ and
$\Phi_{p^\beta k}(a, b) \cdot \Phi_k(a^{p^{\beta - 1}}, b^{p^{\beta - 1}}) =
\Phi_k(a^{p^\beta}, b^{p^\beta})$.

The paper states the second identity as a quotient; here it is cleared of its denominator.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Corollary 1.

articles.title: $7$ is a large Zsigmondy prime for $(2, 1, 3)$
articles.statement:
The prime $7$ is a large Zsigmondy prime
for $(a, b, n) = (2, 1, 3)$: it divides $2^3 - 1 = 7$, divides neither $2^1 - 1$ nor $2^2 - 1$,
and $7 > 3 + 1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Section 1 (definition after Theorem 1).

articles.title: Large Zsigmondy prime
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $n$ and $p$ be natural numbers. Then $p$ is a large
Zsigmondy prime for $(a, b, n)$ when $p$ is a primitive prime divisor of the term $a^n - b^n$ of
the integer sequence $(a^m - b^m)_{m \ge 0}$, that is, $n \ge 1$, $p$ is prime, $p$ divides
$a^n - b^n$ and $p$ divides no $a^m - b^m$ with $1 \le m < n$, and moreover $p^2$ divides
$a^n - b^n$ or $p > n + 1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Section 1 (definition after Theorem 1).

articles.title: $p$-adic valuation of homogenized cyclotomic values at an odd prime
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be
positive integers, let $p$ be an odd prime dividing neither $a$ nor $b$, and let $k$ be the least
positive integer such that $p$ divides $a^k - b^k$. Write $v_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation and
$\Phi_n(a, b)$ for the homogenized cyclotomic value. Then for every positive integer $n$:
$v_p(\Phi_n(a, b)) = v_p(a^k - b^k)$ if $n = k$; $v_p(\Phi_n(a, b)) = 1$ if $n = p^\beta k$ for
some $\beta \ge 1$; and $v_p(\Phi_n(a, b)) = 0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 3 (iv) (quoted from reference [6]).

articles.title: $2$-adic valuation of homogenized cyclotomic values
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be odd positive
integers. Write $v_2$ for the $2$-adic valuation and $\Phi_n(a, b)$ for the homogenized
cyclotomic value. Then for every positive integer $n$: $v_2(\Phi_n(a, b)) = v_2(a - b)$ if
$n = 1$; $v_2(\Phi_n(a, b)) = v_2(a + b)$ if $n = 2$; $v_2(\Phi_n(a, b)) = 1$ if $n = 2^\beta$
for some $\beta \ge 2$; and $v_2(\Phi_n(a, b)) = 0$ if $n$ is not a power of $2$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 3 (v) (quoted from reference [6]).

articles.title: Prime divisors of homogenized cyclotomic values
articles.statement:
Let $a > b$ be coprime positive
integers, let $n \ge 2$, let $\Phi_n(a, b)$ be the homogenized cyclotomic value, let $p$ be a
prime dividing $\Phi_n(a, b)$, and let $k$ be the least positive integer such that $p$ divides
$a^k - b^k$. Then one of the following holds: (i) $p = 2$ and $n = 2^\beta$ for some
$\beta \ge 1$; (ii) $p \ge 3$, $n = k$, and $p$ is a primitive prime divisor of the term
$a^n - b^n$ of the sequence $(a^m - b^m)_{m \ge 0}$; (iii) $p$ is the greatest prime factor of
$n$, $p > 2$, $n = p^\beta k$ for some $\beta \ge 1$, and the $p$-adic valuation of
$\Phi_n(a, b)$ is $1$.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Factorization of $a^n - b^n$ into homogenized cyclotomic values
articles.statement:
For every positive
integer $n$ and all integers $a$ and $b$,

$$a^n - b^n = \prod_{d \mid n} \Phi_d(a, b),$$

where the product runs over the positive divisors $d$ of $n$ and $\Phi_d(a, b)$ is the
homogenized cyclotomic value.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 3 (i) (quoted from reference [6]).

articles.title: Square-root lower bound for Euler's totient
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$,
$\varphi(n) \ge \sqrt{n}/2$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function.

## Sources

- Ömer Avcı, *Large Zsigmondy Primes*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A62, Lemma 1 (quoted from reference [2]).

articles.title: The $5$-adic valuation of Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Writing $F_n$ for the $n$-th Fibonacci number
and $v_5$ for the $5$-adic valuation, $v_5(F_n) = v_5(n)$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Fatehizadeh–Yaqubi, Lemma `Leg1`, citing Lengyel (1995). The source prints `n ≥ 0`, but its p-adic valuation is defined for positive integers, so this formalizes the audited `1 ≤ n` restriction. Only the 5-adic clause is formalized; the source's separate 2-adic and 3-adic clauses are out of scope.

articles.title: Fibonacci parameters for Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
The Fibonacci parameters are the Lucas sequence
parameters $P = 1$ and $Q = -1$; they satisfy the required condition $Q \ne 0$.

These parameters give the Fibonacci and classical Lucas-number sequences.

articles.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind: value at one
articles.statement:
If $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence
of the first kind with integer parameters $P$ and $Q$, then $u_1 = 1$.

articles.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind: value at zero
articles.statement:
If $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence
of the first kind with integer parameters $P$ and $Q$, then $u_0 = 0$.

articles.title: Coprime Lucas sequence parameters
articles.statement:
Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$ are coprime when
there exist integers $x$ and $y$ with $xP + yQ = 1$.

This additional condition is imposed in some applications of Lucas sequences.

articles.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind
articles.statement:
For integers $P$ and $Q$, a sequence of integers
$(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas sequence of the first kind with parameters $P$ and $Q$ when
$u_0 = 0$, $u_1 = 1$, and $u_{n+2} = P u_{n+1} - Q u_n$ for every natural number $n$.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Smyth/smyth2.tex>, lines 114-122.

articles.title: Special primes are the common prime divisors of the parameters
articles.statement:
For integers $P$ and $Q$
and a natural number $p$, $p$ is a special prime for the Lucas parameters $(P, Q)$ if and only if
$p$ is prime and $p$ divides both $P$ and $Q$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Special primes of a Lucas pair
articles.statement:
For integers $P$ and $Q$, a natural number $p$ is a special
prime for the Lucas parameters $(P, Q)$ if $p$ is prime and $p$ divides $\gcd(P, Q)$.

articles.title: Nondegenerate Lucas pair
articles.statement:
A pair of integers $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate when $Q \ne 0$ and,
for all complex numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $\alpha + \beta = P$ and $\alpha \beta = Q$, the
quotient $\alpha / \beta$ is not a root of unity. Such $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the two roots of
$x^2 - P x + Q$, in either order.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Smyth/smyth2.tex>: lines 621-622 say a Lucas sequence is degenerate iff `Q = 0` or `α / β` is a root of unity, where `α` and `β` are the two roots of `x² - P x + Q`. Lines 114-122 establish `α + β = P` and `α * β = Q`.

articles.title: Binet formulas for Lucas sequences over any field
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with
$Q \ne 0$, let $U_n = U_n(P, Q)$ and $V_n = V_n(P, Q)$ be the associated Lucas sequences, and let
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ be elements of a field $K$ with $\alpha + \beta = P$ and $\alpha \beta = Q$
in $K$. If $\alpha \ne \beta$, then for every natural number $n$,
$U_n = (\alpha^n - \beta^n) / (\alpha - \beta)$ and $V_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n$ in $K$. If
$\beta = \alpha$, then for every natural number $n$, $U_n = n \alpha^{n-1}$ and $V_n = 2 \alpha^n$
in $K$, where $\alpha^{n-1}$ is read as $1$ when $n = 0$. Here the integers $U_n$, $V_n$, $P$, $Q$
and $n$ are mapped into $K$.

No assumption on the characteristic of $K$ is made; for example $K$ may be $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$
for a prime $p$, where the coefficient $n$ of the double-root formula is read modulo $p$.

articles.title: Binet formulas for Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with $Q \ne 0$, let
$U_n = U_n(P, Q)$ and $V_n = V_n(P, Q)$ be the associated Lucas sequences, and let $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ be elements of a field $K$ of characteristic zero with $\alpha + \beta = P$ and
$\alpha \beta = Q$ in $K$. If $\alpha \ne \beta$, then for every natural number $n$,
$U_n = (\alpha^n - \beta^n) / (\alpha - \beta)$ and $V_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n$ in $K$. If
$\beta = \alpha$, then for every natural number $n$, $U_n = n \alpha^{n-1}$ and $V_n = 2 \alpha^n$
in $K$, where $\alpha^{n-1}$ is read as $1$ when $n = 0$. Here the integers $U_n$, $V_n$, $P$, $Q$
and $n$ are mapped into $K$.

In the double-root case the hypotheses give $P = 2 \alpha$ and $Q = \alpha^2$.

## Sources

- Christian Ballot, "A Further Generalization of a Congruence of Wolstenholme", Journal of Integer Sequences 15 (2012), Article 12.8.6, sequence definitions and formulas at lines 274–289, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL15/Ballot/ballot4.tex

articles.title: Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
The Lucas numbers are the natural numbers $L_n$ defined by $L_0 = 2$,
$L_1 = 1$ and $L_{n+2} = L_{n+1} + L_n$ for every natural number $n$. They begin
$2, 1, 3, 4, 7, \dots$.

articles.title: Parameters of a Lucas sequence
articles.statement:
Lucas sequence parameters are a pair of integers
$(P, Q)$ with $Q \ne 0$.

The condition $Q \ne 0$ follows the convention of the sources.

articles.title: Recurrence for the Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$
articles.statement:
For Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$ and
every natural number $n$, the Lucas sequence $U = U(P, Q)$ satisfies
$U_{n+2} = P U_{n+1} - Q U_n$.

articles.title: Cassini's identity for Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
For Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$ and every
natural number $n$, the Lucas sequence $U = U(P, Q)$ satisfies
$U_{n+1}^2 - U_n U_{n+2} = Q^n$.

articles.title: The Lucas sequence $U(1, -1)$ is the Fibonacci sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
the $n$-th term of the Lucas sequence $U(1, -1)$ equals the Fibonacci number $F_n$, where
$F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$.

articles.title: Lucas sequence $U(P, Q)$
articles.statement:
For Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$, the Lucas sequence
$U(P, Q)$ is the integer sequence $(U_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$ and
$U_{n+2} = P U_{n+1} - Q U_n$ for every natural number $n$.

articles.title: The Lucas sequence $V(1, -1)$ gives the Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
$n$-th term of the companion Lucas sequence $V(1, -1)$ equals the $n$-th Lucas number $L_n$.

articles.title: Companion Lucas sequence $V(P, Q)$
articles.statement:
For Lucas sequence parameters $(P, Q)$, the
companion Lucas sequence $V(P, Q)$ is the integer sequence $(V_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = P$ and $V_{n+2} = P V_{n+1} - Q V_n$ for every natural number $n$.

articles.title: Lucas sequence of the first kind: the recurrence
articles.statement:
If $(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is the Lucas
sequence of the first kind with integer parameters $P$ and $Q$, then
$u_{n+2} = P u_{n+1} - Q u_n$ for every natural number $n$.

articles.title: Addition formula $2U_{m+n} = U_m V_n + V_m U_n$ for Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
For all integers
$P$ and $Q$ with $Q \neq 0$ and all natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the Lucas sequences
$U_n = U_n(P, Q)$ and $V_n = V_n(P, Q)$ satisfy $2U_{m+n} = U_m V_n + V_m U_n$.

This is the integer specialization of the paper's Proposition 1: its generalized Fibonacci
numbers $F_n$ and Lucas numbers $L_n$, with recurrence $x_{n+2} = a x_{n+1} + b x_n$, are
$U_n(a, -b)$ and $V_n(a, -b)$, and the paper allows real $a$ and $b$.

## Sources

- Vladimir V. Kruchinin and Maria Y. Perminova, "Identities and Hadamard Product of the Generalized Fibonacci, Lucas, Catalan, and Harmonic Numbers", Proposition 1.

articles.title: Primitive divisors of Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Write $F_j$ for the $j$-th Fibonacci number.
For every natural number $n \ge 7$ with $n \ne 12$, $F_n$ has a primitive divisor with respect
to the discriminant $5$: there is a prime $p$ that divides $F_n$ but does not divide
$5 F_1 F_2 \cdots F_{n-1}$.

This is the Fibonacci case of Carmichael's theorem on Lucas sequences, with
$\alpha = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ and $\beta = (1 - \sqrt{5})/2$, so that $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = 5$.

## Sources

- Haojie Hong, *On big primitive divisors of Fibonacci numbers*, arXiv:2312.04354v1, `bigPFn.tex` lines 153–158 (<https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04354>); R. D. Carmichael, *On the numerical factors of the arithmetic forms αⁿ±βⁿ*, Ann. of Math. (2) 15 (1913), 30–70.

articles.title: Primitive divisor relative to a discriminant
articles.statement:
Let $u_0, u_1, u_2, \dots$ be a sequence
of integers and let $D$ be an integer (for a Lucas pair $(\alpha, \beta)$, the discriminant
$D = (\alpha - \beta)^2$). A natural number $p$ is a primitive divisor of $u_n$ when $n \ge 1$, $p$
is prime, $p$ divides $u_n$, and $p$ does not divide $D \, u_1 u_2 \cdots u_{n-1}$ (for $n = 1$ the
product is empty, and the condition is that $p$ does not divide $D$).

articles.title: Primitive divisor of an integer sequence
articles.statement:
Let $(a_s)_{s \ge 0}$ be a sequence of integers
and let $m$ and $u$ be natural numbers. Then $u$ is a primitive divisor of $a_m$ when $m \ge 1$,
$u \ge 2$, $u$ divides $a_m$, and $u$ divides no $a_s$ with $1 \le s < m$.

articles.title: Primitive prime divisor of an integer sequence
articles.statement:
Let $(a_s)_{s \ge 0}$ be a sequence of
integers and let $m$ and $u$ be natural numbers. Then $u$ is a primitive prime divisor of $a_m$ when
$u$ is prime and $u$ is a primitive divisor of $a_m$.

articles.title: A primitive divisor appears at the least positive index
articles.statement:
Let $(a_s)_{s \ge 0}$ be a sequence
of integers and let the natural number $u$ be a primitive divisor of $a_m$. If $n \ge 1$ and $u$
divides $a_n$, then $m \le n$.

articles.title: Somer's primitive divisor theorem
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be integers with $Q \ne 0$, and let
$(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the integer sequence with $u_0 = 0$, $u_1 = 1$ and
$u_{n+2} = Pu_{n+1} - Qu_n$ (the Lucas sequence of the first kind). Suppose the sequence is
nondegenerate: whenever complex numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy $\alpha + \beta = P$,
$\alpha\beta = Q$ and $\beta \ne 0$, no power $(\alpha / \beta)^k$ with $k \ge 1$ equals
$1$. Then for all sufficiently large $n$ the term $u_n$ has a primitive prime divisor: a
prime $p$ that divides $u_n$ but divides no $u_m$ with $0 < m < n$.

Nondegeneracy also excludes the double-root case $\alpha = \beta$.

## Sources

- Chris Smyth, *The Terms in Lucas Sequences Divisible by Their Indices*, Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), Article 10.2.4, invoking Somer's Theorem 1, lines 632–634, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Smyth/smyth2.tex>.

articles.title: A primitive prime divisor occurs at only one index
articles.statement:
Let $(a_s)_{s \ge 0}$ be a sequence of
integers. If a natural number $u$ is a primitive prime divisor of both $a_m$ and $a_n$, then
$m = n$.

articles.title: A primitive divisor occurs at only one index
articles.statement:
Let $(a_s)_{s \ge 0}$ be a sequence of
integers. If a natural number $u$ is a primitive divisor of both $a_m$ and $a_n$, then $m = n$.

articles.title: Zsigmondy's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $0 < b < a$, $a$ and $b$
coprime, and $n \ge 2$, and suppose that $(a, b, n)$ is not a Bang–Zsigmondy exceptional case:
neither $(a, b, n) = (2, 1, 6)$, nor $n = 2$ with $a + b$ a power of two. Then $a^n - b^n$ has a
primitive prime divisor, that is, a prime $p$ that divides $a^n - b^n$ and divides no $a^m - b^m$
with $1 \le m < n$.

## Sources

- Bayarmagnai lines 133–137 invoke the general theorem, with the explicit exception families per Jones Theorem `Bang` lines 211–215.

articles.title: Exceptional cases of Zsigmondy's theorem
articles.statement:
A triple $(a, b, n)$ of natural numbers is a
Bang–Zsigmondy exceptional case when either $(a, b, n) = (2, 1, 6)$, or $n = 2$ and $a + b = 2^k$
for some natural number $k$.

articles.title: The characteristic polynomial annihilates the solutions of its recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
field, $d \ge 0$ and $a_0, \dots, a_{d-1} \in K$. If a sequence $G \colon \mathbb{N} \to K$
satisfies $G_{n+d} = \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} a_i G_{n+i}$ for every $n \ge 0$, then the characteristic
polynomial $X^d - \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} a_i X^i$ of this recurrence annihilates $G$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Lemma 3.4.

articles.title: The Addition-Multiplication Lemma for annihilators
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be the translation operator
$E(G_s) = G_{s+1}$ on sequences. (i) Let $K$ be a field, $I$ a finite index set, and for each
$i \in I$ let $A_i \in K[X]$, $G_i \colon \mathbb{N} \to K$ and $c_i \in K$. If $A_i(E)$
annihilates $G_i$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} A_i(E)$ annihilates the sequence
$s \mapsto \sum_{i \in I} c_i G_i(s)$. (ii) Let $p_1, p_2 \in \mathbb{C}[X]$ be nonzero
polynomials and $G_1, G_2 \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ sequences such that $p_1(E)$
annihilates $G_1$ and $p_2(E)$ annihilates $G_2$. If $r_{1,1}, \dots, r_{1,m}$ and
$r_{2,1}, \dots, r_{2,n}$ are the complex roots of $p_1$ and $p_2$, listed with multiplicity,
then $\prod_{j=1}^{m} \prod_{j'=1}^{n} (E - r_{1,j} r_{2,j'})$ annihilates the termwise product
$s \mapsto G_1(s) G_2(s)$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Lemma 3.8; part (ii) quoted from Jarden.

articles.title: The operator $E - c$ annihilates the powers of $c$
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, $c \in K$, and let
$E$ be the translation operator $E(G_s) = G_{s+1}$ on sequences $G \colon \mathbb{N} \to K$. Then
the operator $E - c$, that is, $p(E)$ for the polynomial $p = X - c \in K[X]$, annihilates the
sequence $s \mapsto c^s$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Lemma 3.7, part (i).

articles.title: Every operator annihilates the zero sequence
articles.statement:
For every semiring $K$ and every polynomial
$p \in K[X]$, the operator $p(E)$ annihilates the zero sequence, where $E$ is the translation
operator $E(G_s) = G_{s+1}$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Section 3 (definition of an annihilator).

articles.title: Annihilator of a sequence
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a semiring, $p = \sum_i a_i X^i \in K[X]$ and
$G \colon \mathbb{N} \to K$ a sequence, and let $E$ be the translation operator
$E(G_s) = G_{s+1}$. The operator $p(E)$ annihilates $G$ when $\sum_i a_i G_{s+i} = 0$ for every
$s \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Section 3 (definitions of the translation operator and of an annihilator).

articles.title: First entries of the left diagonal of the multivariable circuit array
articles.statement:
The multivariable
circuit array $C^M$, with values in the field of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$ in the
variables $X_0, X_1, \dots$, satisfies $C^M_{0,1} = X_1$ and $C^M_{2,2} = X_2$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.5.

articles.title: Row 1 of the multivariable circuit array
articles.statement:
Let $C^M$ be the multivariable circuit array, with
values in the field of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$ in the variables $X_0, X_1, \dots$.
For every integer $s \ge 2$,
$C^M_{1,s} = (9^{s-1} - 1 + X_1)/\bigl(3(X_1 + 3 \cdot 9^{s-2} - 1)\bigr)$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Corollary 4.10.

articles.title: Row 2 of the multivariable circuit array
articles.statement:
Let $C^M$ be the multivariable circuit array, with
values in the field of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$ in the variables $X_0, X_1, \dots$.
For every integer $s \ge 2$,

$$C^M_{2,s} = \frac{\sum_{i,j} c_{i,j}(s) X_1^i X_2^j}{(3 \cdot 9^{s-2} - 1 + X_1)^2},$$

where the sum runs over the six coefficients $c_{2,1}(s) = 9^{s-2}$, $c_{2,0}(s) = 9^{s-2} - 1$,
$c_{1,1}(s) = 4 \cdot 9^{s-2}$, $c_{1,0}(s) = 2 + (16(s-2) - 2) \cdot 9^{s-2}$,
$c_{0,1}(s) = 4 \cdot 9^{s-2}$ and
$c_{0,0}(s) = -1 + 9 \cdot 81^{s-2} - (8 + 16(s-2)) \cdot 9^{s-2}$.
Moreover, writing $E$ for the translation operator on rational sequences, the shifted coefficient
sequences $s \mapsto c_{i,j}(s+2)$, $s \ge 0$, are annihilated as in Table 4: $c_{0,0}$ by
$(E-81)(E-9)^2(E-1)$, $c_{0,1}$ by $(E-1)(E-9)$, $c_{1,0}$ by $(E-9)^2(E-1)$, $c_{1,1}$ by
$E-9$, $c_{2,0}$ by $(E-1)(E-9)$ and $c_{2,1}$ by $E-9$.

The paper's base case is $s = 3$; the identity also holds at $s = 2$. The recursions column of
Table 4 is omitted (its $X_1^0 X_2^1$ entry $G_s = 10G_{s-1} - G_{s-2}$ is misprinted for
$-9G_{s-2}$).

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Corollary 4.12 and Table 4.

articles.title: Row 0 of the multivariable circuit array
articles.statement:
Let $C^M$ be the multivariable circuit array, with
values in the field of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$ in the variables $X_0, X_1, \dots$.
For every integer $s \ge 1$, $C^M_{0,s} = (9^{s-1} - 1 + X_1)/9^{s-1}$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Corollary 4.8.

articles.title: Multivariable circuit array
articles.statement:
Reduce the all-one triangular grid row by row as in Section 2,
and after the $m$-th reduction, for every $m \ge 1$, set every boundary edge (the left edges on the
first diagonal and the right edges on the last diagonal) to the variable $X_m$ of the field of
rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$ in $X_0, X_1, \dots$. The multivariable circuit array
$C^M_{i,j}$ (Table 3) is the circuit array read off these grids: for $j \ge 1$ and
$0 \le i \le 2(j-1)$, it is the left edge for even $i$, or the right edge for odd $i$, of the
triangle in row $2j - 1$ and diagonal $j - \lfloor (i+1)/2 \rfloor$ of the $j$-times reduced
grid (other indices give junk values). In particular $C^M_{2(m-1),m} = X_m$ for every $m \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.5 and Table 3.

articles.title: Circuit array of a boundary assignment
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let $\beta$ assign to each
natural number $m$ either nothing or a value $\beta(m) \in K$. Let $T^0$ be the all-one triangular
grid and, for $m \ge 1$, let $T^m$ be obtained from $T^{m-1}$ by one row reduction followed, when
$\beta(m)$ is given, by setting every boundary edge (left edges on diagonal $1$, right edges on
diagonal $r$ in row $r$) to $\beta(m)$. For natural numbers $i$ and $j$, the entry $C_{i,j}$ of the
circuit array of $\beta$ is the resistance of the left edge (for even $i$) or the right edge (for
odd $i$) of the triangle of $T^j$ in row $2j - 1$ and diagonal $j - \lfloor (i+1)/2 \rfloor$, with
subtraction truncated at $0$. The entries are meaningful for $j \ge 1$ and $0 \le i \le 2(j - 1)$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.3.

articles.title: First entries of the circuit array
articles.statement:
The circuit array satisfies $C_{0,1} = 2/3$,
$C_{0,2} = 26/27$, $C_{1,2} = 13/12$ and $C_{2,2} = 1/2$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Table 1.

articles.title: Column recursion for the one-variable circuit array
articles.statement:
Extend the one-variable circuit array
$C^X$, with entries in the field $\mathbb{Q}(X)$ of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$, to integer
row indices by $C_{i,j} = C^X_{i,j}$ for $i \ge 0$ and $C_{i,j} = 1$ for $i < 0$. For an integer
$i$ and a natural number $j$, let $\tau_{i,j}$ be the triangle with left edge $C_{i,j}$ and right
and base edges $C_{i-1,j}$. Let $\mathcal{P}$, $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{R}$ be the
left-perimeter, left-edge and right-edge functions of the reduction. Then:
(i) $C_{2(c-1),c} = \mathcal{P}(\tau_{2(c-2),c-1}, \tau_{2(c-2),c-1})$ for every natural number
$c \ge 2$;
(ii) $C_{2(c-1),j} = \mathcal{L}(\tau_{2(c-1),j-1}, \tau_{2c-4,j-1}, \tau_{2c-4,j-1})$ for all
natural numbers $c$, $j$ with $2 \le c < j$;
(iii) $C_{2c-3,j} = \mathcal{R}(\tau_{2c-4,j-1}, \tau_{2c-6,j-1}, \tau_{2c-6,j-1})$ for all
natural numbers $c$, $j$ with $2 \le c \le j$;
(iv) $C^X_{0,1} = (X - 3)/X$.

Here $\mathcal{R}$ is the right-edge function of the reduction algorithm, not the misprinted
display (2.4), and the printed $C_{2(c-1-4),j-1}$ in (iii) is read as $C_{2(c-1)-4,j-1}$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Proposition 4.1.

articles.title: Row one of the one-variable circuit array
articles.statement:
For every natural number $s \ge 2$, the
one-variable circuit array $C^X$, with entries in the field $\mathbb{Q}(X)$ of rational functions
over $\mathbb{Q}$, satisfies $C^X_{1,s} = (3 \cdot 9^{s-2} X - 1)/(3 \cdot 9^{s-2} X - 3)$.

The printed denominator $3 \cdot 9^{s-2} X$ is the row-zero formula; Table 2 has
$(3X - 1)/(3X - 3)$ at $s = 2$, which is $13/12$ at $X = 9$, not $26/27$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Corollary 4.5, denominator corrected from Table 2.

articles.title: Row two of the one-variable circuit array
articles.statement:
For every natural number $s \ge 2$, the
one-variable circuit array $C^X$, with entries in the field $\mathbb{Q}(X)$ of rational functions
over $\mathbb{Q}$, satisfies
$C^X_{2,s} = (c_{2,0}(s) - c_{2,1}(s) X + c_{2,2}(s) X^2)/(9^{s-2} X - 1)^2$, where
$c_{2,0}(s) = 27 \cdot 9^{s-3} - 1$, $c_{2,1}(s) = 24(2s - 3) \cdot 9^{s-3}$ and
$c_{2,2}(s) = 81 \cdot 81^{s-3} - 3 \cdot 9^{s-3}$, with integer exponents (so $9^{s-3} = 1/9$
and $81^{s-3} = 1/81$ when $s = 2$).

The printed $c_{2,2}(X^2)$ is read as $c_{2,2}(s) X^2$, as in Remark 4.7.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Corollary 4.6.

articles.title: Row zero of the one-variable circuit array
articles.statement:
For every natural number $s \ge 1$, the
one-variable circuit array $C^X$, with entries in the field $\mathbb{Q}(X)$ of rational functions
over $\mathbb{Q}$, satisfies $C^X_{0,s} = (3 \cdot 9^{s-2} X - 1)/(3 \cdot 9^{s-2} X)$, with an
integer exponent (so $9^{s-2} = 1/9$ when $s = 1$), and the circuit array $C$ satisfies
$C_{0,s} = (9^s/3 - 1)/(9^s/3)$ in $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Corollary 4.4 with (2.6).

articles.title: First entry of the one-variable circuit array
articles.statement:
The one-variable circuit array $C^X$, with
entries in the field $\mathbb{Q}(X)$ of rational functions over $\mathbb{Q}$, satisfies
$C^X_{0,1} = (X - 3)/X$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.4 and Proposition 4.1 (iv).

articles.title: One-variable circuit array
articles.statement:
The one-variable circuit array $C^X_{i,j}$, with entries in
the field $\mathbb{Q}(X)$ of rational functions in one variable over $\mathbb{Q}$, is the circuit
array of the reductions of the all-one triangular grid in which, after the first reduction, every
boundary edge is set to $(X - 3)/X$, and no boundary edge is replaced after any later reduction.
Thus $C^X_{i,j}$ is the left edge (for even $i$) or the right edge (for odd $i$) of the triangle
in row $2j - 1$ and diagonal $j - \lfloor (i+1)/2 \rfloor$ of this grid reduced $j$ times, with
subtraction truncated at $0$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.4 and Table 2.

articles.title: Circuit array
articles.statement:
The circuit array $C_{i,j} \in \mathbb{Q}$ is the circuit array of the
reductions of the all-one triangular grid with no boundary edge replaced: $C_{i,j}$ is the left
edge (for even $i$) or the right edge (for odd $i$) of the triangle in row $2j - 1$ and diagonal
$j - \lfloor (i+1)/2 \rfloor$ of the all-one grid reduced $j$ times, with subtraction truncated
at $0$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.3 and Table 1.

articles.title: Base-edge function
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field. For a triangle with left, right and base
resistances $L$, $R$, $B$ in $K$, its top arm is $\Delta(L, R, B)$, its bottom-right arm is
$\Delta(R, B, L)$ and its bottom-left arm is $\Delta(B, L, R)$, where
$\Delta(x, y, z) = xy/(x + y + z)$. For triangles $t$, $u$, $v$, the base-edge function is
$\mathcal{B}(t, u, v) = Y(a, b, c) = (ab + bc + ca)/a$, where $a$ is the top arm of $t$, $b$ is
the bottom-right arm of $u$ and $c$ is the bottom-left arm of $v$. In a row reduction, for a row
$r$ and a diagonal $d$, the triangles $t$, $u$, $v$ are those in row $r + 2$ and diagonal $d + 1$,
in row $r + 1$ and diagonal $d$, and in row $r + 1$ and diagonal $d + 1$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, equation (2.3).

articles.title: Delta-wye resistance function
articles.statement:
For elements $x$, $y$, $z$ of a field $K$, the delta-wye
resistance function is $\Delta(x, y, z) = \frac{xy}{x + y + z}$.

Division follows the convention $a / 0 = 0$, so $\Delta(x, y, z) = 0$ when $x + y + z = 0$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, equation (2.1).

articles.title: Edges of an upright triangle
articles.statement:
An upright triangle of the grid has three edges: the left
edge $L$, the right edge $R$ and the base $B$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Section 2 (edge labels `L`, `R`, `B`).

articles.title: Reduced circuit grids
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, and for each $m$ let either a boundary value
$\beta_m \in K$ be given or none. The labellings $T^m$, which assign a value $T^m_{r,d,e} \in K$ to
the edge $e$ (left $L$, right $R$ or base $B$) of the upright triangle in row $r$ and diagonal $d$,
are defined by recursion on $m$: $T^0$ is identically $1$, and $T^{m+1}$ is the row reduction of
$T^m$, except that if $\beta_{m+1}$ is given then every left edge with $d = 1$ and every right edge
with $d = r$ takes the value $\beta_{m+1}$.

With no boundary values given this is the numerical reduction of the all-one grid; in
Definitions 2.4 and 2.5 the boundary values are variables.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Section 2 (reductions `T^m`, Definitions 2.4 and 2.5).

articles.title: Bottom-left delta-wye arm
articles.statement:
For an upright triangle whose left, right and base edges carry
the values $L$, $R$, $B$ in a field $K$, the bottom-left arm is
$\Delta(B, L, R) = \frac{BL}{B + L + R}$, where $\Delta$ is the delta-wye resistance function: the
arm of the equivalent star from the centre of the triangle to its bottom-left vertex.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Figure 2 (`Y₈ = Δ(B, L, R)`).

articles.title: Left-edge function
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $\Delta(x, y, z) = xy/(x + y + z)$ and
$Y(a, b, c) = (ab + bc + ca)/a$ be the delta-wye and wye-delta resistance functions, and for an
upright triangle $t$ write $L_t$, $R_t$, $B_t \in K$ for the values on its left, right and base
edges. For triangles $t$, $u$, $v$, the left-edge function is
$\mathcal{L}(t, u, v) = Y(\Delta(R_t, B_t, L_t), \Delta(B_u, L_u, R_u), \Delta(L_v, R_v, B_v))$,
the wye-delta transform of the star formed by the bottom-right arm of $t$, the bottom-left arm of
$u$ and the top arm of $v$, with the arm of $t$ first.

In the row reduction of a labelling $T$ it is applied to $t = T_{r,d-1}$, $u = T_{r,d}$ and
$v = T_{r+1,d}$ for $d \ne 1$, where $T_{r,d}$ is the triangle in row $r$ and diagonal $d$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, equation (2.5).

articles.title: Left-perimeter function
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $\Delta(x, y, z) = xy/(x + y + z)$ be the
delta-wye resistance function, and for an upright triangle $t$ write $L_t$, $R_t$, $B_t \in K$ for
the values on its left, right and base edges. For triangles $t$ and $u$, the left-perimeter
function is $\mathcal{P}(t, u) = \Delta(B_t, L_t, R_t) + \Delta(L_u, R_u, B_u)$, the series
resistance of the bottom-left arm of $t$ and the top arm of $u$.

In the row reduction of a labelling $T$ it is applied to $t = T_{r,1}$ and $u = T_{r+1,1}$, where
$T_{r,d}$ is the triangle in row $r$ and diagonal $d$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, equation (2.2).

articles.title: Row reduction of a labelled triangular grid
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let $T$ be a labelling
that assigns a value $T_{r,d,e} \in K$ to the edge $e$ (left $L$, right $R$ or base $B$) of the
upright triangle in row $r$ (from the top) and diagonal $d$ (from the left); write $T_{r,d}$ for
that triangle and $\Delta(x, y, z) = xy/(x + y + z)$ for the delta-wye resistance function. The
reduced labelling $T'$ is given by $T'_{r,1,L} = \mathcal{P}(T_{r,1}, T_{r+1,1})$ and
$T'_{r,d,L} = \mathcal{L}(T_{r,d-1}, T_{r,d}, T_{r+1,d})$ for $d \ne 1$, where $\mathcal{P}$ is the
left-perimeter function and $\mathcal{L}$ the left-edge function; by $T'_{r,r,R}$ equal to the
bottom-right arm $\Delta(R, B, L)$ of $T_{r,r}$ plus the top arm $\Delta(L, R, B)$ of
$T_{r+1,r+1}$, and $T'_{r,d,R} = \mathcal{R}(T_{r,d}, T_{r,d+1}, T_{r+1,d+1})$ for $d \ne r$, where
$\mathcal{R}$ is the right-edge function; and by
$T'_{r,d,B} = \mathcal{B}(T_{r+2,d+1}, T_{r+1,d}, T_{r+1,d+1})$, where $\mathcal{B}$ is the
base-edge function.

Here $r$ and $d$ range over all natural numbers, with $d - 1$ truncated at $0$; only the values
with $1 \le d \le r$ are meaningful.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Section 2 (row reduction, equations (2.2)-(2.5)).

articles.title: Bottom-right delta-wye arm
articles.statement:
For an upright triangle whose left, right and base edges carry
the values $L$, $R$, $B$ in a field $K$, the bottom-right arm is
$\Delta(R, B, L) = \frac{RB}{R + B + L}$, where $\Delta$ is the delta-wye resistance function: the
arm of the equivalent star from the centre of the triangle to its bottom-right vertex.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Figure 2 (`Y₄ = Δ(R, B, L)`).

articles.title: Right-edge function
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $\Delta(x, y, z) = xy/(x + y + z)$ and
$Y(a, b, c) = (ab + bc + ca)/a$ be the delta-wye and wye-delta resistance functions, and for an
upright triangle $t$ write $L_t$, $R_t$, $B_t \in K$ for the values on its left, right and base
edges. For triangles $t$, $u$, $v$, the right-edge function is
$\mathcal{R}(t, u, v) = Y(\Delta(B_u, L_u, R_u), \Delta(R_t, B_t, L_t), \Delta(L_v, R_v, B_v))$,
the wye-delta transform of the star formed by the bottom-left arm of $u$, the bottom-right arm of
$t$ and the top arm of $v$, with the arm of $u$ first.

In the row reduction of a labelling $T$ it is applied to $t = T_{r,d}$, $u = T_{r,d+1}$ and
$v = T_{r+1,d+1}$ for $d \ne r$, where $T_{r,d}$ is the triangle in row $r$ and diagonal $d$. This
follows Steps 2-5 and Figure 2; the displayed equation (2.4) instead uses $T_{r+1,d}$ in place of
$T_{r+1,d+1}$ and puts the arm of $t$ first, which gives $C_{1,2} = 29/36$ against Table 1's
$13/12$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, equation (2.4) (corrected as above).

articles.title: Top delta-wye arm
articles.statement:
For an upright triangle whose left, right and base edges carry the
values $L$, $R$, $B$ in a field $K$, the top arm is $\Delta(L, R, B) = \frac{LR}{L + R + B}$, where
$\Delta$ is the delta-wye resistance function: the arm of the equivalent star from the centre of
the triangle to its top vertex.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Figure 2 (`Y₁₂ = Δ(L, R, B)`).

articles.title: Variables of the multivariable circuit array
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, $X_m$ is the
indeterminate $X_m$ regarded as an element of the field of fractions
$\mathbb{Q}(X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots)$ of the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Q}[X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots]$ in
countably many variables.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, Definition 2.5 (the variables `X_i`).

articles.title: The Y-Δ resistance function
articles.statement:
For elements $a$, $b$, $c$ of a field $K$, the $Y$-$\Delta$
resistance function is $Y(a, b, c) = (ab + bc + ca)/a$.

When $a = 0$ the value is $0$, by the convention $x/0 = 0$.

## Sources

- Emily J. Evans and Russell Jay Hendel, *Recursions and Characteristic Polynomials of the Rows of the Circuit Array*, Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-4/hendel08232024rev2, equation (2.1).

articles.title: Binet formula for second-order linear recurrences
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let
$P, Q, \alpha, \beta \in K$ with $\alpha \ne \beta$, and suppose that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
both roots of $z^2 - Pz + Q$. If a sequence $u : \mathbb{N} \to K$ satisfies
$u_{n+2} = P u_{n+1} - Q u_n$ for all $n$, then for every natural number $n$,

$$u_n = \frac{(u_1 - \beta u_0)\alpha^n - (u_1 - \alpha u_0)\beta^n}{\alpha - \beta}.$$

## Sources

- Hongshen Chua, "A Study of Second-Order Linear Recurrence Sequences via Continuants," Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023), Article 23.8.8, Theorem [Binet's formula], lines 270–274, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL26/Chua2/chua13.tex>.

articles.title: A tail of a C-finite sequence satisfies a linear recurrence
articles.statement:
If an integer sequence $s$
is C-finite, then there are a shift $q \in \mathbb{N}$, an order $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and integers
$c_0, \dots, c_{p-1}$ such that the shifted sequence $t(n) = s(n + q)$ satisfies
$t(n + p) = \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i \, t(n + i)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Solutions of linear recurrences are C-finite
articles.statement:
Let $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$c_0, \dots, c_{p-1}$ be integers. If an integer sequence $s$ satisfies
$s(n + p) = \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i \, s(n + i)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $s$ is C-finite.

articles.title: C-finite integer sequences
articles.statement:
An integer sequence $s \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is
C-finite if there are $p, q \in \mathbb{N}$ and integers $c_0, \dots, c_{p-1}$ such that
$s(n + p) = \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i \, s(n + i)$ for every $n \ge q$.

## Sources

- JIS VOL26/Fischer–Kotek–Makowsky, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL26/Makowsky/makowsky16.tex>, lines 249–259.

articles.title: Discarding the exceptional prefix of a C-finite recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be an integer
sequence, let $p, q \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $c_0, \dots, c_{p-1}$ be integers. If
$s(n + p) = \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i \, s(n + i)$ for every $n \ge q$, then the shifted sequence
$t(n) = s(n + q)$ satisfies $t(n + p) = \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i \, t(n + i)$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Quadratic form identity for binary recurrences
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let
$A, B \in R$, and let $(G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(H_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be sequences in $R$ with
$G_{n+2} = A G_{n+1} + B G_n$ and $H_{n+2} = A H_{n+1} + B H_n$ for all $n \ge 0$. Put
$C_G = G_1^2 - A G_0 G_1 - B G_0^2$, $C_H = H_1^2 - A H_0 H_1 - B H_0^2$,
$E_{10} = G_1 H_1 - A G_1 H_0 - B G_0 H_0$, $E_{01} = G_1 H_1 - A G_0 H_1 - B G_0 H_0$ and
$\Delta = G_0 H_1 - G_1 H_0$. Then for every $n \ge 0$,

$$C_H G_n^2 - (E_{10} + E_{01}) G_n H_n + C_G H_n^2 = (-B)^n \Delta^2.$$

The source assumes $\Delta \neq 0$; the identity holds without it, since it is polynomial in the
initial values. The notation follows Section 6.1 of arXiv:2308.13817v1.

## Sources

- Kálmán Győry, Attila Pethő and László Szalay, *Decomposable Forms Generated by Linear Recurrences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.5, Theorem 9 (`jis-2024-24.3.5-thm-9`).

articles.title: Decomposable forms taking the values of a power on recurrence sequences
articles.statement:
Let
$\gamma_0, \dots, \gamma_{k-1} \in \mathbb{C}$, let $\chi(x) = x^k - \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i x^i$,
and let $G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(k)} \colon \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ be $\mathbb{C}$-linearly
independent sequences, each satisfying $G_{n+k} = \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i G_{n+i}$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then there are linear forms $L_1, \dots, L_k$ in $k$ variables with complex
coefficients whose product $F = L_1 \cdots L_k$ satisfies
$F(G^{(1)}_n, \dots, G^{(k)}_n) = ((-1)^k \chi(0))^n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

For $k \ge 1$ we have $\chi(0) = -\gamma_0$, so the right side is $((-1)^{k+1} \gamma_0)^n$.

## Sources

- Kálmán Győry, Attila Pethő and László Szalay, *Decomposable Forms Generated by Linear Recurrences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.5, Theorem 2 (`jis-2024-24.3.5-thm-2`).

articles.title: Decomposable forms on consecutive terms of one recurrence sequence
articles.statement:
Let
$\gamma_0, \dots, \gamma_{k-1} \in \mathbb{C}$, let $\chi(x) = x^k - \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i x^i$,
and let $G \colon \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $G_{n+k} = \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i G_{n+i}$ for
every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Suppose that the $k$ vectors
$(G_j, G_{j+1}, \dots, G_{j+k-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^k$ for $0 \le j < k$ are linearly independent.
Then there are linear forms $L_1, \dots, L_k$ in $k$ variables with complex coefficients whose
product $F = L_1 \cdots L_k$ satisfies $F(G_n, G_{n+1}, \dots, G_{n+k-1}) = ((-1)^k \chi(0))^n$
for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

For $k \ge 1$ we have $\chi(0) = -\gamma_0$, so the right side is $((-1)^{k+1} \gamma_0)^n$.

## Sources

- Kálmán Győry, Attila Pethő and László Szalay, *Decomposable Forms Generated by Linear Recurrences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.5, Corollary 3 (`jis-2024-24.3.5-cor-3`).

articles.title: Homogeneous forms taking the values of a power on recurrence sequences
articles.statement:
Let
$\gamma_0, \dots, \gamma_{k-1} \in \mathbb{C}$ and let $\chi(x) = x^k - \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i x^i$
be the characteristic polynomial of the recurrence $G_{n+k} = \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i G_{n+i}$. Let
$G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(k)} \colon \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ be $\mathbb{C}$-linearly independent
sequences, each satisfying this recurrence for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then there is a
homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $k$ in $k$ variables with complex coefficients such that
$F(G^{(1)}_n, \dots, G^{(k)}_n) = ((-1)^k \chi(0))^n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

For $k \ge 1$ we have $\chi(0) = -\gamma_0$, so the right side is $((-1)^{k+1} \gamma_0)^n$.
The source also assumes $\gamma_0 \neq 0$; for $\mathbb{Z}$-indexed solutions, linear
independence already forces it.

## Sources

- Kálmán Győry, Attila Pethő and László Szalay, *Decomposable Forms Generated by Linear Recurrences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.5, Theorem 1 (`jis-2024-24.3.5-thm-1`).

articles.title: Integer decomposable forms on integer recurrence sequences
articles.statement:
Let
$\gamma_0, \dots, \gamma_{k-1} \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $\chi(x) = x^k - \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i x^i$,
suppose $\chi(0) \neq 0$, and let $G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(k)} \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ each
satisfy $G_{n+k} = \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i G_{n+i}$ for every $n \ge 0$. Suppose that the
determinant $\Delta$ of the $k \times k$ matrix of initial values $(G^{(j)}_i)$, with rows
$1 \le j \le k$ and columns $0 \le i < k$, is nonzero. Then there is a polynomial $\tilde F$ in
$k$ variables with integer coefficients that factors over $\mathbb{C}$ as a product of $k$
linear forms and satisfies $\tilde F(G^{(1)}_n, \dots, G^{(k)}_n) = \Delta^k ((-1)^k \chi(0))^n$
for every $n \ge 0$.

For $k \ge 1$ we have $\chi(0) = -\gamma_0$, so the hypothesis says $\gamma_0 \neq 0$ and the
right side is $\Delta^k ((-1)^{k+1} \gamma_0)^n$. The theorem in the source says "homogeneous
form"; decomposability is the paper's description of $\tilde F$ in the introduction and follows
from Theorem 2, since $\tilde F$ is $\Delta^k$ times the form given there. The source's standing
assumption $k \ge 2$ is omitted (for $k \le 1$ the claim holds with $\tilde F$ constant or
linear); definitions are read from arXiv:2308.13817v1.

## Sources

- Kálmán Győry, Attila Pethő and László Szalay, *Decomposable Forms Generated by Linear Recurrences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.5, Theorem 6 (`jis-2024-24.3.5-thm-6`).

articles.title: Algebraic dependence of recurrence sequences and a power sequence
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural
number, let $\gamma_0, \dots, \gamma_{k-1} \in \mathbb{C}$ and let
$\chi(x) = x^k - \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i x^i$. Let
$G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(k)} \colon \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ be sequences such that
$G^{(j)}_{n+k} = \sum_{i\lt k} \gamma_i G^{(j)}_{n+i}$ for every $j$ and every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Then the family of the $k + 1$ sequences $G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(k)}$ and $n \mapsto (-\chi(0))^n$
(integer powers, with $0^n = 0$ for $n < 0$) is not algebraically independent over $\mathbb{C}$
in the $\mathbb{C}$-algebra of all sequences $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$.

For $k \ge 1$ we have $\chi(0) = -\gamma_0$, so the last sequence is $n \mapsto \gamma_0^n$.

## Sources

- Kálmán Győry, Attila Pethő and László Szalay, *Decomposable Forms Generated by Linear Recurrences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.5, Corollary 4 (`jis-2024-24.3.5-cor-4`).

articles.title: Divisor-sum formula for the length-four run count
articles.statement:
For a natural number $B$, let $A_B(4)$
be the number of integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^5$ with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and
$(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have a divisibility run of length at least $4$. For integers $x, y$
let $T_B(x, y)$ be the number of integer triples $(a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^3$ with $x \mid a$,
$y \mid b$, $x + y \mid c$ and $x + 2y \mid a + b + c$, and let $T'_B(x, y)$ be the number of
integer triples $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ with $|\alpha| \le \lfloor B/|x| \rfloor$,
$|\beta| \le \lfloor B/|y| \rfloor$, $|\gamma| \le \lfloor B/|x+y| \rfloor$ and
$x + 2y \mid x\alpha + y\beta + (x+y)\gamma$. Then

$$A_B(4) = \sum_{x, y} \left(T_B(x, y) - 1\right) = \sum_{x, y} \left(T'_B(x, y) - 1\right),$$

where both sums run over the integers $x, y \in [-B, B]$ with $x \ne 0$, $y \ne 0$, $x + y \ne 0$
and $x + 2y \ne 0$.

The second form comes from writing $a = x\alpha$, $b = y\beta$, $c = (x+y)\gamma$; it is the
paper's $\sum \chi_{x,y}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 7.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the length-one run count
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $K$ such that for every
natural number $B \ge 2$ the number $A_B(1)$ of integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^5$
with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and $(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have a divisibility run of length at
least $1$ satisfies $|A_B(1) - 32 B^4 \log B| \le K B^4$; that is,
$A_B(1) = 32 B^4 \log B + O(B^4)$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Run count at bound 1 and length 1
articles.statement:
Exactly $156$ integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c)$ with
all entries in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$, $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and $(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ have a
divisibility run of length at least $1$; that is, $A_1(1) = 156$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Exact formula for the length-one run count
articles.statement:
For every natural number $B$, let
$D(B) = \sum_{m=1}^{B} \lfloor B/m \rfloor$ and let $A_B(1)$ be the number of integer tuples
$(x, y, a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^5$ with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and $(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have
a divisibility run of length at least $1$. Then

$$A_B(1) = 4(2B+1)^3 D(B) + 2B(2B+1)\left((2B+1)^2 - 1\right).$$

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Exact formula for the length-three run count
articles.statement:
For a natural number $B$, let $A_B(3)$ be
the number of integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^5$ with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and
$(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have a divisibility run of length at least $3$, and for integers
$m \ge 1$ let $d_B(m) = 2\lfloor B/m \rfloor + 1$. Then

$$A_B(3) = \sum_{x, y} \left(d_B(|x|)\, d_B(|y|)\, d_B(|x+y|) - 1\right),$$

where the sum runs over the integers $x, y \in [-B, B]$ with $x \ne 0$, $y \ne 0$ and
$x + y \ne 0$, and also

$$
A_B(3) = 2 \sum_{m=1}^{B} \sum_{n=1}^{B} d_B(m)\, d_B(n)\, d_B(m+n) +
4 \sum_{1 \le n < m \le B} d_B(m)\, d_B(n)\, d_B(m-n) - (4B^2 - 2B).
$$

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 6.

articles.title: Asymptotics of the length-two run count
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $K$ such that for every
natural number $B \ge 2$ the number $A_B(2)$ of integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^5$
with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and $(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have a divisibility run of length at
least $2$ satisfies $|A_B(2) - 32 B^3 (\log B)^2| \le K B^3 \log B$; that is,
$A_B(2) = 32 B^3 (\log B)^2 + O(B^3 \log B)$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Exact formula for the length-two run count
articles.statement:
For every natural number $B$, let
$S(B) = \sum_{m=1}^{B} \left(2\lfloor B/m \rfloor + 1\right)$ and let $A_B(2)$ be the number of
integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c) \in [-B, B]^5$ with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and
$(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have a divisibility run of length at least $2$. Then
$S(B) = 2 \sum_{m=1}^{B} \lfloor B/m \rfloor + B$ and $A_B(2) = 4(2B+1) S(B)^2 - 4B^2$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Counting configurations with long divisibility runs
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $B$ and $r$,
$A_B(r)$ is the number of integer tuples $(x, y, a, b, c)$ with all five entries in $[-B, B]$,
$(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ and $(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$ that have a divisibility run of length at
least $r$: for every $i < r$, the Gibonacci number $P_i$ with initial values $P_0 = x$, $P_1 = y$
is nonzero and divides the generalized Tribonacci number $Q_i$ with initial values $Q_0 = a$,
$Q_1 = b$, $Q_2 = c$ (indices start at $0$).

The tuples satisfying the size and nonvanishing conditions form the paper's set
$\mathcal{C}_B$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Equation (2).

articles.title: Divisibility runs have logarithmic length
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $C > 0$ such that for
every natural number $B \ge 2$, all integers $x, y, a, b, c \in [-B, B]$ with $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$
and $(a, b, c) \ne (0, 0, 0)$, and every natural number $L$ such that $(x, y, a, b, c)$ has a
divisibility run of length at least $L$, we have $L \le C \log B$. Here a divisibility run of
length at least $L$ means that for every $i < L$ the Gibonacci number $P_i$ with $P_0 = x$,
$P_1 = y$ is nonzero and divides the generalized Tribonacci number $Q_i$ with $Q_0 = a$,
$Q_1 = b$, $Q_2 = c$.

In the paper's notation this is $E(B) \le C \log B$, where $E(B)$ is the maximal run length
over these configurations.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Basis sequences for generalized Tribonacci sequences
articles.statement:
There are integer sequences
$(u_n)_{n \ge 0}$, $(v_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(w_n)_{n \ge 0}$, each satisfying the Tribonacci
recurrence $s_{n+3} = s_{n+2} + s_{n+1} + s_n$ for all $n \ge 0$, with initial values
$(u_0, u_1, u_2) = (1, 0, 0)$, $(v_0, v_1, v_2) = (0, 1, 0)$ and $(w_0, w_1, w_2) = (0, 0, 1)$,
such that for all integers $a, b, c$ and every $n \ge 0$ the $n$-th term of the generalized
Tribonacci sequence with initial values $a, b, c$ equals $u_n a + v_n b + w_n c$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Divisibility by a Gibonacci sequence forces a Tribonacci sequence to vanish
articles.statement:
Let
$x, y, a, b, c$ be integers, let $(P_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Gibonacci sequence with $P_0 = x$ and
$P_1 = y$, and let $(Q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the generalized Tribonacci sequence with $Q_0 = a$,
$Q_1 = b$ and $Q_2 = c$. If $P_n \ne 0$ and $P_n \mid Q_n$ for every $n \ge 0$, then $Q_n = 0$
for every $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Smirnov, *Finite Divisibility Runs Between Generalized Fibonacci and Tribonacci Sequences*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A122, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Growth bounds for Gibonacci and generalized Tribonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio. For integers $x, y$ let $(P_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the Gibonacci sequence with $P_0 = x$
and $P_1 = y$, and for integers $a, b, c$ let $(Q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the generalized Tribonacci
sequence with $Q_0 = a$, $Q_1 = b$ and $Q_2 = c$. Then (i) for all integers $x, y$ and every
$n \ge 0$, $|P_n| \le (|x| + |y|)\,\varphi^n$; (ii) there are real constants $c_0 > 0$ and
