- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Corollary 3.1.

articles.title: Period and restricted period of Lucas sequences with $Q = 1$
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be the Lucas
sequence with integer parameters $P$ and $Q = 1$, where the pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, and
write $\pi(m)$ and $\rho(m)$ for the period and the restricted period of $U$ modulo $m$. Let
$m \ge 2$. Then $\pi(m) = \rho(m)$ or $\pi(m) = 2\rho(m)$, and if $m = \ell^i$ for an odd prime
$\ell$ and some $i \ge 1$ and $\rho(m)$ is even, then $\pi(m) = 2\rho(m)$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Corollary 3.2.

articles.title: Period of a Lucas sequence modulo 1
articles.statement:
For every Lucas sequence $U = U(P, Q)$, the least
period $\pi_U(1)$ of $U$ modulo $1$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 1.4 (ix).

articles.title: Primes dividing the discriminant when $Q = \pm 1$
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be a Lucas sequence
and let $\ell$ be a prime dividing its discriminant $D = P^2 - 4Q$. Write $\pi_U(m)$ and
$\rho_U(m)$ for the least period and the least restricted period of $U$ modulo $m$. If $Q = -1$,
then $\ell = 2$ or $\ell \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. If $Q = 1$, then $P \equiv 2 \pmod \ell$ or
$P \equiv -2 \pmod \ell$; moreover, if $\ell > 2$ and $P \equiv 2 \pmod \ell$, then
$\pi_U(\ell^i) = \rho_U(\ell^i)$ for every $i \ge 1$, and if $\ell > 2$ and
$P \equiv -2 \pmod \ell$, then $\pi_U(\ell^i) = 2 \rho_U(\ell^i)$ for every $i \ge 1$.

In the paper's notation $W(n + 2) = a W(n + 1) + b W(n)$ one has $a = P$ and $b = -Q$. The
restriction to $\ell > 2$ in the case $P \equiv 2 \pmod \ell$ is needed: for $(P, Q) = (4, 1)$
one has $D = 12$ and $P \equiv 2 \pmod 2$, but $\pi_U(4) = 4$ and $\rho_U(4) = 2$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 3.2.

articles.title: Periods of a Lucas sequence modulo a prime
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be a nondegenerate Lucas
sequence with discriminant $D = P^2 - 4Q$, and let $p$ be a prime. Write $\pi_U(m)$ and
$\rho_U(m)$ for the least period and the least restricted period of $U$ modulo $m$, and
$\left(\frac{x}{p}\right)$ for the Jacobi symbol.
(i) If $p \nmid 2QD$, then $\rho_U(p) > 1$, $\rho_U(p) \mid p - \left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$,
$\rho_U(p) \mid \pi_U(p)$ and $\pi_U(p) / \rho_U(p) \mid p - 1$; if $p = 2$ and $2 \nmid QD$,
then $\pi_U(2) = 3$.
(ii) If $p \nmid 2QD$, then $\rho_U(p) \mid \left(p - \left(\frac{D}{p}\right)\right) / 2$ if and
only if $\left(\frac{Q}{p}\right) = 1$.
(iii) If $p \nmid Q$ and $p \mid D$, then $\rho_U(p) = p$ and $\pi_U(p) \mid p (p - 1)$.
(iv) If $p \nmid 2Q$ and $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right) = 1$, then $\pi_U(p) \mid p - 1$.
(v) If $p \nmid 2Q$ and $\left(\frac{D}{p}\right) = -1$, then $\pi_U(p) \mid p^2 - 1$ and every
prime factor $\ell$ of $\pi_U(p)$ satisfies $2 \ell \le p + 1$.
(vi) If $p \nmid Q$ and $p \mid D$, then $p \mid \pi_U(p)$ and every prime factor of $\pi_U(p)$
is at most $p$.
(vii) If $p \nmid Q$, there is a largest $c \ge 1$ with $\rho_U(p^c) = \rho_U(p)$. If
$p^c \ne 2$, then $\rho_U(p^i) = p^{\max(i - c, 0)} \rho_U(p)$ for every $i \ge 1$. If
$p^c = 2$, there is a largest $d \ge 2$ with $\rho_U(2^d) = \rho_U(4)$, and
$\rho_U(2^i) = 2^{\max(i + 1 - d, 1)} \rho_U(2)$ for every $i \ge 2$.
(viii) If $p \nmid Q$, there is a largest $e \ge 1$ with $\pi_U(p^e) = \pi_U(p)$. If
$p^e \ne 2$, then $\pi_U(p^i) = p^{\max(i - e, 0)} \pi_U(p)$ for every $i \ge 1$. If
$p^e = 2$, there is a largest $g \ge 2$ with $\pi_U(2^g) = \pi_U(4)$, and
$\pi_U(2^i) = 2^{\max(i + 1 - g, 1)} \pi_U(2)$ for every $i \ge 2$.
(ix) $\rho_U(1) = \pi_U(1) = 1$.

In the paper's notation $W(n + 2) = a W(n + 1) + b W(n)$ one has $a = P$ and $b = -Q$. The claim
$\pi_U(p) / \rho_U(p) \mid p - 1$, printed under "if $p \ge 2$", is stated here under the
hypothesis $p \nmid 2QD$ of (i).

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 1.4.

articles.title: Period quotients and seeds of $S(U)$
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be a nondegenerate Lucas
sequence with $Q = -1$, or $Q = 1$, or $Q$ odd and $P = -Q - 1$. Write $\pi_U(m)$ and
$\rho_U(m)$ for the least period and the least restricted period of $U$ modulo $m$, and $S(U)$
for the set of positive integers $n$ coprime to $Q$ with $\pi_U(n) \mid n$. For every prime
$p \nmid Q$, $\rho_U(p)$ divides $\pi_U(p)$, and the quotient $\pi_U(p) / \rho_U(p)$ divides $4$
if $Q = -1$ and divides $2$ if $Q \ne -1$. Moreover, each of the following numbers $s_0$ lies in
$S(U)$: $s_0 = 1$; $s_0 = 6$ if $P \equiv 3 \pmod 6$ and $Q = -1$, or if $P \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 6$
and $Q = 1$; $s_0 = 24$ if $P \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 6$ and $Q = -1$; $s_0 = 12$ if
$P \equiv 3 \pmod 6$ and $Q = 1$; $s_0 = 2$ if $Q$ is odd and $P = -Q - 1$.

In the paper's notation $W(n + 2) = a W(n + 1) + b W(n)$ one has $a = P$ and $b = -Q$. The
paper also characterizes $S(U)$ by chains $n_0 = s_0$, $n_i = n_{i-1} s_i 2^{\varepsilon(s_i)}$
with primes $s_i \mid D U_{n_{i-1}}$, where $D = P^2 - 4Q$ and
$\varepsilon(s_i) = \max(\nu_2(\pi_U(s_i)) - \nu_2(n_{i-1}), 0)$; that characterization is
false as printed in both directions and is omitted. For $(P, Q) = (-10, 1)$ only $s_0 = 1$ is
admissible and $\pi_U(2) = 2$, so $2 \in S(U)$, but the only chain that could end at $2$ has
$s_1 = 2$, and then $\varepsilon(2) = \nu_2(\pi_U(2)) = 1$ gives $n_1 = 4$. For
$(P, Q) = (-11, 1)$, where $D = 117$, the chain $s_0 = 1$, $s_1 = 13$,
$s_2 = 53 \mid U_{13} = 2862615066961$ gives $\varepsilon(53) = \nu_2(26) = 1$ and
$n_2 = 1378$, while $\pi_U(1378) = 78 \nmid 1378$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Period of a Lucas sequence modulo $m$
articles.statement:
For a Lucas sequence $U = U(P, Q)$ and a natural
number $m$, the least period $\pi_U(m)$ of $U$ modulo $m$ is the minimal period of the pair
$(0, 1)$ under the map $(x, y) \mapsto (y, P y - Q x)$ on pairs of residues modulo $m$, that is,
the least $r > 0$ with $U_r \equiv 0 \pmod m$ and $U_{r+1} \equiv 1 \pmod m$, and $0$ if there
is no such $r$.

For $m > 0$, $\pi_U(m) = 0$ exactly when $U$ is not purely periodic modulo $m$, that is, when
$\gcd(m, Q) > 1$. For $m = 0$ the residues are integers and the congruences are equalities; this
value has no meaning in the paper (for the Fibonacci sequence it is $0$).

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Section 1, equation (1.11).

articles.title: Restricted period of the Fibonacci sequence modulo 2
articles.statement:
The least restricted period
modulo $2$ of the Fibonacci sequence $F = U(1, -1)$ equals $3$ (note $F_3 = 2$).

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, equation (1.12).

articles.title: Restricted period of a Lucas sequence modulo 1
articles.statement:
For every Lucas sequence $U = U(P, Q)$,
the least restricted period $\rho_U(1)$ of $U$ modulo $1$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 1.4 (ix).

articles.title: Restricted period of a Lucas sequence modulo $m$
articles.statement:
For a Lucas sequence $U = U(P, Q)$ and
a natural number $m$, the least restricted period $\rho_U(m)$ of $U$ modulo $m$ is the least
$s > 0$ such that $m \mid U_s$ and $U_{s+1}$ is coprime to $m$, and $0$ if there is no such $s$.

In the paper's terms, $U_{s+1} \equiv M \pmod m$ for a multiplier $M$ coprime to $m$; for
$s = \rho_U(m)$ this $U_{s+1}$ is the multiplier $M_U(m)$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Section 1, equations (1.10) and (1.12).

articles.title: Integral averages for $U(P, -1)$
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be a Lucas sequence with $Q = -1$,
so that its discriminant is $D = P^2 + 4$, and let $\pi_U(n)$ be the least period of $U$ modulo
$n$. Call a natural number $n$ good if $n$ lies in the set $S'(U)$ of positive integers $n$
coprime to $Q$ with $\pi_U(n) \mid n$ and $n \mid U_1 + \dots + U_n$, and every integer sequence
$w$ with $w_{k+2} = P w_{k+1} + w_k$ for all $k$ satisfies $n \mid w_1 + \dots + w_n$. Let
$t \ne 1$ be a natural number all of whose prime factors are at least $5$ and divide $D$, and let
$i, j \ge 0$.
(i) If $P \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 6$, then $2^{i+3} 3^{j+1} t$ is good.
(ii) If $P \equiv 3 \pmod 6$, then $2^{i+1} 3^{j+1}$ and $2^{i+2} 3^{j+1} t$ are good.
(iii) If $P \equiv \pm 2 \pmod{12}$, then $2^{i+2} t$ and $2^{i+3} 3^{j+1} t$ are good.
(iv) If $P \equiv 6 \pmod{12}$, then $2^{i+2} 3^j t$ is good.

In the paper's notation $W(n + 2) = a W(n + 1) + b W(n)$ one has $a = P$ and $b = -Q = 1$, and
the paper's $q$ is $t$. The paper's conditions $n > 1$ and $\operatorname{rad}(n) \mid 6 D$
follow from the displayed forms.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Corollary 2.5.

articles.title: Integral averages for $U(P, 1)$
articles.statement:
Let $U = U(P, Q)$ be a nondegenerate Lucas sequence with
$Q = 1$, so that its discriminant is $D = P^2 - 4$, and let $\pi_U(n)$ be the least period of $U$
modulo $n$. Call a natural number $n$ good if $n$ lies in the set $S'(U)$ of positive integers
$n$ coprime to $Q$ with $\pi_U(n) \mid n$ and $n \mid U_1 + \dots + U_n$, and every integer
sequence $w$ with $w_{k+2} = P w_{k+1} - w_k$ for all $k$ satisfies $n \mid w_1 + \dots + w_n$.
(i) Every odd $t > 1$ all of whose prime factors divide $P - 2$ is good.
(ii) Let $t \ne 1$ be odd with all prime factors at least $5$ and dividing $D$, and let
$i, j \ge 0$. If $P \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 6$, then $2^{i+1} 3^{j+1} t$ is good; if
$P \equiv 3 \pmod 6$ or $P \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$, then $2^{i+2} 3^{j+1} t$ is good.
(iii) If $P \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, $t$ is odd with all prime factors dividing $D$, and $i \ge 0$,
then $2^{i+2} t$ is good.

In the paper's notation $W(n + 2) = a W(n + 1) + b W(n)$ one has $a = P$ and $b = -Q = -1$. The
paper's "for all recurrences $W(a, 1)$" is read as $W(a, -1)$, the recurrences of $U(a, -1)$
(Theorem 2.5); as printed it is false: for $a = 5$, $n = 3$ and $W = U(5, 1)$ in the paper's
notation, $W_1 + W_2 + W_3 = 1 + 5 + 26 = 32$, which $3$ does not divide. The paper's condition
$a \ne 0, \pm 1, \pm 2$ in (i) is nondegeneracy.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Corollary 2.6.

articles.title: Smyth's description of the indices $n$ with $n \mid U_n$
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be coprime integers
with $Q \ne 0$ such that the Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $U = U(P, Q)$ be its Lucas
sequence, write $a = P$, $b = -Q$ (so that $U_{k+2} = a U_{k+1} + b U_k$) and $D = P^2 - 4Q$, and
let $T(U)$ be the set of positive integers $n$ coprime to $Q$ with $n \mid U_n$. Call $q_0$
admissible if $q_0 = 1$, or $q_0 = 6$ with $a \equiv 3$ and $b \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 6$, or
$q_0 = 12$ with $a \equiv \pm 1$ and $b \equiv 1 \pmod 6$. Call a finite list of primes
$q_1, \dots, q_r$ ($r \ge 0$, repetitions allowed) a chain from $q_0$ if
$q_i \mid D \, U_{q_0 q_1 \cdots q_{i-1}}$ for each $i$. Then every admissible $q_0$ lies in
$T(U)$; a natural number $n$ lies in $T(U)$ if and only if $n = q_0 q_1 \cdots q_r$ for some
admissible $q_0$ and some chain $q_1, \dots, q_r$ from $q_0$; for every admissible $q_0$ and every
chain $q_1, \dots, q_r$ from $q_0$, each product $q_0 q_1 \cdots q_i$ with $0 \le i \le r$ lies in
$T(U)$; and if $D = 1$, then $T(U) = \{1\}$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 4.1.

articles.title: Members of $S(U)$ of the form $2^i 3^j$
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers with $Q \ne 0$ such that
the Lucas pair $(P, Q)$ is nondegenerate, let $U = U(P, Q)$ be its Lucas sequence, write $a = P$
and $b = -Q$, and suppose $a + b - 1 \ne 0$. Call a positive integer $n$ good if $n$ lies in the
Lucas period set $S(U)$ (the positive integers $n$ coprime to $Q$ whose period $\pi_U(n)$ modulo
$n$ divides $n$) and $n$ divides $w_1 + \dots + w_n$ for every integer sequence $w$ with
$w_{k+2} = a w_{k+1} + b w_k$ for all $k \ge 0$. Then, for all integers $i, j \ge 0$: (i) if
$a \equiv \pm 1$ and $b \equiv 1 \pmod 6$, then $1$ and $2^{i+3} 3^{j+1}$ are good; (ii) if
$a \equiv 1$ and $b \equiv -1 \pmod 6$, then $1$ and $2^{i+1} 3^{j+1}$ are good; (iii) if
$a \equiv 3$ and $b \equiv -1 \pmod 6$, then $1$ and $2^{i+2} 3^{j+1}$ are good; (iv) if $e \ge 1$,
$a \equiv 3 \pmod 6$, $3^e$ divides $a$ but $3^{e+1}$ does not, and
$b \equiv 1 \pmod{2 \cdot 3^{e+1}}$, then $1$ and $2^{i+1} 3^{j+1}$ are good.

The paper's condition $\operatorname{rad}(n) \mid 6$ is implied by these forms of $n$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 2.12.

articles.title: Multiplying a member of $S(U)$ by a number with no new prime factors
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be
integers with $Q \ne 0$, let $U = U(P, Q)$ be their Lucas sequence, write $a = P$ and $b = -Q$, and
let $S(U)$ be the set of positive integers $n$ coprime to $Q$ whose period $\pi_U(n)$ modulo $n$
divides $n$. Let $m > 0$ and $n \in S(U)$ be such that every prime divisor of $m$ divides $n$.
Then $m n \in S(U)$. If moreover $a + b - 1 \ne 0$ and $\gcd(a + b - 1, n) = 1$, or $a + b - 1 = 0$
and $\gcd(-b - 1, n) = 1$, then $m n$ lies in $S'(U)$, the set of $t \in S(U)$ with
$t \mid U_1 + \dots + U_t$, and $m n$ divides $w_1 + \dots + w_{mn}$ for every integer sequence
$w$ with $w_{k+2} = a w_{k+1} + b w_k$ for all $k \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Corollary 2.3.

articles.title: Non-integer period average of a Lucas sequence when $\gcd(n, a, b) > 1$
articles.statement:
Theorem 2.13: for nondegenerate `U(a, b)` with `d = gcd(a, b) > 1` and
`gcd(n, d) > 1`, `A_U(n)` is not an integer.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 2.13.

articles.title: The Lucas average set contains $1$
articles.statement:
For all integers $P, Q$ with $Q \ne 0$, the number $1$
lies in the Lucas average set $S'(U)$ of $U = U(P, Q)$: the set of $n$ in the Lucas period set
$S(U)$ with $n \mid U_1 + \dots + U_n$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Remark 2.2.

articles.title: The index-divisible set of a Lucas sequence contains $1$
articles.statement:
For all integers $P, Q$ with
$Q \ne 0$, the number $1$ lies in the set $T(U)$ of positive integers $n$ coprime to $Q$ with
$n \mid U_n$, where $U = U(P, Q)$ is their Lucas sequence.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Remark 2.2.

articles.title: The Lucas period set contains $1$
articles.statement:
For all integers $P, Q$ with $Q \ne 0$, the number $1$
lies in the Lucas period set $S(U)$ of $U = U(P, Q)$: the set of positive integers $n$ coprime to
$Q$ whose period $\pi_U(n)$ modulo $n$ divides $n$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Remark 2.2.

articles.title: Multiplying a member of $S(U)$ by one of its prime factors
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers with
$Q \ne 0$, let $U = U(P, Q)$ be their Lucas sequence, write $a = P$ and $b = -Q$, and let $S(U)$ be
the set of positive integers $n$ coprime to $Q$ whose period $\pi_U(n)$ modulo $n$ divides $n$. If
$n \in S(U)$ and $\ell$ is a prime dividing $n$, then $\ell n \in S(U)$. If moreover
$a + b - 1 \ne 0$ and $\gcd(a + b - 1, n) = 1$, or $a + b - 1 = 0$ and $\gcd(-b - 1, n) = 1$, then
$\ell n$ lies in $S'(U)$, the set of $t \in S(U)$ with $t \mid U_1 + \dots + U_t$, and $\ell n$
divides $w_1 + \dots + w_{\ell n}$ for every integer sequence $w$ with
$w_{k+2} = a w_{k+1} + b w_k$ for all $k \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 2.3.

articles.title: Sums of a second-order recurrence over whole periods
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers with $Q \ne 0$,
let $U = U(P, Q)$ be their Lucas sequence, write $a = P$ and $b = -Q$, and suppose
$a + b - 1 \ne 0$. Let $n > 0$ be coprime to $b(a + b - 1)$, and let $\pi_U(n)$ be the period of
$U$ modulo $n$: the least $r > 0$ with $U_r \equiv 0$ and $U_{r+1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$, or $0$ if
there is none. Then $\pi_U(n) > 0$, and for every $r \ge 0$ divisible by $\pi_U(n)$ and every
integer sequence $w$ with $w_{k+2} = a w_{k+1} + b w_k$ for all $k \ge 0$, $n$ divides
$w_1 + \dots + w_r$.

Part (ii) of the corollary is false as printed and is omitted: for $(a, b) = (-6, 7)$, so that
$a + b - 1 = 0$, the number $n = 3$ is coprime to $7 \cdot (-8)$ and $\pi_U(3) = 2$, but
$U_1 + U_2 = 1 - 6 = -5$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Corollary 2.2.

articles.title: Sum formula for second-order recurrences
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q$ be integers with $Q \ne 0$ and
$P^2 - 4Q \ne 0$, let $U = U(P, Q)$ be their Lucas sequence, write $a = P$ and $b = -Q$, and let
$w$ be an integer sequence with $w_{k+2} = a w_{k+1} + b w_k$ for all $k \ge 0$. For $n \ge 0$
let $B(n) = w_1 + \dots + w_n$, and for $n > 0$ let $\pi_U(n)$ be the period of $U$ modulo $n$:
the least $r > 0$ with $U_r \equiv 0$ and $U_{r+1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$, or $0$ if there is none.
If $a + b - 1 \ne 0$, then for every $n \ge 0$

$$(a + b - 1) B(n) = w_{n+1} - w_1 + b (w_n - w_0),$$

and for every $n > 0$ coprime to $b$ and every $r \ge 0$ divisible by $\pi_U(n)$, $n$ divides
$w_{r+1} - w_1 + b (w_r - w_0)$. If $a + b - 1 = 0$, then for every $n \ge 0$

$$(-b - 1) B(n) = (w_1 - w_0) U_{n+1} - n (w_1 + b w_0) + w_0 - w_1.$$

The congruence $K(s) \equiv 0 \pmod n$ claimed in part (ii) of the source, for the source's
quantity $K(s)$, is false as printed and is omitted: for $(a, b) = (-6, 7)$, $w = U$ and $n = 3$
one has $\gcd(3, 7) = 1$ and $\pi_U(3) = 2$, but $K(2) = 40$.

## Sources

- Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, *Period Lengths Modulo n and Average of Terms of Second Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A36, Theorem 2.2.

articles.title: Odd Fibonacci numbers $F_n$ with $F_{F_n + 2} \equiv 1 \pmod{F_n}$
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ denote the
$m$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. If $p$ is an odd prime with
$p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ and $p \equiv 2$ or $3 \pmod 5$, and $n = 2p$ or $n = 4p$, then $F_n$ is odd
and $F_{F_n + 2}$ leaves remainder $1$ on division by $F_n$.

## Sources

- Oisín Flynn-Connolly, "On the Divisibility of Sums of Fibonacci Numbers", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Fulton–Morris theorem on Pisano periods equal to the modulus
articles.statement:
Write $F_t$ for the $t$-th
Fibonacci number. Let $m > 1$ be a natural number and let $\pi$ be a positive integer with
$F_\pi \equiv 0 \pmod{m}$ and $F_{\pi+1} \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$ such that $\pi \le t$ for every
positive integer $t$ with $F_t \equiv 0 \pmod{m}$ and $F_{t+1} \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$; that is, $\pi$
is the Pisano period of $m$. Then $\pi = m$ if and only if $m = 24 \cdot 5^{\lambda - 1}$ for some
integer $\lambda \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Amirali Fatehizadeh and Daniel Yaqubi, "Average of the Fibonacci Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.2.6, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Yaqubi/yaq6.tex>, lines 177–189. The theorem is attributed there to John Fulton and William Morris, "On arithmetical functions related to the Fibonacci numbers," Acta Arithmetica 16 (1969), 105–110, DOI 10.4064/aa-16-2-105-110.

articles.title: Infinitely many odd $k$ divide the sum of the first $k$ Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_i$ denote
the $i$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$. There are infinitely many odd positive integers
$k$ such that $k$ divides $F_1 + F_2 + \dots + F_k$.

## Sources

- Oisín Flynn-Connolly, "On the Divisibility of Sums of Fibonacci Numbers", Corollary 2.

articles.title: The Pisano period of $F_n$ divides $2n$ for even $n$
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ denote the $n$-th Fibonacci
number and $\pi(m)$ the Pisano period of $m$. For every even natural number $n > 1$, $\pi(F_n)$
divides $2n$.

## Sources

- Oisín Flynn-Connolly, "On the Divisibility of Sums of Fibonacci Numbers", Proposition 2.

articles.title: Pisano period
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the Pisano period $\pi(n)$ is the minimal period
of the pair $(0, 1)$ under the Fibonacci step $(a, b) \mapsto (b, a + b)$ on
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$: the least $k \ge 1$ such that $k$
applications of the step map $(0, 1)$ back to $(0, 1)$, or $0$ if there is no such $k$ (as for
$n = 0$, where $\mathbb{Z}/0\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$).

articles.title: Sum of the first $p$ Fibonacci numbers modulo a prime $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p > 5$ be a prime, let
$F_i$ denote the $i$-th Fibonacci number, with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, and let
$S = F_1 + F_2 + \dots + F_p$. If $p \equiv 1$ or $4 \pmod 5$, then $S$ leaves remainder $1$ on
division by $p$; if $p \equiv 2$ or $3 \pmod 5$, then $S$ leaves remainder $p - 2$ on division
by $p$; and in every case $p$ does not divide $S$.

## Sources

- Oisín Flynn-Connolly, "On the Divisibility of Sums of Fibonacci Numbers", Theorem 1.

articles.title: The minimum of $\pi(n)/n$ over $1 \le n < N$ tends to zero
articles.statement:
Let $\pi(n)$ denote the Pisano
period of $n$. As $N \to \infty$, the minimum of the real numbers $\pi(n)/n$ over the integers
$1 \le n \le N - 1$ (defined for $N \ge 2$) tends to $0$.

## Sources

- Oisín Flynn-Connolly, "On the Divisibility of Sums of Fibonacci Numbers", Corollary 1.

articles.title: Avila–Chen theorem on Lucas numbers modulo $m$
articles.statement:
Let $L_n$ denote the Lucas numbers. For every
integer $m > 1$, every residue modulo $m$ is attained by the Lucas numbers (for every $r$ with
$0 \le r < m$ there is $n \ge 0$ with $L_n \equiv r \pmod m$) if and only if
$m \in \{2, 4, 6, 7, 14\}$ or $m = 3^k$ for some integer $k \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Brandon Avila and Yongyi Chen, On Moduli For Which the Lucas Numbers Contain a Complete Residue System, Fibonacci Quarterly 51(2) (2013), 151–152, https://doi.org/10.1080/00150517.2013.12427958.

articles.title: Classification of moduli for which the Lucas numbers attain every residue
articles.statement:
The
proposition that for every integer $m > 1$, with $L_n$ the Lucas numbers, every residue modulo
$m$ is attained (for every $r$ with $0 \le r < m$ there is $n \ge 0$ with
$L_n \equiv r \pmod m$) if and only if $m \in \{2, 4, 6, 7, 14\}$ or $m = 3^k$ for some
integer $k \ge 1$.

## Sources

- OPG-37402, Lucas Numbers Modulo m [OpenGarden].

articles.title: Subsequences of a second-order linear recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $(P, Q)$ be Lucas sequence
parameters (integers with $Q \ne 0$), let $U_n$ and $V_n$ be the terms of the Lucas sequence
$U(P, Q)$ and of the companion Lucas sequence $V(P, Q)$, and let $(w_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be an integer
sequence with $w_{n+2} = P w_{n+1} - Q w_n$ for every natural number $n$. Then for all natural
numbers $t > 0$ and $r$, the subsequence $w'_n = w_{tn + r}$ satisfies
$w'_{n+2} = V_t w'_{n+1} - Q^t w'_n$ for every natural number $n$, and
$V_t^2 - 4 Q^t = U_t^2 (P^2 - 4Q)$.

The source writes the recurrence as $w_{n+2} = a w_{n+1} + b w_n$,
with subsequence coefficients $a' = V_t$ and $b' = (-1)^{t+1} b^t$ and discriminant
$D(a, b) = a^2 + 4b$; this is the statement above with $P = a$ and $Q = -b$. The source's
identification of the characteristic roots of the new recurrence as $\alpha^t$ and $\beta^t$ is
not part of this statement.

## Sources

- Somer and Křížek, *Generalization of a Theorem of Vélez on Uniform Distribution in Second-Order Linear Recurrences*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A1, Theorem 2.4.

articles.title: Kalman–Mena generalized Fibonacci sequence
articles.statement:
A Kalman–Mena $(a,b)$-generalized
Fibonacci sequence consists of real parameters $a$ and $b$ together with a real sequence
$(F_n)_{n \ge 0}$ such that $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = a F_{n+1} + b F_n$ for every
$n \ge 0$, and its ordinary generating series in the formal variable $x$ satisfies the
identity of formal power series $(1 - a x - b x^2) \sum_{n \ge 0} F_n x^n = x$, that is,
$\sum_{n \ge 0} F_n x^n = x / (1 - a x - b x^2)$.

articles.title: A convolution of (a, b)-Lucas and (a, d)-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, d$ be complex
numbers with $b \ne d$, and write $L^{a,b}_n$ for the $(a,b)$-Lucas numbers and $F^{a,b}_n$ for
the $(a,b)$-Fibonacci numbers. Then for every natural number $n$,

$$(b - d) \sum_{i=1}^{n} L^{a,b}_{n-i} F^{a,d}_i = L^{a,b}_{n+1} - L^{a,d}_{n+1}$$

and

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} L^{a,b}_{n-i} F^{a,d}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} L^{a,d}_{n-i} F^{a,b}_i.$$

The source states the first identity in divided form,
$\sum_{i=1}^{n} L^{a,b}_{n-i} F^{a,d}_i = (L^{a,b}_{n+1} - L^{a,d}_{n+1})/(b - d)$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Corollary 14(a).

articles.title: Fibonacci, Jacobsthal and Pell convolution identities
articles.statement:
Write $F_n$ and $L_n$ for the
Fibonacci and Lucas numbers (the $(1,1)$-Fibonacci and $(1,1)$-Lucas numbers), $J_n$ and $j_n$
for the Jacobsthal and Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers (the $(1,2)$-Fibonacci and $(1,2)$-Lucas
numbers), and $P_n$ and $Q_n$ for the Pell and Pell–Lucas numbers (the $(2,1)$-Fibonacci and
$(2,1)$-Lucas numbers), all as complex numbers. Then for every natural number $n$:
(i) $\sum_{i=1}^{n} L_{n-i} J_i = j_{n+1} - L_{n+1}$ and
$\sum_{i=1}^{n} j_{n-i} F_i = j_{n+1} - L_{n+1}$;
(ii) $2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i = (Q_{n+1} - 2)/2$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \, Q_{n-i} = (Q_{n+1} - 2)/2$;
(iii) $\sum_{i=1}^{n} L_{2(n-i)} (2^i - 1) = L_{2n+2} - 2^{n+1} - 1$ and
$\sum_{i=1}^{n} (2^{n-i} + 1) F_{2i} = L_{2n+2} - 2^{n+1} - 1$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Corollary 14(b).

articles.title: Discriminant times an (a, b)-Fibonacci number
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be complex numbers with
$a^2 + 4b \ne 0$, and write $F_n$ and $L_n$ for the $(a,b)$-Fibonacci and $(a,b)$-Lucas
numbers. Then for every natural number $m$,

$$(a^2 + 4b) F_{m+1} = L_{m+2} + b L_m.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Corollary 4.

articles.title: Extensionality for Kalman–Mena generalized Fibonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Two Kalman–Mena
$(a,b)$-generalized Fibonacci sequences are equal when they have the same parameter $a$, the same
parameter $b$ and the same sequence $(F_n)_{n \ge 0}$.

articles.title: Recurrence for the (a, b)-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers $a$ and $b$ and every
natural number $n$, the $(a,b)$-Fibonacci numbers satisfy
$F^{a,b}_{n+2} = a F^{a,b}_{n+1} + b F^{a,b}_n$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: First (a, b)-Fibonacci number
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the $(a,b)$-Fibonacci
number $F^{a,b}_1$ equals $1$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: Zeroth (a, b)-Fibonacci number
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the $(a,b)$-Fibonacci
number $F^{a,b}_0$ equals $0$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: The (a, b)-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the $(a,b)$-Fibonacci
numbers $F^{a,b}_n$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, are the complex numbers given by $F^{a,b}_0 = 0$,
$F^{a,b}_1 = 1$ and $F^{a,b}_{n+2} = a F^{a,b}_{n+1} + b F^{a,b}_n$ for every $n$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: Recurrence for the (a, b)-Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers $a$ and $b$ and every
natural number $n$, the $(a,b)$-Lucas numbers satisfy
$L^{a,b}_{n+2} = a L^{a,b}_{n+1} + b L^{a,b}_n$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: First (a, b)-Lucas number
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the $(a,b)$-Lucas number
$L^{a,b}_1$ equals $a$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: Zeroth (a, b)-Lucas number
articles.statement:
For all complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the $(a,b)$-Lucas number
$L^{a,b}_0$ equals $2$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: (a, b)-Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
For complex numbers $a$ and $b$, the $(a, b)$-Lucas numbers are the
sequence $(L_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of complex numbers defined by $L_0 = 2$, $L_1 = a$ and
$L_{n+2} = a L_{n+1} + b L_n$ for all $n \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Section 1 (sequence definition).

articles.title: Sums of (a, b)-Fibonacci numbers weighted by powers of c
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c$ be complex
numbers with $c \ne 0$ and $c^2 - ac - b \ne 0$, and let $(F_n)$ be the $(a, b)$-Fibonacci
numbers. Then for every integer $n \ge 1$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} c^{n-i} F_i = \frac{c^{n+1} - c F_{n+1} - b F_n}{c^2 - ac - b}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 12.

articles.title: Sums of (a, b)-Fibonacci numbers weighted by powers of -b, via Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a, b$
be complex numbers with $\Delta = a^2 + 4b \ne 0$, and let $(F_n)$ and $(L_n)$ be the
$(a, b)$-Fibonacci and $(a, b)$-Lucas numbers. Then for every integer $n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} F_{2i} = \frac{L_{2n+1} + (-1)^{n+1} a b^n}{\Delta}$$

and

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} F_{2i+1} = \frac{L_{2n+2} + 2 (-1)^n b^{n+1}}{\Delta}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 10(a).

articles.title: Sum of even-indexed (a, b)-Fibonacci numbers weighted by powers of -b
articles.statement:
Let $a, b$ be
complex numbers and let $(F_n)$ be the $(a, b)$-Fibonacci numbers. Then for every integer
$n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} F_{2i} = F_n F_{n+1}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Corollary 11.

articles.title: Shifted sums of (a, b)-Lucas numbers weighted by powers of -b
articles.statement:
Let $a, b$ be complex
numbers with $b \ne 0$, and let $(F_n)$ and $(L_n)$ be the $(a, b)$-Fibonacci and
$(a, b)$-Lucas numbers. Then for all integers $m, n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} L_{2(i+m)+1} = F_{2(n+m)+2} + (-1)^n b^{n+1} F_{2m},$$

and this sum also equals $F_{n+m+1} L_{n+m+1} + (-1)^n b^{n+1} F_m L_m$. If moreover $m \ge 1$,
then

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} L_{2(i+m)} = F_{2(n+m)+1} + (-1)^n b^{n+1} F_{2m-1},$$

and this sum also equals $F_{n+m+1} L_{n+m} + (-1)^n b^{n+1} F_m L_{m-1}$.

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 5(b).

articles.title: Sums of (a, b)-Lucas numbers weighted by powers of -b
articles.statement:
Let $a, b$ be complex numbers
with $b \ne 0$, and let $(F_n)$ and $(L_n)$ be the $(a, b)$-Fibonacci and $(a, b)$-Lucas
numbers. Then for every integer $n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} L_{2i+1} = F_{2n+2}
\quad\text{and}\quad \sum_{i=0}^{n} (-b)^{n-i} L_{2i} = F_{2n+1} + (-b)^n.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 5(a).

articles.title: Alternating sums of Fibonacci and Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(F_n)$ and $(L_n)$ be the
Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, that is, the $(1, 1)$-Fibonacci and $(1, 1)$-Lucas numbers, viewed
as complex numbers. Then for every integer $n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i F_{2i} = \frac{(-1)^n L_{2n+1} - 1}{5}, \qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i L_{2i} = (-1)^n F_{2n+1} + 1,$$



$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i F_{2i+1} = \frac{(-1)^n L_{2n+2} + 2}{5}, \qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i L_{2i+1} = (-1)^n F_{2n+2}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 10(b).

articles.title: Weighted alternating sums of Jacobsthal and Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(J_n)$ and
$(j_n)$ be the Jacobsthal and Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers, that is, the $(1, 2)$-Fibonacci and
$(1, 2)$-Lucas numbers, viewed as complex numbers. Then for every integer $n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i 2^{n-i} J_{2i} = \frac{(-1)^n j_{2n+1} - 2^n}{9}, \qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i 2^{n-i} j_{2i} = (-1)^n J_{2n+1} + 2^n,$$



$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i 2^{n-i} J_{2i+1} = \frac{(-1)^n j_{2n+2} + 2^{n+2}}{9}, \qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i 2^{n-i} j_{2i+1} = (-1)^n J_{2n+2}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 10(d).

articles.title: Alternating sums of even-indexed k-Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a complex number, and let
$(F_{k,n})$ and $(L_{k,n})$ be the $k$-Fibonacci and $k$-Lucas numbers, that is, the
$(k, 1)$-Fibonacci and $(k, 1)$-Lucas numbers. Then for all integers $m \ge 1$ and $n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i L_{k,2(i+m)} = (-1)^n F_{k,2(n+m)+1} + F_{k,2m-1}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Corollary 9.

articles.title: Alternating sums of Pell and Pell–Lucas numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(P_n)$ and $(Q_n)$ be the Pell
and Pell–Lucas numbers, that is, the $(2, 1)$-Fibonacci and $(2, 1)$-Lucas numbers, viewed as
complex numbers. Then for every integer $n \ge 0$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i P_{2i} = \frac{(-1)^n Q_{2n+1} - 2}{8}, \qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i Q_{2i} = (-1)^n P_{2n+1} + 1,$$



$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i P_{2i+1} = \frac{(-1)^n Q_{2n+2} + 2}{8}, \qquad
\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i Q_{2i+1} = (-1)^n P_{2n+2}.$$

## Sources

- Emil Daniel Schwab, "Fibonacci Numbers via Dirichlet Convolution and Lucas Numbers via Unitary Convolution", Theorem 10(c).

articles.title: Cassini's identity for associated Pell numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(Q_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of
integers with $Q_0 = Q_1 = 1$ and $Q_{n+2} = 2Q_{n+1} + Q_n$ for every $n \ge 0$. Then for every
natural number $k \ge 1$,

$$Q_{k-1} Q_{k+1} = Q_k^2 + 2(-1)^{k-1}.$$

## Sources

- aBa Mbirika, Janee Schrader, and Jürgen Spilker, "Pell and Associated Pell Braid Sequences as GCDs of Sums of k Consecutive Pell, Balancing, and Related Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 26 (2023), Article 23.6.4, Lemma [Cassini's identity for Q].

articles.title: Even-index Catalan convolution with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer, let $U_n$
and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$, and let $C_j$ be the $j$-th Catalan
number. Then for every natural number $n$, in the rationals,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} C_{2n-2k} C_{2k} U_k V_{n-k} =
\frac{2^{2n}}{2} \cdot \frac{n+2}{2n+1} C_{n+1} U_n.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.4.

articles.title: Shifted Catalan convolution with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer, let $U_n$ and
$V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$, and let $C_j$ be the $j$-th Catalan
number. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $m$ with $m \ge 1$, in the rationals,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} C_{n-k+m} C_{k+m} U_k V_{n-k} =
2 \binom{2m-1}{m} \frac{(n+m+2)(n+1)}{(n+2m+1)(n+2m+2)} C_{n+m+1} U_n.$$

The paper states $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$; at $m = 0$ the printed right side is twice the sum
($p = 1$, $n = 1$: the sum is $2$, the printed right side is $4$), so $m = 0$ is excluded.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.5.

articles.title: Alternating binomial-Catalan sum with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer, let $U_n$
and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$, and let $C_j$ be the $j$-th Catalan
number. Then for every natural number $n$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \binom{4n}{2k} C_k C_{2n-k} U_{2n-k} V_k = (-1)^n C_n C_{2n} U_{2n}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.12.

articles.title: Binomial-Catalan sum with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer, let $U_n$ and $V_n$ be
the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$ and
both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$, and let $C_j$ be the $j$-th Catalan number. Then for
every natural number $n$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{2n}{2k} C_k C_{n-k} U_{n-k} V_k = C_n C_{n+1} U_n.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.11.

articles.title: Dixon-type alternating sum with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer and let $U_n$ and
$V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every natural number $n$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \binom{2n}{k}^3 U_{2n-k} V_k = (-1)^n \binom{3n}{n} \binom{2n}{n} U_{2n},$$

where $\binom{3n}{n} \binom{2n}{n} = (3n)!/(n!)^3$ is the trinomial coefficient.

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Theorem 2.2.

articles.title: Alternating sum of $\binom{2n}{k} \binom{4n}{2k}$ with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an
integer and let $U_n$ and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$,
$U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every
natural number $n$, in the rationals,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \binom{2n}{k} \binom{4n}{2k} U_k V_{2n-k} =
(-1)^n \frac{\binom{6n}{2n} \binom{2n}{n}}{\binom{3n}{n}} U_{2n}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.7.

articles.title: Alternating sum with reciprocal binomial coefficients and Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an
integer and let $U_n$ and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$,
$U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every
natural number $n$, in the rationals,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \frac{\binom{2n}{k}}{\binom{4n}{k} \binom{4n}{2n+k}} U_k V_{2n-k} =
\frac{4n+1}{3n+1} \cdot \frac{1}{\binom{4n}{2n}} U_{2n}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.9.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n}{k} \binom{2n}{n+k} \binom{n+k}{k}$ with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an
integer and let $U_n$ and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$,
$U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every
natural number $n$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \binom{2n}{n+k} \binom{n+k}{k} U_k V_{n-k} = \binom{2n}{n}^2 U_n.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.10.

articles.title: Binomial sums with signs $(-1)^{\binom{k}{2}}$ and Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer
and let $U_n$ and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$,
$U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every
natural number $n$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{4n+1} (-1)^{\binom{k}{2}} \binom{4n+1}{k} U_k V_{4n+1-k} = (-1)^n 2^{2n+1} U_{4n+1}$$

and

$$\sum_{k=0}^{4n+1} (-1)^{\binom{k}{2}} \binom{4n+1}{k} V_k U_{4n+1-k} = (-1)^n 2^{2n+1} U_{4n+1}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 3.1.

articles.title: Alternating squared-binomial sum with Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer and let
$U_n$ and $V_n$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$,
$V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$ and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every natural
number $n$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \binom{2n}{k}^2 U_{2n-k} V_k = (-1)^n \binom{2n}{n} U_{2n}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Theorem 2.1.

articles.title: Alternating two-binomial Catalan convolution of U and V
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer and let $U$
and $V$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so that $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$, and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Writing $C_j$ for the $j$-th Catalan
number, for every natural number $n$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \binom{2n}{k} \binom{4n}{2k} C_k C_{2n-k} U_{2n-k} V_k =
(-1)^n \binom{3n+1}{n} C_n C_{2n} U_{2n}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.13.

articles.title: Squared-binomial convolution of the Lucas sequences U and V
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer and let
$U$ and $V$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so that $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$,
$V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = p$, and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every natural
number $n$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^2 U_{n-k} V_k = \binom{2n}{n} U_n.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.3.

articles.title: Alternating triple-binomial convolution of U and V
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer and let $U$ and
$V$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so that $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$, and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every natural number $n$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{2n} (-1)^k \binom{2n}{k} \binom{4n}{k} \binom{4n}{2n+k} U_k V_{2n-k} =
(-1)^n \binom{2n}{n} \binom{5n}{2n} U_{2n}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.8.

articles.title: Convolution of U and V with shifted binomial weights
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer and let $U$ and
$V$ be the Lucas sequences $U(p, -1)$ and $V(p, -1)$, so that $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$,
$V_1 = p$, and both satisfy $X_{j+2} = p X_{j+1} + X_j$. Then for every natural number $n$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{2n}{k} \binom{2n}{n+k} U_k V_{n-k} = \binom{4n}{n} U_n.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 2.6.

articles.title: Weighted two-sided binomial sums of products of Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer,
let $U$ and $V$ be the two-sided second-order sequences for $p$ with $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$,
$V_0 = 2$ and $V_1 = p$, both satisfying $X_{j+1} = p X_j + X_{j-1}$ for every integer $j$, and
put $\Delta = p^2 + 4$. Then for every natural number $n > 0$ and all integers $m$ and $r$,

$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} k \binom{2n}{n+k} U_{k+m} U_{k+r} = n p \Delta^{n-1} U_{m+r},$$



$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} k \binom{2n}{n+k} V_{k+m} V_{k+r} = n p \Delta^{n} U_{m+r},$$



$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} k \binom{2n}{n+k} U_{k+m} V_{k+r} = n p \Delta^{n-1} V_{m+r},$$



$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} k \binom{2n}{n+k} V_{k+m} U_{k+r} = n p \Delta^{n-1} V_{m+r}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 3.3.

articles.title: Two-sided binomial sums of products of Lucas sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an integer, let $U$
and $V$ be the two-sided second-order sequences for $p$ with $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$, $V_0 = 2$ and
$V_1 = p$, both satisfying $X_{j+1} = p X_j + X_{j-1}$ for every integer $j$, and put
$\Delta = p^2 + 4$. Then for every natural number $n > 0$ and all integers $m$ and $r$,

$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} \binom{2n}{n+k} U_{k+m} U_{k+r} = \Delta^{n-1} V_{m+r},$$



$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} \binom{2n}{n+k} V_{k+m} V_{k+r} = \Delta^{n} V_{m+r},$$



$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} \binom{2n}{n+k} U_{k+m} V_{k+r} = \Delta^{n} U_{m+r},$$



$$\sum_{k=-n}^{n} \binom{2n}{n+k} V_{k+m} U_{k+r} = \Delta^{n} U_{m+r}.$$

## Sources

- John M. Campbell and Emrah Kılıç, *Binomial Sums Involving Second-Order Linearly Recurrent Sequences*, The Fibonacci Quarterly 62 (2024), Article 62-1/campbell10202023, Proposition 3.2.

articles.title: The value $A_k^{(1)} = 2/k$
articles.statement:
For every rational number $k$, the number $A_k^{(1)}$ for
$k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums equals $2/k$, where $2/0$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 1.

articles.title: The value $A_k^{(2)} = 8/k^2$
articles.statement:
For every rational number $k$, the number $A_k^{(2)}$ for
$k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums equals $8/k^2$, where $8/0$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 1.

articles.title: The initial value $A_k^{(0)} = 1$
articles.statement:
For every rational number $k$, the number $A_k^{(0)}$
for $k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums equals $1$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 1.

articles.title: The numbers $A_k^{(p)}$ for $k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums
articles.statement:
For a rational number $k$, the
rational numbers $A_k^{(p)}$, $p \ge 0$, are defined by $A_k^{(0)} = 1$ and, for $p \ge 1$,

$$
A_k^{(p)} = \frac{2}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{\lceil p/2 \rceil} \binom{p}{2j-1} A_k^{(p-2j+1)},
$$

where $2/k$ is read as $0$ when $k = 0$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 1.

articles.title: The polynomial $C_k^{(1)}(n) = n - 2/k$
articles.statement:
For all rational numbers $k$ and $n$, the
coefficient polynomial $C_k^{(1)}$ for $k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums satisfies
$C_k^{(1)}(n) = n - 2/k$, where $2/0$ is read as $0$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 5.

articles.title: The polynomial $C_k^{(0)}$ is constant $1$
articles.statement:
For all rational numbers $k$ and $n$, the
coefficient polynomial $C_k^{(0)}$ for $k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums satisfies $C_k^{(0)}(n) = 1$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 5.

articles.title: The coefficient polynomials $C_k^{(p)}$ for $k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums
articles.statement:
For a rational
number $k$, let $A_k^{(r)}$ be the numbers for $k$-Fibonacci Brousseau sums. For a natural number
$p$ and a rational number $n$,

$$
C_k^{(p)}(n) = \sum_{r=0}^{p} (-1)^r A_k^{(r)} \binom{p}{r} n^{p-r},
$$

where $0^0 = 1$; in particular $C_k^{(p)}(0) = (-1)^p A_k^{(p)}$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Definition 5.

articles.title: Brousseau sums of Fibonacci numbers along an odd step
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci
numbers, $L_n$ the Lucas numbers and $C_k^{(p)}$ the coefficient polynomials. For every odd
natural number $m$ and all $n, p \ge 0$,

$$
L_m \sum_{i=1}^{n} i^p F_{mi} = C_{L_m}^{(p)}(n) F_{m(n+1)} + C_{L_m}^{(p)}(n+1) F_{mn} -
C_{L_m}^{(p)}(0) F_m.
$$

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Corollary 9 (`jis-2024-24.6.4-cor-9`).

articles.title: Brousseau sums of $k$-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For an integer $k$, let $F_{k,n}$ be the
$k$-Fibonacci numbers, the Lucas sequence $U(k, -1)$ ($F_{k,0} = 0$, $F_{k,1} = 1$,
$F_{k,n+2} = k F_{k,n+1} + F_{k,n}$), and let $C_k^{(p)}$ be the coefficient polynomials. For
every nonzero integer $k$ and all $n, p \ge 0$,

$$
k \sum_{i=0}^{n} i^p F_{k,i} = C_k^{(p)}(n) F_{k,n+1} + C_k^{(p)}(n+1) F_{k,n} - C_k^{(p)}(0),
$$

where $0^0 = 1$.

The paper assumes $k \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Theorem 6 (`jis-2024-24.6.4-thm-6`).

articles.title: $k$-Fibonacci numbers as a power-weighted convolution
articles.statement:
For an integer $k$, let $F_{k,n}$
be the $k$-Fibonacci numbers, the Lucas sequence $U(k, -1)$: $F_{k,0} = 0$, $F_{k,1} = 1$ and
$F_{k,n+2} = k F_{k,n+1} + F_{k,n}$. For every integer $k$, every $n \ge 0$ and every $p \ge 1$,

$$
F_{k,n} = n^p + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigl(k i^p -
2 \sum_{j=1}^{\lceil p/2 \rceil} \binom{p}{2j-1} i^{p-2j+1}\Bigr) F_{k,n-i}.
$$

The paper assumes $k \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Theorem 1 (`jis-2024-24.6.4-thm-1`).

articles.title: Power-weighted convolution of k-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a nonzero integer and let
$F_{k,n}$ be the $k$-Fibonacci numbers, the Lucas sequence $U(k, -1)$: $F_{k,0} = 0$,
$F_{k,1} = 1$ and $F_{k,n+2} = k F_{k,n+1} + F_{k,n}$. Let $A_k^{(0)} = 1$ and
$A_k^{(p)} = \frac{2}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{\lceil p/2 \rceil} \binom{p}{2j-1} A_k^{(p-2j+1)}$ for
$p \ge 1$. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $p$, with $0^0 = 1$,

$$
k \sum_{i=0}^{n} i^p F_{k,n-i} = A_k^{(p)} F_{k,n+1} +
\sum_{r=0}^{p} A_k^{(r)} \binom{p}{r} \left((-1)^{p-r} F_{k,n} - n^{p-r}\right).
$$

The source takes $k$ to be a positive integer.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Theorem 4 (`jis-2024-24.6.4-thm-4`).

articles.title: Shifted power-weighted sums of k-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a nonzero integer and let
$F_{k,n}$ be the $k$-Fibonacci numbers, the Lucas sequence $U(k, -1)$: $F_{k,0} = 0$,
$F_{k,1} = 1$ and $F_{k,n+2} = k F_{k,n+1} + F_{k,n}$. Let $A_k^{(0)} = 1$ and
$A_k^{(p)} = \frac{2}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{\lceil p/2 \rceil} \binom{p}{2j-1} A_k^{(p-2j+1)}$ for
$p \ge 1$, and let $C_k^{(p)}(x) = \sum_{r=0}^{p} (-1)^r A_k^{(r)} \binom{p}{r} x^{p-r}$, with
$0^0 = 1$. Then for all natural numbers $m$, $n$ and $p$,

$$
k \sum_{i=1}^{n} i^p F_{k,m+i} = C_k^{(p)}(n) F_{k,m+n+1} + C_k^{(p)}(n+1) F_{k,m+n} -
C_k^{(p)}(0) F_{k,m+1} - C_k^{(p)}(1) F_{k,m}.
$$

The source takes $k$ to be a positive integer.

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Theorem 11 (`jis-2024-24.6.4-thm-11`).

articles.title: Power-weighted Pell sums along odd multiples
articles.statement:
Let $P_n$ be the Pell numbers and $Q_n$ the
Pell–Lucas numbers, the Lucas sequence $V(2, -1)$: $Q_0 = Q_1 = 2$ and
$Q_{n+2} = 2 Q_{n+1} + Q_n$. Let $m$ be an odd natural number and write $k = Q_m$. Let
$A_k^{(0)} = 1$ and
$A_k^{(p)} = \frac{2}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{\lceil p/2 \rceil} \binom{p}{2j-1} A_k^{(p-2j+1)}$ for
$p \ge 1$, and let $C_k^{(p)}(x) = \sum_{r=0}^{p} (-1)^r A_k^{(r)} \binom{p}{r} x^{p-r}$, with
$0^0 = 1$. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $p$,

$$
Q_m \sum_{i=1}^{n} i^p P_{mi} = C_k^{(p)}(n) P_{m(n+1)} + C_k^{(p)}(n+1) P_{mn} -
C_k^{(p)}(0) P_m.
$$

## Sources

- Prabha Sivaraman Nair and Rejikumar Karunakaran, *On k-Fibonacci Brousseau Sums*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.6.4, Corollary 10 (`jis-2024-24.6.4-cor-10`).

articles.title: Cassini identity for Gibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $G_0$ and $G_1$ be integers and let $(G_n)$ be
the Gibonacci sequence with these initial values, so that $G_{n+2} = G_{n+1} + G_n$ for all
$n \ge 0$. Then for every natural number $n \ge 1$,
$G_{n+1} G_{n-1} - G_n^2 = (-1)^n (G_1^2 - G_0 G_1 - G_0^2)$.

## Sources

- Guyer and Mbirika, "GCD of Sums of k Consecutive Fibonacci, Lucas, and Generalized Fibonacci Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.9.8, Proposition 2.5.

articles.title: Gibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For integers $G_0$ and $G_1$, the Gibonacci sequence with initial
values $G_0$ and $G_1$ is the integer sequence $(G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ that starts with $G_0, G_1$ and
satisfies $G_{n+2} = G_{n+1} + G_n$ for every $n \ge 0$.

articles.title: Gibonacci squares recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy
$g(n+2) = g(n+1) + g(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $F_3 = 2$ be the third Fibonacci
number. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$g(n+3)^2 = F_3\, g(n+2)^2 + F_3\, g(n+1)^2 - g(n)^2.$$

The characteristic polynomial $x^3 - 2x^2 - 2x + 1$ of this recurrence has roots $\alpha^2$,
$\beta^2$ and $-1$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $x^2 - x - 1$.

## Sources

- Thomas Koshy, "A Graph-Theoretic Model for a Generalized Fibonacci Gem," Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.4.1, Theorem 2, lines 149–153, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL22/Koshy/koshy7.tex

articles.title: Gibonacci numbers starting from 0 and 1 are the Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n$, the $n$-th Gibonacci number with initial values $G_0 = 0$ and $G_1 = 1$ equals the
$n$-th Fibonacci number $F_n$ (where $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$).

articles.title: Melham's gibonacci sum-of-squares identity
articles.statement:
Let $G : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy
$G(j+2) = G(j+1) + G(j)$ for every integer $j$, with $G(0) \ne 0$ or $G(1) \ne 0$, and let $F_m$
denote the $m$-th Fibonacci number. Then for every integer $k$ and every natural number $n \ge 1$,

$$6\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1} G(k+j)^2\Bigr)^2 =
F_{2n}^2\bigl(G(k+n-2)^4 + 4G(k+n-1)^4 + 4G(k+n)^4 + G(k+n+1)^4\bigr).$$

The hypotheses $G(0) \ne 0$ or $G(1) \ne 0$ and $n \ge 1$ are not needed; they keep the shape of
the source.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL27/Adegoke/adegoke12.tex>, lines 92–103, 877–880, and 1824–1828.

articles.title: Melham's gibonacci sum-of-squares identity, general form
articles.statement:
Let
$G : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $G(j+2) = G(j+1) + G(j)$ for every integer $j$, and let
$F_m$ denote the $m$-th Fibonacci number. Then for every integer $k$ and every natural number $n$,

$$6\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1} G(k+j)^2\Bigr)^2 =
F_{2n}^2\bigl(G(k+n-2)^4 + 4G(k+n-1)^4 + 4G(k+n)^4 + G(k+n+1)^4\bigr).$$

The source states this identity with the additional hypotheses that $G(0) \ne 0$ or $G(1) \ne 0$
and that $n \ge 1$.

articles.title: Binet, Cassini, mixed identity and ratio limit for generalized Fibonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$, $a \ge 0$ and $b > 0$ be integers, and let $m \ge 0$ and $n \ge 0$ be integers.
Let $W, F : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $W_0 = a$, $W_1 = b$, $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$,
$W_{k+2} = p W_{k+1} + W_k$ and $F_{k+2} = p F_{k+1} + F_k$ for every integer $k$. Put
$s = \sqrt{p^2 + 4}$, $\alpha = (p + s)/2$ and $\beta = (p - s)/2$. Then
$W_n = \frac{b - a \beta}{s} \alpha^n + \frac{a \alpha - b}{s} \beta^n$,
$F_{m-2} W_{n-2} - F_{m-3} W_{n-1} = (-1)^{m-1} W_{n-m+1}$,
$W_n W_{n+2} - W_{n+1}^2 = (-1)^n (a^2 + p a b - b^2)$, and $W_{k+1}/W_k$ tends to $\alpha$ as
$k \to \infty$ through the natural numbers.

Here $a^2 + pab - b^2$ is the source's $\Delta$. The four parts also hold separately under weaker
hypotheses; in particular the mixed identity holds for all integers $m$ and $n$.

## Sources

- Abdelhak Taane, Ihab-Eddine Djellas, and Mohammed Mekkaoui, "Total Positivity of Toeplitz Matrices Involving Generalized Hyper-Fibonacci Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.2.5, preliminary-results lemma, lines 192–200, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL29/Djellas/djellas7.tex

articles.title: Binet formula for generalized Fibonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a real number and let
$(W_k)_{k \ge 0}$ be a real sequence with $W_{k+2} = p W_{k+1} + W_k$ for all $k \ge 0$. Put
$s = \sqrt{p^2 + 4}$, and let $\alpha = (p + s)/2$ and $\beta = (p - s)/2$, the roots of
$z^2 - pz - 1$. Then for every $n \ge 0$,
$W_n = \frac{W_1 - W_0 \beta}{s} \alpha^n + \frac{W_0 \alpha - W_1}{s} \beta^n$.

articles.title: Cassini identity for generalized Fibonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let
$p \in R$, and let $(W_k)_{k \ge 0}$ be a sequence in $R$ with $W_{k+2} = p W_{k+1} + W_k$ for
all $k \ge 0$. Then for every $n \ge 0$,
$W_n W_{n+2} - W_{n+1}^2 = (-1)^n (W_0^2 + p W_0 W_1 - W_1^2)$.

articles.title: Mixed identity for generalized Fibonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a real number and let
$W, F : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $W_{k+2} = p W_{k+1} + W_k$ and
$F_{k+2} = p F_{k+1} + F_k$ for every integer $k$, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. Then for all
integers $m$ and $n$, $F_{m-2} W_{n-2} - F_{m-3} W_{n-1} = (-1)^{m-1} W_{n-m+1}$.

articles.title: Ratio limit for generalized Fibonacci sequences
articles.statement:
Let $p > 0$ be a real number and let
$(W_k)_{k \ge 0}$ be a real sequence with $W_0 \ge 0$, $W_1 > 0$ and
$W_{k+2} = p W_{k+1} + W_k$ for all $k \ge 0$. Then $W_{k+1}/W_k$ tends to
$(p + \sqrt{p^2 + 4})/2$ as $k \to \infty$.

articles.title: Generalized Catalan identity for Horadam sequences
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let
$c_1, c_2 \in R$, and let $W, Y, U : \mathbb{N} \to R$ be sequences that each satisfy
$x_{n+2} = c_1 x_{n+1} + c_2 x_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with $U_0 = 0$ and $U_1 = 1$.
Then for all $s, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$W_{s+i}\,Y_{s+j} - W_s\,Y_{s+i+j} = (-c_2)^s\,(W_1 Y_j - W_0 Y_{j+1})\,U_i.$$

The source states the identity over the integers, with integer coefficients, all integer
indices and $c_2 \ne 0$. This version restricts the indices to natural numbers and allows
coefficients in any commutative ring, so no invertibility of $c_2$ is needed; the bi-infinite
version is not claimed.

## Sources

- Aram Tangboonduangjit and Thotsaporn Thanatipanonda, "Determinants Containing Powers of Generalized Fibonacci Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 19 (2016), Article 16.7.1, Proposition "Generalized Catalan Identity," lines 111–126 of <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Tangboonduangjit/aram5.tex>.

articles.title: Generating function of shifted binomial coefficients
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, the
formal power series $\sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{n+r}{r} t^n$ with integer coefficients satisfies
$\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{n+r}{r} t^n\right)(1-t)^{r+1} = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$, that is,
$\sum_{n \ge 0} \binom{n+r}{r} t^n = 1/(1-t)^{r+1}$.

The paper states this for positive $r$; it holds for every $r \ge 0$ and is stated so.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Small values of the hyper-Fibonacci numbers of order one
articles.statement:
The hyper-Fibonacci numbers
$F^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy $F^{(1)}_0 = 0$, $F^{(1)}_1 = 1$, $F^{(1)}_2 = 2$ and
$F^{(1)}_3 = 4$.

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, after Proposition 5 (`F^{(r)}_0 = 0`).

articles.title: Hyper-Fibonacci numbers as partial sums
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r$ and $n$, the
hyper-Fibonacci numbers $F^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $F^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} F^{(r)}_k$.

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, after Proposition 5.

articles.title: Hyper-Fibonacci numbers of order zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the hyper-Fibonacci
number $F^{(0)}_n$ equals the $n$-th Fibonacci number $F_n$ (with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$).

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, after Proposition 5.

articles.title: Hyper-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
The hyper-Fibonacci numbers $F^{(r)}_n$, for natural numbers $r$
and $n$, are the natural numbers defined by $F^{(0)}_n = F_n$, the $n$-th Fibonacci number
(with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$), and $F^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} F^{(r)}_k$.

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, the hyper-Fibonacci numbers `F^{(r)}_{n+1} = ∑_{k=0}^{n+1} F^{(r-1)}_k` displayed after Proposition 5.

articles.title: Convexity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r$ and $n \ge 1$, the
hyper-Leonardo numbers $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n$ satisfy
$2 \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n \le \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_{n-1} + \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Theorem 3, with the definition of convexity displayed before it.

articles.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers in terms of hyper-Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r$
and $n$, the hyper-Leonardo number $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n$ and the hyper-Fibonacci number
$F^{(r)}_{n+1}$ satisfy $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n = 2F^{(r)}_{n+1} - \binom{n+r}{r}$ as integers.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 6, Equation (9).

articles.title: Generating function of the hyper-Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, the
formal power series $\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n t^n$ of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of
order $r$ satisfies
$\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n t^n\right)(1-2t+t^3)(1-t)^r = 1-t+t^2$ in
$\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$, that is,
$\sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n t^n = \frac{1-t+t^2}{(1-2t+t^3)(1-t)^r}$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Theorem 1, Equation (10).

articles.title: Eventual log-concavity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of positive order
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $r \ge 1$ and $n \ge 2$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ of order $r$ satisfy
$Le^{(r)}_{n-1} Le^{(r)}_{n+1} \le (Le^{(r)}_n)^2$.

The source states this for $r \ge 0$, but it fails for the Leonardo numbers $Le_n = Le^{(0)}_n$
at $n = 3$, where $Le_2 Le_4 = 27 > 25 = Le_3^2$; the source's proof starts its induction at
$r = 1$ (Proposition 13).

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 14.

articles.title: Log-convexity and log-concavity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers at index one
articles.statement:
The
hyper-Leonardo numbers $\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_n$ satisfy
$\left(\mathrm{Le}^{(1)}_1\right)^2 \le \mathrm{Le}^{(1)}_0 \mathrm{Le}^{(1)}_2$, and for every
natural number $r \ge 2$ they satisfy
$\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_0 \mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_2 \le \left(\mathrm{Le}^{(r)}_1\right)^2$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 12.

articles.title: Cassini-type identity for hyper-Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r \ge 1$ and
$n \ge 1$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy
$Le^{(r)}_{n-1} Le^{(r)}_{n+1} - (Le^{(r)}_n)^2 =
Le^{(r)}_n Le^{(r-1)}_{n+1} - Le^{(r-1)}_n Le^{(r)}_{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Eventual log-concavity of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of order one
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $n \ge 2$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy
$Le^{(1)}_{n-1} Le^{(1)}_{n+1} \le (Le^{(1)}_n)^2$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 13.

articles.title: First hyper-Leonardo numbers of order one
articles.statement:
The hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(1)}_n$ of
order $1$ satisfy $Le^{(1)}_0 = 1$, $Le^{(1)}_1 = 2$, $Le^{(1)}_2 = 5$ and $Le^{(1)}_3 = 10$.

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 1 (`Le^{(1)}_0 = 1`, `Le^{(1)}_1 = 2`).

articles.title: Consecutive hyper-Leonardo numbers of order one
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(1)}_n$ of order $1$ satisfy
$Le^{(1)}_{n+1} = Le^{(1)}_n + L_{1,n+1}$, where $L_{1,n}$ is the generalized Leonardo number
with $k = 1$, that is, the Leonardo number $Le_n$.

This is the case $r = 1$ of the recurrence $Le^{(r)}_n = Le^{(r)}_{n-1} + Le^{(r-1)}_n$. The
extracted text of the source reads $Le^{(1)}_n = Le_{n-1} + Le_n$, which fails at $n = 2$, where
$Le^{(1)}_2 = 5$ but $Le_1 + Le_2 = 4$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Corollary 1, Equation (5).

articles.title: Generating functions of the hyper-Leonardo numbers of orders one and two
articles.statement:
In the ring
$\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$ of formal power series, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy
$\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} Le^{(1)}_n t^n\right)(1 - 2t + t^3)(1 - t) = 1 - t + t^2$ and
$\left(\sum_{n \ge 0} Le^{(2)}_n t^n\right)(1 - 2t + t^3)(1 - t)^2 = 1 - t + t^2$.

Equivalently, the two generating functions are $\frac{1 - t + t^2}{(1 - 2t + t^3)(1 - t)}$ and
$\frac{1 - t + t^2}{(1 - 2t + t^3)(1 - t)^2}$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Recurrences for the hyper-Leonardo numbers of orders zero, one and two
articles.statement:
The
hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $Le^{(0)}_0 = Le^{(0)}_1 = 1$, $Le^{(1)}_0 = 1$,
$Le^{(1)}_1 = 2$, $Le^{(2)}_0 = 1$ and $Le^{(2)}_1 = 3$, and for every natural number $n \ge 2$,

$$Le^{(0)}_n = Le^{(0)}_{n-1} + Le^{(0)}_{n-2} + 1,$$



$$Le^{(1)}_n = Le^{(1)}_{n-1} + Le^{(1)}_{n-2} + \binom{n-1}{1} + 1,$$



$$Le^{(2)}_n = Le^{(2)}_{n-1} + Le^{(2)}_{n-2} + \binom{n}{2} + \binom{n-1}{1} + 2.$$

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Recurrence for the hyper-Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, the
hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ of order $r$ satisfy $Le^{(r)}_0 = 1$, $Le^{(r)}_1 = r + 1$
and, for every natural number $n \ge 2$,
$Le^{(r)}_n = r + Le^{(r)}_{n-1} + Le^{(r)}_{n-2} + \binom{n+r-2}{r} +
\sum_{j=1}^{r-1} j \binom{n+r-2-j}{r-j}$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Recurrence across consecutive orders of hyper-Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$r \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$, the hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy
$Le^{(r)}_n = Le^{(r)}_{n-1} + Le^{(r-1)}_n$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 3, Equation (4).

articles.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers as partial sums
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $r$ and $n$, the
hyper-Leonardo numbers $Le^{(r)}_n$ satisfy $Le^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} Le^{(r)}_k$.

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Definition 1.

articles.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers of order zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the hyper-Leonardo
number $Le^{(0)}_n$ equals the Leonardo number $L_{1,n}$, the generalized Leonardo number with
$k = 1$, given by $L_{1,0} = L_{1,1} = 1$ and $L_{1,n+2} = L_{1,n+1} + L_{1,n} + 1$.

## Sources

- Spreafico and Catarino, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Definition 1.

articles.title: Hyper-Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers, defined by
$Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$. The hyper-Leonardo numbers are the
integers $Le^{(r)}_n$, for $r, n \ge 0$, defined by $Le^{(0)}_n = Le_n$ and
$Le^{(r+1)}_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} Le^{(r)}_k$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Definition 1, as displayed in the derivation `Le^{(1)}_n = ∑_{k=0}^{n} Le^{(0)}_k` after Proposition 5.

articles.title: Generating function of the Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers
($Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$), and let
$L(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} Le_n t^n$ in the ring $\mathbb{Z}[[t]]$ of formal power series. Then
$L(t)(1 - 2t + t^3) = 1 - t + t^2$ and $L(t)(1 - t - t^2)(1 - t) = 2(1 - t) - (1 - t - t^2)$.

Equivalently, $L(t) = \frac{2}{1-t-t^2} - \frac{1}{1-t} = \frac{1-t+t^2}{1-2t+t^3}$; the
identities above are this equality with the denominators cleared.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Leonardo numbers are log-balanced at index three
articles.statement:
Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo numbers
($Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$). Then $Le_3^2 \le Le_2 Le_4$ and
$\frac{Le_2}{2!} \cdot \frac{Le_4}{4!} \le \left(\frac{Le_3}{3!}\right)^2$, the second
inequality in the real numbers. That is, $(Le_n)$ satisfies the log-convexity inequality at
$n = 3$ and $(Le_n / n!)$ satisfies the log-concavity inequality at $n = 3$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 11, with the definition of log-balanced displayed before Proposition 10.

articles.title: Log-convexity and log-concavity of the Leonardo numbers
articles.statement:
Let $Le_n$ be the Leonardo
numbers ($Le_0 = Le_1 = 1$ and $Le_{n+2} = Le_{n+1} + Le_n + 1$). Then
$Le_n^2 \le Le_{n-1} Le_{n+1}$ for $n = 1$ and $n = 3$, $Le_5^2 = Le_4 Le_6$, and
$Le_{n-1} Le_{n+1} \le Le_n^2$ for $n = 2$, $n = 4$ and every $n \ge 6$.

The paper's "the sequence is log-convex for $n = 1$" is read as the defining inequality at
index $n$.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Proposition 10.

articles.title: The convolution of log-concave sequences is log-concave
articles.statement:
Let $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and
$(y_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be sequences of positive real numbers that are log-concave, that is,
$x_{j-1} x_{j+1} \le x_j^2$ and $y_{j-1} y_{j+1} \le y_j^2$ for every $j \ge 1$. Let
$z_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} x_k y_{n-k}$ be their convolution. Then $z_{j-1} z_{j+1} \le z_j^2$ for
every $j \ge 1$.

Positivity is the paper's standing assumption on log-concave sequences.

## Sources

- Elen Viviani Pereira Spreafico and Paula Maria Machado Cruz Catarino, *A Note on Hyper-Leonardo Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A48, Lemma 3, quoting [1].

articles.title: A small value of $M$ in the family of $r/s$ when $abp + a^2 - b^2 < 0$
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, p$ be
integers with $p \ne 0$ and $abp + a^2 - b^2 < 0$. Let $A(x) = \frac{a(1 - px) + bx}{1 - px - x^2}$
for rational $x$, and for integers $u, v$ let
$M(u, v) = \frac{bu^2 + bv^2 - apu^2 + 2auv}{v^2 - puv - u^2}$, where in both a fraction with
denominator $0$ is read as $0$. Let $r, s$ be coprime integers with $s \ne 0$ such that $A(r/s)$
is an integer, and let $(A^{(r,s)}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be the two-sided sequence with
$A^{(r,s)}_0 = r$, $A^{(r,s)}_1 = s$ and $A^{(r,s)}_{n+1} = pA^{(r,s)}_n + A^{(r,s)}_{n-1}$ for
every integer $n$. If $A^{(r,s)}_n \ne 0$ for every integer $n$, then there is an integer $n$
with $|M(A^{(r,s)}_n, A^{(r,s)}_{n+1})| \le \sqrt{b^2 - a^2 - abp}$.

The hypothesis that no term vanishes is the paper's assumption before Lemma 8 ("we can assume
that the conditions $r \ne 0, s \ne 0, r + ps \ne 0$ automatically hold"). Without it the paper's
claim fails: for $(a, b, p) = (-1, 8, -1)$ and $x = 0$, the members $A_n/A_{n+1}$ of the family
$A^{(0,1)}$ with $A_{n+1} \ne 0$ have $\min |M| = 8 > \sqrt{55}$.

## Sources

- Luu Ba Thang and Nguyen Duy Nguyen, *Integer Values of Generating Functions for a Type of Second-Order Linear Recurrence Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.3, Lemma 9 (`jis-2025-25.8.3-lem-9`).

articles.title: A small value of $M$ in the family of $r/s$ when $abp + a^2 - b^2 \ge 0$
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, p$
be integers with $p \ne 0$ and $abp + a^2 - b^2 \ge 0$. Let
$A(x) = \frac{a(1 - px) + bx}{1 - px - x^2}$ for rational $x$, and for integers $u, v$ let
$M(u, v) = \frac{bu^2 + bv^2 - apu^2 + 2auv}{v^2 - puv - u^2}$, where in both a fraction with
denominator $0$ is read as $0$. Let $r, s$ be coprime integers with $s \ne 0$ such that $A(r/s)$
is an integer, and let $(A^{(r,s)}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be the two-sided sequence with
$A^{(r,s)}_0 = r$, $A^{(r,s)}_1 = s$ and $A^{(r,s)}_{n+1} = pA^{(r,s)}_n + A^{(r,s)}_{n-1}$ for
every integer $n$. If $A^{(r,s)}_n \ne 0$ for every integer $n$, then there is an integer $n$
with $|M(A^{(r,s)}_n, A^{(r,s)}_{n+1})| \le \sqrt{(abp^3 + (a^2 - b^2)p^2)/(p^2 + 4)}$.

The hypothesis that no term vanishes is the paper's assumption before Lemma 8. Without it the
paper's claim fails: for $(a, b, p) = (-3, -8, 5)$ and $x = 0$, the members $A_n/A_{n+1}$ of the
family $A^{(0,1)}$ with $A_{n+1} \ne 0$ have $\min |M| = 8$, while
$(abp^3 + (a^2 - b^2)p^2)/(p^2 + 4) = 1625/29 < 64$.

## Sources

- Luu Ba Thang and Nguyen Duy Nguyen, *Integer Values of Generating Functions for a Type of Second-Order Linear Recurrence Sequence*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.3, Lemma 10 (`jis-2025-25.8.3-lem-10`).

articles.title: Value of the Gibonacci generating function at one
articles.statement:
For all integers $a$ and $b$, the
Gibonacci generating function $G^{(a,b)}(x) = \frac{(b - a)x + a}{1 - x - x^2}$ takes the value
$G^{(a,b)}(1) = -b$ at $x = 1$.

## Sources

- Knapp, *Fibonacci Generating Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.1, Lemma 5 (`jis-2024-24.3.1-lem-5`).

articles.title: Value of the Gibonacci generating function at zero
articles.statement:
For all integers $a$ and $b$, the
Gibonacci generating function $G^{(a,b)}(x) = \frac{(b - a)x + a}{1 - x - x^2}$ takes the value
$G^{(a,b)}(0) = a$ at $x = 0$.

## Sources

- Knapp, *Fibonacci Generating Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.1, Lemma 5 (`jis-2024-24.3.1-lem-5`).

articles.title: Gibonacci generating function
articles.statement:
For integers $a$ and $b$ and a rational number $x$, the
value of the Gibonacci generating function at $x$ is the rational number

$$G^{(a,b)}(x) = \frac{(b - a)x + a}{1 - x - x^2}.$$

It is the generating function of the Gibonacci sequence $(G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $G_0 = a$,
$G_1 = b$ and $G_{n+2} = G_{n+1} + G_n$.

## Sources

- Knapp, *Fibonacci Generating Functions*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.3.1, Lemma 5 (`jis-2024-24.3.1-lem-5`).

articles.title: Generating series of a Gibonacci sequence
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be integers and let
