articles.title: Ramanujan's theta function at $(q, q^2)$
articles.statement:
Let
$f(a,b) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ be Ramanujan's theta function and
$(a;q)_\infty = \prod_{n \ge 0} (1 - a q^n)$. For every complex number $q$ with $|q| < 1$,
$f(q,q^2) \, (q;q^2)_\infty = f(-q^3,-q^3)$, that is, $f(q,q^2) = \varphi(-q^3)/\chi(-q)$ with
the denominator cleared, where $\varphi(q) = f(q,q)$ and $\chi(-q) = (q;q^2)_\infty$.

## Sources

- A. Vanitha, M. P. Chaudhary, and Madiha Khanum, *Modular Relations for the Rogers-Ramanujan-Slater Type Functions of Order Eighteen with Applications to Partitions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A103, Lemma 5, Equation (11).

articles.title: Product of the nonic theta functions
articles.statement:
Let
$f(a,b) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ be Ramanujan's theta function and
write $f(-x) = f(-x,-x^2)$. For every complex number $q$ with $|q| < 1$,
$f(-q,-q^8) f(-q^2,-q^7) f(-q^4,-q^5) f(-q^3) = f(-q) f(-q^9)^3$, that is,
$f(-q,-q^8) f(-q^2,-q^7) f(-q^4,-q^5) = f(-q) f^3(-q^9)/f(-q^3)$ with the denominator cleared.

## Sources

- A. Vanitha, M. P. Chaudhary, and Madiha Khanum, *Modular Relations for the Rogers-Ramanujan-Slater Type Functions of Order Eighteen with Applications to Partitions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A103, Lemma 4, Equation (10).

articles.title: Modular relations for the order-eighteen Rogers–Ramanujan–Slater functions
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be
a complex number with $0 < |q| < 1$. Write $(a;q)_\infty = \prod_{n \ge 0} (1 - a q^n)$ and
$f_k = (q^k;q^k)_\infty$, let $f(a,b) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ be
Ramanujan's theta function, and set $P_n = f(-q^{7n},-q^{11n})/f_{6n}$,
$Q_n = f(-q^{5n},-q^{13n})/f_{6n}$ and $R_n = f(-q^n,-q^{17n})/f_{6n}$. Then the following seven
relations hold.

$$P_1 P_8 + q^3 Q_1 Q_8 + q^{15} R_1 R_8 = \frac{1}{2q f_6 f_{48}} \left(
\frac{f_2^5 f_8^2}{f_1^2 f_4^2 f_{16}} - \frac{f_9^2 f_{72}^2}{f_{18} f_{144}}\right) -
q^8 \frac{f_3 f_{18}^2 f_{24} f_{144}^2}{f_6^2 f_9 f_{48}^2 f_{72}}$$



$$P_2 P_7 + q^3 Q_2 Q_7 + q^{15} R_2 R_7 = \frac{1}{2q f_{12} f_{42}} \left(
\frac{f_2^5 f_{14}^2}{f_1^2 f_4^2 f_{28}} - \frac{f_{18}^2 f_{63}^2}{f_{36} f_{126}}\right) -
q^8 \frac{f_6 f_{21} f_{36}^2 f_{126}^2}{f_{12}^2 f_{18} f_{42}^2 f_{63}}$$



$$P_3 P_6 + q^3 Q_3 Q_6 + q^{15} R_3 R_6 = \frac{1}{2q} \left(
\frac{f_2^5 f_{18}}{f_1^2 f_4^2 f_{36}^2} - \frac{f_{27}^2 f_{54}^2}{f_{18} f_{36} f_{54} f_{108}}
\right) - q^8 \frac{f_9 f_{54}^2 f_{108}^2}{f_{18} f_{27} f_{36}^2 f_{54}}$$



$$P_4 P_5 + q^3 Q_4 Q_5 + q^{15} R_4 R_5 = \frac{1}{2q f_{24} f_{30}} \left(
\frac{f_2^5 f_{20}^2}{f_1^2 f_4^2 f_{40}} - \frac{f_{36}^2 f_{45}^2}{f_{72} f_{90}}\right) -
q^8 \frac{f_{12} f_{15} f_{72}^2 f_{90}^2}{f_{24}^2 f_{30}^2 f_{36} f_{45}}$$



$$P_1 Q_2 - q^3 Q_1 R_2 + q R_1 P_2 = \frac{1}{2q f_6 f_{12}} \left(
\frac{f_9^2 f_{18}}{f_{36}} - \frac{f_1^2 f_2}{f_4}\right) +
q^2 \frac{f_3 f_{18} f_{36}^2}{f_6 f_9 f_{12}^2}$$



$$q^5 P_1 Q_{20} - q^{32} Q_1 R_{20} + R_1 P_{20} = \frac{1}{2q^4 f_6 f_{120}} \left(
\frac{f_9^2 f_{180}^2}{f_{18} f_{360}} - \frac{f_4^2 f_{10}^5}{f_5^2 f_8 f_{20}^2}\right) +
q^{17} \frac{f_3 f_{18}^2 f_{60} f_{360}^2}{f_6^2 f_9 f_{120}^2 f_{180}}$$



$$q^{23} P_1 R_{14} + Q_1 P_{14} - q^6 R_1 Q_{14} = \frac{1}{2q^2 f_6 f_{84}} \left(
\frac{f_9^2 f_{126}^2}{f_{18} f_{252}} - \frac{f_2^2 f_{14}^5}{f_4 f_7^2 f_{28}^2}\right) +
q^{13} \frac{f_3 f_{18}^2 f_{42} f_{252}^2}{f_6^2 f_9 f_{84}^2 f_{126}}$$

These are the source's relations (12)–(18), in order, for $P_n = P(q^n)$, $Q_n = Q(q^n)$ and
$R_n = R(q^n)$, where $P(q) = f(-q^7,-q^{11})/f(-q^6)$, $Q(q) = f(-q^5,-q^{13})/f(-q^6)$ and
$R(q) = f(-q,-q^{17})/f(-q^6)$ are the order-eighteen functions and $f(-q^6) = f_6$.

Deviation: in (14), the third relation, the paper prints $f_{48}$ in the last denominator; that
is false (the coefficients of $q^{56}$ of the two sides are $0$ and $-1$). The statement uses
$f_{54}$, the $f_{6n}$ factor that (12), (13) and (15) carry at this place ($f_{48} = f_{6 \cdot 8}$
is the value from (12)); with $f_{54}$ the relation checks exactly through $q^{198}$.

## Sources

- A. Vanitha, M. P. Chaudhary, and Madiha Khanum, *Modular Relations for the Rogers-Ramanujan-Slater Type Functions of Order Eighteen with Applications to Partitions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A103, Theorem 1, Equations (12)-(18).

articles.title: Relations between the order-eighteen and the nonic Rogers–Ramanujan functions
articles.statement:
Let $q$
be a complex number with $|q| < 1$. Write $(a;q)_\infty = \prod_{n \ge 0} (1 - a q^n)$ and
$f_k = (q^k;q^k)_\infty$, let $f(a,b) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a^{n(n+1)/2} b^{n(n-1)/2}$ be
Ramanujan's theta function, and set $P_n = f(-q^{7n},-q^{11n})/f_{6n}$,
$Q_n = f(-q^{5n},-q^{13n})/f_{6n}$, $R_n = f(-q^n,-q^{17n})/f_{6n}$,
$A_n = f(-q^{4n},-q^{5n})/f_{3n}$, $B_n = f(-q^{2n},-q^{7n})/f_{3n}$ and
$C_n = f(-q^n,-q^{8n})/f_{3n}$. Then

$$P_1 Q_1 R_1 = \frac{(q;q^2)_\infty \, f_{18}^3}{(q^3;q^6)_\infty \, f_6^3},$$



$$\frac{P_1 A_2 + q^3 R_1 C_2}{A_1} = \frac{Q_1 A_2 - q^2 R_1 B_2}{B_1} =
\frac{P_1 B_2 - q Q_1 C_2}{C_1} = \frac{f_9^2}{f_6 f_{18}}$$

and

$$\frac{P_1 A_2 + Q_1 B_2 + q^3 R_1 C_2}{A_1} = \frac{Q_1 A_2 - q^2 R_1 B_2 + P_1 C_2}{B_1} =
\frac{R_1 A_2 + P_1 B_2 - q Q_1 C_2}{C_1} = \frac{f_9^2}{f_6 f_{18}} +
\frac{f_3 f_{18}^2}{f_6^2 f_9}.$$

These are the source's relations (21)–(27). Here $P_n$, $Q_n$, $R_n$ are the order-eighteen
functions of Theorem 1 and $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$ the nonic Rogers–Ramanujan functions
$A(q) = f(-q^4,-q^5)/f(-q^3)$, $B(q) = f(-q^2,-q^7)/f(-q^3)$, $C(q) = f(-q,-q^8)/f(-q^3)$
evaluated at $q^n$, with $f(-q^3) = f_3$; the first relation reads
$P_1 Q_1 R_1 = \chi(-q) f_{18}^3 / (\chi(-q^3) f_6^3)$ with $\chi(-q) = (q;q^2)_\infty$.

## Sources

- A. Vanitha, M. P. Chaudhary, and Madiha Khanum, *Modular Relations for the Rogers-Ramanujan-Slater Type Functions of Order Eighteen with Applications to Partitions*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A103, Theorem 2, Equations (21)-(27).

articles.title: Apéry set and Frobenius number of a compound sequence
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and
let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$ be natural numbers with $0 < a_i < b_i$ for
$1 \le i \le n$ and $\gcd(a_i, b_j) = 1$ whenever $1 \le j \le i \le n$. Let $c_0, \dots, c_n$
be their compound sequence and $S$ the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by
$c_0, \dots, c_n$. Then (Kiers, O'Neill and Ponomarenko) the Apéry set of $S$ with respect to
$c_0$, the set of least elements of $S$ in the residue classes modulo $c_0$, is

$$\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i x_i : x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{N},\ x_i < a_i\Big\},$$

and the largest integer not in $S$, the Frobenius number of $S$, is

$$F(S) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_i - 1) c_i - c_0.$$

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Theorem 2, eq. (2), quoting Kiers, O'Neill, and Ponomarenko.

articles.title: Embedding dimension of the semigroup of a compound sequence
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number
and let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$ be natural numbers with $0 < a_i < b_i$ for
$1 \le i \le n$ and $\gcd(a_i, b_j) = 1$ whenever $1 \le j \le i \le n$; let $c_0, \dots, c_n$
be their compound sequence and $S$ the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by
$c_0, \dots, c_n$. Let $k$ be the number of indices $1 \le i \le n$ with $a_i = 1$. Then the
minimal generating set of $S$, the set of nonzero elements of $S$ that are not a sum of two
nonzero elements of $S$, has exactly $n - k + 1$ elements; that is, the embedding dimension of
$S$ is $n - k + 1$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Theorem 5.

articles.title: When deleting a term of a compound sequence leaves a numerical semigroup
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$
and let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$ be natural numbers with $0 < a_i < b_i$ for
$1 \le i \le n$ and $\gcd(a_i, b_j) = 1$ whenever $1 \le j \le i \le n$; let $c_0, \dots, c_n$
be their compound sequence. For $0 \le j \le n$, the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$
generated by the terms $c_i$ with $0 \le i \le n$ and $i \ne j$ has finite complement in
$\mathbb{N}$ (so it is a numerical semigroup) if and only if either $0 < j < n$ and
$\gcd(a_j, b_{j+1}) = 1$, or $j = n$ and $a_n = 1$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Deletions from a compound sequence that keep the Frobenius number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and let $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ and $(b_i)_{i \ge 0}$ be sequences of natural numbers with
$0 < a_i < b_i$ for $1 \le i \le n$ and $\gcd(a_i, b_j) = 1$ whenever $1 \le j \le i \le n$; let
$c_0, \dots, c_n$ be their compound sequence. Let $0 \le j \le n$ and suppose that the terms
$c_i$ with $0 \le i \le n$ and $i \ne j$ have greatest common divisor $1$. Let $S$ be the
additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $c_0, \dots, c_n$ and $S^\star$ the one
generated by the $c_i$ with $0 \le i \le n$ and $i \ne j$. Then some integer is both the largest
integer not in $S^\star$ and the largest integer not in $S$, that is, $S^\star$ and $S$ have the
same Frobenius number, if and only if $a_j = 1$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Theorem 4.

articles.title: The minimal generating set as the least Frobenius-preserving subset
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, \dots, b_n$ be natural numbers with $0 < a_i < b_i$
for $1 \le i \le n$ and $\gcd(a_i, b_j) = 1$ whenever $1 \le j \le i \le n$; let
$C = \{c_0, \dots, c_n\}$ be the set of terms of their compound sequence and $S$ the additive
submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $C$. Say that a set $G$ of natural numbers has the same
Frobenius number as $S$ if some integer is both the largest integer not in the submonoid
generated by $G$ and the largest integer not in $S$. Let $M$ be the minimal generating set of
$S$, the set of nonzero elements of $S$ that are not a sum of two nonzero elements of $S$. Then
$M \subseteq C$ and $M$ has the same Frobenius number as $S$, and every subset $C' \subseteq C$
with the same Frobenius number as $S$ has at least as many elements as $M$, with the same number
of elements only if $C' = M$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Last term of a compound sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and all sequences $a$, $b$
of natural numbers, the compound sequence $c$ of $a$ and $b$ satisfies $c_n = b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Section 2, eq. (1).

articles.title: First term of a compound sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and all sequences $a$, $b$
of natural numbers, the compound sequence $c$ of $a$ and $b$ satisfies $c_0 = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Section 2, eq. (1).

articles.title: Compound sequence
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $a = (a_i)$ and $b = (b_i)$ be
sequences of natural numbers. For a natural number $j$, the $j$-th term of the compound sequence
of $a$ and $b$ is

$$c_j = \Big(\prod_{i=1}^{j} b_i\Big) \Big(\prod_{i=j+1}^{n} a_i\Big),$$

so that $c_j = b_1 b_2 \cdots b_j \, a_{j+1} \cdots a_n$ for $0 \le j \le n$, the range of
interest; for $j > n$ the second product is empty and $c_j = b_1 \cdots b_j$.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Section 2, eq. (1) (after Kiers, O'Neill, and Ponomarenko).

articles.title: Brauer–Shockley formula for the Frobenius number
articles.statement:
Let $A_1, \dots, A_k$ be positive
integers with $\gcd(A_1, \dots, A_k) = 1$, let $S$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ they
generate, and let $a = A_i$ be one of them with $a \ge 2$. For $1 \le x \le a - 1$ let $m_x$ be
the least element of $S$ congruent to $x$ modulo $a$. If $M$ is the largest of the numbers $m_x$,
then $M - a$ is the largest integer not in $S$, that is, the Frobenius number of $S$.

The case $a = 1$, where the maximum would be over an empty set, is excluded.

## Sources

- Edgar Federico Elizeche and Amitabha Tripathi, *A Note on Deletions from Compound Sequences That Leave the Frobenius Number Invariant*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A6, Lemma 1, quoting Brauer and Shockley.

articles.title: Frobenius numbers of three consecutive star numbers for $6 \le n \le 9$
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for
the $m$-th star number $6m(m-1)+1$. For natural numbers $n$ and $p$ with $6 \le n \le 9$ and
$p \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, there is a natural number $g$ such that at most $p$ triples $(x, y, z)$ of
natural numbers satisfy $x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = g$, every natural number larger than
$g$ has more than $p$ such triples, and $g = 2n S_{n+1} + (p + 2) n S_{n+2} - S_n$. That is,
the $p$-Frobenius number of $S_n, S_{n+1}, S_{n+2}$ is $2n S_{n+1} + (p + 2) n S_{n+2} - S_n$.

## Sources

- "On p-Frobenius Numbers for the Numerical Semigroups Generated by Three Consecutive Star Numbers", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Frobenius numbers of three consecutive star numbers for $n \ge 10$
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the
$m$-th star number $6m(m-1)+1$. For natural numbers $n$ and $p$ with $n \ge 10$ and
$p \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, there is a natural number $g$ such that at most $p$ triples $(x, y, z)$ of
natural numbers satisfy $x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = g$, every natural number larger than
$g$ has more than $p$ such triples, and $g = (2n - 11) S_{n+1} + (p + 3) n S_{n+2} - S_n$. That
is, the $p$-Frobenius number of $S_n, S_{n+1}, S_{n+2}$ is
$(2n - 11) S_{n+1} + (p + 3) n S_{n+2} - S_n$.

## Sources

- "On p-Frobenius Numbers for the Numerical Semigroups Generated by Three Consecutive Star Numbers", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Three consecutive star numbers are relatively prime
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$, $\gcd(S_n, S_{n+1}, S_{n+2}) = 1$.

## Sources

- "On p-Frobenius Numbers for the Numerical Semigroups Generated by Three Consecutive Star Numbers", Lemma 2.

articles.title: $p$-Frobenius number of three consecutive star numbers
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For natural numbers $p$, $n$ and $g$, $g$ is the $p$-Frobenius number of
$S_n, S_{n+1}, S_{n+2}$ when at most $p$ triples $(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers satisfy
$x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = g$, and every natural number $N > g$ has more than $p$ triples
$(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers with $x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = N$.

articles.title: $1$-Sylvester number of three consecutive star numbers
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For every natural number $n \ge 6$, the number of natural numbers $N$ for
which at most one triple $(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers satisfies
$x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = N$ is $25n^3 + 23n^2 + 14n + 1$.

## Sources

- "On p-Frobenius Numbers for the Numerical Semigroups Generated by Three Consecutive Star Numbers", Theorem 2.

articles.title: $2$-Sylvester number of three consecutive star numbers
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For every natural number $n \ge 6$, the number of natural numbers $N$ for
which at most two triples $(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers satisfy
$x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = N$ is $33n^3 + 35n^2 + 20n + 2$.

## Sources

- "On p-Frobenius Numbers for the Numerical Semigroups Generated by Three Consecutive Star Numbers", Theorem 2.

articles.title: $0$-Sylvester number of three consecutive star numbers
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For every natural number $n \ge 6$, the number of natural numbers that
cannot be written as $x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2}$ with $x, y, z$ natural numbers is
$n(15n^2 + 8n + 7)$.

## Sources

- "On p-Frobenius Numbers for the Numerical Semigroups Generated by Three Consecutive Star Numbers", Theorem 2.

articles.title: $p$-Sylvester number of three consecutive star numbers
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For natural numbers $p$ and $n$, the $p$-Sylvester number of
$S_n, S_{n+1}, S_{n+2}$ is the number of natural numbers $N$ for which at most $p$ triples
$(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers satisfy $x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = N$.

For $n \ge 1$ the three star numbers are relatively prime, so this set of natural numbers is
finite.

articles.title: Representation count for three consecutive star numbers
articles.statement:
Write $S_m$ for the $m$-th star
number $6m(m-1)+1$. For natural numbers $n$ and $N$, the representation count of $N$ is the
number of triples $(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers with $x S_n + y S_{n+1} + z S_{n+2} = N$.

The star numbers are positive, so there are only finitely many such triples.

articles.title: Star numbers
articles.statement: For a natural number $n$, the $n$-th star number is $S_n = 6n(n-1)+1$.

articles.title: Representation counts between consecutive two-generator Frobenius numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$
be coprime positive integers. For a natural number $r$ let $g(a, b; r)$ be the generalized
Frobenius number of $(a, b)$ at $r$, and for an integer $m$ let $d(m; a, b)$ be the number of
representations of $m$ by $(a, b)$. Let $i$ and $s$ be natural numbers, let $c$ be a positive
integer divisible by $a$ or by $b$, and let $j$ be an integer. Then $d(g(a, b; s) + jc; a, b) = i$
if and only if $g(a, b; s) + jc \le g(a, b; i)$ and, in case $i \ge 1$, also
$g(a, b; i - 1) < g(a, b; s) + jc$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Lemma 3, quoted from Subwattanachai, *Generalized Frobenius number of three variables*.

articles.title: Representation counts above a shifted two-generator Frobenius number
articles.statement:
Let $a < b$ be
coprime positive integers, let $s$ and $k$ be natural numbers, let $g$ be the generalized Frobenius
number $g(a, b; s)$, and for an integer $m$ let $d(m; a, b)$ be the number of representations of
$m$ by $(a, b)$. If $m$ is an integer with $m > g + ka$, then for every natural number $j$,
$d(m - ja; a, b) \ge d(g + (k - j)a; a, b)$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Lemma 4, quoted from Subwattanachai, *Generalized Frobenius number of three variables*.

articles.title: Representation count of the reduced triangular triple at a shifted Frobenius number
articles.statement:
For a
natural number $r$ write $t_r = r(r+1)/2$. Let $n$, $k$, $i$ be natural numbers with $i \le 2k + 1$
and put $s = k(k+1) + i$. Let $N_s = 6\lfloor\sqrt{s+1}\rfloor - 6$ if $n$ is even and
$N_s = 6\lfloor(\sqrt{4s+5} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$ if $n$ is odd, and suppose $n > N_s$. For even $n$
let $(x_s, y_s) = (i, 2(k - i))$ if $i \le k$ and $(x_s, y_s) = (i - k - 1, 4k - 2i + 3)$ if
$i > k$; for odd $n$ let $(x_s, y_s) = (2i, k - i)$ if $i \le k$ and
$(x_s, y_s) = (2(i - k) - 1, 2k - i + 1)$ if $i > k$. Put $d_1 = \gcd(t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$,
$a = t_{n+1}/d_1$ and $b = t_{n+2}/d_1$. If $g$ is the generalized Frobenius number
$g(a, b; x_s)$, then the number of representations of $g + y_s t_n$ by $(t_n, a, b)$ is $s$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Splitting off the first generator of the reduced triangular triple
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$r$ write $t_r = r(r+1)/2$, and for an integer $m$ and natural numbers $a_1, \dots, a_k$ let
$d(m; a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be the number of representations of $m$ by $(a_1, \dots, a_k)$. Let
$n \ge 1$, $d_1 = \gcd(t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$, $a = t_{n+1}/d_1$ and $b = t_{n+2}/d_1$. Then for every
natural number $m$,

$$d(m; t_n, a, b) = \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/t_n \rfloor} d(m - j t_n; a, b).$$

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Beck–Kifer reduction by a common factor of all generators but the first
articles.statement:
Let $K \ge 2$,
let $a_1$ and $\ell$ be positive integers, and let $a'_2, \dots, a'_K$ be positive integers with
$\gcd(a'_2, \dots, a'_K) = 1$ such that $\gcd(a_1, \ell a'_2, \dots, \ell a'_K) = 1$. Let $s$ be a
natural number. If $g'$ is the generalized Frobenius number $g(a_1, a'_2, \dots, a'_K; s)$, then
$\ell g' + a_1(\ell - 1)$ is the generalized Frobenius number
$g(a_1, \ell a'_2, \dots, \ell a'_K; s)$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Lemma 1, quoted from Beck and Kifer, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Generalized Frobenius numbers of the reduced triangular triple
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$
write $t_r = r(r+1)/2$. Let $n$, $k$, $i$ be natural numbers with $i \le 2k + 1$ and put
$s = k(k+1) + i$. Let $N_s = 6\lfloor\sqrt{s+1}\rfloor - 6$ if $n$ is even and
$N_s = 6\lfloor(\sqrt{4s+5} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$ if $n$ is odd, and suppose $n > N_s$. For even $n$
let $(x_s, y_s) = (i, 2(k - i))$ if $i \le k$ and $(x_s, y_s) = (i - k - 1, 4k - 2i + 3)$ if
$i > k$; for odd $n$ let $(x_s, y_s) = (2i, k - i)$ if $i \le k$ and
$(x_s, y_s) = (2(i - k) - 1, 2k - i + 1)$ if $i > k$. Put $d_1 = \gcd(t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$,
$a = t_{n+1}/d_1$ and $b = t_{n+2}/d_1$. Then $(x_s + 1)ab - a - b$ is the generalized Frobenius
number $g(a, b; x_s)$, and $(x_s + 1)ab - b - a + y_s t_n$ is the generalized Frobenius number
$g(t_n, a, b; s)$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Komatsu's conjecture on generalized Frobenius numbers of triangular triples
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $r$ write $t_r = r(r+1)/2$. Let $n$ and $s$ be natural numbers, let
$N_{s+1} = 6\lfloor\sqrt{s+2}\rfloor - 6$ if $n$ is even and
$N_{s+1} = 6\lfloor(\sqrt{4s+9} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$ if $n$ is odd, and suppose $n > N_{s+1}$. Let
$g_s$ and $g_{s+1}$ be the generalized Frobenius numbers of $(t_n, t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$ at $s$ and at
$s + 1$, and put $P = (n+1)(n+2)$. Then: (i) if $s + 1$ is neither $k^2$ nor $k(k+1)$ for any
integer $k \ge 1$, then $4(g_{s+1} - g_s) = 6P$; (ii) if $n$ is even and $s + 1 = k^2$ or
$s + 1 = k(k+1)$ for an integer $k \ge 1$, then $4(g_{s+1} - g_s) = (n - 6k + 6)P$; (iii) if $n$ is
odd and $k \ge 1$ is an integer, then $4(g_{s+1} - g_s) = (n - 6k + 9)P$ when $s + 1 = k^2$, and
$4(g_{s+1} - g_s) = (n - 6k + 3)P$ when $s + 1 = k(k+1)$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Generalized Frobenius numbers of triangular triples in parametrized form
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $r$ write $t_r = r(r+1)/2$. Let $n$, $k$, $i$ be natural numbers with $i \le 2k + 1$ and
put $s = k(k+1) + i$. Suppose that $s \le 2$ or that $s$ is neither $m^2$ nor $m(m+1)$ for any
integer $m \ge 1$. Let $N_s = 6\lfloor\sqrt{s+1}\rfloor - 6$ if $n$ is even and
$N_s = 6\lfloor(\sqrt{4s+5} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$ if $n$ is odd, and suppose $n \ge 2$ and $n > N_s$.
For even $n$ let $(x_s, y_s) = (i, 2(k - i))$ if $i \le k$ and
$(x_s, y_s) = (i - k - 1, 4k - 2i + 3)$ if $i > k$; for odd $n$ let $(x_s, y_s) = (2i, k - i)$ if
$i \le k$ and $(x_s, y_s) = (2(i - k) - 1, 2k - i + 1)$ if $i > k$. Then the generalized Frobenius
number $g$ of $(t_n, t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$ at $s$ exists and satisfies
$4(g + 1) = (n+1)(n+2)\bigl((2x_s + y_s + 3)n + 6x_s\bigr)$ if $n$ is even and
$4(g + 1) = (n+1)(n+2)\bigl((x_s + 2y_s + 3)n + 3(x_s - 1)\bigr)$ if $n$ is odd.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Explicit generalized Frobenius numbers of triangular triples at levels 11 to 20
articles.statement:
For a
natural number $r$ write $t_r = r(r+1)/2$. For a natural number $n$, a natural number $s$ and an
integer $L$, say that $s$ has value $L$ when the generalized Frobenius number $g$ of
$(t_n, t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$ at $s$ exists and satisfies $4(g + 1) = (n+1)(n+2)L$. Then for every
natural number $n$: $11$ has value $8n + 12$ if $n = 12$ or $n \ge 14$; $12$ has value $9n$ for
even $n \ge 14$ and $9n - 3$ for odd $n \ge 17$; $13$ has value $9n + 6$ for even $n \ge 12$ and
$9n + 3$ for odd $n \ge 15$; $14$ has value $9n + 12$ for even $n \ge 12$ and $9n + 9$ for odd
$n \ge 15$; $15$ has value $9n + 18$ for even $n \ge 18$ and $9n + 15$ for odd $n \ge 15$; $16$
has value $10n$ if $n = 17$ or $n \ge 19$; $17$ has value $10n + 6$ if $n = 15$ or $n \ge 17$; $18$
has value $10n + 12$ if $n = 17$ or $n \ge 19$; $19$ has value $10n + 18$ if $n = 20$ or
$n \ge 22$; $20$ has value $11n$ for even $n \ge 18$ and $11n - 3$ for odd $n \ge 21$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Generalized Frobenius numbers of three consecutive triangular numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$j$ write $t_j = j(j+1)/2$. Let $n$ and $s$ be natural numbers, let $r = \lfloor\sqrt{s}\rfloor$,
let $\delta_s = 1$ if $s \ge r^2 + r$ and $\delta_s = 0$ otherwise, and put
$q_s = 2r + 2 + \delta_s$ and $c_s = s - r^2 - \delta_s r$. Suppose that
$n > 6\lfloor\sqrt{s+1}\rfloor - 6$ if $n$ is even and $n > 6\lfloor(\sqrt{4s+5} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$
if $n$ is odd. Then the generalized Frobenius number $g$ of $(t_n, t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$ at $s$ exists
and satisfies $4(g + 1) = (n+1)(n+2)(q_s n + 6c_s)$ if $n$ is even and
$4(g + 1) = (n+1)(n+2)(q_s n + 6c_s - 3\delta_s)$ if $n$ is odd.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Triangular Frobenius threshold at $s = 0$
articles.statement:
At $s = 0$ the triangular Frobenius threshold
$N_s$ equals $0$ for $n = 0$ (the even case, $N_0^{\mathrm{even}} = 6\lfloor\sqrt{1}\rfloor - 6$)
and $-3$ for $n = 1$ (the odd case, $N_0^{\mathrm{odd}} = 6\lfloor(\sqrt{5} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$).

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, equation (4).

articles.title: Triangular Frobenius threshold
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $s$, the threshold $N_s$ is
the integer $N_s^{\mathrm{even}} = 6\lfloor\sqrt{s+1}\rfloor - 6$ when $n$ is even and
$N_s^{\mathrm{odd}} = 6\lfloor(\sqrt{4s+5} - 1)/2\rfloor - 3$ when $n$ is odd.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, equation (4).

articles.title: The parameter $x_s$ of the triangular Frobenius formula
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $k$
and $i$, let $x$ be $i$ if $i \le k$ and $i - k - 1$ if $i > k$ when $n$ is even, and $2i$ if
$i \le k$ and $2(i - k) - 1$ if $i > k$ when $n$ is odd. For $s = k(k+1) + i$ with
$0 \le i \le 2k+1$ this is the integer $x_s$ (written $x_s^{\mathrm{even}}$ or
$x_s^{\mathrm{odd}}$ by the parity of $n$).

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Definition 1.

articles.title: Triangular Frobenius parameters at $s = 5$
articles.statement:
Take $k = 1$ and $i = 3$, so that
$s = k(k+1) + i = 5$. Then $(x_s, y_s) = (1, 1)$ for $n = 0$ (the even case) and
$(x_s, y_s) = (3, 0)$ for $n = 1$ (the odd case).

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Definition 1 and Table 2.

articles.title: The parameter $y_s$ of the triangular Frobenius formula
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$, $k$
and $i$, let $y$ be $2(k - i)$ if $i \le k$ and $4k + 3 - 2i$ if $i > k$ when $n$ is even, and
$k - i$ if $i \le k$ and $2k + 1 - i$ if $i > k$ when $n$ is odd, where a difference that would
be negative is replaced by $0$ (this happens only for $i > 2k + 1$). For $s = k(k+1) + i$ with
$0 \le i \le 2k+1$ this is the integer $y_s$ (written $y_s^{\mathrm{even}}$ or
$y_s^{\mathrm{odd}}$ by the parity of $n$).

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Definition 1.

articles.title: Triangular triple at $n = 1$
articles.statement:
The three consecutive triangular numbers
$(t_1, t_2, t_3)$, where $t_m = m(m+1)/2$, are $(1, 3, 6)$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction.

articles.title: Three consecutive triangular numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the triangular triple of
$n$ is $(t_n, t_{n+1}, t_{n+2})$, where $t_m = m(m+1)/2$ is the $m$-th triangular number.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction.

articles.title: Negative integers have no representations
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a_1, \dots, a_k$ and
every integer $m < 0$, the representation count $d(m; a_1, \dots, a_k)$ is $0$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction (definition of `d(n; a₁, …, a_k)`).

articles.title: Finitely many representations for positive generators
articles.statement:
If $a_1, \dots, a_k$ are positive
natural numbers, then for every integer $m$ the representation count $d(m; a_1, \dots, a_k)$ is
finite.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction (definition of `d(n; a₁, …, a_k)`).

articles.title: Number of representations by a vector of generators
articles.statement:
For natural numbers
$a_1, \dots, a_k$ and an integer $m$, the representation count $d(m; a_1, \dots, a_k)$ is the
number of tuples $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of natural numbers with $x_1 a_1 + \dots + x_k a_k = m$,
counted as an extended natural number, so that it is $\infty$ when there are infinitely many such
tuples.

It is $0$ for $m < 0$, and finite when every $a_i$ is positive.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction (definition of `d(n; a₁, …, a_k)`).

articles.title: Generalized Frobenius number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a_1, \dots, a_k$ and $s$, write
$d(m; a)$ for the number of representations of an integer $m$ by $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$. An
integer $g$ is the generalized Frobenius number $g(a; s) = \max \{m \in \mathbb{Z} \mid
d(m; a) \le s\}$ when $d(g; a) \le s$ and $d(m; a) > s$ for every integer $m > g$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction (definition of `g(A; s)`).

articles.title: Uniqueness of the generalized Frobenius number
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a_1, \dots, a_k$ and
$s$, if the integers $g$ and $g'$ are both the generalized Frobenius number $g(a_1, \dots, a_k; s)$,
then $g = g'$.

## Sources

- Kittipong Subwattanachai, *Formulas for the Generalized Frobenius Number of Triangular Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A63, Introduction (definition of `g(A; s)` as a maximum).

articles.title: Tripathi's pseudo-Frobenius formula
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $d$, $h$ and $k$ be positive integers with
$\gcd(a, d) = 1$, and let $q$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $1 \le r \le k$ and
$a - 1 = qk + r$. Let $S$ be the set of all sums $c_0 a + \sum_{i=1}^{k} c_i (ha + id)$ with
natural numbers $c_0, \dots, c_k$, that is, the additive monoid generated by
$a, ha + d, \dots, ha + kd$. Then the natural numbers $y \notin S$ such that $y + s \in S$ for
every nonzero $s \in S$ are exactly the numbers

$$y = ha \left\lfloor \frac{x - 1}{k} \right\rfloor + (h - 1)a + dx$$

with $x$ a natural number satisfying $a - r \le x \le a - 1$.

The case $a = 1$ cannot occur, since then $a - 1 = qk + r$ with $r \ge 1$ is impossible. When
$k \ge a$, these numbers are exactly $(h - 1)a + dx$ for $1 \le x \le a - 1$.

## Sources

- Amitabha Tripathi, "The Frobenius Problem for Modified Arithmetic Progressions," Journal of Integer Sequences 16 (2013), Article 13.7.4, Theorem, lines 235–238, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Tripathi/trip22.tex It follows from `tripathi_pseudo_frobenius_arithmetic_progression_general`; the hypothesis `hd` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Tripathi's pseudo-Frobenius formula without assuming $d > 0$
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $h$ and $k$ be
positive integers and $d$ a natural number with $\gcd(a, d) = 1$, and let $q$ and $r$ be natural
numbers with $1 \le r \le k$ and $a - 1 = qk + r$. Let $S$ be the set of all sums
$c_0 a + \sum_{i=1}^{k} c_i (ha + id)$ with natural numbers $c_0, \dots, c_k$. Then the natural
numbers $y \notin S$ such that $y + s \in S$ for every nonzero $s \in S$ are exactly the numbers

$$y = ha \left\lfloor \frac{x - 1}{k} \right\rfloor + (h - 1)a + dx$$

with $x$ a natural number satisfying $a - r \le x \le a - 1$.

The hypotheses force $d > 0$: if $d = 0$, then $\gcd(a, d) = a = 1$, and $a - 1 = qk + r$ with
$r \ge 1$ is impossible.

articles.title: Dutch–Rickett conductor recursion for semigroups of $k$-th powers
articles.statement:
Fix an integer
$k \ge 1$. For $m \ge 1$ let $S_m$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by
$m^k, (m+1)^k, (m+2)^k, \ldots$, and let $\tau(S_m)$ be its conductor, the least natural number
$c$ such that every $j \ge c$ lies in $S_m$. Then for every integer $n \ge 1$,

$$\tau(S_n) \le 2^k \, \tau(S_{\lceil n/2 \rceil}) + (2^k - 1)(2n)^k.$$

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Proposition 2, inequality (3), quoting K. Dutch and C. Rickett.

articles.title: Dutch–Rickett conductor inequality for a union of generating sets
articles.statement:
For a set $X$ of
natural numbers, let $\tau(X)$ be the conductor of the additive submonoid $\langle X \rangle$ of
$\mathbb{N}$ generated by $X$, the least natural number $c$ such that every $j \ge c$ lies in
$\langle X \rangle$. Let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty sets of natural numbers such that $1$ is the only
natural number dividing every element of $A \cup B$, let $t$ be a natural number dividing every
element of $A$, and let $C = \{a / t : a \in A\}$ (with $a / 0 = 0$). Then

$$\tau(A \cup B) \le t \, \tau(C \cup B) + \tau(B \cup \{t\}).$$

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Lemma 3, quoting K. Dutch and C. Rickett.

articles.title: Embedding dimension bound from linear growth of first appearances
articles.statement:
Let
$x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers. For $m \ge 1$
let $S_m$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $x_m, x_{m+1}, \ldots$; call a
nonzero element of $S_m$ that is not the sum of two nonzero elements of $S_m$ a minimal generator
of $S_m$, and let the embedding dimension $e(S_m)$ be the number of minimal generators of $S_m$.
For $k \ge 1$ let $r_k$ be the least $m \ge 1$ such that $x_k$ is a minimal generator of $S_m$.
If $\alpha > 0$ is a real number with $r_k \ge \alpha k$ for all $k \ge 1$, then
$e(S_n) \le \lfloor n / \alpha \rfloor - n + 1$ for all $n \ge 1$.

The paper's standing assumption $\gcd(x_n, x_{n+1}, \ldots) = 1$ is not needed and is dropped.

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Semigroups of squares have embedding dimension $O(n)$
articles.statement:
For $n \ge 1$ let $S_n$ be the
additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $n^2, (n+1)^2, (n+2)^2, \ldots$, and let $e(S_n)$
be its embedding dimension, the number of nonzero elements of $S_n$ that are not the sum of two
nonzero elements of $S_n$. There is a natural number $C$ with $e(S_n) \le C n$ for all $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Four squares with large nonzero parts
articles.statement:
There is a real constant $C > 0$ such that every
positive integer $n$ can be written as $n = a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2 + a_4^2$ with integers
$a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$, each of which is either $0$ or at least $\sqrt{n} / C$.

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Lemma 2, quoting A. Moscariello.

articles.title: Frobenius numbers of semigroups of $k$-th powers are $O(n^{k+\varepsilon})$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 2$
be an integer and $\varepsilon > 0$ a real number. For $n \ge 1$ let $S_n$ be the additive
submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $n^k, (n+1)^k, (n+2)^k, \ldots$. Then there is a real
constant $K$ such that for every $n \ge 1$, if $S_n$ has a Frobenius number $F$ (the largest
natural number not in $S_n$), then $F \le K n^{k + \varepsilon}$.

Since $S_1 = \mathbb{N}$ has no Frobenius number, the case $n = 1$ is vacuous.

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Minimal generators of the tail semigroups of an increasing sequence
articles.statement:
Let
$x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots$ be a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers. For $m \ge 1$
let $S_m$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $x_m, x_{m+1}, \ldots$, and let
$\beta(S_m)$ be its set of minimal generators, the nonzero elements of $S_m$ that are not the sum
of two nonzero elements of $S_m$. For $k \ge 1$ let $r_k$ be the least $m \ge 1$ with
$x_k \in \beta(S_m)$. Then for all integers $k, n \ge 1$, $x_k \in \beta(S_n)$ if and only if
$r_k \le n \le k$; and the embedding dimension $e(S_n) = |\beta(S_n)|$ equals the number of
integers $j \ge 1$ with $r_j \le n \le j$.

The paper's standing assumption $\gcd(x_n, x_{n+1}, \ldots) = 1$ is not needed and is dropped.

## Sources

- Fabián Arias, Jerson Borja and Jaider Terán, *A Note on Numerical Semigroups Generated by k-th Powers*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A11, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Asymptotic count of primes with more than $\ell$ representations
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $\ell$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $C$ such that the following
holds for all coprime natural numbers $c$ and $d$ with $C \le c < d$. Put
$g_\ell(c, d) = (\ell + 1)cd - c - d$, and let $\pi_{\ell,c,d}$ be the number of primes
$n \le g_\ell(c, d)$ such that the equation $n = cx + dy$ has more than $\ell$ solutions
$(x, y)$ in natural numbers. Then, with $\pi$ the prime-counting function,

$$
\left|\pi_{\ell,c,d} - \frac{\pi(g_\ell(c, d))}{2\ell + 2}\right| <
\varepsilon \, \frac{\pi(g_\ell(c, d))}{2\ell + 2}.
$$

That is, $\pi_{\ell,c,d} \sim \pi(g_\ell(c, d))/(2\ell + 2)$ as $c \to \infty$, uniformly over
coprime $d > c$.

## Sources

- Yuchen Ding and Takao Komatsu, *On a Conjecture of Ramírez Alfonsín and Skałba, III*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A51, Theorem 1, with `g_ℓ(c, d)` from equation (1).

articles.title: Counting primes with more than $\ell$ representations
articles.statement:
Let $c$ and $d$ be coprime
natural numbers with $1 < c < d$, let $\ell$ be a natural number, and put
$g_\ell(c, d) = (\ell + 1)cd - c - d$. Write $\pi_{\ell,c,d}$ for the number of primes
$n \le g_\ell(c, d)$ such that the equation $n = cx + dy$ has more than $\ell$ solutions
$(x, y)$ in natural numbers. Then $\pi_{\ell,c,d}$ equals the number of primes $n$ with
$\ell cd < n \le g_\ell(c, d)$ of the form $n = \ell cd + cx_0 + dy_0$ for some natural numbers
$x_0 \le d$ and $y_0 \le c$.

## Sources

- Yuchen Ding and Takao Komatsu, *On a Conjecture of Ramírez Alfonsín and Skałba, III*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A51, Lemma 3, with `g_ℓ(c, d)` from equation (1).

articles.title: Normal form of a number with exactly $\ell$ representations
articles.statement:
Let $c$ and $d$ be coprime
positive integers, and let $n$ and $\ell$ be natural numbers such that the equation
$n = cx + dy$ has exactly $\ell$ solutions $(x, y)$ in natural numbers. Then there are natural
numbers $x_0 < d$ and $y_0 < c$ with $n = (\ell - 1)cd + cx_0 + dy_0$ in the integers.

The identity is stated over the integers, so $\ell = 0$ is included (then $\ell - 1 = -1$). The
paper's standing assumption $1 < c < d$ is weakened to $0 < c$, $0 < d$.

## Sources

- Yuchen Ding and Takao Komatsu, *On a Conjecture of Ramírez Alfonsín and Skałba, III*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A51, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Two representations by coprime generators
articles.statement:
Let $c$ and $d$ be coprime natural numbers.
If natural numbers $x, y, x', y'$ satisfy $cx + dy = cx' + dy'$, then $c$ divides $y - y'$ and
$d$ divides $x - x'$ in the integers.

The paper's standing assumption $1 < c < d$ is not needed and is dropped.

## Sources

- Yuchen Ding and Takao Komatsu, *On a Conjecture of Ramírez Alfonsín and Skałba, III*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A51, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Weighted count of primes in the $\ell$-numerical semigroup
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$\ell$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a natural number $C$ such that the following holds
for all coprime natural numbers $c$ and $d$ with $C \le c < d$. For a natural number $k$ put
$g_k(c, d) = (k + 1)cd - c - d$, so that $g_0(c, d) = cd - c - d$, and let $\psi_{\ell,c,d}$ be
the sum of the von Mangoldt function $\Lambda(n)$ over the natural numbers $n$ with
$\ell cd < n \le g_\ell(c, d)$ of the form $n = \ell cd + cx_0 + dy_0$ for some natural numbers
$x_0 \le d$ and $y_0 \le c$. Then

$$
\left|\psi_{\ell,c,d} - \frac{g_0(c, d)}{2}\right| < \varepsilon \, \frac{g_0(c, d)}{2}.
$$

That is, $\psi_{\ell,c,d} \sim g_0(c, d)/2$ as $c \to \infty$, uniformly over coprime $d > c$.

## Sources

- Yuchen Ding and Takao Komatsu, *On a Conjecture of Ramírez Alfonsín and Skałba, III*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A51, Proposition 1, with `g_ℓ(c, d)` from equation (1).

articles.title: Sylvester's coin theorem for two distinct odd primes
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct odd
primes. Then the number of natural numbers $n$ that cannot be written as $n = px + qy$ with
natural numbers $x, y$ is $(p-1)(q-1)/2$.

Distinct odd primes are coprime, so this is a special case of Sylvester's count for coprime
$p$ and $q$.

## Sources

- Damanvir Singh Binner, "Generalization of a Result of Sylvester Related to the Frobenius Coin Problem", Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), Article 21.8.4, Theorem `Sylvester'` (the Special Case of Sylvester's theorem), source lines 123–127, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Binner/binner13.tex>. The paper attributes the general coprime statement to Sylvester (1882).

articles.title: Sylvester's coin theorem
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be coprime natural numbers. Then the number of
natural numbers $n$ that cannot be written as $n = ax + by$ with natural numbers $x, y$ is
$(a - 1)(b - 1)/2$.

Subtraction here is truncated at $0$: if $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, coprimality forces the other number
to be $1$, every natural number is representable, and both sides are $0$.

## Sources

- J. J. Sylvester on the Frobenius coin problem (1882); the count of gaps is `(a - 1) * (b - 1) / 2` for coprime `a b`.

articles.title: Telescopic sequences
articles.statement:
Let $G = (g_1, \dots, g_k)$ be a finite sequence of natural numbers.
For $0 \le i \le k$ let $d_i$ be the greatest common divisor of $g_1, \dots, g_i$, with $d_0 = 0$,
and for $1 \le j \le k$ let $c_j = d_{j-1} / d_j$ be the successive gcd quotient, taken to be $0$
when $d_j = 0$. The sequence $G$ is telescopic when $k \ge 2$, $g_1 + g_2 > 0$, and for every $j$
with $2 \le j \le k$ the number $c_j g_j$ lies in the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated
by $g_1, \dots, g_{j-1}$.

articles.title: Successive gcd quotients
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $G = (g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of natural numbers,
let $d_i$ be the greatest common divisor of the first $i$ entries of $G$ (of all of $G$ when
$i > k$), with $d_0 = 0$. For $j \ge 1$ the successive gcd quotient is $c_j = d_{j-1} / d_j$,
taken to be $0$ when $d_j = 0$, that is, when the first $j$ entries are all zero; and $c_0 = 0$.

The source always assumes $g_1 > 0$ or $\gcd(G) = 1$, which avoids the degenerate case
$d_j = 0$. For example, $(660, 550, 352, 50, 201)$ has $(c_2, \dots, c_5) = (6, 5, 11, 2)$ and
$(3, 4, 5)$ has $(c_2, c_3) = (3, 1)$.

articles.title: Prefix gcds of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence $G = (g_1, \dots, g_k)$ of natural numbers
and a natural number $j$, $d_j$ is the greatest common divisor of the first $j$ entries of $G$
(of all of $G$ when $j > k$), with $d_0 = 0$.

articles.title: Dyadic upper half interval
articles.statement:
For a natural number $e$, $I_e$ is the finite set of natural
numbers $i$ with $2^{e-1} < i \le 2^e$, where $e - 1$ is truncated subtraction, so that $I_0$ is
empty.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of I_e.

articles.title: A 2-adic limit of normalized odd double factorials
articles.statement:
Write $(2^e - 1)!!$ for the product of
the odd natural numbers from $1$ to $2^e - 1$. There is a 2-adic integer $w$ such that for every
natural number $e \ge 3$, $2^{e-1}$ divides $w - \lfloor ((2^e - 1)!! - 1) / 2^e \rfloor$ in
$\mathbb{Z}_2$.

For $e \ge 3$ the division is exact. The paper writes $e \ge 2$, but at $e = 2$ the quotient
$(3 - 1)/4$ is not an integer.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition after Corollary 10.

articles.title: A 2-adic limit of the odd parts of $(2^e)!$
articles.statement:
There is a 2-adic integer $z \in \mathbb{Z}_2$
such that $z \equiv \operatorname{od}((2^{e-1})!) \pmod{2^e}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ for every natural
number $e \ge 1$, where $\operatorname{od}(n)$ is the odd part of $n$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Corollary 8.

articles.title: A 2-adic constant relating unstable and stable bits
articles.statement:
Write
$\mathrm{od}(n)$ for the odd part of a natural number $n$, and for natural numbers $d$ and $e$ let
$\mathrm{uns}(e, d) = \lfloor \mathrm{od}((2^e)!) / 2^{e+1} \rfloor \bmod 2^d$ and
$\mathrm{stab}(e + 1, d) = \lfloor \mathrm{od}((2^{e+d})!) / 2^{e+1} \rfloor \bmod 2^d$. There is a
2-adic integer $K$ such that for all natural numbers $d < e$, $2^d$ divides
$\mathrm{uns}(e, d) + K - \mathrm{stab}(e + 1, d)$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Four copies of the residues $1 \bmod 8$ below $2^e$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $e$, this is the
multiset of integers containing exactly four copies of each natural number $n < 2^e$ with
$n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, that is, of each of $1, 9, \dots, 2^e - 7$ when $e \ge 3$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 21.

articles.title: Four copies as a multiset scalar multiple
articles.statement:
For every natural number $e$, the multiset of four
copies of the residues $1 \bmod 8$ below $2^e$ equals $4 \cdot M$, the sum of four copies of $M$,
where $M$ is the integer multiset of the set of natural numbers $n < 2^e$ with $n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 21.

articles.title: Cardinality of the integer multiset
articles.statement:
For every finite set $s$ of natural numbers, the integer
multiset of $s$ has the same number of elements, counted with multiplicity, as $s$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Convention for finite multisets.

articles.title: Integer multiset of a finite set of naturals
articles.statement:
For a finite set $s$ of natural numbers, its
integer multiset is the multiset of integers obtained by sending each element $n \in s$ to $n$
viewed as an integer, so each element of $s$ occurs exactly once.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Convention for finite multisets.

articles.title: Membership in the dyadic upper half
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $e$ and $i$, $i$ belongs to the
dyadic upper half $I_e$ if and only if $2^{e-1} < i$ and $i \le 2^e$, where $e - 1$ is truncated
subtraction.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of I_e.

articles.title: Membership in the odd numbers below $2^e$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $e$ and $i$, $i$ belongs to the
set $S_e$ of odd positive integers below $2^e$ if and only if $1 \le i$, $i < 2^e$ and $i$ is odd.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of S_e.

articles.title: Membership in the residues one modulo eight below a power of two
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $e$
and $n$, $n$ lies in the set of natural numbers below $2^e$ that are congruent to $1$ modulo $8$
if and only if $n < 2^e$ and $n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 21 notation.

articles.title: Odd numbers below a power of two
articles.statement:
For a natural number $e$, $S_e$ is the finite set of odd
natural numbers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of S_e.

articles.title: Odd double factorial below a power of two as an odd-range product
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$e$, $(2^e-1)!!$ equals the product of the odd natural numbers in the closed interval
$[1, 2^e-1]$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of (2^e-1)!!.

articles.title: Congruence of normalized odd double factorials
articles.statement:
For every natural number $e \ge 3$, writing
$(2^k-1)!!$ for the product of the odd numbers from $1$ to $2^k-1$, the integer $2^e$ divides
$(2^e-1)!! - 1$, the integer $2^{e+1}$ divides $(2^{e+1}-1)!! - 1$, and

$$\frac{(2^e-1)!! - 1}{2^e} \equiv \frac{(2^{e+1}-1)!! - 1}{2^{e+1}} \pmod{2^{e-1}}.$$

The source states this for $e \ge 2$, but at $e = 2$ the first quotient is not an integer:
$(2^2-1)!! - 1 = 2$ is not divisible by $4$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Corollary 10.

articles.title: Odd double factorial below a power of two
articles.statement:
For a natural number $e$, $(2^e-1)!!$ is the
product of the odd natural numbers in the closed interval $[1, 2^e-1]$. The parameter is the
exponent $e$, not the odd endpoint $2^e-1$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of (2^e-1)!!.

articles.title: Odd parts biject the upper dyadic half onto the odd numbers below a power of two
articles.statement:
For every natural number $e \ge 1$, the map sending each natural number to its odd part restricts
to a bijection from $I_e = \{i \in \mathbb{N} : 2^{e-1} < i \le 2^e\}$ onto the set $S_e$ of odd
natural numbers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Odd part as a quotient by a power of two
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$\mathrm{od}(n) = n / 2^{\nu_2(n)}$, where $\mathrm{od}(n)$ is the odd part of $n$ and
$\nu_2(n)$ is the exponent of $2$ in the prime factorization of $n$, with $\nu_2(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of od.

articles.title: Odd parts of consecutive dyadic factorials agree modulo a power of two
articles.statement:
For every natural
number $e \ge 3$, $\mathrm{od}((2^{e-1})!) \equiv \mathrm{od}((2^e)!) \pmod{2^e}$, where
$\mathrm{od}(n)$ denotes the odd part of $n$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Corollary 7.

articles.title: Normalized difference of odd parts of dyadic factorials
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{od}(n)$ for the odd
part of $n$, $(2^e-1)!!$ for the product of the odd numbers from $1$ to $2^e-1$, and
$\lfloor x \rfloor$ for the floor of $x$; congruences are taken in the $2$-adic integers
$\mathbb{Z}_2$. Let $z, w \in \mathbb{Z}_2$ satisfy $z \equiv \mathrm{od}((2^{e-1})!) \pmod{2^e}$
for every $e \ge 1$ and $w \equiv \lfloor ((2^e-1)!! - 1)/2^e \rfloor \pmod{2^{e-1}}$ for every
$e \ge 3$. Then for every $e \ge 3$,

$$\lfloor (\mathrm{od}((2^e)!) - \mathrm{od}((2^{e-1})!))/2^e \rfloor \equiv zw \pmod{2^{e-1}}.$$

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Theorem 12.

articles.title: Odd part of a dyadic factorial as a product of odd blocks
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$e \ge 1$,

$$\mathrm{od}((2^e)!) = \prod_{m=2}^{e} h(m)^{e+1-m},$$

where $\mathrm{od}(n)$ is the odd part of $n$ and $h(m)$ is the product of the odd numbers from
$2^{m-1}+1$ to $2^m-1$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Odd part
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n \ge 1$, the odd part $\operatorname{od}(n)$ is
$n / 2^{\nu_2(n)}$, where $2^{\nu_2(n)}$ is the largest power of $2$ dividing $n$; it is the odd
factor of $n$ left after removing that power of $2$. For $n = 0$ the definition gives
$\operatorname{od}(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of od.

articles.title: Initial-segment congruence for the odd product block
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$ and $u$ write
$\operatorname{odpr}(l, u)$ for the product of the odd integers $j$ with $l \le j \le u$, and let
$h(m) = \operatorname{odpr}(2^{m-1}+1, 2^m-1)$. Let $m \ge 4$ and $B$ be natural numbers with
$m - 1 \le B \le 3m - 7$, and put $d = \lfloor (B + 4 - m)/2 \rfloor$, that is,
$d = 2 + \lfloor (B - m)/2 \rfloor$ (so $d = 1$ when $B = m - 1$). Then

$$
h(m) \equiv \operatorname{odpr}\bigl(2^{m-1}+1,\ 2^{m-1}+2^d-1\bigr)^{2^{m-1-d}} \pmod{2^B}.
$$

The paper prints the hypotheses $2 \le m - 1 \le B \le 3m - 7$, which also allow $(m, B) = (3, 2)$.
There $d = 1$, $h(3) = 35$ and the right-hand side is $5^2 = 25$, but $35 - 25 = 10$ is not
divisible by $4$. Requiring $m \ge 4$ removes exactly that case and keeps every other printed case.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Odd product block as an odd-range product
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$, the odd product block
$h(m)$ equals $\operatorname{odpr}(2^{m-1}+1, 2^m-1)$, the product of the odd integers $j$ with
$2^{m-1}+1 \le j \le 2^m-1$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of h.

articles.title: Odd product block
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, the odd product block $h(m)$ is the product of
the odd integers $j$ with $2^{m-1}+1 \le j \le 2^m-1$. In particular $h(0) = h(1) = 1$, as empty
products.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of h.

articles.title: Odd-range product as a filtered product
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $l$ and $m$, the odd-range
product $\operatorname{odpr}(l, m)$ equals the product $\prod j$ over the odd natural numbers $j$ in
the closed interval $[l, m]$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of odpr.

articles.title: Odd-range product
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$ and $m$, the odd-range product
$\operatorname{odpr}(l, m)$ is the product of the odd natural numbers $j$ with $l \le j \le m$;
it equals $1$ when there are none.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of odpr.

articles.title: Shifting the odd numbers below $2^e$ by $2^e$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $e \ge 2$, let $S_e$ be
the set of odd integers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$. Then

$$
\prod_{i \in S_e} i \equiv \prod_{i \in S_e} (2^e + i) \pmod{2^{2e}}.
$$

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Proposition 9.

articles.title: Product of the odd numbers below $2^e$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $e \ge 3$, the product of the
odd integers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$ is congruent to $2^e + 1$ modulo $2^{e+1}$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Shifting the odd numbers below $2^e$ by a multiple of $2^e$
articles.statement:
For every integer $A$ and every
natural number $e \ge 2$, let $S_e$ be the set of odd integers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$. Then

$$
\prod_{i \in S_e} (A \cdot 2^e + i) \equiv \prod_{i \in S_e} i \pmod{2^{3e-1}}.
$$

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Powers of shifted products over the odd numbers below $2^e$
articles.statement:
For all integers $A$ and $B$ and
all natural numbers $j$ and $e$ with $e \ge 2$, let $S_e$ be the set of odd integers $i$ with
$1 \le i < 2^e$. Then

$$
\prod_{i \in S_e} (A \cdot 2^e + i)^{2^j} \equiv \prod_{i \in S_e} (B \cdot 2^e + i)^{2^j}
\pmod{2^{3e-1+j}}.
$$

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Corollary 17.

articles.title: Numbers below $2^e$ congruent to $1$ modulo $8$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $e$, this is the
finite set of natural numbers $n$ with $n < 2^e$ and $n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$.

For $e \ge 3$ its elements are $1, 9, \dots, 2^e - 7$, the sequence displayed in Lemma 21 of
the source.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 21 notation.

articles.title: Unfolding the reversed elementary symmetric function
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$,
natural number $i$ and finite multiset $S$ of elements of $R$ with $n$ elements counted with
multiplicity, the reversed elementary symmetric function satisfies
$\hat\sigma_i(S) = \sigma_{n-i}(S)$, the elementary symmetric function of $S$ of degree $n - i$,
where $n - i$ is truncated subtraction.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of σ̂_i.

articles.title: $\hat\sigma_1$ of four copies of the numbers $1 \bmod 8$ below $2^e$
articles.statement:
Let $e \ge 3$ and let
$M_e$ be the multiset of integers containing each natural number $n < 2^e$ with
$n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ (that is, $1, 9, \dots, 2^e - 7$) exactly four times, let $N$ be the
number of elements of $M_e$ counted with multiplicity, and write $\sigma_k$ for the elementary
symmetric function of degree $k$. Then the reversed elementary symmetric function
$\hat\sigma_1(M_e) = \sigma_{N-1}(M_e)$ satisfies $\hat\sigma_1(M_e) \equiv 2^{e-1} \pmod{2^e}$
in $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 21.

articles.title: $\hat\sigma_1$ of the odd numbers below $2^e$
articles.statement:
Let $e \ge 2$ and let $S_e$ be the set of odd
natural numbers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$, regarded as a multiset of integers with $n$ elements,
and write $\sigma_k$ for the elementary symmetric function of degree $k$. Then the reversed
elementary symmetric function $\hat\sigma_1(S_e) = \sigma_{n-1}(S_e)$ satisfies
$\hat\sigma_1(S_e) \equiv 2^{2e-2} \pmod{2^{2e-1}}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 18.

articles.title: $\hat\sigma_2$ of the odd numbers below $2^e$
articles.statement:
Let $e \ge 2$ and let $S_e$ be the set of odd
natural numbers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$, regarded as a multiset of integers with $n$ elements,
and write $\sigma_k$ for the elementary symmetric function of degree $k$. Then the reversed
elementary symmetric function $\hat\sigma_2(S_e) = \sigma_{n-2}(S_e)$ satisfies
$\hat\sigma_2(S_e) \equiv 2^{e-2} \pmod{2^{e-1}}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 19.

articles.title: Reversed elementary symmetric functions
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let $S$ be a
finite multiset of elements of $R$ with $n$ elements counted with multiplicity, and let $i$ be a
natural number. The reversed elementary symmetric function $\hat\sigma_i(S)$ is
$\sigma_{n-i}(S)$, the elementary symmetric function of degree $n - i$ in the elements of $S$.
Here $n - i$ is truncated subtraction, so $\hat\sigma_i(S) = \sigma_0(S) = 1$ whenever $i \ge n$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of σ̂_i.

articles.title: Each residue $1 \bmod 8$ has four odd square roots modulo $2^e$
articles.statement:
Let $e \ge 3$ and let $S_e$
be the set of odd natural numbers $i$ with $1 \le i < 2^e$. For every natural number $v < 2^e$
with $v \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, exactly four elements $i \in S_e$ satisfy $i^2 \bmod 2^e = v$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Lemma 20.

articles.title: Formula for the stable bits
articles.statement:
Write $\operatorname{od}(n)$ for the odd part of a natural
number $n$. For all natural numbers $s$ and $d$, the stable bits are
$\operatorname{stab}(s, d) = \lfloor \operatorname{od}((2^{s+d-1})!) / 2^s \rfloor \bmod 2^d$,
where $s + d - 1$ is read as $0$ when $s = d = 0$.

For $s = e + 1$ the factorial is that of $2^{e+d}$, the shift is by $e + 1$ binary digits and the
modulus is $2^d$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of stab.

articles.title: The stable bits $\operatorname{stab}(5, 2)$ vanish
articles.statement:
Writing $\operatorname{od}(m)$ for the odd
part of $m$, the binary digits of $\operatorname{od}(64!)$ in positions $5$ and $6$ (the units
digit being position $0$) are both $0$; that is,
$\operatorname{stab}(5, 2) = \lfloor \operatorname{od}(64!) / 2^5 \rfloor \bmod 4 = 0$.

This small instance checks the same factorial, shift and remainder convention as the source's
larger worked example $\operatorname{stab}(18, 7) = 55$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Worked example after Theorem 1.

articles.title: Stable bits of the odd part of a factorial
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $s$ and $d$, let
$\operatorname{stab}(s, d)$ be the number whose binary digits are the digits of
$\operatorname{od}((2^{s+d-1})!)$ in positions $s, \dots, s + d - 1$ (position $0$ being the
units digit), where $\operatorname{od}(m)$ is the odd part of $m$ and $s + d - 1$ is truncated
subtraction. That is,

$$\operatorname{stab}(s, d) = \lfloor \operatorname{od}((2^{s+d-1})!) / 2^s \rfloor \bmod 2^d.$$

For $s = e + 1$ this is the source's $\operatorname{stab}(e + 1, d)$, the digits in positions
$e + 1, \dots, e + d$ of $\operatorname{od}((2^{e+d})!)$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of stab.

articles.title: Squared products of the odd residues omitting one factor
articles.statement:
Let $e \ge 1$ and let
$S_e$ be the set of odd positive integers below $2^e$. Then, as integers,

$$\sum_{i \in S_e} \Bigl(\prod_{j \in S_e \setminus \{i\}} j\Bigr)^2 \equiv 2^{e-1} \pmod{2^e}.$$

Each squared product equals the paper's $((2^e-1)!!)^2/i^2$; the product form avoids an exact
division for every summand.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Proposition 22.

articles.title: Formula for the unstable bits
articles.statement:
Write $\operatorname{od}(n)$ for the odd part of a natural
number $n$. For all natural numbers $e$ and $d$, the unstable bits are
$\operatorname{uns}(e,d) = \lfloor \operatorname{od}((2^e)!) / 2^{e+1} \rfloor \bmod 2^d$.

The binary digits of this number, least significant first, are the paper's first $d$ unstable
bits of $\operatorname{od}((2^e)!)$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of uns.

articles.title: The unstable bits for $e = 4$ and $d = 2$
articles.statement:
The unstable bits $\operatorname{uns}(4,2)$ equal
$3$; that is, $\lfloor \operatorname{od}(16!) / 2^5 \rfloor \bmod 2^2 = 3$, where
$\operatorname{od}(16!)$ is the odd part of $16!$.

This small case stands in for the paper's worked example $\operatorname{uns}(17,7) = 74$.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Worked example after Theorem 1.

articles.title: Unstable bits
articles.statement:
Write $\operatorname{od}(n)$ for the odd part of a natural number $n$. For
natural numbers $e$ and $d$, the unstable bits $\operatorname{uns}(e,d)$ are the natural number
$\lfloor \operatorname{od}((2^e)!) / 2^{e+1} \rfloor \bmod 2^d$, whose binary digits are the $d$
bits of $\operatorname{od}((2^e)!)$ at positions $e+1, \dots, e+d$ (position $0$ being the least
significant bit).

The paper assumes $e > d$ only when stating Theorem 1, so the definition itself is total.

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Definition of uns.

articles.title: The unstable translation constant equals $-zw$
articles.statement:
Write $\operatorname{od}(n)$ for the odd part
of a natural number $n$, $(2^e-1)!!$ for the product of the odd numbers from $1$ to $2^e-1$,
$\operatorname{uns}(e,d) = \lfloor \operatorname{od}((2^e)!)/2^{e+1} \rfloor \bmod 2^d$ and
$\operatorname{stab}(e+1,d) = \lfloor \operatorname{od}((2^{e+d})!)/2^{e+1} \rfloor \bmod 2^d$.
Let $K$, $z$ and $w$ be $2$-adic integers such that, with congruences in $\mathbb{Z}_2$,
$\operatorname{uns}(e,d) + K \equiv \operatorname{stab}(e+1,d) \pmod{2^d}$ for all natural
numbers $d < e$, $z \equiv \operatorname{od}((2^{e-1})!) \pmod{2^e}$ for all $e \ge 1$, and
$w \equiv \lfloor ((2^e-1)!! - 1)/2^e \rfloor \pmod{2^{e-1}}$ for all $e \ge 3$. Then $K = -zw$.

The three hypotheses are the defining properties of $K$ (Theorem 1), $z$ (Corollary 8) and $w$
(the definition after Corollary 10).

## Sources

- Donald M. Davis, *Some 2-adic Integers Related to the Odd Part of 2^e!*, Journal of Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Article 26.3.1, Theorem 14.

articles.title: Absolute values on finite fields are trivial
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a finite field and $v$ a
real-valued absolute value on $K$. Then $v(x) = 1$ for every nonzero $x \in K$.

articles.title: Absolute values inducing the same topology are equivalent
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and
$v$, $w$ real-valued absolute values on $K$. The topologies induced on $K$ by $v$ and by $w$
are equal if and only if $v$ and $w$ are equivalent.

This is about equality of the induced topologies on $K$, not about equality
of the absolute values themselves: inequivalent absolute values may still agree
on many elements while inducing different topologies.

articles.title: Topology induced by an absolute value
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued absolute
value on $K$. The topology induced by $v$ on $K$ is the topology pulled back along the identity
map from $K$ to $K$ equipped with the norm $v$; equivalently, it is the metric topology of the
distance $d(x, y) = v(x - y)$ on $K$.

articles.title: Nonarchimedean criterion using positive integers
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued
absolute value on $K$. Then $v$ is nonarchimedean, that is, $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for
all $x, y \in K$, if and only if $v(n) \le 1$ for every positive integer $n$, viewed as the
element $n \cdot 1$ of $K$.

The case $n = 0$ may be omitted because $v(0) = 0 \le 1$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI, Section 1.2, Lemma 1.4 (in the book's form).

articles.title: Nonarchimedean criterion for absolute values
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued
absolute value on $K$. Then $v$ is nonarchimedean, that is, $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for
all $x, y \in K$, if and only if $v(n) \le 1$ for every natural number $n$, viewed as the element
$n \cdot 1$ of $K$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI, Section 1.2, Lemma 1.4.

articles.title: Absolute values in positive characteristic are nonarchimedean
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field of
characteristic $p > 0$. Then every real-valued absolute value $v$ on $K$ is nonarchimedean:
$v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K$.

articles.title: Absolute values bounded by one on the natural numbers are nonarchimedean
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $K$. If $v(n) \le 1$ for every natural
number $n$, viewed as the element $n \cdot 1$ of $K$, then $v$ is nonarchimedean:
$v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K$.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI, Section 1.2, backward direction of Lemma 1.4.

articles.title: Values of a power of an absolute value
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a semiring, $v$ a real-valued
absolute value on $R$ and $c$ a real number with $0 < c \le 1$. The $c$-th power of $v$ takes
the value $v(x)^c$ at every $x \in R$.

articles.title: Powers of an absolute value
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a semiring, $v$ a real-valued absolute value
on $R$ and $c$ a real number with $0 < c \le 1$. The $c$-th power of $v$ is the real-valued
absolute value $x \mapsto v(x)^c$ on $R$.

articles.title: Cassels' embedding theorem
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and $S$ a finite
subset of $K$. Then there are a prime $p \ge 3$ and an injective ring homomorphism from the subring
of $K$ generated by $S$ into the ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers.

## Sources

- J. W. S. Cassels, "An embedding theorem for fields", Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. 14 (1976), 193–198.

articles.title: For odd $p$, a binary unit form over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ represents a unit square
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an
odd prime and let $u, v$ be units of $\mathbb{Z}_p$. Then there are $x_0, y_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_p$ and
a unit $z_0$ of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with $z_0^2 = u x_0^2 + v y_0^2$.

## Sources

- Lemma 10.5, key step.

articles.title: Unit diagonal forms in at least three variables over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ are isotropic for odd $p$
articles.statement:
**Unit diagonal forms in at least three variables over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ are isotropic for odd
$p$.** Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $n > 2$, and let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be units of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
Then there is a nonzero vector $(x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathbb{Q}_p^n$ with
$a_1 x_1^2 + \dots + a_n x_n^2 = 0$.

## Sources

- ArithmeticGeometry:75.

articles.title: Real Hilbert symbol equal to $-1$
articles.statement:
For nonzero real numbers $a$ and $b$, the real Hilbert
symbol of $a$ and $b$ equals $-1$ if and only if there are no real numbers $x, y$ with
$a x^2 + b y^2 = 1$.

articles.title: Sign rule for the real Hilbert symbol
articles.statement:
For nonzero real numbers $a$ and $b$, the real
Hilbert symbol of $a$ and $b$ equals $-1$ if and only if $a < 0$ and $b < 0$.

articles.title: When the $p$-adic Hilbert symbol is $-1$
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and nonzero
$a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_p$, the $p$-adic Hilbert symbol $(a, b)_p$ equals $-1$ if and only if there
are no $x, y \in \mathbb{Q}_p$ with $ax^2 + by^2 = 1$.

articles.title: Real Hilbert symbol equal to $1$
articles.statement:
For nonzero real numbers $a$ and $b$, the real Hilbert
symbol of $a$ and $b$ equals $1$ if and only if there are real numbers $x, y$ with
$a x^2 + b y^2 = 1$.

articles.title: When the $p$-adic Hilbert symbol is $1$
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and nonzero
$a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_p$, the $p$-adic Hilbert symbol $(a, b)_p$ equals $1$ if and only if there
exist $x, y \in \mathbb{Q}_p$ with $ax^2 + by^2 = 1$.

articles.title: The $p$-adic Hilbert symbol is $\pm 1$
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and all nonzero
$a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_p$, the $p$-adic Hilbert symbol $(a, b)_p$ equals $1$ or $-1$.

articles.title: The real Hilbert symbol is $\pm 1$
articles.statement:
For nonzero real numbers $a$ and $b$, the real Hilbert
symbol of $a$ and $b$ equals $1$ or $-1$.

articles.title: The Hilbert symbol of a field is $\pm 1$
articles.statement:
For every field $F$ and all nonzero
$a, b \in F$, the Hilbert symbol $(a, b)_F$ of $a$ and $b$ over $F$ equals $1$ or $-1$.

articles.title: The Hilbert symbol of two $p$-adic units is trivial for odd $p$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime
and let $u, v$ be units of $\mathbb{Z}_p$. Then the $p$-adic Hilbert symbol of $u$ and $v$, viewed
as units of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, equals $1$.

## Sources

- Lemma 10.5.

articles.title: Hilbert symbol of a field
articles.statement:
For a field $F$ and nonzero elements $a, b \in F$, the Hilbert
symbol $(a, b)_F$ is the integer $1$ if there exist $x, y \in F$ with $ax^2 + by^2 = 1$, and $-1$
otherwise.

articles.title: Solvability of $ax^2 + by^2 = 1$
articles.statement:
For a field $F$ and nonzero elements $a, b \in F$, the
equation $ax^2 + by^2 = 1$ is solvable over $F$ if there exist $x, y \in F$ with
$ax^2 + by^2 = 1$.

articles.title: The $p$-adic Hilbert symbol
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and nonzero $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_p$, the
$p$-adic Hilbert symbol $(a, b)_p$ is the integer $1$ if there exist $x, y \in \mathbb{Q}_p$ with
$ax^2 + by^2 = 1$, and $-1$ otherwise.

articles.title: Real Hilbert symbol
articles.statement:
For nonzero real numbers $a$ and $b$, the real Hilbert symbol of $a$
and $b$ is the integer $1$ if there are real numbers $x, y$ with $a x^2 + b y^2 = 1$, and the
integer $-1$ otherwise.

articles.title: Value of the inclusion of $p$-adic integer units
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$ and a unit $u$ of
$\mathbb{Z}_p$, the image of $u$ under the inclusion of the units of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ into the units
of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, viewed as an element of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, equals $u$ viewed as an element of
$\mathbb{Q}_p$.

articles.title: Inclusion of $p$-adic integer units
articles.statement:
For a prime $p$, this is the map from the units of
$\mathbb{Z}_p$ to the units of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ induced by the inclusion
$\mathbb{Z}_p \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_p$.

articles.title: p-adic integrality is equivalent to norm at most one
articles.statement:
An element of the algebraic closure of `ℚ_[p]` is integral over `ℤ_[p]`
if and only if its norm is at most one.

articles.title: Krasner's lemma for closest conjugates
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a complete nontrivially normed field
whose norm is ultrametric, with algebraic closure $\overline{K}$, and let
$\alpha, \beta \in \overline{K}$. If $\alpha$ is the closest conjugate to $\beta$ and $\alpha$ is
separable over $K$, then $K(\alpha) \subseteq K(\beta)$.

articles.title: Closest conjugate roots of nearby monic polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a complete nontrivially
normed field whose norm is ultrametric, with algebraic closure $\overline{K}$, and let
$f \in K[X]$ be monic, irreducible and separable. Then there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that for
every monic $g \in K[X]$ with $\lVert f - g \rVert_1 < \delta$, where $\lVert \cdot \rVert_1$ is
