$L_1, L_2$ are the products of two disjoint sets of primes, and $k_1, k_2$ come from Lemmas 4 and
5; the statement keeps only the hypotheses the conclusion uses.

## Sources

- Thomas Wright, *(a,a)-Carmichael Numbers and Greatest Common Divisors of p-a*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A123, Section 5 (definition of `𝒫^i_k`) and Lemma 6.

articles.title: Primes are $(a, a)$-Carmichael numbers
articles.statement:
For every integer $a$, every prime $p$ is an
$(a, a)$-Carmichael number.

## Sources

- Thomas Wright, *(a,a)-Carmichael Numbers and Greatest Common Divisors of p-a*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A123, characteristic lemma of the definition in Section 1.

articles.title: $(a, a)$-Carmichael numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an integer. A natural number $n$ is an
$(a, a)$-Carmichael number if $n$ is squarefree and $p - a$ divides $n - a$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ for
every prime $p$ dividing $n$.

## Sources

- Thomas Wright, *(a,a)-Carmichael Numbers and Greatest Common Divisors of p-a*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A123, abstract and Section 1 (definition read from the arXiv version, arXiv:2607.02738; the journal display could not be checked).

articles.title: Size of the auxiliary primes in the construction
articles.statement:
For a natural number $z$, let $J$ be the
product of the primes $r$ with $z/2 \le r \le z$, and write $\omega(g)$ for the number of distinct
prime factors of $g$. For every real $A$ and all sufficiently large natural numbers $z$ the
following holds: if $j$, $g$ and $q$ are natural numbers with $1 \le j \le (\log z)^{2A}$,
$g \mid J$, $\omega(g) = \lfloor \log z \rfloor$, $q$ prime and $q = gj + 1$, then

$$(z/6)^{\log z} \le q \le 2 z^{\log z} (\log z)^{2A}.$$

In the paper the bound is stated for the primes $q$ of a chosen set $\mathcal{Q}_i$ of such primes
with a fixed $j = j_0$, and $A \ge 2$ is the constant of Conjecture 2; the statement here covers
every such $j$ and $q$, and every real $A$.

## Sources

- Thomas Wright, *(a,a)-Carmichael Numbers and Greatest Common Divisors of p-a*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A123, Section 3 (definitions of `J`, `𝓡_j`, `𝒬ᵢ`) and Lemma 1.

articles.title: Infinitely many Fibonacci pseudoprimes at twice-prime indices
articles.statement:
Let $F_m$ denote the
$m$-th Fibonacci number. There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $n = F_{2p}$ satisfies
$n > 1$, $n$ is not prime, and $n$ divides $F_{n - \left(\frac{5}{n}\right)}$, where
$\left(\frac{5}{n}\right)$ is the Jacobi symbol. In other words, $F_{2p}$ is a Fibonacci
pseudoprime: a composite number $n$ that divides $F_{n - \left(\frac{5}{n}\right)}$.

## Sources

- Y. Hamahata and Y. Kokubun, "Cipolla Pseudoprimes," Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Article 07.8.6, Corollary 4 [Lehmer], lines 321–324 (Fibonacci-pseudoprime definition at lines 313–318), https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL10/Hamahata2/hamahata44.tex

articles.title: Lucas–Lehmer test with a general seed
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an odd natural number, let
$M_n = 2^n - 1$, and let $s_1$ be an integer. Define $s_{k+1} = s_k^2 - 2$ for $k \ge 1$. If the
Jacobi symbols satisfy $\left(\frac{s_1 + 2}{M_n}\right) = -1$ and
$\left(\frac{s_1 - 2}{M_n}\right) = 1$, then $M_n$ is prime if and only if $M_n$ divides
$s_{n-1}$.

In the terminology of Roettger and Williams, such a seed $s_1$ is acceptable: the Lucas–Lehmer
test started at $s_1$ decides the primality of $M_n$ (their Assertion A).

Proof: Following Mathlib's Lucas-Lehmer order argument, sufficiency uses a quadratic extension
and the least prime factor; necessity uses the Jacobi conditions and Frobenius conjugation as in
Lehmer (1930) and Roettger-Williams (2025).

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, "Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test," Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Theorem, lines 814–819; Assertion A at lines 187–190, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Roettger/roettger15.tex

articles.title: Condition (etar) fails for some reduced residue when $s_1^- \equiv 3 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let
$s_1 \ge 3$ be an integer, let $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ be the odd squarefree parts of $s_1 - 2$ and
$s_1 + 2$, and let $\Omega = \Omega(s_1^- s_1^+)$ be the order of $2$ modulo $s_1^- s_1^+$,
doubled when it is odd. If $s_1^- \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, then there is a natural number $n$ with
$1 \le n < \Omega$ and $\gcd(n, \Omega) = 1$ for which condition (etar) for $s_1^-$, $s_1^+$
and $n$ fails.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Lemma 13.

articles.title: Condition (etar) fails for some reduced residue when $s_1^+ \equiv 1 \pmod 4$
articles.statement:
Let
$s_1 \ge 3$ be an integer, let $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ be the odd squarefree parts of $s_1 - 2$ and
$s_1 + 2$, and let $\Omega = \Omega(s_1^- s_1^+)$ be the order of $2$ modulo $s_1^- s_1^+$,
doubled when it is odd. If $s_1^+ \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then there is a natural number $n$ with
$1 \le n < \Omega$ and $\gcd(n, \Omega) = 1$ for which condition (etar) for $s_1^-$, $s_1^+$
and $n$ fails.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Lemma 14.

articles.title: Infinitely many acceptable seeds with the same odd squarefree parts
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ be a
natural number and $M_n = 2^n - 1$. For an integer $S$ put $S_1 = S$ and $S_{k+1} = S_k^2 - 2$,
and call $S$ an acceptable seed for $M_n$ if $M_n$ is prime exactly when $M_n$ divides
$S_{n-1}$. Let $s_1 \ge 3$ be an integer that is an acceptable seed for $M_n$, and let $s_1^-$
and $s_1^+$ be the odd squarefree parts of $s_1 - 2$ and $s_1 + 2$. Then there are infinitely
many integers $S \ge 3$ that are acceptable seeds for $M_n$ and for which $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$
are the odd squarefree parts of $S - 2$ and $S + 2$.

Seeds are taken $\ge 3$ (the paper's seeds are nonnegative, and the odd squarefree part of
$S - 2$ needs $S - 2 > 0$).

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Theorem 10.

articles.title: The odd squarefree part of $360$
articles.statement:
The number $5$ is the odd squarefree part of $360$:
$5$ is odd and squarefree, and $360 = 2^a m^2 \cdot 5$ for some natural number $a$ and some
integer $m$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 7 (example `10 = sqf(360)`).

articles.title: Odd squarefree part
articles.statement:
For an integer $N$ and a natural number $k$, $k$ is an odd
squarefree part of $N$, written $N^* = k$, when $k$ is odd and squarefree and $N = 2^a m^2 k$
for some natural number $a$ and some integer $m$.

For positive $N$ such a $k$ is unique: it is the squarefree part of $N$ when that is odd, and
half of it otherwise.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 7 (definition of `N^*`).

articles.title: Fourth-order recurrence of Lehmer's companion sequence
articles.statement:
For all integers $R$ and $Q$ and
every natural number $k$, Lehmer's companion sequence satisfies
$\bar V_{k+4}(R, Q) = (R - 2Q)\,\bar V_{k+2}(R, Q) - Q^2\,\bar V_k(R, Q)$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 2, recurrence (4thLehmer).

articles.title: Lehmer's companion sequence for $R = 2$ and $Q = -1$
articles.statement:
For $R = 2$ and $Q = -1$, Lehmer's
companion sequence has $\bar V_2(2, -1) = 4$, $\bar V_4(2, -1) = 14$ and
$\bar V_8(2, -1) = 194$.

These are the parameters giving the seed $4$, and $14 = 4^2 - 2$ and $194 = 14^2 - 2$, as the
doubling formula (LehmerV2n) predicts.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 2 (formula (LehmerV2n) and the case `R = 2`, `Q = -1` after Theorem 6).

articles.title: Lehmer's companion sequence
articles.statement:
For integers $R$ and $Q$, Lehmer's companion sequence
$\bar V_k(R, Q)$, $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, is the integer sequence with $\bar V_0 = 2$,
$\bar V_1 = 1$, $\bar V_2 = R - 2Q$, $\bar V_3 = R - 3Q$ and
$\bar V_{k+4} = (R - 2Q)\,\bar V_{k+2} - Q^2\,\bar V_k$ for every $k \ge 0$.

With $P = \sqrt R$ and the Lucas sequence $V_k(P, Q)$ given by $V_0 = 2$, $V_1 = P$ and
$V_{k+2} = P V_{k+1} - Q V_k$, for $R \ne 0$ the term $\bar V_k(R, Q)$ equals $V_k(\sqrt R, Q)$
for even $k$ and $V_k(\sqrt R, Q)/\sqrt R$ for odd $k$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 2 (definition of `V̄_n` and recurrence (4thLehmer)).

articles.title: Divisibility of Lehmer's companion sequence by a Mersenne prime, Diophantine form
articles.statement:
Let
$n \ge 3$ be an odd natural number such that $M_n = 2^n - 1$ is prime, and let $r$, $d$, $q$,
$X$, $Y$, $Z$ be integers with $\gcd(M_n, Y) = 1$ and $4qY^2 = rX^2 - dZ^2$. Put $R = rX^2$ and
$Q = qY^2$, and let $\bar V_k(R, Q)$ denote Lehmer's companion sequence. If the Jacobi symbols
$\left(\frac{rd}{M_n}\right)$ and $\left(\frac{qr}{M_n}\right)$ are both $-1$, then $M_n$ divides
$\bar V_{(M_n+1)/2}(R, Q) = \bar V_{2^{n-1}}(R, Q)$.

Here $D = R - 4Q = dZ^2$, and since $M_n$ is prime the Jacobi symbols are Legendre symbols.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Divisibility of Lehmer's companion sequence by a Mersenne prime
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an odd
natural number such that $M_n = 2^n - 1$ is prime, let $R$ and $Q$ be integers, let
$\bar V_k(R, Q)$ denote Lehmer's companion sequence, and put $D = R - 4Q$. If the Jacobi symbols
$\left(\frac{DR}{M_n}\right)$ and $\left(\frac{QR}{M_n}\right)$ are both $-1$, then $M_n$
divides $\bar V_{(M_n+1)/2}(R, Q) = \bar V_{2^{n-1}}(R, Q)$.

Since $M_n$ is prime, these Jacobi symbols are Legendre symbols.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Condition (etar) for the seed $37$
articles.statement:
For the seed $s_1 = 37$, the odd squarefree parts of
$s_1 - 2 = 35$ and $s_1 + 2 = 39$ are $s_1^- = 35$ and $s_1^+ = 39$. Condition (etar) for
$s_1^- = 35$ and $s_1^+ = 39$ holds for $n = 7$ and fails for $n = 1$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 7 (example `s_1 = 37`, `𝒜(37) = {7}`).

articles.title: Condition (etar) fails for some reduced residue when the seed is odd
articles.statement:
Let $s_1 \ge 3$ be
an odd integer, let $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ be the odd squarefree parts of $s_1 - 2$ and $s_1 + 2$,
and let $\Omega = \Omega(s_1^- s_1^+)$. Then the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n < \Omega$
and $\gcd(n, \Omega) = 1$ for which condition (etar) holds for $s_1^-$, $s_1^+$ and $n$ is not
equal to $\varphi(\Omega)$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Corollary 16.

articles.title: Condition (etar) on Jacobi symbols of $M_n$
articles.statement:
Let $s^-$, $s^+$ and $n$ be natural
numbers and let $M_n = 2^n - 1$. For a natural number $s$ write $\left(\frac{M_n}{s}\right)$ for
the Jacobi symbol, the product of the Legendre symbols $\left(\frac{M_n}{p}\right)$ over the
prime factors $p$ of $s$ counted with multiplicity (so it is $1$ for $s = 0$ and $s = 1$).
Condition (etar) holds for $s^-$, $s^+$ and $n$ when $s^- = 1$ or
$\left(\frac{M_n}{s^-}\right) = (-1)^{(s^- - 1)/2}$, and moreover
$\left(\frac{M_n}{s^+}\right) = (-1)^{(s^+ + 1)/2}$. Here the exponents are rounded down, and
$s^- - 1$ is read as $0$ when $s^- = 0$.

In the source, $s^-$ and $s^+$ are the odd squarefree parts $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ of $s_1 - 2$
and $s_1 + 2$ for a seed $s_1$. For squarefree $s$ the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{M_n}{s}\right)$
is the product of $\eta_n(p) = \left(\frac{M_n}{p}\right)$ over the primes $p$ dividing $s$,
which is how the source states the condition.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 7, condition (etar).

articles.title: $\Omega$ for the seed $37$
articles.statement:
We have $\Omega(1365) = 12$, where $\Omega(m)$ is the
multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $m$, doubled when that order is odd. Here $1365 = 35 \cdot 39$
is the product of the odd squarefree parts $35$ of $37 - 2$ and $39$ of $37 + 2$, the parts
$s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ for the seed $s_1 = 37$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 7 (example `s_1 = 37`).

articles.title: The order $\Omega(m)$ of $2$, doubled when odd
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, let $\omega(m)$
be the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $m$, taken to be $0$ when no positive power of $2$ is
congruent to $1$ modulo $m$ (that is, when $m$ is even). Then $\Omega(m) = 2\omega(m)$ if
$\omega(m)$ is odd, and $\Omega(m) = \omega(m)$ otherwise.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Section 7 (definitions of `ω(m)` and `Ω(m)`).

articles.title: Lucas–Lehmer test with the rational seed $6/5$
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$, let $M_n = 2^n - 1$, and
define $s_1 = 6 \cdot 5^{-1}$ and $s_{k+1} = s_k^2 - 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}/M_n\mathbb{Z}$. If
$n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, then $M_n$ is prime if and only if $s_{n-1} = 0$. If $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$,
then $M_n$ is prime if and only if $s_{n-2} = 0$.

In both cases $n$ is odd, so $5$ does not divide $M_n$ and $5^{-1}$ is the inverse of $5$
modulo $M_n$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Theorem 17.

articles.title: Lehmer-sequence primality criterion for Mersenne numbers
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ be odd, let
$M_n = 2^n - 1$, and let $R$ and $Q$ be integers with $\gcd(M_n, Q) = 1$. If $M_n$ divides
Lehmer's companion term $\bar V_{2^{n-1}}(R, Q)$, then $M_n$ is prime.

Here $2^{n-1} = (M_n + 1)/2$. No coprimality of $R$ and $Q$ and no condition on $D = R - 4Q$
is assumed.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Residues mod $4$ of $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ when (etar) always holds
articles.statement:
Let $s_1 \ge 3$ be an
integer, let $s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ be the odd squarefree parts of $s_1 - 2$ and $s_1 + 2$, and let
$\Omega = \Omega(s_1^- s_1^+)$. If the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n < \Omega$ and
$\gcd(n, \Omega) = 1$ for which condition (etar) holds for $s_1^-$, $s_1^+$ and $n$ equals
$\varphi(\Omega)$, then $s_1^- \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $s_1^+ \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Theorem 15.

articles.title: A zero Legendre symbol forces $\gcd(n, \Omega) > 1$
articles.statement:
Let $s_1 \ge 3$ be an integer, let
$s_1^-$ and $s_1^+$ be the odd squarefree parts of $s_1 - 2$ and $s_1 + 2$, and let
$\Omega = \Omega(s_1^- s_1^+)$. Let $p$ be a prime dividing $s_1^- s_1^+$, let $n$ be a natural
number and let $M_n = 2^n - 1$. If the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{M_n}{p}\right)$ is $0$, then
$\gcd(n, \Omega) > 1$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Proposition 12.

articles.title: Order of $2$ modulo a product of coprime odd numbers
articles.statement:
Let $m_1$ and $m_2$ be coprime odd
natural numbers, and write $\omega(m)$ for the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $m$. Then
$\omega(m_1 m_2) = \operatorname{lcm}(\omega(m_1), \omega(m_2))$.

The printed $\operatorname{lcm}(\omega(m_1)\omega(m_2))$ is read as
$\operatorname{lcm}(\omega(m_1), \omega(m_2))$; the product reading fails, since $\omega(15) = 4$
while $\omega(3)\omega(5) = 8$.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Proposition 11.

articles.title: Euler's family of solutions of $aT^2 - bU^2 = c$
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be integers
with $ab > 1$, $ab$ not a perfect square and $c \ne 0$, and let $T_1$, $U_1$ be integers with
$aT_1^2 - bU_1^2 = c$. Let $\varepsilon = x_1 + y_1\sqrt{ab}$ be the fundamental solution of
$x^2 - ab\,y^2 = 1$ and, for every natural number $j$, write
$\varepsilon^j = x_j + y_j\sqrt{ab}$. Then for every $j \ge 0$ the integers
$T = T_1 x_j + b U_1 y_j$ and $U = a T_1 y_j + U_1 x_j$ satisfy $aT^2 - bU^2 = c$, and different
$j$ give different pairs $(T, U)$.

The hypothesis $c \ne 0$ is added to the source statement: for $c = 0$ the only integer solution
is $(0, 0)$, since $ab$ is not a square.

## Sources

- E. L. Roettger and H. C. Williams, *Some Remarks Concerning the Lucas-Lehmer Primality Test*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.2.5, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Pocklington's criterion for $N = Kp^e + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $N$, $K$ and $e$ be natural numbers and
let $p$ be a prime, with $0 < K < p^e$ and $N = Kp^e + 1$. If some natural number $a$ satisfies
$a^{N-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{N}$ and $\gcd\big(a^{(N-1)/p} - 1, N\big) = 1$, where $(N-1)/p$ is the
quotient of $N - 1$ by $p$ rounded down and $a^{(N-1)/p} - 1$ is truncated at $0$, then $N$ is
prime.

Proof: The proof follows Pocklington's standard least-prime-factor order argument, from
Pocklington (1914) as stated by Grau and Oller-Marcen, arXiv:1011.4836v3, lines 60-69.

## Sources

- Pocklington (1914), as stated in Grau and Oller-Marcen, "A primality test for Kp^n+1 numbers", arXiv:1011.4836v3, lines 60-69, which give the complete condition, including gcd(a^((N-1)/p)-1,N)=1. The source's integer witness a ∈ ℤ is represented here by a natural residue representative a : ℕ, using Nat.ModEq and Nat.gcd with natural subtraction in the exponents.

articles.title: Proth's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $h$ odd and $h < 2^k$, and let
$N = h \cdot 2^k + 1$. Then $N$ is prime if and only if there is a residue class $a$ modulo $N$
with $a^{(N-1)/2} = -1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.

Proof: The forward implication uses a nonsquare and Euler's criterion; the reverse uses Proth's
least-prime-factor order argument. Sources: Proth (1878), p. 926, and the Wikipedia exposition.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proth%27s_theorem

articles.title: Number of Fermat pseudoprime bases (Monier; Baillie–Wagstaff)
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be a
composite natural number. Then the number of integers $b$ with $1 \le b < n$ such that $n$ is a
Fermat pseudoprime to the base $b$, that is, $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, equals
$\prod_p \gcd(n - 1, p - 1)$, where $p$ runs over the distinct prime divisors of $n$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Monier's formula for the number of strong pseudoprime bases
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be an odd composite
natural number, let $r$ be the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, and let $v$ be the least
of the $2$-adic valuations of $p - 1$ over the prime divisors $p$ of $n$. Write $d$ for the odd
part of $n - 1$ and $d_p$ for the odd part of $p - 1$. Then the number of integers $b$ with
$1 \le b < n$ such that $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $b$ equals, as a rational number,

$$\left(1 + \frac{2^{vr} - 1}{2^r - 1}\right) \prod_p \gcd(d, d_p),$$

where the product runs over the distinct prime divisors $p$ of $n$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 3, Formula (5).

articles.title: Strong pseudoprime bases $2^{2^{k-1}+t} \pm 2^t$ of composite Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
natural number such that the Fermat number $F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1$ is composite. Then for every
natural number $t$, $F_k$ is a strong pseudoprime to both bases $2^{2^{k-1}+t} + 2^t$ and
$2^{2^{k-1}+t} - 2^t$, computed modulo $F_k$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Composite Fermat numbers are strong pseudoprimes to every power of $2$
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
natural number such that the Fermat number $F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1$ is composite. Then for every
integer $t$, $F_k$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $2^t$, where the power is taken in the
unit group of $\mathbb{Z}/F_k\mathbb{Z}$ (in which $2$ is a unit because $F_k$ is odd).

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Corollary 5.

articles.title: A subgroup of strong pseudoprime bases of a composite Fermat number
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural
number such that the Fermat number $F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1$ is composite, and let $S_k$ be the set of
residues modulo $F_k$ of the form $2^t$, $2^{2^{k-1}+t} + 2^t$ or $2^{2^{k-1}+t} - 2^t$ with $t$ a
natural number. Then the units of $\mathbb{Z}/F_k\mathbb{Z}$ that lie in $S_k$ form a subgroup of
the unit group of order $2^{k+2}$, and $F_k$ is a strong pseudoprime to every base in $S_k$.

The source also asserts that this subgroup is isomorphic to $C_{2^{k+1}} \times C_2$. This is
false: the residue $2^{16} + 1$ has multiplicative order $128 = 2^{k+2}$ modulo $F_5$, so the
subgroup is cyclic for $k = 5$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 8.

articles.title: The subgroup criteria for strong pseudoprime bases hold almost always
articles.statement:
For an odd
composite natural number $n$, let $r$ be the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, let $v$ be
the least of the $2$-adic valuations of $p - 1$ over the prime divisors $p$ of $n$, and consider
the conditions: (a) the units $b$ of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ such that $n$ is a strong
pseudoprime to the base $b$ form a subgroup of the unit group; (b) the number of integers $b$
with $1 \le b < n$ to which $n$ is a strong pseudoprime divides the number of integers $b$ with
$1 \le b < n$ to which $n$ is a Fermat pseudoprime; (c) $v = 1$ or $r = 1$; (d) some prime
$p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ divides $n$, or $n$ is a prime power. Then the set of odd composite natural
numbers $n$ for which at least one of (a)–(d) fails has natural density $0$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Strong pseudoprime bases almost always form a subgroup
articles.statement:
The set of odd composite natural
numbers $n$ for which the units $b$ of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ such that $n$ is a strong
pseudoprime to the base $b$ do not form a subgroup of the unit group has natural density $0$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Products of two distinct primes have a square number of Fermat pseudoprime bases
articles.statement:
Let
$p$ and $q$ be distinct primes. Then the number of integers $b$ with $1 \le b < pq$ such that
$pq$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to the base $b$, that is, $b^{pq-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{pq}$, is a perfect
square.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Corollary 1.

articles.title: 2047 is a strong pseudoprime to base 2
articles.statement:
The number $2047 = 23 \cdot 89$ is a strong
pseudoprime to the base $2$.

Indeed $2046 = 2 \cdot 1023$ with $1023$ odd, and $2^{1023} = (2^{11})^{93} = 1$ modulo $2047$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Section 1 (first strong pseudoprime to base 2 in the list given there).

articles.title: Unfolded definition of strong pseudoprimes
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $b$ a residue
class modulo $n$. Then $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $b$ if and only if $n > 1$, $n$ is
not prime, $n$ is odd, and there are natural numbers $k$ and $d$ with $n - 1 = 2^k d$ and $d$ odd
such that $b^d = 1$ or $b^{2^i d} = -1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ for some $i < k$.

articles.title: Composite divisors of primitive parts without their intrinsic factor are strong pseudoprimes
articles.statement:
**Composite divisors of primitive parts without their intrinsic factor are strong
pseudoprimes.** Let $b > 1$ and $m > 2$ be natural numbers, and let $\Phi_j$ denote the $j$-th
cyclotomic polynomial. If a composite natural number $c > 1$ divides
$\Phi_m(b) / \gcd(\Phi_m(b), m)$ or $\Phi_{2m}(b) / \gcd(\Phi_{2m}(b), m)$, then $c$ is a strong
pseudoprime to the base $b$.

Here $\Phi_m(b)$ and $\Phi_{2m}(b)$ are the primitive parts of $b^m - 1$ and $b^m + 1$, and
dividing by the greatest common divisor with $m$ removes the intrinsic prime factor, if any.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Every odd composite is a strong pseudoprime to base 1
articles.statement:
Every odd composite number $n$
is a strong pseudoprime to the base $1$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, proof of Theorem 6 ("every composite `n` is spsp(1)").

articles.title: Strong pseudoprime bases are closed under powers and negation
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number and $b$ a unit of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ such that $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the
base $b$. Then for every integer $t$, $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $b^t$, and $n$ is a
strong pseudoprime to the base $-b$.

Requiring $b$ to be a unit loses nothing, since every strong pseudoprime base $b$ satisfies
$b^{n-1} = 1$; it also gives meaning to negative exponents.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Composite divisors of primitive parts without the intrinsic factor are strong pseudoprimes to every power of the base
articles.statement:
**Composite divisors of primitive parts without the intrinsic factor are strong pseudoprimes to
every power of the base.** Let $b > 1$ and $m > 2$ be natural numbers, write $\Phi_j(b)$ for the
value at $b$ of the $j$-th cyclotomic polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}$, and let $c > 1$ be a natural
number that is not prime. If $c$ divides $\Phi_m(b) / \gcd(\Phi_m(b), m)$ or
$\Phi_{2m}(b) / \gcd(\Phi_{2m}(b), m)$, then for every unit $u$ of $\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}$ equal
to the residue class of $b$ and every integer $t$, $c$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $u^t$.

These two quotients are the primitive parts of $b^m - 1$ and $b^m + 1$ with the intrinsic factor
removed.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Strong pseudoprime
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and $b$ a residue class modulo $n$. Then
$n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $b$ if $n$ is an odd composite number (that is, $n > 1$,
$n$ is odd and $n$ is not prime) and there are natural numbers $k$ and $d$ with $d$ odd and
$n - 1 = 2^k d$ such that either $b^d = 1$ or $b^{2^i d} = -1$ for some $i < k$, where the
powers are computed in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

For odd composite $n$ the decomposition $n - 1 = 2^k d$ with $d$ odd is unique, so the
existential agrees with the usual definition for the fixed $k$ and $d$. An integer base is used
through its residue class modulo $n$.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Section 1, Congruences (2) and (3).

articles.title: Strong pseudoprimes are not prime
articles.statement:
If $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to some base $b$
modulo $n$, then $n$ is not prime.

articles.title: Strong pseudoprimes are odd
articles.statement:
If $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to some base $b$ modulo $n$,
then $n$ is odd.

articles.title: Strong pseudoprimes exceed one
articles.statement:
If $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to some base $b$ modulo
$n$, then $n > 1$.

articles.title: When the strong pseudoprime bases form a subgroup
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be an odd number that is
not prime, let $r$ be the number of distinct prime factors of $n$, and let $v$ be the least
exponent of $2$ in $p - 1$ over the prime factors $p$ of $n$. Then the following are equivalent:
(a) there is a subgroup of the unit group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ whose elements are
exactly the units $u$ such that $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $u$; (b) the number of
$b$ with $1 \le b < n$ such that $n$ is a strong pseudoprime to the base $b$ divides the number
of $b$ with $1 \le b < n$ such that $n$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to the base $b$, that is,
$n \mid b^{n-1} - 1$; (c) $v = 1$ or $r = 1$; (d) some prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ divides $n$,
or $n$ is a prime power.

## Sources

- Samuel S. Wagstaff, Jr., *Pseudoprimes and Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A23, Theorem 4.

articles.title: $s$-Cullen numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $s$ and $n$, write $C_{n,s} = n s^n + 1$ for the
$s$-Cullen value. A natural number $m$ is an $s$-Cullen number when $s \ge 2$ and $m = C_{n,s}$
for some natural number $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Grantham/gran4.tex>.

articles.title: The $s$-Cullen value
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $s$ and $n$, the $s$-Cullen value is
$C_{n,s} = n s^n + 1$.

## Sources

- Jon Grantham and Hester Graves, *The abc Conjecture Implies That Only Finitely Many s-Cullen Numbers Are Repunits*, Journal of Integer Sequences 24 (2021), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Grantham/gran4.tex>.

articles.title: Coprime representatives of a residue class
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ be natural
numbers with $\gamma > 0$ and $\gcd(\alpha, \beta) = 1$. Then there is a natural number $c > 0$
with $\gcd(c, \gamma) = 1$ and $c \equiv \beta \pmod{\alpha}$.

The numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$ need not be positive.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 10 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-10`).

articles.title: Prime divisors of Fermat numbers and the period of Fermat residues
articles.statement:
Write
$F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$ for the $n$-th Fermat number. Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $h$ be a natural
number and let $k$ be a positive integer such that the sequence $n \mapsto F_{h+n} \bmod p$ is
periodic with period $k$ and every positive period of it is a multiple of $k$. Then $p$ divides
$F_n$ for some natural number $n$ if and only if $k = 1$.

Any such $h$ is at least the preperiod of $n \mapsto F_n \bmod p$, and $k$ is then the primitive
period of $n \mapsto F_n \bmod p$, which does not depend on $h$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Proposition 18 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-prop-18`).

articles.title: Every preperiod of Fermat residues occurs for a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$
articles.statement:
Write
$F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$. For every natural number $v$ there is a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ such that
the sequence $n \mapsto F_n \bmod p$ has preperiod exactly $v$: the sequence
$n \mapsto F_{v+n} \bmod p$ is periodic with some positive period, and for no $h < v$ is the
sequence $n \mapsto F_{h+n} \bmod p$ periodic with a positive period.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Theorem 23 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-thm-23`).

articles.title: A primitive root in which a residue has index $(p-1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be
a prime and let $a$ be a nonzero residue modulo $p$, of multiplicative order
$\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$. Then there is a primitive root $g$ modulo $p$ (an element of order
$p - 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) with $g^{(p-1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} = a$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Proposition 11 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-prop-11`).

articles.title: Uniqueness of the $2$-adic decomposition of the index of $2$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and
write $p - 1 = 2^r u$ with $u$ odd. Then there is exactly one pair $(s, t)$ of natural numbers
with $s \le r$ and $t \mid u$ such that $g^{2^s t} = 2$ for some primitive root $g$ modulo $p$
(an element of order $p - 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$).

Since $2^s t$ divides $p - 1$, it lies in $\{1, \dots, p - 1\}$, so it is the index
$\operatorname{ind}_g(2)$ of $2$ with respect to $g$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Corollary 14 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-cor-14`); also Theorem 15 (i).

articles.title: Indices dividing $p - 1$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $g$ be a primitive root modulo $p$ (an
element of order $p - 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$), let $a \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and let
$i$ be a natural number with $g^i = a$. Then $i$ divides $p - 1$ if and only if
$i = (p - 1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$, where $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ is the multiplicative order
of $a$.

For $i$ outside $\{1, \dots, p - 1\}$ both sides are false, so the statement concerns the index
$\operatorname{ind}_g(a)$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Proposition 13 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-prop-13`).

articles.title: Congruences between Fermat numbers propagate
articles.statement:
Write $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$. Let $m$, $i$ and
$j$ be natural numbers with $F_i \equiv F_j \pmod m$. Then $F_{i+t} \equiv F_{j+t} \pmod m$ for
every natural number $t$.

No condition on $m$, $i$ or $j$ is needed.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 4 (i) (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-4`).

articles.title: Two of $F_0, \dots, F_p$ are congruent modulo $p$
articles.statement:
Write $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$. For every
positive integer $p$ there are natural numbers $i < j \le p$ with $F_i \equiv F_j \pmod p$.

This is the pigeonhole principle; $p$ need not be prime.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 2 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-2`).

articles.title: Coincidences among Fermat residues
articles.statement:
Write $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$. Let $p$ be a prime, and let
$h$ and $k$ be the preperiod and the period of $n \mapsto F_n \bmod p$ in the following sense:
$k > 0$, the sequence $n \mapsto F_{h+n} \bmod p$ is periodic with period $k$, every positive
period of it is a multiple of $k$, and for no $h' < h$ is the sequence $n \mapsto F_{h'+n} \bmod p$
periodic with a positive period. Then for all natural numbers $i < j$, $F_i \equiv F_j \pmod p$
if and only if $i \ge h$ and $i \equiv j \pmod k$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 6 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-6`).

articles.title: Preperiod and period of Fermat numbers modulo an odd prime
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime
and write the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $p$ as $2^v w$ with $v, w$ natural numbers and
$w$ odd. Let $k$ be the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $w$ (so $k = 1$ when $w = 1$), and
let $F_m = 2^{2^m} + 1$ be the $m$-th Fermat number. Then the sequence $n \mapsto F_{v+n} \bmod p$
is periodic with period $k$; for every $h < v$, the sequence $n \mapsto F_{h+n} \bmod p$ has no
positive period; and every positive period of the sequence $n \mapsto F_{v+n} \bmod p$ is
divisible by $k$.

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL28/Klaska/klaska22.tex>, Theorem, lines 593--606. This is the complete selected theorem statement, not a prerequisite stage.

articles.title: Preperiod and period of Fermat residues from the index of $2$
articles.statement:
Write $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$.
Let $p$ be an odd prime, write $p - 1 = 2^r u$ with $u$ odd, and let $s \le r$ and $t \mid u$ be
natural numbers such that $g^{2^s t} = 2$ for some primitive root $g$ modulo $p$ (an element of
order $p - 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$). Let $k$ be the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo
$u/t$, with $k = 1$ when $t = u$. Then the sequence $n \mapsto F_{r-s+n} \bmod p$ is periodic
with period $k$, every positive period of it is a multiple of $k$, and for no $h < r - s$ is the
sequence $n \mapsto F_{h+n} \bmod p$ periodic with a positive period. Thus $n \mapsto F_n \bmod p$
has preperiod $r - s$ and primitive period $k$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Theorem 15 (ii) and (iii) (`jis-2025-25.8.7-thm-15`).

articles.title: Non-congruence of Fermat numbers passes to smaller indices
articles.statement:
Write $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$ for
the $n$-th Fermat number. Let $m$ be a natural number and let $i \le j$. If
$F_j \not\equiv F_{j+t} \pmod{m}$ for every $t \ge 1$, then $F_i \not\equiv F_{i+t} \pmod{m}$
for every $t \ge 1$.

The statement holds for every modulus $m$ and allows $i = j$; the paper takes $m = p$ prime and
$i < j$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 4 (ii) (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-4`).

articles.title: The index of a residue and its multiplicative order
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $g$ be a
primitive root modulo $p$ (an element of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ of multiplicative order
$p - 1$), and let $a \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. If $g^i = a$ for a natural number $i$, then
$\gcd(p - 1, i) = (p - 1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$, where $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ is the
multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $p$.

This holds for every natural number $i$ with $g^i = a$; the paper's index
$\operatorname{ind}_g(a)$, which lies between $1$ and $p - 1$, is one of them.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 8 (iv) (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-8`).

articles.title: Fermat prime
articles.statement:
A natural number $p$ is a Fermat prime if $p$ is prime and
$p = 2^{2^k} + 1$ for some natural number $k$, that is, $p$ is a prime Fermat number.

articles.title: The power of $2$ dividing the order of $2$ modulo a prime
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let
$\operatorname{ord}_p(2)$ be the multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $p$. If $p \equiv 7 \pmod 8$,
then $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)$ is odd. If $p \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, then $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)$ is
divisible by $2$ but not by $4$. If $p \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, then $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)$ is
divisible by $4$ but not by $8$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Theorem 22, order statements (`jis-2025-25.8.7-thm-22`).

articles.title: Prime divisors of Fermat numbers and the order of $2$
articles.statement:
Write $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$ for the
$n$-th Fermat number. An odd prime $p$ divides $F_n$ if and only if the multiplicative order of
$2$ modulo $p$ equals $2^{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Jiří Klaška, *Fermat Numbers Modulo a Prime*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.8.7, Lemma 17 (`jis-2025-25.8.7-lem-17`).

articles.title: Gandhi's formula for the $n$th prime
articles.statement:
For $i \ge 1$ let $p_i$ be the $i$th prime, so that
$p_1 = 2$, and for $n \ge 1$ let $P_{n-1} = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_{n-1}$, the empty product $1$ when
$n = 1$. Let $\mu$ be the Möbius function. Then for every $n \ge 1$,

$$p_n = \left\lfloor 1 - \log_2 \left( -\frac{1}{2} + \sum_{d \mid P_{n-1}} \frac{\mu(d)}{2^d - 1}
\right) \right\rfloor.$$

## Sources

- J. M. Gandhi, "Formulae for the nth prime," Proc. Washington State University Conference on Number Theory (1971), 96--107. The displayed formula and indexing follow the secondary source Eric S. Rowland, "A Natural Prime-Generating Recurrence," Journal of Integer Sequences 11 (2008), Article 08.2.8, lines 90--103 of the official TeX, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Rowland/rowland21.tex, where `f(n)` is the `n`th prime `pₙ` and `Pₙ = p₁ p₂ ⋯ pₙ`.

articles.title: Generalized Fermat number
articles.statement:
For an even natural number $b$ and a positive integer $n$,
the generalized Fermat number is $F_n(b) = b^{2^n} + 1$ (also written $F_{b,n}$).

## Sources

- <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL15/Castillo/castillo2.tex> and <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL24/Witno/witno8.tex>.

articles.title: Fortunate numbers
articles.statement:
Write $q\#$ for the primorial of a natural number $q$, the product of
all primes $p \le q$. For natural numbers $q$ and $m$, $m$ is the Fortunate number of $q$ when
$q$ is prime, $m > 1$, $q\# + m$ is prime, and $q\# + k$ is not prime for any $k$ with
$1 < k < m$.

## Sources

- Antonín Čejchan, Michal Křížek, and Lawrence Somer, *On Remarkable Properties of Primes Near Factorials and Primorials*, Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.1.4.

articles.title: Composite numbers from Mersenne shifts of an arithmetic progression
articles.statement:
For a natural
number $j$ let $M_j = 2^j - 1$ be the $j$-th Mersenne number (so $M_0 = 0$). For every natural
number $t$ there are natural numbers $a$ and $d > 0$ such that, for every natural number $r$,
every natural number $j \le t$ and every natural number $n$, the number
$(a + rd + M_j) \cdot 2^n + 1$ is composite.

## Sources

- Carrie E. Finch-Smith and R. Scottfield Groth, "Arbitrarily Long Sequences of Sierpiński Numbers that are the Sum of a Sierpiński Number and a Mersenne Number", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Infinitely many Riesel repdigits in every base $b > 509203$
articles.statement:
Let $b > 509203$ be a
natural number. Then there are infinitely many Riesel numbers of the form $k(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ with
$1 \le k < b$ and $t \ge 1$, that is, $b$-repdigits: the digit $k$ written $t$ times in base $b$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Corollary 3.8.

articles.title: Covering-produced Riesel numbers give infinitely many Riesel repintegers
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
Riesel number that has Riesel covering data, so that $k$ is produced as a Riesel number by the
covering system method. Then for every natural number $b \ge 2$ there are infinitely many $t \ge 1$
such that the $b$-repinteger $k_b^{(t)} = k\,(b^{\ell t} - 1)/(b^{\ell} - 1)$, where $\ell$ is the
number of base-$b$ digits of $k$ (so $k_b^{(t)}$ is $k$ written $t$ times in base $b$), is a Riesel
number.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.4.

articles.title: Infinitely many Riesel repunits in bases $b \equiv 16518444216571 \pmod{2^{64} - 1}$
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a natural number with $b \equiv 16518444216571 \pmod{18446744073709551615}$, where
$18446744073709551615 = 2^{64} - 1$. Then there are infinitely many Riesel numbers among the
$b$-repunits $(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ with $t \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Corollary 3.14.

articles.title: Infinitely many Riesel repunits from primitive divisors of $2^{2^j} - 1$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau$ be a
natural number. For $1 \le j \le \tau$ let $p_j$ be a primitive prime divisor of $2^{2^j} - 1$ in
the sequence $(2^m - 1)_{m \ge 0}$, let $q \ne p_\tau$ be a primitive prime divisor of
$2^{2^\tau} - 1$ in the same sequence, and put $P = p_1 \cdots p_\tau$. Let $b > 2$ be a natural
number with $b \equiv 1 \pmod P$, and suppose that (i) $q \mid b$, or (ii) $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$, or
(iii) $q \nmid b$, $b \not\equiv 1 \pmod q$ and $\gcd(P, \operatorname{ord}_q(b)) = 1$, where
$\operatorname{ord}_q(b)$ is the multiplicative order of $b$ modulo $q$. Then there are infinitely
many Riesel numbers among the $b$-repunits $(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ with $t \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.13.

articles.title: Infinitely many Narayana numbers are Sierpiński numbers
articles.statement:
There are infinitely many
natural numbers $k$ that are Sierpiński numbers and terms of Narayana's cows sequence $(N_t)$,
that is, $k = N_t$ for some $t$; here a Sierpiński number is an odd $k$ such that
$k \cdot 2^n + 1$ is not prime for every $n \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Katherine Franzone and Joshua Harrington, *Sierpiński and Riesel Numbers in Narayana's Cow Sequence*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A10, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Infinitely many Sierpiński repdigits in every base $b > 78557$
articles.statement:
Let $b > 78557$ be a
natural number. Then there are infinitely many Sierpiński numbers of the form $k(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$
with $1 \le k < b$ and $t \ge 1$, that is, $b$-repdigits: the digit $k$ written $t$ times in
base $b$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Corollary 3.7.

articles.title: Covering-produced Sierpiński numbers give infinitely many Sierpiński repintegers
articles.statement:
Let $k$
be a Sierpiński number that has Sierpiński covering data, so that $k$ is produced as a Sierpiński
number by the covering system method. Then for every natural number $b \ge 2$ there are infinitely
many $t \ge 1$ such that the $b$-repinteger $k_b^{(t)} = k\,(b^{\ell t} - 1)/(b^{\ell} - 1)$, where
$\ell$ is the number of base-$b$ digits of $k$ (so $k_b^{(t)}$ is $k$ written $t$ times in base
$b$), is a Sierpiński number.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.3.

articles.title: Infinitely many Sierpiński repunits in bases $b \equiv 1, 147, 265, 378 \pmod{641}$ with $b \not\equiv 1 \pmod 5$
articles.statement:
**Infinitely many Sierpiński repunits in bases $b \equiv 1, 147, 265, 378 \pmod{641}$ with
$b \not\equiv 1 \pmod 5$.** Let $b > 2$ be a natural number with $b \equiv c \pmod{641}$ for some
$c \in \{1, 147, 265, 378\}$ and $b \not\equiv 1 \pmod 5$. Then there are infinitely many
Sierpiński numbers among the $b$-repunits $(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ with $t \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Corollary 3.12.

articles.title: Infinitely many Sierpiński repunits from primitive divisors of $2^{2^j} - 1$
articles.statement:
Let $\tau$
be a natural number. For $1 \le j \le \tau$ let $p_j$ be a primitive prime divisor of
$2^{2^j} - 1$ in the sequence $(2^m - 1)_{m \ge 0}$, and let $q \ne p_\tau$ be a primitive prime
divisor of $2^{2^\tau} - 1$ in the same sequence. Let $b > 2$ be a natural number with $q \nmid b$.
For $1 \le j \le \tau$ put $\ell_j = 1$ if $p_j \mid b$, $\ell_j = p_j$ if $p_j \nmid b$ and
$b \equiv 1 \pmod{p_j}$, and otherwise $\ell_j = \operatorname{ord}_{p_j}(b)$, the multiplicative
order of $b$ modulo $p_j$; let $L = \operatorname{lcm}(2, \ell_1, \dots, \ell_\tau)$. Suppose that
either (i) $b \equiv 1 \pmod q$ and $q \nmid L$, or (ii) $b \not\equiv 1 \pmod q$ and there is a
natural number $s \equiv 1 \pmod L$ with $(b^s - 1)/(b - 1) \equiv -1 \pmod q$. Then there are
infinitely many Sierpiński numbers among the $b$-repunits $(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ with $t \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.11.

articles.title: Riesel covering data
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number and let $S$ be a finite set of triples
$(r, m, p)$ of natural numbers. Then $S$ is Riesel covering data for $k$ (data producing $k$ as a
Riesel number by the covering system method) when every integer is congruent to $r$ modulo $m$
for some $(r, m, p) \in S$, distinct triples in $S$ have distinct third entries $p$, and every
$(r, m, p) \in S$ has $m \ge 1$, $p$ prime, $p \mid 2^m - 1$ and $p \mid k \cdot 2^r - 1$ (for
$k \ge 1$ the last condition says $k \equiv 2^{-r} \pmod p$).

Subtraction is in the natural numbers, so for $k = 0$ the condition $p \mid k \cdot 2^r - 1$ reads
$p \mid 0$ and holds trivially.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 2, Equation (3).

articles.title: Narayana numbers that are Riesel numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(N_t)$ be Narayana's cows sequence, with
$N_0 = 0$ and $N_1 = N_2 = 1$. If $t$ is congruent modulo $718391520$ to one of the $27$ residues
$3629412$, $13386852$, $73151172$, $96325092$, $101203812$, $119499012$, $175604292$,
$198778212$, $212194692$, $240247332$, $268299972$, $328064292$, $337821732$, $360995652$,
$384169572$, $402464772$, $425638692$, $467107812$, $476865252$, $495160452$, $564682212$,
$587856132$, $592734852$, $611030052$, $629325252$, $652499172$, $703725732$, then $N_t$ is a
Riesel number: $N_t$ is odd and $N_t \cdot 2^n - 1$ is not prime for every $n \ge 1$.

With this indexing, $N_t$ is odd exactly when $t \bmod 7 \in \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$.

## Sources

- Katherine Franzone and Joshua Harrington, *Sierpiński and Riesel Numbers in Narayana's Cow Sequence*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A10, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Riesel repdigits with digit $101$ in bases $b \equiv 180 \pmod{11184810}$
articles.statement:
Let $b$ and $t$
be natural numbers with $b \equiv 180 \pmod{11184810}$ and $t \equiv 171 \pmod{240}$. Then the
$b$-repinteger $101_b^{(t)}$, which is the repdigit $101\,(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ because $101 < b$, is
a Riesel number.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.10.

articles.title: Binary repstrings of 659 that are Riesel numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $t$ with
$t \equiv 1369 \pmod{2730}$ or $t \equiv 2599 \pmod{2730}$, the binary repstring
$659_2^{(2;t)} = 659\,(2^{12t} - 1)/(2^{12} - 1)$ is a Riesel number. Its binary expansion is that
of $659$ (ten binary digits) written $t$ times with two zeros between consecutive copies.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 4.4.

articles.title: Binary repintegers of 18107 that are Riesel numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$t \equiv 31 \pmod{56}$, the binary repinteger $18107_2^{(t)} = 18107\,(2^{15t} - 1)/(2^{15} - 1)$,
whose binary expansion is that of $18107$ (fifteen binary digits) written $t$ times, is a Riesel
number.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.6.

articles.title: Riesel number
articles.statement:
A natural number $k$ is a Riesel number if $k$ is odd and, for every
integer $n \ge 1$, the number $k \cdot 2^n - 1$ is not prime.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, abstract and Section 1.

articles.title: Sierpiński covering data
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number and $S$ a finite set of triples
$(r, m, p)$ of natural numbers. Then $S$ is Sierpiński covering data for $k$ if every integer is
congruent to $r$ modulo $m$ for some $(r, m, p) \in S$, distinct triples in $S$ have distinct
third entries, and every $(r, m, p) \in S$ has $m \ge 1$, $p$ prime, $p \mid 2^m - 1$ and
$p \mid k \cdot 2^r + 1$.

This is the input of the covering system method for Sierpiński numbers; the last condition says
that $k \equiv -2^{-r} \pmod{p}$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 2, Equation (2).

articles.title: Repdigits with digit 41 that are Sierpiński numbers
articles.statement:
Let $b$ and $t$ be natural numbers
with $b \equiv 87 \pmod{11184810}$ and $t \equiv 59 \pmod{120}$. Then the base-$b$ repdigit
$41_b^{(t)} = 41\,(b^t - 1)/(b - 1)$ is a Sierpiński number. Since $b \ge 87 > 41$, its $t$
base-$b$ digits all equal $41$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.9.

articles.title: Binary repstrings of 659 that are Sierpiński numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number $t$ with
$t \equiv 131 \pmod{2730}$ or $t \equiv 1361 \pmod{2730}$, the binary repstring
$659_2^{(2;t)} = 659\,(2^{12t} - 1)/(2^{12} - 1)$ is a Sierpiński number. Its binary expansion is
that of $659$ (ten binary digits) written $t$ times with two zeros between consecutive copies.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Binary repintegers of 18107 that are Sierpiński numbers
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$t \equiv 25 \pmod{56}$, the binary repinteger $18107_2^{(t)} = 18107\,(2^{15t} - 1)/(2^{15} - 1)$,
whose binary expansion is that of $18107$ (fifteen binary digits) written $t$ times, is a
Sierpiński number.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.5.

articles.title: Sierpiński number
articles.statement:
A natural number $k$ is a Sierpiński number if $k$ is odd and,
for every integer $n \ge 1$, the number $k \cdot 2^n + 1$ is not prime.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, abstract and Section 1.

articles.title: The empty set is not Riesel covering data
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the empty set is
not Riesel covering data for $k$, because its residue classes do not cover $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 2.

articles.title: One is not a Riesel number
articles.statement:
The number $1$ is not a Riesel number, since
$1 \cdot 2^2 - 1 = 3$ is prime.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 1.

articles.title: Empty Sierpiński covering data
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the empty set is not
Sierpiński covering data for $k$: the empty family of residue classes does not cover $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 2.

articles.title: Theorem 3.2 (no Sierpiński $2$-repdigits from coverings)
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$t \ge 1$, the covering system method cannot produce the $2$-repdigit $2^t - 1$ as a
Sierpiński number: no finite set of triples $(r_j, m_j, p_j)$ is Sierpiński covering data
for $2^t - 1$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 3.2.

articles.title: $1$ is not a Sierpiński number
articles.statement:
The number $1$ is not a Sierpiński number, since
$1 \cdot 2 + 1 = 3$ is prime.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 1.

articles.title: A $10$-repstring
articles.statement:
The $10$-repstring with $k = 1$, $z = 2$ and $t = 3$ is
$1_{10}^{(2;3)} = 1001001$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 4.

articles.title: The three-digit $2$-repunit
articles.statement:
The $2$-repstring with $k = 1$, $z = 0$ and $t = 3$, that is,
the $2$-repunit $1_2^{(3)}$ with three digits, equals $7$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Section 1.

articles.title: Repstrings
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $b$, $k$, $z$ and $t$, let $\ell$ be the number of base-$b$
digits of $k$. The $b$-repstring is

$$k_b^{(z;t)} = \left\lfloor \frac{k\,(b^{(z+\ell)t} - 1)}{b^{z+\ell} - 1} \right\rfloor,$$

where subtraction is truncated at $0$ and the integer division gives $0$ when the denominator is
$0$. For $z = 0$ it is the $b$-repinteger $k_b^{(t)}$.

For $b \ge 2$ and $k \ge 1$ the division is exact, and $k_b^{(z;t)}$ is the number whose base-$b$
expansion is $k$ written $t$ times with $z$ zeros between consecutive copies.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Sections 1 and 4.

articles.title: Theorem 4.6 (Sierpiński and Riesel repstring coverings correspond)
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$,
$\mathfrak{t} \ge 1$, $w \ge 1$ and $z \ge 0$ be natural numbers. There is a single finite set
of triples that is Sierpiński covering data for the $2$-repstring $k_2^{(z;t)}$ for every
$t \ge 1$ with $t \equiv \mathfrak{t} \pmod{w}$ if and only if there is a single finite set
of triples that is Riesel covering data for $k_2^{(z;t')}$ for every $t' \ge 1$ with
$t' \equiv -\mathfrak{t} \pmod{w}$.

## Sources

- Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, *On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A12, Theorem 4.6.

articles.title: Distinct factorial residues modulo a socialist prime
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a socialist prime. If $a$
and $b$ are distinct natural numbers with $2 \le a \le p - 1$ and $2 \le b \le p - 1$, then
$a!$ and $b!$ have different remainders modulo $p$.

articles.title: Socialist primes
articles.statement:
A natural number $p$ is a socialist prime if $p$ is prime, $p > 5$, and
the factorials $2!, 3!, \ldots, (p-1)!$ have pairwise distinct remainders modulo $p$.

## Sources

- Trudgian, arXiv:1310.6403v2, line 24.

articles.title: Infinitely many primes are not Sophie Germain primes
articles.statement:
The set of primes $q$ that are not
Sophie Germain primes, that is, the primes $q$ for which $2q + 1$ is not prime, is infinite.

## Sources

- Takashi Agoh, *A Note on Sophie Germain Primes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A83, Theorem 3.1.

articles.title: Characterization of Sophie Germain primes
articles.statement:
A natural number $p$ is a Sophie Germain prime
if and only if $p$ is prime and $2p + 1$ is prime.

articles.title: Wilson-type characterization of Sophie Germain primes
articles.statement:
Let $a \ge 2$ be a natural number.
Then $a$ is a Sophie Germain prime other than $2$ if and only if
$(a - 1)! \equiv 2a - 1 \pmod{a(2a + 1)}$ or $(a - 1)! \equiv -(6a + 1) \pmod{a(2a + 1)}$, the
congruences being taken in the integers.

The paper states this for all positive integers $a$; at $a = 1$ the first congruence holds
($0! = 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$) while $1$ is not prime (the proof's appeal to Wilson's theorem modulo
$a$ needs $a \ge 2$).

## Sources

- Takashi Agoh, *A Note on Sophie Germain Primes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A83, Theorem 5.3.

articles.title: Sophie Germain primes
articles.statement:
A natural number $p$ is a Sophie Germain prime if $p$ is prime and
$2p + 1$ is prime. The case $p = 2$ is not excluded.

## Sources

- arXiv:2311.13375, lines 83–85.

articles.title: Safe prime of a Sophie Germain prime
articles.statement:
If $p$ is a Sophie Germain prime, then $2p + 1$ is
prime.

articles.title: Sophie Germain primes are prime
articles.statement: If $p$ is a Sophie Germain prime, then $p$ is prime.

articles.title: Primes that are not Sophie Germain primes
articles.statement:
For an odd prime $p$, let
$A(p) = \{pr + (p - 1)/2 : r = 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$, and let $A$ be the union of the sets $A(p)$ over
all odd primes $p$. A prime is not a Sophie Germain prime if and only if it lies in $A$;
equivalently, the Sophie Germain primes are exactly the primes outside $A$.

## Sources

- Takashi Agoh, *A Note on Sophie Germain Primes*, INTEGERS 25 (2025), Article A83, Theorem 2.1.

articles.title: Divisibility of later generalized Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $m$
write $F_m(a, b) = a^{b^m} + 1$. Let $a, b, D \ge 2$ and $n$ be natural numbers such that $D$
divides $F_n(a, b)$. If $b$ is odd, then $D$ divides $F_{n+k}(a, b)$ for every $k \ge 1$. If $b$
is even and $D \ge 3$, then $D$ does not divide $F_{n+k}(a, b)$ for any $k \ge 1$.

The source states the even case for $D \ge 2$; its proof gives $F_{n+k}(a, b) \equiv 2 \pmod D$,
which excludes only $D = 2$, and the even case is false there: for $a = 3$, $b = 2$, $n = 0$ and
$k = 1$, $2$ divides both $F_0(3, 2) = 4$ and $F_1(3, 2) = 10$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Greatest common divisors of generalized Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and
$k$ write $F_k(a, b) = a^{b^k} + 1$, and let $a, b \ge 2$ and $m$, $n$ be natural numbers. If
$n < m$ and $a$ and $b$ are both even, then $\gcd(F_m(a, b), F_n(a, b)) = 1$. If $n < m$, $a$ is
odd and $b$ is even, then $\gcd(F_m(a, b), F_n(a, b)) = 2$. If $n \le m$ and $b$ is odd, then
$\gcd(F_m(a, b), F_n(a, b)) = F_n(a, b)$.

The source assumes $a, b > 2$ and $0 \le n \le m$; its proof uses only $a, b \ge 2$ and treats
$m > n$ ("Since $m > n$"), and the first two cases fail for $m = n$: for $a = b = 4$ and
$m = n = 0$ the gcd is $\gcd(5, 5) = 5$, and for $a = 3$, $b = 4$ and $m = n = 0$ it is
$\gcd(4, 4) = 4$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Start of the period of generalized Fermat numbers modulo the square of a prime
articles.statement:
For
natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $k$ write $F_k(a, b) = a^{b^k} + 1$. Let $a, b \ge 2$, let $p$ be a
prime, and let $n_0$ be the least natural number with $p^2 \mid F_{n_0}(a, b)$. Say that the
sequence $(F_k(a, b))_k$ is periodic modulo $p^2$ from index $m$ if there is a $T > 0$ with
$F_{m+k+T}(a, b) \equiv F_{m+k}(a, b) \pmod{p^2}$ for every $k \ge 0$. If $b$ is odd, then $n_0$
is the least index from which the sequence is periodic modulo $p^2$; if $b$ is even, this least
index is $n_0 + 1$.

In the source's terms, $n_0$ is the index of the first term of the period when $b$ is odd, and
the index of the last term of the pre-period when $b$ is even.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the number of prime factors of generalized Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
For natural
numbers $a$, $b$ and $n$ write $F_n(a, b) = a^{b^n} + 1$, and let $\Omega(N)$ be the number of
prime factors of $N$ counted with multiplicity. If $a, b \ge 2$ and $b$ is odd, then
$\Omega(F_n(a, b)) \le \Omega(F_m(a, b))$ for all natural numbers $n \le m$.

The source writes $\varphi_n(a, b)$ for $\Omega(F_n(a, b))$. Its open question on
$\varphi_n(2, 2)$ and its list of values of $\varphi_n(2, 2)$ are not stated here.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Corollary 1.

articles.title: Smaller iterated powers are not congruent to one
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, m \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$ be
natural numbers with $a^{b^n} \not\equiv 1 \pmod m$. Then $a^{b^t} \not\equiv 1 \pmod m$ for every
natural number $t < n$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Wieferich primes to base $a$ via multiplicative orders
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $a$ a
natural number not divisible by $p$. Then $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$, that is, $p$ is a
Wieferich prime to base $a$, if and only if the multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $p^2$ equals
the multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $p$.

The congruence $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is the source's equation (8) defining $p \in W(a)$.
The source assumes $a \ge 2$; both sides also hold for $a = 1$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Lemma 1 (iii).

articles.title: Squared prime factors of Fermat numbers via Wieferich primes and orders
articles.statement:
Let
$F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$ be the $n$-th Fermat number. For every natural number $n$ and every odd prime
$p$, $p^2$ divides $F_n$ if and only if $p$ is a Wieferich prime (to base $2$) and the
multiplicative order of $2$ modulo $p$ is $2^{n+1}$.

This follows from the criterion that a prime $p$ dividing $F_n$ satisfies $p^2 \mid F_n$ exactly
when $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$, since an odd prime $p$ divides $F_n$ exactly when the order
of $2$ modulo $p$ is $2^{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Theorem 5, Equation (11).

articles.title: Squared prime factors of Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$ be the $n$-th Fermat
number, and let $p$ be a prime dividing $F_n$. Then $p^2$ divides $F_n$ if and only if
$2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Theorem 3, citing Křížek, Luca, and Somer.

articles.title: Squared prime factors of generalized Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $n$
write $F_n(a, b) = a^{b^n} + 1$. Let $a, b \ge 2$, let $n$ be a natural number, let $p$ be an odd
prime coprime to $ab$, and write $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ for the multiplicative order of $a$
modulo $p$. If $p^2$ divides $F_n(a, b)$, then $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ (that is, $p$ is a
Wieferich prime to base $a$) and $\operatorname{ord}_p(a)$ divides $2b^n$. Conversely, if
$a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ and $\operatorname{ord}_p(a) = 2b^n$, then $p^2$ divides $F_n(a, b)$.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Squared prime factors of $a^{2^n} + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $a$ be a natural
number not divisible by $p$, and let $n$ be a natural number. Then $p^2$ divides $a^{2^n} + 1$ if
and only if $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ (that is, $p$ is a Wieferich prime to base $a$) and the
multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $p$ is $2^{n+1}$.

The congruence $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is the source's equation (8) defining $p \in W(a)$.
The source assumes $a \ge 2$; for $a = 1$ both sides are false.

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Warren–Bray congruence for prime divisors of Fermat numbers
articles.statement:
Let $F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1$ be
the $n$-th Fermat number. For every $n \ge 2$ and every odd prime $p$ dividing $F_n$, we have
$2^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{F_n}$. This result is due to Warren and Bray (1967).

## Sources

- Klaška, *Several Notes on Jakóbczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A77, Theorem 2, citing Warren and Bray.

articles.title: Wieferich primes via congruences
articles.statement:
For every natural number $p$, $p$ is a Wieferich prime
if and only if $p$ is prime and $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$.

articles.title: Wieferich primes via remainders
articles.statement:
For every natural number $p$, $p$ is a Wieferich prime
if and only if $p$ is prime and the remainder of $2^{p-1}$ on division by $p^2$ is $1$.

articles.title: Wieferich primes
articles.statement:
A natural number $p$ is a Wieferich prime (to base $2$) if $p$ is
prime and $p^2$ divides $2^{p-1} - 1$.

articles.title: Closure of a prime in Macías's coprime topology
articles.statement:
If $p$ is a prime number, then the
closure of $\{p\}$ in the positive integers with Macías's coprime topology is the set of
positive integers divisible by $p$.

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, "Another Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers", Lemma 1.

articles.title: Positive integers coprime to a given integer
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$, $\Omega_n$ is the
set of positive integers $m$ with $\gcd(n, m) = 1$.

articles.title: Coprime arithmetic progressions are dense in the comaximal space
articles.statement:
Equip the positive
integers with the comaximal topology, the topology generated by the sets
$\{m : \gcd(n, m) = 1\}$ for positive integers $n$. If $a$ and $b$ are coprime positive integers,
then the arithmetic progression $\{ak + b : k \in \mathbb{N}\} = \{b, a + b, 2a + b, \dots\}$,
with $k$ ranging over the natural numbers including $0$, is dense in this topology.

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, *A Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A39, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Density of the primes passes from the subspace without 1
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be the positive
integers with Macías's coprime topology and $X_1$ the subspace of positive integers different
from $1$. If the set of prime numbers is dense in $X_1$, then it is dense in $X$.

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, "Another Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers", Lemma 2.

articles.title: The primes are dense in the coprime topology without 1
articles.statement:
The set of prime numbers is dense
in the set of positive integers different from $1$, with the subspace topology induced by
Macías's coprime topology on the positive integers.

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, "Another Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers", Theorem 3.

articles.title: A nonempty set of primes is dense in the comaximal space iff it is infinite
articles.statement:
Equip the
positive integers with the comaximal topology, the topology generated by the sets
$\{m : \gcd(n, m) = 1\}$ for positive integers $n$. A nonempty set $A$ of primes is infinite if
and only if it is dense in this topology.

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, *A Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers in Certain Arithmetic Progressions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A39, Lemma 1 (quoting Macías, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A47).

articles.title: Infinitude of the primes as density
articles.statement:
There are infinitely many prime numbers if and only
if the set of prime numbers is dense in the positive integers with Macías's coprime topology.

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, "Another Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers", Theorem 2.

articles.title: Macías's coprime sets form a basis
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$ let $\Omega_n$ be the set
of positive integers coprime to $n$. The family $\beta = \{\Omega_n : n \ge 1\}$ is a basis of
the topology on the positive integers that it generates (Macías's coprime topology).

## Sources

- Jhixon Macías, "Another Topological Proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Macías's coprime basis
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$ let $\Omega_n$ be the set of positive
integers coprime to $n$. Macías's coprime basis is the family $\beta = \{\Omega_n : n \ge 1\}$ of
subsets of the positive integers.

articles.title: Macías's coprime topology without 1
articles.statement:
The topology $\tau_1$ on the set of positive integers
different from $1$ is the subspace topology induced by Macías's coprime topology $\tau$ on the
positive integers.

articles.title: Macías's coprime topology
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$ let $\Omega_n$ be the set of positive
integers coprime to $n$. Macías's coprime topology $\tau$ is the topology on the positive integers
generated by the sets $\Omega_n$, $n \ge 1$, that is, the coarsest topology in which every
$\Omega_n$ is open.

articles.title: Primes among the positive integers different from 1
articles.statement:
Within the set of positive integers
different from $1$, this is the subset consisting of the prime numbers.

articles.title: Primes among the positive integers
articles.statement:
The set of positive integers that are prime
numbers.

articles.title: Conway–Schneeberger fifteen theorem
articles.statement:
Let $Q$ be a positive definite symmetric
$n \times n$ matrix with integer entries, with quadratic form $Q(x) = \sum_{i,j} Q_{ij} x_i x_j$
on $\mathbb{Z}^n$. Then $Q$ is universal, that is, it represents every positive integer, if and
only if it represents every integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le 15$.

The forward direction is immediate; the content is the converse. Bhargava's refinement reduces
the critical set to $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 14, 15\}$.

## Sources

- Conway–Schneeberger 1993 (unpublished, communicated by Conway in lectures); full proof M. Bhargava, 'On the Conway–Schneeberger fifteen theorem', in *Quadratic Forms and their Applications* (Contemp. Math. 272, AMS 2000). Listed as §95 in O. Knill, *Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics* (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `conway_schneeberger_fifteen` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Critical numbers of the 290 theorem
Quadratic form of a matrix
articles.statement:
For a ring $R$ and an $n \times n$ matrix $M$ with entries
in $R$, the value of the quadratic form of $M$ at a vector $x \in R^n$ is
$x \cdot (M x) = \sum_{i,j} x_i M_{ij} x_j$, where $i$ and $j$ range over $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

No symmetry of $M$ is assumed, and $R$ need not be commutative.

articles.title: Quadratic form of an integer matrix
articles.statement:
For an $n \times n$ matrix $Q$ with integer
entries, the quadratic form of $Q$ is the map $\mathbb{Z}^n \to \mathbb{Z}$ sending $x$ to
$Q(x) = \sum_{i,j} Q_{ij} x_i x_j$, where $i$ and $j$ range over $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. No
symmetry of $Q$ is assumed.

articles.title: Integer-valued quadratic forms
articles.statement:
For a ring $R$, an $n \times n$ matrix $M$ with entries
in $R$ is integral if its quadratic form takes integer values at integer vectors: for every
$x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, the value $\sum_{i,j} x_i M_{ij} x_j$ computed in $R$ lies in the image
of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $R$.

articles.title: Universal quadratic forms over a ring
articles.statement:
For a ring $R$, an $n \times n$ matrix $M$ with
entries in $R$ is universal if it represents every positive integer: for every positive
integer $m$ there is $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with $\sum_{i,j} x_i M_{ij} x_j = m$ in $R$.

articles.title: Universal integer-matrix quadratic forms
articles.statement:
An $n \times n$ matrix $Q$ with integer
entries is universal if its quadratic form $Q(x) = \sum_{i,j} Q_{ij} x_i x_j$ represents every
positive integer, that is, for every positive integer $m$ there is $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with
$Q(x) = m$.

articles.title: Natural numbers represented by a quadratic form
articles.statement:
For a ring $R$, an $n \times n$ matrix
$M$ with entries in $R$ represents a natural number $m$ if there is an integer vector
$x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with $\sum_{i,j} x_i M_{ij} x_j = m$, where the entries of $x$ and the
number $m$ are viewed as elements of $R$.

articles.title: Integers represented by an integer-matrix quadratic form
articles.statement:
An $n \times n$ matrix $Q$
with integer entries represents an integer $m$ if $Q(x) = m$ for some $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$,
where $Q(x) = \sum_{i,j} Q_{ij} x_i x_j$.

articles.title: The 290 theorem
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $M$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix
that is positive definite (symmetric, with $x^{\top} M x > 0$ for every nonzero
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$) and integral (for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, the value $x^{\top} M x$ is
an integer). If $M$ represents each of the 29 critical numbers of the 290 theorem, that is,
for each critical number $m$ there is $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with $x^{\top} M x = m$, then $M$
is universal: for every positive integer $m$ there is $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with
$x^{\top} M x = m$.

## Sources

- M. Bhargava, J. Hanke, Universal quadratic forms and the 290-theorem, preprint (2011). See also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_and_290_theorems. Problem `two_ninety_theorem` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Rational representations of an arithmetic progression scale to integral ones
articles.statement:
Let
$a, b, c$ be integers, $n$ a natural number and $u_0, d$ rational numbers. If for every natural
number $i < n$ there are rational numbers $x, y$ with $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 = u_0 + id$, then there
is a nonzero integer $k$ such that for every natural number $i < n$ there are integers $x, y$
with $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 = k^2(u_0 + id)$.

The nonzero condition on $k$ is the paper's common-denominator choice; it also excludes the
trivial zero scaling.

## Sources

- Ajai Choudhry, "Arithmetic Progressions Represented by Binary Quadratic Forms", Lemma 1.

articles.title: Binary quadratic forms with non-square discriminant represent nine-term progressions
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c$ be integers such that the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ is not a perfect square. Then
there are integers $u_0$ and $d \ne 0$ such that for every natural number $i < 9$ there are
integers $x, y$ with $u_0 + id = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$.

The condition $d \ne 0$ excludes constant progressions.

## Sources
