$$\sum_{l} \binom{n}{l_1, \dots, l_m} B_{l_r}(x_r + l_r) \prod_{j \neq r} (x_j + l_j)^{l_j} =
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \frac{(m + k - 2)!}{(m - 2)!} B_{n-k}(x_1 + \dots + x_m + n),$$

where the sum on the left runs over all $l = (l_1, \dots, l_m) \in \mathbb{N}^m$ with
$l_1 + \dots + l_m = n$, and $\binom{n}{l_1, \dots, l_m}$ is the multinomial coefficient.

The source states the identity for arbitrary real or complex parameters; this statement records
its specialization to rational $x_1, \dots, x_m$.

## Sources

- Claudio de J. Pita Ruiz V., "Carlitz-Type and Other Bernoulli Identities," Journal of Integer Sequences 19 (2016), Article 16.1.8, Proposition [Abel-Hurwitz-Bernoulli identity] (a), equation (5.16), lines 821–829, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Pita/pita23.tex

articles.title: Carlitz's Bernoulli identity
articles.statement:
Let $B_j$ denote the $j$-th Bernoulli number, with
$B_1 = -1/2$. For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$,

$$(-1)^m \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k} B_{n+k} = (-1)^n \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} B_{m+k}.$$

## Sources

- Pita Ruiz, “Carlitz-Type and Other Bernoulli Identities”; original L. Carlitz, Problem 795, Mathematics Magazine 44 (1971), p. 107.

articles.title: Euler's convolution identity for Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
Let $B_j$ denote the $j$-th
Bernoulli number, with $B_1 = -1/2$. For every natural number $n \ge 1$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} B_i B_{n-i} = -n B_{n-1} - (n-1) B_n.$$

## Sources

- Ken Kamano, "Sums of Products of Bernoulli Numbers, Including Poly-Bernoulli Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 13 (2010), <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL13/Kamano/kamano2.tex>. Lines 98–104.

articles.title: Gessel's Bernoulli-number identity
articles.statement:
Let $B_j$ denote the $j$-th Bernoulli number, with
$B_1 = -1/2$. For all natural numbers $n$, $r$ and $m$ with $r$ odd and $m \ge 1$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n+r} m^{n+r-k} \binom{n+r}{k} \binom{n+k+r}{r} B_{n+k} =
\frac{r+1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} \sum_{j=0}^{r+1} \binom{n+r}{j} \binom{n+r}{r+1-j}
k^{j+n-1} (k-m)^{n+r-j}.$$

The powers on the right have integer exponents and nonzero rational bases: for $n = 0$ the terms
$j = 0$ and $j = r + 1$ have exponent $-1$.

## Sources

- Redha Chellal and Farid Bencherif, *An Identity for Generalized Bernoulli Polynomials*, Journal of Integer Sequences 23 (2020), Article 20.11.2, formula `t5` (the special case `ℓ = n` with `r` odd), lines 142–149, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL23/Chellal/chellal7.tex>. Quoted there from H. Belbachir and M. Rahmani, *On Gessel-Kaneko's identity for Bernoulli numbers*, Appl. Anal. Discrete Math. 7 (2013), 1–10. Original: I. M. Gessel, *Applications of the classical umbral calculus*, Algebra Universalis 49 (2003), 397–434.

articles.title: Gould's alternating identity for Bernoulli polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $B_i$ denote the $i$-th
Bernoulli number, with $B_1 = -1/2$, and let $B_j(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{j} \binom{j}{i} B_i x^{j-i}$
be the $j$-th Bernoulli polynomial. For every natural number $n$ and every rational number $x$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} B_{n+1}(x - k) = \frac{(n+1)!}{2} (2x - n - 1).$$

## Sources

- Claudio de J. Pita Ruiz V., "Carlitz-Type and Other Bernoulli Identities", Journal of Integer Sequences 19 (2016), Article 16.1.8, Proposition (Gould-Bernoulli identities), equation (5.3), lines 727-732, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Pita/pita23.tex>.

articles.title: Kaneko's Stirling-number formula for the Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
Let $B_n$ denote the $n$-th
Bernoulli number, with $B_1 = -1/2$, and let $S(n, j)$ denote the Stirling numbers of the second
kind. For every natural number $n$,

$$B_n = \sum_{m=1}^{n+1} \frac{(-1)^{m-1} (m-1)!\, S(n, m-1)}{m}.$$

This is Kaneko's explicit formula for the poly-Bernoulli numbers $B_n^{(k)}$ at $k = 1$. That
formula carries a factor $(-1)^n$, which cancels against $B_n^{(1)} = (-1)^n B_n$ (the numbers
$B_n^{(1)}$ come from the generating series $t/(1 - e^{-t})$).

## Sources

- Y. Hamahata and H. Masubuchi, "Special Multi-Poly-Bernoulli Numbers," Journal of Integer Sequences 10 (2007), Article 07.4.1, Theorem [Kaneko1], lines 144–152, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL10/Hamahata/hamahata3.tex citing M. Kaneko, "Poly-Bernoulli numbers," Journal de Théorie des Nombres de Bordeaux 9 (1997), 221–228.

articles.title: Tuenter's power-sum identity for Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be nonzero complex
numbers and let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number with $b^n \ne a^n$. Let $\sigma_x(i) \in \mathbb{C}$,
for $x \in \mathbb{C}$ and $i \in \mathbb{N}$, satisfy
$(i+1)\,\sigma_x(i) = B_{i+1}(x+1) - B_{i+1}$ for all $x$ and $i$, where $B_m(t)$ denotes the
Bernoulli polynomial and $B_m$ the Bernoulli number, with $B_1 = -\tfrac{1}{2}$. Then

$$B_n = \frac{1}{b^n - a^n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \binom{n}{i} B_{n-i}
\left( a^{n-1-i} \, b^i \, \sigma_{a-1}(i) - a^i \, b^{n-1-i} \, \sigma_{b-1}(i) \right),$$

where the exponents $n - 1 - i$ are integers, equal to $-1$ when $i = n$.

For a natural number $x$ and $i \ge 1$ the relation gives $\sigma_x(i) = 1^i + 2^i + \dots + x^i$.

## Sources

- Jitender Singh, *On an Arithmetic Convolution*, Journal of Integer Sequences 17 (2014), Article 14.6.7, Corollary with equation `eq23`, lines 339–344, identified there as Tuenter's identity at `c = 0`, line 348, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Singh/singh8.tex>.

articles.title: Apostol–Bernoulli numbers
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a complex number and let $\log$ denote the
principal branch of the complex logarithm. A sequence $(\beta_k)_{k \ge 0}$ of complex numbers
is the sequence of Apostol–Bernoulli numbers $\beta_k(\alpha)$ when $\alpha \ne 0$,
$\alpha \ne 1$, and for every complex number $t$ with $|t| < |\log \alpha|$ the series
$\sum_{k \ge 0} \beta_k t^k / k!$ converges unconditionally to $t / (\alpha e^t - 1)$.

articles.title: Appell sequence
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field of characteristic zero. A sequence of polynomials
$(p_n)_{n \ge 0}$ over $R$ is an Appell sequence when, for every $n$, the polynomial $p_n$ has
degree exactly $n$ (in particular $p_n \ne 0$) and the formal derivative of $p_{n+1}$ equals
$(n + 1)\, p_n$.

articles.title: Kummer's congruence
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime, let $B_j$ denote the $j$-th Bernoulli number,
with $B_1 = -1/2$, and let $t$ be a natural number. Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers, neither
divisible by $p - 1$, with $m \equiv n \pmod{(p-1)p^t}$. Then the rational numbers

$$\frac{(1 - p^{m-1}) B_m}{m} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{(1 - p^{n-1}) B_n}{n}$$

are either equal, or their difference has $p$-adic valuation at least $t + 1$.

In other words, the two numbers agree modulo $p^{t+1}$; equality is listed as a separate case
because the $p$-adic valuation of $0$ is taken to be $0$.

Proof: We use Voronoi's finite-sum congruence in p-adic norm form, following
Ireland--Rosen, Ch. 15 §2, and Washington, Cor. 5.14, back to Kummer's 1851 paper.

## Sources

- Ernst Eduard Kummer, "Über eine allgemeine Eigenschaft der rationalen Entwickelungscoefficienten einer bestimmten Gattung analytischer Functionen," Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 41 (1851), 368–372, DOI 10.1515/crll.1851.41.368, https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1851.41.368.

articles.title: Binary run lengths
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the binary run lengths of $n$ form the list
of the lengths of the maximal runs of $1$s in the binary expansion of $n$, in the order in which
the runs occur when the digits are read from the least significant one. This is the paper's list
$\mathcal{L}(n)$, whose order does not matter there; for $n = 0$ the list is empty.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Definition 1.

articles.title: Run lengths of a digit list
articles.statement:
Given a list $b_1, \dots, b_k$ of natural numbers (binary
digits) and a natural number $c$, this is the list, in order of occurrence, of the lengths of the
maximal runs of $1$s in the sequence consisting of $c$ ones followed by $b_1, \dots, b_k$, where
every digit other than $1$ ends a run.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Definition 1.

articles.title: Linear recurrences via powers of the companion matrix
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number, let
$d_0, \dots, d_r$ be integers, and let $S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $S(0) = 1$ and
$S(m + 1) = d_0 S(m) + d_1 S(m - 1) + \dots + d_r S(m - r)$ for every $m \ge r$. Let $\gamma(1)$
be the $(r + 1) \times (r + 1)$ integer matrix with rows and columns indexed by $0, \dots, r$
whose row $i < r$ has a $1$ in column $i + 1$ and zeros elsewhere, and whose last row is
$(d_r, d_{r-1}, \dots, d_0)$. With $v = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$ and $w = (S(0), \dots, S(r))^{T}$,
we have $S(n) = v \, \gamma(1)^n \, w$ for every natural number $n$.

The values $S(1), \dots, S(r)$ are arbitrary.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+5k}{2k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
Let
$S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $S(0) = 1$, $S(1) = S(2) = 2$, $S(3) = 3$ and
$S(m) = S(m - 1) + S(m - 2) - S(m - 3) + S(m - 4)$ for every $m \ge 4$. Then for every natural
number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+5k}{2k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$ equals the
value at $n$ of the run length transform of $S$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 11.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+5k}{2n+2k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
Let
$S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $S(0) = S(1) = S(2) = S(3) = 1$ and
$S(m) = S(m - 1) + S(m - 2) - S(m - 3) + S(m - 4)$ for every $m \ge 4$. Then for every natural
number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+5k}{2n+2k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$ equals
the value at $n$ of the run length transform of $S$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 10.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+7k}{3n+k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+7k}{3n+k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$
equals the value at $n$ of the run length transform of the shifted Padovan sequence $P$, given by
$P(0) = 1$, $P(1) = 0$, $P(2) = 1$ and $P(i + 3) = P(i + 1) + P(i)$, that is,
$1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, \dots$ (the Padovan numbers, OEIS A000931, from offset $3$).

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 13.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+k}{n-k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+k}{n-k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$
equals the value at $n$ of the run length transform of the sequence $S(i) = i + 1$ of positive
integers $1, 2, 3, \dots$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 6.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+3k}{6k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+3k}{6k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$
equals the value at $n$ of the run length transform of the sequence
$S(i) = \lfloor i / 2 \rfloor + 1$ of doubled positive integers $1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, \dots$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 8.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+2k}{2n-k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+2k}{2n-k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$
equals the value at $n$ of the run length transform of the sequence $S$ with $S(0) = S(1) = 1$
and $S(i) = L_{i-2}$ for $i \ge 2$, where $L_0 = 2, L_1 = 1, L_2 = 3, \dots$ are the Lucas
numbers; that is, $S$ is $1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, \dots$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 9.

articles.title: Sum of $\binom{n+2k}{2k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2$ as a run length transform
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $n$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \bigl(\binom{n+2k}{2k}\binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\bigr)$
equals the value at $n$ of the run length transform of the sequence $S$ with $S(0) = 1$ and
$S(i) = 2$ for $i \ge 1$, that is, $1, 2, 2, 2, \dots$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 5.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 15
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the run length transform of the periodic sequence
$S$ with $S(i) = 0$ if $i \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ and $S(i) = 1$ otherwise, i.e. of
$1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, \dots$. Then for every natural number $n$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{8k - 2n}{n + k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$, where a binomial
coefficient $\binom{a}{b}$ with $a < 0$ is $0$.

Equivalently, a negative top entry $8k - 2n$ may be replaced by $0$, since the bottom entry $n + k$
is then positive.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 15.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 12
articles.statement:
Let $(p_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be the shifted Padovan sequence,
$p_0 = 1$, $p_1 = 0$, $p_2 = 1$ and $p_{j+3} = p_{j+1} + p_j$, and let $T$ be the run length
transform of $S(i) = p_{i+2}$, i.e. of $1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, \dots$ (the Padovan numbers,
OEIS A000931, from offset $5$). Then for every natural number $n$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{7k - n}{n + k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$, where a binomial
coefficient $\binom{a}{b}$ with $a < 0$ is $0$.

Equivalently, a negative top entry $7k - n$ may be replaced by $0$, since the bottom entry $n + k$
is then positive.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 12.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 14
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the run length transform of the sequence $S$ with
$S(i) = 1$ for even $i$ and $S(i) = (i + 1)/2$ for odd $i$, i.e. of $1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4, \dots$.
Then for every natural number $n$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{6k}{n + 3k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 14.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 7
articles.statement:
Let $(N_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be Narayana's cows sequence, $N_0 = 0$,
$N_1 = N_2 = 1$ and $N_j = N_{j-1} + N_{j-3}$ for $j \ge 3$, and let $T$ be the run length
transform of $S(i) = N_{i+1}$, i.e. of $1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, \dots$. Then for every natural
number $n$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{n - k}{6k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 7.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 2
articles.statement:
Let $(F_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be the Fibonacci numbers, $F_0 = 0$,
$F_1 = 1$, and let $T$ be the run length transform of $S(i) = F_{i+1}$, i.e. of
$1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots$. Then for every natural number $n$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{n - k}{2k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 3
articles.statement:
Let $(F_j)_{j \ge 0}$ be the Fibonacci numbers, $F_0 = 0$,
$F_1 = 1$, and let $T$ be the run length transform of $S(i) = F_{i+2}$, i.e. of
$1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots$. Then for every natural number $n$,
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{3k}{k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 4
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the run length transform of the sequence $S$ with
$S(0) = 1$ and $S(i) = 2^{i-1}$ for $i \ge 1$, i.e. of $1, 1, 2, 4, 8, \dots$. Then for every
natural number $n$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left(\binom{n}{2k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2\right) = T(n)$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 4.

articles.title: Run length transform at eleven
articles.statement:
For every sequence $S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$, the run
length transform $T$ of $S$ satisfies $T(11) = S(1) S(2)$: in binary $11$ is $1011$, whose maximal
runs of $1$s have lengths $2$ and $1$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, example after Definition 1.

articles.title: Run length transform of a linear recurrence (Rampersad–Wiebe Theorem 1)
articles.statement:
Let $r \ge 0$, let
$d_0, \dots, d_r$ be integers, and let $S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $S(0) = 1$ and
$S(m + 1) = d_0 S(m) + d_1 S(m - 1) + \dots + d_r S(m - r)$ for all $m \ge r$. Let $T$ be the run
length transform of $S$, let $v = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$ and $w = (S(0), \dots, S(r))^\top$, let
$\gamma(0)$ be the $(r + 1) \times (r + 1)$ matrix with first column $w$ and zeros elsewhere, and
let $\gamma(1)$ be the $(r + 1) \times (r + 1)$ companion matrix with ones on the superdiagonal,
last row $(d_r, \dots, d_0)$ and zeros elsewhere. Then for every natural number $n$ with binary
digits $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_t$, most significant first,
$T(n) = v \, \gamma(b_1) \gamma(b_2) \cdots \gamma(b_t) \, w$, where for $n = 0$ the product of
matrices is empty and equals the identity.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Run length transform at zero
articles.statement:
For every sequence $S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$, the run
length transform of $S$ takes the value $1$ at $0$, since $0$ has no runs of $1$s in binary.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Definition 1.

articles.title: Run length transform
articles.statement:
For a sequence $S : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$, the run length
transform of $S$ is the sequence $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ given by
$T(n) = \prod_{\ell \in \mathcal{L}(n)} S(\ell)$, where $\mathcal{L}(n)$ is the list of the
lengths of the maximal runs of $1$s in the binary expansion of $n$, so that each run contributes
one factor.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Definition 1.

articles.title: Binomial parity sums detect run length divisibility
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $n$,
the sum

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( \binom{2^m k}{n + k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2 \right)$$

equals $1$ if every maximal run of $1$s in the binary expansion of $n$ has length divisible by
$m$, and $0$ otherwise.

The paper takes $m \ge 2$; the statement holds for every $m$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Theorem 16.

articles.title: Binomial parity sums at one less than a power of two
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and
$\ell$, with $n = 2^\ell - 1$, the sum

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \left( \binom{2^m k}{n + k} \binom{n}{k} \bmod 2 \right)$$

equals $1$ if $m$ divides $\ell$, and $0$ otherwise.

The paper takes $m \ge 2$; the statement holds for every $m$, where $0$ divides $\ell$ only
when $\ell = 0$.

## Sources

- Narad Rampersad and Max Wiebe, *Sums of Products of Binomial Coefficients Mod 2 and 2-Regular Sequences*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A73, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Lex-minimal extensions are closed under addition
articles.statement:
If $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ are
lex-minimal extensions, then their componentwise sum $\eta_1 + \eta_2$ is a lex-minimal
extension.

Since the zero sequence is also a lex-minimal extension, the set $L$ of lex-minimal extensions
is a monoid under componentwise addition.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Corollary 1.

articles.title: A lex-minimal extension periodic from its second entry is periodic
articles.statement:
Let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a lex-minimal extension and let $p \ge 1$. If $e_{i+p} = e_i$
for every $i \ge 2$, then $e_{1+p} = e_1$, so the whole sequence $\eta$ is periodic with
period $p$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Lex-minimal extensions satisfy the Average Condition
articles.statement:
Every lex-minimal extension
satisfies the Average Condition.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Constant sequences satisfy the Average Condition
articles.statement:
For every natural number $c$, the
constant sequence $(c, c, c, \dots)$ satisfies the Average Condition.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Lemma 3.

articles.title: The Average Condition
articles.statement:
A sequence $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of nonnegative integers
satisfies the Average Condition when its upper average $A_0(\eta)$, the limit superior as
$n \to \infty$ of the averages $A_{n,0}(\eta) = (e_1 + \dots + e_n)/n$ taken in the extended
real line, equals $A_{i,0}(\eta)$ for some $i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Averages of a constant sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $c$ and every $i \ge 1$,
the average $A_{i,0}$ of the first $i$ entries of the constant sequence $(c, c, c, \dots)$
equals $c$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Section 3.

articles.title: The largest of the first $m$ averages is the largest average
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 0$ and let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries, with averages
$A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$ for $i \ge 1$. If $1 \le j \le m$ and
$A_j = \max \{A_i \mid 1 \le i \le m\}$, then $A_i \le A_j$ for every $i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Lemma 1.

articles.title: The first average is the first entry
articles.statement:
For every sequence $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of
nonnegative integers, the initial average $A_{1,0}(\eta)$ of its first entry equals $e_1$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 2.

articles.title: Averages of a binomid index
articles.statement:
Let $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a binomid index, write
$s_n = e_1 + \dots + e_n$, and for $i \ge 1$ and $l \ge 0$ let $A_{i,l} = (s_{i+l} - s_l)/i$
be the average of $e_{l+1}, \dots, e_{l+i}$. Then for all $i, l \ge 1$: $A_{i,l} \ge A_{i,0}$;
$A_{ki,0} \ge A_{i,0}$ for every $k \ge 1$; and
$A_{i+l,0} = \frac{i}{i+l} A_{i,l} + \frac{l}{l+i} A_{l,0}$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Initial averages of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a sequence $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of
nonnegative integers and $i \ge 1$, the average $A_{i,0}(\eta)$ is the rational number
$s_i / i$, where $s_i = e_1 + \dots + e_i$ is the sum of the first $i$ entries; for $i = 0$
the value is $A_{0,0}(\eta) = 0$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Section 3; the same average is the sequence `Ave(η)` of Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 2.

articles.title: Distinct shifts of lex-minimal extensions meet only in zero
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be the set of
lex-minimal extensions, and for a natural number $l$ let $\sigma^l$ be the right shift that
prepends $l$ zeros to a sequence. For natural numbers $l \neq m$,
$\sigma^l(L) \cap \sigma^m(L) = \{(0, 0, 0, \dots)\}$: the only sequence in both images is
the zero sequence.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Proposition 6.

articles.title: Shifting by zero places is the identity
articles.statement:
For every sequence $\eta$ of nonnegative
integers, $\sigma^0(\eta) = \eta$, where $\sigma^l$ is the right shift that prepends $l$ zeros.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53.

articles.title: Right shift of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a natural number $l$, the right shift $\sigma^l$ sends a
sequence $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of nonnegative integers to the sequence
$(0, \dots, 0, e_1, e_2, \dots)$ obtained by prepending $l$ zeros: its first $l$ entries are $0$
and its $(l + i)$-th entry is $e_i$ for every $i \ge 1$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53; definition as restated in arXiv:2505.20018, Section 1.

articles.title: Upper average of a constant sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $c$, the upper average
$A_0$ of the constant sequence $(c, c, c, \dots)$ equals $c$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Section 3.

articles.title: The upper average of a binomid index is the supremum of its averages
articles.statement:
Let $\eta$ be a
binomid index, let $s_i$ be the sum of its first $i$ entries, let $A_{i,0}(\eta) = s_i / i$ for
$i \ge 1$, and let $A_0(\eta) = \limsup_{i \to \infty} A_{i,0}(\eta)$ be its upper average.
Then, in the extended real numbers, $A_0(\eta) = \sup_{i \ge 1} A_{i,0}(\eta)$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Upper average of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a sequence $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of nonnegative
integers with partial sums $s_i = e_1 + \dots + e_i$ and averages $A_{i,0}(\eta) = s_i / i$,
the upper average of $\eta$ is $A_0(\eta) = \limsup_{i \to \infty} A_{i,0}(\eta)$, taken in
the extended real numbers; it is $+\infty$ when $s_i / i$ is unbounded.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Section 3.

articles.title: Spans of lex-minimal extensions of a fixed length are finitely presented
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 0$
let $L_k$ be the set of sequences of nonnegative integers that are the lex-minimal extension of
their first $k$ entries, and let $\langle L_k \rangle$ be the submonoid of $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$
(under componentwise addition) generated by $L_k$. Then there are $n \ge 0$, a surjective
monoid homomorphism $f \colon \mathbb{N}^n \to \langle L_k \rangle$ and a finite set $R$ of
pairs of elements of $\mathbb{N}^n$ such that the congruence on $\mathbb{N}^n$ generated by $R$
is the kernel congruence of $f$, which relates $x$ and $y$ exactly when $f(x) = f(y)$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Lemma 6.

articles.title: Partial sums of a lex-minimal extension solve a knapsack problem
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$, let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries, and write
$S_i = e_1 + \dots + e_i$. Then for every $c \ge 1$ there are nonnegative integers
$n_1, \dots, n_m$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m n_i i = c$ and $S_c = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i S_i$ that solve the
unbounded knapsack problem with values $S_i$, weights $i$ and capacity $c$: all nonnegative
integers $n'_1, \dots, n'_m$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m n'_i i \le c$ satisfy
$\sum_{i=1}^m n'_i S_i \le \sum_{i=1}^m n_i S_i$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Lex-minimal extensions have a nomid coefficient equal to one
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$, let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries, and let $p$ be a
prime. Write $f_i = p^{e_i}$ for $i \ge 1$ and, for $1 \le k \le n$, let
$[n, k]_f = \frac{f_n f_{n-1} \cdots f_{n-k+1}}{f_k f_{k-1} \cdots f_1}$ be the $f$-nomid
coefficient, the generalized binomial coefficient of $f$. Then for every $n > m$ there is some $k$
with $1 \le k < n$ and $[n, k]_f = 1$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Late partial sums of a lex-minimal extension split
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $k$ entries, and write
$S_i = e_1 + \dots + e_i$. Then for every $l$ there is a map $\pi \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
such that $1 \le \pi(i) < i$ and $S_i = S_{\pi(i)} + S_{i - \pi(i)}$ for every $i$ with
$k < i \le l$.

The paper takes the specific bound $l = l(k)$ from its proof of the preceding lemma; the
statement here holds for every $l$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Lemma 4.

articles.title: A preperiod bound for lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 0$, let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries, with averages
$A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$, and let $1 \le k \le m$ with
$A_k = \max \{A_i \mid 1 \le i \le m\}$. Then $\eta$ is periodic after position
$N = k m (m + 1)/2$: there is $p \ge 1$ with $e_{i+p} = e_i$ for all $i > N$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Spans of lex-minimal extensions of a fixed length are finitely generated
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 0$
let $L_k$ be the set of sequences of nonnegative integers that are the lex-minimal extension of
their first $k$ entries. Then the submonoid of $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ (under componentwise
addition) generated by $L_k$ is finitely generated, and only finitely many elements of $L_k$
are atomic binomid indices, that is, nonzero binomid indices that are not the sum of two
nonzero binomid indices.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Lemma 5.

articles.title: The gcd of the maximizing indices divides the minimal period
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$, let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries, with averages
$A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$, and let $g$ be the greatest common divisor of the indices
$1 \le i \le m$ with $A_i = \max \{A_j \mid 1 \le j \le m\}$. If $p$ is the least $q \ge 1$
such that $e_{i+q} = e_i$ for all sufficiently large $i$, then $g$ divides $p$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Every index with maximal average is a multiple of the gcd of those up to $m$
articles.statement:
Let
$m \ge 0$, let $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries,
with averages $A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$, let $J$ be the set of indices $1 \le j \le m$ with
$A_j = \max \{A_{j'} \mid 1 \le j' \le m\}$, and let $g = \gcd J$. Then $g$ divides every
$i \ge 1$ such that $A_i = A_j$ for some $j \in J$.

Since every element of $J$ is such an index, $g$ is also the greatest common divisor of all
$i \ge 1$ with $A_i = A_j$ for some $j \in J$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Lemma 2.

articles.title: The monoid of lex-minimal extensions is a directed union
articles.statement:
For $k \ge 0$ let $L_k$ be the
set of sequences of nonnegative integers that are the lex-minimal extension of their first $k$
entries, let $\langle L_k \rangle$ be the submonoid of $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ (under
componentwise addition) generated by $L_k$, and let $\mathcal{A}_k$ be the set of elements of
$L_k$ that are atomic binomid indices, that is, nonzero binomid indices that are not the sum of
two nonzero binomid indices. Then $\langle L_k \rangle \subseteq \langle L_{k'} \rangle$ and
$\mathcal{A}_k \subseteq \mathcal{A}_{k'}$ whenever $k \le k'$; the union of the sets
$\langle L_k \rangle$ over all $k$ is the set $L$ of all lex-minimal extensions; and for every
$k$ the submonoid generated by $\mathcal{A}_k$ is $\langle L_k \rangle$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Theorem 3.

articles.title: Primes divide all inner binomial coefficients of infinitely many rows
articles.statement:
For every prime
$p$ there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that $p$ divides the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ for every $k$ with $1 \le k < n$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Corollary 3.

articles.title: Primes divide all inner Fibonomial coefficients of infinitely many rows
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be
the Fibonacci numbers and $F_n! = F_1 F_2 \cdots F_n$ the Fibonacci factorial. For every prime
$p$ there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that for every $k$ with $1 \le k < n$ the
Fibonomial coefficient $F_n! / (F_k! \, F_{n-k}!)$ is an integer multiple of $p$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Corollary 4.

articles.title: Nomid coefficients of binomid indices that are not lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
Let
$\mu = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a binomid index such that for no $m$ is $\mu$ the lex-minimal
extension of its first $m$ entries, and let $p$ be a prime. Write $f_i = p^{e_i}$ for $i \ge 1$
and let $[n, k]_f = \frac{f_n f_{n-1} \cdots f_{n-k+1}}{f_k f_{k-1} \cdots f_1}$ be the
$f$-nomid coefficient. Then there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that for every $k$
with $1 \le k < n$ the coefficient $[n, k]_f$ is an integer multiple of $p$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Corollary 2.

articles.title: Basis of the span of the lex-minimal extensions of length $k$
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 0$ and let
$L_k$ be the set of sequences $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of nonnegative integers that are the
lex-minimal extension of $(e_1, \dots, e_k)$. A set $B$ of sequences of nonnegative integers is
a basis of the submonoid generated by $L_k$ under componentwise addition if and only if $B$ is
the set of nonzero atomic binomid indices that belong to $L_k$. Hence that set is the unique
basis of this submonoid.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Proposition 5.

articles.title: The empty set is a basis of the zero submonoid
articles.statement:
In every additive commutative monoid,
the empty set is a basis of the subset $\{0\}$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 4.

articles.title: Atoms are the unique basis of an atom-generated submonoid
articles.statement:
Let $\iota$ be a type and
let $M$ be a submonoid of $\mathbb{N}^\iota$ under componentwise addition. Let $A$ be the set
of atoms of $M$: the elements $a \in M$ with $a \ne 0$ such that $y = 0$ or $z = 0$ whenever
$a = y + z$ with $y, z \in M$. If every element of $M$ is a finite sum of elements of $A$, then
a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}^\iota$ is a basis of $M$ if and only if $B = A$; that is, $A$ is
the unique basis of $M$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Basis of the monoid of lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be the set of lex-minimal
extensions, viewed inside the sequences of nonnegative integers under componentwise addition.
A set $B$ of sequences of nonnegative integers is a basis of $L$ if and only if $B$ is the set
of nonzero atomic binomid indices that belong to $L$. Hence that set is the unique basis of $L$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Proposition 5.

articles.title: Basis of a submonoid
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $B$ be subsets of an additive commutative monoid.
Then $B$ is a basis of $M$ when $M$ is the submonoid $\langle B \rangle$ generated by $B$ and
no element of $B$ is a nonnegative integer combination of elements of $B$ in which its own
coefficient is $0$: for all pairwise distinct $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n \in B$, all nonnegative
integers $c_1, \dots, c_n$ and every $j$, if $\beta_j = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \beta_i$ then
$c_j \ge 1$.

The elements $\beta_i$ are required to be distinct: the paper's wording allows repeated
entries, under which $\beta = (b, b)$ and $b = 0 \cdot b + 1 \cdot b$ would rule out every
nonempty $B$; its uniqueness proof uses distinct entries.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 4 (definition of a basis).

articles.title: The constant sequence $1$ is atomic
articles.statement:
The constant sequence $(1, 1, 1, \dots)$ is a
nonzero atomic binomid index: it is a nonzero binomid index that is not the sum of two nonzero
binomid indices.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 4 (example of `(E_m)^∞` with `m = 1`).

articles.title: Atomic binomid index
articles.statement:
A sequence $\eta$ of nonnegative integers is a nonzero atomic
binomid index (an element of the paper's set $\mathrm{Atom}$) when $\eta$ is a nonzero binomid
index that is not the sum of two nonzero binomid indices: whenever $\eta = \eta_1 + \eta_2$
termwise with $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ binomid indices, $\eta_1 = 0$ or $\eta_2 = 0$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 4 (definition of atomic).

articles.title: Constant sequences are binomid indices
articles.statement:
For every natural number $c$, the constant
sequence $(c, c, c, \dots)$ is a binomid index.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53.

articles.title: Partial-sum characterization of binomid indices
articles.statement:
Let $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a
sequence of nonnegative integers with partial sums $s_n = e_1 + \dots + e_n$ (so $s_0 = 0$).
Then $\eta$ is a binomid index if and only if $s_{n-k} + s_k \le s_n$ for all $k$ and $n$ with
$1 \le k < n$. Moreover, for every $m$, if $\eta$ is the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$
entries, then for every $n > m$

$$s_n = \max_{1 \le k < n} (s_{n-k} + s_k),$$

where the maximum over the empty range (for $n = 1$) is taken to be $0$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Monotone sequences are binomid indices
articles.statement:
Every non-decreasing sequence
$e_1 \le e_2 \le \cdots$ of nonnegative integers is an infinite binomid index.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Binomid index
articles.statement:
An infinite binomid index is a sequence $(e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of
nonnegative integers such that $\sum_{i=n-k+1}^{n} e_i \ge \sum_{i=1}^{k} e_i$ for all
$1 \le k \le n$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53; definition as restated in arXiv:2505.20018, Section 1.

articles.title: Minimal period of a lex-minimal extension
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be the lex-minimal extension of $(e_1, \dots, e_m)$. For
$1 \le i \le m$ let $A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$, and let $A_{\max}$ be the largest of
$A_1, \dots, A_m$. Let $g$ be the greatest common divisor of the indices $1 \le i \le m$ with
$A_i = A_{\max}$. Then $g$ is the minimal eventual period of $\eta$: $g \ge 1$,
$e_{i+g} = e_i$ for all sufficiently large $i$, and every $q \ge 1$ with $e_{i+q} = e_i$ for
all sufficiently large $i$ satisfies $g \le q$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Theorem 1.

articles.title: The Average Condition gives eventually periodic lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
If an
infinite binomid index $e = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ satisfies the Average Condition, then $e$ is
a lex-minimal extension, that is, the lex-minimal extension of $(e_1, \dots, e_m)$ for some
$m \ge 0$, and $e$ is eventually periodic: there are $N$ and $p \ge 1$ such that
$e_{n+p} = e_n$ for all $n \ge N$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Partial-sum criterion for lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let
$\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a sequence of nonnegative integers and write
$S_i = e_1 + \dots + e_i$. Suppose $S_i + S_j \le S_{i+j}$ for all $i, j \ge 1$ with
$i + j \le k$. Then $\eta$ is the lex-minimal extension of $(e_1, \dots, e_k)$ if and only if,
for every $r > k$, $S_i + S_j \le S_r$ for all $i, j \ge 1$ with $i + j = r$, with equality for
at least one such pair $(i, j)$.

In the paper's notation, the condition says that $\Delta_\eta(r) = 0$ for every $r > k$, where
$\Delta_\eta(r) = \min \{S_r - S_i - S_j : i + j = r,\ i, j \ge 1\}$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Proposition 1.

articles.title: The lex-minimal extension is computed greedily
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let
$f = (f_1, f_2, \dots)$ be a sequence of nonnegative integers whose first $m$ entries form a
finite binomid index, that is, $\sum_{i=n-k+1}^{n} f_i \ge \sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i$ for all
$1 \le k \le n \le m$. Suppose that for every $n > m$ the entry $f_n$ equals the maximum,
over $1 \le k < n$, of the integers $\sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i - \sum_{i=n-k+1}^{n-1} f_i$. Then $f$
is the lex-minimal extension of $(f_1, \dots, f_m)$.

The differences are taken in the integers and may be negative; the condition says that
$f_n + \sum_{i=n-k+1}^{n-1} f_i \ge \sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i$ for every $1 \le k < n$, with equality
for some such $k$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Monotone finite binomid indices extend periodically
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let
$e_1 \le e_2 \le \cdots \le e_m$ be nonnegative integers. Then the periodic sequence
$(e_1, \dots, e_m, e_1, \dots, e_m, \dots)$ is the lex-minimal extension of $(e_1, \dots, e_m)$.

A non-decreasing finite sequence is automatically a finite binomid index.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Periodic binomid indices are lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
If an infinite binomid index
$e = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ is periodic, that is, there is $p \ge 1$ with $e_{i+p} = e_i$ for all
$i$, then $e$ is a lex-minimal extension: it is the lex-minimal extension of
$(e_1, \dots, e_m)$ for some $m \ge 0$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53, Proposition 5.

articles.title: The zero sequence is lex-minimal
articles.statement:
For every $m \ge 0$, the zero sequence
$(0, 0, \dots)$ is the lex-minimal extension of its first $m$ entries.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53.

articles.title: Lex-minimal extension
articles.statement:
Let $e = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a sequence of nonnegative integers
and $m \ge 0$. Then $e$ is the lex-minimal extension of $(e_1, \dots, e_m)$ when $e$ is an
infinite binomid index and, for every infinite binomid index $g$ with $g_i = e_i$ for all
$i \le m$, either $g = e$ or $e$ is lexicographically smaller than $g$: there is a $j$ with
$e_i = g_i$ for all $i < j$ and $e_j < g_j$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53; definition as restated in arXiv:2505.20018, Section 1.

articles.title: Lex-minimal extensions
articles.statement:
A sequence $e = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of nonnegative integers is a
lex-minimal extension when, for some $m \ge 0$, it is the lex-minimal extension of
$(e_1, \dots, e_m)$. The set of all lex-minimal extensions is denoted $L$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Lexicographically Minimal Extension of a Finite Binomid Index*, INTEGERS 24 (2024), Article A53.

articles.title: Maximal-average indices for $m = 1$
articles.statement:
Let $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ be a sequence of
nonnegative integers and $A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$. For $m = 1$, the set of indices
$1 \le i \le m$ at which $A_i$ is maximal among $A_1, \dots, A_m$ is $\{1\}$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 3.

articles.title: Indices of maximal average
articles.statement:
For a sequence $\eta = (e_1, e_2, \dots)$ of nonnegative
integers and $m \ge 0$, let $A_i = (e_1 + \dots + e_i)/i$ be the average of the first $i$
entries of $\eta$. The set of maximal-average indices of $\eta$ up to $m$ is the set of all $i$
with $1 \le i \le m$ such that $A_j \le A_i$ for every $j$ with $1 \le j \le m$; for
$m \ge 1$ these are the $i$ with $1 \le i \le m$ and $A_i = A_{\max}$, where
$A_{\max} = \max \{A_i \mid 1 \le i \le m\}$, and for $m = 0$ the set is empty.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 3 (the set `{i ≤ m | A_max = A_i}`).

articles.title: Summands of a lex-minimal extension are lex-minimal
articles.statement:
Let $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ be
infinite binomid indices and let $k \ge 0$. If the termwise sum $\eta_1 + \eta_2$ is the
lex-minimal extension of its first $k$ entries, then $\eta_1$ is the lex-minimal extension of
its first $k$ entries and $\eta_2$ is the lex-minimal extension of its first $k$ entries.

Since every lex-minimal extension is the lex-minimal extension of its first $k$ entries for some
$k$, this contains the first claim of the source: if $\eta_1 + \eta_2$ is a lex-minimal
extension, then so are $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Proposition 3.

articles.title: A monoid basis does not contain zero
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid and
let $M$ and $B$ be subsets of $\alpha$. If $B$ is a basis of $M$, then $0 \notin B$.

## Sources

- Caalim and Tanaka, *Generalized Binomial Coefficients and the Monoid of Lexicographically Minimal Extensions*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A113, Section 4.

articles.title: Cubed central binomial coefficients as diagonal coefficients
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
the coefficient of $x^n y^n z^n$ in the polynomial
$(1 + x + y + z)^{2n} (1 + x + y - z)^n (1 + x - y + z)^n$ in three variables $x, y, z$ with
integer coefficients equals $\binom{2n}{n}^3$.

## Sources

- Formal proof of the A002897 diagonal-coefficient identity (methods of Tsoukalas et al. [arXiv/2605.22763]), https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/a32396489dcb8f86c3549b93aa358ac6a10a3a1f/FormalConjectures/OEIS/2897.wip.lean#L408.

articles.title: Diagonal-coefficient property of the cubed central binomial coefficients
articles.statement:
This is the
proposition that for every natural number $n$, the coefficient of $x^n y^n z^n$ in the
polynomial $(1 + x + y + z)^{2n} (1 + x + y - z)^n (1 + x - y + z)^n$ in three variables
$x, y, z$ with integer coefficients equals $\binom{2n}{n}^3$.

articles.title: Cubed central binomial coefficients
articles.statement: For a natural number $n$, $a(n) = \binom{2n}{n}^3$.

articles.title: Product polynomial for the cubed central binomial coefficients
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$,
this is the polynomial $(1 + x + y + z)^{2n} (1 + x + y - z)^n (1 + x - y + z)^n$ in three
variables $x, y, z$ (indexed by $0, 1, 2$) with integer coefficients.

articles.title: Indices for three variables
articles.statement:
Three polynomial variables are indexed by the set
$\{0, 1, 2\}$.

articles.title: Exponent vector of $x^n y^n z^n$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the exponent vector assigning
exponent $n$ to each of the three variables $x, y, z$, that is, the monomial $x^n y^n z^n$.

articles.title: Large valuations in short runs of consecutive integers are rare
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$x$ let $K = \lfloor \exp(0.8 \sqrt{\log x}) \rfloor$ and, for a prime $p$, let
$D_p = 1 + \lfloor \log x / \log p \rfloor$. Write $v_p(n)$ for the exponent of $p$ in a
positive integer $n$. Then the number of integers $m$ with $1 \le m \le x$ for which some prime
$p < 2K$ satisfies $\max \{ v_p(m + i) : 1 \le i \le K \} > D_p / \log D_p$ is $o(x)$ as
$x \to \infty$.

For large $x$ every prime $p < 2K$ is at most $x$, so $D_p \ge 2$ and $\log D_p > 0$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Lemma 5.

articles.title: Small valuations of the middle binomial coefficient are rare
articles.statement:
For a natural number $x$
let $K = \lfloor \exp(0.8 \sqrt{\log x}) \rfloor$ and, for a prime $p$, let
$D_p = 1 + \lfloor \log x / \log p \rfloor$. Write $v_p(n)$ for the exponent of $p$ in a
positive integer $n$. Then the number of integers $m$ with $1 \le m \le x$ for which some prime
$p \le 2K$ satisfies $v_p\bigl(\binom{2m}{m}\bigr) \le D_p / \log D_p$ is $o(x)$ as $x \to \infty$.

For large $x$ every prime $p \le 2K$ is at most $x$, so $D_p \ge 2$ and $\log D_p > 0$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Binomial coefficients dividing the middle binomial coefficient
articles.statement:
The set of natural
numbers $m$ such that $\binom{m+k}{k}$ divides $\binom{2m}{m}$ for every integer $k$ with
$1 \le k \le \exp(0.8 \sqrt{\log m})$ has natural density $1$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Theorem 2.

articles.title: Valuations of the middle binomial coefficient on a set of density one
articles.statement:
Write $v_p(n)$ for
the exponent of a prime $p$ in a positive integer $n$, and for $m \ge 2$ let
$\alpha_p(m) = v_p\bigl(\binom{2m}{m}\bigr) / (\log m / \log p)$. There is a set $S$ of natural
numbers of natural density $1$ such that: $\alpha_2(m) \to 1/2$ as $m \to \infty$ within $S$; for
every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\alpha_3(m) \ge 34/81 - \varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large
$m \in S$; and $\alpha_p(m) \ge 0.39$ for every $m \in S$ and every prime $p$ with
$3 < p < 2 \log m$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Products of consecutive integers dividing the middle binomial coefficient
articles.statement:
Let $\eta$ be
a real number with $\eta < 1 / \log 4$. The set of natural numbers $m$ such that
$(m+k)!/m! = (m+1)(m+2) \cdots (m+k)$ divides $\binom{2m}{m}$ for every integer $k$ with
$1 \le k \le \eta \log m$ has natural density $1$.

The constant $1 / \log 4$ is the threshold imposed by the prime $2$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Short runs of consecutive integers have small valuations almost always
articles.statement:
Write $v_p(n)$
for the exponent of a prime $p$ in a positive integer $n$. The set of natural numbers $m$ such
that $\max \{ v_p(m + i) : 1 \le i \le k \} \le 3 \log k / \log p$ for every integer $k$ with
$\frac{1}{2} \log m < k < \log m$ and every prime $p \le 2k$ has natural density $1$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Valuation of a product of consecutive integers
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers and
$p$ a prime, and write $v_p(n)$ for the exponent of $p$ in a positive integer $n$. Then
$v_p\bigl((m+k)!/m!\bigr) \le v_p(k!) + \max \{ v_p(m + i) : 1 \le i \le k \}$, where the
maximum is $0$ when $k = 0$.

The quotient $(m+k)!/m! = (m+1) \cdots (m+k)$ is an integer. Unlike the source, the inequality
is stated also for $m = 0$ and $k = 0$.

## Sources

- Carl Pomerance, *Remarks on the Middle Binomial Coefficient*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A47, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Central binomial products with $a + b \le 10$
articles.statement:
Let $x$, $a$, $b$ be positive integers
with $a + b \le 10$. Then $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$ if and only if
$x = 1$ and $a = 1$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 1.

articles.title: Central binomial products with $x = 1$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers. Then
$\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{1+2b}{b}$ if and only if $a = 1$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Proposition 2.

articles.title: Allen's theorem on central binomial products
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $b$ be positive integers and
let $a$ be a nonnegative integer. Then $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$ if
and only if $x = 1$ and $a = 1$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Theorem 1.

articles.title: Allen's inequality for central binomial products
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $b$ be positive integers
and let $a$ be a nonnegative integer with $a \le x$. Then
$\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \le \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$, and equality holds if and only if
$x = 1$ and $a = 1$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Proposition 1.

articles.title: Central binomial products in the case $x = a - 2$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be natural numbers
with $4 < 2a \le a + b$. Then $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{a+2b-2}{b}$, so the
equation $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$ has no solution with $x = a - 2$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 3.

articles.title: Central binomial products in the case $x = a - 3$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be natural numbers
with $4 < 2a \le a + b$. Then $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{a+2b-3}{b}$, so the
equation $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$ has no solution with $x = a - 3$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 4.

articles.title: Central binomial products in the case $x = a - 1$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be natural numbers
with $4 < 2a \le a + b$. Then $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{a+2b-1}{b}$, so the
equation $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$ has no solution with $x = a - 1$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 2.

articles.title: Central binomial products in the balanced range
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers,
let $x \ge 2$ be an integer, and put $k = a + b$. If $k \ge 75$, $a \le \tfrac{9}{10}k$ and
$b \le \tfrac{4}{5}k$, then $\binom{2k}{k} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 11.

articles.title: Central binomial products with $a \ge b \ge 3$
articles.statement:
Let $x$, $a$, $b$ be natural numbers with
$x \ge 1$ and $3 \le b \le a$. Then $\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 7.

articles.title: Central binomial products with $x \ge 2$ and $a \ge b$
articles.statement:
Let $x$, $a$, $b$ be natural
numbers with $x \ge 2$ and $1 \le b \le a$. Then
$\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 8.

articles.title: No large solutions of the central binomial product equation with a dominant central factor
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $x$ with $b \ge 1$, $x \ge 2$, $a + b \ge 150$ and
$a \ge \frac{171}{121} x$, we have
$\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 12.

articles.title: No large solutions of the central binomial product equation with shift at least two
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $x$ with $a \ge 1$, $b \ge 1$, $x \ge 2$ and $a + b \ge 150$, we have
$\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Proposition 3.

articles.title: Central binomial products with $x \ge 2$ and $a + b < 150$
articles.statement:
Let $x$, $a$, $b$ be natural
numbers with $a \ge 1$, $b \ge 1$, $x \ge 2$ and $x < a + b < 150$. Then
$\binom{2(a+b)}{a+b} \ne \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Proposition 4.

articles.title: Stănică's bounds for the binomial coefficient $\binom{mn}{rn}$
articles.statement:
Let $m$, $n$ and $r$ be
natural numbers with $1 \le r < m$ and $n \ge 1$, and put

$$B = \frac{m^{mn + 1/2}}{(m-r)^{(m-r)n + 1/2}\, r^{rn + 1/2}}.$$

Then

$$\frac{e^{-1/(8n)}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sqrt{n}}\, B < \binom{mn}{rn} <
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sqrt{n}}\, B.$$

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 6, quoting Stănică.

articles.title: A prime factor above $4.42m$ in a product of consecutive integers
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be
natural numbers with $m > 3$, $n > 4m$ and $n + m \ge 150$. Then the product
$n(n+1)\cdots(n+m-1)$ has a prime divisor $p$ with $p > 4.42\,m$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 10, quoting Nair and Shorey.

articles.title: A prime factor above $9m/5$ in a product of consecutive integers
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be
natural numbers with $2 < m < n$ and $n + m \ge 150$. Then the product $n(n+1)\cdots(n+m-1)$ has
a prime divisor $p$ with $p > 9m/5$.

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 9, quoting Shanta and Shorey.

articles.title: Hanson's theorem on a prime factor above $3m/2$ in consecutive integers
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$
be natural numbers with $0 < m < n$. The product $n(n+1)\cdots(n+m-1)$ has a prime divisor $p$
with $p > 3m/2$ if and only if $(n, m)$ is none of the pairs $(3, 2)$, $(8, 2)$ and $(6, 5)$
(the products $3 \cdot 4$, $8 \cdot 9$ and $6 \cdot 7 \cdot 8 \cdot 9 \cdot 10$).

## Sources

- Meaghan Allen, *Solvability of $\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2a}{a}\binom{x+2b}{b}$*, INTEGERS 26 (2026), Article A26, Lemma 5, quoting Hanson.

articles.title: Recurrence of the alternating-sign Fibonacci sequence
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$,
the alternating-sign Fibonacci sequence $d$ satisfies $d_{m+2} = d_{m+1} + d_m + (-1)^{m+2}$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 2.2.

articles.title: First values of the alternating-sign Fibonacci sequence
articles.statement:
The alternating-sign Fibonacci
sequence $d$ satisfies $d_0 = 0$, $d_1 = 1$, $d_2 = 2$, $d_3 = 2$ and $d_4 = 5$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Example 5.

articles.title: Alternating-sign Fibonacci sequence
articles.statement:
The alternating-sign Fibonacci sequence
(OEIS A181716) is the integer sequence $(d_m)_{m \ge 0}$ defined by $d_0 = 0$, $d_1 = 1$ and
$d_{m+2} = d_{m+1} + d_m + (-1)^{m+2}$ for every natural number $m$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 2.2 (definition before Lemma 3).

articles.title: Every factorial is at most a positive power of the golden ratio
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the
golden ratio. For every natural number $n$ there is an integer $m \ge 1$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$.

Thus the set of positive integers $m$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$, whose least element is the
golden factorial exponent of $n$, is nonempty.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 2.2, definition (4).

articles.title: Existence of the Lambert sequences
articles.statement:
Let $h(y) = y e^y$ be the Lambert map. For every
natural number $n \ge 4$ and every real number $c$ with $0 < c \le 1$ there is a real number
$a \ge n - 1$ with

$$h\left(-\frac{a}{n-1}\right) = -\frac{1}{n-1} \, c^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Equivalently, $a = -(n-1) \, W_{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{n-1} c^{1/(n-1)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$ is the
lower real branch of the Lambert W function. With $c = 4/7$ this is the paper's $a_n$, and with
$c = 4/(7m)$ for an integer $m \ge 1$ it is the paper's $A_{n,m}$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 3.1 (the lower branch `W₋₁` defining `a n` and `A n m`).

articles.title: Minimality of the golden factorial exponent
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and,
for a natural number $n$, let $\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with
$n! \le \varphi^m$. If $n$ and $m$ are natural numbers with $m \ge 1$ and $n! \le \varphi^m$,
then $\alpha(n) \le m$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 2.2, definition (4).

articles.title: Defining property of the golden factorial exponent
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio
and, for a natural number $n$, let $\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with
$n! \le \varphi^m$. For every natural number $n$, $\alpha(n) \ge 1$ and
$n! \le \varphi^{\alpha(n)}$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 2.2, definition (4).

articles.title: Golden factorial exponent of $1$
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and, for a natural
number $n$, let $\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$. Then
$\alpha(1) = 1$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Table 3.

articles.title: Increment bounds for the golden factorial exponent
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio
and, for a natural number $n$, let $\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with
$n! \le \varphi^m$. For every natural number $n > 1$,

$$\alpha(n-1) + \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor \le \alpha(n) \le
\alpha(n-1) + \lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor + 1.$$

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Lemma 2 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-lem-2`).

articles.title: Golden factorial exponent of $2$
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be the golden ratio and, for a natural
number $n$, let $\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$. Then
$\alpha(2) = 2$.

This holds because $\varphi < 2 \le \varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Table 3.

articles.title: Golden factorial exponent
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the golden factorial exponent
$\alpha(n)$ is the least positive integer $m$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$, where $\varphi$ is the golden
ratio. This is the sequence OEIS A214048.

Equivalently $\alpha(n)$ is the positive integer $m$ with $\varphi^{m-1} \le n! \le \varphi^m$; the
number $n!$ is never a power of $\varphi$ for $n \ge 2$, and $\alpha(1) = 1$.

## Sources

- Aleksandar Petojević, Marjana Gorjanac Ranitović, Dragan Rastovac and Milinko Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 2.2, definition (4).

articles.title: Left factorial bounds at the golden factorial exponent
articles.statement:
For every integer $n \ge 1$, let
$!n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k!$ be the left factorial, let
$K_n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k \, dt$ be Kurepa's partial integral, and let
$\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$, where $\varphi$ is the
golden ratio. Then $\beta(n) = K_n(\alpha(n))$ satisfies $\beta(n) < {!n} < \beta(n) + 1$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Theorem 12 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-thm-12`).

articles.title: Two-parameter Lambert bounds for the left factorial
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 5$ and $m \ge 1$ be
integers, let $!n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k!$ be the left factorial, let
$K_n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k \, dt$ be Kurepa's partial integral, let
$h(y) = y e^y$ be the Lambert map, and let $A$ be a real number with $A \ge n - 1$ and

$$h\left(-\frac{A}{n-1}\right) = -\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7m}\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Then $K_n(A) < {!n} < K_n(A) + \frac{1}{m}$.

The two conditions on $A$ say exactly that
$A = -(n-1)\, W_{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7m}\right)^{1/(n-1)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$
is the lower real branch of the Lambert $W$ function; this is the paper's $A(n, m)$, and
$K_n(A)$ is its $B(n, m)$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Theorem 14 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-thm-14`).

articles.title: Lambert bounds for the left factorial
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 5$ be an integer, let
$!n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k!$ be the left factorial, let
$K_n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k \, dt$ be Kurepa's partial integral, let
$h(y) = y e^y$ be the Lambert map, and let $a$ be a real number with $a \ge n - 1$ and

$$h\left(-\frac{a}{n-1}\right) = -\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Then $K_n(a) < {!n} < K_n(a) + 1$.

The two conditions on $a$ say exactly that
$a = -(n-1)\, W_{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n-1)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$
is the lower real branch of the Lambert $W$ function; this is the paper's $a(n)$, and $K_n(a)$
is its $b(n)$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Theorem 10 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-thm-10`).

articles.title: Kurepa's partial integral vanishes at zero
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, Kurepa's partial
integral $K_n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k \, dt$ satisfies $K_n(0) = 0$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 1.

articles.title: Kurepa's partial integral
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a real number $x$, Kurepa's partial
integral is

$$K_n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k \, dt,$$

an oriented integral, so for $x < 0$ it is minus the integral over $[x, 0]$.

The paper writes it as $!n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \frac{t^n - 1}{t - 1} \, dt$; the geometric sum
agrees with $\frac{t^n - 1}{t - 1}$ for $t \ne 1$, and the singularity at $t = 1$ is removable.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Section 1 (the function `!z(x)`) and Sections 3.1-3.3.

articles.title: The golden factorial exponent exceeds the Lambert sequence
articles.statement:
Let $n > 4$ be an integer, let
$h(y) = y e^y$ be the Lambert map, and let $a$ be a real number with $a \ge n - 1$ and

$$h\left(-\frac{a}{n-1}\right) = -\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Then $a < \alpha(n)$, where $\alpha(n)$ is the least positive integer $m$ with $n! \le \varphi^m$
and $\varphi$ is the golden ratio.

The two conditions on $a$ say exactly that
$a = -(n-1)\, W_{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n-1)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$
is the lower real branch of the Lambert $W$ function; this is the paper's $a(n)$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Theorem 6 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-thm-6`).

articles.title: Floor formulas for the left factorial
articles.statement:
Let $!n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k!$ be the left
factorial, let $K_n(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k \, dt$ be Kurepa's partial integral,
let $h(y) = y e^y$ be the Lambert map, and let $\alpha(n)$ be the least positive integer $m$ with
$n! \le \varphi^m$, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio. Then the following hold.
(i) For every integer $n \ge 1$, $\lfloor K_n(\alpha(n)) \rfloor + 1 = {!n}$.
(ii) For every integer $n > 4$ and every real $a \ge n - 1$ with
$h(-\frac{a}{n-1}) = -\frac{1}{n-1} (\frac{4}{7})^{1/(n-1)}$, we have
$\lfloor K_n(a) \rfloor + 1 = {!n}$.
(iii) For all integers $n > 4$ and $m \ge 1$ and every real $A \ge n - 1$ with
$h(-\frac{A}{n-1}) = -\frac{1}{n-1} (\frac{4}{7m})^{1/(n-1)}$, we have
$\lfloor K_n(A) + \frac{1}{m} \rfloor = {!n}$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Corollary 15 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-cor-15`).

articles.title: Counting integers by their golden-ratio logarithm
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be the integer sequence with
$d(0) = 0$, $d(1) = 1$ and $d(m) = d(m-1) + d(m-2) + (-1)^m$ for $m \ge 2$, and let $\varphi$ be
the golden ratio. For every integer $m \ge 1$, the number of positive integers $n$ with
$\lfloor \log_\varphi n \rfloor = m$ equals $d(m)$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Lemma 3 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-lem-3`).

articles.title: Partial exponential sums at the Lambert sequence
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 5$ and $k$ be natural numbers
with $k < n - 2$, let $h(y) = y e^y$ be the Lambert map, and let $a$ be a real number with
$a \ge n - 1$ and

$$h\left(-\frac{a}{n-1}\right) = -\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n-1)}.$$

Then

$$\sum_{t=0}^{k} \frac{a^t}{t!} < \frac{a^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}.$$

The two conditions on $a$ say exactly that
$a = -(n-1)\, W_{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n-1)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$
is the lower real branch of the Lambert $W$ function; this is the paper's $a(n)$.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Lemma 9 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-lem-9`).

articles.title: A linear lower bound for the Lambert sequence
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 4$ be a natural number, write
$h(y) = y e^y$ for the Lambert map, and let $a$ be a real number with $a \ge n - 1$ such that

$$h\left(-\frac{a}{n - 1}\right) = -\frac{1}{n - 1} \left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{1/(n - 1)}.$$

Then $2n - 4 < \frac{3}{4} a$.

These conditions determine $a$ uniquely: it is the paper's
$a_n = -(n - 1) W_{-1}\bigl(-\frac{1}{n - 1} (4/7)^{1/(n - 1)}\bigr)$, where $W_{-1}$ is the lower
real branch of the Lambert W function.

## Sources

- Petojević, Gorjanac Ranitović, Rastovac and Mandić, *The Golden Ratio, Factorials, and the Lambert W Function*, Journal of Integer Sequences 27 (2024), Article 24.5.7, Lemma 8 (`jis-2024-24.5.7-lem-8`).

articles.title: Kimball–Webb congruence for Fibonomial coefficients modulo $p^3$
articles.statement:
Let $F_n$ be the
Fibonacci numbers, with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, and write $F_n! = F_1 F_2 \cdots F_n$, with $F_0! = 1$.
Let $p \ge 7$ be a prime and $\varepsilon \in \{1, -1\}$, and suppose that $\rho = p - \varepsilon$
is the rank of appearance of $p$, that is, $p \mid F_\rho$ and $p \nmid F_m$ for $0 < m < \rho$.
Then for every natural number $k$ the Fibonomial coefficient

$$\binom{(k+1)\rho - 1}{\rho - 1}_F = \frac{F_{(k+1)\rho - 1}!}{F_{\rho - 1}!\, F_{k\rho}!}$$

is congruent to $\varepsilon^k$ modulo $p^3$.

The quotient is taken in the natural numbers; it is exact because Fibonomial coefficients are
integers. This is the Fibonacci case only, not Ballot's general theorem for Lucasnomial
coefficients.

## Sources

- Christian Ballot, *The Congruence of Wolstenholme for Generalized Binomial Coefficients Related to Lucas Sequences*, Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.5.4, <https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Ballot/ballot14.tex>, Theorem `thm:KW` (rewriting Lemma 3 of Kimball and Webb), equation `eq:Fib`, lines 144-150.

articles.title: Vanishing $p$-adic valuation of Fibonomial coefficients at prime powers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a
prime with $p \ne 2$ and $p \ne 5$, and let $a, b$ be integers with $0 < a \le b$ such that
$p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 5$ or $a \equiv b \pmod 2$. Write $F_n$ for the $n$-th Fibonacci number
and $F_n! = F_1 F_2 \cdots F_n$ for the Fibonacci factorial, with $F_0! = 1$. Then the $p$-adic
valuation of the Fibonomial coefficient

$$\binom{p^b}{p^a}_F = \frac{F_{p^b}!}{F_{p^a}! \, F_{p^b - p^a}!},$$

where the quotient is taken by division of natural numbers, is $0$.

## Sources

- Phunphayap–Pongsriiam, Example `rem18`, equation `eq1remark2`.

articles.title: Lifting the exponent for Fibonacci numbers
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $m \ge 1$ an
integer such that $p$ divides the Fibonacci number $F_m$, and write $v_p$ for the $p$-adic
valuation. Then $v_p(F_{mj}) = v_p(F_m) + v_p(j)$ for every integer $j \ge 1$.

articles.title: Explicit formula for A265233 in terms of Franel numbers
articles.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be the
sequence A265233 and let $f_m = \sum_{k=0}^{m} \binom{m}{k}^3$ be the $m$-th Franel number. For
every integer $n \ge 1$,

$$a_n = \frac{1}{6} \sum_{m=0}^{n} \binom{n}{m} 4^{n-m} f_m.$$

## Sources

- Juntao Jin, "An Explicit Formula and a Recurrence for OEIS A265233", Theorem 1.

articles.title: Asymptotics of A265233
articles.statement:
The sequence $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ A265233 satisfies

$$a_n \sim \frac{\sqrt{3}}{6\pi} \cdot \frac{12^n}{n} \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$

## Sources
